expected_answer: The weaker photoluminescence redshift in the complete device can arise because selective contacts extract photocarriers and reduce the carrier accumulation that drives emissive iodide-rich domain formation in an isolated film. This does not immobilize the halides. Illumination, internal electric fields, defects, and chemical-potential gradients can still drive iodide through the absorber and transport layers. Silver acts as a reactive iodide sink: formation of AgI consumes migrated iodide, perturbs interfacial stoichiometry, and makes part of the redistribution chemically irreversible. The resulting ionic polarization, interfacial defects, and contact degradation can increase hysteresis and lower photovoltaic performance even when the bulk PL spectrum shows only weak demixing or later recovers. A decisive test would compare otherwise identical devices with Ag and an inert, iodide-blocking electrode or diffusion barrier while simultaneously tracking depth-resolved iodide/AgI formation, hysteresis, and PL under the same illumination protocol. Suppression of AgI and hysteresis without a major change in the initial PL response would support the proposed interfacial sink mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Selective carrier extraction can reduce photocarrier-driven emissive phase segregation relative to a bare film.
Mobile iodide can still migrate under light, field, and defect gradients even when the PL redshift is small.
A reactive Ag contact can trap iodide as AgI, causing irreversible interfacial stoichiometric loss and hysteresis.
A controlled electrode/barrier substitution with operando ion-distribution and device measurements can test the mechanism.
accepted_equivalents: Reduced quasi-Fermi-level splitting or carrier density suppresses visible demixing without stopping ion migration.
Silver functions as a chemical sink or getter for iodide.
Depth-resolved ToF-SIMS, XPS, or operando scattering may be used to track interfacial iodide accumulation.
An inert electrode such as Au or a suitable diffusion-blocking interlayer is an acceptable mechanistic control if other stack variables are held constant.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that a smaller PL redshift proves the complete device is intrinsically more stable.
Attributing AgI only to moisture without connecting it to iodide migration from the absorber.
Treating hysteresis as a purely electronic capacitance effect unrelated to ionic redistribution.
Claiming that recovery of the PL peak guarantees recovery of interfacial composition and device performance.

expected_answer: Equal photon dose does not guarantee an equivalent degradation pathway because dark periods permit partial ionic back-diffusion, defect-state relaxation, strain redistribution, and crystallite reorientation. Repeating those transitions can create path-dependent fatigue that a continuous test may miss or mis-rank. The minimum defensible design should compare repeated light/dark cycling with continuous illumination at matched dose, a dark-aging control, and a temperature-matched light-off thermal-cycle control. After every light and dark segment, it should measure an optical indicator such as PL, structural indicators such as GIWAXS peak position, residual secondary-phase intensity, microstrain, and texture/orientation, and device indicators such as stabilized MPP output and hysteresis. A material fails the fatigue criterion if the dark-rest PL largely recovers but the post-dark structural baseline or device performance drifts cumulatively beyond reproducibility limits. Direct mitigation should combine absorber-level suppression of ion motion and strain, for example composition/cation/lattice engineering, with interface-level protection such as an iodide-blocking interlayer or a less reactive electrode.
scoring_key_points: Explains why matched light dose does not reproduce path-dependent light/dark relaxation and fatigue.
Includes cyclic, continuous-light, dark-aging, and temperature-matched light-off controls.
Tracks optical recovery together with residual phase, lattice, microstrain/texture, MPP, and hysteresis after each cycle.
Defines cumulative post-dark drift as failure and proposes both absorber-level and interface/electrode-level mitigation.
accepted_equivalents: Cycle-count dependence, memory effects, or noncommutative stress history are acceptable descriptions of structural fatigue.
In situ or operando XRD may substitute for GIWAXS if it resolves lattice shift, secondary phases, strain, and orientation.
Halide-vacancy reduction, lattice stiffening, strain relaxation, or compositional redesign are acceptable absorber interventions.
A diffusion barrier, chemically inert metal, or contact redesign is an acceptable interface intervention.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming equal integrated photon dose makes continuous and cyclic tests equivalent.
Using only PL recovery as the pass criterion.
Comparing light cycling only with a hot dark control and omitting continuous-light and dark-aging baselines.
Proposing generic encapsulation without targeting ion migration, structural fatigue, or contact reactivity.

expected_answer: The translation strategy should replace expensive bulk noble-metal protection with a corrosion-resistant low-cost foil carrying only a thin catalyst layer, while preserving continuous electrical contact and chemical isolation from the electrolyte. The foil-to-tandem bond must combine low sheet/contact resistance with solvents and cure conditions that do not attack the perovskite or recombination junction; a graded or multilayer conductive adhesive can be screened against pure highly resistive and highly aggressive extremes. Edge seals and barrier layers should be redesigned as a multilayer system that blocks acid and water, tolerates gas evolution and thermal expansion, and prevents electrolyte access to the TCO and bond line. Qualification must include light, temperature, electrical load, acidic electrolyte, gas-bubble/mechanical, and light-dark cycling both in combination and as isolated controls. During aging, report Faradaic-efficiency-corrected STH, catalyst polarization curves, subcell-resolved EQE or luminescence, series/contact resistance, leakage current, and spatial ingress maps. A design is economically meaningful only if its measured degradation law and yield-adjusted added cost reduce projected lifetime-normalized hydrogen cost; for example, a barrier that doubles area cost but does not move the extrapolated service life toward the multi-year threshold should be rejected.
scoring_key_points: Redesigns the catalyst support and protection as a thin-catalyst, corrosion-resistant, low-cost foil rather than relying on bulk noble metal.
Co-optimizes a low-resistance, chemically compatible bond and multilayer electrolyte barrier without damaging the buried tandem.
Uses combined and isolated light, heat, bias, acid, gas/mechanical, and cycling stresses with catalyst- and subcell-specific diagnostics.
Judges changes by lifetime- and yield-adjusted hydrogen cost, not by area cost or short-term STH alone.
accepted_equivalents: Catalyst-coated stainless steel, titanium, or another corrosion-resistant support is acceptable if compatibility is justified.
A conductive laminate, anisotropic adhesive, or diffusion-barrier contact is acceptable if both contact resistance and solvent damage are addressed.
Equivalent economic metrics such as LCOH, hydrogen yield per replacement cycle, or discounted lifetime energy output are acceptable.
A physics-based acceleration model may replace direct multi-year testing if it is calibrated against multiple coupled-stress conditions.
common_wrong_answers: Focusing only on replacing Pt while ignoring electrolyte sealing and electrical bonding.
Using a single damp-heat or continuous-light test as a proxy for immersed operating conditions.
Calling a design successful because initial STH is higher despite faster degradation.
Comparing uncorrected photocurrent without checking Faradaic efficiency or catalyst polarization.

expected_answer: Direct transfer is not justified because SHJ, TOPCon, and PERC expose different passivation stacks, doped contacts, transparent conductors, metallization schemes, and thermal budgets. The first gate is architecture mapping: identify which layers contact the encapsulant and solvent, then test whether the delamination temperature, polar solvents, toluene, and ultrasonication alter passivation, tunnel oxides, poly-Si contacts, dielectric layers, Ag/Al contacts, or adhesion. The second gate is selective removal: the perovskite and transport layers must be removed below a defined Pb/I residue limit without etching or swelling the retained layers, verified by XPS/ToF-SIMS, morphology, thickness, adhesion, and contact-resistance measurements. The third gate is retained function after each recycling loop, including lifetime or iVOC, reflectance/EQE, sheet and contact resistance, and performance of a rebuilt bottom cell and tandem; trend limits should be specified rather than accepting one successful loop. The scale gate must include solvent recovery, worker and environmental hazards, water and energy demand, throughput, yield, and the value retained in the silicon cell. A process should proceed only when yield-adjusted recovered-cell value and avoided embodied energy exceed the environmental and manufacturing burden, and design-for-disassembly changes should be considered if opening the package dominates cost or damage.
scoring_key_points: Requires architecture-specific compatibility tests for passivation, contacts, metallization, adhesion, and thermal budget before transfer.
Defines residue-removal and retained-layer integrity gates using chemical, morphological, and electrical diagnostics.
Requires loop-by-loop lifetime/iVOC, optical, resistance, and rebuilt-device performance with explicit degradation limits.
Includes solvent recovery, toxicity, energy, throughput, yield, retained value, and design-for-disassembly in the go/no-go decision.
accepted_equivalents: Tunnel-oxide integrity, poly-Si contact selectivity, dielectric passivation, or Al-BSF stability are valid architecture-specific concerns.
A life-cycle assessment, technoeconomic analysis, or material-flow analysis is acceptable for the scale gate.
A validated alternative solvent or dry-removal process may pass if it meets the same selectivity and environmental criteria.
A cumulative efficiency-loss or value-retention threshold across recycling loops is an acceptable repeatability rule.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming all crystalline-silicon bottom cells tolerate the same solvents and thermal exposure.
Using visual cleanliness as the only release criterion.
Demonstrating one rebuilt device without evaluating yield or repeated-loop degradation.
Claiming circularity from device reuse while ignoring solvent toxicity, recovery, and process energy.

expected_answer: The top-cell voltage gain can add to tandem voltage only if the recombination contact remains selective and low loss, the top cell does not introduce shunts, and its quasi-Fermi-level splitting is preserved after integration. The fill-factor gain translates only if large-area uniformity, series resistance, and recombination-layer resistance do not dominate the tandem. Because the subcells are series connected, tandem current is limited by the lower photocurrent; additive-induced changes in film thickness, parasitic absorption, or transmission can therefore erase a Voc/FF benefit by worsening current matching. Aging should combine full-spectrum and spectrally selective stress, with periodic subcell EQE, electroluminescence/PL, Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV, dark J-V/impedance, and contact-resistance measurements. The top-cell branch should track Sn2+/Sn4+ chemistry, halide redistribution, trap density, and spectral PL. The CIGS branch should track its filtered EQE, junction voltage, and luminescence. The interconnect branch should be diagnosed by voltage loss, resistance growth, or injection nonuniformity that cannot be assigned to either absorber. Comparing isolated single-junction controls with complete tandems under the same environment is required to identify integration-specific failure.
scoring_key_points: States that top-cell Voc gains translate only if recombination-contact selectivity and quasi-Fermi-level splitting are preserved.
Explains that series-current matching and top-cell transmission/thickness can offset voltage or fill-factor gains.
Recognizes that tandem FF can be dominated by interconnect, series resistance, shunts, and area nonuniformity.
Proposes subcell-resolved optical, electrical, and chemical aging diagnostics plus isolated single-junction controls.
accepted_equivalents: Pseudo-JV, Suns-Voc, luminescence coupling analysis, or voltage-dependent EQE may be used to separate recombination and resistive losses.
Filtered JV/EQE or optical-bias EQE is acceptable for subcell-resolved current diagnosis.
Sn oxidation may be tracked by XPS/XANES and halide motion by depth profiling or bias-stress methods.
A statement that the tandem voltage is approximately the sum of subcell voltages is acceptable only if interconnect losses are addressed.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a higher single-junction PCE automatically produces the same relative tandem-PCE gain.
Ignoring current matching because the top-cell bandgap is unchanged.
Attributing all tandem aging to Sn oxidation without testing the recombination layer or CIGS subcell.
Using only the two-terminal tandem J-V curve to localize degradation.

expected_answer: Transient photocurrent and TRPL probe different rate processes. A faster photocurrent transient can indicate more rapid extraction or collection through the electron-contact interface, provided the measured decay is not dominated by the external RC time constant. A longer TRPL lifetime indicates that photogenerated carriers survive longer because nonradiative recombination and interfacial trapping are reduced; it does not imply slower extraction when measured on a film or under a different boundary condition. Observing faster extraction together with longer radiative survival is therefore the expected combination for a better-passivated, better-aligned buried interface. The unchanged bandgap and nearly unchanged Jsc argue against bulk halide alloying or enhanced absorption as the main origin, while the Voc and FF gains point to lower interfacial recombination, stronger built-in selectivity, and reduced transport loss. The inference should be validated by controlling excitation density, detection geometry, film thickness, and device capacitance/series resistance, and by corroborating it with TPV, impedance, SCLC, bottom-side PL, or Mott-Schottky measurements.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes faster transient photocurrent extraction/collection from carrier recombination lifetime.
Interprets longer TRPL as reduced nonradiative recombination or trapping rather than slower extraction.
Uses unchanged bandgap/Jsc and increased Voc/FF to localize the dominant gain to the buried interface and charge selectivity.
Identifies RC, geometry, excitation-density, or fitting artifacts and requires an orthogonal electrical/optical control.
accepted_equivalents: TPC may be described as an extraction time constant and TRPL as an effective recombination lifetime.
Enhanced built-in field, improved band alignment, or reduced interface trap density are acceptable dominant improvements.
TPV, intensity-dependent Voc, impedance, SCLC, or bottom-illumination PL are acceptable corroborating measurements.
A warning that faster TPC decay can also result from a smaller device capacitance is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the faster photocurrent decay evidence of faster recombination without considering extraction.
Claiming that longer TRPL necessarily means carriers are extracted more slowly.
Attributing the performance gain to bulk bandgap widening despite unchanged bandgap and Jsc.
Ignoring RC and measurement-geometry differences between TPC and TRPL.

expected_answer: Use an orthogonal design rather than testing only the complete champion stack. At minimum, vary the buried contact between the baseline monolayer and the coverage-improved co-assembled contact, and vary the upper interface among no bulky-ammonium treatment, conventionally annealed treatment, and vacuum-annealed treatment. Fabricate these combinations at coupon and module-relevant area, with replicated lots and matched absorber, ETL, electrode and encapsulation. This separates buried-contact, top-interface and area-scaling effects and exposes interactions between them. Apply a stress matrix that includes the original 55 °C/N2 MPP condition as a bridge control, 85 °C MPP in inert gas, 85 °C MPP in controlled humidity or damp heat, thermal cycling, and light-soak bias conditions. Unencapsulated and encapsulated specimens should be distinguished because barrier performance can mask intrinsic interface failure. Diagnose buried-contact failure through reverse dark current, shunt resistance, FF, local hot spots, EL/LBIC maps and spatial KPFM or contact-potential maps. Diagnose top-interface failure through QFLS/PLQY loss, ideality-factor changes, surface-sensitive diffraction or PL phase evolution, UPS/Kelvin-probe shifts, and ToF-SIMS or related depth profiling for PEA, halide and metal migration. Diagnose scale nonuniformity through thickness and composition mapping, sheet/contact-resistance maps, module-segment J-V, EL/PL imaging and statistics of dead or weak regions. A defensible go/no-go rule should be predefined at the module level, for example retention of at least 90% of stabilized power after the target 85 °C humid-light MPP duration, with no progressive local shunts, no unacceptable segment mismatch, and no treatment-specific ion accumulation. Passing only 55 °C/N2 or dark storage is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Uses an orthogonal buried-contact × top-treatment × area design with proper baseline and processing controls.
Includes bridge, thermal, humid, illuminated MPP and cycling stresses while separating encapsulated from intrinsic-interface behavior.
Maps distinct failure signatures to buried leakage, top-interface chemistry or ion migration, and large-area nonuniformity using spatial or operando diagnostics.
Defines a predeclared module-level go/no-go criterion based on stabilized power plus local failure and ion-migration evidence.
accepted_equivalents: A statistically powered fractional factorial design is acceptable if it still resolves the three requested failure origins.
Lock-in thermography, photoluminescence imaging, electroluminescence imaging, LBIC or segment-resolved J-V are acceptable spatial diagnostics.
SIMS, XPS depth profiling, isotope tracing, solid-state NMR or operando X-ray methods are acceptable ion-migration probes when correctly applied.
A different quantitative retention threshold is acceptable if it is declared in advance and tied to the intended qualification standard.
common_wrong_answers: Testing only the full optimized device against one control, which cannot separate the two interfaces or scale effects.
Treating 55 °C nitrogen MPP stability as proof of 85 °C humid-air module reliability.
Reporting only average module PCE and overlooking localized shunts, segment mismatch, or coating gradients.
Using dark shelf storage as a substitute for illuminated operational testing.

expected_answer: The single-dipole claim is underdetermined because the interlayer simultaneously changes liquid-solid interactions, film formation, chemical coordination and contact electrostatics. Orthogonal controls should vary one function at a time. A chemically inert surface-energy modifier should reproduce the contact angle with minimal dipole and minimal Lewis-acid/base passivation; if it reproduces grain-size, nucleation-density, morphology, lifetime and part of the QFLS gain, wetting-mediated crystallization is causal. A dipolar analogue with similar anchoring and coverage but weak defect-binding chemistry should reproduce the UPS/KPFM work-function shift; if Voc and contact selectivity follow the energetic shift without comparable morphology or PL-lifetime changes, electrostatic alignment is causal. A passivating but nearly non-dipolar analogue should reduce surface recombination, raise PLQY/QFLS and lower ideality factor without a large work-function shift; that supports chemical passivation. A patterned or porous insulating interlayer that changes the real contact fraction while preserving local chemistry can test contact-area effects; reduced interfacial recombination and higher Voc may occur, but excessive area reduction should increase series resistance and lower FF. In situ or early-stage GIWAXS, optical microscopy and SEM/AFM should track nucleation and morphology; UPS/KPFM and contact-potential mapping should quantify electrostatics; excitation-side-resolved PLQY/QFLS, TRPL and ideality-factor analysis should localize recombination; transfer-length/contact-resistance measurements and area-dependent J-V should test contact restriction. Causality requires that the targeted control reproduces the corresponding intermediate variable and device response while non-target variables remain unchanged. A multivariate correlation in the original device alone is not sufficient.
scoring_key_points: Rejects a single-mechanism inference because the interlayer simultaneously changes wetting, chemistry, electrostatics and contact geometry.
Proposes function-matched controls for wetting, dipole, passivation and effective contact area rather than only a no-interlayer control.
Maps each mechanism to distinct intermediate measurements and device signatures, including nucleation, UPS/KPFM, PLQY/QFLS and contact resistance.
Requires selective reproduction of both the intermediate variable and device response while non-target variables remain controlled.
accepted_equivalents: A designed molecular series with independently varied terminal dipole, anchoring group and passivating group is acceptable.
Surface-energy matching by solvent treatment, plasma-free chemistry or an inert polymer is acceptable if it does not introduce confounding damage.
Localized-contact test structures, patterned dielectrics or current-crowding simulations may be used to evaluate effective contact area.
Steady-state PLQY, transient PL, microwave conductivity or surface-recombination-velocity analysis may be combined when the localization limits are acknowledged.
common_wrong_answers: Treating a work-function shift as proof that all morphology and lifetime changes are dipole-driven.
Using only a treated versus untreated comparison without function-matched analogues.
Assigning longer TRPL entirely to better bulk material without separating surface extraction and recombination effects.
Assuming that reducing contact area always improves FF, ignoring current crowding and series resistance.

expected_answer: The conclusion is not justified. Approximately threefold Voc is useful evidence that the three subcells are electrically connected in series, but it does not establish low interconnect resistance, absence of shunts, high photocurrent matching, uniform segment performance or durable laser scribes. Likewise, dark ambient T90 measures shelf stability under a relatively mild condition; it does not test photochemical degradation, bias-driven ion migration, thermal stress, humidity ingress, encapsulation reliability or outdoor cycling. Qualification should first verify P1/P2/P3 geometry and electrical isolation with optical microscopy, profilometry or cross-sectional imaging, resistance measurements across each scribe, and EL/LBIC or thermography to identify local shunts and dead zones. Segment-resolved J-V should confirm voltage addition, current matching and series resistance. Report total, aperture and active areas separately, together with geometrical fill factor and both active-area and aperture-area efficiency, so dead-area losses are not hidden. Next, run replicated stabilized-MPP tests under illumination at relevant temperatures, damp-heat or humidity-bias tests, thermal cycling, UV exposure and light-dark cycling, with encapsulated and unencapsulated controls. Outdoor exposure may follow after laboratory screens. Track module power, Voc, Jsc, FF, scribe resistance, insulation resistance, EL/LBIC maps and failure propagation. Manufacturing evidence requires multiple substrates and lots, yield distributions, scribe-position tolerance, debris/redeposition control and process windows rather than one champion module. A failure that begins locally at P2/P3 and spreads should be assigned to interconnect or scribe damage; uniform photocurrent loss with stable scribe resistance suggests absorber/contact degradation; edge-driven humidity failure implicates encapsulation. Passing dark storage alone cannot support outdoor readiness.
scoring_key_points: Explains that voltage scaling verifies series connection only, not interconnect loss, shunt freedom, current matching or durability.
Distinguishes dark shelf T90 from illuminated, biased, thermal, humid and cyclic operational reliability.
Specifies scribe, segment and area-accounting diagnostics, including active/aperture/total area and geometrical fill factor.
Defines replicated stress testing and spatial failure interpretation that separates scribe, absorber/contact and encapsulation failure while assessing manufacturing yield.
accepted_equivalents: Electroluminescence, photoluminescence, LBIC, lock-in thermography or infrared imaging may be used to localize scribe and segment defects.
IEC-style damp heat, thermal cycling, UV and outdoor tests are acceptable; exact sequences may vary if dark storage is clearly distinguished from operation.
Four-wire interconnect resistance, transfer-length structures or segment-resolved impedance may be used to quantify laser-interconnect loss.
A different area terminology is acceptable if active, aperture and total substrate areas are unambiguously separated.
common_wrong_answers: Treating threefold Voc as proof of high module efficiency and robust interconnects.
Equating dark ambient storage with maximum-power-point or outdoor stability.
Reporting only active-area efficiency and omitting dead-area and scribe losses.
Qualifying a process from one champion minimodule without yield, tolerance or spatial-failure data.

expected_answer: The key is to decouple vacancy population from lattice strain. First, vary the iodide-vacancy chemical potential independently of the framework—for example by halide-rich/halide-poor processing, controlled electrical bias, illumination, or thermal stressing—while matching composition, morphology, and residual strain. Phase stability should then follow vacancy concentration if vacancy accumulation is causal. Second, quantify ion motion and defect buildup during stress using temperature-dependent ionic conductivity or current drift, SCLC, transient ion-current measurements, or depth-sensitive ion profiling; the framework should reduce the growth or aggregation of mobile-vacancy signatures. Third, follow the black-to-yellow transformation in situ by XRD or Raman during identical heating cycles and correlate the onset kinetics with the independently measured defect evolution. Finally, compare a rotatable framework with a chemically similar nonrotatable analogue and a conventional static passivant, supported by calculations of vacancy migration/aggregation barriers and strain-only phase energetics. A vacancy-suppression mechanism is supported only if phase stabilization tracks reduced vacancy kinetics and survives controls that preserve strain or passivation but remove framework dynamics.
scoring_key_points: Independently vary or quantify iodide-vacancy population while controlling strain, composition, and morphology.
Measure ion migration and stress-induced defect accumulation with an electrical, spectroscopic, or compositional probe.
Track phase-transition kinetics in situ and correlate them with vacancy evolution rather than static lattice distortion.
Use nonrotatable/static-passivant controls plus migration and phase-energy calculations to falsify strain-only explanations.
accepted_equivalents: Halide chemical-potential control, defect-doping control, or bias-induced vacancy generation as a way to decouple vacancies from strain
Temperature-dependent conductivity, transient ionic current, SCLC, Kelvin-probe drift, ToF-SIMS, or isotope tracing as vacancy diagnostics
In situ GIWAXS in place of XRD, or temperature-dependent Raman in place of diffraction
A rigid structural analogue, nonrotatable 2D phase, or matched molecular passivant as the critical control
common_wrong_answers: Treating higher room-temperature PL or larger grains alone as proof of a vacancy-migration mechanism
Inferring causality only from a calculated migration barrier without stress-dependent experimental validation
Attributing all phase stabilization to compressive strain without independently measuring vacancy accumulation
Comparing only additive versus control films without a nonrotatable or strain-matched control

expected_answer: A viable candidate must first be structurally dynamic in the relevant processing and operating range: its reconfiguration should be reversible, thermally compatible with perovskite annealing, and free of decomposition or irreversible secondary-phase growth. Second, it must alter the defect kinetics that matter—raising halide-vacancy migration or aggregation barriers, reducing field-driven ionic redistribution, or buffering local stress—while preserving the wide-bandgap absorber's optical gap, carrier mobility, and band alignment. Third, dose and deposition must have a finite process window: the candidate should localize at surfaces or grain boundaries without forming a thick transport-blocking 2D phase, disrupting current matching, or creating compositional segregation. A rigid analogue and a conventional passivant should be included to separate dynamic behavior from ordinary passivation. Finally, the candidate must be tested under coupled illumination, electrical bias, heat, and thermal cycling at stabilized maximum power, with in situ phase, ion-migration, recombination, and extraction diagnostics. Scale-up should proceed only if the benefit persists in encapsulated larger-area devices with uniform coating and no new hysteresis or series-resistance penalty.
scoring_key_points: Require reversible structural motion and thermal/process compatibility without decomposition or irreversible secondary phases.
Show reduced vacancy migration or aggregation while preserving optical absorption, band alignment, and carrier extraction.
Establish a dose and coating window that avoids a thick insulating low-dimensional phase and include rigid/passivant controls.
Validate under coupled light-bias-heat cycling at stabilized MPP and confirm persistence in uniform larger-area devices.
accepted_equivalents: Dynamic lattice accommodation, reversible orientational motion, or entropy-assisted defect buffering
Migration-barrier calculations combined with bias-temperature ion-drift experiments
Grain-boundary-selective incorporation or ultrathin interfacial localization instead of bulk incorporation
Mini-module, large-area cell, or statistically sampled submodule validation as the scale-up gate
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the candidate solely because it increases initial PL intensity or PCE
Assuming that more low-dimensional phase is always beneficial
Testing only shelf stability in inert atmosphere without electrical bias or illumination
Ignoring current matching, contact resistance, or coating uniformity in the tandem context

expected_answer: A minimal model contains a fast electronic state—carrier generation, extraction, and recombination—and a slow ionic/interfacial state such as vacancy redistribution and ionic screening at TiO2/perovskite or perovskite/carbon interfaces. A very fast scan freezes the ionic distribution and samples a favorable initial internal field, so the apparent PCE can be inflated. A slow scan allows ions and interfacial charge to approach a less favorable steady state, reducing collection. At an intermediate scan time, the voltage sweep crosses the ionic relaxation time, producing delayed field redistribution and a transient current overshoot or bump. The light-induced capacitance increase and dark discharge are consistent with stored interfacial ionic/electronic charge, but are not sufficient alone. The mechanism should show systematic dependence on prebias, scan direction, dwell time, temperature, frequency, and light intensity, with Arrhenius-like ionic time constants that agree between J-V, step-current, and capacitance measurements. Interface and geometry controls—changing mesoporous TiO2, carbon surface chemistry, spacer thickness, porosity, or adding an ion-blocking layer—should shift the effect. A pure instrument RC artifact would follow cable/device capacitance and sweep settings but would not exhibit chemically sensitive activation energies, preconditioning memory, or interface-specific scaling.
scoring_key_points: Model fast electronic transport and slow ionic/interfacial polarization as coupled state variables.
Explain fast-, slow-, and intermediate-scan behavior by the relation between sweep time and ionic relaxation time.
Require prebias, direction, dwell, temperature, frequency, and time-domain tests with consistent kinetic scaling.
Use interface/geometry controls and distinguish chemical activation and memory from a simple instrumental RC response.
accepted_equivalents: Mobile halide vacancies, protonic defects, or ionic double-layer formation as the slow variable
Dynamic internal-field screening, interfacial band bending, or delayed charge collection as the coupling mechanism
Intensity-modulated photocurrent/photovoltage, transient photocurrent, or bias-step relaxation
Ion-blocking interlayers, altered mesoporous TiO2, carbon functionalization, or device-thickness series as localization controls
common_wrong_answers: Treating the fastest-scan PCE as the true steady-state efficiency
Explaining the bump only as random measurement noise without testing time-scale dependence
Using capacitance magnitude alone as definitive proof of bulk ion migration
Ignoring preconditioning and scan direction when comparing hysteresis data

expected_answer: PL quenching in a contacted stack is ambiguous because both faster charge extraction and faster nonradiative recombination reduce the emitted intensity. The unchanged neat-film QFLS and TRPL indicate that the treatment neither strongly passivates nor strongly worsens bulk/surface recombination in the isolated absorber, so the mechanism must be tested at the contact. Dark and illuminated UPS, Kelvin-probe/KPFM measurements, and depth- or core-level-sensitive XPS should establish the sign and magnitude of the molecular dipole, the change in surface band bending, and the valence-band offset to the hole-transport material. Charge-selectivity must then be demonstrated dynamically using transient surface photovoltage, transient photocurrent or charge extraction, contact-selective devices, and measurements of electron leakage to the hole contact. Improved Voc/FF or electroluminescence efficiency should correlate with faster hole extraction and reduced minority-carrier leakage without a loss of QFLS. Concentration, molecular-dipole, and nonpolar-analogue controls are needed to rule out morphology, solvent, or chemical-damage explanations.
scoring_key_points: State that PL quenching can arise from either extraction or nonradiative trapping and is therefore ambiguous.
Use unchanged neat-film QFLS/TRPL to constrain large passivation or trap-creation explanations.
Map dark/light work function, band bending, and VBM-to-HTL alignment with UPS/Kelvin probe/XPS-type measurements.
Demonstrate faster hole extraction and lower electron leakage with dynamic/contact-selective controls and device correlation.
accepted_equivalents: Photoluminescence efficiency or absolute PL in place of PLQY-derived QFLS
Contact-potential difference mapping, surface photovoltage spectroscopy, or capacitance profiling for band bending
Time-resolved microwave conductivity combined with selective contacts, transient absorption, or charge-extraction measurements
A dipole-reversed molecule, nonpolar analogue, or solvent-only control
common_wrong_answers: Interpreting stronger PL quenching as automatic proof of better extraction
Calling the treatment a strong passivant despite unchanged neat-film QFLS and lifetime
Using only ex situ work-function data without the hole-transport layer or illumination
Ignoring minority-carrier leakage and contact selectivity when explaining Voc and FF gains

expected_answer: PL quenching and lifetime shortening are kinetically ambiguous. They may indicate rapid hole transfer into the HTM, but they can also result from a new interfacial nonradiative sink. Faster extraction should therefore be demonstrated by a carrier-specific observable, such as the prompt appearance of an HTM hole-polaron signal in transient absorption, faster transient photocurrent, or charge-transfer kinetics that scale with contact formation. Bulk HTM transport must be evaluated independently through mobility or SCLC, conductivity, thickness-dependent series resistance, and spatial current mapping; lower energetic disorder should manifest as less field/temperature sensitivity, more uniform local current, and reduced transport-related fill-factor loss. Interfacial recombination should be judged by quasi-Fermi-level splitting or absolute PLQY of device-relevant stacks, nonradiative voltage loss, dark saturation current, light-intensity-dependent open-circuit voltage/ideality factor, and transient photovoltage under open-circuit conditions. A genuinely superior HTM should combine fast carrier transfer with preserved or increased quasi-Fermi-level splitting, lower dark recombination and ideality factor, higher built-in potential, and lower series resistance. If PL is strongly quenched but quasi-Fermi-level splitting and voltage fall, the interface is acting as a recombination sink. If interfacial metrics improve but fill factor remains thickness-sensitive, bulk HTM transport is still limiting. The causal claim is strongest when these measurements are made at matched thickness, doping level, optical absorption, and perovskite quality.
scoring_key_points: States that PL quenching and shorter TRPL are ambiguous between productive charge transfer and interfacial nonradiative quenching.
Uses carrier-specific transfer measurements to identify faster hole extraction rather than inferring it from PL alone.
Separates bulk HTM transport using mobility/conductivity, thickness dependence, energetic disorder, or local-current mapping.
Requires improved QFLS/voltage and reduced recombination indicators together with fast transfer and low series resistance for a superior HTM.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz spectroscopy, or ultrafast interfacial spectroscopy may establish productive hole transfer.
Absolute PLQY-derived QFLS, electroluminescence efficiency, dark J0, ideality factor, or transient photovoltage are acceptable recombination diagnostics.
SCLC mobility, four-point conductivity, C-AFM, or thickness-dependent device resistance are acceptable bulk-transport diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Equates stronger PL quenching directly with lower recombination without checking QFLS or voltage loss.
Attributes all fill-factor improvement to energy-level alignment while ignoring HTM disorder and conductivity.
Uses only one transient lifetime measurement and does not separate transfer, transport, and recombination.

expected_answer: The meaning of PL kinetics depends on whether an extracting contact is present. On insulating glass, carriers cannot be selectively removed, so higher PL and a longer lifetime normally indicate fewer bulk or grain-boundary nonradiative pathways and improved crystallization/passivation. On SnO2, lower PL and a shorter lifetime can instead reflect faster electron transfer into the electron-selective layer. That interpretation becomes credible when the modifier also passivates SnO2 defects and improves band alignment, but the PL trend alone remains ambiguous because a defective interface would produce the same quenching. Minimum controls should include identical perovskite films on glass, untreated SnO2, modifier-treated SnO2, and an inert or electronically blocking substrate; thickness and excitation density must be matched. Productive extraction should be verified by transient absorption or another carrier-selective probe showing faster electron population of SnO2, by faster short-circuit photocurrent or reduced extraction time, and by improved device QFLS/open-circuit voltage rather than a reduced QFLS. Interfacial recombination should be checked through absolute PLQY, dark saturation current, ideality factor, transient photovoltage, or electroluminescence efficiency. XPS/oxygen-vacancy analysis and SCLC can establish defect passivation, while UPS supports reduced energetic barriers. The consistent result pattern is longer lifetime on glass, faster transfer on SnO2, lower trap density and recombination current, and higher QFLS/Voc. Faster decay accompanied by lower QFLS or higher dark recombination would instead diagnose harmful interfacial quenching.
scoring_key_points: Explains that longer lifetime on glass diagnoses reduced nonradiative loss, whereas shorter lifetime on an extracting SnO2 contact may diagnose faster electron transfer.
Recognizes that contact-induced PL quenching is ambiguous and requires matched substrate, thickness, and excitation controls.
Requires a carrier-selective extraction measurement together with defect/passivation and energy-alignment evidence.
Uses QFLS/Voc or dark-recombination metrics to distinguish productive extraction from a new nonradiative interface.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved terahertz, surface photovoltage, or ultrafast charge-transfer spectroscopy may prove electron extraction.
Absolute PLQY, electroluminescence efficiency, dark J0, ideality factor, or transient photovoltage may diagnose interfacial recombination.
An insulating oxide, passivated SnO2, or a blocking interlayer may serve as the nonextracting control.
common_wrong_answers: Calls the two PL trends contradictory without considering selective carrier extraction by SnO2.
Assumes every shorter lifetime on a transport layer is beneficial extraction.
Uses only UPS alignment or XPS coordination as proof that interfacial recombination is reduced.

expected_answer: A minimum 2 by 2 factorial design is required: neither treatment, buried modifier only, top passivator only, and both treatments, with identical absorber batches, thicknesses, contacts, and processing history. Replicated devices and analysis of main effects plus the interaction term prevent the combined device from being attributed automatically to the buried layer. Buried-interface readouts should include SnO2 surface chemistry/defect density, UPS or contact potential, electron-only SCLC, substrate-dependent PL or transient extraction, and interface-specific recombination. Top-interface readouts should include surface PLQY, surface chemistry, and hole-extraction or recombination measurements. Device outputs should include QFLS or nonradiative voltage loss, ideality factor, dark current, stabilized power, and scan-rate-dependent hysteresis. To test migration causally, ion redistribution must be measured during or before electrical degradation under controlled heat, light, and bias, using time-resolved ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, EDS, ion-conductivity/activation-energy measurements, or transient ionic-current methods. A causal claim is strengthened if the buried-only treatment suppresses ion motion before the performance diverges, if the suppression scales with modifier coverage or binding while initial PCE is held similar, and if deliberately increasing ionic stress reverses both migration and stability benefits. If lower migration appears only after the untreated device has already decomposed, it may be a consequence of different damage severity. The full factorial also reveals synergy: the combined device may outperform the sum of individual effects, but that interaction must be reported rather than assigned to either layer alone.
scoring_key_points: Specifies the four-group 2 by 2 factorial design and analyzes buried, top, and interaction effects separately.
Assigns interface-specific chemical, energetic, extraction, and recombination readouts to the buried and top treatments.
Uses stabilized device metrics, QFLS/voltage loss, ideality, and hysteresis rather than champion PCE alone.
Tests migration causally by measuring ion motion before or during degradation under controlled stress and by perturbing migration independently of initial device quality.
accepted_equivalents: ANOVA, linear mixed models, or an equivalent interaction analysis may be used for the factorial attribution.
ToF-SIMS, isotope labeling, EDS, Kelvin-probe transients, impedance-based ionic relaxation, or activation-energy measurements are acceptable migration probes.
Matched initial Voc/PCE cohorts or dose-dependent modifier coverage may be used to decouple ion migration from initial device quality.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only untreated and doubly passivated devices, making the two interfaces inseparable.
Attributes all stability gains to the buried layer despite the presence of an independent top passivator.
Treats lower post-mortem ion accumulation as causal without showing that migration changed before degradation.

expected_answer: The additive should combine a flexible backbone and reversible interactions with selective coordination to undercoordinated Sn/Pb sites, but it must remain electronically and optically innocuous at low loading. Desirable criteria include precursor compatibility, limited redox activity toward Sn2+, appropriate molecular weight and solubility, a modulus/Tg that permits stress dissipation over the operating range, and a thermodynamic tendency to enrich grain boundaries or interfaces rather than forming an insulating continuous phase. Screening must map concentration because too little additive may not form a percolating mechanical network, whereas too much can retard crystallization, create amorphous inclusions, increase series resistance, block vertical charge transfer, alter residual stress excessively, or promote phase separation and delamination. STEM-EDS or chemical mapping should verify localization; GIWAXS/XRD and microscopy should assess texture, grain growth, and secondary phases; nanoindentation, adhesion/fracture tests, and in situ stress measurements should quantify mechanics. Electronic qualification should include mobility or vertical conductivity, QFLS/PLQY, ideality factor, SCLC trap density, Sn4+/Sn2+ and PbI2 analysis, and ion-migration diagnostics. Module-relevant testing should combine thermal cycling with illumination at maximum power, electrical bias, humidity, and oxygen exposure, while monitoring tandem current matching and recombination-layer integrity. A viable additive should retain mechanical and chemical benefits across the concentration window without a transport penalty and should suppress crack growth, oxidation, and ionic redistribution under coupled stress. Improvement only in dark nitrogen thermal cycling is insufficient for transfer.
scoring_key_points: Defines polymer chemistry, mechanics, redox compatibility, and grain-boundary localization criteria appropriate for Sn-Pb perovskites.
Identifies a concentration window and at least one overloading failure mode involving crystallization, insulation, phase separation, or excessive residual stress.
Requires linked structural, mechanical, electronic, and Sn-oxidation/ion-migration diagnostics.
Uses coupled light-heat-bias-humidity/oxygen testing with tandem-module constraints rather than dark thermal cycling alone.
accepted_equivalents: Hydrogen bonding, dynamic coordination, ionic interactions, or other reversible supramolecular bonds are acceptable dissipation mechanisms.
STEM-EDS, ToF-SIMS, XPS mapping, fluorescence labeling, or atom-probe methods may verify grain-boundary localization.
Maximum-power tracking with thermal cycles, damp heat under bias, or combined light-soak/temperature/humidity testing are acceptable coupled-stress protocols.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that more polymer always gives better crack resistance and ignores electrical insulation or crystallization disruption.
Selects the additive solely by binding strength to Sn/Pb without considering redox chemistry, modulus, localization, or transport.
Qualifies only unencapsulated films in dark nitrogen thermal cycling and extrapolates directly to tandem modules.

expected_answer: The key is to create interventions that preserve one mechanism while suppressing the others. For templating, compare precursor-added material with a substrate seed layer or an early-stage nucleation pulse of the additive, and contrast these with a chemically identical post-anneal treatment that cannot alter initial crystallization. Time-resolved XRD/GIWAXS during drying and annealing should show whether the additive forms early, changes intermediate-phase disappearance, and increases vertical texture; device performance should track texture and vertical transport if templating dominates. For n-phase redistribution, use depth-resolved absorption/PL, excitation from opposite sides, and transient absorption to quantify small-n/high-n populations and energy-transfer kinetics while holding texture as constant as possible. A dominant phase-distribution mechanism should change the spectral population and funneling dynamics even when grain-boundary passivation is matched. For electronic passivation, compare a post-deposition grain-boundary treatment, a nonbinding structural analogue, and loading-dependent samples. SCLC, absolute PLQY/QFLS, trap spectroscopy, XPS/KPFM, and recombination ideality should improve without substantial changes in GIWAXS texture or n-phase spectra if passivation dominates. Vertical conductivity and selective-contact TRPL are essential controls because a wide-gap low-dimensional phase can improve lifetime yet block extraction. The strongest causal conclusion would come from mediation analysis or matched samples showing that only one variable—texture, phase distribution, or trap density—predicts Voc/FF after the other two are experimentally held constant.
scoring_key_points: Uses timing/location perturbations such as precursor addition, seeding, and post-deposition treatment to separate crystallization from passivation.
Defines distinct time-resolved structural and vertical-transport signatures for a templating/orientation mechanism.
Defines depth-resolved spectral and energy-funneling signatures for an n-phase redistribution mechanism.
Defines passivation-specific trap/QFLS signatures at unchanged texture/phase distribution and checks that the low-dimensional phase does not block extraction.
accepted_equivalents: Pre-nucleation seeding, additive timing during coating, or surface-only post-treatment are acceptable causal perturbations.
GIWAXS orientation factors, polarized absorption, out-of-plane mobility, or vertical conductivity may quantify orientation-related transport.
Depth-resolved PL, transient absorption, cathodoluminescence, or compositional nano-imaging may quantify n-phase redistribution.
common_wrong_answers: Lists GIWAXS, PL, and SCLC without experimental perturbations that isolate causal mechanisms.
Assumes improved vertical orientation automatically proves that orientation caused the voltage gain.
Interprets a longer lifetime as beneficial without testing whether a wide-bandgap low-dimensional phase blocks charge extraction.

expected_answer: The longer TRPL lifetime should first be interpreted in the geometry in which it was measured. With excitation and collection dominated by the perovskite side of an incomplete stack, a longer decay can arise because interfacial nonradiative recombination has been suppressed; it does not necessarily mean that holes cross the selective contact more slowly. Faster extraction is instead supported by the lower contact resistance and the reduced valence-band offset, which indicate a smaller energetic/kinetic barrier for hole transfer. The lower trap density and narrower KPFM potential distribution independently support chemical passivation and reduced microscopic energetic disorder at the buried interface. A rigorous separation requires matched measurements in different geometries or stacks—for example, TRPL from both excitation directions on an inert-substrate control and on the selective-contact stack, supplemented by transient photocurrent or time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity. If the interlayer lengthens lifetime on an inert or weakly extracting substrate but accelerates quenching or current extraction in the complete selective-contact geometry, passivation and extraction enhancement are simultaneously demonstrated rather than confused.
scoring_key_points: Interprets the longer TRPL lifetime as suppressed interfacial nonradiative recombination in the stated measurement geometry, not automatically as slower extraction.
Uses lower contact resistance and reduced valence-band offset as evidence for a smaller hole-extraction barrier and improved transport.
Links lower trap density and narrower KPFM potential variation to chemical passivation and reduced local energetic disorder.
Proposes a geometry- or stack-matched control that decouples recombination lifetime from extraction kinetics, such as front/back TRPL plus transient photocurrent or an inert-substrate comparison.
accepted_equivalents: Quasi-Fermi-level splitting or photoluminescence quantum-yield measurements may replace inert-substrate PL controls for diagnosing nonradiative loss.
Transient photovoltage, transient photocurrent, impedance spectroscopy, or selective-contact-dependent PL quenching may be used to separate recombination and extraction.
A reduced HOMO/VBM offset may be described as improved energetic alignment or a lower hole-transfer activation barrier.
common_wrong_answers: Claims that any longer PL lifetime proves poorer charge extraction.
Uses improved wetting or contact angle alone as proof of chemical passivation.
Treats an energy-level shift alone as sufficient evidence that trap-assisted recombination is reduced.
Ignores excitation direction, stack completeness, or the presence of a selective contact when interpreting TRPL.

expected_answer: The transfer should be treated as a coverage-window problem rather than as a single additive concentration. Molecular dose, coating speed, solvent activity, drying time, and post-deposition annealing should be varied to identify the narrow regime that gives complete anchoring without a thick, disordered organic overlayer. At minimum, the study needs bare NiOx, a conventional phosphonic-acid SAM, and preferably a wetting-matched but weakly anchoring molecular control; these distinguish anchoring/topology effects from generic surface-energy changes. Spatial validation should combine chemical coverage mapping or representative XPS/ToF-SIMS coupons with KPFM or surface-potential mapping, PL or electroluminescence mapping, contact-resistance mapping, and buried-interface morphology from peeled or cross-sectional samples. The module must then be evaluated under stabilized maximum-power-point operation, ideally with elevated temperature and controlled humidity, while tracking local hot spots, shunts, series resistance, and area-normalized yield. Storage retention alone is insufficient because it does not test whether the molecular layer remains electronically and chemically functional under carrier flux, heat, and field.
scoring_key_points: Defines a coating and annealing process window that targets complete anchored coverage while avoiding multilayer aggregation or excessive organic thickness.
Includes mechanistically discriminating controls: bare NiOx, a standard SAM, and/or a wetting-matched nonbridging analogue.
Requires spatially resolved chemical, energetic, optical, and electrical uniformity diagnostics rather than only average contact angle or small-area J-V data.
Uses stabilized MPP testing under operationally relevant thermal/humidity stress and monitors area-dependent failure modes such as shunts, hot spots, and series resistance.
accepted_equivalents: Ellipsometry, quartz-crystal microbalance calibration, angle-resolved XPS, or infrared spectroscopy may be used to constrain molecular-layer thickness and anchoring.
LBIC, electroluminescence imaging, photoluminescence imaging, or lock-in thermography are acceptable module-uniformity diagnostics.
Continuous-light thermal aging under load is acceptable if true MPP tracking is unavailable and the limitation is stated.
common_wrong_answers: Optimizes only contact angle and assumes the most hydrophilic condition is automatically best.
Uses only champion-cell efficiency without spatial yield or module-scale statistics.
Omits a control that separates molecular anchoring from generic solvent or wetting effects.
Relies only on dark storage or shelf-life data to claim operational stability.

expected_answer: A credible study needs a factorial control matrix rather than a single treated-versus-untreated comparison. Additive and control films should be processed to matched thickness and, where possible, matched grain size; an additive analogue that preserves solvent/crystallization effects but lacks strong Sn coordination is especially useful. Devices and films should then be exposed to independently controlled oxygen, water vapor, temperature, illumination, and electrical bias, including continuous MPP operation, so that chemical oxidation can be separated from purely thermal or field-driven changes. Sn4+/Sn2+ ratios, carrier density or dark conductivity, and Fermi-level shifts should be tracked over time to diagnose oxidation/self-doping. UPS/PYS, built-in potential, contact resistance, and interfacial recombination measurements should be followed to test whether energetic alignment remains stable. In parallel, XRD/GIWAXS, microscopy, and strain or texture measurements should determine whether the benefit is fixed at film formation or continues to suppress chemical degradation. Persistent suppression of Sn4+, carrier-density drift, and trap growth under O2/H2O supports chemical stabilization; unchanged chemistry but stable contact resistance supports an energetic effect; a benefit present only at time zero and explained by matched morphology indicates a crystallization-only origin.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched additive, untreated, and preferably coordination-deficient analogue controls to separate chemical binding from crystallization effects.
Applies independently controlled O2, H2O, heat, light, and electrical-bias/MPP stresses rather than relying on inert storage alone.
Tracks oxidation/self-doping and energetic-contact observables over time, including Sn4+/Sn2+, carrier density/conductivity, energy levels, contact resistance, or interfacial recombination.
Defines distinct result patterns for oxidation suppression, persistent energetic alignment, and a one-time morphology benefit.
accepted_equivalents: Operando XPS, XANES, Mössbauer-like tin speciation methods, or chemical titration may replace conventional XPS for Sn oxidation-state tracking.
Hall effect, capacitance-voltage, Kelvin probe, or Seebeck measurements may be used to monitor self-doping and Fermi-level drift.
Thermal cycling or damp-heat under illumination is acceptable in addition to constant-temperature MPP testing.
common_wrong_answers: Treats nitrogen storage retention as proof of resistance to oxygen and moisture.
Measures only PCE decay without identifying the changing chemical or electronic state variable.
Allows grain size, thickness, or interface stack to change simultaneously with additive chemistry.
Assumes any stability improvement must arise from lower trap density at time zero.

expected_answer: The red-shifted EQE edge and smaller bandgap directly explain part of the Jsc gain because the absorber harvests a wider portion of the solar spectrum; the integrated EQE should quantify this optical contribution. The voltage comparison must not be made from Voc alone because the maximum attainable voltage scales with bandgap. The appropriate quantity is the voltage deficit, Eg/q minus Voc, or an equivalent nonradiative loss derived from quasi-Fermi-level splitting, absolute PLQY, or electroluminescence quantum efficiency. A smaller-bandgap crystal can still exhibit a higher absolute Voc if its reduction in nonradiative and trap-assisted recombination exceeds the voltage penalty associated with the modest bandgap reduction. Stronger PL, longer TRPL, a lower ideality factor, and a longer transient-photovoltage lifetime are mutually consistent with this reduced recombination loss. Optical thickness, reflection, and collection efficiency should also be controlled so that the red-shifted EQE is not incorrectly attributed to transport alone.
scoring_key_points: Attributes the principal Jsc increase to broader spectral absorption verified by the red-shifted and integrated EQE response.
Evaluates voltage using Eg/q minus Voc or another bandgap-normalized loss metric rather than comparing Voc alone.
Explains that sufficiently reduced nonradiative/SRH loss can produce a higher Voc despite a modestly smaller bandgap.
Uses PLQY/QFLS/EL efficiency, ideality factor, TRPL/TPV, and optical controls to separate recombination and absorption contributions.
accepted_equivalents: The radiative-limit voltage loss and nonradiative voltage loss may be reported separately instead of a single Voc deficit.
Absolute photoluminescence quantum yield or external electroluminescence efficiency is acceptable for estimating nonradiative voltage loss.
Transfer-matrix optical modeling may replace empirical reflection/thickness controls.
common_wrong_answers: States that a smaller bandgap must always produce a lower measured Voc.
Attributes the entire Jsc gain to better charge transport without using the EQE edge.
Uses stronger PL alone as proof of higher extraction efficiency.
Compares absolute Voc without normalizing to bandgap or radiative limit.

expected_answer: The coating process should be controlled through a coupled mass- and heat-transfer window: additive-to-solvent ratio, wet-film thickness, line speed, gas-knife or vacuum-flash intensity, web temperature, and residence time must be co-optimized so that the desired intermediate forms transiently but is removed before conversion is complete. Flexible substrates require lower peak temperature, so longer residence time, staged drying, controlled gas flow, or reduced-pressure extraction may replace aggressive annealing. Acceptance cannot be based on one central coupon. Edge, center, leading, and trailing regions should be sampled or mapped for residual solvent, stoichiometry, phase/orientation, strain, PL lifetime or QFLS, and surface potential; calibrated GC-MS/thermal desorption on witness coupons can complement depth-resolved ToF-SIMS. Module validation should include electroluminescence or PL imaging, LBIC, sheet/series resistance, shunt mapping, cell-to-cell mismatch, aperture-area efficiency, and yield across multiple modules. Durability should combine stabilized MPP illumination with thermal cycling or moderate-temperature damp heat compatible with the polymer substrate, while tracking whether degradation initiates in high-residue regions. A credible acceptance limit is a narrow spatial distribution of residue below a prevalidated defect threshold, no systematic edge-center gradient, and module performance/stability that correlate with the same residue-sensitive descriptors established in small cells.
scoring_key_points: Controls the coupled coating, drying, and low-temperature annealing window so the intermediate is retained transiently but final residue is removed.
Defines spatially resolved acceptance measurements for residual solvent, stoichiometry, phase/strain, and electronic quality across the full module area.
Validates module electrical uniformity and yield with imaging/mapping and aperture-area metrics rather than only a champion subcell.
Uses flexible-compatible MPP and environmental/thermal-cycling durability tests and correlates failure initiation with local residual-solvent metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Infrared solvent mapping, inline mass spectroscopy, or spectroscopic ellipsometry may serve as scalable residual-solvent process monitors after calibration.
Lock-in thermography, electroluminescence, photoluminescence, or scanning photocurrent are acceptable electrical-uniformity tools.
A statistically defined process-capability index for residue and module-cell mismatch is an acceptable quantitative acceptance criterion.
common_wrong_answers: Copies the small-area annealing recipe without considering web-scale mass transfer or substrate temperature limits.
Samples only the module center and ignores edge, flow-direction, or drying gradients.
Reports only total module PCE without cell-to-cell mismatch, shunt, or spatial-yield analysis.
Uses only dark shelf storage and does not test illumination, bias, or flexible-substrate thermal cycling.

expected_answer: Use independent measurement of the inorganic flux and the total or substrate-level deposited flux so the organic contribution can be estimated by calibrated mass balance, but do not rely on a single local QCM. Add spatially distributed or traversing rate sensors and at least one independent composition-sensitive signal, such as residual-gas or optical-emission monitoring of the organic precursor, in situ ellipsometry, reflectometry, or spectroscopic absorption. Calibrate tooling factors against witness substrates across the web and update them as source geometry and fill level change. The controller should combine feed-forward warm-up and depletion models with feedback to source temperature, shutters, pressure, and substrate speed; it should explicitly manage rate ramps and reject data during unstable transients. Reference runs, redundant sensors, zero checks, and periodic witness-sample composition measurements are needed to detect QCM drift or coating. Qualification must be based on run-to-run and cross-web distributions of thickness, stoichiometry, phase/texture, pinholes/voids, and stabilized device metrics, together with source utilization, uptime, and process capability. A higher rate is manufacturable only if it remains inside predefined control limits over source lifetime and multiple batches, with acceptable yield and degradation after encapsulation; a single high-efficiency pixel or a temporarily stable rate trace is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Uses independent inorganic and total/substrate-level rate information with calibration or mass balance, rather than treating one local sensor as a complete composition measurement.
Adds spatial sensing and an independent composition/thickness signal, plus calibration for tooling factors, source depletion, and precursor-batch changes.
Specifies feed-forward plus feedback control of warm-up, ramps, source temperature, shutters/pressure, and substrate speed, with redundancy and drift detection.
Defines manufacturability through multi-run spatial uniformity, yield, process capability, source-life stability, and stabilized device/encapsulation performance rather than a champion cell.
accepted_equivalents: Multiple QCMs, moving QCMs, quartz-crystal arrays, or calibrated optical rate monitors are acceptable spatial-sensing implementations.
Mass spectrometry, tunable-diode absorption, optical emission, or precursor-specific spectroscopy may serve as the independent organic-flux signal.
Statistical process control indices, control charts, or a formally specified yield window are acceptable manufacturability criteria.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing source temperature until the desired nominal rate is reached, without independent composition feedback.
Assuming the rate measured at one QCM is spatially representative of a meter-scale substrate.
Ignoring source depletion, sensor coating/drift, or warm-up transients.
Defining success solely by the best PCE obtained from a small sampled area.

expected_answer: Both mechanisms predict later appearance of the perovskite optical and diffraction signatures, so a global time shift does not reveal whether nuclei are merely born later or are spatially prevented from colliding. The decisive experiment must resolve spatial statistics and mass transport during film formation. Use operando high-speed fluorescence or scattering microscopy, optionally combined with micro-GIWAXS/SAXS or interferometric thickness mapping, to track nucleation positions, growth fronts, pair-correlation distances, collision/coalescence frequency, and the locations where cracks later emerge. Map additive/intermediate-rich domains with a chemically sensitive channel if possible. Include controls that decouple coordination from viscosity, evaporation rate, and steric size: a weakly coordinating additive with matched rheology/volatility, and a comparably coordinating molecule with different intermediate size or persistence. Also vary seed density or impose matched global nucleation timing. A physical barrier is supported if, at matched overall nucleation rate and solvent-loss trajectory, intermediate-rich regions create persistent spatial exclusion, reduce nuclei encounters and local solute depletion, and predict where cracks are suppressed. Under a simple kinetic-delay model, spatial distributions and collision statistics should collapse onto the control after rescaling time; the film would crystallize later but follow the same coalescence and depletion pathway.
scoring_key_points: Explains that both uniform kinetic slowing and physical separation can produce delayed global PL/absorption/XRD transitions, so temporal delay alone is non-diagnostic.
Proposes operando spatial tracking of nuclei positions, growth, pair correlations, collisions/coalescence, solute or thickness fields, and later crack locations.
Includes matched controls that separate coordination/intermediate formation from viscosity, volatility, steric size, or initial nucleation density.
Gives a falsifiable contrast: persistent spatial exclusion and fewer collisions at matched global kinetics support a barrier, whereas time-rescaled spatial statistics support simple slowing.
accepted_equivalents: Liquid-cell electron microscopy, coherent X-ray imaging, grazing-incidence scattering with spatial resolution, or super-resolution optical imaging may replace high-speed fluorescence microscopy.
Raman, infrared, or fluorescence labeling of the adduct may serve as the chemically sensitive intermediate map.
A reaction-diffusion model fitted jointly to spatial and temporal data is acceptable if it makes and tests the stated barrier-versus-delay predictions.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that a longer crystallization time by itself proves physical separation of nuclei.
Comparing only final grain size or final crack density without observing the formation pathway.
Using an unmatched solvent additive control that changes viscosity and evaporation as well as coordination.
Describing the barrier mechanism qualitatively without a prediction that could falsify it.

expected_answer: The two strategies should be compared at matched halide composition, bandgap, thickness, morphology, and interface stack. Initial screening should quantify segregation kinetics by time-resolved PL or absorption under controlled carrier density, then measure ionic transport with temperature- and illumination-dependent impedance or another transport method to obtain a reproducible migration barrier and prefactor. Operando structural or compositional mapping should verify that reduced spectral evolution corresponds to reduced halide redistribution rather than optical masking. Device testing must track stabilized power, Jsc, Voc, FF, hysteresis, and recovery during and after combined light/heat stress, because a formulation can suppress a PL shift yet still accumulate ions at interfaces or damage extraction. A candidate should fail if its benefit disappears at realistic temperature or bias, if dark recovery reveals reversible hidden segregation, if ion accumulation shifts interfacial energetics, or if improved short-term spectra are offset by phase instability, bandgap drift, current loss, or poor reproducibility. The preferred strategy is the one that raises the kinetic barrier and preserves device output without creating a new thermodynamic or transport penalty; uncertain incorporation is acceptable only when localization and mechanism are experimentally bounded.
scoring_key_points: Defines matched-composition and matched-device controls so steric, passivation, bandgap, morphology, and interface effects are not confounded.
Requires agreement among segregation kinetics, a quantitative ionic-transport metric, and operando structural/compositional evidence.
Evaluates stabilized device parameters under combined light, heat, and relevant electrical bias, including recovery or reversibility behavior.
States explicit rejection criteria for transient optical masking, hidden interfacial ion accumulation, phase/bandgap penalties, current loss, or poor reproducibility.
accepted_equivalents: Ion kinetics may be measured by impedance, transient ion-drift methods, bias-stress relaxation, thermally stimulated current, or isotope/depth profiling.
Operando segregation may be monitored by PL mapping, absorption, XRD/GIWAXS, XRF, or composition-sensitive microscopy.
A-site steric modification and vacancy passivation may be combined if factorial controls identify a genuine cooperative effect.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the candidate with the smallest initial PL redshift without testing temperature, bias, reversibility, or device output.
Assuming that uncertain bulk incorporation invalidates a passivator, or conversely assuming that any additive necessarily enters the A-site lattice.
Using only shelf storage or a single J-V scan as evidence of operational ion-migration stability.

expected_answer: The first level is solvent compatibility: quantify 3D perovskite solubility, mass loss, roughness, crystallinity, and optical changes after solvent-only exposure, using a deliberately damaging solvent as a positive control. The second level is chemical lineage and spatial localization. Isotopically or elementally labeled large cations, depth profiling, cross-sectional EDS/EELS, and time-resolved composition measurements should determine whether the deposited layer remains on top or exchanges into the 3D lattice. The third level is formation kinetics: in situ absorption/PL/GIWAXS should establish whether a low-dimensional phase forms directly from precursor colloids without first erasing or reconstructing the 3D diffraction/absorption signature. A structurally distinct, continuous bilayer with preserved 3D lattice and minimal cation penetration supports deterministic stacking; loss and regrowth support dissolution-reprecipitation; progressive large-cation penetration and altered near-surface 3D composition support exchange. GIWAXS then determines whether the low-dimensional slabs are oriented for through-plane transport. UPS/KPFM and band-edge measurements must show whether the interface produces a hole-selective cascade/upward bending for n-i-p or the opposite energetics needed for p-i-n. Device transients should confirm that the structural and energetic assignment predicts extraction rather than merely correlating with PCE.
scoring_key_points: Begins with quantitative solvent-only damage and solubility controls to test whether the underlying 3D film is truly orthogonal to the coating solvent.
Uses labeled-species or depth-resolved chemical analysis to distinguish a retained top layer from cation exchange into the 3D absorber.
Uses in situ formation and diffraction/optical evidence to discriminate direct deposition from dissolution-reprecipitation while confirming preservation of the 3D phase.
Links GIWAXS orientation and UPS/KPFM band bending to architecture-specific carrier extraction and validates the link with transport or transient measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Depth analysis may use ToF-SIMS, XPS sputter profiling, nano-XRF, atom-probe methods, or labeled-cation spectroscopy.
Direct formation may be assessed by in situ PL/absorption, GIWAXS, ellipsometry, or synchronized mass/thickness monitoring.
Architecture-specific energetics may be phrased as hole-extraction versus electron-blocking selectivity in regular and inverted stacks.
common_wrong_answers: Treating a new excitonic peak as sufficient proof of an intact, deterministically stacked bilayer.
Assuming that any low-solubility solvent prevents all surface exchange or reconstruction.
Choosing the same low-dimensional phase for n-i-p and p-i-n devices without measuring orientation and interfacial band bending.

expected_answer: Scale-up should start with a solvent-composition map that measures 3D-film dissolution, precursor solubility, viscosity, surface tension, contact angle, evaporation rate, and toxicity/safety constraints. Blade speed, gap, substrate temperature, airflow, and drying profile should be varied with statistically designed experiments, while in situ thickness and scattering measurements identify the region that gives a continuous low-dimensional layer without redissolving the 3D film. Phase number and thickness must be co-optimized because too low an n or excessive thickness can create an extraction barrier, whereas too high an n or incomplete coverage may lose passivation and ion-blocking benefits. GIWAXS, UPS/KPFM, PLQY, transport transients, and spatial mapping should verify orientation, energetics, recombination, and coating uniformity across the full module. Mechanism-specific stability evidence requires matched encapsulation and identical module layouts, followed by thermal/light stress, damp heat, and bias operation. ToF-SIMS or another depth probe should quantify iodide migration into the transport layer; temperature-dependent ionic kinetics should show a higher barrier; spectroscopy should verify crosslinking/polymerization or iodine capture. Subcell-resolved electroluminescence, resistance mapping, and post-mortem analysis should exclude encapsulation leaks and scribe failures as the sole cause of improvement.
scoring_key_points: Builds a solvent and coating-process map that includes 3D-film damage, precursor solubility, wetting, rheology, evaporation, and blade-drying variables.
Co-optimizes low-dimensional phase number, thickness, coverage, orientation, and architecture-specific band alignment rather than transferring the spin-coated optimum directly.
Uses full-area structural, optical, and electrical mapping plus stabilized module output to verify uniformity and transport.
Requires matched encapsulation and mechanism-specific ion-migration/crosslinking evidence, while diagnosing scribe, interconnect, and encapsulation failures separately.
accepted_equivalents: A designed-experiments or response-surface method may be used instead of a full factorial process map.
Ion blocking may be assessed by ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, bias-induced PL/XRF mapping, impedance, or thermally activated drift measurements.
Crosslinking may be verified by Raman, FTIR, solid-state NMR, insolubility, mechanical modulus, or chemical-resistance tests.
