common_wrong_answers: Using the spin-coating solvent ratio, phase number, and thickness unchanged in blade coating without re-establishing the drying and wetting window.
Attributing better damp-heat retention to ion blocking when the treated module simply has superior encapsulation or fewer edge leaks.
Reporting only total module PCE without subcell mapping, interconnect resistance, or spatial failure analysis.

expected_answer: Williamson-Hall microstrain describes local lattice-spacing distributions, whereas sin-squared-psi stress analysis probes the macroscopic in-plane stress state of the constrained film; similar microstrain therefore does not contradict a large difference in global residual stress. Equal initial toughness and similar morphology weaken the claims that the additive simply improved initial adhesion or grain size. A tensile pre-stress increases the cyclic crack-driving force when thermal-expansion mismatch adds alternating stress, so repeated cycling can nucleate cracks and progressively degrade the buried interface even if the initial toughness is identical. The later divergence in toughness, cross-sectional damage, and diffraction intensity is consistent with fatigue-induced delamination and structural disorder; absence of new low-angle or secondary-phase peaks argues against a phase transformation as the primary early cause. A key limitation is that residual stress extraction depends on assumed elastic constants, texture, stress uniformity, and the representativeness of a simplified device-like stack. It should be checked with independent curvature, Raman, synchrotron, or spatial stress measurements and, ideally, tracked through temperature cycles rather than only ex situ at room temperature.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes macroscopic biaxial residual stress from Williamson-Hall microstrain and explains why similar microstrain does not invalidate the stress mechanism.
Uses equal initial toughness and similar grain size/morphology to rule against improved initial adhesion or grain-size effects as the primary explanation.
Explains how tensile pre-stress and thermal-expansion mismatch raise cyclic crack-driving force, producing progressive cracking, delamination, toughness loss, and structural disorder.
Identifies a valid limitation of sin-squared-psi stress inference or ex situ measurement and proposes an independent or in-cycle validation.
accepted_equivalents: Macroscopic stress may be described as film-average residual stress, while microstrain is a distribution of local lattice distortions/coherent-domain effects.
Crack-driving force may be discussed using energy-release rate, stress-intensity range, fatigue threshold, or accumulated interfacial damage.
Independent validation may use wafer curvature, Raman mapping, digital image correlation, synchrotron XRD, or temperature-dependent diffraction.
common_wrong_answers: Treating Williamson-Hall microstrain and macroscopic residual stress as the same quantity.
Claiming that higher initial interfacial toughness caused the improved cycling despite the stated equality before cycling.
Attributing diffraction-intensity loss directly to a new chemical phase without evidence of new phase peaks or temporal ordering.

expected_answer: The experiment must separate precursor chemistry, precursor access, and external barrier formation. Use matched thermal/vacuum-only, precursor-A-only, co-reactant-only, full-ALD, and physically deposited oxide-cap controls, all with the same temperature and exposure time. Then vary HTL thickness and permeability while keeping its conductivity and energetics as constant as possible; an infiltration mechanism should weaken when precursor transport is blocked and strengthen with controlled access, whereas a top barrier should not require a porous HTL. Depth-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS, cross-sectional TEM/EELS, or isotope-labeled precursor profiling should locate Al-containing species and any PbI2 enrichment specifically near the buried junction rather than only above the electrode or HTL. Optical/electrical localization should use perovskite/HTL half-cells, low-temperature PL, wavelength-resolved TRPL, ELQY-derived nonradiative voltage loss, and impedance or ideality-factor measurements. The infiltration model is supported if the spiro-induced sub-bandgap emission disappears, band-edge recombination dominates, and the reduction in nonradiative voltage loss quantitatively tracks the VOC gain only when precursor access and buried chemical conversion occur. A barrier-only treatment may improve moisture or vacuum stability, but should not reproduce the same immediate buried-interface spectroscopic signature; thermal conditioning alone should likewise fail to generate the chemical and voltage-loss correlations.
scoring_key_points: Use matched full-ALD, single-precursor, thermal/vacuum-only, and external oxide-cap controls.
Vary HTL permeability or thickness to test whether the effect requires precursor transport to the buried junction.
Localize Al/PbI2 chemistry with depth-resolved or cross-sectional analysis rather than detecting only a top oxide.
Require buried-interface spectroscopy and ELQY-derived voltage-loss changes to track the VOC gain quantitatively.
accepted_equivalents: TMA-only exposure as the chemically active precursor control
A dense blocking interlayer, cross-linked HTL, or permeability-matched HTL series as the infiltration control
Angle-resolved XPS, sputter-depth profiling, ToF-SIMS, STEM-EDS/EELS, or labeled-precursor neutron/X-ray methods
QFLS from absolute PL in place of ELQY, provided the nonradiative voltage loss is quantitatively compared with VOC
common_wrong_answers: Treating improved shelf stability by itself as proof of buried-interface passivation
Using only top-view XPS that cannot distinguish a surface oxide from buried precursor penetration
Attributing the VOC gain to reduced bulk defect density despite nearly unchanged photocurrent and no bulk-localized control
Comparing treated and untreated devices without matching ALD temperature, vacuum, and exposure history

expected_answer: First determine whether the new HTL admits a controlled precursor flux. Permeation coupons and depth profiles should measure precursor uptake, reaction depth, and lateral uniformity as functions of HTL thickness, cross-linking, ALD pulse time, temperature, and dose. If the dense HTL blocks access, increasing dose is not automatically acceptable because precursor accumulation can attack the electrode or create uncontrolled surface oxide; the chemically active step should instead be moved to the exposed perovskite surface before HTL deposition, or replaced by a noninfiltrative passivant. The useful process window must produce only a thin, self-limited buried conversion region: excess PbI2, insulating Al2O3, HTL de-doping, contact corrosion, shunting, and series-resistance growth are rejection criteria. Large-area electroluminescence or absolute-PL/QFLS mapping, contact-resistivity and sheet-resistance mapping, cross-sectional chemistry, and local J-V statistics should verify uniform passivation without transport loss. Qualification must then compare encapsulated modules under stabilized MPP in light, heat, humidity, and relevant vacuum/outgassing conditions, using thermal-only and barrier-only controls. Post-assembly infiltration is retained only if buried chemistry is uniform and the voltage/stability gains persist without electrode or transport penalties; pre-HTL treatment is preferred if access is blocked but the same interfacial state can be reproduced; the route is abandoned if the benefit requires an unscalable permeability or a damaging precursor dose.
scoring_key_points: Measure precursor permeability, reaction depth, and lateral uniformity in the dense HTL before selecting the process route.
Define a self-limited dose window that avoids excess PbI2/oxide, HTL de-doping, corrosion, shunts, and series resistance.
Use area-resolved QFLS/EL, contact-resistance, and chemical mapping to verify uniform buried passivation.
Make the post-assembly versus pre-HTL decision from encapsulated module MPPT stability and transport integrity, not initial PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Quartz-crystal microbalance or witness-film uptake measurements combined with depth profiling
Spatial PLQY, luminescence imaging, Suns-VOC, or implied-VOC maps as QFLS uniformity diagnostics
Transmission-line, four-point-probe, impedance, or dark-injection measurements for contact and series resistance
Moving only the TMA-like conversion step before the HTL while applying a benign barrier after assembly
common_wrong_answers: Increasing precursor exposure until a voltage gain appears without checking electrode or HTL damage
Assuming a dense polymer will behave like porous spiro-OMeTAD
Qualifying the process only on small cells or shelf storage
Treating a thicker oxide as universally beneficial even when it blocks charge transport

expected_answer: Build a field-time-temperature-illumination response map rather than selecting a single bias. During poling, track crystallographic orientation, strain, and domain evolution by in situ GIWAXS/XRD or microscopy, while simultaneously monitoring PL peak position and splitting, absorption edge, and spatial luminescence for mixed-halide segregation. Ion accumulation should be quantified by transient current/impedance, Kelvin-probe drift, or depth profiling, with field-polarity reversal and dark relaxation used to test reversibility. A safe window produces a structural state that persists after removing the field but shows no new low-energy PL band, no halide-composition gradient, and no growing ionic hysteresis. The optical and electrical gains must then be validated in the tandem context: EQE/current matching, QFLS and subcell VOC, stabilized MPP, spectral stability, and thermal cycling should be measured on statistically sampled areas. Field uniformity across the top cell and edge-field concentration must also be checked before scale-up. The route is rejected if the gain disappears on relaxation, depends on a segregated low-bandgap phase, worsens current matching, or accelerates bias-light degradation; it advances only if a reproducible structural orientation/scattering or polarization benefit survives coupled light-bias-heat stress without compositional drift.
scoring_key_points: Map field, duration, temperature, and illumination while measuring ferroelastic structure and mixed-halide spectral segregation in situ.
Use polarity reversal, relaxation, and ion-transport diagnostics to separate persistent domain restructuring from ionic accumulation.
Require no low-energy phase, composition gradient, increasing hysteresis, or current-matching penalty after poling.
Validate spatially uniform benefit under tandem EQE/QFLS and stabilized light-bias-heat cycling before scale-up.
accepted_equivalents: Operando micro-PL/Raman mapping together with GIWAXS as a segregation and structure monitor
Bias-stress activation-energy measurements or ToF-SIMS instead of transient ion-current measurements
A reversible AC-conditioning step followed by a lower DC hold as an alternative poling protocol if independently validated
Subcell-selective electroluminescence or luminescence-coupling analysis for tandem voltage/current attribution
common_wrong_answers: Transferring the MAPbI3 field and duration unchanged to a mixed-halide absorber
Using a higher initial JSC as evidence of success without checking spectral phase segregation
Equating persistence after field removal with ferroelasticity even when ionic composition remains redistributed
Testing only isolated top cells and ignoring tandem current matching and coupled operating stress

expected_answer: The reactor must first be operated at controlled methanol and water partial pressures, temperature, photon flux, residence time, and total flow, with calibrated inlet/outlet composition and blank-reactor controls. Rate should be reported per absorbed photon, catalyst area or mass, and Pt amount; varying flow and film geometry should reveal external mass-transfer or vapor-depletion limitations. Continuous GC or GC-MS must quantify H2, formaldehyde, CO, CO2, and other carbon products so that hydrogen production, donor conversion, and carbon balance are tracked rather than inferred from H2 alone. At selected times, operando or interrupted XRD/PL should test the perovskite lattice, while TEM/EDS, XPS, ICP analysis of the film and downstream trap, and contact-sensitive transient spectroscopy should quantify Pt loss, aggregation, oxidation state, and loss of electron extraction. Orthogonal regeneration tests are essential: redeposit Pt without rebuilding the perovskite, wash/desorb products without adding Pt, restore vapor composition, and compare with a fresh film. Recovery only after Pt renewal supports cocatalyst loss/contact failure; recovery after purge or wash supports poisoning; irreversible optical/structural loss supports perovskite degradation. Stability should be demonstrated in replicated long-duration flow runs with steady partial pressures and periodic activity/selectivity checks, not by cumulative batch yield or a short high-rate window.
scoring_key_points: Control and vary vapor partial pressure, flow, residence time, photon flux, and geometry to expose transport limitations.
Measure continuous product selectivity and carbon/hydrogen balance rather than hydrogen alone.
Track perovskite integrity and Pt mass, morphology, oxidation state, and charge-transfer contact during deactivation.
Use selective regeneration tests and replicated long-duration flow MP-like operation before claiming scalable stability.
accepted_equivalents: A differential reactor or low-conversion regime to minimize reactant depletion
Online mass spectrometry instead of GC-MS if quantitatively calibrated
Quartz microbalance, ICP of condensate, or downstream Pt capture as evidence of cocatalyst loss
Operando diffuse-reflectance spectroscopy or transient absorption in place of interrupted PL for contact evolution
common_wrong_answers: Calling preserved XRD alone proof that the catalyst interface remains functional
Attributing the activity loss to perovskite decomposition without measuring Pt retention or contact
Using only a sealed batch reactor where methanol pressure and product buildup change with time
Reporting cumulative hydrogen after catalyst regeneration as uninterrupted operational stability

expected_answer: The carboxyl head can coordinate undercoordinated Sn2+/Pb2+ and reduce Sn oxidation or surface traps, while EDA supplies favorable surface n-type character. Increasing chain length or coverage can also separate the perovskite electronically and chemically from C60, suppressing C60-induced trap formation and moisture/oxygen access; therefore PLQY and VOC may initially improve. The trend should not be assumed monotonic. A very long or densely packed hydrocarbon layer increases tunneling distance, weakens electronic coupling to C60, raises contact resistance, and can reduce FF and eventually JSC even when PLQY remains high. The mechanisms should be resolved with XPS/FTIR for carboxylate-metal bonding and Sn4+ fraction, UPS/KPFM for Fermi-level and work-function shifts, and PLQY plus illumination-side-dependent TRPL before and after C60 deposition for interface-specific recombination. Electron-only devices, contact-resistivity measurements, impedance, and temperature-dependent transport should identify a tunneling barrier. GIWAXS/XRD and microscopy should rule out a low-dimensional bulk phase or morphology change. A chain-length-by-dose matrix is needed because sparse long chains and dense short chains may produce similar nominal carbon content but different spacing and resistance. The optimum is where C60-induced recombination and oxidation are minimized without a measurable extraction or series-resistance penalty.
scoring_key_points: Link the carboxyl head to Sn/Pb coordination and reduced surface oxidation/traps, with EDA-related surface doping retained.
Predict initial recombination/VOC improvement from C60 separation but a long-chain/high-coverage transport penalty.
Use XPS/FTIR, UPS/KPFM, and C60-side versus glass-side PLQY/TRPL to separate chemistry, energetics, and interface recombination.
Use contact-resistance/electron-only transport plus structural controls and a chain-length-dose matrix to locate the optimum.
accepted_equivalents: Metal-carboxylate coordination or Lewis-base passivation of undercoordinated B-site cations
Thermionic/tunneling barrier, reduced wave-function overlap, or increased electron-transfer distance
Time-resolved microwave conductivity or transient photovoltage/current as supporting transport diagnostics
Transient reflection, grazing-incidence scattering, or cross-sectional spectroscopy to rule out bulk-phase formation
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the longest ligand must provide the best device because it is most hydrophobic
Using higher PLQY alone to claim better device extraction
Assigning all VOC change to surface passivation without measuring energy-level movement
Ignoring chain coverage and testing only one concentration per ligand

expected_answer: Begin with spatially resolved diagnostics rather than another champion pixel. Map electroluminescence, absolute PL/QFLS, Kelvin-probe potential, and local J-V or contact resistance across the Pb-Sn subcell before and after C60. Chemical mapping of ligand carbon/carboxylate signal and Sn4+/Sn2+ ratio should be correlated with these maps; nonuniform chemistry should produce local QFLS or VOC loss, whereas uniformly high QFLS with low FF points more strongly to a transport barrier. A ligand dose, drying, and annealing process window must be established for the large-area coating, including solvent orthogonality, edge accumulation, C60 coverage/nucleation, and sheet/contact resistance. Electron-only structures and temperature-dependent resistance can confirm excessive tunneling distance. The tandem must then be decomposed optically and electrically using subcell EQE/current matching, filtered-light tests, subcell luminescence, and comparison with the same treated NBG single junction. Early decay may arise from NBG interface chemistry or from tandem-specific near-UV filtering/current imbalance. Encapsulated stabilized-MPP testing under light, heat, and controlled humidity must use the same electrode/contact system as the performance device, or explicitly disclose any Cu-versus-Ag change. Scale-up proceeds only if coverage and work function are uniform, Sn oxidation remains suppressed, contact resistance stays below a predefined limit, current matching is preserved, and the benefit is reproducible across modules and stress conditions.
scoring_key_points: Correlate area-resolved QFLS/EL, work function, ligand chemistry, Sn oxidation, and contact resistance.
Establish a large-area dose/drying/annealing window that avoids edge accumulation, C60-contact defects, and tunneling resistance.
Separate NBG-interface failure from tandem current-matching or spectral effects with subcell-selective measurements and controls.
Require encapsulated stabilized-MPP replication with protocol-matched electrodes before scale-up.
accepted_equivalents: Photoluminescence imaging, Suns-VOC mapping, or hyperspectral luminescence in place of absolute-QFLS maps
Nano-XPS, ToF-SIMS, infrared mapping, or Raman/chemical imaging for ligand and oxidation uniformity
Transmission-line measurements, impedance mapping, dark injection, or electron-only devices for interface resistance
Bias-light or spectral-filter decomposition of tandem subcell behavior
common_wrong_answers: Averaging the module result and ignoring spatially localized low-FF regions
Increasing ligand dose to improve stability without checking tunneling/contact resistance
Attributing all early tandem decay to the Pb-Sn subcell without subcell-selective tests
Comparing stability devices with a different electrode system as though the protocols were identical

expected_answer: The process should be controlled by an integrated moisture-temperature exposure, not by nominal relative humidity alone. Humidity, temperature, residence time, gas-flow uniformity, film thickness, and texture-dependent diffusion length jointly determine whether the buried framework converts before the already formed perovskite degrades. The first stage should therefore be a deliberately short, high-transport step, terminated when an endpoint metric indicates that the buried precursor or residual PbI2 has fallen below a defined threshold. A rapid purge followed by a drier and typically lower-temperature stage should then remove the water-assisted kinetic driving force, suppress volatile-organic loss, and allow residual PbI2 or imperfect crystallites to recrystallize without extended humid exposure. Scale-up qualification must use wafer maps rather than center-point measurements. A minimum package includes phase-sensitive mapping such as XRD or optical signatures calibrated to XRD, representative cross-sectional or depth-composition measurements to verify buried conversion, and PL or quasi-Fermi-level-splitting mapping to detect nonradiative hot spots. Completed tandem devices should be checked for spatially resolved yield, fill factor, V_OC, current matching, and damp-heat or light-soak stability. The recipe must be re-optimized when texture, thickness, gas transport, or deposition route changes; a fixed coupon time cannot be assumed transferable.
scoring_key_points: Controls the coupled humidity-temperature-time dose together with gas flow, film thickness, and texture-dependent diffusion length.
Uses a buried-conversion endpoint to trigger rapid drying or purging and a lower-damage second stage rather than a fixed high-humidity dwell.
Requires wafer-scale phase, depth-composition, and PL/QFLS uniformity mapping to detect incomplete conversion and recombination hot spots.
Validates transfer using tandem-device yield, FF/V_OC/current matching, and accelerated stability, with re-optimization for changed geometry or deposition routes.
accepted_equivalents: A moisture-dose or water-activity-time-temperature process window
Model-predictive or feedback control based on an optical or diffraction endpoint
Representative destructive depth profiling combined with nondestructive full-wafer mapping
common_wrong_answers: Copies one coupon annealing time and RH value without accounting for spatial nonuniformity or diffusion length.
Maximizes humidity to force complete conversion and ignores decomposition during overexposure.
Qualifies only surface morphology or average XRD and does not verify the buried interface.
Uses initial efficiency alone and omits yield, spatial uniformity, and accelerated stability.

expected_answer: The wavelength dependence primarily diagnoses vertical heterogeneity. Blue excitation is absorbed close to the illuminated surface, so the initial carrier distribution overlaps strongly with surface recombination sites. Carriers then both recombine and diffuse into the film, producing a rapid early PL loss. Red excitation generates carriers more deeply and therefore weights the bulk more strongly. If surface passivation suppresses the blue-red difference, that is strong evidence that a high front-surface recombination velocity, rather than a change in intrinsic bulk recombination order, contributed to the fast shallow-excitation decay. The region-of-interest dependence diagnoses lateral heterogeneity: enlarging the sampled area mixes domains with different local lifetimes or photon-escape conditions, broadening the rate distribution and lowering beta. The preferred analysis is a global diffusion-recombination model using the wavelength-dependent generation profile, a common diffusion coefficient and bulk recombination term, and separate boundary recombination velocities for the two surfaces. Spatial FLIM or local TRPL can constrain the lateral lifetime distribution. A stretched exponential may summarize distributed kinetics, but beta is descriptive rather than a unique microscopic identifier; arbitrary biexponential lifetimes should not be labeled as distinct traps or layers unless independent evidence supports those assignments.
scoring_key_points: Attributes the faster shallow-excitation decay to near-surface generation coupled to surface recombination and carrier diffusion.
Uses the reduced wavelength dependence after passivation as evidence for a surface-recombination contribution.
Interprets the decreasing beta at larger ROI as averaging over greater lateral heterogeneity.
Proposes a global depth-dependent diffusion/SRV model and treats stretched or biexponential fit parameters as non-unique without independent constraints.
accepted_equivalents: Front-surface versus bulk weighting by different optical penetration depths
A globally constrained PDE or rate-equation model with depth-dependent generation and two surface boundary conditions
A distribution-of-rates model constrained by FLIM instead of a stretched exponential
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the faster blue-excited decay to Auger or bimolecular recombination despite the stated low-injection regime.
Interprets two fitted exponentials as direct measurements of surface and bulk lifetimes without a transport model.
Uses beta as a unique fingerprint of one trap species or one microstructural defect.
Ignores ROI size and treats a macroscopic TRPL decay as spatially homogeneous.

expected_answer: The transfer should begin with matched solvent-only controls, untreated devices, and iodide treatments using more than one counter-cation. A non-iodide salt or cation-matched control helps separate the iodide effect from generic ionic strength, solvent exposure, or cation chemistry. Surface-sensitive composition and chemical-state measurements should verify iodide enrichment while checking for residual metal species, oxidation, or reactions with the transport layer. The electronic consequences must be evaluated before aging: PLQE or QFLS, V_OC, FF, series resistance, hysteresis, dark current, and extraction-sensitive measurements should reveal whether the treatment passivates defects without creating an insulating layer, unfavorable band alignment, or a mobile-ion reservoir. Stability testing must be performed on complete devices under combined illumination, electrical bias or maximum-power-point tracking, heat, and controlled humidity, with operando optical absorption or XRD used to follow phase fraction. Ion-migration or interfacial accumulation should also be monitored. The treatment is disqualified if it lowers initial performance, increases hysteresis or ionic drift, reacts with contacts, produces a benefit only in dark model-film tests, or fails to preserve power output and phase integrity under realistic stress. A slower isolated-film JMAK rate is necessary evidence, not sufficient device validation.
scoring_key_points: Uses untreated, solvent-only, counter-cation, and non-iodide or cation-matched controls to isolate the chemical origin of the effect.
Verifies surface chemistry and checks band alignment, extraction, recombination, resistance, hysteresis, and ion-migration consequences in the full stack.
Tests complete devices operando under light, bias or MPP, heat, and humidity while tracking both power output and phase evolution.
Rejects the treatment if it harms initial performance, contacts, or ionic stability, or if the model-film benefit does not persist under operating stress.
accepted_equivalents: UPS/KPFM or contact-selective spectroscopy for interface energetics
Operando XRD, GIWAXS, or calibrated optical phase-fraction tracking
Transient ion-drift, impedance, or bias-stress diagnostics for mobile-ion effects
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that a fivefold slower model-film transformation guarantees a fivefold longer device lifetime.
Tests only dark humidity exposure and omits illumination, bias, temperature, and contact interactions.
Measures only TRPL and ignores extraction, energetics, hysteresis, and ion migration.
Attributes all benefits to iodide without solvent, cation, or non-iodide controls.

expected_answer: The three functions must be separated with matched controls rather than inferred from correlated properties. To isolate solvent orthogonality, compare the normal solution-deposited QD process with a solvent-free or transfer-deposited QD layer, or chemically crosslink/protect the otherwise soluble control HTM without changing its frontier levels. Cross-sectional microscopy, thickness mapping, and AFM before and after QD coating should verify whether the underlying HTM is removed or roughened. If the target HTM loses most of its EQE advantage when all HTMs are preserved equally, solvent resistance was a dominant contributor; if the advantage remains, solvent integrity alone is insufficient. To isolate injection and transport, independently tune the controls' energy alignment with a very thin dipole/interlayer or controlled p-doping, and adjust HTM thickness so that series resistance and hole-only current are matched. UPS, SCLC or conductivity, transient electroluminescence, capacitance, and charge-balance measurements should then be compared at equal interfacial morphology. If matching HOMO offset and bulk hole conductance reproduces the turn-on voltage, recombination-zone position, and EQE, transport is causal. If EQE remains lower despite matched injection, another mechanism dominates. Excessively shallow alignment or very high mobility can also overinject holes; a shift toward charge imbalance and stronger efficiency roll-off would falsify the assumption that more hole current is always beneficial. Passivation should be tested by placing an ultrathin layer of the candidate molecule, or a nonconducting analogue retaining the same binding groups, at the QD interface while using a common bulk HTM. Conversely, a structural analogue with matched HOMO/mobility but without the proposed passivating group should be tested. Absolute PLQY, bias-dependent PL/EL, trap-filled-limit measurements, transient absorption, and nonradiative loss should improve at unchanged film integrity and hole conductance if passivation is independently effective. A longer TRPL alone is not decisive because slower extraction can also lengthen lifetime; PLQY and device charge balance must agree. A factorial experiment combining preserved/damaged HTM films, matched/unmatched injection, and passivating/nonpassivating interfaces permits variance or mediation analysis. The mechanism assignment is credible only when the targeted perturbation selectively removes or restores the corresponding performance contribution.
scoring_key_points: Uses a solvent-free, transferred, crosslinked, or protected control to isolate whether QD-ink exposure destroys the underlying HTM.
Independently matches HOMO alignment, HTM thickness, and hole conductance to test injection/transport while monitoring charge balance and roll-off.
Uses interface-only passivating layers or nonpassivating structural analogues plus PLQY/trap diagnostics to separate passivation from transport.
States explicit supporting and falsifying outcomes and rejects TRPL lifetime alone as a unique passivation indicator.
accepted_equivalents: Dry transfer, orthogonal-vapor deposition, a sacrificial barrier, or crosslinking are acceptable solvent-integrity controls.
Transient EL, impedance, single-carrier devices, recombination-zone mapping, or charge-balance analysis are acceptable injection diagnostics.
Absolute PLQY/QY, transient absorption, SCLC trap density, deep-level spectroscopy, or bias-dependent luminescence are acceptable passivation readouts.
common_wrong_answers: Lists UPS, AFM, SCLC, and TRPL without perturbations that isolate the three causal functions.
Attributes the entire EQE increase to the shallowest HOMO or highest mobility without testing charge balance.
Treats a longer PL lifetime as conclusive proof of passivation even if carrier extraction has changed.

expected_answer: Blue transfer requires re-optimizing the energetic and excitonic landscape because the wider-bandgap QD generally has a deeper valence level and greater sensitivity to interfacial quenching. The HTM HOMO should minimize the hole-injection barrier without driving severe hole overinjection relative to electron supply. Its optical gap and triplet/excited-state energies must be high enough to confine excitons in the blue QD and avoid energy transfer or exciplex formation. Thus, a still shallower HOMO or higher mobility can increase charge imbalance, move the recombination zone toward a damaging interface, enhance Auger/polaron quenching, or increase electron leakage rather than raising EQE. Molecular screening should retain solvent orthogonality and film compactness while increasing morphological robustness: appropriate glass-transition temperature, resistance to Joule-heating-induced crystallization, and possibly crosslinkable or higher-cohesion motifs. Substituent tuning should adjust HOMO and interfacial Lewis-base strength separately so that ligand stripping, halide exchange, or overly strong binding to blue QDs is avoided. Direct surface spectroscopy or controlled ligand-exchange studies should verify the interfacial chemistry instead of relying only on PL lifetime. At the device level, HTM thickness, electron-transport layer, injection layers, and interfacial dipoles should be co-optimized for balanced current. Hole-only/electron-only currents, transient EL, recombination-zone mapping, bias-dependent PL, EQE-current-density roll-off, spectral shift, and thermal imaging should determine whether the blue loss is caused by injection barriers, imbalance, exciton quenching, or heating. Controls with matched film morphology and solvent exposure are required. Reliability claims need encapsulated operational testing under constant current and constant initial luminance at several brightness levels, with T50 or extrapolation based on a disclosed acceleration law. Temperature, humidity, and pulsed-display duty cycle should be included, while monitoring voltage rise, spectral drift, dark spots, leakage, and interfacial chemical change. A transferable platform must show reproducible large-area blue EQE, limited roll-off, stable color, and a lifetime increase by orders of magnitude over a minutes-scale ambient screen; a single peak-EQE demonstration is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes HOMO alignment, excited-state confinement, and charge balance for the deeper-valence, wider-bandgap blue emitter.
Explains how excessive hole mobility or an overly shallow HOMO can cause overinjection, recombination-zone shift, leakage, or high-current quenching.
Requires solvent/morphology robustness and direct validation that interfacial binding passivates rather than strips ligands or quenches blue QDs.
Demands encapsulated, brightness-dependent operational lifetime, roll-off, spectral, thermal, and reproducibility evidence beyond minutes-scale ambient testing.
accepted_equivalents: High triplet energy, sufficiently wide optical gap, or explicit exciton-blocking ability are equivalent confinement criteria.
Crosslinking, higher Tg, stronger amorphous stability, or a robust intermolecular network are acceptable morphology-stability strategies.
Constant-current, constant-luminance, pulsed-duty, or accelerated multi-luminance lifetime protocols are acceptable if conditions and extrapolation are disclosed.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes the green-device HOMO and HTM thickness are automatically optimal for blue QDs.
Treats maximum hole mobility as an unconditionally beneficial design target and ignores electron-hole balance.
Uses only peak EQE or an unencapsulated minutes-scale test to claim display-level operational stability.

expected_answer: The first distinction is spatial. Angle-resolved XPS/UPS, sputter- or cluster-depth profiling, cross-sectional ToF-SIMS, and Kelvin-probe potential mapping should determine whether the donor and Fermi-level shift are confined to the top few nanometers, penetrate grain boundaries, or fill the bulk. Bulk doping should give a roughly uniform dopant/charge profile and survive removal of the top surface; a surface-compensation layer should decay strongly with depth and be altered by rinsing or gentle etching. Thickness scaling is especially diagnostic. For uniform bulk doping, the Hall-derived volume carrier density and conductivity should be approximately thickness-independent once morphology is controlled. For a fixed compensating sheet charge at the surface or grain boundaries, the apparent change in volume carrier density should scale approximately as inverse thickness, and the effect should saturate when the available surface charge is filled. Grain-size variation at fixed thickness can further separate external-surface from grain-boundary contributions: a grain-boundary mechanism should grow with internal interfacial area. Contact geometry must then be changed. Compare van der Pauw/four-probe films, bottom-contact and top-contact transistors, vertical diodes with the donor placed either below or above the absorber, and devices in which the treated surface contacts an inert layer rather than the electron-transport layer. A contact-modification mechanism should strongly change transfer length, contact resistance, band bending, and perovskite/ETL recombination while leaving the bulk four-probe transport less affected. A genuine bulk carrier-density change should appear in contact-independent transport. Charge transfer and passivation must also be separated. Donor oxidation, EPR or NMR evidence of chemical dissociation, Seebeck sign/magnitude, and a systematic Fermi-level shift support electronic compensation. Trap passivation should lower trap-assisted recombination and subgap-state density even when the equilibrium free-carrier density is held constant. Absolute PLQY/QFLS, deep-level or SCLC measurements, and temperature-dependent Hall data can test this. Unchanged XRD only excludes large average structural conversion; it does not prove bulk doping. The most defensible conclusion would combine chemical oxidation evidence with the predicted depth, thickness, grain-size, and contact dependencies.
scoring_key_points: Uses depth-resolved composition and electronic-potential measurements to distinguish a top-surface layer, grain-boundary penetration, and uniform bulk doping.
Predicts thickness and grain-size scaling: bulk carrier density is thickness-independent, whereas fixed interfacial compensation scales with surface or grain-boundary area.
Changes contact geometry and treatment location to separate bulk transport from electron-contact or band-alignment effects.
Separates donor charge transfer from trap passivation using donor oxidation/Fermi-level evidence together with trap and recombination measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Angle-resolved photoemission, gentle depth profiling, atom-probe analysis, or cross-sectional chemical imaging are acceptable spatial tests.
Surface removal, capping-before-treatment, opposite-side treatment, or film-thickness scaling are acceptable localization perturbations.
Seebeck, EPR, NMR, oxidized-dopant spectroscopy, or quantitative work-function measurements may establish charge transfer.
common_wrong_answers: Calls the process bulk doping solely because Hall analysis reports a lower volume hole density.
Uses unchanged XRD as proof that the donor is uniformly incorporated without altering the lattice.
Attributes the device improvement entirely to carrier compensation without testing contact resistance or interface recombination.

expected_answer: Optimization must target a carrier-density window, not the minimum possible hole density. A dose matrix should vary concentration, soak time, solvent activity, drying, post-anneal, absorber thickness, and grain size. Hall/Seebeck, conductivity, mobility, work function, and capacitance should identify the point at which intrinsic p-type self-doping is compensated without type inversion or a large loss of majority-carrier transport. Because a post-treatment may provide a nearly fixed interfacial dose, the required concentration and time must be recalibrated for a micrometer absorber; surface saturation cannot be assumed to control the entire volume. The electronic stopping criteria are a plateau or reversal in voltage/current gain, rising series or contact resistance, falling fill factor, reduced vertical conductivity, a mobility collapse, or a new low-frequency capacitive/interfacial feature. Chemical and morphological criteria include dopant aggregation, a continuous organic overlayer, impaired wetting or deposition of the electron-transport layer, new deep states, and nonuniform surface coverage. ToF-SIMS/XPS mapping, AFM, contact-angle measurements, transfer-length analysis, and cross-sectional microscopy should be paired with trap/recombination and carrier-density measurements. The optimum is the lowest dose that reaches the desired compensation while keeping the overlayer discontinuous or electronically transparent. For scale-up, treatment delivery must control areal dose and solvent residence time across the module. Slot-die or spray parameters, drying gradients, edge accumulation, and batch-to-batch dopant oxidation should be monitored with work-function, PL, sheet-resistance, or hyperspectral maps. A small-cell champion at one concentration is not transferable if spatial tails produce locally blocking regions. Reliability testing should combine light, heat, electrical bias or maximum-power operation, oxygen, and moisture because the dopant and Sn-rich host can both oxidize. Depth-resolved chemistry after aging should distinguish dopant loss, further oxidation, Sn oxidation, and migration into adjacent layers. Encapsulated module tests should track voltage rise, fill factor, leakage, spectral response, and spatial electroluminescence. Precursor incorporation should be treated as a separate process because it may disturb crystallization and distribute the molecule in the bulk; it is not automatically equivalent to surface treatment. Transfer succeeds only within a reproducible process window that preserves compensation, contact selectivity, and stability under coupled stress.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes to a target carrier-density and mobility window rather than maximizing compensation or dopant concentration.
Defines electronic and chemical stopping criteria for surface accumulation, contact blocking, mobility loss, aggregation, or new deep states.
Recalibrates areal dose, penetration, drying, and spatial uniformity for thick absorbers and large-area coating.
Uses coupled light-heat-bias-oxygen/moisture aging with depth-resolved postmortem analysis and module-level spatial metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Dose may be expressed through concentration-time product, adsorbed areal density, or integrated solvent exposure if calibrated.
Transfer-length, impedance, vertical single-carrier devices, or contact-resistance extraction are acceptable blocking-layer diagnostics.
Maximum-power tracking, constant-bias light soak, damp-heat under bias, or thermal cycling in controlled oxygen are acceptable coupled-stress protocols.
common_wrong_answers: Selects the highest dose because it produces the lowest Hall hole density.
Ignores the distinction between a surface treatment and uniform bulk doping in a thick absorber.
Qualifies only initial PCE and does not test dopant oxidation, contact blocking, or large-area dose nonuniformity.

expected_answer: The starting state must first be established with the lowest possible probe dose. Dark-equilibrated absorption and spatial PL maps, collected over multiple synthesis routes and storage histories, should test whether low-energy domains exist before deliberate stress. Persistent compositional domains in the dark, strong dependence on precursor route or annealing history, and direct low-dose chemical heterogeneity support intrinsic immiscibility or site preference rather than a purely photoinduced process. For reversible photoinduced segregation, illumination-intensity and time-dependent PL/absorption should show growth of a low-bandgap emissive population with conserved overall halide content. The signal should substantially reverse after a reproducible dark-recovery time, and repeated light-dark cycles should be possible without cumulative stoichiometric loss. Spatially resolved measurements should show domain formation and dissolution rather than permanent material removal. Temperature and electric-field dependence may change kinetics but should not produce irreversible mass loss under benign conditions. Halide expulsion requires evidence beyond spectral segregation. It should produce incomplete recovery, cumulative changes over cycles, a measurable loss or redistribution of halide, halide-deficient or Pb-rich products, and possibly molecular iodine/bromine or redox products. Dependence on oxygen, redox-active solvent, carrier extraction, or hole accumulation would support a redox-coupled pathway. Time-resolved mass spectrometry, halogen trapping, XPS/chemical analysis, and mass-balance measurements should test whether iodide is lost before bromide rather than merely concentrated in low-bandgap domains. Probe artifacts must be treated as an experimental variable. XRD, electron beams, and ToF-SIMS should be repeated over a dose series with beam-off controls, rastered versus stationary acquisition, cryogenic or low-dose conditions, and comparison to non-destructive optical measurements. A feature that appears only after the characterization beam, grows with probe dose, or differs between first and subsequent scans cannot be assigned confidently to the unstressed material. The decision tree should therefore classify the phenomenon only when pre-stress state, reversibility, mass conservation, environmental dependence, and probe-dose dependence agree.
scoring_key_points: Establishes a low-dose dark baseline and uses synthesis/history dependence to identify pre-existing immiscibility or site preference.
Defines reversible photo-segregation by light-dose-dependent spectral/domain formation, substantial dark recovery, and conserved halide content.
Defines redox-coupled expulsion by cumulative irreversibility, chemical or mass loss, degradation products, and environmental/carrier dependence.
Uses explicit X-ray/electron/ion-beam dose controls and non-destructive cross-checks to exclude probe-induced segregation.
accepted_equivalents: Spatial PL, hyperspectral microscopy, transient absorption, or cathodoluminescence may be used to track domain formation if beam effects are controlled.
Halogen traps, evolved-gas analysis, quartz-crystal mass sensing, XPS stoichiometry, or isotope balance are acceptable expulsion tests.
Beam-dose series, cryogenic acquisition, repeated first-scan comparison, or optical-before/after characterization are acceptable artifact controls.
common_wrong_answers: Calls every red-shifted PL feature photoinduced segregation without checking whether heterogeneity existed in the dark.
Equates partial dark recovery with proof that no irreversible halide loss occurred.
Uses XRD or ToF-SIMS maps as artifact-free ground truth without controlling irradiation dose.

expected_answer: The relevant design variable is competitive and kinetic coordination, not maximum binding strength. An additive weaker than DMSO may fail to displace the solvent from PbI2 and therefore have little influence on precursor speciation or nucleation, although it can still remain in the film and passivate defects. A moderately stronger ligand can replace part of the solvent coordination shell, alter intermediate structure, raise the nucleation barrier so that fewer nuclei form, and then release or reorganize during annealing quickly enough to permit complete perovskite conversion. If binding is too strong, concentration is too high, or ligand exchange is too slow, the additive can sequester Pb, stabilize a persistent adduct, retard organic-cation insertion/desolvation, and leave residual intermediate or PbI2. The resulting morphology can therefore be nonmonotonic with coordinating strength. The useful window should be mapped over additive concentration, solvent donor strength or DMSO fraction, water content, annealing temperature/rate, and drying rate. Solution NMR, FTIR/Raman, absorption, or calorimetry can quantify competitive complexation and ligand exchange. In situ CLSFM or another nucleation-imaging method should measure nucleus density, while in situ UV-vis and GIWAXS/XRD should resolve intermediate formation, conversion onset, phase-completion time, and residual phases. A beneficial condition should delay or reduce nucleation yet complete conversion rapidly enough to avoid persistent adducts. Growth regulation must be separated from passivation by timing and location controls. Add the molecule to the PbI2 precursor, introduce it only with the organic-salt step, and apply it after the film has fully crystallized. A post-treatment that lowers trap density or increases PLQY without changing grain size, texture, or in situ conversion kinetics demonstrates a passivation-only contribution. Conversely, early-stage changes in nucleation and intermediate phases that persist even when final trap density is matched support genuine growth regulation. Finally, morphology-matched and trap-matched controls should be compared using SEM/GIWAXS, SCLC or subgap-state spectroscopy, absolute PLQY/QFLS, TRPL, XPS for additive retention/residual solvent, and device voltage/fill factor. The optimum is the condition that completes the desired phase, improves morphology and nonradiative loss, and does not create an insulating residue; stronger coordination beyond that point is harmful rather than beneficial.
scoring_key_points: Explains the solvent-competition threshold and the nonmonotonic transition from weak/no growth control to useful intermediate regulation to over-stabilized adducts.
Maps concentration, solvent strength/composition, drying, and annealing while using in situ nucleation and phase-conversion measurements.
Uses precursor-stage, conversion-stage, and post-deposition timing controls to separate growth regulation from passivation.
Requires complete phase conversion plus morphology, trap, recombination, residue, and device checks to define the beneficial window.
accepted_equivalents: Ligand-exchange kinetics, coordination lifetime, precursor speciation, or a binding-energy margin relative to the solvent are acceptable formulations.
In situ GIWAXS/XRD, UV-vis, fluorescence microscopy, light scattering, or calorimetry may be combined to track nucleation and conversion.
Surface post-treatment, delayed additive injection, or orthogonal passivator controls are acceptable ways to isolate post-growth passivation.
common_wrong_answers: States that the strongest Pb-binding molecule must always produce the largest grains and best device.
Uses final SEM and trap density alone without measuring precursor competition, nucleation, or conversion kinetics.
Attributes all performance gains to grain enlargement and ignores a passivation-only pathway.

expected_answer: The additive must be evaluated relative to the actual solvent coordination and process timescale. Replacing DMSO with NMP or another donor changes PbI2 speciation, ligand-exchange thermodynamics, viscosity, evaporation, and the duration for which complexes remain mobile. An additive that barely outcompetes DMSO may not displace a stronger or longer-lived solvent, whereas one that worked at spin-coating timescales may over-stabilize an intermediate during slow blade drying. Therefore the portable descriptors are a competitive coordination margin and exchange/conversion kinetics relative to drying and annealing, not a single gas-phase or dilute-solution binding energy. A solvent-additive matrix should measure precursor speciation and exchange by NMR, FTIR/Raman, UV-vis, calorimetry, or mass spectrometry over realistic concentrations and temperatures. Candidate solubility, aggregation, redox activity, volatility, and chemical stability must also be checked. In situ GIWAXS/optical monitoring during blade coating should track solvent-complex intermediates, supersaturation, nucleation position and density, conversion completion, and texture as functions of coating speed, wet-film thickness, substrate temperature, gas-knife flow, humidity, and annealing profile. The useful additive window may require changing loading or using staged addition because the wet-film residence time is much longer than in spin coating. Large-area validation must be spatial. Across-web maps of thickness, composition, residual solvent/additive, phase, grain size/orientation, PLQY or QFLS, trap density proxies, and sheet/vertical conductivity should be correlated with local device performance. Edge accumulation and center-to-edge drying gradients must be quantified; a high average performance with defective tails is not acceptable. Post-deposition XPS/ToF-SIMS or thermal-desorption analysis should verify that the intended passivator remains while the coordinating solvent and harmful adduct are removed. The stability program should compare no-additive, original-process, and recalibrated-process films under humidity, heat, illumination, and maximum-power operation. Residual additive/adduct may either passivate defects or accelerate ion migration, moisture uptake, and interfacial reactions, so aging must track chemical redistribution, phase change, nonradiative loss, and module-area uniformity. Successful transfer requires complete conversion, reproducible morphology and passivation across the coating width, no persistent solvent complex, and stable devices; matching the original additive concentration or calculated binding energy is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Replaces absolute binding energy with solvent-relative coordination and ligand-exchange/conversion timescales referenced to blade-coating drying.
Builds a solvent-additive-process matrix with realistic precursor speciation and in situ nucleation/intermediate/conversion measurements.
Requires spatially resolved large-area maps for drying gradients, residual solvent/additive, phase, morphology, electronic quality, and device tails.
Validates complete conversion and retained passivation under coupled environmental/operational aging while checking redistribution and ionic/interfacial failure.
accepted_equivalents: A coordination-energy difference, equilibrium constant ratio, donor-number comparison, or ligand-exchange rate ratio relative to drying is acceptable.
Slot-die, meniscus, or blade-coating process variables may replace one another if wet-film residence, thermal history, and mass transfer are treated explicitly.
Spatial PL/QFLS, hyperspectral reflectance, XRD/GIWAXS mapping, ToF-SIMS, thermal desorption, or equivalent inline/offline maps are acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Reuses the spin-coating additive concentration because the molecular structure and PbI2 are unchanged.
Ranks candidates only by isolated additive-PbI2 binding energy and ignores the new solvent and drying kinetics.
Validates only center-area small cells and does not measure edge accumulation, residual adducts, or distribution tails.

expected_answer: No. Making the gap direct removes a momentum-conservation penalty, but it does not repair the other microscopic properties that determine photovoltaic quality. First, a direct gap can still have a weak absorption onset if the band-edge transition has low oscillator strength because of orbital character or symmetry; the absorber would then require greater thickness to harvest near-gap photons, increasing collection demands. Second, hole masses above 1 m0 imply low band dispersion and, all else equal, reduced mobility and diffusion, so photocarriers are less likely to reach selective contacts before recombining. Third, nonbonding N-2p and localized transition-metal-d band edges do not reproduce the antibonding, highly dispersive, spin-orbit-modified band-edge chemistry associated with lead-halide defect tolerance. A low-energy nitrogen vacancy with a deep transition level can therefore be abundant and act as a Shockley-Read-Hall recombination center. The direct-gap change is beneficial but not decisive: advancement would require a strong allowed absorption onset, small and reasonably balanced carrier masses, and dominant intrinsic defects that are shallow or energetically costly to form.
scoring_key_points: A direct gap removes momentum mismatch but does not guarantee a strong, symmetry-allowed near-edge transition or steep absorption onset.
Heavy, weakly dispersive holes predict poor transport and more stringent thickness/collection requirements.
Nonbonding N-2p and localized d-derived band edges do not reproduce lead-halide antibonding/SOC-enabled defect-tolerant chemistry.
A low-formation-energy deep nitrogen-vacancy level would promote Shockley-Read-Hall recombination, so several properties must improve together.
accepted_equivalents: Oscillator strength, dipole matrix element, or selection-rule arguments may be used for the optical point.
Trap-assisted recombination, deep-center recombination, or Shockley-Read-Hall recombination are equivalent descriptions.
Low mobility, short diffusion length, or poor collection caused by large effective mass are acceptable transport formulations.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring the material suitable solely because the bandgap is direct and close to the tandem optimum.
Discussing only the numerical bandgap while ignoring transition strength, effective masses, and defect transition levels.
Assuming a large dielectric constant automatically makes every low-energy defect shallow or harmless.

expected_answer: The student's inference is invalid because steady-state PL intensity is not a stand-alone measure of non-radiative loss. It depends on the absorbed photon flux, film thickness, optical interference, scattering and outcoupling, collection geometry, and whether a contact extracts or quenches carriers. A monocrystal on a charge-selective substrate can therefore emit less while still having fewer traps if carriers are transferred efficiently rather than accumulating radiatively. The longer TRPL components and lower SCLC trap density support reduced trap-assisted recombination in the monocrystal. Faster transient photocurrent is consistent with more efficient extraction, while the longer transient-photovoltage lifetime indicates slower recombination under device-relevant conditions; the higher fill factor is the expected electrical consequence of lower recombination and resistance losses. The PL contrast should be re-evaluated using matched absorbed-photon density and matched thickness/active area, identical substrates and optical geometry, and preferably absolute PL quantum yield in an integrating sphere. Bare-film and contacted-film measurements, together with wavelength-resolved absorptance and calibrated collection, would separate intrinsic radiative efficiency from contact quenching and optical artifacts.
scoring_key_points: Steady-state PL intensity is confounded by absorption, thickness, optics/outcoupling, geometry, and contact-induced extraction or quenching.
Longer TRPL and lower SCLC trap density support fewer trap-assisted losses rather than worse material quality.
Faster TPC, slower TPV recombination, and higher FF form a consistent device-level extraction/recombination chain.
Valid controls include matched absorbed flux/thickness/stack and calibrated absolute PLQY or bare-versus-contacted comparisons.
accepted_equivalents: External PL, internal radiative efficiency, and absolute PLQY may be distinguished using equivalent terminology.
Contact quenching, interfacial charge transfer, or efficient carrier extraction are acceptable explanations for low PL in a contacted film.
Integrating-sphere PLQY, calibrated absorptance, or front/back collection controls are acceptable optical controls.
common_wrong_answers: Equating lower steady-state PL intensity directly with a higher non-radiative recombination rate.
Using the longer TRPL lifetime alone while ignoring extraction, trap-density, and device-transient evidence.
Claiming that high PL is always beneficial even when it results from poor carrier extraction.

expected_answer: The evidence first implicates textured-surface nonconformality together with current mismatch. In a two-terminal tandem, the operating current is limited by the lower-current subcell, so valley thinning can reduce top-cell absorption and create local current deficits even when the top-cell chemistry on planar witnesses is good. The spatially localized electroluminescence dark regions and valley thinning further suggest pinholes, incomplete coverage, local shunts, or recombination-active interfaces; these defects can lower fill factor without causing a proportionate loss in the spatially averaged open-circuit voltage. The interconnecting layer remains a second, independent suspect: parasitic absorption lowers the matched current, whereas inadequate recombination contact, sheet resistance, or sputter damage raises series resistance and depresses FF. The mechanisms can be separated by bias-light subcell EQE, reflectance/absorptance measurements and optical transfer-matrix modeling; PL/EL mapping and cross-sectional compositional microscopy; Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV comparison with measured JV to isolate resistive FF loss; and impedance, contact-resistance, or ICL-thickness studies. Comparing planar, intermediate-texture, and fully textured devices, or replacing only the ICL while holding the absorber constant, provides decisive process perturbations.
scoring_key_points: In a two-terminal tandem, EQE current mismatch makes the lower-current subcell limit tandem Jsc; valley thinning can drive that mismatch.
Localized EL-dark regions plus nonconformal valley coverage indicate pinholes, shunts, or local interface recombination that can reduce FF.
An ICL can cause separate optical-current loss through parasitic absorption and electrical FF loss through resistance, damage, or poor recombination contact.
Use subcell-resolved EQE/optical modeling, spatial luminescence/microscopy, pseudo-JV versus JV, and texture/ICL perturbations to discriminate causes.
accepted_equivalents: Current-limiting subcell, series-connected current matching, or bottleneck-current language is acceptable.
Suns-Voc, implied JV, intensity-dependent Voc, or pseudo-fill-factor analysis may be used to separate recombination from resistance.
TLM, impedance spectroscopy, contact-resistivity extraction, or four-point sheet-resistance measurements are acceptable ICL diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all losses to the perovskite bandgap because the integrated Voc is nearly unchanged.
Treating EQE mismatch as independent of textured-film thickness and optical field distribution.
Blaming the ICL only for series resistance while ignoring its parasitic absorption and process-damage roles.

expected_answer: The ICL must be judged as a multifunctional component, not only as a resistor. It must provide efficient electron-hole recombination or an ohmic interconnection, high optical transmission over the spectrum needed by the silicon bottom cell, low lateral and contact resistance, chemical and solvent compatibility, and protection of the underlying perovskite during subsequent processing. Candidate A should therefore be tested for sputter-induced defect creation, voltage loss, and shunting; Candidate B should be tested for near-infrared parasitic absorption, current-matching loss, thermal creep, delamination, and contact evolution. The electrical and optical contributions should be quantified separately using subcell EQE, transmission/reflectance, contact-resistivity or impedance measurements, Suns-Voc/pseudo-JV, and stabilized tandem MPP. Qualification must then move to large-area devices and modules, measuring uniformity, yield, process throughput, and compatibility with textured surfaces and encapsulation. Finally, IEC-relevant damp heat, thermal cycling, humidity-freeze, UV/light soaking, and prolonged MPP testing should track absolute JV parameters, adhesion, interdiffusion, and localized failure. A slightly more resistive ICL can be commercially superior if it preserves current, causes less process damage, survives qualification, and yields a longer lifetime and lower lifetime-adjusted energy cost.
scoring_key_points: Evaluate recombination/contact function, optical transparency, resistance, chemical compatibility, and damage protection together.
Quantify candidate-specific risks: sputter damage for A versus NIR absorption, softening, and delamination for B.
Use subcell EQE/optics, contact-resistance and pseudo-JV diagnostics, then assess large-area uniformity, yield, and process compatibility.
Require IEC-relevant environmental and MPP durability; lifetime and energy yield can outweigh the lowest initial resistance.
accepted_equivalents: Recombination layer, tunnel/recombination junction, or interconnection contact are acceptable terms for the ICL function.
Accelerated damp heat, thermal cycling, UV, light-soak, humidity-freeze, or equivalent IEC 61215 stress sequences are acceptable.
LCOE, lifetime energy yield, bankability, or warranty-relevant lifetime may be used for the commercial decision metric.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting Candidate A solely because its initial sheet resistance is lower.
Evaluating only cell efficiency without subcell-resolved optical loss, process damage, or module yield.
Treating a short inert-atmosphere aging test as equivalent to IEC-relevant qualification.

expected_answer: No. Suppressing the visible separation between forward and reverse JV scans does not prove that ionic redistribution no longer screens the operating field. The downward MPP current drift and concurrent PL rise show that extraction is still deteriorating and carriers are accumulating under the actual operating condition. Acceptance should require stable current and power during extended MPP tracking, convergence of fast and slow JV scans, disappearance or strong reduction of the coupled current/PL transient after bias steps, and a substantially smaller slow ionic charge density or longer displacement time measured by BACE/CELIV or an equivalent method. The result should also be robust to illumination level, temperature, and bias-history tests and should not merely shift the transient outside the scan window. Materials strategies include reducing the concentration of mobile ionic defects through composition control and defect passivation, raising migration barriers in the bulk and at grain boundaries, and chemically stabilizing interfaces. Device strategies include contacts or interlayers that block ionic accumulation without blocking electronic carriers, reduce interfacial recombination, and maintain a strong extraction field even after partial ionic screening. Long-duration MPP and accelerated aging are needed because ion accumulation can couple to irreversible interface reactions even when short-term hysteresis appears small.
scoring_key_points: Near-zero JV hysteresis is not equivalent to eliminating ionic field screening; MPP current loss plus PL rise proves extraction loss remains.
Acceptance requires stable MPP, fast/slow-scan convergence, suppressed current/PL transients, and reduced slow ionic charge or mobility.
Target mobile-defect concentration and migration pathways through composition, passivation, grain-boundary, and lattice design.
Use ion-blocking/selective interfaces and field-robust device design, then verify under bias, temperature, and long-duration aging.
accepted_equivalents: Reducing ion density, reducing ion mobility, increasing migration activation energy, or preventing interfacial accumulation are acceptable mitigation targets.
Stabilized power output, steady-state efficiency, or prolonged MPPT may be used as the operating-condition acceptance metric.
Interfacial dipole control, ionic blocking layers, or more selective transport layers are acceptable device interventions.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring success solely because forward and reverse scans overlap.
Using only a very fast JV scan that outruns the ions and therefore hides the loss.
Proposing thicker absorbers or higher illumination without addressing field screening and interfacial accumulation.

expected_answer: The most likely failure is over-treatment: a thicker or more continuous low-n quantum-well layer has passivated surface traps and confined carriers, increasing PL intensity and lifetime, but it has also created a high-bandgap, poorly connected barrier to out-of-plane extraction. The broad GIWAXS azimuthal distribution indicates that the quantum wells are not preferentially oriented for vertical transport, and increasing n=1 content strengthens dielectric and quantum confinement relative to higher-n phases. Thus, a stronger PQW diffraction peak is not automatically beneficial. The mechanisms should be separated structurally and electrically. GIWAXS azimuthal analysis and phase-resolved XRD should quantify orientation and n distribution; cross-sectional HRTEM or related microscopy should measure layer thickness and whether PQWs occupy only surfaces/grain boundaries or form a continuous cap. SCLC can show whether trap density falls, but mobility, impedance/transport resistance, carrier-selective-contact PL quenching, transient extraction, and EQE must determine whether carriers can cross the layer. Beneficial treatment should reduce traps while preserving rapid contact quenching, low transport resistance, high FF/Jsc, and a thin, vertically connected mixed-phase layer. If PL improves but extraction and EQE decline as n=1/misorientation increases, the treatment has crossed from passivation into transport blocking.
scoring_key_points: Over-treatment can create a thick, high-bandgap low-n layer that passivates traps yet blocks out-of-plane extraction.
Broad GIWAXS azimuth and rising n=1 fraction diagnose misorientation and stronger confinement; peak intensity alone is not sufficient.
Use phase/orientation/thickness mapping to determine whether PQWs are thin and localized at surfaces/grain boundaries or form a continuous cap.
Combine trap-density measurements with mobility, resistance, contact-quenching, transient extraction, and EQE to separate passivation from blocking.
accepted_equivalents: Over-passivation, spacer overloading, insulating 2D capping, or excessive low-n phase formation are equivalent failure descriptions.
GIWAXS pole figures, azimuthal-width analysis, or texture coefficients are acceptable orientation diagnostics.
EIS, SCLC mobility, TPC, transient absorption extraction, or contact-dependent TRPL are acceptable transport diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that stronger PL and longer TRPL necessarily predict higher device efficiency.
Treating a stronger PQW diffraction peak as sufficient evidence of favorable vertical orientation.
Attributing the Jsc and FF loss only to increased trap density despite the passivation signatures.

expected_answer: Scale-up should begin by defining a process window for spacer concentration, deposited dose, solvent exposure, reaction time, drying rate, and substrate temperature. Uniform delivery by a scalable coating method must be shown not to dissolve or roughen the underlying perovskite, and the window must tolerate realistic variations in grain size and surface PbI2. Across the module area, GIWAXS/XRD mapping should verify the desired phase mixture and out-of-plane texture, while microscopy and chemical analysis should confirm thin PQW coverage at the top surface and grain boundaries without pinholes or a continuous blocking cap. Spatial PL/EL, TRPL, contact-quenching, EQE, impedance, and stabilized JV maps should then demonstrate that passivation and low transport resistance coexist, with high manufacturing yield rather than only a champion pixel. Durability must be tested in encapsulated large-area devices under prolonged MPP illumination, damp heat, thermal cycling, humidity-freeze, and UV or equivalent IEC-relevant stresses. Results should report absolute post-aging PCE, Voc, Jsc, FF, leakage, and spatial failure maps, not only normalized retention. Post-mortem structural and chemical analysis should determine whether failure arises from spacer desorption, PQW phase evolution, ion migration, contact reaction, moisture ingress, or delamination. A valid scale-up claim requires reproducible structure, transport, yield, and module-level lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Define and demonstrate a scalable dose/solvent/time/temperature process window that does not damage the 3D film.
Map PQW phase, orientation, thickness, and surface/grain-boundary coverage across the large area to prevent blocking or nonuniform regions.
Verify passivation and transport simultaneously with spatial optical/electrical diagnostics, stabilized performance, and yield statistics.
Use encapsulated module-level MPP and IEC-relevant stress tests with absolute JV reporting and post-mortem failure analysis.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, blade, spray, meniscus, or another scalable deposition route is acceptable if dose and uniformity are controlled.
Spatial PL/EL, LBIC, thermography, or mapped EQE may be used to demonstrate large-area uniformity.
Damp heat, thermal cycling, humidity-freeze, UV, or equivalent standardized module stresses are acceptable durability tests.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling by increasing spacer dose until PL is maximized without checking orientation or transport resistance.
Using normalized PCE retention of a few small unencapsulated cells as proof of commercial durability.
Reporting only champion efficiency and omitting module-area uniformity, yield, and failure-mode analysis.

expected_answer: A credible causal decomposition requires chemically orthogonal controls rather than only untreated versus acidic-fluoride samples. At minimum, the study should compare: an untreated oxide; a nonfluorinated acid treatment matched in proton activity and exposure time; a fluoride treatment delivered with little or no added acidity and matched for fluoride dose; and the combined acidic-fluoride treatment. A chloride or other halide analogue can be added as a specificity control. All samples should be processed to comparable oxide roughness, perovskite thickness, grain size, and optical absorption so that morphology does not absorb the causal attribution. The proton-cleaning contribution should be diagnosed on the bare oxide. Acid-only treatment should lower the O 1s hydroxyl-to-lattice-oxygen ratio and reduce hydroxyl-related trap or superoxide signatures, but it need not produce an F 1s signal or the same work-function shift as fluoride. Surface-sensitive XPS, contact-angle measurements, EPR or illumination-dependent oxygen chemistry, and trap-sensitive electrical measurements on oxide-only test structures can establish this branch. The oxide-fluorination branch requires evidence that fluoride is bound at oxide surface sites and changes electronic extraction without merely etching the film. F 1s and cation-core-level shifts, UPS/Kelvin-probe work function, conduction-band position, contact resistance, transient photocurrent, and electron-only-device measurements should be compared across the fluoride-only and acid-only controls. If fluoride occupancy is important, the fluoride-containing samples should show the energetic or extraction change even when proton cleaning is held approximately constant. Excess etching, an insulating fluoride-rich layer, or over-reduction of the oxide would instead increase resistance and can reverse the fill-factor benefit. Perovskite-side passivation must be localized to the buried interface. Lift-off or peel-exposed bottom-surface XPS, angle- or depth-resolved spectroscopy, ToF-SIMS, solid-state NMR/FTIR, or chemically selective calculations should show fluoride concentrated near the bottom interface and interacting with undercoordinated Pb and/or N-H groups. Bottom-side PLQY, TRPL, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, light-intensity-dependent Voc, and ideality factor should then show reduced trap-assisted recombination. This branch is most directly linked to Voc gain; improved alignment and reduced charge accumulation contribute to fill factor and hysteresis. Bulk fluoride alloying is falsified if fluoride remains interfacially localized, the bulk lattice constants, absorption edge and perovskite energy levels remain unchanged, and no composition-dependent bulk phase shift is detected. A genuine bulk-alloying mechanism would require fluoride distributed through the absorber and reproducible bulk structural or band-edge changes, not merely buried-interface chemical bonding.
scoring_key_points: Uses orthogonal acid-only, fluoride-only, combined-treatment and untreated controls while holding morphology and dose-related variables comparable.
Assigns oxide hydroxyl removal to surface-chemistry evidence distinct from fluoride binding and work-function/extraction changes.
Localizes perovskite-side passivation to the buried interface and connects recombination diagnostics primarily to Voc, with extraction/charge accumulation linked to FF and hysteresis.
Falsifies bulk alloying through interfacial fluoride localization plus unchanged bulk lattice, absorption edge and absorber energy levels.
accepted_equivalents: A matched-pH nonfluoride acid and a neutral or weakly acidic fluoride salt are acceptable implementations of the orthogonal controls.
Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, cross-sectional STEM-EELS, neutron depth profiling or isotope-labelled fluoride may substitute for ToF-SIMS when they establish depth localization.
Surface photovoltage, time-resolved microwave conductivity, photo-CELIV or impedance-derived contact resistance may substitute for one of the extraction diagnostics.
Pb-F coordination and F···H-N hydrogen bonding may be expressed more generally as anion coordination of undercoordinated lead and stabilization of cation-vacancy environments.
common_wrong_answers: Treating the combined treatment as proof of a single fluoride mechanism without acid-only and fluoride-only controls.
Using higher PL alone as proof of improved electron extraction or favorable band alignment.
Calling a lower hydroxyl signal proof that fluoride passivates the perovskite bottom surface.
Claiming bulk fluoride substitution despite unchanged bulk structure and fluoride confined to the buried interface.

expected_answer: The transfer should preserve functions, not copy the original reagent. The primer must remove or neutralize hydroxyl-related SnO2 defects, supply a controlled amount of fluoride or an equivalent hard anion to passivate oxide and perovskite-side undercoordination, and create a favorable electron-selective contact. It should not rely on strong free acid that etches transparent conductors, corrodes coating equipment, or changes SnO2 stoichiometry unpredictably. A practical design is a surface-anchoring fluoride donor, ion-paired salt, or ultrathin bifunctional molecule whose oxide-binding group immobilizes the anion and whose total loading is self-limiting. Low-temperature rinsing or conversion should remove unbound ions and residual counterions. The electrical design window is narrow. The layer must be sub-monolayer to a few nanometres, laterally complete enough to passivate but thin and electronically transparent enough to avoid tunnelling or injection barriers. Dose and thickness series should be evaluated by UPS/KPFM, contact resistance, electron-only devices, voltage-dependent EQE, transient extraction and illuminated J-V.
