The observed S-shape after aging suggests that the primer has become too insulating, has altered the SnO2/perovskite band offset, or has redistributed under bias. A successful redesign should retain the Voc/QFLS benefit without increasing series resistance or producing carrier accumulation. Architecture-specific controls are essential because SnO2 is not TiO2. The matrix should include untreated SnO2, acid-only, nonacid fluoride, anchored fluoride, and a nonfluorinated anchored analogue, all deposited with the same wetting and thermal history. Surface hydroxyls, Sn oxidation state, work function, perovskite bottom-side chemistry, adhesion and morphology should be measured. Depth profiling before and after stress must verify that the active species remains at the buried interface and does not enter the bulk absorber, transport layers or electrodes. Validation must go beyond dark shelf storage. Use maximum-power-point operation under one-sun illumination with elevated temperature, humid-air or damp-heat exposure with appropriate encapsulation controls, sustained electrical bias, thermal cycling, and repeated bending. Track J-V shape, QFLS, ideality factor, impedance/contact resistance, electroluminescence uniformity, ion-distribution profiles and interfacial adhesion. A defensible rejection criterion is any formulation that gives a statistically significant initial Voc gain but develops persistent S-shaped J-V behaviour, increasing interfacial resistance, or stress-induced fluoride migration beyond the interface before the required lifetime, even if dark-storage PCE retention remains high. Those signatures show that passivation has been purchased at the cost of transport or ionic stability.
scoring_key_points: Redesigns around immobilized, dose-controlled interfacial fluoride chemistry rather than directly substituting another soluble fluoride or strong acid.
Defines a thin-layer energetic and transport window and interprets the aged S-shape as a barrier, resistance or redistribution problem requiring electrical diagnostics.
Uses SnO2-specific factorial controls and verifies interfacial localization before and after stress.
Specifies combined light, heat, humidity, bias and bending validation with a go/no-go rule that rejects migration or transport-barrier formation despite good initial PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Covalently tethered fluoride, an oxide-chelating cation-fluoride ion pair, a self-assembled monolayer or a self-limiting plasma/chemical fluorination are acceptable immobilization strategies.
An equivalent nonmobile hard-base passivator may replace fluoride if it reproduces the defect and energetic functions without creating new barriers.
Operando XPS is not required; ex situ depth profiling at multiple stress intervals, isotope tracing or cross-sectional spectroscopy is acceptable.
Mechanical validation may use cyclic bending, peel testing, nanoindentation or interfacial-fracture measurements when appropriate to the flexible stack.
common_wrong_answers: Recommending a higher fluoride concentration to recover Voc without addressing the S-shape or migration.
Assuming that a treatment optimized on TiO2 will have identical surface chemistry and band alignment on SnO2.
Using only dark-storage stability as proof of operational stability.
Accepting a formulation solely because average PCE remains high while ion migration or contact resistance is worsening.

expected_answer: The first step is to avoid treating the higher PLQY and Voc as a complete mechanism. Glass-side PLQY, absolute QFLS, electroluminescence efficiency, light-intensity-dependent Voc and ideality factor can establish that recombination at or near the buried contact has decreased. If those improve while current extraction worsens, passivation and transport have become decoupled. The characteristic device signature is a higher Voc but lower FF/Jsc, possibly an S-shaped illuminated J-V curve, voltage-dependent EQE, slow transient photocurrent, charge accumulation or a low-frequency impedance feature. A dipole or band-offset claim requires direct energetic and electrostatic evidence. UPS on model stacks, Kelvin-probe or KPFM measurements, surface photovoltage, built-in-potential measurements and band-edge estimates should show that the modifier changes the SnO2/perovskite offset in the direction predicted by the J-V response. The energetic shift must correlate with dose and with extraction kinetics. If QFLS improves but the conduction-band barrier exceeds the useful extraction window, electrons accumulate and FF falls. Conversely, if the work function and contact potential are unchanged while resistance rises strongly with modifier thickness, a simple insulating-layer explanation is more likely. Bottom-side morphology and chemistry must be measured directly rather than inferred from top-view SEM. Lift-off or peeling followed by SEM/AFM, nano-FTIR, XPS, glass-side confocal PL, cross-sectional TEM, and grazing-incidence scattering can reveal porous regions, unreacted precursor, altered nucleation or compositional inhomogeneity at the buried surface. A wetting/crystallization mechanism should produce bottom-side structural or chemical changes that co-vary with the electrical loss, even when the top surface looks similar. Strain requires an independent structural branch. Depth-sensitive GIWAXS/GIXRD, Raman mapping or microdiffraction should quantify residual strain and its spatial distribution; thermal-expansion or curvature measurements can test whether the modifier changes mechanical constraint. Strain-induced loss should track lattice distortion, defect formation or local nonradiative hot spots rather than only contact resistance. Finally, series resistance should be tested through dark and illuminated impedance, transfer-length or contact-resistance structures, four-point measurements on the ETL stack, and a modifier-thickness series. A dominant dipole/band-offset mechanism is justified only when direct energetic shifts, carrier accumulation/extraction signatures and dose dependence agree, while bottom-side morphology, strain and simple ohmic resistance are insufficient to explain the loss.
scoring_key_points: Separates recombination metrics such as glass-side PLQY/QFLS and ideality factor from current-extraction metrics and recognizes the higher-Voc/lower-FF trade-off.
Requires direct energetic/electrostatic evidence plus dose-correlated extraction signatures before assigning the loss to a dipole or band offset.
Uses buried-side or cross-sectional characterization to test wetting, crystallization and chemical inhomogeneity that top-view SEM cannot reveal.
Includes independent strain and series-resistance branches and states how their signatures would compete with or falsify the energetic-barrier hypothesis.
accepted_equivalents: Hard-X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, cross-sectional scanning probes or peel-transfer spectroscopy may substitute for lift-off XPS/nano-FTIR.

Transient photovoltage/photocurrent, photo-CELIV, time-resolved microwave conductivity or voltage-dependent photoluminescence may substitute for one another when used to diagnose extraction and accumulation.
Wafer curvature, synchrotron nano-XRD or Raman peak shifts may serve as strain diagnostics.
A tunnelling barrier, low vertical conductivity or modifier-induced depletion may be treated as variants of the extraction-barrier mechanism if distinguished from bulk series resistance.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that higher PLQY proves the interface improves every aspect of device operation.
Using only top-view SEM to rule out buried morphology or wetting changes.
Claiming a favorable dipole solely from a higher Voc without measuring energy levels or extraction kinetics.
Ignoring modifier thickness, contact resistance and strain when interpreting the FF and Jsc losses.

expected_answer: The first gate should test whether the modifier performs the necessary electronic function within a manufacturable dose window. Each candidate should be screened for reduction of buried-interface recombination, suitable majority-carrier band alignment, negligible minority-carrier leakage, and low vertical contact resistance. QFLS/PLQY, ideality factor, UPS/KPFM, contact-resistance structures, transient extraction and thickness-series J-V are more informative than a single champion PCE. A candidate that passivates only at a loading that creates an extraction barrier should not advance. The second gate addresses chemical and crystallization compatibility with the exact tandem stack. The modifier must survive the perovskite solvent, not corrode the charge-transport layer or recombination junction, and must not introduce mobile or hygroscopic ions that accelerate bias- or moisture-driven degradation. Wetting, nucleation, bottom-side morphology, residual solvent and phase purity should be mapped over a realistic process window. Candidate A therefore needs immobilization and humidity testing; B needs an upper thickness limit and conductivity check; C needs aggregation and solvent-partition control; D needs proof that the coherent phase forms reproducibly across stoichiometric and thermal variations. The third gate is specific to a flexible tandem. Mechanical adhesion, fracture energy, residual strain, thermal-expansion mismatch and bending durability must be measured together with optical parasitic absorption and reflectance. The modifier must be compatible with the low thermal budget and must not damage the underlying subcell or alter current matching. A polymer may help adhesion yet fail electrically; an inorganic salt may passivate yet crystallize or migrate during bending and humidity; a conductive 2D layer may be optically or mechanically anisotropic; a self-formed layer may relieve lattice mismatch but have a narrow processing window. The fourth gate evaluates scale and uniformity. Slot-die or blade-coated coupons should be mapped by PL/EL, LBIC, sheet/contact resistance, thickness and buried-side spectroscopy across the coating width. Statistical yield, not the best cell, determines progression. The modifier must tolerate line-speed, drying, roughness and precursor-batch variations without local shunts or contact barriers. The final gate is a mini-module factorial stress program. Compare no-modifier controls and the best dose of each candidate under maximum-power-point light soaking, elevated temperature, damp heat or controlled humidity, thermal cycling and cyclic bending, including encapsulated and unencapsulated diagnostic sets. Track subcell-resolved voltage, current matching, series resistance, EL/PL nonuniformity, ion redistribution, adhesion and phase evolution. Advancement requires retention of both electrical selectivity and mechanical integrity with narrow spatial dispersion; a candidate is rejected if its apparent PCE benefit depends on a narrow dose, degrades current matching, or creates stress-induced ionic, optical or contact losses.
scoring_key_points: Uses electronic selectivity, recombination and vertical-transport gates rather than champion PCE to define the first screening stage.
Evaluates solvent/chemical compatibility, mobile-ion risk and bottom-side crystallization with candidate-specific failure modes.
Includes flexible-tandem constraints: adhesion, strain, bending, thermal budget, parasitic optics and current matching.
Defines statistically mapped scale-up and combined-stress mini-module validation with explicit advancement or rejection logic.
accepted_equivalents: A weighted multi-objective score or Pareto-front selection is acceptable if hard failure gates are retained.
Mechanical integrity may be quantified by peel strength, interfacial fracture energy, cyclic curvature, crack-density imaging or equivalent methods.
Spatial uniformity may be evaluated by electroluminescence, photoluminescence, lock-in thermography, LBIC, hyperspectral imaging or contact-potential mapping.
Tandem current matching may be monitored through subcell-resolved EQE, bias-light J-V, luminescent coupling analysis or equivalent subcell diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Ranking the four candidates by the highest reported small-area PCE from different device stacks.
Assuming that a polymer is mechanically superior without checking its vertical resistance and solvent swelling.
Ignoring hygroscopicity or mobile-ion risk because the initial QFLS improves.
Declaring module readiness after a single dark-storage or bending test without simultaneous light, heat, humidity and electrical operation.

expected_answer: The causal claim requires first proving a distinct spatial distribution at equal total loading. The fullerene should be isotope-labelled or tracked by a chemically unique fragment using calibrated ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved or sputter-depth XPS, cross-sectional spectroscopy, or a carbon-free inorganic-perovskite model stack that removes absorber-carbon background. The waiting sample should show reproducible enrichment near the ETL/perovskite interface and little accumulation at the top surface, whereas the premixed sample should be comparatively uniform and the no-wait overcoat should show a sharper or less penetrated interfacial layer. Top-surface solvent-rinse analysis or NMR can independently test whether the molecule reaches the upper surface. Depth profiles must be corrected for sputter mixing and compared at matched total fullerene content. Next, morphology and chemistry must be controlled. Film thickness, absorption, grain size, roughness, crystallinity and residual solvent should be similar, or any differences must be explicitly modelled. A nonfullerene analogue with similar wetting but no electron-accepting orbital, and a fullerene analogue with poor precursor miscibility, can distinguish chemical/electronic function from generic solvent or nucleation effects. The gradient should produce a location-specific electronic signature. Bottom-side or substrate-side PL quenching, cross-sectional KPFM, electron-beam-induced current, selective-contact transient photocurrent, impedance/contact resistance and electron-only mobility should show faster extraction or lower interfacial accumulation specifically at the bottom contact. The expected device pattern is a strong FF and extraction improvement for bottom enrichment, while homogeneous mixing can raise Voc through distributed defect passivation. QFLS and ideality-factor changes should therefore be interpreted separately from mobility and contact resistance. Finally, the gradient must be perturbed without changing total loading. Vary the waiting time, solvent activity, substrate temperature or drying rate to tune diffusion; plot bottom enrichment against FF and extraction rate. Reverse the distribution by depositing the fullerene from the top after perovskite formation, or immobilize it on the ETL so that infiltration cannot occur. If the gradient is causal, erasing bottom enrichment should remove the FF advantage, and a reversed top-rich profile should not reproduce the same electron-contact benefit. The hypothesis is falsified if performance follows only total fullerene concentration, bulk trap density or morphology while depth distribution changes independently, or if an equal-loading uniform sample gives the same extraction signatures and FF.
scoring_key_points: Demonstrates bottom enrichment with depth-resolved, artefact-controlled profiling at matched total loading and distinguishes premixed, no-wait and waiting distributions.
Controls for morphology, wetting and generic additive effects so that spatial fullerene distribution remains the manipulated variable.
Links bottom enrichment to location-specific electron extraction, mobility/contact resistance and FF while separating those metrics from bulk-passivation/Voc effects.
Uses waiting-time/diffusion or reversed-gradient perturbations and states a clear falsification condition.
accepted_equivalents: Neutron reflectometry, resonant soft X-ray scattering, cross-sectional STEM-EELS or fluorescence-labelled analogues may replace ToF-SIMS if they resolve the vertical distribution without changing chemistry materially.
Substrate-side excitation PL, interface-selective transient absorption or cross-sectional EBIC may provide spatially selective electronic evidence.
A no-wait, diffusion-blocked or covalently tethered ETL fullerene control may serve as the gradient-erasure perturbation.
The distinction may be phrased as bulk trap passivation controlling Voc versus contact-selective extraction controlling FF.
common_wrong_answers: Inferring a vertical gradient solely because a waiting step was used.
Using one uncorrected sputter-depth profile without equal-loading or sputter-mixing controls.
Treating higher electron mobility as proof of a gradient without spatial localization.
Ignoring the possibility that altered crystallization or wetting, rather than fullerene position, caused the FF change.

expected_answer: Continuous processing should convert the laboratory waiting step into a controlled diffusion and partitioning zone. The molecule needs enough affinity for the polar precursor to enter the lower perovskite region, but a larger equilibrium affinity for the ETL or the early-forming bottom lattice so that it remains bottom-enriched. This can be achieved with an ETL-anchoring group such as phosphonate, carboxylate, silane or a specifically binding heteroatom, while retaining a fullerene frontier-orbital alignment that accepts electrons and blocks holes. Side chains should provide precursor miscibility without making the molecule excessively bulky or insulating. Because operation exceeds the reported glass transition, the gradient must be kinetically locked. Options include covalent or multidentate anchoring to the ETL, a post-diffusion crosslinkable side group, a higher-Tg rigid or branched substituent, or conversion into a lightly networked interfacial phase after the desired distribution forms. Crosslinking must occur after sufficient infiltration and must not shift the LUMO/HOMO unfavourably, generate traps or create a thick insulating layer. The optimal loading remains low and should be established through contact resistance and recombination measurements. The process can use sequential slot-die heads, a wet-on-wet overcoat, controlled solvent orthogonality, a short heated or solvent-vapour residence zone, and directed gas flow. Line speed, gap between coating heads, wet-film thickness, substrate temperature and solvent activity define the diffusion length before crystallization arrests the profile. A transport model or dimensionless diffusion/drying analysis should be calibrated with depth profiles, then used to choose a robust operating window rather than copying the spin-coating time. Scale-up proof requires depth-resolved mapping across the web and through the module before and after annealing. Equal-loading homogeneous and no-anchor controls should separate gradient function from total fullerene effects. Spatial PL/EL, contact-potential maps, transient extraction, electron mobility, contact resistance and FF uniformity should confirm that bottom enrichment improves electron collection without adding recombination. Stability tests must specifically challenge redistribution: maximum-power-point light soaking at 70-85 °C, sustained bias, thermal cycling, damp heat and shelf storage. Repeat depth profiling and molecular-aggregation measurements after stress, and monitor FF, hysteresis, series resistance and spatial nonuniformity. The design fails if the fullerene migrates toward the top or electrodes, aggregates, loses the FF advantage, or creates a contact barrier even when average dark-storage PCE remains acceptable.
scoring_key_points: Redesigns the molecule to combine precursor miscibility, correct electron-selective energy levels and preferential ETL/bottom-interface affinity.
Addresses operation above Tg by anchoring, crosslinking or increasing Tg without creating an insulating or trap-forming layer.
Replaces the waiting step with a continuous wet-on-wet/diffusion process window controlled by line speed, solvent activity, temperature and drying.
Validates gradient location and electronic function before and after high-temperature light/bias/humidity stress using equal-loading controls and spatial/depth-resolved measurements.
accepted_equivalents: A block-copolymer, supramolecular anchor or reactive fullerene that binds selectively to SnO2/TiO2 may substitute for phosphonate/carboxylate anchoring.
A dual-slot-die, gravure-overcoat, spray-assisted interlayer or in-line solvent-vapour zone is acceptable if it creates a reproducible diffusion interval.
Higher Tg may be achieved through rigidification, branching, controlled oligomerization or interfacial network formation.
Gradient stability may be measured by isotope-labelled depth profiling, neutron reflectometry, cross-sectional spectroscopy or equivalent methods.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing fullerene concentration to compensate for the shorter process time without controlling where it accumulates.
Ignoring the fact that operation above Tg can enable molecular redistribution and aggregation.
Crosslinking before diffusion, thereby trapping the fullerene as a sharp insulating layer on the ETL.
Declaring success from initial small-cell PCE without remeasuring the gradient after heat, illumination and bias.

expected_answer: At the molecular level, the additive should retain complementary hydrogen-bonding and Pb-coordination motifs that buffer ambient crystallization and passivate residual undercoordination. However, interaction strength and dose must be optimized for complete conversion and electrical transparency. Too little additive will not control nucleation; too much can over-retard crystallization, leave an insulating residue, alter stoichiometry or increase ion mobility. A dose and molecular-analogue series should therefore measure complexation, residual content, QFLS and vertical contact resistance, not only grain size or PCE. A modest hydrophobic or anchoring feature may improve moisture tolerance, but it must not disrupt precursor solubility or phase formation. The coating process must control the spatial thermal and mass-transfer field. Across the 100 cm² width, map wet-film thickness, meniscus shape, substrate temperature, airflow velocity/direction, solvent evaporation and local RH. Closed-loop control of airflow, substrate heating and line speed should hold the nucleation window uniform. In situ or line-scan PL/reflectance/GIWAXS can identify where the crystallization front becomes nonuniform. Coupons cut from centre, edge, leading and trailing regions should be compared at identical device area to separate chemistry from coating position. The fill-factor loss must then be decomposed electrically. EL/PL imaging, LBIC, lock-in thermography, dark J-V, sheet/contact-resistance mapping and subcell/interconnect measurements should distinguish shunts, dead-area and electrode resistance from an interfacial extraction barrier. If small coupons taken from the same coated sheet retain high QFLS but the module loses FF through resistive or interconnection patterns, the dominant problem is scale architecture rather than additive chemistry. If low-QFLS regions coincide with drying or void nonuniformity, the additive/process window is not spatially robust. Stability attribution requires direct degradation evidence. Use encapsulated and unencapsulated diagnostic modules under maximum-power-point light soaking, elevated temperature, humidity cycling and damp heat, with edge-seal variants. Track PbI2 and nonphotoactive phase formation by XRD/GIWAXS, bottom voids and interfacial delamination by cross-sectional imaging, ion redistribution by ToF-SIMS, and spatial voltage/current loss by EL/LBIC. Edge-first failure may originate from seal permeability, lateral moisture transport along voids or additive-rich regions, not simply insufficient passivation. A passivation-based stability claim is justified only if the optimized additive lowers nonradiative recombination and suppresses PbI2/nonphotoactive-phase formation at matched coating uniformity, while the same chemistry remains localized and electrically benign after stress. Module success additionally requires uniform FF and no edge-localized failure after combined operation. Dark shelf retention alone, or delayed visual degradation without MPP and phase/ion diagnostics, is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes interaction strength and dose for crystallization control, passivation, complete conversion and vertical conductivity, including overbinding/residue failure modes.
Controls and maps large-area airflow, temperature, RH, wet-film thickness and nucleation so additive chemistry can be separated from hydrodynamic nonuniformity.
Decomposes module FF loss using spatial electrical and interconnection diagnostics rather than assigning it automatically to recombination.
Requires combined MPP/heat/humidity testing with phase, ion, interface and edge-seal evidence before claiming passivation-driven module stability.
accepted_equivalents: Meniscus coating, slot-die or scalable blade coating may replace the stated process if the same spatial mass-transfer controls are used.
Hyperspectral PL, electroluminescence, thermography, LBIC or distributed resistance extraction may be combined in different ways for spatial loss mapping.
A hydrophobic substituent, polymerizable anchor or grain-boundary-affine group may be proposed if precursor compatibility and electronic transparency are verified.
Humidity cycling, IEC-inspired damp heat, light-soak at controlled RH or edge-ingress tests are acceptable components of the stability matrix.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing additive concentration to stop edge degradation without checking residue, conductivity or crystallization completion.
Attributing all module fill-factor loss to traps while ignoring sheet resistance, interconnect geometry and local shunts.
Using centre-point morphology to represent the entire coated area.
Claiming operational stability from ambient shelf storage or visual colour retention alone.

expected_answer: The observations point primarily to spatially heterogeneous contact-induced nonradiative recombination, not to an absorption or current-generation limitation. Dark regions appearing only after formation of the buried hole contact implicate incomplete wetting, pinholes, or nonuniform molecular coverage on rough flexible ITO; this should be verified by contact-stack PLQY or QFLS mapping together with direct coverage or wetting measurements. Additional nonuniform PL loss after the fullerene layer implicates top-interface coverage, selectivity, or energetic mismatch; morphology and thickness mapping should therefore be paired with UPS or Kelvin-probe energetics and PLQY measured before and after the electron contact. The voltage and lifetime gain from the chloride-containing surface treatment, without a meaningful current gain, is consistent with suppressed interfacial or near-surface nonradiative recombination and improved selectivity rather than improved absorption. Bulk halide segregation must be tested independently under relevant illumination by reversible time-dependent spectral red-shifts or peak splitting in PL, electroluminescence, absorption, or diffraction; its absence would rule out segregation as the main cause of the original spatial voltage loss.
scoring_key_points: High bare-film QFLS, unchanged bandgap, and unchanged EQE identify a contact-induced voltage loss rather than an optical-generation deficit.
Dark patches introduced by the hole contact indicate incomplete or nonuniform buried-contact coverage on rough ITO; verify with spatial PLQY/QFLS plus direct wetting or coverage characterization.

Further loss after the fullerene layer indicates top-interface morphology, selectivity, or energy-alignment problems; verify with ETL coverage/thickness, interfacial PLQY, and UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements.

A treatment-driven lifetime and voltage gain with little current change supports recombination passivation; bulk phase segregation requires separate light-soak spectral or structural evidence and reversibility tests.
accepted_equivalents: contact-induced voltage loss or interface-induced QFLS-to-VOC loss
SAM pinholes, incomplete monolayer coverage, or poor wetting
electron-contact selectivity or energetic-barrier loss
illumination-induced halide demixing detected by reversible spectral red-shift or peak splitting
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the entire voltage deficit to the perovskite bulk despite the high bare-film QFLS.
Treating every decrease in PL after adding an extraction layer as proof of beneficial charge extraction.
Claiming a low-dimensional surface phase or bulk chloride incorporation without composition-sensitive evidence.
Ruling out phase segregation solely because the dark J-V curve is unchanged.

expected_answer: A valid comparison requires paired treated and control cohorts operated for identical durations and conditions at maximum power, with sufficient replicates to report T80 or another survival metric rather than retention at different stopping times. A factorial aging matrix should separate and combine light, heat, humidity, electrical bias, oxygen, and encapsulation; dark and open-circuit controls help distinguish photochemical, thermal, and field-driven mechanisms, while contact angle alone cannot measure water-vapor permeation through grain boundaries or interfaces. Chemical decomposition should be tracked by phase-sensitive diffraction or spectroscopy and composition profiling; ion or metal migration by depth-resolved mass spectrometry or microscopy; and interfacial failure by adhesion, cross-sectional imaging, electroluminescence/PLQY, impedance, and local shunt mapping. Transfer to large-area flexible devices additionally requires area-scaled statistics, module/interconnect testing, standardized bending radius and cycle protocols before and after environmental aging, compatible encapsulation, and equal-condition ISOS-style operational tests. Until those requirements are met, the defensible claim is improved laboratory-scale unencapsulated durability, not certified module lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Run equal-duration, equal-condition MPPT tests with replicated treated/control cohorts and report a common survival metric such as T80 rather than unequal endpoint retention.
Use a factorial stress matrix that separates and combines light, heat, humidity, bias, oxygen, and encapsulation; contact angle alone is not a moisture-barrier or operational-stability metric.

Assign mechanism-specific diagnostics: structural/compositional probes for decomposition and ion/metal migration, and adhesion/cross-section plus luminescence, impedance, or shunt mapping for interfacial failure.

Require area-scaled flexible devices or modules, interconnect and encapsulation compatibility, standardized bending before/after aging, and ISOS-style operational statistics before making a transferable lifetime claim.
accepted_equivalents: equal-duration paired MPPT or common T80 comparison
factorial multi-stress aging
depth-resolved ion or electrode migration analysis
combined environmental and mechanical qualification of large-area flexible devices
common_wrong_answers: Comparing retention percentages measured at different MPPT durations as if they were directly equivalent.
Using a higher water contact angle as sufficient proof of humidity or operational stability.
Collapsing shelf, humidity, light-bias, and bending tests into one generic stability number.
Claiming module or commercial lifetime from unencapsulated small-area laboratory devices.

expected_answer: Initial curling is governed by the net residual force and bending moment produced by mismatch stress and asymmetric layer placement, whereas cyclic cracking is governed mainly by the tensile or compressive strain experienced by brittle ITO during bending. Thinning the polymer reduces ITO strain at a given radius but also lowers bending stiffness, so the same sputter stress generates much larger free curvature. A back-side oxide can supply an opposing residual moment; there is an optimum thickness-modulus product at which curvature is cancelled, while excess compensation can reverse the curl and introduce a second brittle layer prone to cracking or delamination. Flatness alone does not prove low cyclic ITO strain because the back layer also moves the neutral axis; if it shifts the neutral axis away from ITO, bending durability may worsen even though the sheet is initially flat. The design must therefore be verified on a released specimen by free-curvature or residual-stress measurement, layer-resolved strain or neutral-axis analysis, in-situ resistance versus bending radius and cycle count, and post-mortem crack/delamination imaging rather than by flatness while temporarily bonded to a rigid support.
scoring_key_points: Separate residual-stress curvature, controlled by laminate force/moment balance, from cyclic brittle-film strain, controlled by distance from the neutral axis and bending radius.
Recognize that a thinner polymer reduces ITO bending strain but also reduces laminate stiffness and therefore amplifies free curvature from sputter stress.
Explain the optimum back-oxide thickness/modulus that cancels curvature, the possibility of reverse curl or oxide cracking when overcompensated, and the independent neutral-axis shift.
Verify on released laminates using free-curvature/residual-stress measurements, neutral-axis or strain mapping, in-situ resistance during bending, and crack/delamination imaging.
accepted_equivalents: residual bending moment versus outer-fiber strain
Stoney-type curvature or multilayer force-moment balance
neutral-axis shift
released-sample curvature plus in-situ resistance cycling
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a perfectly flat laminate must also have minimum ITO strain during folding.
Assuming substrate thinning always reduces curling because it improves flexibility.
Ignoring reverse curvature, brittle back-oxide cracking, or interfacial delamination at excessive oxide thickness.
Evaluating flatness only while the ultrathin sheet is attached to a rigid carrier.

expected_answer: Mesh line width, pitch, and thickness must balance sheet resistance and current crowding against optical shading and pattern visibility; this requires spatial sheet-resistance and transmittance measurements together with module electroluminescence or thermal maps under current. Embedding and planarization must suppress steps that cause incomplete perovskite coverage and shunts, but added planarization thickness and cure stress can alter flexibility and adhesion; profilometry/AFM, cross-sectional imaging, PL or electroluminescence uniformity, and shunt statistics should be correlated. The back oxide and any front protective overlayer must jointly cancel residual curvature and place brittle conductors and active layers near the neutral plane while also providing barrier function; finite-element strain analysis must be validated by in-situ resistance and photovoltaic measurements over radius-dependent cyclic folds and environmental aging. Finally, P1/P2/P3 scribes must be registered relative to mesh lines and intended fold axes so that dead area, interconnect resistance, local heating, shorts, and crack propagation are minimized; full-module J-V, subcell voltage distribution, EL/IR imaging, insulation tests, and post-fold cross-sections are required. Module qualification must include repeated folding in multiple directions under or after illumination, heat, and humidity, not only static TCE resistance.
scoring_key_points: Co-optimize mesh width, pitch, and thickness for resistance/current spreading versus shading and transparency; validate with spatial electrical/optical maps and EL or thermal current-crowding diagnostics.
Co-optimize embedding and planarization for low topography versus added stress, thickness, and adhesion; validate morphology, luminescence uniformity, and shunt yield.

Co-optimize back-oxide and protective-overlayer thickness for anti-curling, barrier function, and neutral-plane placement; validate modelled strain with radius-dependent cyclic electrical and photovoltaic tests before and after environmental aging.

Register P1/P2/P3 scribes, mesh, and fold axes to minimize dead area, contact resistance, heating, shorts, and crack propagation; validate on complete modules with J-V, EL/IR, insulation, and post-fold structural analysis.
accepted_equivalents: mesh shading versus sheet resistance
planarity versus added stress or thickness
neutral-plane and barrier co-design
scribe-to-mesh and scribe-to-fold-axis registration
common_wrong_answers: Optimizing sheet resistance and transmittance on a flat TCE coupon without fabricating the full device stack.
Assuming an embedded mesh is automatically planar enough for defect-free absorber coating.
Testing only one bending radius or direction and only before environmental aging.
Ignoring local heating and crack propagation at laser scribes and mesh intersections.

expected_answer: Fluorination changes several variables simultaneously, including solubility, hydrogen bonding, surface energy, organic-inorganic interaction strength, frontier levels, hydrophobicity, and crystallization kinetics, so the observed chain is underdetermined. Solution aggregation should be tested as a function of concentration, solvent, temperature, and aging by DLS or scattering, then linked directly to nucleation and growth by in-situ optical monitoring and GIWAXS during drying; aggregation should also be perturbed independently, for example with solvent or seed changes, while holding spacer chemistry fixed. Direct passivation and electronic effects can be isolated by applying the spacer as a post-treatment to preformed films, or by using matched analogues with similar aggregation but different dipole or fluorination; PLQY/QFLS, trap spectroscopy, XPS, UPS, and interfacial extraction should then be compared at matched morphology. Phase distribution and orientation require depth- and direction-sensitive GIWAXS plus phase-resolved front/back PL or transient spectroscopy, followed by anisotropic mobility or extraction measurements; processing should be adjusted to match grain size while varying orientation. Only if independent perturbations reproduce the expected changes in recombination, transport, and fill factor can the proposed causal pathway be assigned rather than inferred from correlation.
scoring_key_points: State that fluorination simultaneously changes multiple chemical, interfacial, and processing variables, so correlation among dipole, aggregate size, morphology, lifetime, and fill factor is not causal proof.
Isolate aggregation/nucleation with solution-condition-dependent DLS or scattering, in-situ crystallization measurements, and an independent aggregation perturbation at fixed spacer chemistry.
Isolate direct passivation/energetics using post-treatment or matched analogues at comparable morphology, measured by PLQY/QFLS, trap, XPS/UPS, and extraction diagnostics.

Isolate phase distribution/orientation using depth/direction-sensitive GIWAXS and phase-resolved spectroscopy with grain size controlled, then connect anisotropic transport or extraction to fill factor.
accepted_equivalents: in-situ GIWAXS during nucleation and growth
post-treatment to decouple crystallization from passivation
matched analogue with similar aggregation but different dipole
front/back phase-resolved spectroscopy or anisotropic transport
common_wrong_answers: Assuming larger precursor aggregates necessarily produce larger grains and better devices.
Treating a longer PL lifetime as unambiguous evidence of faster charge extraction.
Using a fill-factor increase alone to prove lower trap density.
Attributing all effects to hydrophobicity or fluorine without controlling morphology and phase distribution.

expected_answer: Static contact angle measures the initial wetting of the outer surface, not water-vapor sorption, diffusion through grain boundaries, permeability of the complete stack, or moisture reactions at buried interfaces and electrodes. Fluorination may strengthen the layered lattice, suppress defect-assisted photochemistry, and improve thermal or light stability while simultaneously changing phase distribution, residual stress, adhesion, ionic mobility, or interfacial chemistry in a way that makes the complete device more vulnerable under humid bias. A useful screen should therefore include water sorption and permeation measurements, humidity-dependent structural and optical monitoring, ion-migration or composition profiling, and adhesion or interfacial electrical diagnostics, all on films with matched thickness and morphology. Candidates must then be compared in replicated devices under equal-duration dark humidity, damp heat, illumination, and maximum-power-point conditions, both unencapsulated and with the intended encapsulation, using T80 or degradation-rate statistics. The correct conclusion is that fluorination can improve some degradation pathways without universally maximizing humidity stability.
scoring_key_points: Explain that contact angle reports surface wetting, not water-vapor uptake, grain-boundary transport, buried-interface reactions, or complete-stack permeability.

Recognize that fluorination can improve lattice, thermal, or photochemical stability while worsening another pathway through phase distribution, stress, adhesion, ion migration, or interface chemistry.
Screen water sorption/permeation, humidity-dependent structure and luminescence, ion/composition movement, and interfacial adhesion/electrical quality at matched film morphology.
Use replicated equal-duration multi-stress device aging, with and without intended encapsulation and under MPP where relevant, and rank by T80 or degradation rate rather than contact angle.
accepted_equivalents: surface hydrophobicity versus water-vapor permeability
condition-specific rather than universal stability
dynamic vapor sorption or humidity-dependent mass uptake
equal-duration multi-stress T80 screening
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the more hydrophobic spacer must always give the best humidity stability.
Using film XRD stability alone to infer complete-device stability.
Comparing different stress durations or initial efficiencies without normalized degradation statistics.
Ignoring buried contacts, electrode reactions, ion migration, and encapsulation.

expected_answer: Contact passivation mainly lowers the first-order coefficient k1 associated with trap- or interface-assisted nonradiative loss. High-fluence transients are dominated by k2 n^2 and eventually k3 n^3, so they can remain almost unchanged, as can the extracted bimolecular coefficient, even though low-density device performance improves. The low-density differential-lifetime plateau should increase from approximately 1/k1, while the first-to-second-order crossover should move to lower carrier density: the rate-balance scale is n approximately k1/k2, with a factor-of-two adjustment if the derivative-based differential lifetime is used. At a fixed one-sun generation rate, lowering k1 raises the steady-state carrier density and therefore the quasi-Fermi-level splitting and open-circuit voltage, although the exact increase must be obtained from the full rate equation if second-order recombination becomes significant. The slope of VOC versus log light intensity should move away from strongly trap-assisted behavior toward the bimolecular/radiative limit, usually toward a lower ideality factor, but it need not become ideal if bulk traps, transport, ions, or contact barriers remain. Thus an unchanged k2 is entirely compatible with successful suppression of first-order interface loss.
scoring_key_points: Identify the treatment as primarily reducing k1, so low-density nonradiative loss improves while high-density k2/k3-dominated TAS and the extracted k2 can remain unchanged.

Predict a longer low-density differential-lifetime plateau and a first-to-second-order crossover shifted to lower density when k1 decreases (rate-balance scale n approximately k1/k2; derivative-lifetime definitions may introduce a factor of two).
Predict higher one-sun steady-state carrier density, QFLS, and VOC at fixed generation, using the full rate equation if the device approaches the k2-dominated regime.
Predict a VOC-light-intensity slope or ideality factor that moves away from trap-assisted first-order behavior toward bimolecular/radiative behavior, without claiming it must become perfectly ideal.
accepted_equivalents: lower first-order recombination coefficient or lower surface recombination velocity
higher low-density lifetime plateau
crossover density k1/k2 shifts downward
higher steady-state carrier density and lower ideality factor
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that unchanged high-fluence TAS proves the passivation had no effect.
Expecting the bimolecular coefficient to decrease whenever VOC improves.
Predicting that the first-to-second-order crossover moves to higher density after k1 is reduced.
Assuming the VOC-light slope must become exactly kT/q regardless of remaining losses or ionic effects.

expected_answer: The primary comparison must use identical TiO2/ZrO2/carbon scaffolds with and without PAN, identical precursor loading, pore filling, thickness, and encapsulation. Initial Voc, Jsc, FF, and optical density should be matched or included as covariates. An inert-polymer control with comparable rheology is valuable for separating a generic diffusion barrier from nitrile-specific phase stabilization, and bare-film or scaffold witness samples should be aged alongside complete devices to distinguish absorber chemistry from electrode masking. The stress matrix should include controlled-humidity storage, elevated-temperature humidity, and one-sun MPP operation; dark heat or thermal cycling can identify polymer softening or pore-blocking failure. Operando or time-resolved XRD/GIWAXS should track the δ-FAPbI3 signature, while hyperspectral PL, Raman/absorption mapping, and D2O-ToF-SIMS or gravimetric uptake should distinguish phase conversion from delayed water arrival. At module scale, edge, centre, and print-direction positions should be monitored by PL/EL or LBIC imaging, subcell-resolved J-V/EQE, and mismatch/shunt analysis. Successful transfer requires that PAN delay or suppress δ-phase formation and preserve QFLS and stabilized MPP output at equivalent internal water exposure across the module, not merely that a high-starting-PCE module retains a favourable percentage for a short time.
scoring_key_points: Uses architecture-matched PAN and no-PAN devices, with initial performance, pore filling, optical density, and encapsulation controlled or statistically normalized.
Applies humidity, temperature, and operational MPP stresses rather than relying on ambient dark storage alone.
Directly tracks δ-FAPbI3 formation and water ingress with spatially and temporally resolved phase/chemical diagnostics.
Defines module success by uniform suppression of phase conversion and retention of stabilized electrical output, not normalized PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: An isotopically labelled-water experiment is acceptable for equalizing or quantifying internal moisture exposure.
Environmental XRD, GIWAXS, Raman, absorption, or hyperspectral PL may be used to identify δ-phase formation.
Cell-resolved electroluminescence, photoluminescence, lock-in thermography, or LBIC are acceptable module-uniformity tools.
common_wrong_answers: Compares PAN and control devices with different pore filling, thickness, or encapsulation.
Uses only dark shelf aging and assumes it predicts illuminated module operation.
Attributes better retention to phase stabilization without directly measuring δ-FAPbI3 or water ingress.
Reports only whole-module PCE and ignores edge failure, print gradients, and subcell mismatch.

expected_answer: The full molecule should be compared with three matched deletion analogues: one lacking F but retaining pyridine N and COOH, one lacking pyridine N but retaining F and COOH, and one lacking COOH but retaining pyridine N and F. Positional isomers or a second set may be needed if deletion strongly changes solubility, acidity, sterics, or dipole; all compounds must be dosed at matched surface exposure and residual concentration. Pb coordination should be assigned only when Pb-core-level or vibrational shifts, reduced Pb-related trap signatures, and a corresponding loss of effect in the N- or COOH-deletion controls agree. FA interaction should be tested by FA-containing-solution NMR or vibrational shifts and by comparison with an MA-rich control, not inferred from device PCE. A fluorine-dependent effect on halide-vacancy chemistry should be supported by vacancy-sensitive calculations or spectroscopy, ion-migration/activation measurements, halide-depth mapping, or reduced light/bias-induced ionic response, and should disappear when F is removed. XRD/GIWAXS peak positions and depth-resolved chemical analysis should show that the molecule is not incorporated as a bulk lattice component. UPS/Kelvin-probe data should verify that any average energy-level shift is small or insufficient, while PLQY/QFLS, surface-recombination velocity, tDOS/SCLC, and perovskite/C60 extraction or adhesion demonstrate the actual passivation/contact pathway.
scoring_key_points: Uses the full molecule plus deletion controls for F, pyridine N, and COOH, with matched dose and attention to solubility/dipole confounders.
Assigns Pb and FA interactions through functional-group-dependent spectroscopic/chemical evidence rather than through efficiency alone.
Requires a fluorine-dependent vacancy/ion-migration diagnostic to support the halide-vacancy function.
Rules out bulk lattice incorporation and dominant work-function shifting using diffraction/depth profiling and energy-level measurements.
accepted_equivalents: A fractional-factorial molecular library with positional isomers is acceptable if it independently varies the three functional motifs.
DFT-calculated binding energies may support, but cannot replace, functional-group deletion experiments.
Thermally stimulated current, transient ion drift, bias-dependent PL, ToF-SIMS, or activation-energy measurements are acceptable vacancy/ion-migration probes.
common_wrong_answers: Uses only the full molecule and an untreated control.
Assigns all three functions from one Pb 4f shift or from higher PCE.
Treats fluorine detection as proof that halide vacancies are passivated.
Interprets a small UPS shift as sufficient explanation for all Voc and FF gains without recombination diagnostics.

expected_answer: The transfer should begin in single-junction top-cell structures using a fixed more-Br-rich composition, fixed thickness, identical contacts, and a passivator concentration series with an untreated control. Because the bandgap is changing relative to the original system, voltage must be compared through Eg/q − Voc, radiative-limit voltage loss, QFLS, or external electroluminescence efficiency rather than absolute Voc alone. EQE and optical modelling should separate any absorption or thickness change from extraction, and the top-cell thickness should be adjusted only in a controlled current-matching step. Chemical transfer requires evidence that the passivator still reduces Pb/halide-related traps, surface-recombination velocity, and perovskite/C60 contact loss in the Br-rich film; unchanged or improved adhesion is also important on texture. Operando PL spectra and maps under one-sun open circuit and MPP, optionally with electrical bias and temperature variation, should track iodide-rich emission, while GIWAXS/XRD, ion-depth profiling, or transient ion-drift tests assess structural segregation and halide migration. Only after these criteria are met should matched textured tandems be fabricated. Success is lower bandgap-normalized voltage loss and higher stabilized FF/Voc with no loss of EQE current matching, no accelerated phase segregation, and improved MPP durability. A higher reverse-scan tandem PCE caused by a thinner top cell or altered current balance is not sufficient.
scoring_key_points: Uses a fixed Br-rich composition and stack with a passivator dose series before transferring to tandems.
Normalizes voltage to bandgap/radiative limit and controls EQE, thickness, and current matching when interpreting Voc and Jsc.
Tests defect passivation, perovskite/C60 extraction/adhesion, and operando mixed-halide segregation or ion migration.
Defines tandem success by stabilized, current-matched Voc/FF and durability gains rather than scan PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Absolute PLQY-derived QFLS, EQEEL, or detailed-balance voltage loss are acceptable bandgap-normalized voltage metrics.
Bias-dependent hyperspectral PL, environmental GIWAXS, or time-resolved electroluminescence may diagnose phase segregation.
A four-terminal optical/electrical screening stage is acceptable before committing to two-terminal current-matched tandems.
common_wrong_answers: Compares absolute Voc between different bandgaps without normalization.
Changes Br fraction, absorber thickness, and passivator dose simultaneously and attributes all effects to passivation.
Uses only dark storage and ignores illumination-driven mixed-halide segregation.
Claims successful transfer from a higher scan PCE despite worsened current matching or stabilized output.

expected_answer: UPS or another mean work-function measurement spatially averages over covered domains, uncovered ITO, dipole patches, and molecular aggregates. Two layers can therefore have the same average energy level but very different local extraction barriers and electric fields. A patchy HSL produces nonuniform precursor wetting and nucleation, local contact gaps, and lateral variations in band bending. These variations create recombination hotspots and spatially nonuniform carrier accumulation. They can also generate heterogeneous crystal orientation and residual strain; strain gradients and local electrostatic/chemical-potential gradients lower the barrier for halide redistribution. Under illumination, the same regions accumulate carriers and drive iodide-rich domain formation, reducing QFLS, Voc, and FF. Aggregation should be varied without changing the molecular ratio—for example by changing ethanol/water content, concentration, temperature, aging time, filtration, sonication, or deposition method while verifying identical surface stoichiometry by XPS. DLS should confirm aggregate-size changes, KPFM and coverage mapping should confirm altered local potential variance, and wetting must be measured as a covariate. If reduced aggregation at fixed composition systematically narrows CPD, lowers microstrain by Williamson–Hall/GIWAXS analysis, suppresses operando PL segregation, and improves recombination/FF metrics, aggregation-driven interfacial heterogeneity is causal rather than merely correlated.
scoring_key_points: Explains that mean work function averages over local coverage/dipole variations and cannot capture nanoscale extraction barriers or uncovered regions.
Links patchy HSL coverage to nonuniform wetting/nucleation, local fields, recombination, and carrier accumulation.
Connects strain/electrostatic heterogeneity to illumination-driven halide redistribution and iodide-rich phase formation.
Proposes a fixed-composition processing experiment that varies aggregation and verifies DLS, KPFM/coverage, strain, operando PL, and device responses.
accepted_equivalents: Local density-of-states mapping, scanning Kelvin probe, photoelectron microscopy, or conductive AFM may replace conventional KPFM.
Co-solvent, temperature, concentration, aging, filtration, or vapour-deposition controls are acceptable if molecular composition and dose remain fixed.
Microstrain may be quantified by Williamson–Hall analysis, grazing-incidence diffraction, Raman mapping, or nanodiffraction.
common_wrong_answers: Treats identical average work function as proof of identical interfacial energetics.
Attributes phase segregation only to bulk halide composition and ignores buried-interface heterogeneity.
Changes the molecular blend ratio while claiming to isolate aggregation.
Uses DLS alone without verifying the deposited monolayer, perovskite strain, or operando phase behaviour.

expected_answer: The experiment should compare each HSL in both a wide-bandgap single-junction cell and an otherwise identical full tandem, while keeping the organic rear subcell and interconnection process fixed. Organic-only cells and interconnection witness structures should be aged in parallel. To make the single-junction and tandem comparisons meaningful, the wide-bandgap absorber should experience the same absorbed photon flux, temperature, and approximate operating voltage; spectral bias or four-terminal monitoring can be used to achieve this. Stress should include MPP operation, open-circuit illumination—which maximizes carrier density and phase-segregation driving force—and dark thermal aging. Operando hyperspectral PL should track iodide-rich emission and recovery, while QFLS/EL, subcell-resolved EQE, transient or impedance measurements, and tandem-voltage decomposition identify recombination and contact losses. The organic subcell should be monitored for absorption/EQE loss, morphology or burn-in, and the interconnection for series resistance or recombination-layer degradation. The mixed HSL can be credited with top-cell stabilization only if suppressed segregation and preserved top-cell QFLS/Voc precede and quantitatively explain the tandem-voltage/MPP retention, while organic-only and interconnection controls age similarly across HSL cases. If tandem FF falls through rising interconnection resistance or the organic Jsc declines without a top-cell spectral/voltage signature, the lifetime gain cannot be assigned to perovskite stabilization.
scoring_key_points: Compares HSL variants in matched wide-bandgap single-junctions and full tandems while aging organic-only and interconnection controls.
Matches top-cell photon flux, temperature, and operating point and includes MPP, open-circuit illumination, and thermal stresses.
Uses operando phase-segregation, QFLS/EL, subcell-EQE, and electrical-loss diagnostics together with organic/interconnection monitoring.
Attributes the lifetime gain to the top cell only when suppressed segregation and preserved top-cell voltage causally account for tandem retention.
accepted_equivalents: Spectral-bias illumination, luminescent coupling analysis, or four-terminal test structures may be used to equalize/resolve subcell stress.
Electroluminescence imaging, impedance, Suns-Voc, transient photovoltage/current, or voltage-dependent PL may supplement subcell-resolved diagnostics.
An equivalent failure-attribution model based on time-resolved parameter decomposition is acceptable if it distinguishes top cell, organic cell, and interconnection.
common_wrong_answers: Tests only complete tandems and attributes every retention difference to the HSL.
Uses unmatched light spectra or temperatures for single-junction and tandem comparisons.
Monitors only total tandem PCE without subcell-resolved spectral or voltage diagnostics.
Interprets lower phase-segregation PL as sufficient even when organic-subcell current or interconnection resistance dominates failure.

expected_answer: There is no contradiction because the dominant decay channel changes with stack configuration. In the bare treated film, stronger steady-state emission and a longer lifetime indicate that the nonradiative recombination rate has fallen, consistent with passivation of surface or grain-boundary traps exposed during reconstruction. After C60 is added, an additional interfacial electron-transfer rate competes with radiative decay; therefore, stronger quenching and a faster decay can indicate more rapid extraction rather than a higher trap-assisted loss rate. Photoluminescence quenching by itself is non-unique and cannot separate charge transfer from nonradiative recombination. The assignment becomes credible only when the optical result is combined with controls and independent electrical evidence: pristine, solvent-only, interlayer-only, and full-treatment films measured both with and without C60; absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting on the bare films; transient extraction or photocurrent measurements on C60 stacks; and trap-density, mobility, energy-level, Voc-ideality, or electroluminescence measurements. A genuine dual-function treatment should increase bare-film radiative quality while accelerating extraction in the contacted stack and simultaneously reducing voltage loss and trap signatures.
scoring_key_points: Explains higher bare-film PL/lifetime as a reduction in the nonradiative recombination rate after defect passivation.
Explains stronger quenching after C60 as a possible increase in the interfacial charge-transfer rate rather than an optical contradiction.
States explicitly that PL quenching alone is ambiguous and cannot distinguish extraction from newly introduced nonradiative loss.
Proposes matched treatment/contact controls plus at least two independent optical-electrical diagnostics that test passivation and extraction separately.
accepted_equivalents: Rate-equation reasoning using radiative, trap-assisted, and charge-transfer rate constants
Absolute photoluminescence quantum yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting as the bare-film recombination metric
Transient photocurrent, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or selective-contact spectroscopy as an extraction diagnostic
Electroluminescence efficiency or nonradiative Voc loss as an alternative device-level corroboration
common_wrong_answers: Treating every decrease in PL intensity as proof of improved charge extraction
Claiming that a longer bare-film lifetime necessarily means slower carrier extraction in the finished device
Using only morphology or a single PL trace to assign both passivation and band alignment

expected_answer: Persistence of the voltage and vacuum-level shift across a chemically inert spacer argues against a mechanism that requires direct defect coordination. An oriented dipole should produce a reproducible sign and magnitude of work-function or vacuum-level shift, often saturating once an interfacial molecular layer is complete, while leaving the absorber bandgap essentially unchanged. Reversing molecular orientation, changing the anchoring group or counterion, disordering the layer thermally, or placing the same dipole in an architecture where the required extraction direction is reversed should predictably weaken or reverse the device effect. Charge-transfer doping would instead alter carrier density, conductivity, Fermi-level position relative to band edges, core-level spectra, capacitance, or Seebeck response and need not show the same orientation-dependent sign. Direct passivation should require physical access to defects and should primarily improve PLQY/QFLS or trap spectroscopy even without an adjacent transport layer. Generic dielectric screening should correlate mainly with dielectric constant and thickness, not molecular dipole orientation or halide-dependent vacuum-level shifts. Improved lifetime or VTFL alone is not decisive because reduced interfacial energy loss can change those observables secondarily.
scoring_key_points: Uses spacer persistence and a signed vacuum-level/work-function shift to support a non-contact electrostatic dipole mechanism.
Identifies orientation, counterion/anchoring, thermal disorder, thickness saturation, or architecture reversal as decisive dipole perturbations.
Separates charge-transfer doping by its carrier-density, conductivity, Fermi-level/core-level, capacitance, or thermopower signatures.
Explains why passivation and dielectric screening predict different contact, PLQY/QFLS, dielectric-constant, thickness, and orientation dependencies.
accepted_equivalents: Surface-potential mapping, UPS, Kelvin probe, or contact-potential difference measurements for dipole sign
Hall effect, Mott-Schottky analysis, field-effect measurements, or conductivity as doping diagnostics
Intentional molecular inversion or switching between n-i-p and p-i-n selective contacts as orientation tests
Absolute PLQY, QFLS, or deep-level spectroscopy as direct passivation tests
common_wrong_answers: Calling any UPS shift proof of chemical doping without checking carrier density or core levels
Treating longer PL lifetime or lower VTFL as unique evidence of direct defect passivation
Ignoring the predicted sign reversal or performance penalty when the dipole is placed against the wrong selective contact

expected_answer: The interlayer must be redesigned around the required sign of the potential step, not copied by chemical name. A molecule should be selected whose anchoring group binds reproducibly to either the perovskite or C60-side surface while its terminal ionic or polar group points so that the vacuum level lowers the electron-extraction barrier. Molecular head-tail polarity, counterion, spacer length, surface coverage, and packing should be tuned to obtain a monolayer-scale dipole without forming a thick low-dimensional perovskite or blocking layer. The sequence should use orthogonal solvents, controlled humidity and temperature, and preferably crosslinking or strong anchoring so that subsequent C60 deposition does not dissolve, randomize, or invert the dipoles. Validation requires UPS/Kelvin-probe confirmation of the potential-step sign after the full overlayer process, thickness-dependent transport and series resistance, transient electron-extraction or impedance measurements, Voc/FF/hysteresis and electroluminescence loss analysis, and comparison with a deliberately reversed-dipole control. Thermal, illumination, and solvent-aging tests must show that the energy shift and device benefit persist rather than arising from transient processing chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Selects or reverses molecular head-tail orientation so the potential step lowers the electron-extraction barrier in p-i-n architecture.
Limits coverage and thickness to avoid a resistive 2D or organic barrier while controlling counterion, packing, and anchoring.
Uses orthogonal-solvent, ordered-deposition, crosslinking, or robust anchoring strategies that preserve dipole orientation during C60 coating.
Validates post-processing dipole sign, electron extraction, resistance/Voc losses, reversed-dipole controls, and thermal/light/solvent stability.
accepted_equivalents: Using a molecule with reversed permanent dipole moment or swapping the surface anchoring end
A self-assembled monolayer, zwitterion, or ultrathin polymer with controlled dipole orientation
Inverse photoemission or contact-potential mapping as alternatives for energy-level validation
Transient photocurrent, impedance spectroscopy, or charge-extraction measurements for electron-transfer validation
common_wrong_answers: Applying the same PEABr layer and assuming chemical passivation will overcome an unfavorable dipole direction
Increasing interlayer thickness to maximize surface coverage without checking tunneling or series-resistance penalties
Measuring UPS before C60 deposition but not verifying that the dipole survives the subsequent solvent, vacuum, or thermal process

expected_answer: A coherent model is that SCN− temporarily coordinates undercoordinated Pb or forms soluble/intermediate lead-thiocyanate complexes, increasing local ionic mobility and enabling partial surface or grain-boundary dissolution followed by recrystallization into larger grains. During washing or annealing, SCN-containing intermediates decompose, desorb, or leave the film, explaining the absence of residual sulfur. PEAI can remain near surfaces or boundaries and form a thin layered-perovskite-like phase that passivates the final structure; this residual phase is therefore chemically distinct from the transient regrowth agent. The critical controls are MASCN-only, PEAI-only, the mixed treatment, a noncomplexing methylammonium salt, and time/temperature/dose series. In-situ GIWAXS/XRD, optical microscopy, mass spectrometry of evolved species, and time-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS should show transient SCN-containing intermediates before grain enlargement and sulfur loss after annealing. Isotopically labeled SCN would strengthen the mass balance. The mixed treatment should exceed PEAI-only grain growth, while PEAI-only may retain surface passivation without the same topological regrowth. Permanent-SCN passivation would instead require measurable residual sulfur correlated with the final electronic benefit.
scoring_key_points: Proposes transient SCN-Pb complexation or partial dissolution that increases ionic mobility and drives grain-boundary regrowth.
Interprets sulfur disappearance as removal of the transient species while the n = 2 feature is assigned mainly to residual PEAI-derived surface passivation.
Includes MASCN-only, PEAI-only, mixed, noncomplexing-salt, and time/temperature/dose controls.
Uses time-resolved structural and depth/composition measurements with predicted intermediate formation, grain growth, and final sulfur loss.
accepted_equivalents: SCN-assisted Ostwald ripening, defect-mediated recrystallization, or transient solvate/intermediate formation
In-situ synchrotron GIWAXS, Raman, infrared, XPS, ToF-SIMS, or evolved-gas analysis
Stable-isotope tracing of sulfur or nitrogen to demonstrate removal
Cross-sectional microscopy showing reduced horizontal boundary continuity as a regrowth outcome
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that undetectable sulfur proves thiocyanate never participated in the process
Assigning grain enlargement solely to a permanent 2D PEAI cap without a transient reconstruction step
Calling SCN a permanent passivator while providing no residual-composition or time-resolved evidence

expected_answer: The main risks are nonuniform wetting and reaction time over large area, uncontrolled solvent penetration to the buried interface, spatially varying grain regrowth, excess PEAI-derived layered phase that raises contact resistance, and compatibility of the treated surface with C60, ALD SnO2, and sputter damage. Wide-bandgap films also require checks for halide segregation, stress redistribution, and nonuniform optical thickness. The process should replace uncontrolled spin dosing with a metered meniscus, slot-die, spray, or vapor-assisted step, followed by tightly controlled dwell, drying, wash, and anneal conditions. Spatial maps of thickness, grain topology, composition, PLQY/QFLS, and side-selective lifetime should be linked to electroluminescence, series-resistance, shunt, and local photocurrent maps. The semitransparent device must retain transmission and top-cell EQE, with the filtered silicon response used to verify tandem current and optical balance. Area-dependent statistics, stabilized power, thermal/light soaking, bias stress, and post-stress phase/luminescence maps are required. A voltage gain accompanied by lower FF, reduced transmission, local shunts, or accelerated phase segregation is not a successful transfer.
scoring_key_points: Identifies large-area wetting/reaction nonuniformity, buried-interface penetration, excess 2D-phase resistance, and contact-process compatibility as primary risks.
Proposes metered scalable coating with controlled dwell, drying, washing, and annealing rather than simple spin-process replication.
Requires spatially resolved morphology/composition and recombination maps linked to local electrical loss diagnostics.
Verifies semitransparent EQE/transmission, filtered bottom-cell response, area statistics, and operational/phase-segregation stability with no FF or optical penalty.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, slot-die, ultrasonic spray, or vapor transport as scalable post-treatment delivery
Hyperspectral PL, EL imaging, LBIC, lock-in thermography, or microwave photoconductance mapping
Four-terminal power summation or two-terminal current-matching analysis depending on tandem architecture
Bias-light stress and compositional mapping to test light-induced halide segregation
common_wrong_answers: Judging scale-up only by champion Voc from one large-area device
Ignoring the possibility that a thicker layered passivation phase improves Voc but lowers FF and transparency
Testing film stability alone without the C60/SnO2/transparent-electrode process stack

expected_answer: PL quenching and a short lifetime are supportive but not sufficient because both interfacial transfer and trap-assisted recombination remove photocarriers. The extraction interpretation becomes strong when independent measurements align. A favorable SnO2 work-function shift measured by Kelvin probe or KPFM establishes a reduced electron-extraction barrier but does not prove low recombination. Higher and more spatially uniform c-AFM current establishes that the mixed layer does not behave as an insulating dipole film. Lower trap-filled-limit voltage and XPS evidence for fewer oxygen-vacancy or hydroxyl-related SnO2 defects support chemical passivation rather than new trap creation. Suppression of cathodic reverse-current or other charge-accumulation signatures under operation provides the most direct dynamic link to reduced interfacial carrier storage and ion-migration driving force. Unchanged perovskite crystallinity, thickness, and morphology rule out gross film-quality changes. The full interpretation should also be consistent with higher Voc or lower hysteresis, improved PEC onset/current, and ideally absolute PLQY/QFLS or selective-contact controls. No single listed technique is decisive; the necessary evidence is convergence of energetics, conductivity, trap chemistry, and operating-state accumulation diagnostics.
scoring_key_points: States that PL quenching and shorter TRPL are intrinsically ambiguous between extraction and nonradiative loss.
Uses work-function alignment and c-AFM conductivity together to show a lower barrier without an insulating interlayer.
Uses lower VTFL and XPS defect reduction to support genuine chemical passivation rather than new trap formation.
Treats suppressed reverse-current/charge accumulation plus unchanged morphology and improved device/PEC behavior as the dynamic corroboration required for the extraction assignment.
accepted_equivalents: Transient photocurrent, transient photovoltage, impedance, TAS, or operando potential mapping as charge-accumulation diagnostics
Absolute PLQY or QFLS measured with and without the selective contact as an additional recombination control
Electron-only devices, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or contact-resistance measurements as alternatives to c-AFM
Oxygen-vacancy, hydroxyl, or undercoordinated-Sn passivation as equivalent SnO2 defect descriptions
common_wrong_answers: Declaring faster extraction solely because PL intensity and lifetime decrease
Treating a work-function shift alone as proof that interfacial recombination has been suppressed
Ignoring the possibility that an organic dipole layer can improve alignment while simultaneously increasing resistance

expected_answer: The redesign should shorten and lower the resistance of the electron path by placing the HER catalyst as close as possible to the electron-selective contact, using a direct vertical contact, conductive grid, low-resistance transparent electrode, or chemically compatible conductive encapsulant rather than a long lateral SnO2-to-TCO-to-Pt route. The SnO2/TCO junction should be engineered with an ohmic, defect-passivated interlayer, and catalyst loading must be optimized without shading or damaging the perovskite. Photovoltage and current matching between photoanode and photocathode must be retained. Diagnose each electrode first in a three-electrode configuration, then in the coupled unbiased system. Use EIS, transient current/voltage, operando potential mapping, and local current or thermal imaging to locate resistance and accumulation. Compare gas evolution and Faradaic efficiency with photocurrent and solar-to-hydrogen efficiency. Post-operation XPS/ToF-SIMS/XRD/PL should test interfacial ion migration, phase damage, and catalyst/contact corrosion. Acceptance requires lower series and charge-transfer resistance, disappearance of accumulation transients, stable electrode potentials, unchanged gas selectivity, and longer coupled-system retention. If degradation simply shifts to the catalyst, encapsulation, or photoanode, the bottleneck has moved rather than been eliminated.
scoring_key_points: Redesigns the photocathode to shorten the electron path and reduce SnO2/TCO/Pt contact and lateral-transport resistance.
Includes ohmic/passivated contact engineering and catalyst integration while preserving optical transmission and current/photovoltage matching.
Uses isolated-electrode and coupled-system tests with impedance, transients, operando potential/current mapping, and gas/Faradaic-efficiency measurements.
Defines materials post-mortem and system-level criteria that distinguish elimination of the bottleneck from merely shifting degradation elsewhere.
accepted_equivalents: Direct catalyst deposition on a protected electron-selective contact, a metal mesh, or a conductive adhesive/carbon interlayer
Reference-electrode probes in the two-photoelectrode system to resolve individual electrode potentials
Scanning electrochemical microscopy, distributed voltage probes, or lock-in thermography for local loss mapping
Hydrogen evolution rate, Faradaic efficiency, and STH retention as system-level outputs
common_wrong_answers: Adding more Pt without addressing the long resistive electron path or buried charge accumulation
Testing only the full unbiased device, so the failing electrode cannot be identified
Calling the redesign successful when initial current rises but Faradaic efficiency, optical transmission, or long-term retention worsens

expected_answer: A shorter perovskite/ETL PL lifetime can reflect rapid electron transfer into the ETL, but it can also reflect newly introduced nonradiative interface states; lifetime shortening is therefore ambiguous without an absolute photon-balance or device-voltage measurement. The GIWAXS and electron-only mobility results support a packing-controlled transport mechanism: enantiopure molecules can form a more coherent, oriented network with fewer energetic or structural bottlenecks even though their isolated-molecule HOMO and LUMO levels are unchanged. Higher bulk mobility should reduce electron accumulation, series resistance, and recombination under load, improving fill factor and potentially Voc. To separate the steps, first measure absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting for bare perovskite, perovskite/ETL bilayers, and complete contact stacks at matched absorbed flux. Efficient transfer with low added recombination gives strong quenching but preserves a high implied voltage; defective quenching lowers both PLQY and implied voltage. Second, determine thickness- and temperature-dependent ETL conductivity or mobility in electron-only and contactless measurements. A bulk-mobility origin should persist away from the perovskite interface and scale with packing and thickness. Third, use ultrafast or time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy, transient absorption, or field-dependent transient photocurrent to measure transfer kinetics separately from recombination. Finally, compare electroluminescence efficiency, ideality factor, impedance, and Voc versus light intensity.
