Interfacial nonradiative recombination produces larger nonradiative voltage loss and recombination signatures, whereas improved transfer and transport should increase collection and reduce charge accumulation without an implied-voltage penalty.
scoring_key_points: Explains the fundamental ambiguity of PL quenching between charge transfer and nonradiative recombination.
Links enantiopure molecular packing and orientational order to bulk transport without invoking a frontier-energy-level change.
Separates bulk mobility, interfacial transfer kinetics, and interfacial recombination using orthogonal measurements and sample structures.
States distinct predicted signatures, especially whether strong quenching preserves or reduces quasi-Fermi-level splitting and electroluminescence efficiency.
accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved microwave conductivity, Hall measurements, or space-charge-limited current with rigorous injection corrections may be used for ETL transport.
Surface photovoltage, photo-CELIV, charge-extraction-by-linearly-increasing-voltage, or transient photovoltage may replace one of the listed dynamic probes.
Reciprocity-derived nonradiative voltage loss may replace direct electroluminescence-efficiency analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Equating faster PL decay automatically with more efficient electron extraction.
Attributing the performance gain to different HOMO or LUMO levels despite the stated energetic equivalence.
Using SCLC mobility alone to prove faster interfacial transfer.
Failing to provide contrasting predictions for transport improvement versus added interface recombination.

expected_answer: Use untreated, optimized, and excessive-additive formulations in Sn-only cells, Sn-Pb subcells, tandem-relevant half stacks, and complete encapsulated tandems. Apply a blocked factorial stress matrix that separates dry oxygen, controlled humidity, illumination, temperature, and electrical operating point, followed by combined maximum-power-point stress representative of service. Include dark heat, light without bias, open circuit, short circuit, MPP, and reverse-bias or current-mismatch conditions because oxidation and ion motion can be field dependent. Operando or interrupted measurements should track Sn(IV)/Sn(II) by XPS, X-ray absorption, or calibrated chemical spectroscopy; structural evolution by GIWAXS; absolute PLQY or implied voltage; stabilized power; hysteresis, impedance, and ionic capacitance; and depth profiles of acetate, ammonium, halide, Sn, and interconnect metals. Contact-angle measurements are only supporting evidence and cannot establish oxidative stability. Half-stack comparisons should reveal whether residual ionic liquid reacts with PEDOT:PSS or alternative hole contacts, C60, recombination layers, or encapsulants, and whether it changes adhesion or outgassing. A credible benefit requires slower Sn(IV) accumulation and lower nonradiative voltage loss under oxygen-containing operational stress, no harmful additive migration or interfacial resistance growth, preserved tandem current matching and interconnect voltage, and statistically improved T80 or integrated energy yield across multiple batches. Reject the transfer if the benefit disappears outside nitrogen, depends on an excessive dose, or merely delays initial crystallization while long-term oxidation, ion accumulation, or contact degradation accelerates.
scoring_key_points: Separates oxygen, humidity, light, heat, and bias effects before applying realistic combined MPP stress.
Tracks Sn oxidation, phase evolution, nonradiative loss, ionic response, and depth-resolved additive or halide redistribution rather than relying on contact angle or scan PCE.
Tests compatibility with transport layers, recombination contacts, encapsulants, and tandem current or voltage matching using half stacks and complete tandems.
Defines quantitative acceptance around slower Sn(IV) growth, stabilized energy yield or T80, absence of migration or resistance penalties, and batch reproducibility.
accepted_equivalents: Isotope-labeled acetate or ammonium tracing is an acceptable enhanced method for additive migration.
Indoor-spectrum or concentrated-light operation may be substituted for one-sun testing if the intended application is explicitly defined.
A hermeticity-normalized comparison is acceptable when different encapsulation systems are evaluated.
common_wrong_answers: Treating nitrogen storage or nitrogen heating as sufficient evidence for air-operational stability.
Using water contact angle as the principal proof of oxidation resistance.
Ignoring field-driven additive or halide migration into tandem contacts.
Reporting only initial and final J-V scans without stabilized MPP or chemical-state tracking.

expected_answer: The toughness increase can contain several additive terms. Silane groups can hydrolyze and condense with hydroxylated glass or TCO, raising the local adhesive strength inside an infiltrated scribe. A scribe perpendicular to crack advance can interrupt the weak planar interface, force crack deflection into a tougher path, and create polymer bridges that stretch or pull out; a parallel scribe may guide the crack and engage less bonded area. The polymer also dissipates energy through rate- and temperature-dependent viscoelastic deformation, so a high measured Gc is not automatically evidence of stronger covalent bonding. Thermal cycling may promote further silane condensation, improve wetting and infiltration, relax lamination voids, or change polymer crystallinity, but it could also introduce residual stresses. The control matrix should include silane-grafted and ungrafted POE matched in modulus and thickness, blocked or hydrolysis-inhibited silane chemistry, hydroxylated versus deliberately dehydroxylated oxide surfaces, filled versus empty scribes, and geometries with equal area fraction but varied orientation and pitch. DCB tests should span crack velocities and temperatures; covalent-bond gains should remain relatively less rate dependent, whereas viscoelastic dissipation should follow time-temperature superposition. In situ crack imaging, compliance calibration, and cohesive-versus-adhesive surface analysis by profilometry, XPS, ToF-SIMS, or microscopy should locate failure. Pre- and post-cycle chemical spectroscopy should test siloxane growth, while modulus and crystallinity measurements test polymer evolution. A finite-element or cohesive-zone model fitted across orientations can then separate geometrical crack-path effects from intrinsic interfacial toughness.
scoring_key_points: Separates chemical adhesion, geometrical crack deflection or bridging, polymer pull-out, and rate-dependent viscoelastic dissipation.
Explains why perpendicular and parallel scribes can engage the crack differently even at similar area fraction.
Uses matched chemical, surface, infiltration, and geometry controls plus rate- and temperature-dependent DCB testing.
Includes failure-surface localization and pre/post-cycling chemical or polymer-state measurements to test the cause of post-cycle strengthening.
accepted_equivalents: Peel, wedge, four-point-bend, or mixed-mode fracture tests may supplement DCB if mode mixity and energy release rate are quantified.
Dynamic mechanical analysis and time-temperature superposition are acceptable ways to isolate viscoelastic contributions.
Cohesive-zone, phase-field, or extended finite-element modeling may be used for the crack-path decomposition.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all fracture-energy gain to silane covalent bonds without considering geometry or polymer dissipation.
Assuming more scribe area alone explains the orientation effect.
Using one crack speed and one temperature, which cannot separate viscoelasticity from adhesion.
Claiming thermal cycling is beneficial without checking residual stress, polymer crystallinity, or continued silane reaction.

expected_answer: The design variable should be treated as a multiobjective problem, not as a search for maximum DCB fracture energy. Build a parameter matrix over scribe width, pitch, transverse-anchor spacing, orientation, oxide exposure, silane density, lamination temperature, and encapsulant rheology. Use realistic P1-P3 patterns and registration distributions from the production tool. Measure geometric fill factor, dead-area optical loss, series resistance, shunt resistance, isolation voltage, leakage current, and subcell mismatch together with DCB or mixed-mode toughness and crack-growth resistance. Because brittle module failure is statistical, test many specimens and fit Weibull or survival distributions rather than compare only mean Gc. Couple experiments to finite-element or cohesive-zone models that include thermal-expansion mismatch, crack orientation, and local stress concentration. Qualification should include thermal cycling, damp heat, humidity-freeze, mechanical load, hail or impact surrogates, flexure, and combined bias-temperature-humidity stress. Cross-sectional imaging and moisture tracing must verify that filled scribes remain void-free and do not become diffusion channels; electrical mapping after stress should detect scribe-edge shunts. The commercial optimum is a Pareto point that meets a minimum lower-confidence-bound toughness or crack-arrest probability while preserving target geometric fill factor, insulation, stabilized power, and manufacturing yield. Acceptance also requires robustness to worst-case scribe width, offset, incomplete POE fill, and silane-lot variation. A layout should be rejected if its mechanics benefit depends on laboratory-perfect alignment, degrades electrical isolation, or produces post-aging moisture ingress despite a favorable initial Gc.
scoring_key_points: Frames the task as multiobjective optimization over geometry, chemistry, lamination, and manufacturing-error distributions rather than maximizing toughness alone.
Measures fracture distributions together with fill factor, optical dead area, resistance, isolation, leakage, mismatch, and stabilized module output.
Uses coupled environmental, thermal, electrical, and mechanical qualification with imaging or moisture tracing of filled scribes.
Defines commercialization criteria using lower-confidence mechanical reliability, electrical safety and performance, process tolerance, and manufacturing yield.
accepted_equivalents: Bayesian optimization, robust design of experiments, or Pareto-front analysis are acceptable optimization frameworks.
Peel strength, crack-growth rate, or probability of crack arrest may replace a single Gc threshold if statistically justified.
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, or dark-current mapping are acceptable scribe-edge failure diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing the densest scribe pattern solely because it maximizes fracture energy.
Ignoring insulation resistance, leakage, or scribe-edge shunting.
Using only mean toughness from a few specimens instead of reliability distributions.
Assuming laboratory scribe width, alignment, and encapsulant filling can be reproduced without tolerance analysis.

expected_answer: First define the target use case and outcomes: stabilized top-cell efficiency or tandem energy yield, voltage loss relative to detailed balance, current collection relative to the bandgap limit, area and yield, and operational stability under a specified protocol. Clean impossible records, retain provenance, and normalize Voc, Jsc, and PCE to bandgap-dependent limits rather than compare raw values across Eg. Stratify or model jointly by composition, device polarity, transport layers, additives, area, year, and measurement protocol. A multilevel or causal model should include laboratory or publication random effects and propensity or overlap checks so that a transport stack is not credited for being used only in easier compositions or by high-performing groups. Report uncertainty intervals and require adequate effective sample size. Stability missingness is likely not random; therefore describe reporting propensity, perform complete-case and inverse-probability or pattern-mixture sensitivity analyses, and do not impute long lifetime from absent data. Rank candidate stacks by a conservative lower-confidence utility combining normalized performance, reproducibility, area scaling, and standardized MPP durability, with penalties for sparse evidence and protocol heterogeneity. Then prospectively fabricate a preregistered factorial subset using matched absorbers and identical measurement conditions. Measure stabilized J-V, implied and device Voc losses, light-soaking behavior, phase segregation, and encapsulated MPP stability with multiple batches. Advance a stack only if the prospective result agrees with the database prediction within a predefined tolerance and improves the lower-bound utility, not merely the champion value. A stack with excellent reported PCE but poor overlap, high missingness, or unstable prospective performance should be rejected.
scoring_key_points: Defines application-relevant normalized outcomes and cleans records while retaining provenance and measurement metadata.
Controls composition, polarity, contacts, area, year, laboratory, and protocol using stratification, multilevel modeling, or causal-overlap methods.
Treats stability missingness as potentially informative and reports uncertainty, effective sample size, and sensitivity to missing-data assumptions.
Requires preregistered matched fabrication and standardized MPP or segregation validation before advancing a stack, using a conservative lower-bound decision rule.
accepted_equivalents: Targeted maximum likelihood, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, causal forests, or doubly robust estimators are acceptable if overlap and confounding assumptions are addressed.
External validation on a held-out laboratory or time period may supplement prospective fabrication but should not replace it entirely.
A Pareto rule over voltage loss, current collection, stability, area, and evidence quality may replace a scalar utility.
common_wrong_answers: Ranking architectures by raw median or champion PCE without bandgap normalization.
Treating missing stability reports as zero degradation or as missing completely at random.
Ignoring laboratory, year, device area, and measurement-protocol confounding.
Using database correlations as the final decision without matched prospective validation.

expected_answer: Because the conventional film-quality and defect metrics are matched, the remaining plausible advantage of additive B is a grain-boundary electrostatic ion-caging effect. A symmetric negative-positive-negative potential can repel a migrating halide or charged vacancy from either neighboring grain and raise the effective migration barrier in both directions, whereas an asymmetric dipole may assist migration on one side even if it binds undercoordinated Pb. The mechanism requires B to be localized at grain boundaries rather than incorporated randomly into the lattice. A decisive test set should therefore combine chemical localization with ion-transport measurements. ToF-SIMS, labeled-molecule depth profiling, nano-IR, or cross-sectional spectroscopy should show grain-boundary enrichment; KPFM or electrostatic-force microscopy should reveal a reproducible local potential pattern. Temperature-dependent ionic conductivity, bias-stress transient current, impedance, or isotope-tracer diffusion should yield a higher activation energy or lower halide diffusivity for B despite matched electronic trap density. Operando PL mapping and XRD under light plus forward/reverse bias should test whether suppression follows ion-driving force and remains spatially uniform. Finally, depth-resolved GIXRD, strain mapping, and a strain-matched control must show that the segregation difference persists without a corresponding strain difference. Computed migration barriers for the matched additives can support, but not replace, these experimental discriminants.
scoring_key_points: Identify symmetric bidirectional electrostatic repulsion at grain boundaries as the extra ion-migration barrier beyond matched passivation.
Require direct evidence that the macrocycle is localized at grain boundaries and produces a distinct local electrostatic potential.
Measure ionic activation energy or diffusivity under temperature and bias while holding electronic defect density and morphology constant.
Use operando segregation measurements plus strain-matched GIXRD or strain mapping to reject strain and ordinary film-quality explanations.
accepted_equivalents: Electrostatic grain-boundary cage, Coulombic ion confinement, or symmetric field barrier
Halide-vacancy migration may be discussed instead of direct halide-ion migration
Isotope exchange, scanning-probe ion microscopy, transient ion-drift, or bias-dependent ToF-SIMS as ion-transport measurements
Finite-element electrostatics and NEB calculations as supporting evidence when paired with experimental validation
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the result only to larger grains or fewer traps even though those variables are explicitly matched
Claiming that any strong molecular dipole must suppress migration in both directions
Using PL intensity alone as proof that halide diffusion is slower
Treating a calculated barrier or a single ex situ XRD scan as decisive without localization and operando ion-transport evidence

expected_answer: The molecular gate is not simply maximum binding strength. The cavity and electrostatic pattern must remain compatible with the local Pb-halide coordination environment, the molecule must be chemically and thermally stable, and its loading must be low enough to avoid an insulating grain-boundary network. An analog and concentration matrix should measure Pb binding, precursor-colloid behavior, nucleation, grain-boundary localization, energy levels, carrier mobility, and ionic activation energy. The process gate must establish compatibility with slot-die solvents, drying gradients, coating speed, and large-area crystallization. Area-resolved PL/QFLS, composition, thickness, and ToF-SIMS or chemical mapping should verify uniform distribution without edge accumulation, phase precipitation, pinholes, or excessive series resistance. The stability gate must separate intrinsic mixed-halide stabilization from environmental barrier effects. Compare encapsulated and unencapsulated films/devices under one-sun and MPP in dry N2, controlled oxygen, controlled humidity, and heat, with dark-rest remixing tests and operando PL/XRD or spectral-EQE tracking. Dry-N2 light/bias tests isolate photo/bias-driven segregation; humidity tests evaluate the additional barrier function. Tandem qualification must also preserve top-cell bandgap, voltage, current matching, recombination-junction compatibility, and module-scale uniformity. The route is accepted only if reduced segregation and voltage loss persist under dry MPP stress while electronic transport, tandem current matching, and reproducibility remain within predefined limits.
scoring_key_points: Screen cavity/electrostatic compatibility and loading against Pb binding, ionic migration, carrier transport, and insulating-boundary risk.
Establish a slot-die process window with area-resolved chemical, optical, and electrical uniformity rather than relying on small spin-coated cells.
Separate intrinsic light/bias segregation suppression from moisture-barrier effects using dry-N2, humidity, heat, dark-remixing, and operando tests.
Qualify the tandem on bandgap, voltage loss, current matching, recombination-junction compatibility, MPP stability, and module reproducibility.
accepted_equivalents: Blade coating, inkjet coating, or other scalable wet coating in place of slot-die coating
Absolute PL, EL imaging, hyperspectral PL, or implied-VOC mapping for spatial voltage-loss assessment
Temperature-dependent bias stress or isotope diffusion as intrinsic ion-migration qualification
A pass/fail criterion based on no measurable FF or mobility penalty together with reduced segregation under dry MPP
common_wrong_answers: Increasing additive concentration until segregation disappears without checking electronic transport
Using only damp-heat or shelf storage to claim intrinsic photostability
Assuming molecular behavior and localization are unchanged when moving from spin coating to slot-die coating
Ignoring tandem current matching and recombination-junction losses because the single-junction film appears stable

expected_answer: Higher PLQY and VOC indicate lower nonradiative recombination, but they do not prove efficient extraction. Excessive low-n material can passivate traps while forming a thick quantum-confined, electronically resistive layer; this should increase contact resistance, produce strong low-n optical or diffraction signatures, and cause a coverage- or dose-dependent FF/JSC penalty. Unfavorable orientation can give the same chemistry and phase fraction but place insulating organic spacers perpendicular to the desired transport direction. Angle- and depth-resolved GIWAXS should distinguish in-plane from out-of-plane orientation, and polarization-resolved spectroscopy or anisotropic transport can support the assignment. Energetic misalignment can preserve passivation yet create a hole- or electron-extraction barrier. UPS/IPES, KPFM, and temperature-dependent contact transport should reveal an adverse band offset or interfacial dipole. The sequence should first quantify phase fraction and n-value distribution by low-angle XRD, absorption, and depth-resolved PL; then determine orientation by GIWAXS; then measure band alignment and work-function changes; finally connect these results to transient absorption, excitation-side-dependent TRPL, impedance, TPC, and selective-carrier devices. Ligand dose, annealing, and molecular structure should be varied independently. Reducing concentration or favoring higher-n phases addresses overconversion; promoting vertical orientation addresses spacer geometry; tuning fluorination, aromatic substitution, chain length, or terminal functionality addresses the band offset while retaining passivation.
scoring_key_points: Recognize that passivation can raise PLQY/VOC while a low-n transport barrier lowers FF or JSC.
Use angle/depth-resolved structural measurements to separate excessive phase fraction from unfavorable crystallite orientation.
Measure interface energetics and temperature/contact transport to identify a chemically passivated but misaligned junction.
Correlate dose and molecular modifications with phase, orientation, energetics, and extraction rather than relying on PL alone.
accepted_equivalents: Quasi-2D phase distribution or n-value distribution in place of low-n coverage
NEXAFS, polarized GIWAXS, or polarized absorption as orientation probes
Inverse photoemission, ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy, surface photovoltage, or Kelvin probe for energetic alignment
SCLC, contact-resistivity, impedance, or carrier-selective half-cells for transport-barrier diagnosis
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that higher PLQY necessarily means faster charge extraction
Treating all 2D phases as equivalent regardless of n value or orientation
Assigning the lower FF only to bulk defects despite the higher VOC and PLQY
Changing ligand chemistry and processing simultaneously so that phase, orientation, and energetics cannot be separated

expected_answer: The screen should be architecture-specific. In an inverted device the ligand-derived phase must be localized at the intended bottom or top interface without blocking the carrier that must cross that junction. Molecular descriptors should include binding functionality toward undercoordinated Pb/halide vacancies, ammonium multiplicity, aromaticity or fluorination, chain length, dipole, rigidity, hydrophobicity, thermal stability, and the propensity to form low-n versus higher-n phases. Long hydrophobic chains and strong 2D formation may improve moisture resistance but can create transport barriers; diammonium, multipoint-bonding, cross-linkable, or moderately fluorinated ligands may better suppress ion motion and interdiffusion if orientation and thickness are controlled. Computational screening can rank binding, band offsets, and migration barriers, but the process screen must measure solubility, solvent orthogonality, coating rheology, drying sensitivity, and phase/orientation uniformity across the blade-coated area. Use GIWAXS/XRD, depth-resolved PL, UPS/KPFM, PLQY/QFLS, ion-drift measurements, and contact-resistance maps to impose go/no-go limits on n-value distribution, orientation, energetic offset, and transport. Stability qualification should use encapsulated modules under stabilized MPP at heat, damp heat, light-soak, and thermal cycling, with chemical depth profiling to detect ligand/cation interdiffusion and ion migration. The winning ligand is not the most hydrophobic or the highest-PL candidate; it is the one that reproducibly maintains QFLS, FF, phase distribution, and interfacial chemistry over large area and stress.
scoring_key_points: Define architecture-specific ligand location and carrier selectivity before choosing molecular chemistry.
Balance binding, hydrophobicity, ion blocking, thermal/interdiffusion resistance, low-n formation, orientation, and electronic coupling.
Include scalable-solvent, rheology, drying, and large-area phase/energetic/transport uniformity gates for blade coating.
Select from encapsulated mini-module MPP, damp-heat, thermal-cycling, and post-aging depth-profile evidence, not initial PL or PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die coating or another scalable meniscus coating in place of blade coating
Molecular dynamics or high-throughput DFT for ligand binding, band alignment, and ion-migration ranking
Cross-linked polymer-ligand networks as an interdiffusion-suppression strategy
EL/QFLS imaging, hyperspectral PL, or Suns-VOC mapping as large-area recombination diagnostics
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the longest alkyl ligand solely for hydrophobicity
Ignoring whether the ligand-derived layer is at the correct interface for an inverted architecture
Screening only spin-coated small cells and assuming blade-coated phase distribution will match
Using storage stability without stabilized MPP, damp heat, or evidence of interdiffusion and ion migration

expected_answer: The redesign must decouple electronic selectivity from a brittle, abrupt interface. The low-dimensional phase should be kept ultrathin or graded rather than converted deeply, and its ligand can be modified toward a more compliant, multipoint-binding, or cross-linkable spacer that anchors both the perovskite and carbon without creating a thick insulating layer. A mixed-n or composition gradient can distribute strain while retaining an electron-blocking conduction offset and hole-accessible valence alignment. On the scaffold side, carbon surface functionalization, controlled porosity, smaller interfacial pores, compliant conductive binders, or an ultrathin elastic conductive interlayer can improve contact area and accommodate differential expansion. Changes must preserve solvent compatibility and printability. Validation should quantify thermal-expansion coefficients, modulus, adhesion energy, and fracture behavior of the relevant interfaces, followed by thermal cycling and 85 °C aging under open circuit and MPP. In situ or periodic impedance/contact-resistance measurements, EL/PL imaging, cross-sectional SEM/TEM, acoustic or X-ray tomography, and peel/nanoindentation tests should determine whether electrical loss tracks delamination or cracking. GIWAXS/XRD and chemical depth profiles should verify that the low-dimensional phase and FA-rich absorber remain chemically stable and do not interdiffuse. UPS/KPFM, EQE, QFLS, and stabilized J-V must confirm that the redesigned compliant interface retains the desired selectivity. Success requires simultaneous preservation of adhesion, low contact resistance, VOC, FF, and MPP output after thermal stress.
scoring_key_points: Use an ultrathin or graded low-dimensional phase and compliant/multipoint/cross-linkable anchoring to reduce an abrupt brittle interface.
Modify carbon/scaffold porosity or add a compliant conductive contact layer while preserving printable transport pathways.
Measure thermal expansion, modulus, adhesion/fracture, and contact resistance during thermal cycling and 85 °C MPP stress.
Verify that phase chemistry and type-II selectivity remain intact with structural, depth-profile, energetic, optical, and stabilized-device measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Elastomeric conductive binder, molecular bridge, self-assembled linker, or flexible carbon-surface functionalization
Mixed-n 2D/3D gradient, Dion-Jacobson-like linker, or polymer-reinforced interphase
Digital image correlation, wafer-curvature stress, microcantilever, or finite-element thermomechanical analysis
Acoustic microscopy, X-ray nanotomography, cross-sectional FIB-SEM, or electroluminescence mapping for contact failure
common_wrong_answers: Adding a thicker hydrophobic 2D layer without considering brittleness or contact resistance
Attributing all 85 °C loss to perovskite phase decomposition without testing mechanical contact failure
Improving adhesion with an insulating polymer while ignoring hole extraction and FF
Qualifying the redesign by room-temperature shelf storage rather than thermal cycling and stabilized MPP

expected_answer:
The scale-up target should be a time-dependent state path: wet-film temperature, solvent activity, intermediate fraction, supersaturation, nucleation onset, phase-conversion rate, and final solvent removal. A large-area process should not be considered equivalent merely because the substrate set point equals the laboratory hot-plate temperature.

The process can be tuned through solvent donor strength and volatility, solids concentration, ink temperature, coating speed and gap, wet thickness, substrate preheating, zoned heating, gas-knife intensity, vacuum or solvent-extraction steps, and staged annealing. These variables should be combined in a design-of-experiments window that deliberately perturbs line speed, ambient humidity, ink age, and edge-to-center thermal gradients. The objective is a broad operating window, not a single optimum.

Inline IR thermography and thickness/interference measurements should verify thermal and drying uniformity. Spectrally resolved reflectance or PL can detect conversion and low-n/high-n evolution; in-line or rapid off-line GIWAXS can verify orientation and phase distribution. Final maps should include thickness, roughness, PL/QFLS, electroluminescence, sheet/contact resistance, and subcell performance across the full area.

Acceptance requires narrow spatial distributions, reproducible stabilized MPP efficiency and yield, and no systematic edge or web-direction loss. The selected phase distribution need not reproduce a presumed vertical n-value gradient if it delivers low non-radiative loss and efficient out-of-plane extraction. Stability criteria should include humidity/thermal/light-bias ageing, phase redistribution, ion migration, and adhesion or cracking under thermal cycling. A scaled process passes only if its structural trajectory and degradation behavior remain robust across batches and realistic manufacturing perturbations.
scoring_key_points: Defines the scale-up target as a matched supersaturation/intermediate/conversion trajectory rather than a copied temperature set point.
Identifies coating, solvent, thermal, gas-flow, wet-thickness, and post-treatment variables that can control that trajectory.
Uses inline thermal, drying, optical, structural, and spatially resolved electrical observables.
Requires robust yield, stabilized performance, and combined-stress structural stability across the full coated area.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, slot-die, meniscus, or another large-area coating method is acceptable.
Gas quenching, vacuum extraction, solvent-vapor control, or zoned annealing are acceptable tools for controlling supersaturation.
A uniform or otherwise non-graded n-phase distribution is acceptable if transport, recombination, and stability criteria are met.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only by using the same substrate temperature and annealing time as the small-area hot-cast recipe.
Accepting a high center-cell PCE while ignoring edge-to-center gradients, yield, and web-direction nonuniformity.
Treating vertical quantum-well grading as a mandatory endpoint without measuring extraction, recombination, and ageing.

expected_answer:
The test must separate oxygen, water, light, heat, and electric field because each can activate a different tin-perovskite failure pathway. A minimum factorial matrix should include dry N2, dry O2 or air, controlled humidity in N2, humid air, light-only, heat-only, and combined light-heat-humidity under MPP bias. Encapsulated and unencapsulated devices are both needed: encapsulation distinguishes intrinsic bulk/contact chemistry from ingress-limited failure.

Controls should include the untreated perovskite, the optimized additive dose, at least one higher dose that approaches the pinhole regime, and a molecular analogue that alters ink rheology or nucleation but lacks one of the Sn-binding or iodide-binding functions. Film thickness, grain size, coverage, and initial efficiency should be matched or included as covariates so that a smoother starting film is not mistaken for antioxidant chemistry.

At scheduled times, Sn4+/Sn2+ ratio, iodide/iodine chemical state, phase decomposition, additive redistribution, and electrode or transport-layer reactions should be measured by oxidation-sensitive spectroscopy, XRD, and depth profiling. PLQY/QFLS, trap density, mobility, EQE, stabilized MPP output, hysteresis, and spatial shunt maps should connect chemistry to device loss. Cross-sectional imaging should identify pinholes and ingress channels.

A go decision requires the optimized dose to slow Sn oxidation, trap growth, and power loss under oxygen- and moisture-containing combined stress, not only in N2, while retaining morphology and contact integrity. The benefit should persist in encapsulated devices and across batches without additive migration or a dose-sensitive shunt penalty. If gains disappear when morphology is matched, or if chemical protection is offset by pinholes, hygroscopicity, or contact reactions, the additive has not demonstrated transferable stability.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial stress matrix that separates and combines oxygen, humidity, light, heat, and MPP bias.
Includes untreated, optimized-dose, overdosed/pinhole, molecular-analogue, and encapsulated controls with morphology accounted for.
Tracks Sn oxidation, iodide chemistry, phase/additive redistribution, traps, transport, and stabilized device output over time.
Defines transfer as chemistry-linked durability under realistic combined stress without migration, pinholes, shunts, or contact failure.
accepted_equivalents: Dry air may substitute for dry O2 if oxygen partial pressure is controlled.
XPS/XANES and ToF-SIMS may be replaced by equivalent oxidation-state and depth-profiling methods.
Operational stability may be evaluated by MPP tracking with periodic EQE, QFLS, or pseudo-JV diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Treating long nitrogen shelf storage as proof of resistance to oxygen and humidity.
Comparing only initial and final PCE without measuring Sn4+, phase decomposition, traps, or pinhole-mediated ingress.
Assuming more additive is always more protective despite the observed morphology and shunting penalty at high loading.

expected_answer:
The reacted layer depends on the amount and accessibility of surface PbI2, which can vary with drying, stoichiometry, grain termination, and position on a large substrate. Too little reaction leaves uncovered recombination and migration sites; too much reaction can form rough crystallites or an electronically resistive layer. Coating flow can also accumulate material at edges and menisci. In laser-scribed modules, ionic-liquid residue or redistributed halide may contaminate P2/P3 overlap regions, increase contact resistance, bridge scribes, or alter laser ablation and debris removal.

The acceptance map should combine chemistry, structure, and electrical function at subcell resolution. Spatial XRF/XPS or another composition map should quantify Br and residual PbI2; profilometry or cross-sectional sampling should verify thickness and roughness. PL/QFLS and electroluminescence maps should locate recombination-active regions, while lock-in thermography, dark current, and local sheet/contact resistance should identify shunts and resistive stripes. Scribe width, isolation resistance, contact resistance, and dead-area fraction must be measured separately rather than absorbed into module FF.

True transfer requires a narrow distribution of subcell Voc, FF, QFLS, and contact resistance; the summed module Voc should scale with the number of active subcells, and the module gain should persist after correcting for aperture area and scribe loss. The capping layer should not increase series resistance or leakage at edges and scribes. Heat-humidity-light-bias ageing should repeat the maps to test whether Br, iodine, or the ionic liquid redistributes toward contacts and scribes.

A module passes only when the passivation and energetic benefits are spatially continuous, the scribe regions remain electrically isolated and chemically stable, and batch-to-batch yield and stabilized MPP power improve without a compensating loss in fill factor or dead area.
scoring_key_points: Identifies nonuniform surface-PbI2 reaction, incomplete/excessive thickness, rough crystallites, edge accumulation, and scribe contamination as distinct risks.
Maps capping chemistry and thickness together with PL/QFLS, electroluminescence, resistance, shunting, and scribe quality.
Requires narrow subcell distributions and module Voc/FF scaling after aperture and dead-area corrections.
Repeats spatial diagnostics after combined ageing to exclude ionic-liquid or halide redistribution and contact/scribe failure.
accepted_equivalents: XRF, XPS, Raman, hyperspectral imaging, or another calibrated surface-composition map is acceptable.
Lock-in thermography, luminescence imaging, local dark current, or equivalent methods may locate shunts and resistive defects.
P1-P2-P3 may be described generically as series-interconnection scribe regions if their electrical functions are correctly addressed.
common_wrong_answers: Using one module-average J-V curve as proof that every subcell received a uniform capping layer.
Assuming a small-cell thickness optimum automatically applies at edges, menisci, and laser scribes.
Ignoring scribe isolation, contact resistance, dead area, and post-ageing ion redistribution.

expected_answer: The transferred search space should be expressed through the physics of wet-film formation rather than literal spin-coating settings. Relevant variables include wet-film thickness, coating speed, solution and substrate temperature, solvent-removal or quench flux, gas flow, drying time, meniscus residence time, ambient humidity, and the timing of crystallization relative to solvent loss. The objective should combine area-resolved PL intensity, peak energy, spatial variance, thickness and coverage, pinhole or shunt indicators, and preferably a radiative-quality metric such as PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting. Bayesian optimization should include replicated center points, batch and day blocking, uncertainty-aware constraints, and deliberate environmental perturbations so that it selects a robust operating window rather than a narrow optimum. A statistically designed subset of complete cells and mini-modules must test whether absorber proxies predict Voc, Jsc, fill factor, stabilized power, subcell uniformity, and interconnect losses; the other layers cannot remain an unexamined manual boundary. Stability must be assessed under relevant light, heat, humidity, and electrical bias, not inferred from inert-atmosphere small-cell aging. Failure criteria include high average PL with poor spatial tails, non-transferable proxy-device correlation, excessive process sensitivity, module-localized shunts, or a stability advantage that disappears under realistic combined stress.
scoring_key_points: Reparameterizes the process using wet-film, drying, quench, temperature, airflow, and humidity variables rather than directly copying spin-coating settings.
Defines a constrained multiobjective target that includes spatial optical quality, coverage/thickness or defect metrics, and not merely mean PL.
Uses replication, environmental perturbation, uncertainty-aware optimization, and full-device or mini-module subsets to test proxy transferability and robustness.
Requires realistic combined-stress MPP validation and rejects narrow optima, spatial tails, module shunts, or absorber proxies that fail to predict device performance.
accepted_equivalents: Drying physics may be parameterized with evaporation rate, solvent activity, Peclet number, gas-knife flux, or residence time in a controlled drying zone.
Radiative quality may be represented by PLQY, implied Voc, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, electroluminescence efficiency, or calibrated hyperspectral PL.
Robust optimization may use Bayesian constraints, multiobjective Pareto optimization, chance constraints, or response-surface designs with random effects.
common_wrong_answers: Copying the small-area numerical recipe directly to blade coating and treating coating speed as equivalent to spin speed.
Optimizing only champion-cell PCE or mean PL without spatial distributions, replicate uncertainty, or module-level defect statistics.
Claiming field-relevant stability from a short inert-atmosphere test of small cells while other layers and interconnects remain unvalidated.

expected_answer: An area-averaged absorption spectrum can reveal that several quantum-well phases exist, but it cannot determine where they are located or whether their inorganic slabs provide a cross-plane transport path. Top- versus substrate-side excitation in transient absorption, excitation-dependent PL, or depth-resolved spectroscopy should identify whether lower-n and higher-n members are vertically ordered and should measure the direction and time scale of population transfer. GIWAXS or pole-figure analysis is then needed to distinguish vertically oriented slabs from in-plane or randomly oriented quantum wells; integrated phase fractions alone are insufficient. A beneficial gradient requires a band-edge sequence compatible with the two selective contacts and rapid transfer into the phase that feeds extraction, without long-lived carrier accumulation behind a wide-bandgap barrier. Ultrafast rise/decay kinetics, TRPL, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, SCLC, light-intensity-dependent Voc, EIS, or recombination resistance should show faster extraction and less trap-assisted loss. The energy-funnel claim is falsified if the proposed gradient is present but transfer remains slow, carriers accumulate at a buried phase boundary, orientation is unfavorable, or matched devices with the same depth profile do not improve after contact energetics and trap density are controlled.
scoring_key_points: Explains why conventional absorption or average phase fraction cannot resolve depth sequence, quantum-well orientation, or transport barriers.
Uses top/bottom or otherwise depth-sensitive spectroscopy to map n-phase location and the direction and kinetics of interphase carrier transfer.
Uses GIWAXS/pole figures plus kinetic and recombination measurements to distinguish vertical transport from in-plane barriers and trap-rich inclusions.
Defines a falsification condition: the phase gradient must align energetically with the contacts and accelerate extraction without interfacial accumulation or hidden recombination.
accepted_equivalents: Depth profiling may use front/back transient absorption, variable-angle PL, cross-sectional cathodoluminescence, nano-XRD, or depth-resolved photoemission.
Orientation may be quantified by GIWAXS azimuthal distributions, pole figures, grazing-incidence XRD, or polarized spectroscopy with appropriate controls.
Carrier accumulation may be detected by transient absorption signatures, charge-extraction transients, Kelvin-probe mapping, capacitance, or bias-dependent PL.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a dominant n = 3 absorption peak guarantees a single-phase film with efficient vertical transport.
Calling every lower-n phase beneficial because it can transfer energy to a lower-bandgap phase, without considering spatial position, band offsets, or extraction direction.
Using only surface SEM or steady-state PL to distinguish depth sequence, orientation, and trap-mediated recombination.

expected_answer: The solvent and acid recipe is not universal because a new spacer changes lattice energy, acid-base chemistry, solubility, precursor coordination, colloid stability, and drying kinetics. The goal is to retain target-like coordinated fragments or colloids long enough to guide crystallization, not to maximize aggregate size or merely dissolve the crystal. Precursor screening should compare single-crystal, stoichiometric-mixture, and Pb-halide controls using absorption, DLS or scattering, spectroscopy of lead-halide coordination, and time/temperature stability; excessive sedimentation or large particles is a failure, not proof of templating. Slot-die transfer also requires rheology, wetting, in situ drying/crystallization measurements, and a coating-window study because residence time and solvent removal differ from hot spin coating. Films must show the intended n distribution, depth profile, and vertical orientation by complementary optical and GIWAXS methods, together with uniform thickness, low roughness, and low trap density. Devices should demonstrate stabilized extraction and recombination improvements across area and batches. Operational light/heat/humidity testing must confirm that phase narrowing does not create a 3D-rich unstable surface or lower-n transport barrier. The mechanism is rejected if crystal and stoichiometric precursors become indistinguishable, colloids are unstable, phase/orientation control vanishes at scale, or performance derives only from changed wetting or morphology.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that spacer chemistry and target n change solubility, coordination, colloid stability, and drying, so the original solvent/acid recipe cannot be assumed transferable.
Requires single-crystal, stoichiometric, and lead-halide precursor controls with colloid/coordination measurements and rejects sedimentation or uncontrolled aggregation.
Adapts rheology and drying to slot-die coating and verifies phase distribution, depth sequence, vertical orientation, uniformity, and trap density in the film.

Demands reproducible stabilized devices and combined-stress testing, with go/no-go failure for loss of template-specific behavior, scale nonuniformity, or unstable/barrier-forming phase distributions.
accepted_equivalents: Precursor coordination may be assessed by UV-visible absorption, Raman, NMR, X-ray scattering, mass spectrometry, or other lead-halide complex probes.
In situ film formation may be tracked by GIWAXS, optical interferometry, absorption, PL, or environmental scattering during coating and drying.
A different weakly coordinating solvent family is acceptable if matched controls show target-specific precursor memory and reproducible film consequences.
common_wrong_answers: Treating a larger DLS particle size as sufficient proof that target-phase single-crystal templates are preserved.
Keeping the same acid fraction and solvent ratio while changing the spacer and coating method, without measuring precursor coordination or drying kinetics.
Claiming mechanism transfer from one improved J-V scan even if phase depth, orientation, batch reproducibility, and operational stability are unknown.

expected_answer: The process must first control the density and uniformity of surface hydroxyl/oxide binding sites through cleaning, UV-ozone or plasma dose, storage time, and contamination monitoring. SAM concentration, solvent, deposition time, temperature, and rinsing should be mapped as a coverage window: undercoverage creates exposed FTO and local recombination/shunts, whereas overcoverage leaves insulating or weakly bound multilayers that can desorb, impede transport, or disrupt perovskite wetting. Large-area acceptance should combine representative XPS or ToF-SIMS, ellipsometry, contact-angle mapping, Kelvin-probe/work-function mapping, and a coverage-sensitive electrical or fluorescence marker, followed by local dark-current and electroluminescence maps. Blade-coated ink wetting, nucleation, pinholes, thickness, and buried-interface roughness must be verified on the actual textured substrate. Adhesion and chemical durability should be tested by solvent exposure, thermal cycling, humidity, bias, and mechanical peel or scratch methods. Mini-modules require subcell-resolved stabilized MPP, interconnect loss analysis, and matched encapsulated light-heat-humidity testing. A short unencapsulated low-humidity run is only a screening result; failure criteria include work-function tails, exposed-FTO shunts, residual multilayer, wetting defects, delamination, or stability that collapses after encapsulation/process integration or combined stress.
scoring_key_points: Controls substrate activation/cleanliness and maps a SAM concentration-deposition-rinse window that separates exposed FTO from unbound multilayer residues.
Requires spatial coverage, thickness/wetting, work-function, and electrical-defect mapping on the actual textured large-area substrate.
Verifies blade-coated perovskite nucleation/coverage and buried-interface adhesion or chemical durability under solvent, heat, humidity, bias, and mechanical stress.
Qualifies subcell-resolved stabilized mini-modules under matched encapsulated combined stress and rejects short low-humidity small-cell testing as a module-stability claim.
accepted_equivalents: Work-function uniformity may be assessed by scanning Kelvin probe, KPFM, photoelectron mapping, or calibrated contact-potential methods.
Coverage may be monitored by XPS/ToF-SIMS sampling, labeled tracer molecules, infrared spectroscopy, ellipsometry, or surface-sensitive electrochemistry.
Mechanical reliability may be evaluated by peel, scratch, nanoscratch, bend, thermal-cycle adhesion, or fracture-energy measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing SAM concentration until contact angle saturates, without checking unbound multilayer, electrical resistance, or rinsing stability.
Assuming a uniform average work function guarantees complete coverage on textured FTO.
Claiming module readiness from a 100 h unencapsulated MPP trace without spatial defect mapping, encapsulation, interconnect analysis, or combined stress.

expected_answer: The minimum design crosses polymer identity with anilinium dose, including untreated surfaces where deposition is possible, the treatment on a reference HTM or inert surface, and a chemically different wetting treatment adjusted to the same contact angle. This separates polymer electronic structure from generic wetting and from iodide/anilinium chemistry. Surface-sensitive XPS/ToF-SIMS, contact-angle maps, ellipsometry, and UPS/Kelvin probe before and after treatment should quantify coverage, energetic shifts, and whether treatment levels differ among polymers. Perovskite growth must then be measured independently by time-resolved/in situ crystallization, SEM/AFM, thickness, XRD/GIWAXS, and Sn2+/Sn4+ or defect-sensitive spectroscopy. Only after morphology and oxidation are bounded should TCSPC, PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, hole-only SCLC, transient photocurrent, and EIS be used to separate extraction, transport, and recombination. A short PL lifetime is not uniquely favorable because it can also arise from interfacial traps. Full devices should be analyzed with matched absorber thickness and batch statistics. The intrinsic polymer claim is supported only if its advantage persists at matched anilinium coverage and matched film morphology; an interaction term may instead show that a specific polymer organizes or binds the surface treatment more effectively.
scoring_key_points: Uses a polymer-by-anilinium factorial design with untreated, reference-surface, dose, and matched-wetting chemical controls.
Quantifies treatment coverage and treatment-induced energy-level changes separately for each polymer using surface-sensitive and contact-potential measurements.
Measures perovskite nucleation, morphology, thickness, crystallinity, and Sn oxidation/defects before interpreting PL, mobility, or recombination results.
Explains that short PL decay is not unique proof of extraction and requires PLQY/QFLS, SCLC/transients/EIS, matched morphology, and statistical device validation.
accepted_equivalents: A matched-wetting control may use another ammonium salt, neutral surfactant, plasma treatment, or surface-energy modification that does not reproduce the same iodide chemistry.
Treatment distribution may be measured by XPS, ToF-SIMS, infrared spectroscopy, isotope labeling, or angle-resolved photoemission.
Tin oxidation may be assessed by XPS, Mössbauer spectroscopy, optical signatures, conductivity/doping measurements, or chemical titration with appropriate controls.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only treated devices and attributing all differences to polymer structural isomerism.
Using contact angle alone to conclude that the anilinium layer is chemically identical on every polymer.
Treating the shortest PL lifetime as proof of fastest useful extraction without testing trap-assisted quenching, morphology, or Sn oxidation.

expected_answer: Transfer cannot be inferred from the all-tin result because mixed Sn-Pb compositions have different valence-band energies, solvent/additive chemistry, nucleation kinetics, oxidation equilibria, and light-induced ionic/phase behavior. The polymer's dopant-free thermal and moisture advantages may transfer, but its HOMO alignment must be remeasured on the actual thin film by UPS or contact-potential methods; solution electrochemistry is insufficient. The polymer surface and any anilinium pretreatment must be reoptimized for the mixed precursor, with contact angle, in situ crystallization, morphology, thickness, orientation, and large-area uniformity compared at matched conditions. Sulfur coordination could passivate under-coordinated Sn/Pb or suppress Sn4+, but it could also bind precursors too strongly, alter crystallization, or create interfacial dipoles; matched sulfur-free/isomer controls and XPS/FTIR/NMR or related coordination probes are required. PLQY/QFLS, TRPL, transient extraction, SCLC and EIS should separate passivation from transport barriers. Under light, heat, bias, and humidity, the study must track Sn oxidation, ion accumulation, spectral phase segregation, stabilized power, Voc/FF, and recovery. Go requires reproducible efficiency and lower nonradiative loss without new segregation, extraction, or process-window penalties; otherwise the molecule must be redesigned or the interface treatment changed.
scoring_key_points: Rejects automatic transfer and remeasures thin-film energetics because mixed Sn-Pb composition changes band alignment and interfacial chemistry.
Reoptimizes wetting, any anilinium treatment, and crystallization on the actual mixed precursor with matched morphology and uniformity controls.
Tests whether sulfur coordination passivates Sn/Pb or instead overcoordinates/changes dipoles and growth using matched structural controls and chemical spectroscopy.
Requires combined light-heat-bias-humidity MPP testing with Sn oxidation, ion accumulation, phase-segregation, extraction, and recovery diagnostics before go/no-go.
accepted_equivalents: Thin-film energetic alignment may use UPS, Kelvin probe, photoelectron yield spectroscopy, or calibrated contact-potential measurements.
Coordination may be probed by XPS core-level shifts, FTIR/Raman, solid-state NMR, absorption, or computation paired with matched molecular controls.
Ion/phase stability may be evaluated by operando PL/absorption, GIWAXS, XRF, impedance, bias-stress relaxation, or depth profiling.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a dopant-free, hydrophobic polymer is universally stable regardless of absorber composition and band alignment.
Using the all-tin HOMO value, contact angle, or dark shelf lifetime without remeasuring the mixed Sn-Pb interface.
Interpreting any sulfur-containing polymer as a passivator without testing overcoordination, altered crystallization, interfacial dipoles, or light-induced segregation.

expected_answer: UPS primarily establishes electronic doping and energy-level movement: a Fermi level closer to the HOMO is consistent with increased hole density and a reduced energetic barrier, but it does not show that holes can move efficiently through the film in the device-normal direction. Likewise, a conventional conductivity measurement can be dominated by lateral transport and therefore may not predict vertical extraction through an anisotropic semicrystalline polymer. If P3HT remains edge-on, its favorable pi-stacking pathway is poorly oriented for transport from the perovskite to the electrode, so a highly doped film can still suffer vertical resistance and charge accumulation. Face-on-enriched packing provides a more favorable out-of-plane transport network and can convert the electronic doping benefit into device-level extraction and fill factor. Strong PL quenching and a shorter lifetime in a perovskite/HTL bilayer are consistent with faster interfacial hole transfer, while lower transport resistance and higher recombination resistance support, respectively, easier carrier passage and less interfacial/back recombination. PL quenching alone is not definitive because additional nonradiative traps can also quench PL. It should therefore be triangulated with selective-contact controls and measurements such as absolute PL or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, time-resolved interfacial transfer, and device dark-current or recombination analysis. The correct diagnosis is that an effective HTL requires coordinated energetic doping, favorable vertical microstructure, rapid selective extraction, and suppressed recombination; no single UPS or conductivity result proves all four.
scoring_key_points: Explains that UPS diagnoses p-type doping/energy-level movement but not transport directionality or interfacial selectivity.
Explains why lateral conductivity can coexist with poor device-normal transport when the polymer remains edge-on, whereas face-on packing favors vertical extraction.
Correctly maps bilayer PL/TRPL and impedance evidence to extraction, transport resistance, and recombination rather than treating them as redundant measurements.
Recognizes that PL quenching can arise from either charge transfer or added traps and proposes an orthogonal method to distinguish them.
accepted_equivalents: Transport anisotropy or mobility-tensor mismatch between in-plane testing and through-plane device operation
Face-on pi-stacking or an out-of-plane percolation pathway favorable for vertical hole transport
Use of quasi-Fermi-level splitting, absolute photoluminescence, transient extraction, or selective-contact controls to disambiguate PL quenching
common_wrong_answers: Claims that a UPS shift alone proves fast hole extraction and low recombination.
Assumes that the largest measured film conductivity must yield the best fill factor regardless of molecular orientation.
Treats all PL quenching as beneficial charge transfer without considering trap-assisted nonradiative loss.
Explains the improvement only by energy alignment and ignores vertical microstructure and interfacial recombination.

expected_answer: A thicker and more continuous SiOx layer suppresses direct carrier exchange with defective crystalline silicon and limits dopant in-diffusion during annealing, so it can preserve surface passivation and a high implied voltage. The same continuity also raises the tunneling barrier; once the oxide is too thick or too stoichiometric, carrier transmission becomes inefficient and the contact can show very high resistivity or Schottky-like nonlinearity. At low oxidation severity, many thin or missing regions provide easy conduction and low measured contact resistance, but they also permit deeper dopant penetration and expose poorly passivated silicon, increasing Auger and interface recombination after annealing. On a textured surface, the key variable is not the mean oxide thickness but its distribution. Valley regions with locally missing oxide can act as large pinholes: they carry a disproportionate fraction of current, create current crowding and local Joule loss, and may dominate recombination even if most sidewalls are well passivated. An intermediate condition can work when the background oxide is sufficiently passivating while a controlled density of nanoscale thin regions provides transport; uncontrolled valley openings are not equivalent to deliberately distributed transport paths. The average-thickness model should be tested with site-specific TEM/EELS or tomography, conductive AFM or tunneling-current mapping, EBIC or luminescence/lifetime mapping, and spatial dopant profiling. Correlation of valley locations with local current and recombination would support the heterogeneous-pathway model, whereas uniform current and recombination despite strong thickness variation would falsify it.
scoring_key_points: Explains why a continuous/thicker oxide improves passivation and suppresses dopant in-diffusion but impedes tunneling and raises contact resistivity.
Explains why thin or missing oxide lowers contact resistance yet promotes dopant penetration and local interface/Auger recombination after annealing.
Treats valley pinholes as spatially concentrated transport and recombination sites that can cause current crowding, not merely as a change in average thickness.
Proposes at least one local structural/current measurement and one local recombination or dopant-profile measurement that can test the heterogeneous-pathway model.
accepted_equivalents: Percolative transport through sparse oxide-thin regions or pinholes
A conductance-recombination distribution dominated by textured valleys rather than the area-average oxide
Conductive AFM, EBIC, micro-PL, lock-in thermography, TEM/EELS, atom-probe, or spatial ECV/SIMS as falsification tools
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that thicker SiOx must always improve both passivation and contact transport.
Treats pinholes only as beneficial conduction channels and ignores their recombination and dopant-diffusion penalties.
Explains the result solely by optical texturing and does not address contact physics.
Relies on a single average oxide thickness and proposes no spatially resolved diagnostic.

expected_answer: The most coherent interpretation is a slow interfacial or surface-conditioning process, such as redistribution and binding of a passivating additive at undercoordinated Sn/halide sites, reduction of surface defect density, or gradual relaxation of near-surface strain. The decrease in hole density is especially important: it indicates reduced self-p-doping rather than creation of additional acceptor-like defects. In an oxygen-free environment, beneficial Sn2+ oxidation is chemically implausible, and oxidation to Sn4+ would not by itself explain a simultaneous reduction in p-type carrier density. The unchanged absorption edge and bulk diffraction pattern argue against a large change in bulk composition, dimensionality, or phase fraction. Higher Voc and longer PL lifetime with a weaker surface-trap signature instead point to lower nonradiative recombination at the surface or transport-layer interface. To distinguish mechanisms, depth-sensitive XPS/UPS or Kelvin-probe measurements should track surface oxidation state, band bending, and work function; front- versus back-excited TRPL or surface-photovoltage can localize the recombination change; time-resolved GIWAXS or diffraction-peak analysis can test strain relaxation; and impedance, transient photovoltage, contact-resistance, or selective-contact measurements can reveal whether the dominant change occurs at the electrode interface. Chemical mapping or isotope-labeled additive profiling would directly test redistribution. A causal claim requires the temporal evolution of the proposed surface species or strain metric to track the electrical improvement, not merely a post-storage PCE increase.
scoring_key_points: Identifies slow surface/interface passivation, additive redistribution, or near-surface relaxation as more plausible than a bulk phase change.
Uses the falling hole density and oxygen-free condition to reject beneficial oxidation as the main explanation.
Uses unchanged bulk XRD and absorption to argue against major bulk reconstruction while linking higher Voc/lifetime to reduced nonradiative recombination.
Proposes depth/localization-sensitive chemical, strain, and contact/recombination measurements that can discriminate among the candidate mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Slow passivation of undercoordinated Sn or halide sites
Additive migration to grain boundaries or the top interface followed by defect binding
Near-surface strain relaxation or contact dipole evolution, provided it is experimentally distinguished from chemical passivation
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the improvement to oxygen-induced Sn4+ formation despite oxygen-free storage and decreasing hole density.
Claims that unchanged bulk XRD proves that no structural or interfacial evolution can occur.
Treats the PCE increase alone as proof of a specific passivation mechanism.
Proposes only bulk XRD and steady-state IV, which cannot localize a surface or contact process.

expected_answer: The first stage is precursor and redox control. Starting salts and solvents should be purified to minimize pre-existing Sn4+, processed under controlled oxygen/water activity, and combined with a reducing or complexing strategy that does not introduce unstable residues. Acceptance requires reproducible Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio, low background hole density, controlled stoichiometry, and stable precursor aging. The second stage is bulk film formation: nucleation, grain growth, dimensionality, and A-site/additive chemistry should suppress Sn vacancies, pinholes, and high-defect grain boundaries while preserving the target bandgap and transport. Acceptance should include morphology, defect density, carrier lifetime, doping density, and phase stability under heat and light. The third stage targets surfaces and contacts with chemically selective passivation and energy alignment; it should reduce interface recombination without blocking extraction or reacting with Sn2+. Quasi-Fermi-level splitting, surface spectroscopy, contact resistance, and bias-dependent recombination are appropriate criteria. The fourth stage is packaging: oxygen and moisture barriers, edge seals, electrode compatibility, and capture of volatile/acidic products must be assessed in area-scaled devices. Qualification should use separated and combined oxygen, humidity, heat, illumination, and MPP-bias stresses, plus thermal cycling and leakage analysis, because Sn perovskites can still form HI and corrode interfaces. A Sn-Pb absorber may offer excellent low-bandgap performance and improved stability, but it reintroduces lead and therefore fails a fully lead-free requirement. Short inert storage can conceal oxygen/moisture sensitivity, post-storage activation, bias-driven ion movement, and package failure; it is not evidence of decades-long outdoor reliability.
scoring_key_points: Separates precursor purification/redox control from later film and device interventions and defines a Sn4+/doping/stoichiometry acceptance criterion.
Includes bulk crystallization, Sn-vacancy/grain-boundary control, and phase/morphology diagnostics under thermal and optical stress.
Includes surface/contact passivation and package/edge-seal qualification with electrical selectivity, barrier, and corrosion criteria.
Explains that Sn-Pb violates the fully lead-free objective and that short inert storage does not test coupled environmental, bias, or module-scale failure.
accepted_equivalents: Reducing-agent, complexation, or tin-powder purification routes that lower pre-existing Sn4+ without degrading film formation
Vacancy suppression through chemical-potential control, A-site engineering, 2D/3D design, or morphology control
Combined damp-heat, oxygen/light, MPP-bias, thermal-cycle, and edge-ingress testing on encapsulated area-scaled devices
common_wrong_answers: Treats one additive as a complete solution to precursor oxidation, vacancies, interfaces, and packaging.
Uses only initial PCE and ignores hole density, Sn4+ content, defects, and phase stability.
Counts a Sn-Pb tandem absorber as fully lead-free.
Equates storage activation or retention in a glovebox with operational outdoor stability.

expected_answer: The location of the coating outside the electrically active stack, together with unchanged Voc and fill factor, already favors an optical rather than electronic mechanism. A downshifting layer should absorb photons in a spectral region that is weakly used or damaging and re-emit at wavelengths where the perovskite has stronger collection. The resulting device signature is a wavelength-localized EQE and Jsc increase that follows the coating's excitation-emission action spectrum. Similar UV absorbance in a nonemissive control rules out absorption or UV screening alone; if antireflection were dominant, the reflectance and EQE changes would follow optical interference over a broader spectral range and should be reproduced by a nonluminescent film of matched refractive index and thickness. The spray/spin comparison shows that molecular loading is not sufficient: aggregation in the spin-coated film can create excimers, nonradiative channels, or self-quenching, whereas a deposition route that limits aggregation preserves emissive states and usable PLQY. A convincing measurement set includes integrating-sphere absorption, reflection, and absolute PLQY; excitation/emission spectra and overlap with perovskite EQE; wavelength-resolved EQE or an action spectrum with and without the coating; thickness-dependent optical modeling; and a luminescent-versus-nonluminescent index/thickness-matched control. Time-resolved PL or geometry/spacer experiments can test whether emitted photons are transferred or reabsorbed by the perovskite, while integrated Jsc from EQE should match the IV gain. The causal claim fails if the current gain can be fully explained by reduced reflection or if the low-PLQY film gives the same gain.
scoring_key_points: Uses the external location, unchanged Voc/FF, and wavelength-localized Jsc/EQE gain to identify a primarily optical mechanism.
Distinguishes downshifting from UV filtering and antireflection using nonemissive, index/thickness-matched controls and spectral correspondence.
Explains why aggregation-induced nonradiative quenching makes deposition method and solid-film PLQY decisive despite similar molecular loading.
Specifies a coherent minimum set of PLQY, absorption/reflection, action-spectrum or EQE, thickness/modeling, and current-consistency measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Luminescent solar concentration or radiative wavelength conversion followed by perovskite reabsorption
Aggregation-caused excimer formation, triplet quenching, or other nonradiative decay channels
Monochromatic external quantum efficiency, spectral response under UV excitation, or integrating-sphere photon-balance measurements
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the Jsc increase to improved perovskite crystallization even though the coating is on the external glass.
Treats UV absorption alone as proof of downshifting.
Ignores antireflection and refractive-index controls.
Assumes equal molecular loading guarantees equal optical function and disregards aggregation-dependent PLQY.

expected_answer: The minimum causal design is a full 2^3 factorial experiment containing the untreated control, each single-location treatment, all three two-location combinations, and the full three-location treatment. Dose at each location should be optimized within a common range, and at least one dose-matched control should place the same total amount of molecule at only one location or distribute an inert analogue similarly. This prevents total loading from being confused with spatial function. The buried treatment should be evaluated through precursor wetting/contact angle, nucleation density, buried-interface voids, interfacial chemistry, and hole-extraction or buried-interface recombination. The bulk treatment should be diagnosed through wet-film intermediates, crystallization rate, grain orientation, residual solvent, strain, defect density, and bulk carrier lifetime. The top treatment should be diagnosed through surface composition, undercoordinated-site passivation, surface recombination, energy alignment with the electron contact, and contact resistance. A statistical model should include the three main effects and bottom-by-bulk, bottom-by-top, bulk-by-top, and three-way interaction terms. If the full treatment equals the sum of independently measured main effects within uncertainty, the response is additive. A significant positive interaction after dose matching supports synergy—for example, bottom-controlled nucleation may enable the bulk additive to form a low-strain film that the top treatment can then passivate efficiently. If a dose-matched single-location treatment reproduces the full response, spatial synergy is not established. Mechanistic claims should also require that the predicted location-specific intermediate changes precede the device improvement, rather than relying only on final PCE.
scoring_key_points: Specifies a full bottom/bulk/top factorial design including all single, pairwise, and three-location combinations plus an untreated control.
Uses total-dose-matched and preferably inert-analogue controls to separate spatial function from simple additive loading.
Assigns distinct diagnostics to buried-interface wetting/voids, bulk crystallization/strain/defects, and top-surface passivation/contact energetics.
Defines additivity versus synergy using statistically significant interaction terms and requires mechanism-specific intermediate evidence, not only higher PCE.
accepted_equivalents: A response-surface or hierarchical factorial design that estimates main and interaction effects
Buried-interface PL/SEM/wetting, bulk GIWAXS/XRD/TA, and surface XPS/UPS/TRPL/contact diagnostics
Mediation analysis showing that location-specific structural or recombination changes account for the device response
common_wrong_answers: Compares only untreated and full three-location devices.
Calls the result synergistic simply because the full treatment has the highest PCE.
Does not control total molecular dose across treatment architectures.
Uses the same bulk-averaged characterization for all three locations and cannot assign spatial mechanisms.

expected_answer: Down-selection should start from factorial evidence, not the champion architecture. Each placement is retained only if it addresses a failure mode that the remaining placements cannot control. A bottom treatment is non-redundant when poor wetting, excessive nucleation, residual-solvent voids, or buried-interface recombination persist without it. A bulk treatment is non-redundant when orientation, strain, A-site vacancy formation, grain-boundary defects, or bulk lifetime remain limiting. A top treatment is non-redundant when surface traps, electron-contact recombination, or top-interface energetics dominate after the film is formed. For each candidate subset, dose and drying must be reoptimized because excessive additive can retard conversion, leave ionic residue, alter band alignment, block extraction, or migrate under bias. Large-area qualification should map thickness, wetting, crystallization timing, grain orientation/strain, buried voids, surface chemistry, PL lifetime or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, contact resistance, and electroluminescence/thermal nonuniformity across the substrate. The smallest subset that reproduces the critical intermediates and device yield should be advanced. Stability selection must use area-scaled encapsulated devices under MPP illumination, heat/humidity storage, thermal cycling, and bias stress, while monitoring ion migration, phase change, contact degradation, and spatially localized failure. A treatment set is acceptable only if its efficiency distribution, yield, and degradation rate remain within guardbands; a statistically insignificant PCE advantage from the third step does not justify it. Conversely, a step with modest initial PCE impact may still be retained if it uniquely prevents a long-term buried-interface, bulk-phase, or top-contact failure.
scoring_key_points: Uses factorial/mechanistic evidence to retain a placement only when it controls a unique bottom, bulk, or top failure mode.
Recognizes process risks such as over-retarded crystallization, residue, energy barriers, solvent incompatibility, and field-driven additive migration.
Requires spatially resolved large-area measurements of wetting/crystallization, voids, orientation/strain, recombination, contact resistance, and device uniformity/yield.
Selects the minimum treatment set using area-scaled MPP and environmental stability guardbands, allowing a step to be removed or retained based on unique long-term value rather than champion PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Pareto down-selection based on yield, process complexity, efficiency, and degradation rate
Ablation studies with reoptimization of dose for every retained treatment subset
Spatial PL/EL, GIWAXS, impedance, thermal imaging, buried-interface microscopy, and ion-migration profiling on large-area devices
common_wrong_answers: Keeps all three steps automatically because the full treatment has the highest small-area PCE.
Removes a step based only on its initial PCE contribution and ignores a unique stability function.
Assumes that additive doses optimized in the three-step process remain optimal after one placement is removed.
Uses only average large-area IV and cannot detect localized voids, contact barriers, or degradation hot spots.

expected_answer: The isolated-film PL QFLS represents the absorber's bulk/material potential under optical generation. A drop when selective contacts are added points to contact-induced nonradiative recombination, surface damage, or poor interfacial selectivity rather than an intrinsic bulk-bandgap limit. The additional gap between PL-derived and EL-derived pseudo-JV behavior indicates a carrier-injection/extraction or energy-alignment penalty: PL creates carriers inside the absorber, whereas EL requires them to traverse the contacts, so selectivity barriers, interfacial band offsets, or contact transport can reduce the electrically accessible QFLS. Because that PL-EL gap is already reproduced in the matched single-junction cell, it cannot primarily originate from tandem integration or the recombination interconnect. The near agreement between the sum of the subcell EL pseudo-VOCs and the measured tandem VOC further argues that the interconnect adds little open-circuit voltage penalty; a significant shortfall of tandem VOC from that sum would instead implicate interconnect recombination or leakage.
