Finally, the gap between pseudo-fill factor and measured fill factor is assigned mainly to transport, series resistance, contact resistance, and current-matching losses that are excluded or strongly reduced in the luminescence-derived pseudo-JV curves. EL must be recorded after a defined steady-state history—such as identical light soaking or dark-VOC biasing followed by stabilization—because ion redistribution and especially low-gap-subcell conditioning can change ELQY and the inferred pseudo-JV curve.
scoring_key_points: Assigns the isolated-film-to-contacted-stack PL-QFLS loss to contact/surface-induced nonradiative recombination or selectivity loss.
Assigns the PL-to-EL pseudo-JV gap to electrically accessed energy alignment, injection/extraction, or contact-transport penalties.
Uses the single-junction reproduction and the summed subcell pseudo-VOC agreement to rule out a dominant interconnect VOC loss.
Assigns the pseudo-FF-to-measured-FF gap to transport/resistive/current-matching losses and requires controlled steady-state EL conditioning.
accepted_equivalents: Contact-induced QFLS loss, interface recombination, or imperfect carrier selectivity
An injection barrier, extraction barrier, non-ohmic contact, or energy-offset loss for the PL-EL discrepancy
Suns-VOC or luminescence pseudo-JV versus electrical J-V as a separation of recombination and resistive losses
A standardized prebias, light-soak, dark-VOC, or time-to-steady-state protocol
common_wrong_answers: Attributes every voltage difference to the recombination interlayer without using the single-junction control.
Treats PL-derived QFLS, EL-derived QFLS, and electrical VOC as interchangeable quantities with identical loss sensitivity.
Explains the fill-factor deficit only by nonradiative recombination and ignores series resistance or current matching.
Ignores measurement-history effects and interprets a transient ELQY as a steady-state subcell property.

expected_answer: The process should be qualified as a sequence of partial stacks, not only as a finished tandem. Identical high-gap witness cells and PL-capable coupons should be measured before and after each potentially damaging step—fullerene deposition, nanoparticle/ALD oxide formation, ultrathin recombination layer deposition, solution coating of the low-gap-side contact, and low-gap absorber processing. Absolute, spectrally selective PLQY/QFLS maps should identify when and where the high-gap luminescence potential is lost; microscopy, absorption, and chemical analysis can then distinguish physical/chemical damage from unchanged bulk quality. Completed devices should undergo wavelength-filtered or otherwise subcell-selective EL pseudo-JV analysis. If the sum of subcell pseudo-VOCs falls only after the interconnect step, or if dark leakage/shunt signatures appear, the interconnect is implicated; if the high-gap PL QFLS falls before electrical completion, processing damage is implicated. Electrical J-V, Suns-VOC or pseudo-JV, electroluminescence mapping, sheet/contact resistance mapping, and spectral EQE/current-matching analysis should separate recombination-free pseudo-FF from area-dependent resistive and current-mismatch losses. Controls must include small-area devices from the same coating, interconnect-free or deliberately altered interconnect controls, and process-exposed witness single junctions. Finally, all PL/EL comparisons require identical preconditioning and time-to-steady-state criteria, followed by maximum-power-point operation with periodic subcell-selective diagnostics to determine whether spatial voltage loss is permanent damage, reversible ion redistribution, or progressive contact/interconnect degradation. Manufacturing acceptance should require a narrow spatial distribution of subcell QFLS, negligible loss added by each integration step, stable summed subcell voltage, and an electrical FF consistent with mapped resistance and current matching.
scoring_key_points: Uses process-exposed witness cells and partial stacks to locate the exact integration step that degrades high-gap PLQY/QFLS.
Uses subcell-selective PL/EL plus summed subcell voltages and leakage controls to distinguish absorber/contact damage from interconnect loss.
Uses spatial resistance, EL, EQE/current-matching, and pseudo-JV versus electrical J-V measurements to diagnose large-area FF loss.
Requires standardized conditioning and MPP-aged repeated diagnostics to separate reversible history effects from progressive degradation.
accepted_equivalents: A process-of-record split lot with stop points after every tandem-integration layer
Hyperspectral PL, luminescence imaging, or area-resolved QFLS mapping
Dark J-V, shunt mapping, impedance, or contact-resistivity measurements for interconnect and transport diagnosis
Repeated characterization after controlled light soaking, prebias, and operational aging
common_wrong_answers: Compares only final tandem efficiency and assumes the lowest-performing layer is the cause.
Uses one global PL or J-V value and ignores spatial nonuniformity in a large-area device.
Blames current mismatch for a subcell QFLS loss that appears before the low-gap cell is electrically connected.
Declares the process stable from a short initial scan without steady-state conditioning or MPP operation.

expected_answer: The test requires a matched scaffold series in which one interaction channel is removed at a time while framework size, porosity, loading, and processing are held as constant as possible. For example, the imine/Lewis-base site can be blocked or electronically weakened to suppress Pb coordination; the arene electron deficiency can be reduced while preserving a hydrogen-bond acceptor to weaken anion-pi interaction; and the A-site-cation hydrogen-bond acceptor can be removed or sterically shielded while retaining comparable Pb binding and framework morphology. Small-molecule or monomer analogues and an inert hydrophobic COF are useful controls for framework effects and water repellence. Precursor-doped and post-deposition surface-treated versions must be compared, because a surface passivator cannot by itself establish control of the wet-film phase pathway. Solution-state NMR or vibrational shifts should probe A-site-cation binding; UV-vis/Raman/speciation measurements should probe halide and PbIx complexes; and XPS or related spectroscopy should confirm Pb/halide interactions in films. Synchronized in situ GIWAXS/XRD with in situ PL or optical absorption should measure nucleation time, intermediate-phase population, and direct alpha-phase formation. Genuine all-component control is supported if removing any one interaction channel weakens the delayed, intermediate-free phase pathway even when Pb coordination or hydrophobicity remains similar, and if the fully functional additive produces a larger-than-additive improvement in phase selection, trap density/QFLS, and morphology. A Pb 4f shift, disappearance of residual PbI2, or longer crystallization time alone is insufficient, because each can arise from simple Lewis-base binding or over-retardation without coordinated control of all precursor components.
scoring_key_points: Proposes matched one-site-at-a-time molecular ablations that separately perturb Pb coordination, halide interaction, and A-site-cation hydrogen bonding.
Includes precursor-doped versus surface-only and inert-hydrophobic/framework controls to separate crystallization control from passivation.
Combines solution speciation/binding probes with synchronized in situ phase and luminescence measurements.
Defines synergy as loss of the desired phase pathway when any interaction channel is removed despite comparable Pb binding or hydrophobicity.
accepted_equivalents: A factorial substituent series or chemically protected functional groups that isolate the three interaction channels
NMR for FA/MA interaction, optical or Raman probes of iodoplumbate speciation, and XPS for Pb/halide coordination
In situ GIWAXS, XRD, PL, UV-vis, or scattering measurements of intermediate phases and nucleation kinetics
A non-additive epistasis-style response in which the complete multifunctional additive outperforms the sum of single-site controls
common_wrong_answers: Concludes all-component control solely from the strongest Pb 4f shift.
Uses only final ex situ XRD and cannot distinguish phase-pathway control from post-crystallization passivation.
Changes several molecular features simultaneously, making dipole, hydrophobicity, framework size, and binding inseparable.
Treats the longest crystallization time as automatically optimal without checking phase selection or film quality.

expected_answer: The transferable variable is not the original additive volume or spin time but the relationship among precursor-additive complexation, solvent removal, supersaturation, nucleation, phase conversion, and COF formation/distribution. In a slower slot-die process, the same loading may over-retard nucleation, promote premature COF aggregation or gelation, or leave an electronically resistive excess at the top surface and grain boundaries. A development matrix should therefore cross additive concentration and molecular functionality with solvent coordination strength, solids content, substrate temperature, gas-knife/drying rate, coating speed, and annealing profile. Filtration/dispersion controls and, if needed, delayed or sequential delivery should keep the COF nanoscale and spatially localized rather than embedded as a continuous insulating phase. In situ or rapid-line GIWAXS/XRD and optical/PL monitoring should verify a reproducible intermediate-free alpha-phase pathway and a controlled nucleation-to-growth window across the coating width. Cross-web maps of thickness, roughness, orientation, PLQY/QFLS, trap density, and composition should establish uniformity. Excellent PL must be paired with contact-selective extraction tests—TRPL with the electron contact, contact resistance, impedance, transient photocurrent, or pseudo-JV versus electrical J-V—to detect COF accumulation that passivates but blocks electron transfer. Acceptance should require a wide process window, low defect and shunt dispersion, stable MPP output, and retention under humidity, heat, and illumination, together with verification of lead immobilization/leakage control. A single champion module or high PL signal does not establish scalable crystallization control.
scoring_key_points: Preserves the relative timescales of complexation, supersaturation, nucleation, phase conversion, drying, and COF formation rather than copying the spin-coating recipe.
Uses a multivariable coating matrix and dispersion/localization controls to avoid aggregation, gelation, and insulating COF accumulation.
Requires in situ phase-pathway monitoring plus cross-web film/QFLS uniformity and selective-contact extraction diagnostics.
Defines scale-up success through process-window robustness, MPP stability, environmental aging, and lead-leakage control rather than champion efficiency alone.
accepted_equivalents: A Damkohler-like or timescale-ratio framing between binding/crystallization kinetics and solvent evaporation
Gas quenching, substrate heating, solvent engineering, sequential coating, or reduced additive loading
Inline GIWAXS, reflectometry, hyperspectral PL, or spatially resolved luminescence and resistance mapping
TRPL/contact controls, impedance, transient photocurrent, or Suns-VOC/pseudo-FF tests for extraction blockage
common_wrong_answers: Uses the same additive concentration and anneal schedule solely because it worked in spin coating.
Optimizes only for the longest wet-film lifetime and ignores over-retardation or aggregation.
Accepts high PL as proof of good devices without testing selective electron extraction.
Claims stability from unencapsulated shelf storage alone and omits operational, thermal, or leakage testing.

expected_answer: The molecular series should independently vary dipole and binding chemistry. One pair should have similar surface-binding groups but different dipole magnitude or orientation; another pair should have similar dipole moments but one molecule unable to coordinate Pb; an inert spacer with comparable size/thickness should test physical C60 displacement. Surface coverage and morphology must be matched, and each molecule should be tested over a submonolayer-to-overlayer dose or thickness series. A dipole-dominated effect produces a systematic vacuum-level/work-function or surface-potential shift in UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements that follows molecular dipole orientation and improves the perovskite/C60 band offset and built-in potential; reversing orientation should reverse or weaken the shift. It need not remove Pb0 or strongly change trap spectroscopy. A passivation-dominated effect produces disappearance/reduction of metallic Pb or undercoordinated-Pb signatures, higher absolute PLQY/QFLS and longer selective-contact lifetime, lower ideality factor/SRH recombination, and reduced trap density even when the vacuum-level shift is small. A spacer/displacement mechanism should show a nonmonotonic thickness dependence: an ultrathin layer may reduce C60-induced interfacial quenching or recombination, but excess thickness raises contact/series resistance, slows transient extraction, lowers FF and eventually JSC, and may require tunneling. The strongest causal conclusion comes from orthogonal agreement among UPS/KPFM, XPS, PLQY/QFLS, transient extraction, impedance/contact resistance, and light-intensity recombination analysis. Similar VOC/FF gains from chemically nonbinding but correctly oriented dipoles support electrostatics; similar gains from low-dipole strong binders support passivation; a sharp thickness optimum and transport penalty at excess dose support a spacer/tunneling contribution.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched molecules that independently vary dipole magnitude/orientation and Pb-binding chemistry, plus an inert spacer control.
Assigns UPS/KPFM and built-in-potential shifts that track dipole orientation to electrostatic energy-alignment effects.
Assigns Pb0/defect removal, QFLS/lifetime improvement, and reduced SRH/trap signatures to chemical passivation.
Uses a thickness-dependent extraction/resistance optimum and excess-layer FF/JSC loss to identify tunneling or C60-displacement effects.
accepted_equivalents: A two-factor molecular design with orthogonal dipole and Lewis-base/ionic binding strength
Kelvin probe, surface photovoltage, UPS, or core-level/vacuum-level measurements for the dipole
Absolute PL, Suns-VOC, ideality factor, TAS/DLTS, or XPS for passivation
Contact resistivity, TPC, impedance, temperature-dependent transport, or thickness-dependent tunneling tests
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the entire improvement to the largest calculated molecular dipole without testing orientation or surface coverage.
Treats a Pb 4f shift as proof of better energy alignment.
Assumes a thicker molecular layer must passivate better and ignores tunneling/contact resistance.
Uses unchanged JSC to claim that transport is irrelevant, even though FF is transport-sensitive.

expected_answer: Retained VOC with unchanged JSC but reduced FF points first to nonuniform contact transport rather than an optical-generation problem. On a textured, large-area surface, solution pooling in valleys, incomplete facet coverage, crystallized salt islands, variable molecular orientation, or a locally thick low-dimensional/insulating phase can create contact resistance and current crowding while still passivating enough area to preserve the average VOC. The process should target a conformal submonolayer or ultrathin layer using a highly dilute orthogonal solvent, controlled meniscus/spray coating, vapor-assisted delivery, or another method with tight drying and surface-coverage control. A dose-by-drying-rate-by-texture matrix should define the window between incomplete coverage and transport-blocking excess. KPFM/UPS or surface-potential mapping should test dipole magnitude and orientation across facets; XPS/ToF-SIMS and cross-sectional microscopy should map chemical coverage and salt accumulation. Electroluminescence and PL/QFLS maps should separate spatial recombination from current crowding. Suns-VOC or luminescence-derived pseudo-FF compared with electrical FF, together with contact resistivity, impedance, dark J-V, and transient extraction, distinguishes a resistive contact loss from a true increase in nonradiative recombination. The qualified tandem must then undergo stabilized MPP operation and thermal cycling over the intended temperature range, with periodic resistance and luminescence mapping; damp-heat/moisture testing and ion-migration or interlayer-redistribution checks should be added because salts and textured interfaces can move or hydrate. Success requires uniform molecular coverage, preserved energy shift, low contact resistance, and stable FF/VOC—not merely retention of the small-cell VOC gain.
scoring_key_points: Diagnoses texture-driven nonuniform coverage, pooling/aggregation, orientation variation, or an insulating salt-rich phase as likely causes of retained VOC but lost FF.
Proposes a conformal ultrathin deposition and dose/drying/texture process window rather than simply increasing salt loading.
Uses spatial dipole/chemistry/luminescence mapping plus pseudo-FF versus electrical FF and contact-resistance diagnostics.
Requires stabilized MPP, thermal cycling, moisture testing, and repeated mapping to verify tandem durability and interlayer immobility.
accepted_equivalents: Spray, vapor, meniscus, or orthogonal-solvent deposition that yields conformal molecular coverage
KPFM, UPS mapping, ToF-SIMS, XPS imaging, conductive AFM, or cross-sectional analysis
Suns-VOC, pseudo-JV, impedance, TLM/contact resistivity, or transient photocurrent for resistance-recombination separation
IEC-like thermal cycling plus operational and damp-heat testing of encapsulated tandems
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the FF loss to reduced absorption even though JSC is unchanged.
Raises the interlayer concentration to improve coverage without checking for an insulating overlayer.
Uses only average UPS/XPS values and misses facet- or area-dependent nonuniformity.
Claims stability from initial encapsulated efficiency without operational or thermal-cycle testing.

expected_answer: Absorber decomposition is indicated by loss or spectral change of perovskite absorption/PL, reduced recovered QFLS, new crystalline/decomposition phases, and chemical changes inside the protected stack; these changes can occur before or together with loss of photocurrent. Protection-layer failure is instead indicated by rising dark leakage or shunt current, electrolyte penetration, pinhole-localized corrosion/delamination, and detection of Pb/halide or other absorber species in the electrolyte by ICP-MS/ion analysis, often with spatially localized electroluminescence or photocurrent failure. Catalyst deactivation is diagnosed when the absorber optical/electrical quality and barrier integrity remain largely intact but catalytic overpotential and interfacial charge-transfer resistance rise, product rate/Faradaic efficiency falls, and catalyst oxidation state, surface area, or selectivity changes; stable photocurrent with declining desired-product FE can indicate competing reactions rather than absorber failure. A still-intact but electronically degraded interface is supported by preserved absorber spectrum/QFLS and no electrolyte leakage, combined with slower carrier extraction, increased interfacial impedance, altered photovoltage/photocurrent transients, and stronger interfacial recombination. The decision tree should continuously pair chronoamperometry and impedance/photovoltage with online gas or liquid-product quantification, periodic absolute PL/absorption or operando spectroscopy, dark-leakage testing, post-test cross-sectional microscopy/adhesion analysis, and electrolyte elemental analysis. No single current trace can distinguish these mechanisms because current may fall from optical destruction, barrier breach, catalyst kinetics, or charge-selective-contact loss.
scoring_key_points: Assigns absorber optical/QFLS/phase changes to perovskite decomposition.
Assigns dark leakage, localized corrosion/delamination, and absorber-ion release to protection-layer pinholes or failure.
Assigns increased catalytic overpotential/charge-transfer resistance and product-selectivity loss with intact absorber/barrier to catalyst deactivation or side reactions.

Assigns slower extraction and increased interfacial recombination with intact chemistry and no leakage to electronic interface degradation, using online product analysis and orthogonal operando tests.
accepted_equivalents: ICP-MS, ion chromatography, or elemental analysis of electrolyte for barrier breach
Operando XRD, Raman, absorption, PL/QFLS, or postmortem spectroscopy for absorber decomposition
EIS, intensity-modulated photocurrent/photovoltage, transient absorption, or surface photovoltage for interfacial kinetics
Online gas chromatography, mass spectrometry, or liquid-product analysis for Faradaic efficiency and selectivity
common_wrong_answers: Interprets photocurrent decay alone as proof that the perovskite decomposed.
Uses stable crystal structure to claim the whole photoelectrode is stable without checking pinholes or catalyst activity.
Equates high photocurrent with high oxygen Faradaic efficiency and ignores parasitic reactions.
Measures only the dry postmortem absorber and omits electrolyte/product and operando electrical evidence.

expected_answer: The electrically isolated PV-electrolyzer is the preferred architecture under these constraints because it keeps the lead-halide absorber dry and physically separated from neutral aqueous electrolyte, allows the CO2 electrolyzer and catalyst to be replaced independently, and avoids relying on a defect-free immersed barrier for 1000 h. The perovskite PV should be encapsulated as a conventional photovoltaic module and connected to a separate CO2 electrolyzer. Its operating voltage—not merely VOC—must exceed the electrolyzer's thermodynamic potential plus kinetic, ohmic, membrane, and mass-transport overpotentials at the desired current. Tandem/series PV connection, cell-area ratio, catalyst area, or power electronics should match the PV maximum-power point to the electrolyzer load across irradiance and temperature. The primary metric is stabilized solar-to-CO or solar-to-fuel efficiency based on incident sunlight and verified CO production, together with CO Faradaic efficiency/selectivity, energy efficiency, current density, carbon balance, and continuous operating time; PV PCE or short photocurrent alone is insufficient. Containment validation should include encapsulation aging, damp heat, thermal cycling, mechanical stress, deliberate fault/pinhole tests, and sensitive Pb/halide analysis of all fluids and condensates. The electrolyzer requires catalyst/membrane durability, gas-crossover and product-purity tests, while the coupled system requires MPP/load tracking and start-stop cycling. A directly suspended lead perovskite fails the exposure and containment constraints, and a protected photoelectrode is a secondary option only if a scalable, conductive, catalytic, pinhole-free barrier can independently demonstrate the same 1000 h and zero-release requirement.
scoring_key_points: Selects the isolated PV-electrolyzer because it physically decouples the lead-perovskite absorber from neutral aqueous electrolyte and permits catalyst replacement.
Matches PV MPP voltage/current to electrolyzer thermodynamic plus kinetic/ohmic/mass-transport requirements using tandem/series design, area matching, or power electronics.
Requires solar-to-CO/fuel efficiency, Faradaic efficiency/selectivity, energy efficiency, carbon balance, and stabilized duration rather than PV PCE alone.
Includes encapsulation fault/aging and sensitive Pb-release tests plus electrolyzer catalyst, membrane, crossover, and coupled-load durability tests.
accepted_equivalents: A dry encapsulated perovskite tandem powering a separate CO2 electrolyzer
Series-connected PV cells, monolithic tandems, DC-DC conversion, or area-ratio matching
Solar-to-chemical efficiency verified by calibrated product quantification and full carbon balance
ICP-MS containment testing under damp heat, thermal cycling, mechanical damage, and start-stop operation
common_wrong_answers: Chooses direct lead-perovskite suspension because it has the shortest charge-transfer distance, ignoring water stability and lead release.
Uses PV open-circuit voltage as the electrolyzer operating voltage and ignores the MPP/load curve and overpotentials.
Reports only photovoltaic efficiency or photocurrent without product selectivity and Faradaic efficiency.
Assumes encapsulation is perfect and omits fault testing or elemental analysis of the electrolyte.

expected_answer: The unchanged absorption edge and shallow fluorine profile argue against bulk alloying or bulk doping. Longer bare-film decay, higher radiative quality, and an ideality factor moving toward unity are consistent with fewer surface or near-surface Shockley-Read-Hall pathways. A reproducible work-function or band-edge shift can additionally reduce selective-contact offsets, but it is not by itself proof of chemical passivation because an oriented molecular dipole can produce the same observation. The low-angle peak appearing only at high dose, together with loss of Voc or fill factor, indicates that an initially beneficial interfacial reconstruction has crossed into a thicker or more continuous low-dimensional layer that impedes extraction or increases series resistance. Causality requires a dose series and orthogonal controls: post-treatment versus precursor addition; a nonfluorinated hydrazine analogue and a fluorinated molecule lacking the anchoring group; direct-contact and inert-spacer configurations; depth-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS; absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting; UPS or Kelvin-probe measurements; angle-resolved diffraction or cross-sectional microscopy; and contact-resolved extraction or impedance measurements. The dominant mechanism at the optimum is therefore coupled surface passivation and favorable interfacial energetics, not the mere presence of a quasi-2D peak.
scoring_key_points: Uses the unchanged bulk optical response and shallow molecular distribution to reject bulk compositional modification as the primary mechanism.
Assigns lifetime and ideality-factor improvement to reduced trap-assisted recombination while treating the work-function shift as an additional, non-unique interfacial energetic effect.
Identifies the high-dose quasi-2D phase and declining Voc or fill factor as an over-treatment or transport-barrier boundary.
Proposes matched chemical, placement, dose, depth-profile, energetic, recombination, structural, and extraction controls that can distinguish the three mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Surface dipole, vacuum-level shift, or contact-selectivity improvement as equivalent descriptions of the energetic contribution
Absolute photoluminescence quantum yield, electroluminescence efficiency, or nonradiative Voc loss as alternatives to quasi-Fermi-level-splitting measurements
A blocked hydrazine, nonfluorinated aromatic hydrazine, or fluorinated nonbinding analogue as a structure-function control
GIWAXS, grazing-incidence XRD, or cross-sectional TEM as acceptable methods for resolving low-dimensional interfacial phase formation
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that any work-function shift proves defect passivation or bulk doping
Treating the appearance of a quasi-2D peak as necessarily beneficial at every concentration
Using longer PL lifetime alone to prove improved extraction in the completed device

expected_answer: A first-order transient-absorption lifetime is not a complete descriptor of extraction. It can be dominated by recombination in the 3D bulk and remain similar even when the vertical connectivity, energetic cascade, and transport barrier of the capping region differ. A surface-rich low-n layer may passivate defects yet impose strong quantum confinement and a poorly conducting barrier. A mixed distribution containing more high-n phases can preserve passivation while providing smaller band offsets, electronically coupled pathways, and faster transfer toward the 3D absorber or electron contact, thereby increasing diffusion length and fill factor without greatly changing the fitted first-order lifetime. The mechanism should be tested by combining angle- or depth-resolved GIWAXS with excitation-depth-dependent and spectrally resolved PL, ultrafast transfer dynamics, contact-induced PL quenching, electron mobility or diffusion measurements, and temperature-dependent transport. Absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting should quantify passivation independently. Matched ligand chemistry with solvent-only controls, and samples engineered to have similar integrated phase fractions but different vertical distributions, are especially decisive. If performance tracks defect density but not phase location or transfer kinetics, passivation dominates; if it tracks high-n connectivity and contact-directed transfer at comparable radiative quality, phase distribution is causal.
scoring_key_points: Explains that a similar first-order recombination lifetime can coexist with different vertical phase connectivity, energetic barriers, and extraction kinetics.
Contrasts a passivating but transport-blocking low-n surface layer with a mixed high-n network that supports energy funneling and carrier continuity.
Requires depth-resolved structure plus spectrally or spatially resolved transfer, mobility, diffusion, and contact-extraction measurements.
Separates passivation using PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting and states a decision rule linking performance either to defect density or to phase connectivity.
accepted_equivalents: Reduced quantum-confinement penalty, smaller interwell barrier, or improved electronic coupling as explanations for the high-n benefit
Angle-dependent GIWAXS, grazing-incidence scattering tomography, or cross-sectional nano-diffraction for vertical phase mapping
Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz spectroscopy, or diffusion-length measurements for transport diagnosis
Wavelength-selective excitation or front-versus-back excitation as an alternative depth-sensitive transfer test
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that identical fitted lifetimes prove identical interfaces and transport
Assuming that the lowest-n phase always gives the best stability and therefore the best device performance
Using stronger steady-state PL alone to claim faster charge extraction

expected_answer: A slower tail in a complete device is not evidence of improved lifetime because contacts and mobile ions can store charge and feed carriers back into the perovskite. The experiment should compare matched samples before and after aging in a ladder: bare perovskite, perovskite/electron-contact bilayer, ITO/hole-contact/perovskite partial stack, and full cell. For each geometry, measure differential TPL versus quasi-Fermi-level splitting over multiple fluences, temperatures, repetition rates, and external conditions such as open circuit, short circuit, controlled bias, and bias preconditioning. Add absolute PLQY or QFLS, electroluminescence, transient current and voltage, impedance or capacitance-frequency spectra, internal-versus-terminal voltage lag, and Kelvin-probe or ion-depth-profile measurements. True recombination improvement should appear in the bare or minimally contacted stack, raise radiative efficiency and QFLS, and remain broadly insensitive to electrode capacitance and bias history. A charging or re-injection artifact should emerge mainly in contacted structures, strengthen at low fluence or after bias preconditioning, correlate with increased capacitance or potential lag, and coexist with lower EL efficiency and Voc. Drift-diffusion modeling must reproduce the entire stack ladder and bias dependence before assigning a recombination lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Rejects the inference that a slower full-device PL tail necessarily means less recombination and identifies charge storage, ions, and re-injection as alternatives.
Uses a pre-aging and post-aging stack ladder from bare film through bilayer and partial stack to full device.
Varies fluence, temperature, repetition rate, terminal condition, bias, and bias history while combining QFLS or PLQY with electrical transients, capacitance, and potential or ion diagnostics.
Defines contrasting decision criteria for genuine recombination improvement versus contact-, capacitance-, ion-, or re-injection-dominated slow decay.
accepted_equivalents: Pulsed-bias, light-soaking, or voltage-preconditioning sequences as probes of ionic and capacitive memory
Electroabsorption, surface-potential mapping, or operando X-ray methods as alternatives for internal-field diagnosis
Intensity-dependent photoluminescence quantum yield or Suns-Voc as alternatives for QFLS validation
Equivalent-circuit analysis combined with drift-diffusion modeling
common_wrong_answers: Calling the aged cell better because its PL decay is slower despite lower Voc and electroluminescence efficiency
Measuring only the full cell and omitting the stack ladder needed to localize the new slow component
Ignoring excitation fluence and bias history even though capacitive and ionic effects are strongly state dependent

expected_answer: The design should cross HTL chemistry and Li content with ferrocene dose, wet thickness, and deposition or drying conditions. Required controls are no ferrocene at each Li level, a conventional LiTFSI/tBP formulation, a low-Li formulation, a Li-free or alternative-dopant formulation, and ideally a nonbinding redox analogue. Spiro oxidation state, conductivity, and mobility determine whether ferrocene still assists HTL doping; PLQY/QFLS, transient extraction, impedance, and series resistance determine whether direct interfacial electronic benefits persist. Li NMR or binding measurements and aged depth profiles establish whether Li immobilization remains relevant. Large-area acceptance requires coverage and thickness maps, Fe or composition mapping, PL/EL uniformity, sheet resistance, shunt and dark-current imaging, and yield statistics. The useful window is monolayer-like or ultrathin: below it, uncovered regions allow Li accumulation and recombination; above it, series resistance, energetic decoupling, or ferrocene aggregation should appear. Damp-heat, dry heat, illumination at MPP, and thermal cycling must be run separately. If the stability benefit collapses as Li approaches zero but extraction remains improved, Li binding was the main durability function while surface modification remains transferable; if all benefits vanish, the original effect was formulation-specific.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial matrix spanning HTL chemistry or Li level, ferrocene dose or thickness, and coating or drying conditions with matched no-interlayer controls.
Separately measures spiro oxidation and transport, interfacial recombination and extraction, and residual Li binding or migration.
Defines a bounded ultrathin coverage window and large-area spatial acceptance tests for coverage, resistance, shunts, luminescence, and yield.
Includes distinct humidity, dry-heat, MPP-illumination, and cycling stresses and explains how results identify formulation-specific versus transferable functions.
accepted_equivalents: Alternative stable dopants, dopant-free small-molecule HTLs, or self-assembled hole contacts as the low-Li or Li-free comparison
X-ray fluorescence, SIMS, Raman, ellipsometry, or hyperspectral imaging for large-area ferrocene coverage mapping
Transient photocurrent, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or charge-extraction measurements as alternatives to impedance
Statistical thickness-design-of-experiments or response-surface optimization
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the same ferrocene concentration is optimal after removing LiTFSI
Judging transfer only by champion PCE and ignoring interlayer nonuniformity or series resistance
Running only humid storage and failing to separate Li-related, thermal, and illumination-driven degradation

expected_answer: Equal PCE does not imply equal heat generation because the modules can absorb different total optical power and dissipate losses in different layers. Sub-bandgap absorption in the TCO, encapsulant, backsheet, or inactive semiconductor becomes heat without producing current. Above-bandgap thermalization and nonradiative or resistive electrical losses also become heat, whereas escaped or reflected photons do not heat the module. Strong light trapping can therefore improve current while simultaneously trapping otherwise escaping near-infrared photons and increasing parasitic heat. Spectral reflectance, transmittance, absorptance, and EQE should be combined with layer-resolved optical modeling to locate absorbed power. MPP I-V data, electroluminescence or recombination analysis, and series-resistance measurements constrain electrical heat generation. Calorimetry or controlled infrared thermography, measured emissivity, through-plane thermal resistance, and identical wind-tunnel boundary conditions separate heat generation from heat rejection. Increasing wind raises the convective heat-transfer coefficient, so a similar difference in generated heat produces a much smaller temperature difference. The diagnosis is credible only if one coupled optical-electrical-thermal model predicts temperature over wind speed and irradiance, rather than fitting temperature alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains why equal PCE can coexist with different absorbed optical power and heat generation, especially from sub-bandgap parasitic absorption.
Separates non-heating photon escape or reflection from thermalization, parasitic absorption, nonradiative recombination, and resistive losses.
Requires spectral and layer-resolved optical measurements, electrical-loss diagnostics, and calorimetric or thermographic measurements under controlled thermal boundaries.
Explains wind-driven convergence through the convective heat-transfer coefficient and requires a coupled model across irradiance and wind speed.
accepted_equivalents: Spectral calorimetry or photothermal deflection as alternatives for locating parasitic absorption
Lock-in thermography, infrared microscopy, or heat-flux sensors for spatial heat-generation validation
External radiative efficiency or Suns-Voc analysis as alternatives for nonradiative-loss quantification
A calibrated finite-element thermal model in place of a one-dimensional heat-balance model
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the hotter module must have lower PCE when both modules have the same measured efficiency
Counting all photons not converted to electricity as heat, including photons that escape or reflect
Attributing the high-wind convergence to reduced optical absorption rather than stronger convective heat removal

expected_answer: The catalyst should be tested under continuous time-on-stream illumination at controlled photon flux, temperature, oxygen activity, toluene concentration, and water content, with matched dark, no-substrate, and no-oxygen controls. Batch recycling alone should be replaced or complemented by a long continuous run because washing and dark storage can hide reversible processes. Activity, selectivity, carbon balance, and apparent quantum yield should be tracked at short intervals. Ligand desorption is diagnosed by loss of surface nitrogen/organic signatures using XPS, FTIR, TGA or elemental analysis and by ligand detected in the liquid or gas phase; re-dosing the ligand should restore ordering/charge-transfer behavior and activity if desorption is causal. Renewed disorder is diagnosed by a decrease in the superstructure ordering ratio and peak coherence, ideally supported by total-scattering/PDF, Raman, or local coordination probes; a simple ligand wash that does not restore order would distinguish irreversible cation rearrangement. Halide corrosion requires solution-phase Br analysis by ion chromatography or ICP-compatible methods, changes in Bi/Ag oxidation states, new phases, or mass loss; activity should not recover by removing adsorbates alone. Poisoning is indicated by accumulated carbonaceous surface species, altered adsorption signatures, and recovery after a mild oxidative or solvent-cleaning treatment without restoring lost ligand or halide. PL/TRPL, SPV/KPFM, and EIS collected during aging link each structural or chemical change to carrier separation and interfacial transfer. The study should report whether failure is reversible, partially reversible, or irreversible and should preserve the reaction history before ex situ washing.
scoring_key_points: Uses a continuous, controlled time-on-stream protocol with appropriate light/dark/reactant controls and tracks activity, selectivity, and photon-normalized performance.
Assigns ligand desorption through surface/compositional measurements plus a ligand re-dosing recovery test.
Separates renewed cation disorder from halide corrosion using ordering/local-structure probes versus dissolved-halide/chemical-state analysis.
Diagnoses surface poisoning through carbonaceous-species detection and selective cleaning recovery, while linking degradation to carrier-dynamics measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Operando XAS or neutron/total scattering as alternatives for cation-order tracking
Mass spectrometry, NMR, or chromatographic analysis of leached ligand and reaction products
Photothermal or electrochemical regeneration as an alternative selective poisoning-recovery test
common_wrong_answers: Using only before/after XRD and final activity retention
Calling every reversible activity loss structural degradation
Washing the catalyst before characterization without preserving evidence of desorbed ligand or adsorbed poisons

expected_answer: The ideality factor is the slope of Voc versus the logarithm of light intensity over a selected range; it indicates how the dominant voltage-dependent recombination pathway scales, not the absolute magnitude of recombination or the quality of carrier extraction. A buried low-dimensional layer can change carrier densities, injection conditions, or the dominant pathway and therefore lower the apparent slope while still causing a large absolute voltage loss. It can create a conduction-band or tunneling barrier, accumulate charge, increase contact-selective recombination, or reduce electron collection, all of which can depress Voc and fill factor. The hierarchy should start with absolute quasi-Fermi-level splitting from calibrated PLQY or electroluminescence and compare it with device Voc: a large QFLS-Voc gap implicates contact/interface loss, whereas a low QFLS already in the bare film points to bulk or phase-defect recombination. Next, Suns-Voc and intensity-dependent measurements should be checked across a broad range to exclude slope artifacts. Dark J-V, impedance, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, mobility or conductivity, and temperature-dependent transport can identify extraction barriers and series/contact resistance. Finally, depth-resolved SIMS/GIWAXS, cross-sectional microscopy, and phase-selective PL correlate the buried organic-rich low-dimensional phase with the electrical loss. A lower ideality factor is therefore compatible with a worse device when the dominant recombination mechanism changes or when transport/contact losses become controlling.
scoring_key_points: States that ideality factor is a slope/mechanism indicator and does not measure the absolute recombination rate or extraction quality.
Explains how a buried low-dimensional organic-rich phase can create energetic/tunneling barriers, charge accumulation, or contact recombination despite a lower apparent ideality factor.
Uses calibrated PLQY/QFLS or electroluminescence and the QFLS-Voc gap to separate bulk from contact/interface voltage losses.
Adds transport/contact diagnostics and depth-resolved phase mapping, with attention to intensity-range artifacts in the fitted ideality factor.
accepted_equivalents: Pseudo-JV or Suns-Voc analysis as an equivalent method for separating transport from recombination losses
Temperature-dependent impedance, charge-extraction, or time-of-flight measurements as transport-barrier diagnostics
Cross-sectional nano-XRD, TOF-SIMS, or electron microscopy as alternatives for buried-phase localization
common_wrong_answers: Equating an ideality factor closer to one with universally lower recombination
Ignoring the absolute Voc and QFLS because the slope metric appears favorable
Attributing the entire loss to optical absorption even though the phase is concentrated at the charge-selective contact

expected_answer: More negative adsorption is not automatically better because an overly strong or densely packed surface layer can block electronic coupling to the transport layer, create an unfavorable dipole or band offset, reduce wetting, or produce a locally insulating region. Likewise, a longer film TRPL lifetime can indicate fewer nonradiative traps, but it can also reflect slower charge extraction when the selective contact is added; the device fill factor exposes this transport penalty. Poor thermal stability may arise from ligand volatility, desorption, chemical reaction with FA/halide or the transport layer, phase separation, or thermally activated migration. The go/no-go matrix should therefore include a concentration/thickness sweep and contact-complete measurements: calibrated PLQY and QFLS before and after contact deposition; UPS/Kelvin-probe band alignment; dark J-V, series resistance, impedance, transient photocurrent, and electroluminescence to quantify extraction and interface loss. Chemical robustness should be tested by TGA/thermal desorption, temperature-dependent XPS or IR, TOF-SIMS depth profiles before and after aging, and analysis of decomposition products or ligand loss. Manufacturability requires solubility, coating uniformity, solvent orthogonality, drying-window tolerance, and mapping of large-area PL/QFLS and sheet resistance. It should advance only if a lower dose or altered deposition route preserves the recombination benefit while recovering FF and if the molecule remains chemically and spatially stable under combined heat, light, and electrical bias. If the transport penalty persists at submonolayer coverage or degradation is intrinsic, the analog should be rejected despite favorable adsorption and TRPL.
scoring_key_points: Explains that overly strong/dense adsorption can create an insulating layer, unfavorable dipole, poor wetting, or contact-coupling barrier.
Explains that longer film TRPL can result from slower extraction and must be reconciled with contact-complete QFLS, FF, and transport diagnostics.
Includes thermal-desorption, chemical-compatibility, migration, and decomposition tests under combined heat/light/bias stress.
Defines a practical go/no-go decision using dose/process optimization, large-area uniformity and solvent compatibility, and recovery of FF without losing stability.
accepted_equivalents: Pareto optimization of passivation, extraction, stability, and manufacturability rather than single-metric ranking
Contacted-PL, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or impedance spectroscopy as alternatives for distinguishing lifetime from extraction
Blade-coating, slot-die, spray, or vapor deposition as equivalent module-relevant process screens
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the analog solely because its adsorption energy is most negative
Interpreting every increase in TRPL lifetime as faster carrier extraction
Testing shelf storage only and ignoring thermal desorption, bias-driven migration, or contact compatibility

expected_answer: The controls must hold final alkali content and processing history constant while changing whether a phase-defined seed exists. At minimum, compare delta-phase seeds with equivalent molar amounts of soluble CsI/RbI or molecular precursors, a seed-free ionic-strength control, and inert or composition-matched particles lacking the delta crystal structure; include seed-size or number-density series at constant total Cs/Rb. True heterogeneous nucleation requires phase-specific evidence before conversion: the delta reflections or local structure should persist in the first-step intermediate, and in situ GIWAXS or optical scattering should show an altered nucleation onset, induction time, or spatial nucleation density that scales with seed number/surface area. The seed route should create a reproducible intermediate morphology, such as porosity that accelerates FA/MA penetration, even when the final Cs/Rb composition is matched to soluble-salt controls. Time-resolved conversion measurements should then connect this intermediate to faster or more complete disappearance of PbI2, different grain-number evolution, and a depth distribution not explained by simple bulk doping. A generic solvent/ionic-strength mechanism would be reproduced by non-seed salts with similar coordination chemistry; nonspecific templating would be reproduced by inert particles of comparable size and surface energy; simple doping would primarily change final composition/bandgap and would not require a phase-identified intermediate or seed-number-dependent nucleation kinetics. Device-level Voc and recombination gains are supportive consequences, not proof of the nucleation mechanism by themselves.
scoring_key_points: Uses soluble Cs/Rb, ionic-strength/solvent, inert-particle, and seed-size/number-density controls while matching final alkali content.
Requires phase-specific seed evidence in the first-step intermediate and time-resolved nucleation kinetics that depend on seed surface area or number.
Connects seed-specific intermediate porosity/penetration to conversion completeness, residual PbI2, grain evolution, and depth distribution.
Explains the distinct predictions of simple doping, generic solution effects, and nonspecific particulate templating, and does not use device efficiency as sole proof.
accepted_equivalents: In situ XRD, GIWAXS, SAXS, Raman, or electron diffraction for seed-phase and nucleation tracking
Silica, alumina, PbI2 nanoparticles, or amorphized seed material as inert/nonspecific particulate controls
Isotopically or chemically labeled seed components as a route to trace seed-derived material
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only a seed-added film with a seed-free film while changing Cs/Rb composition at the same time
Calling larger grains proof of heterogeneous nucleation without measuring the intermediate or nucleation kinetics
Using higher Voc or lower residual PbI2 alone to infer a seed-specific pathway

expected_answer: The scale-up target is not the spin speed or nominal bake time but the sequence of physical states that enables seed-assisted conversion. The first ink must maintain stable seed dispersion, an appropriate seed-number density, PbI2-solvent coordination, and colloid/rheology behavior without settling or nozzle filtration; DLS or laser scattering, rheology, turbidity, and periodic composition analysis are suitable controls. During first-layer drying, the relevant variables are wet thickness, solvent-removal rate, substrate temperature, ambient humidity, and residence time that produce the intended porous but continuous intermediate. Inline reflectance/scattering, interferometric thickness, infrared solvent signatures, and rapid GIWAXS/XRD or imaging can monitor this state. The second step must preserve the diffusion-reaction balance of FA/MA salts through the intermediate, so coating dose, solvent activity, contact time before crystallization, and evaporation rate should be controlled; residual-PbI2 mapping, conversion kinetics, and spatial PL/absorption are rapid indicators. Annealing must complete conversion and additive removal without driving cation segregation, excessive grain coarsening, or film stress, requiring temperature-history rather than furnace set-point matching. A multivariate design of experiments should map line speed, coating gap, drying-zone profile, humidity, and seed loading to intermediate porosity, residual PbI2, QFLS, and device uniformity. Closed-loop limits should reject drift in ink scattering, wet thickness, intermediate optical signature, or residual-PbI2/PL maps. Qualification must include large-area yield and MPP light/thermal/humidity aging because a process that gives high initial PCE but leaves spatially variable residual phases or mobile alkali distributions is not stable.
scoring_key_points: Preserves seed dispersion/number density, PbI2-solvent coordination, colloid stability, and rheology, with ink-level scattering/rheology/composition controls.
Controls wet thickness, drying/solvent-removal history, humidity, and residence time to reproduce the required porous continuous intermediate, with inline optical/thickness/structural indicators.
Controls second-step diffusion-reaction and annealing histories using conversion kinetics, residual-PbI2, PL/absorption, and temperature-profile mapping rather than copied spin-coating times.
Defines multivariate/closed-loop process limits and qualifies large-area yield plus combined MPP, heat, and humidity stability.
accepted_equivalents: Roll-to-roll gravure, blade, curtain, or spray coating as equivalent continuous-process contexts
Inline hyperspectral imaging, Raman, XRF, ellipsometry, or machine-vision scattering as equivalent rapid indicators
Statistical process control, response-surface DOE, or model-predictive control as equivalent scale-up frameworks
common_wrong_answers: Copying spin speed, solution concentration, and oven set point without matching wet-film and drying kinetics
Monitoring only final film color or champion-cell PCE
Ignoring seed sedimentation, nozzle filtration, humidity sensitivity, or spatial residual-PbI2 variation

expected_answer:
A new low-energy PL peak is suggestive of I-rich domains because photocarriers can funnel into a small volume fraction of lower-bandgap material, but PL alone does not establish compositional segregation. The first branch of the decision tree should test kinetics and reversibility. Phase segregation typically shows an illumination-dose-dependent emergence of the low-energy emission and at least partial dark recovery; the rate should depend on temperature, excitation density, electric field, and defect/ion-migration history. A static defect-tail state may saturate rapidly and need not show the same reversible compositional memory.

Heating must be excluded by measuring the actual film temperature, reproducing the temperature rise in the dark or at low excitation, and comparing the expected bandgap-temperature shift with the observed spectral change. A smooth thermally induced bandgap shift differs from the growth of a distinct low-energy population. Spectrally resolved absorption, photothermal deflection, or sensitive EQE can determine whether a new lower-gap absorption edge appears; pure carrier funneling into pre-existing traps can strongly alter PL without creating a measurable new absorber fraction.

Composition-sensitive and spatial probes are then required. Time-resolved or nano-focused GIWAXS, nano-XRF, cathodoluminescence, hyperspectral PL mapping, and correlative chemical imaging can detect nanoscale I-rich/Br-rich heterogeneity. Conventional XRD can remain unchanged because the segregated volume fraction may be small, domains may be nanoscale or strained, and PL disproportionately weights the lowest-gap regions through carrier funneling. Therefore, lack of bulk peak splitting does not rule out segregation.

Finally, contact effects should be separated by repeating measurements on contact-free films, partial stacks, and complete devices under open circuit, short circuit, and controlled bias. Absolute PL-derived QFLS and electroluminescence can distinguish absorber changes from interface recombination. If the red peak occurs in the bare film with a new low-gap absorption/composition signal and reversible ion-migration kinetics, phase segregation is supported. If it appears only after a selective contact or under a particular bias while the absorber spectrum and composition remain unchanged, interfacial carrier accumulation or recombination is the more likely cause.
scoring_key_points: Uses illumination-dose, temperature, field, and dark-recovery kinetics to test reversible ion-migration-driven segregation.
Separates heating and pre-existing defect/tail funneling with temperature controls and absorption or sensitive-EQE measurements.
Requires nanoscale spatial/composition-sensitive probes and explains why a small segregated fraction can evade conventional XRD yet dominate PL.
Compares bare films, partial stacks, bias conditions, QFLS, and electroluminescence to identify contact-induced recombination or accumulation.
accepted_equivalents: Nano-XRD, nano-XRF, STEM-EDS/EELS, ToF-SIMS, or another composition-sensitive nanoscale method may be used to detect segregated domains.
Photothermal deflection, sub-bandgap EQE, absorption, or photocurrent spectroscopy may test for a new low-gap absorber population.
Reversible spectral recovery in the dark is supportive but not sufficient without composition or absorption evidence.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring phase segregation solely from a red PL peak without excluding heating, traps, or interface effects.
Ruling out phase segregation because conventional XRD shows no split peak.
Measuring only a complete device and assigning every spectral change to bulk halide motion.

expected_answer:
Thermodynamic control should reduce the driving force for demixing while retaining the target bandgap. Composition can be adjusted through mixed cations, carefully selected halide ratios, or a third halide/additive that improves miscibility and lattice compatibility. The trade-off is that composition changes can shift the bandgap, introduce new defects, or create another unstable phase; high configurational entropy is not proof of operational miscibility.

Kinetic control should suppress the motion pathways that allow the system to reach a segregated state. Lowering halide-vacancy density, passivating grain boundaries and surfaces, increasing migration barriers, and using thin 2D or crosslinked boundary layers can slow ion motion. The trade-offs are reduced carrier mobility, blocked extraction, altered band alignment, or merely delayed rather than eliminated segregation. A successful strategy should lower mobile-defect density without creating a resistive network.

Mechanical control should minimize strain gradients and stress concentrations that bias local composition. Matching thermal expansion, controlling crystallization rate, reducing wrinkling and residual compressive stress, and using compliant or graded interfaces can remove nucleation sites for segregation. Excessive lattice stiffening or constraint can cause cracking, delamination, or different defect formation. Large-area coating must therefore control thickness, drying, and temperature uniformity, not only average composition.

Interfacial control should avoid carrier accumulation and electric fields that drive ion redistribution. Selective contacts with low recombination, appropriate band alignment, low ionic reactivity, and minimal fixed charge can reduce local quasi-Fermi-level and field gradients. Very thick 2D/passivation layers, however, can lower fill factor and current. The evidence must include stabilized MPP operation under light, heat, realistic spectrum, and electrical bias for long durations; periodic absorption/PL/EL and spatial composition or diffraction maps; dark-recovery and restart behaviour; QFLS/VOC and series-resistance tracking; and post-stress ion/defect analysis. Stability requires unchanged composition, voltage, and extraction over relevant time and area, not simply the absence of a red PL peak during a brief contact-free illumination test.
scoring_key_points: Provides a thermodynamic miscibility strategy while recognizing bandgap, defect, and competing-phase trade-offs.
Provides kinetic vacancy/ion-migration suppression without assuming that slower segregation equals thermodynamic stability.
Addresses strain, crystallization, and large-area mechanical nonuniformity as drivers of local segregation.
Controls interfacial fields/recombination and requires long-duration MPP, spectral, spatial-composition, voltage, and transport evidence.
accepted_equivalents: Triple-halide, mixed-cation, entropy engineering, or another justified miscibility intervention is acceptable.
Grain-boundary crosslinking, 2D capping, vacancy passivation, or lattice stiffening may be used as kinetic barriers if transport trade-offs are discussed.
Nano-XRF, nano-XRD, ToF-SIMS, hyperspectral PL, or equivalent spatial methods may demonstrate compositional stability.
common_wrong_answers: Proposing only a wider-bandgap composition without addressing defects, strain, ion migration, or contact fields.
Calling a film stable because no red PL peak appears in the first few minutes of illumination.
Using a thick insulating 2D layer as a universal solution without considering current extraction and fill-factor loss.

expected_answer:
Chemical passivation predicts functionality-specific behaviour. Molecular analogues that preserve thickness and morphology but remove the coordinating group should lose the QFLS benefit, while spectroscopy should show removal or neutralization of specific surface-defect signatures. If the interlayer improves only the perovskite-C60 stack and not the neat film, chemical healing of the bulk is already unlikely; surface chemical passivation remains possible but must correlate with functional-group chemistry rather than simply with coverage.

Physical contact displacement predicts that a chemically inert spacer of comparable thickness, coverage, and tunnelling distance should recover a similar fraction of QFLS. The benefit should correlate with reduced direct perovskite-C60 contact area or increased separation measured by microscopy, scattering, ellipsometry, or depth profiling. A common non-monotonic thickness response across unrelated materials would support this mechanism: initial coverage suppresses interfacial recombination, whereas excessive separation impedes electron transfer. If an inert, conformal spacer fails despite matching geometry, pure separation is insufficient.

A dipole or band-alignment mechanism predicts systematic work-function, vacuum-level, or band-offset shifts measured by UPS/Kelvin probe/photoelectron spectroscopy, and corresponding changes in contact selectivity, built-in field, or injection/extraction activation energy. The QFLS gain should track dipole orientation or magnitude, not merely thickness. If two interlayers produce the same QFLS recovery but opposite or negligible energetic shifts, a common dipole explanation is weakened.

Protection from C60-deposition damage predicts that the untreated perovskite changes chemically or electronically during energetic C60 evaporation and that the interlayer suppresses this change. Compare evaporated C60 with a softer-deposited electron contact, vary deposition rate or substrate temperature, and measure the perovskite before and after deposition using XPS, PLQY/QFLS, and defect-sensitive spectroscopy. If soft deposition removes the loss even without an interlayer, protection is strongly supported. The full matrix should hold optical generation constant and include time-resolved extraction, series resistance, and FF so that a QFLS gain caused by blocked electron transfer is not mistaken for a useful contact.
scoring_key_points: Uses functional-group analogues and defect-sensitive chemistry to test surface chemical passivation independently of bulk passivation.
Uses inert geometry-matched spacers, coverage/contact-area measurements, and thickness trends to test physical separation or contact displacement.
Uses work-function/band-offset and activation-energy measurements to test a dipole or band-alignment mechanism.
Varies C60 deposition severity or contact method and checks pre/post-deposition damage while confirming that extraction and FF remain acceptable.
accepted_equivalents: MgF2, an inert organic monolayer, or another non-coordinating spacer may serve as the geometry-matched separation control.
UPS, Kelvin probe, surface photovoltage, inverse photoemission, or device temperature dependence may probe energetic changes.
Soft lamination, solution-processed ETL, low-energy evaporation, or another reduced-damage contact can test deposition protection.
common_wrong_answers: Calling both interlayers bulk passivants even though the neat-film QFLS is unchanged.
Assigning the mechanism from a single XPS shift without geometry, energetic, and deposition controls.
Treating the highest stack QFLS as optimal while ignoring electron-transfer resistance and device fill factor.

expected_answer:
The key manufacturing variable is local effective coverage and tunnelling distance, not nominal deposited mass. On a textured or rough surface, the same average thickness can leave pinholes at peaks and form thick pools in valleys. The process must therefore control surface cleaning, roughness, precursor wetting or evaporation angle, deposition rate, substrate temperature, and any post-treatment. Cross-sectional microscopy, ellipsometry or X-ray reflectivity on representative geometries, and chemical-depth mapping should establish conformality and pinhole statistics across the full area.

Recombination and extraction must be mapped separately. Absolute PL-derived QFLS maps of neat perovskite, perovskite/interlayer, and perovskite/interlayer/C60 partial stacks should identify where C60-induced loss is suppressed. Electroluminescence or implied-VOC maps, sensitive sub-bandgap EQE, and contactless PL can reveal recombination nonuniformity. Four-point or transmission-line resistance, impedance, transient extraction, FF, and temperature-dependent J-V should detect thick or insulating regions. The acceptable window is the overlap where interface QFLS is high and series/contact resistance remains low.

Large-area qualification should use distributions and yield: subcell VOC, FF, leakage, shunt density, contact resistance, and stabilized MPP must be mapped from edge to centre and across multiple batches. Nominal thickness should be deliberately perturbed to determine process latitude. A robust interlayer tolerates realistic roughness and deposition variations without creating bimodal devices or local hot spots.

Durability testing should combine light, heat, electrical bias, thermal cycling, and realistic tandem current. Operando QFLS/EL, impedance, and resistance tracking can distinguish renewed interfacial recombination from transport-barrier growth. Post-ageing depth profiles and microscopy should check interlayer diffusion, chemical reaction with C60 or perovskite, pinhole growth, delamination, and ion accumulation. The interlayer passes only if it retains spatially uniform QFLS/VOC gains and extraction over time; a high initial QFLS followed by rising resistance or local recombination is a failed transfer.
scoring_key_points: Controls and measures local conformality, pinholes, and effective thickness on textured large-area surfaces rather than nominal thickness alone.
Maps partial-stack QFLS/recombination independently from contact resistance, extraction, FF, and transport activation.
Defines a reproducible process window using spatial distributions, perturbation tolerance, module yield, and stabilized MPP.
Uses combined-stress ageing and post-mortem chemistry/morphology to distinguish recombination return, barrier growth, diffusion, and delamination.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional TEM/SEM, tomography, AFM, XRR, ellipsometry, or another justified combination may quantify coverage and thickness.
PLQY/QFLS mapping, electroluminescence, implied-VOC imaging, or luminescence tomography may map non-radiative losses.
Sheet/contact resistance, impedance, TLM, transient photocurrent, or temperature-dependent transport may diagnose extraction barriers.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling by depositing the same nominal thickness used on a flat small-area substrate.
Optimizing only QFLS while ignoring pinholes, series resistance, fill factor, and spatial yield.
Reporting a short shelf-life test without light, bias, heat, tandem current, or interlayer diffusion analysis.

expected_answer:
The passivant cannot be judged by one trap-density number or one-sun PLQY. The first step is to determine the distribution of trap energies and capture kinetics, not merely the total state density. Temperature- and fluence-dependent steady-state PLQY/QFLS, thermal admittance or deep-level methods used cautiously, and trap-depth-aware SRH fitting should determine whether the treatment removes efficient deep recombination centres or converts them into shallow states with rapid trapping/detrapping. Capture coefficients for both carrier types matter because a shallow state can be benign, recombination active, or strongly photodoping depending on asymmetry.

The second step is a carrier-density and history matrix. Measure absolute PLQY, QFLS, kdiff or differential lifetime, and an independent n+p observable from low-light to above one sun, after dark storage, illumination preconditioning, and electrical bias. Charge-neutrality calculations should fit n, p, and trap occupancy. If the improved one-sun PLQY arises because shallow traps are filled or because photodoping creates a favourable majority-carrier population, performance may collapse at low injection or reverse after the illumination history changes.

The third step is to distinguish electronic trap occupancy from evolving ionic defects. Operando PL/QFLS, current-voltage, impedance, electroluminescence, and spatial potential or composition measurements during light-bias ageing should track timescales. Reversible fast changes with carrier population suggest trapping/photodoping; slower bias-direction-dependent drift, hysteresis, spatial segregation, or contact accumulation indicates ion migration or chemically evolving defects. Post-ageing spectroscopy and depth profiling should test whether the passivant or mobile ions redistribute.

Acceptance should be based on the intended operating envelope: stabilized MPP VOC and efficiency, low-light response, temperature dependence, recovery after dark and restart, and long-duration combined light/heat/bias stability. A passivant passes only if a single physically consistent model explains steady-state and transient behaviour and if the reduction of deep losses is not replaced by unstable shallow-trap photodoping, rising interfacial recombination, or mobile-ion drift. A higher one-sun PLQY with history-dependent voltage is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Separates trap concentration from energetic depth and electron/hole capture coefficients using trap-depth-aware, temperature- and fluence-dependent analysis.
Measures PLQY/QFLS and differential recombination versus carrier density and illumination/bias history while solving charge neutrality and photodoping.
Distinguishes fast electronic occupancy effects from slower ion-migration or chemical evolution with operando electrical, optical, spatial, and post-ageing diagnostics.
Bases acceptance on stabilized MPP, low-light, thermal, restart, and long-duration performance across the real operating envelope, not one-sun PLQY alone.
accepted_equivalents: Admittance, DLTS-like methods, thermally stimulated current, or optical spectroscopy may inform trap depth if their assumptions and limitations are acknowledged.
Transient absorption, conductivity, charge extraction, or another calibrated carrier-density probe may supplement PL/QFLS.
KPFM, ToF-SIMS, nano-XRF, electroluminescence imaging, or equivalent methods may identify ion redistribution and spatial degradation.
common_wrong_answers: Accepting the passivant because it lowers an SCLC or admittance-derived trap-density value at one condition.
Assuming shallow traps are always harmless or deep traps are always the only source of non-radiative recombination.
Treating illumination-history-dependent VOC as measurement noise without testing photodoping, trap occupancy, or ion migration.

expected_answer: The redox hypothesis contains two coupled half-reactions: trapped or long-lived holes oxidize iodide toward polyiodide species, while electrons reduce Pb2+ toward Pb0. These products create or accompany mobile defect complexes that are expelled toward grain boundaries and participate in formation of I-rich perovskite and PbI2. Charge-selective extraction should therefore interrupt the causal chain. Efficient hole extraction should suppress iodide oxidation and reduce polyiodide formation; efficient electron extraction should suppress Pb2+ reduction and reduce Pb0 formation. Because the mechanism requires a coupled redox pair and charge neutrality, either intervention should delay or reduce I-rich boundary nucleation, with the strongest suppression expected when both carrier populations are rapidly extracted or when selective redox scavengers are used. The contacts must be chemically inert and thickness-matched, and illumination should be adjusted so that comparisons are not merely caused by different absorbed photon flux, temperature, or gross steady-state carrier density. Time-resolved PL alone is insufficient. The experiment should track segregation kinetics by hyperspectral PL or absorption, boundary phase formation by in situ AFM/work-function mapping or nano-XRD, and redox species by operando or rapid-transfer XPS, Raman, or optical signatures. A causal redox model is supported if suppression of the relevant half-reaction selectively removes its chemical marker and proportionally delays boundary nucleation. A strain/polaron model becomes more plausible if I-rich domains still form with similar kinetics after both Pb0 and polyiodide signals are suppressed, and if segregation instead scales with lattice strain, elastic heterogeneity, or polaron population under matched carrier conditions. Intermediate results would indicate that redox and lattice effects are coupled rather than mutually exclusive.
scoring_key_points: Link hole extraction to suppression of iodide oxidation/polyiodide and electron extraction to suppression of Pb2+ reduction/Pb0.
Predict delayed or reduced grain-boundary I-rich nucleation when either coupled redox half-reaction is interrupted.
Use chemically inert, thickness-matched contacts and matched optical, thermal, and carrier-density conditions with orthogonal redox and phase measurements.
Favor a strain/polaron mechanism if segregation persists with similar kinetics despite suppression of both redox markers and instead tracks lattice or polaron observables.
accepted_equivalents: Selective chemical electron or hole scavengers may replace transport layers if they do not react directly with halides or Pb.
Operando XPS, rapid-transfer XPS, Raman, electron paramagnetic resonance, or chemically specific optical probes are acceptable redox diagnostics.
Nano-XRD, GIWAXS, AFM work-function mapping, or hyperspectral PL are acceptable segregation diagnostics.
A coupled redox-strain mechanism is acceptable if the proposed experiment can quantify both contributions.
common_wrong_answers: Using lower PL intensity as the sole evidence that redox has been suppressed.
Comparing contacts that change film chemistry, morphology, or temperature without matched controls.
Assuming that the absence of detectable Pb0 alone falsifies all redox involvement.
Treating polaron, strain, vacancy, and redox mechanisms as necessarily mutually exclusive.

expected_answer: The first gate is electronic rather than purely crystallographic. For each candidate, determine whether the bandgap is direct or indirect, the orbital character and dispersion at the band edges, effective masses, dielectric screening, exciton binding energy, and whether the electronic network is actually connected in the direction required for extraction. A structurally 3D double perovskite can still have an indirect, weakly absorbing gap; a 0D or 2D material can have localized carriers and strong excitons even if its nominal optical gap is attractive. The second gate is defect and lattice physics. Calculate and measure dominant defect formation energies, transition depths, capture cross-sections, multiphonon capture propensity, and electron-phonon coupling. Low defect density is not enough if the remaining defects are deep or have large capture coefficients, and strong lattice relaxation can cause self-trapping. The third gate is form factor and processing. Measure phase purity, orientation, grain-boundary connectivity, attainable thickness, absorption coefficient, minority-carrier diffusion length, and contact compatibility in the actual deposition route. Structural dimensionality must be separated from film texture; a layered material may work if vertically oriented but fail when sheets lie parallel to the substrate. The stability gate must use identical encapsulation, illumination, temperature, humidity, bias, and MPP conditions, with chemical and structural post-mortem analysis. Dark shelf survival only tests one low-stress axis and can favor wide-gap or kinetically inert materials that perform poorly. The final down-select should use device-relevant weighted metrics such as absorptance at target thickness, QFLS deficit, mobility-lifetime product, nonradiative voltage loss, stabilized efficiency, and normalized degradation rate. A candidate advances only if its electronic dimensionality, defect tolerance, processable texture, interfaces, and operational stability are jointly acceptable.
scoring_key_points: Prioritize directness, band-edge dispersion, effective masses, dielectric screening, exciton binding, and extraction-direction electronic connectivity.
Evaluate defect transition depth, capture cross-section, lattice relaxation, and self-trapping rather than defect density alone.
Separate structural dimensionality from film orientation and form factor using phase, texture, absorption, transport, and interface measurements.
Compare candidates under normalized MPP stability protocols and select on joint performance-stability metrics, not dark shelf life.
accepted_equivalents: Mobility-lifetime product, diffusion length, QFLS, or nonradiative voltage deficit may be used as the principal transport/recombination metric.
High-throughput DFT plus experimental validation is acceptable for the initial electronic and defect screen.
A Pareto-front or weighted decision matrix is acceptable if the weights and rejection thresholds are explicit.
The protocol may include tandem-specific bandgap and current-matching constraints.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the structurally 3D candidate automatically because 3D implies good transport.
Selecting the longest shelf-life material without testing illumination, bias, heat, and interfaces.
Using low defect concentration as proof of defect tolerance without capture kinetics.
Ignoring texture and transport direction in layered candidates.

expected_answer: The treatment should not advance on the fresh maps alone. Uniform SPV and higher local photocurrent may reflect better extraction, but they may also be produced by tip-induced contact changes, altered surface charging, or redistribution of current into a small fraction of conductive paths. More importantly, those measurements do not show that ion migration or chemical degradation has been reduced under the actual combined stress.
