Qualification should use the same device-relevant stack, illumination, bias polarity, temperature, and controlled humidity as the lifetime test. Fiducial markers should enable repeated imaging of identical grains and boundaries before stress, during interruptions, and after defined dose increments. Calibrated KPFM should track both spatial CPD and relaxation kinetics after light or bias removal; slower or larger relaxation after aging can indicate increased mobile ionic species rather than improved stability. pc-AFM or c-AFM should map whether current remains broadly distributed or collapses into hotspots, with force and contact-area controls to limit probe damage. PFIR/PTIR or nano-IR should identify degradation products and organic-cation changes, while topography records roughening or grain-boundary opening. Time-resolved or G-mode electrical imaging can separate fast electronic response from slower ionic redistribution. The nanoscale data must be correlated with area-matched QFLS or PL imaging, stabilized MPP, EQE, impedance, hysteresis, and post-aging chemical depth profiles. Sampling must cover many locations and multiple coated batches so that a visually favorable region is not treated as representative. The treatment advances only if the initial SPV/current gains persist under stress, ionic relaxation and chemical-degradation rates decrease, current remains spatially distributed, and those changes predict improved device-level lifetime without new series resistance or leakage. If local electrical uniformity improves but chemical and ionic degradation remain unchanged, the passivation is a performance treatment, not a stability solution.
scoring_key_points: Reject fresh KPFM/pc-AFM improvement as sufficient evidence and reproduce the actual combined humidity, bias, light, and temperature stress.
Use fiducial same-location time series to track CPD relaxation, current distribution, morphology, and local chemical degradation at grains and boundaries.
Control probe perturbation and separate fast electronic response from slow ionic/electrochemical changes with time-resolved measurements.
Advance only when nanoscale changes correlate across batches with improved stabilized MPP lifetime and no transport, leakage, or hotspot penalty.
accepted_equivalents: FF-tr-EFM, G-mode KPFM, scanning microwave impedance microscopy, or time-resolved EFM may substitute for time-resolved electrical imaging.
Nano-FTIR, PFIR, PTIR, Raman mapping, or SIMS may be used for local chemical-degradation evidence.
EL/QFLS imaging or Suns-VOC may replace area-matched PL as the macroscopic recombination cross-check.
A statistically designed sampling grid across a mini-module is acceptable for the scale-up representativeness test.
common_wrong_answers: Advancing the process because the fresh KPFM map looks more uniform.
Treating higher pc-AFM current as proof of lower ion migration.
Imaging different regions before and after stress and interpreting the difference as temporal evolution.
Ignoring conductive-tip damage, contact-force variation, and the mismatch between film-only maps and device operating conditions.

expected_answer:
The first gate is a normalized resource metric, not indium per cell. Indium use should be expressed per rated watt and, more importantly, per lifetime energy delivered at module level, including deposition utilization, grid and interconnect materials, yield losses, inactive-area penalties, and efficiency degradation. A low-indium architecture can displace more indium per terawatt than a nominally indium-free option if it preserves higher yield, efficiency, and service life.

The second gate is coupled optoelectronic and interface performance. Sheet resistance, near-infrared transparency, contact resistivity, work function, recombination-junction selectivity, and optical coupling must be measured in the complete tandem. Process compatibility must include sputter/plasma damage to perovskite, a-Si:H, or self-assembled monolayers; thermal budget; nucleation of ultrathin films; adhesion; and metal diffusion. A strong standalone electrode is not acceptable if it damages the buried interface or raises recombination.

The third gate is reliability under relevant combined stresses: damp heat, thermal cycling, UV/light bias, electrical bias, mechanical loading, and encapsulated module aging. AZO requires special attention to grain-boundary water ingress and conductivity loss; the ultrathin TCO route must be checked for pinholes and grid corrosion; the TCO-free junction must be checked for contact selectivity, process complexity, and long-term interdiffusion. Track Rs/FF, Voc, EQE, electroluminescence uniformity, adhesion, and chemical depth profiles.

Finally, perform a rebound audit. If AZO needs an ITO cap, or an alternative architecture requires indium-containing barriers elsewhere, those additions count in the inventory. Selection should be made from a Pareto frontier of lifetime energy yield, indium intensity, reliability, manufacturability, and cost, not from a binary material label.
scoring_key_points: Normalizes indium use to module watts or lifetime energy, including yield and efficiency effects.
Evaluates complete-stack electrical, optical, recombination-junction, and interface/process compatibility.
Defines combined accelerated-stress tests with mechanism-sensitive observables for each architecture.
Identifies rebound or burden shifting when caps, barriers, or yield losses undermine a nominally indium-free route.
accepted_equivalents: Energy-payback-adjusted or service-life-adjusted indium intensity is equivalent to lifetime-energy normalization.
A multi-criteria decision analysis or Pareto-front approach is acceptable if the stated gates are retained.
Module-level annual energy yield may replace lifetime energy if degradation and service life are explicitly modeled.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting AZO solely because zinc is abundant.
Comparing sheet resistance and transmittance only on isolated films.
Calling a stack indium-free while ignoring an indium-containing cap, interlayer, or manufacturing yield penalty.

expected_answer:
The replacement must first pass an atomistic plausibility gate. The divalent ion should have a credible low-energy incorporation site, compatible radius and coordination, and sufficiently strong metal–halide bonding to reduce vacancy formation or halide escape without creating deep electronic states. Formation energies and migration barriers from DFT are useful hypotheses, but they must be tested experimentally. Redox instability, volatile or toxic by-products, poor precursor solubility, and a tendency to form insulating secondary phases are early rejection risks.

Next use a concentration-resolved factorial design: control, candidate-MI2 only, alkali iodide only, dual additive, matched excess-iodide control, and—where chemically possible—candidate metal with a different counter-anion. XRD/GIWAXS and microscopy assess phase and morphology; XPS/EXAFS and depth-resolved mapping test oxidation state, coordination, and spatial location. The candidate should not merely enlarge grains: it should improve absolute PLQY/QFLS, reduce trap density, preserve carrier mobility, and maintain favorable band alignment and selective-contact extraction.

The ion-migration gate requires more than lower hysteresis. Measure bias- and temperature-dependent ionic transients, low-frequency impedance, operando elemental or potential redistribution, and activation energy. The expected division of labor should be recoverable: bulk-site stabilization by the divalent ion and interfacial/interstitial immobilization by the alkali ion, with a dual effect exceeding either component and the iodide-only control.

Finally, test MPP operation, thermal/light bias, humidity, and composition transfer with statistically meaningful device populations. Reject the candidate if it introduces a deep trap or unstable oxidation state; forms a secondary phase or segregates; improves PCE only through transient morphology while QFLS or mobility worsens; fails to suppress ionic redistribution; or requires a concentration that damages transport, reproducibility, or environmental safety.
scoring_key_points: Defines atomistic site, bonding, deep-state, redox, and precursor-compatibility criteria for the replacement metal.
Uses factorial metal, alkali, dual, iodide-only, and counter-anion controls with structural and spatial verification.
Requires optoelectronic and direct ion-migration evidence beyond morphology or initial J–V improvement.
Specifies operational stability, statistical transfer tests, and clear rejection criteria.
accepted_equivalents: First-principles defect thermodynamics plus experimental spectroscopy is equivalent to the atomistic plausibility gate.
XANES/EXAFS, solid-state NMR, or atom-probe methods may replace the listed coordination and location tools.
A non-cadmium bivalent ion need not occupy exactly the Pb site if an alternative verified bulk-stabilizing mechanism is demonstrated.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing a replacement only by ionic radius.
Accepting larger grains and higher initial PCE as proof of dual-site defect engineering.
Ignoring counter-anion, excess-iodide, oxidation-state, or environmental-safety confounders.

expected_answer:
A hybrid dynamic-network claim requires two coupled bond populations: anchoring interactions between the polymer and perovskite, such as carbonyl–Pb coordination, and reversible polymer–polymer hydrogen bonds that break and reform during deformation. A plasticizer can lower modulus and delay cracking, but it does not require bond-specific anchoring, sacrificial-bond kinetics, or recovery of local chemical order.

Use molecular controls at the same loading and molecular weight: a PDMS-like soft segment without coordinating urea, a urea-containing analog with blocked or strongly immobilized hydrogen bonding, and, if possible, a non-dynamic covalently cross-linked analog. In situ FTIR or Raman under strain should track reversible shifts/intensity changes of coordinated carbonyl and N–H bands. Stress-relaxation, creep, cyclic hysteresis, fracture energy, and strain-rate/temperature dependence should reveal a characteristic bond-exchange timescale; a dynamic network should dissipate energy but recover stiffness and hysteresis after rest or mild conditioning, whereas a plasticized film should show persistent creep or flow.

Correlate mechanics with chemistry and optoelectronics. In situ GIWAXS or diffraction can measure lattice-strain relaxation; XPS should quantify strain-induced Pb0; confocal PL/PLQY mapping should resolve crack-adjacent nonradiative loss; cross-sectional microscopy should track crack deflection and polymer localization. Matched grain size and wettability remove two common alternative explanations.

Stronger self-association can be inferior because polymer A may aggregate or lock its urea groups into polymer–polymer bonds, reducing access to perovskite surfaces and slowing chain rearrangement. Its dense network can store stress and fracture brittly. Polymer B can maintain sufficient grain anchoring while allowing sacrificial bonds and mobile chains to redistribute stress, giving a non-monotonic optimum rather than ‘more cross-linking is always better.’
scoring_key_points: Defines a hybrid network as perovskite anchoring plus reversible sacrificial interchain bonds, distinct from simple softening.
Proposes structure-matched controls that separately remove coordination, dynamic hydrogen bonding, or chain mobility.
Uses bond-sensitive in situ spectroscopy and rate-/temperature-dependent mechanical tests to establish exchange-mediated dissipation and recovery.
Explains why excessive self-association can cause aggregation, unavailable binding groups, slow relaxation, and brittle stress concentration.
accepted_equivalents: Dynamic mechanical analysis, rheology, nanoindentation relaxation, or single-edge fracture tests may substitute for the named mechanical methods.
Coordination can be demonstrated by solid-state NMR or X-ray absorption instead of FTIR/Raman.
A supramolecular network with other reversible bonds is acceptable if both grain anchoring and exchange kinetics are verified.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the softer film a dynamic network without bond-specific evidence.
Attributing all improvements to larger grains or hydrophobicity despite those variables being matched.
Assuming stronger hydrogen bonding must always produce better toughness.

expected_answer:
Scale-up should be treated as preservation of two coupled functions across area, not as reproduction of a single small-cell PCE. Process-critical variables include monolayer surface coverage and binding to NiOx, solution residence time and blade speed, substrate temperature, precursor contact angle and drying front, and tolerance to surface contamination or roughness. A concentration/process window should be mapped rather than transferring the spin-coating concentration directly.

Uniformity must be checked spatially. Contact-angle and surface-potential maps should verify homogeneous wetting and dipole; large-area PL/PLQY or hyperspectral maps should identify uncovered regions, nonuniform crystallization or local nonradiative losses; GIWAXS/XRD mapping and cross-sectional microscopy should assess texture, grain growth and voids; sheet/contact resistance, electroluminescence or lock-in thermography should locate extraction bottlenecks and shunts. Coupon cells cut from multiple web or plate positions should be statistically compared with full mini-modules.

Stability qualification should include encapsulated maximum-power-point operation at elevated temperature and humidity, thermal cycling to probe NiOx/SAM/perovskite adhesion, light-soaking and bias stress to reveal ion accumulation, and damp-heat or storage controls that separate moisture barrier effects from intrinsic interface stability. Pre/post-aging XPS or depth profiling, impedance, ideality factor and spatial PL can determine whether degradation originates from molecular desorption, dipole drift, local dewetting, contact corrosion or bulk decomposition.

A formulation should be rejected even if its best small-area or module PCE is high when it shows a narrow coating window, strong edge-to-center variation, local uncovered/shunted regions, rising contact resistance, molecular redistribution, or rapid MPP loss. Acceptance should require both yield/uniformity and retention of the coupled wetting-plus-extraction signatures under accelerated operation.
scoring_key_points: Defines scale-relevant process variables and maps a coating/process window rather than copying the spin-coating recipe.
Uses spatially resolved wetting, potential, luminescence, structure and electrical diagnostics across the coated area or module.
Includes operational, thermal/humidity and bias/light stresses with post-mortem tests that localize the failure mechanism.
States a rejection rule based on nonuniformity, poor yield, interfacial drift or rapid MPP degradation even when champion efficiency is high.
accepted_equivalents: Roll-to-roll or slot-die qualification in place of blade coating, provided the same uniformity and interfacial criteria are addressed.
Use of PL/EL imaging, LBIC, thermography, KPFM, GIWAXS mapping or equivalent large-area diagnostics.
T80/T95, degradation-rate or statistically defined retention criteria rather than a specific lifetime number.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only the active area while measuring one champion device.
Using average contact angle or average PCE without spatial maps or yield statistics.
Testing dark shelf storage only and calling the result operational stability.
Accepting a high initial PCE despite a narrow process window or rapid contact-resistance growth.

expected_answer:
At low-to-moderate loading, the polymer can bind undercoordinated ions or vacancies, moderate nucleation and growth, bridge grain boundaries and dissipate mechanical strain. This can increase radiative efficiency or lifetime in an inert-film measurement, reduce trap density and suppress crack initiation during bending. At excessive loading, the polymer may precipitate or segregate, create an electrically insulating phase at grain boundaries or interfaces, alter solvent coordination so strongly that conversion is incomplete, or interrupt perovskite connectivity. Low crack density therefore does not prove an electronically useful film.

The diagnosis should use a concentration series and separate structural, chemical, electronic and mechanical observables. GIWAXS/XRD and SEM/AFM should track phase purity, orientation, grain size, residual precursor and polymer-rich domains. XPS/FTIR or solid-state spectroscopy should verify binding and detect whether passivating interactions saturate before performance falls. SCLC and temperature-dependent conductivity or mobility should test whether trap density continues to fall while transport becomes activation-limited. PL/TRPL should be measured both on inert substrates and on complete transport-layer stacks: longer lifetime on an inert substrate with slower extraction or weaker quenching on a selective contact indicates blocking rather than improved collection. Impedance, dark J–V, ideality factor and series resistance should reveal interfacial/contact resistance and recombination.

Mechanical tests should record retention versus bending radius and cycle number, while microscopy maps cracks and delamination. The beneficial regime is where trap density, nonradiative loss and strain decrease without increased series resistance or loss of extraction. The detrimental regime is identified when morphology or phase purity deteriorates, polymer-rich regions emerge, mobility/contact transfer falls and FF/JSC decline despite continued mechanical compliance. The optimum is therefore a multi-objective window, not the concentration giving the longest PL lifetime or fewest cracks alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains the low-loading benefits as passivation/crystallization control and mechanical stress absorption.
Identifies high-loading failure modes such as polymer segregation/precipitation, insulating barriers, disrupted crystallization or incomplete conversion.
Uses substrate-selective PL/TRPL plus transport/recombination measurements to separate longer intrinsic lifetime from blocked extraction.
Defines the optimum as a concentration window balancing electrical and mechanical metrics rather than maximizing one indicator.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent use of GIWAXS, SCLC, impedance, conductivity, dark J–V, PLQY, transient absorption or time-resolved microwave conductivity.
Describing a Pareto optimum between bend durability and electronic transport.
Calling the high-loading regime percolation loss or formation of a dielectric grain-boundary phase.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that longer TRPL always means better device extraction.
Choosing the formulation with the lowest crack density without examining FF, mobility or contact resistance.
Attributing the JSC/FF loss only to optical absorption without checking phase purity and electrical connectivity.
Using one polymer concentration and one substrate, which cannot reveal a transition or distinguish bulk lifetime from extraction.

expected_answer:
A fixed-cation anion series is suggestive but not sufficient, because ionic strength, viscosity, precursor complexation and drying can covary. The design should include: the matched imidazolium salts with different anions at equal molar loading; anion-only controls using noncoordinating counter-cations; cation analogues in which the candidate donor nitrogen is blocked or electronically deactivated; and a neutral imidazole-like donor or an inert salt control matched for ionic strength and solvent content. Precursor viscosity, water content and drying history should be controlled.

Primary cation–Pb coordination would be supported if PbI2 titration produces systematic cation-resonance shifts, if XPS and vibrational spectroscopy show charge redistribution at Pb and the cationic N, and if a donor-blocked cation loses the passivation benefit even with the same anion. DFT or another binding analysis should predict stronger adsorption and charge transfer for the cation donor than for the anion, and the trend should survive after controlling morphology. Anion-only controls may alter nucleation rate, texture, solubility or hydrophobicity, but should not reproduce the full Pb-defect suppression or recombination improvement.

The anion's tuning role is established when the magnitude of cation–Pb spectroscopic perturbation, precursor adduct lifetime, nucleation/texture and optimum loading changes across the anion series while the same cationic donor motif remains necessary. Structural and electronic consequences should then converge: reduced SCLC trap density, lower trap-assisted recombination, higher mobility or recombination resistance and improved PL/EL metrics. If an inert salt produces the same result, or if the anion-only control reproduces all chemical and device signatures, the specific cation-coordination mechanism is falsified.
scoring_key_points: Requires matched fixed-cation salts plus anion-only, donor-blocked cation and inert ionic-strength/solvent controls.
Defines direct cation–Pb evidence from solution and film spectroscopy/computation, not only improved device metrics.
Separates the anion's role in precursor chemistry, nucleation, texture or hydrophobicity from the cation's donor-dependent passivation role.
States a falsification criterion, such as inert-salt or anion-only controls reproducing the complete effect.
accepted_equivalents: Use of isotopically labeled ions, solid-state NMR, pair-distribution analysis or operando spectroscopy as direct coordination evidence.
A two-factor cation-by-anion matrix rather than a single fixed-cation series.
Equivalent controls that hold viscosity, water, solvent and total ion concentration constant.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the cation is primary solely because its calculated adsorption energy is more negative.
Treating the best anion as proof of anion passivation without testing the cation donor site.
Ignoring precursor viscosity, residual water or drying kinetics that can independently change crystallization.
Using PL lifetime or PCE alone as evidence for a specific chemical bond.

expected_answer:
The three contributions should be perturbed independently. To isolate transient crystallization control, compare thiourea in PbI2 with a volatile or removable thiourea treatment, a chemically similar Lewis base that forms an adduct but does not remain at the interface, and a post-crystallization thiourea treatment that cannot influence nucleation. In situ GIWAXS/XRD, optical microscopy or calorimetry should track formation and disappearance of any low-dimensional/adduct phase, conversion rate to α-FAPbI3, nucleation density, orientation and residual PbI2. A route that changes these time-resolved signatures before the final film forms supports the intermediate mechanism.

Persistent buried-interface passivation should be tested with bottom-only, bulk-only and top-only placement at comparable retained thiourea content, verified by depth profiling or labeled thiourea. XPS/UPS on peeled interfaces, Pb0 quantification, trap-density measurements, selective-contact PL/TRPL, dark J–V and interface-sensitive impedance should show fewer Pb-related defects and faster electron extraction specifically when thiourea remains near SnO2. A post-crystallization bottom-interface analogue that improves these metrics without changing bulk crystallization would isolate passivation.

Stress relief must be separated from both chemistry and grain size. Wafer-curvature or Raman/GIXRD strain mapping should quantify residual stress across identical film thicknesses, while thermal-cycling and substrate-CTE controls vary mechanical constraint. If stress is independently reduced with little change in chemical passivation, crack formation, ion-migration signatures and degradation should improve; conversely, a passivated but mechanically constrained film may retain low trap density yet age poorly.

A factorial analysis should determine whether the two routes weight the mechanisms differently: precursor addition is expected to affect the transient conversion pathway more strongly, whereas SnO2 treatment should emphasize buried-interface retention and extraction. Full causality requires route-specific time-resolved, depth-resolved and strain-resolved evidence rather than assigning all improvements to one multifunctional label.
scoring_key_points: Separates transient crystallization using time-resolved conversion measurements and controls that alter adduct formation without persistent interface retention.
Separates buried-interface passivation using location-specific treatments, depth verification and interface-sensitive defect/extraction diagnostics.
Measures residual stress independently and uses mechanical/CTE controls to distinguish stress relief from chemistry or grain-size effects.
Recognizes that precursor and SnO2 routes can weight the three mechanisms differently and calls for factorial causal analysis.
accepted_equivalents: Use of isotope-labeled thiourea, TOF-SIMS, angle-resolved XPS or cross-sectional nanospectroscopy to verify location.
In situ absorption, GIWAXS, synchrotron scattering or calorimetry as crystallization-kinetics probes.
Raman peak mapping, wafer curvature, nano-beam diffraction or sin²ψ GIXRD as stress measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Using only final grain size or XRD intensity to claim competitive crystallization.
Treating lower trap density as proof that stress was relieved.
Assuming thiourea remains at the buried interface without a depth- or location-sensitive measurement.
Comparing only the two optimized routes, which changes location, concentration and crystallization history simultaneously.

expected_answer:
The redesign should decouple conversion kinetics from thermal budget. Possible routes include stronger solvent/antisolvent control, vacuum- or gas-assisted solvent extraction, photonic or rapid localized heating, a lower-barrier precursor complex, or sequential dosing in which a small bottom-interface thiourea reservoir is retained while excess bulk thiourea is removed. The concentration and dwell time must be re-optimized because slower low-temperature conversion can stabilize an unwanted thiourea–PbI2 or low-dimensional phase. A flexible interlayer or substrate with better CTE matching may be used, but it must not block electron extraction.

In situ or quasi-in situ GIWAXS/XRD and optical spectroscopy should verify complete conversion to the desired photoactive phase, absence of persistent low-angle thiourea-rich reflections, low residual PbI2 and acceptable texture. Depth profiling and buried-interface XPS should confirm that a limited thiourea population remains where passivation is needed rather than throughout the bulk. SEM/cross-sectional imaging, SCLC and PL/TRPL on inert and SnO2-like contacts should check morphology, bulk recombination and electron extraction. Residual strain should be mapped before and after bending and thermal cycling.

Mechanical viability requires efficiency and resistance to be measured during repeated bending at defined radius, together with crack/delamination imaging. Operational qualification should include MPP illumination at elevated temperature, humidity exposure and bias stress, because lower-temperature processing can leave mobile residual species that accelerate hysteresis or ion migration. Pre/post-aging depth profiles and impedance can test thiourea redistribution and interface stability.

The process should fail qualification if low-temperature conversion leaves a persistent low-dimensional/adduct phase, residual PbI2, strong hysteresis, rising series resistance, poor extraction, thiourea migration, or rapid crack-assisted degradation—even if initial PCE is competitive. Acceptance requires complete phase conversion, localized passivation, low residual stress and stable performance under combined bending and operation.
scoring_key_points: Proposes a credible low-temperature conversion route and re-optimizes thiourea dose/dwell time rather than simply lowering the anneal temperature.
Requires phase-sensitive and depth-sensitive evidence that conversion is complete and thiourea remains localized rather than forming an insulating bulk phase.
Includes electrical/extraction, residual-strain and bending diagnostics appropriate to the flexible stack.
Defines operational and mechanical failure criteria, including residual phase, hysteresis, migration, contact resistance or crack-assisted degradation.
accepted_equivalents: Photonic curing, microwave/infrared heating, vacuum flash, gas quenching or solvent-engineered low-temperature conversion.
Use of an alternative low-temperature ETL provided its chemistry and extraction are controlled.
Combined mechanical-environmental MPP testing rather than separate tests, if the failure modes remain distinguishable.
common_wrong_answers: Reducing the annealing temperature without checking for incomplete α-phase conversion or residual adduct.
Increasing thiourea concentration to compensate for low temperature, which may create an insulating/2D-rich phase.
Using bending retention alone while ignoring operational ion migration and hysteresis.
Assuming better CTE matching automatically preserves electron extraction.

expected_answer:
The program should separate phase stability, molecular mobility and tandem electrical compatibility. Operando hyperspectral PL or electroluminescence mapping should be performed under one-sun and elevated-intensity illumination, at maximum power point and at open circuit, across a controlled temperature range. The key phase-segregation observables are emergence and growth of a red-shifted low-bandgap emission, spatial nucleation sites, recovery in the dark and changes in absorption/EQE. Treated and untreated films/devices should be compared at matched halide composition, thickness and initial bandgap.

Molecular mobility should be tested under light, heat and electric field. Isotopically labeled or marker-enabled depth profiling before and after stress should determine whether the bridge leaves the intended interfaces, accumulates at electrodes or enters the bulk. Complementary XPS/UPS/KPFM and impedance should detect dipole drift, band-alignment change, ionic capacitance or contact-resistance growth. Operando PL alone cannot distinguish suppressed segregation from accelerated carrier extraction or a changed starting bandgap, so absorption, EQE and composition measurements are required.

The top cell should then be integrated with the intended bottom cell or an optically/electrically representative simulator. Four-terminal tests can first isolate top-cell stability; two-terminal tandems must be evaluated for current matching, spectral response, stabilized MPP efficiency and luminescent-coupling changes before and after aging. Thermal cycling and damp-heat/encapsulation controls should be added because interface-localized molecules may desorb or redistribute during module processing.

Acceptance requires: no significant stress-induced red-shifted phase or spatial segregation relative to control; no adverse redistribution of the bridge; stable interfacial energetics and resistance; retention of the designed WBG EQE onset and current; and durable two-terminal MPP performance without new current mismatch. A higher initial top-cell PCE or unchanged average PL peak is insufficient if local segregation, molecular drift or tandem current loss appears.
scoring_key_points: Uses operando, spatially resolved spectral measurements under relevant illumination, bias and temperature to quantify halide phase segregation.
Separates phase stabilization from changed extraction or initial bandgap using absorption/EQE/composition controls.
Tracks bridge-molecule redistribution and interfacial energetic/resistive drift before and after light/heat/field stress.
Defines tandem-level acceptance through current matching, stabilized MPP and retained WBG spectral response, not top-cell PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Use of cathodoluminescence, Raman, XRD, transient absorption or nano-XRF alongside hyperspectral PL to map segregation.
A four-terminal-to-two-terminal staged tandem validation.
Equivalent current-matching criteria based on EQE-integrated subcell currents and mismatch evolution.
common_wrong_answers: Using dark shelf stability as evidence that light-induced halide segregation is suppressed.
Interpreting a smaller PL redshift as proof without checking starting bandgap, extraction and spatial heterogeneity.
Ignoring molecular migration because the additive was initially localized at the interfaces.
Testing the WBG subcell alone and assuming tandem current matching will be preserved.

expected_answer: The combined evidence supports an interface-dominated improvement rather than a bulk-crystallization effect. The inserted polymer likely provides favorable electron-selective energetics and/or stronger chemical contact with the tin-perovskite surface, thereby increasing electron-transfer rate, passivating electrically active interfacial defects, and reducing leakage and trap-assisted recombination. Faster photoluminescence decay by itself cannot distinguish beneficial carrier extraction from harmful non-radiative quenching; it becomes evidence for extraction only when accompanied by higher quasi-Fermi-level splitting or device voltage, lower dark leakage, reduced ideality factor, lower trap signatures, or direct charge-transfer measurements. A decisive follow-up would compare time-resolved photoluminescence with an extraction-sensitive measurement such as transient absorption showing electron population in the transport layer, time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity, or calibrated photoluminescence quantum yield/quasi-Fermi-level splitting under identical excitation. Beneficial extraction should increase interfacial electron-transfer yield without lowering the achievable quasi-Fermi-level splitting, whereas a new recombination center would accelerate decay while reducing it.
scoring_key_points: Attributes the improvement primarily to the absorber/ETL interface, not to changed bulk crystallinity or morphology.
Links selective transport and interfacial passivation to lower leakage, weaker trap-assisted recombination, and reduced electron-trap signatures.
States that shorter PL lifetime alone is non-unique because extraction and non-radiative quenching can produce the same trend.
Proposes a direct discriminating measurement and predicts opposite outcomes for productive extraction versus parasitic quenching.
accepted_equivalents: Interfacial dipole or improved band alignment may substitute for favorable electron-selective energetics.
Transient absorption, time-resolved photoinduced absorption, TRMC/THz conductivity, or PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting are acceptable discriminating probes.
Reduced Shockley-Read-Hall recombination is equivalent to reduced trap-assisted recombination.
common_wrong_answers: Treating faster PL decay as proof of lower defect density without acknowledging extraction-versus-quenching ambiguity.
Assigning the performance gain to larger grains or a new crystal phase despite unchanged structural data.
Claiming hydrophobicity alone explains the electrical diagnostics.

expected_answer: The oxidant transfers charge from the hole-transport molecule, creating mobile holes and dopant counterions. The increased carrier density raises conductivity even if the drift mobility decreases, so the contact becomes sufficiently conductive and the extraction barrier responsible for the s-shaped curve is removed. The mobility loss can arise because ionized dopant counterions create long-range Coulomb potentials that trap or scatter holes; therefore conductivity and mobility need not move in the same direction. The basic additive can coordinate to, reduce, or otherwise shift the redox equilibrium of the doped species, causing dedoping and loss of conductivity. To distinguish Coulomb trapping from morphology, compare mobility across dopant concentration and temperature while independently measuring structure. Coulomb trapping predicts a systematic mobility decrease with ionized dopant density, stronger field/temperature activation, and recovery when the counterion is made larger or more weakly interacting, even when GIWAXS, AFM, and glass-transition/morphology metrics remain similar. A morphology mechanism should correlate with new packing disorder, phase separation, or roughness and may persist even with a counterion change at the same carrier density.
scoring_key_points: Explains that p-doping raises carrier density, so conductivity can increase despite reduced mobility.
Connects restored conductivity to removal of extraction/contact limitation and the s-shaped J-V curve.
Attributes the mobility penalty plausibly to Coulomb trapping/scattering by ionized dopant counterions and dedoping to the basic additive shifting the redox equilibrium.
Proposes concentration/temperature/counterion tests combined with structural measurements to discriminate Coulomb trapping from morphology.
accepted_equivalents: Ionized-impurity scattering, electrostatic trapping, or dopant-counterion potential fluctuations are equivalent descriptions.
The basic additive may be described as complexing the oxidant or neutralizing the oxidized HTM, provided dedoping is explicit.
GIWAXS, DSC, AFM, ellipsometry, or microscopy may be used as morphology controls.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming higher conductivity necessarily means higher mobility.
Explaining the s-shaped curve only by absorber defects while ignoring HTL conductivity/contact extraction.
Attributing the mobility loss to morphology without proposing any independent structural test.

expected_answer: First, the additive decomposition window must overlap reproducibly with solvent removal and perovskite nucleation: its absorption, photolysis quantum yield, and thermal decomposition kinetics must be compatible with the coating/annealing temperature and line speed. Second, the products must be chemically beneficial and mass-balanced: retained fragments should passivate or regulate crystallization at low concentration, while volatile products must leave cleanly and no corrosive, mobile, or electronically deep species should remain. Third, photon dose must be spatially uniform and scalable, accounting for lamp spectrum, film optical density, web speed, temperature, and oxygen; the process should have a wide enough dose tolerance that small variations do not switch from incomplete decomposition to film damage. Fourth, the final stack must remain compatible with transport layers, encapsulation, and operational stress, because improved initial crystallization does not prove suppressed ion migration or photochemical aging. Inline control should combine calibrated irradiance mapping and closed-loop substrate temperature with spatially resolved photoluminescence or reflectance to track nucleation and disappearance of additive emission. Periodic off-line verification by mass spectrometry/FTIR, XRD, trap diagnostics, and damp-heat plus MPP tests should set acceptance limits for residual additive, phase purity, defect density, and stability across the full module area.
scoring_key_points: Requires matched photochemical/thermal kinetics with the coating, solvent-removal, and crystallization time window.
Requires benign retained fragments, clean removal of volatile products, and absence of mobile, corrosive, or deep-trap residues.
Controls spectral photon dose, temperature, oxygen, and lateral uniformity with a sufficiently broad processing window.
Uses inline optical feedback plus spatially resolved chemical/structural/electrical and MPP/damp-heat validation of the finished module.
accepted_equivalents: Roll-to-roll web speed or slot-die coating residence time may substitute for generic line speed.
Hyperspectral PL, Raman, optical coherence, or reflectance can serve as inline conversion/crystallization monitors.
Accelerated UV, thermal, humidity, and bias stress may supplement MPP and damp heat.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the laboratory lamp intensity can be scaled directly without dose mapping or spectral calibration.
Checking only initial module efficiency and not residual chemistry or spatial uniformity.
Treating complete additive disappearance as sufficient even if harmful decomposition products remain.

expected_answer: Use a matched molecular analogue matrix rather than comparing only additive versus no additive. To isolate Pb coordination, replace or sterically block the carbonyl/Lewis-base site while retaining N-H and fluorinated groups; loss of Pb core-level shifts, reduced defect passivation, and lower PLQY/lifetime at similar morphology would support the coordination role. To isolate N-H···halide bonding, use an N-methylated analogue that preserves the carbonyl and fluorinated tail but removes hydrogen-bond donation; increased halide migration under bias, larger ionic hysteresis, or weaker halide core-level shifts would support the N-H contribution. To isolate crystallization retardation, compare precursor incorporation with a post-deposition surface treatment at matched surface coverage and use in situ PL/XRD; only the precursor route should delay nucleation and alter grain size if coordination-controlled crystallization is causal. To isolate hydrophobicity, use a nonfluorinated analogue with similar binding groups and film morphology; lower contact angle, faster water uptake, and poorer humidity stability without a major change in dry-state recombination would identify the fluorinated contribution. Dose matching and checks of additive retention, energy levels, and film thickness are required to avoid confounding the analogue comparison.
scoring_key_points: Uses a carbonyl/Lewis-base-disabled analogue and chemical/electronic defect diagnostics to isolate Pb coordination.
Uses an N-H-disabled analogue and ion-migration or halide-interaction diagnostics to isolate hydrogen bonding.
Compares precursor addition with post-deposition treatment and in situ crystallization probes to isolate kinetic grain-growth regulation.
Uses a nonfluorinated but otherwise matched analogue and water-uptake/humidity tests to isolate hydrophobicity while controlling morphology and dry-state electronics.
accepted_equivalents: Phosphine-oxide, amide, or carbonyl substitutions are acceptable if they selectively change Lewis basicity.
Bias-dependent PL, Kelvin-probe mapping, impedance, ToF-SIMS, or hysteresis may serve as ion-migration diagnostics.
Contact angle should be accompanied by sorption or humidity degradation; either may be named as the primary hydrophobicity probe.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning all improvements to a single generic passivation effect.
Using unrelated analogue molecules that change binding, size, polarity, and energy levels simultaneously.
Claiming a higher contact angle proves reduced ion migration.

expected_answer: First determine the optical consequence with subcell-resolved EQE and an optical transfer-matrix or measured absorptance model using the actual layer thicknesses and complex refractive indices. Vary front- and rear-cell thicknesses to find the current-matched region under the reference spectrum, and verify that the front-cell EQE gain does not excessively reduce photons reaching the organic rear cell. Second separate electrical losses by comparing the tandem open-circuit voltage with the sum of subcell voltages, measuring recombination-junction resistance/selectivity, and using electroluminescence or intensity-dependent voltage to identify non-radiative and interconnection losses. A genuine material gain should raise front-cell voltage or fill factor and permit a higher matched current, not simply make the front cell overcurrent while the rear cell limits the series tandem. Third test phase stability and defect evolution under MPP with spectrally varied illumination, temperature, and bias, because mixed-halide front-cell current and bandgap can drift under blue-rich or high-intensity conditions. Track subcell EQE, spectral PL, tandem current, voltage, and luminescence coupling over time. Finally calculate energy yield using time-dependent spectra and temperature rather than only AM1.5G efficiency; the composition is beneficial only if its lower recombination and phase stability maintain current matching and voltage across realistic operating conditions.
scoring_key_points: Uses subcell EQE plus optical modeling or absorptance measurements to optimize thickness and quantify current matching, including photon loss to the rear cell.
Separates electrical losses through tandem-versus-subcell voltage, recombination-junction/contact diagnostics, and recombination-sensitive measurements.
States that a useful front-cell gain must improve matched current and/or voltage/FF, not merely create front-cell overcurrent while the rear cell limits the tandem.
Tests MPP stability under spectral, intensity, and temperature variation and evaluates time-dependent energy yield with subcell-resolved diagnostics.
accepted_equivalents: Transfer-matrix, ray-tracing, or experimentally calibrated optical modeling is acceptable.
Electroluminescence, photoluminescence quantum yield, Suns-Voc, impedance, or transient methods may diagnose electrical losses.
Outdoor spectral datasets or indoor spectral perturbation matrices are acceptable for energy-yield assessment.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming higher front-cell EQE automatically raises series-tandem current.
Optimizing only the perovskite thickness under AM1.5G without checking rear-cell photon supply.
Using shelf stability alone and ignoring light-induced bandgap/phase changes and spectral current mismatch.

expected_answer: The measurements must be interpreted in the boundary condition in which they were acquired. On inert glass, stronger PL and a longer lifetime indicate that photocarriers survive longer because nonradiative bulk, grain-boundary, or surface recombination has been reduced, provided excitation density, thickness, and optical outcoupling are controlled. Absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting would be a more decisive passivation test. In a perovskite/hole-transport-layer stack, faster decay accompanied by stronger PL quenching can instead mean that holes are transferred out of the perovskite more rapidly. The UPS shift makes that interpretation plausible because it reduces the energetic penalty for extraction; selective-contact transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or transient photocurrent would test it directly. The nearly unchanged absorption and JSC imply that the additive does not mainly increase photogeneration. The VOC gain is therefore consistent with lower nonradiative recombination, while the fill-factor gain can arise from reduced recombination and more selective, lower-resistance extraction. The disappearance of hysteresis cannot be established by PL, TRPL, UPS, or SCLC alone. It requires an ionic diagnostic, such as bias-dependent transient ion-drift measurements, mobile-ion capacitance, pre-bias relaxation, temperature-dependent hysteresis, or operando depth profiling. A reduction in mobile ionic charge, ionic relaxation amplitude, or field-driven redistribution would support ion-migration suppression; otherwise, the hysteresis change could be caused by improved interfacial extraction rather than true ionic immobilization.
scoring_key_points: Interprets longer PL lifetime on an inert substrate as reduced nonradiative recombination, subject to controlled optical conditions.
Explains that faster PL decay in a contacted stack can indicate faster hole extraction rather than a shorter intrinsic carrier lifetime, especially with improved band alignment.
Uses the nearly unchanged absorption/JSC to assign VOC and fill-factor gains mainly to recombination and extraction rather than increased photogeneration.
States that hysteresis suppression requires a direct ionic-transport or bias-relaxation measurement and cannot be inferred from photophysics alone.
accepted_equivalents: Absolute PLQY, calibrated QFLS, or external electroluminescence efficiency may be used to quantify nonradiative loss.
Transient absorption, transient photocurrent, surface photovoltage, or contact-selective TRPL are acceptable extraction diagnostics.
Transient ion drift, bias-stress relaxation, low-frequency capacitance, ToF-SIMS under bias, or activation-energy measurements are acceptable ion-migration tests.
common_wrong_answers: Claims that the faster contacted-stack TRPL proves that recombination has become worse.
Attributes the performance gain mainly to stronger absorption despite nearly unchanged JSC.
Treats a lower SCLC trap density as direct proof that mobile ions have been immobilized.
Uses a single forward/reverse J-V scan as sufficient evidence for suppressed ion migration.

expected_answer: The transfer should use a factorial process matrix rather than one nominal concentration. Additive dose, wet-film residence time, coating speed, drying temperature or gas flow, and the halogen substituent should be varied while the absorber composition, thickness, and contacts are held fixed. Controls should include an untreated film, a potassium-salt control that lacks the multifunctional organic anion, and an anion-bearing analogue with a different non-potassium counter-cation or another matched method of suppressing the K contribution. These controls separate generic ionic-strength or K effects from the designed anion chemistry. Spatially resolved measurements are essential: K/F/halogen depth and lateral distributions should be mapped by ToF-SIMS, XPS mapping, nano-XRF where feasible, or cross-sectional elemental analysis, and combined with GIWAXS, PL/QFLS imaging, microscopy, and wetting maps from the coating leading edge to trailing edge and across interconnects. A beneficial window should show dilute, reproducible incorporation or interfacial enrichment without discrete salt-rich domains, secondary phases, or local film-thickness defects. Electrical testing should separate passivation from transport blockage by combining QFLS or electroluminescence efficiency, recombination ideality, transient extraction, series resistance, fill factor, and shunt maps. Direct ion diagnostics should quantify mobile ionic charge, bias-induced redistribution, hysteresis relaxation, and interfacial accumulation. At module level, subcell-resolved EL/PL or LBIC mapping and stabilized MPP operation are more informative than champion scan PCE. The go condition is a concentration/drying window that lowers nonradiative loss and mobile-ion response without increasing series resistance, local shunts, or interconnect contamination, and that maintains uniform output under combined light, heat, humidity, and electrical bias. A condition that gives a high initial VOC but develops K/F-rich patches, FF loss, or edge/interconnect degradation should be rejected.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial dose-and-drying process matrix with untreated, cation-focused, and anion-focused controls while holding the device stack fixed.
Requires lateral and depth-resolved additive/phase mapping across the module rather than relying on average composition.
Separates passivation from transport blockage and directly measures mobile-ion behavior, local resistance, shunts, and stabilized output.
Defines a go/no-go window by uniform MPP durability under combined environmental and electrical stress, not by champion small-cell PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Matched controls may use potassium halides, non-potassium aryltrifluoroborates, or another chemically justified cation/anion decomposition strategy.
Nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved XPS, STEM-EDS/EELS, or calibrated fluorescence tagging are acceptable distribution probes.
ISOS-style MPP aging, thermal cycling, damp heat, or bias-light stress are acceptable if local module failure is mapped.
common_wrong_answers: Transfers the small-cell optimum concentration directly without re-optimizing coating and drying kinetics.
Uses only average XPS or EDS composition and misses rare salt-rich domains or interconnect contamination.
Equates lower hysteresis with lower ion migration without a direct ionic measurement.
Selects the highest reverse-scan PCE despite increased series resistance or poor module uniformity.

expected_answer: The study should use a designed matrix in which additive concentration is crossed with coating speed, wet-film thickness, solvent composition, drying-gas flow, annealing and cooling profile, substrate temperature, and web tension. The absorber composition and downstream contacts should remain fixed, and untreated runs should be interleaved rather than produced on a different day. A molecular analogue or two-functional-group control can help determine whether any process benefit requires the complete multifunctional structure. Across-web and machine-direction maps should quantify thickness, composition, additive distribution, grain size/orientation, PL or QFLS, and residual stress. Suitable tools include hyperspectral PL, inline reflectometry, GIWAXS at representative positions, Raman or diffraction strain mapping, AFM/profilometry, and cross-web contact-angle or surface-energy measurements. Web edges, splice regions, and acceleration/deceleration zones must be included because they often define yield. Qualification should use matched dry cyclic bending to isolate mechanical stress relief, controlled humidity/light exposure to test hydrophobic and defect-passivation functions, and combined bending plus illumination/heat/humidity to expose coupling between cracks and ingress. Module or strip-level EL/PL imaging, local series/shunt resistance, stabilized MPP, adhesion, and crack-density evolution should be measured. A robust window is one that gives a narrow spatial distribution of residual stress and optoelectronic quality, no additive-rich residue or dewetting, acceptable series resistance, and reproducible retained MPP after specified bending and combined aging. A single high-PCE coupon from the web centre is not sufficient; failure at edges or under web-tension transients is a no-go even if average efficiency improves.
scoring_key_points: Crosses additive dose with roll-to-roll drying, temperature, coating-speed, and web-tension variables while interleaving untreated controls.
Maps crystallization, additive distribution, optoelectronic quality, and residual stress across the full web and along the coating direction.
Separates dry mechanical bending from humidity/light aging and then applies combined stresses to test coupled failure.
Defines acceptance by spatially uniform, reproducible stabilized output and retained mechanical integrity, not a centre-coupon champion result.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, blade, gravure, or meniscus roll-to-roll coating is acceptable if wet-film dose and drying history are controlled.
Raman, GIWAXS, curvature, polarized optical mapping, or digital image correlation may be used for stress/strain mapping.
EL, PL, LBIC, thermography, or four-point resistance mapping may be used to quantify strip or module uniformity.
common_wrong_answers: Optimizes only additive concentration while leaving web tension and drying gradients unmeasured.
Samples only the centre of the coated web and ignores edges or transient coating regions.
Uses humidity aging alone as proof of improved mechanical flexibility.
Changes the perovskite composition between control and additive runs, making stress comparisons uninterpretable.

expected_answer: The critical comparison must keep the treated electron-transport-layer chemistry constant while changing only the residence time or population of the intermediate. On identically treated substrates, films should be annealed immediately, held at room temperature for several controlled dwell times, or subjected to different heating ramps that bypass or prolong the delta-like state. In situ GIWAXS/XRD and optical scattering or absorption should quantify intermediate fraction, nucleation onset, conversion rate, and alpha-phase orientation. Replicate films should be quenched at selected times to measure precursor complexes and nucleation density, then all samples should receive the same final thermal budget so that residual delta phase is absent. Final grain-size distribution, buried-void density, microstrain, trap density, and QFLS should be compared. A matched ETL-passivation control that improves SnO2 oxygen defects or conductivity without stabilizing the same intermediate is needed to show what ETL passivation alone can achieve. Causality is supported if, within the same treated-surface chemistry, the final morphology and strain vary systematically with the measured intermediate residence time; if a rapid ramp that suppresses the intermediate also removes much of the film-quality advantage, and a dwell that restores the intermediate rescues it, the intermediate is a mediator. If all treated films remain equally improved regardless of whether the intermediate is bypassed, or if an ETL-only control reproduces the final film quality without the intermediate, the delta-like peak is likely a correlated marker rather than the causal growth pathway. The final absence of delta phase is necessary to rule out apparent improvement caused by retaining a nonperovskite phase.
scoring_key_points: Holds the treated ETL chemistry fixed while independently varying intermediate residence time through dwell or heating-ramp interventions.
Uses in situ phase/nucleation measurements and identical final annealing, then quantifies final grains, voids, microstrain, traps, and QFLS.
Includes an ETL-passivation control that does not stabilize the same intermediate to separate surface passivation from crystallization mediation.
Defines causality by loss-and-rescue or dose-response of final film quality with intermediate lifetime, and defines a falsifying outcome.
accepted_equivalents: Temperature-jump experiments, rapid thermal annealing, solvent-vapour dwell, or controlled room-temperature aging may tune the intermediate lifetime.
In situ GIWAXS, XRD, Raman, optical interferometry, or calorimetry may monitor intermediate formation and conversion.
Nucleation density, grain orientation, void fraction, Williamson-Hall strain, PLQY, or SCLC may be used as downstream response variables.
common_wrong_answers: Claims causality solely because a longer-lived intermediate and better final film are observed in the same treated sample.
Compares different surface chemistries without independently tuning the intermediate lifetime.
Allows different final annealing budgets, so residual phase and thermal history confound the result.
Treats the absence of residual delta phase after annealing as proof that the intermediate caused the improvement.

expected_answer: All devices must use identical encapsulation, absorber thickness, contacts, and processing except for the controlled variables. Residual PbI2 at the buried interface should be varied independently of the pseudo-halide treatment, for example through a narrow precursor-stoichiometry or annealing series, while initial PCE and recombination loss are matched as closely as possible. A complementary control should improve electron extraction or reduce recombination without using the pseudo-halide, so that general electronic improvement can be separated from PbI2 chemistry. Light-soaking should be performed at controlled temperature and atmosphere under open circuit, MPP, and short circuit because carrier accumulation and interfacial potential differ across these states. Operando or time-sequenced GIWAXS/XRD should track PbI2 and Pb0 signatures; depth-sensitive XPS or ToF-SIMS on sacrificial samples should localize the products; PL/EL, impedance, transient extraction, and cross-sectional microscopy should track recombination, transport, voids, and crack formation. The time order is decisive. A causal residual-PbI2/Pb0 mechanism is supported if buried Pb0 appears before major electrical and structural failure, if its formation rate scales with independently controlled buried PbI2 even at similar initial QFLS/extraction, and if reducing buried PbI2 or applying the treatment suppresses both Pb0 and later cracking. A reintroduction or rescue experiment strengthens the claim. The mechanism is falsified as primary if PCE and morphology fail before detectable Pb0, if Pb0 does not scale with buried PbI2, or if an extraction-only control prevents degradation equally well while Pb0 evolution is unchanged.
scoring_key_points: Uses identical encapsulation and independently varies buried residual PbI2 while matching initial electronic quality as closely as possible.
Applies controlled light stress under multiple electrical boundary conditions and includes a non-pseudo-halide extraction/passivation control.
Tracks the temporal and spatial sequence of PbI2/Pb0 formation, recombination, transport loss, voids, cracks, and PCE degradation.
Defines a causal and a falsifying result based on whether Pb0 precedes and predicts failure independently of initial recombination/extraction.
accepted_equivalents: Synchrotron GIWAXS, laboratory XRD, hard-XPS, ToF-SIMS, X-ray fluorescence, or electron microscopy may be combined to locate Pb-containing phases.
Open-circuit, MPP, short-circuit, or controlled forward-bias stress are acceptable electrical boundary conditions when carrier accumulation is explained.
An alternative SnO2 passivator or band-alignment modifier is an acceptable extraction-focused control.
common_wrong_answers: Compares differently encapsulated devices and attributes all stability differences to buried chemistry.
Measures metallic Pb only after catastrophic failure and assumes it was the initiating cause.
Changes precursor stoichiometry so widely that bandgap, morphology, and initial PCE are no longer comparable.
Uses only dark shelf storage to test a proposed photo-reduction mechanism.

expected_answer: The two effects should not be treated as independent voltage sources, because improved band bending can raise VOC mainly by suppressing interfacial recombination. First, calibrated absolute PLQY or QFLS should be measured on the bare absorber under one-sun-equivalent excitation. A higher absorber QFLS at unchanged bandgap directly quantifies a reduction in nonradiative loss before the electron contact is added. Second, QFLS or PLQY should be repeated after adding C60, and device external electroluminescence efficiency should be measured at a current density near JSC. The decrease from bare-film QFLS to contacted-stack QFLS, and from contacted QFLS to device VOC, separates bulk/surface passivation from contact-induced and transport-related losses. Third, UPS/KPFM and capacitance or Mott-Schottky measurements should map the surface work function, band offsets, and depletion behavior, but these measurements alone cannot assign a VOC gain. Surface-photovoltage, bias-dependent KPFM, temperature-dependent VOC, and selective-contact transient extraction can test whether the cap creates stronger carrier selectivity without a resistive barrier. Fourth, transient photovoltage, transient photocurrent, or intensity-dependent recombination measurements should show whether carrier lifetime at operating carrier density increases while extraction remains fast. If most of the VOC increase is reproduced by the bare-film QFLS gain, passivation dominates. If bare-film QFLS changes little but the C60-induced QFLS penalty and device nonradiative loss shrink, improved surface electrostatics/contact selectivity dominates. Unchanged bandgap, absorption, and JSC rule out an optical-generation explanation. A higher built-in potential is supportive but not sufficient, because capacitance-derived values can be affected by mobile ions and interfacial charge.
scoring_key_points: Uses calibrated bare-film PLQY/QFLS at unchanged bandgap to quantify intrinsic nonradiative-loss reduction.
Compares bare absorber, electron-contact stack, and full-device QFLS/EQEEL to separate bulk/surface, contact, and device voltage losses.
Uses spatial or bias-dependent electrostatic and transient extraction measurements rather than treating UPS or Mott-Schottky alone as proof.
Recognizes that band bending improves VOC through contact selectivity/recombination suppression and that unchanged JSC excludes an optical origin.
accepted_equivalents: Absolute PL, Suns-QFLS, implied VOC, or calibrated electroluminescence may be used for the voltage-loss decomposition.
Surface photovoltage, Kelvin-probe mapping, impedance/capacitance profiling, or temperature-dependent VOC may probe electrostatics.
Transient absorption, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, charge-extraction, or recombination-order measurements may test selectivity and kinetics.
common_wrong_answers: Adds the built-in-potential increase directly to the QFLS increase as two independent contributions to VOC.
Uses only longer TRPL lifetime and concludes that all voltage gain is bulk passivation.
Treats a Mott-Schottky intercept as an unambiguous measure of the device's internal voltage despite ionic effects.
Attributes the VOC and fill-factor gains to increased light absorption despite unchanged JSC.

expected_answer: The two-terminal transfer must begin with an optical-electrical current-matching model, because the tandem current is limited by the lower-current subcell. The wide-bandgap absorber thickness, Br fraction, transparent-contact thickness, and parasitic absorption of C60, buffer, TCO, and recombination layers should be varied in controlled steps while the cap dose is initially held fixed. Subcell EQE under appropriate optical bias must verify current matching; a four-terminal sum cannot be used as the two-terminal target. The cap must then survive sequential deposition. Witness samples should be characterized before and after C60 deposition, ALD or solution buffer growth, sputtered TCO, and recombination-layer processing using angle-resolved XPS/GIWAXS, PLQY/QFLS, contact-angle or chemical mapping, and cross-sectional microscopy. Soft-deposition or shielding conditions should be optimized if sputter or ALD precursors damage or displace the cap. Transport qualification requires contact resistivity, dark J-V, impedance, transient extraction, and fill-factor analysis to ensure that the low-dimensional layer remains passivating but not tunnelling-limited. The recombination junction must support high current with minimal voltage loss. Stability must be tested under tandem-relevant electrical conditions: operando spectrally resolved PL/EL of the top cell at open circuit and MPP, temperature-controlled one-sun or concentrated stress, and depth/phase measurements to detect mixed-halide segregation or cap interdiffusion. Successful transfer requires near-current-matched subcell EQE, a tandem VOC close to the sum of the stabilized subcell voltages minus a small interconnect loss, high stabilized fill factor and MPP output, no cap-induced series-resistance penalty, and slower phase-segregation or voltage-loss growth than an uncapped control. A high scan PCE or arithmetic sum of separate cells is not sufficient.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes optical thickness and composition for two-terminal current matching and verifies subcell EQE under optical bias.
Tests cap chemistry and passivation after each electron-contact, buffer, TCO, and recombination-layer deposition step.
Quantifies contact/interconnect resistance and extraction so that a passivating cap is not mistaken for a transport barrier.
Requires stabilized two-terminal voltage, fill factor, current matching, and operando phase-segregation durability rather than a four-terminal efficiency sum.
accepted_equivalents: Optical transfer-matrix, ray-tracing, or experimentally calibrated EQE modelling may be used for current matching.
ALD-SnO2, evaporated buffers, sputtered ITO/IZO, or alternative recombination contacts are acceptable if process damage is evaluated.
Hyperspectral PL, EL, GIWAXS, Raman, or ion-migration measurements may be used to diagnose top-cell segregation under operation.
common_wrong_answers: Adds the independent top- and bottom-cell efficiencies and calls the result a two-terminal tandem prediction.
Assumes the cap survives sputtering or ALD because the pre-contact film PL was high.
Optimizes top-cell passivation without checking current matching or recombination-junction resistance.
Uses only nitrogen shelf storage and ignores bias- and illumination-driven mixed-halide segregation.

expected_answer: The controls should vary anchoring/void filling and bromine functionality independently. A practical set includes the primary monolayer alone; post-assembled nonhalogenated short-chain phosphonic acid; post-assembled brominated phosphonic acid at matched surface coverage; a brominated non-anchoring analogue that is removed by rinsing or cannot fill FTO vacancies; and, where possible, a surface-energy control that reproduces the contact angle without bromine-perovskite chemistry. A co-assembled version is useful to test whether sequential assembly is required. Before perovskite deposition, physical void filling should be diagnosed by PiFM or chemical-force mapping, KPFM potential variance, angle-resolved XPS, conductive-AFM leakage, and surface coverage statistics. A void-filling contribution is present if both nonhalogenated and brominated anchored second molecules reduce nanoscale potential/leakage heterogeneity relative to the primary monolayer, even before any perovskite is deposited. Wetting-mediated crystallization should be tested by matching or deliberately varying precursor contact angle and then following early-stage nucleation with in situ GIWAXS, optical microscopy, or drying interferometry. If film coverage, grain distribution, and strain track contact angle across chemically different surfaces, wetting is a major mediator. Direct bromine-mediated passivation requires an additional benefit at matched coverage and wetting: reproducible NMR or XPS chemical shifts, lower interfacial recombination velocity or higher QFLS, lower trap density/ideality factor, and improved extraction without a new transport barrier. A brominated molecule that lacks persistent anchoring may show solution interaction but should not deliver durable buried-interface benefit. If the brominated surface improves only contact angle and crystallization while no independent chemical or recombination signature remains after matching wetting, the data support wetting rather than direct halogen passivation.
scoring_key_points: Uses controls that independently vary anchoring/void filling and bromine functionality, including primary-only and matched-coverage post-assembly conditions.
Assigns physical void filling from pre-perovskite nanoscale coverage, potential, or leakage measurements.
Tests wetting-mediated crystallization by matching contact angle or tracking nucleation/film formation across chemically different surfaces.
Requires a bromine-specific chemical and recombination benefit at matched coverage and wetting before claiming direct passivation.
accepted_equivalents: PiFM, AFM phase/current mapping, KPFM, XPS mapping, ellipsometry, or molecular labelling may quantify void filling.
In situ GIWAXS, optical microscopy, interferometry, or time-resolved scattering may diagnose wetting-dependent nucleation.
NMR/XPS, QFLS/PLQY, surface-recombination velocity, SCLC, ideality factor, or transient extraction may support bromine-specific passivation.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only the primary monolayer with the brominated post-assembled layer and attributes every improvement to bromine.
Uses lower contact angle alone as proof of direct defect passivation.
Measures coverage only after perovskite deposition, when crystallization has obscured the original SAM defects.
Ignores the possibility that an excess second component forms an insulating overlayer.

expected_answer: The process design should vary primary-SAM dose and rinse, second-component concentration, dwell time, coating method, rinse strength, drying history, and FTO roughness or supplier lot. The aim is to span incomplete filling, near-monolayer completion, and excess-overlayer regimes. Interconnect regions should be masked or deliberately exposed in separate trials because residual phosphonic acid can change contact resistance or scribe isolation. Coverage and thickness must be mapped across the full area using a combination of calibrated XPS or fluorescence mapping, Kelvin-probe or surface-potential mapping, ellipsometry on witness coupons, contact-angle maps, and representative PiFM/AFM or conductive-AFM measurements. Perovskite wetting, nucleation, PL/QFLS, thickness, and defect maps should be recorded at module edges, centre, coating-direction extremes, and around P1/P2/P3 lines. Transport qualification should combine contact resistivity or transfer-length measurements, transient extraction, series resistance and fill-factor analysis, dark leakage, and temperature-dependent transport. Incomplete filling should appear as local recombination/shunts and broad potential distributions; excessive post-assembly should appear as increased contact resistance, slow extraction, FF loss, or poor adhesion even if PL is high. Module EL/PL, LBIC, thermography, and subcell J-V or resistance maps should quantify spatial yield. Qualification should include stabilized MPP under illumination and elevated temperature, followed by humidity or thermal-cycle testing with attention to edges and interconnects. A robust window is one in which coverage and wetting are uniform, local shunts decrease, contact resistance does not increase, subcell PCE dispersion narrows, and the module retains stabilized output without drift or interconnect degradation. A champion coupon or static contact-angle maximum is not an adequate process criterion.
scoring_key_points: Explores incomplete, near-complete, and excessive post-assembly regimes while controlling rinsing, drying, substrate roughness, and interconnect exposure.
Maps SAM coverage/thickness and perovskite wetting/quality across the full module, including edges and laser-scribed regions.
Uses contact-resistance, extraction, leakage, fill-factor, and temperature-dependent diagnostics to distinguish pinholes from an insulating overlayer.
Defines qualification by narrow subcell dispersion and durable stabilized MPP under combined thermal/environmental stress, not by a champion coupon.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, spray, dip, blade, or vapour-assisted post-assembly is acceptable if dose and rinse uniformity are quantified.
Kelvin-probe, XPS, fluorescence, ellipsometry, PiFM, AFM, or conductive-AFM may be combined for spatial coverage metrology.
EL/PL imaging, LBIC, thermography, Suns-VOC, or distributed-resistance modelling may be used for module-level loss mapping.
common_wrong_answers: Selects the condition with the lowest contact angle without checking contact resistance or extraction.
Characterizes only witness coupons and assumes the same coverage at module edges and interconnects.
Uses only average module J-V and misses local shunts or series-resistance hotspots.
Claims scalable stability from dry-box storage without MPP, heat, or interconnect stress.

expected_answer: The result requires a multi-channel mechanism rather than a single grain-size explanation. First, the polymer acts as a kinetic crystallization regulator: because nucleation is unchanged but annealing conversion is delayed, polymer-cation and polymer-Pb interactions slow crystal growth and permit larger, better-oriented grains with fewer defective boundaries. Second, it provides chemical defect passivation. Electron-rich fluorinated groups can coordinate under-coordinated Pb species and interact with organic cations, suppressing metallic Pb0 and lowering both electron and hole trap populations; this reduces Shockley-Read-Hall recombination and raises the quasi-Fermi-level splitting and open-circuit voltage. Third, it changes interfacial energetics: the downward conduction-band shift reduces the energetic mismatch to SnO2, facilitating electron transfer and decreasing extraction-related loss without changing the absorber bandgap. The matched slow-annealing film isolates the kinetic contribution: reproducing morphology but not Pb0 removal or the full voltage gain shows that chemical passivation and electronic alignment add benefits beyond texture. The optical observations are substrate-dependent, not contradictory. On inert glass, a longer lifetime indicates slower non-radiative decay inside the absorber. On SnO2, stronger quenching can indicate faster transfer of surviving electrons into the contact; it is beneficial only when accompanied by higher quasi-Fermi-level splitting or photoluminescence quantum yield on an inert substrate and improved electrical extraction, rather than by increased non-radiative interface loss.
scoring_key_points: Identifies kinetic crystallization control as a distinct contribution that improves grain growth and texture without changing initial nucleation.
Identifies fluorine-mediated chemical passivation of under-coordinated Pb/organic-cation environments, linking Pb0 and trap suppression to lower non-radiative recombination.
Identifies improved conduction-band alignment with SnO2 as an additional extraction/contact contribution while recognizing that the optical bandgap is unchanged.
Uses the matched slow-annealing control to reject a morphology-only model and correctly reconciles inert-substrate lifetime extension with contact-induced PL quenching.
accepted_equivalents: Crystallization templating, growth retardation, or kinetic coordination may be used for the first contribution.
Lewis-base passivation, Pb-F coordination, hydrogen bonding to FA/MA, or suppression of deep lead-related traps are acceptable chemical descriptions.
Reduced electron-extraction barrier, improved ETL energetic matching, or reduced contact loss are acceptable electronic descriptions.
PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level-splitting evidence may replace lifetime language when used to distinguish passivation from interfacial quenching.
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the entire voltage improvement to larger grains or preferential orientation.
Claims that the polymer raises the bandgap and therefore raises the open-circuit voltage.
Treats any shorter or more strongly quenched PL signal as proof of lower recombination without considering extraction and substrate configuration.
Ignores the matched slow-annealing control and merely lists measurements without causal separation.

expected_answer: A simple dipole explanation is insufficient because the three monolayers produce nearly the same FTO work function, while their device and recombination metrics diverge. Bulk morphology is also an unlikely cause because XRD and SEM are unchanged. Genuine interfacial passivation should raise the absorber's absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting and lengthen its lifetime when measured without an extracting contact, while lowering trap density, reducing the light-intensity Voc slope or ideality factor toward unity, and decreasing non-radiative voltage loss. Efficient hole transfer must then be tested on the actual FTO/SAM/perovskite contact. A selective contact may quench or shorten PL because carriers are extracted; this is beneficial only if transient photocurrent or extraction measurements become faster, contact resistance and charge accumulation decrease, and Voc/FF do not collapse.
