By contrast, blocked hole transfer can also produce a long lifetime or high PL because carriers remain in the absorber, but it should yield slow extraction, interfacial charge buildup, higher impedance/contact resistance, possible S-shaped J-V behavior, and reduced current or fill factor. The strongest diagnosis therefore compares the same absorber on inert glass, bare FTO, and each SAM-coated FTO; combines absolute PLQY/QFLS with TRPL, transient photocurrent or transient absorption, impedance/contact-resistance measurements, and trap/ideality diagnostics; and attributes the O-S-Se ranking to semiconductor-specific interfacial bonding/passivation only if the optical and electrical signatures are mutually consistent.
scoring_key_points: Uses the nearly identical work functions and unchanged film morphology to exclude simple dipole and bulk-film explanations for the O-S-Se device ranking.
Defines passivation signatures on an inert or non-extracting configuration: higher PLQY/QFLS or longer lifetime, lower trap density, and lower ideality factor/non-radiative voltage loss.
Distinguishes beneficial contact-induced PL quenching from blocked transfer using extraction kinetics, contact resistance/impedance, charge accumulation, and J-V behavior.
Proposes matched substrate-dependent controls that connect chemical interface quality, optical recombination and actual hole-selective transport.
accepted_equivalents: Suns-Voc, electroluminescence quantum efficiency, or quasi-Fermi-level splitting may be used instead of an ideality-factor or PLQY metric.
Transient surface photovoltage, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or selective-excitation transient absorption may replace transient photocurrent if extraction is directly probed.
Interfacial Lewis-acid/base interaction, stronger heteroatom-Pb interaction, or reduced under-coordinated-Pb defects are acceptable passivation mechanisms.
A hole-only device or transfer-length measurement may be used to quantify contact transport.
common_wrong_answers: Claims that the Se molecule wins because it creates a larger work-function shift despite the premise that all three shifts are nearly identical.
Treats a long PL lifetime as automatic proof of efficient extraction.
Attributes the ranking to larger grains or improved crystallinity despite the matched XRD and SEM results.
Lists characterization methods without predicting how passivation and blocked transfer would differ.

expected_answer: Selection should be based on a modular interface screen, not on the best small-area efficiency alone. Anchor-to-electrode robustness should be assessed on the actual textured oxide using XPS or elemental coverage before and after solvent rinsing, thermal treatment and aging, together with adhesion/desorption tests. Monolayer quality requires thickness and coverage mapping, work-function or Kelvin-probe mapping, contact-angle/wetting uniformity, and pinhole-sensitive leakage or shunt tests across large areas; a favorable mean work function is inadequate if roughness leaves exposed TCO. Absorber-specific screening must then be repeated for each semiconductor because the same head group can interact differently with ionic perovskite defects and with an organic donor-acceptor surface. Required metrics include nucleation or wetting effects, PLQY/QFLS and trap-assisted recombination for perovskites, interfacial charge-transfer and recombination metrics for organics, selectivity against electron leakage, and contact resistance or extraction kinetics. Durability should include maximum-power-point light soaking, heat and humidity, thermal cycling, solvent/process exposure, electrode corrosion, and post-stress work-function/coverage mapping, with module-scale yield and spatial uniformity. Cross-platform success is valuable because it suggests robust anchoring and broadly favorable hole selectivity, but it does not establish universal passivation: defect chemistry, surface energy, molecular packing, energetic offsets and degradation reactions differ among absorbers and textured electrodes. The selected SAM is therefore the one with the best worst-case combination of coverage, selectivity, interfacial recombination and retention, not necessarily the champion small-cell PCE.
scoring_key_points: Separates and tests phosphonic-acid anchoring/adhesion to the actual textured transparent electrode, including resistance to rinsing, heat and aging.
Assesses monolayer coverage, work-function uniformity, packing and pinholes spatially rather than relying on a mean work function from a smooth coupon.
Requires absorber-specific tests of wetting, passivation, charge selectivity and extraction for both perovskite and organic semiconductor systems.
Includes module-relevant operational durability and explains why two-system success supports breadth but does not prove universal interface compatibility.
accepted_equivalents: Angle-resolved XPS, ellipsometry, AFM phase mapping, fluorescence tagging, or electrochemical probes may be used for monolayer coverage and pinholes.
Kelvin-probe force microscopy, ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy mapping, or contact-potential mapping are acceptable dipole-uniformity methods.
Accelerated MPP, ISOS-style protocols, damp heat, or thermal cycling may be used for durability if the stress condition and failure metric are explicit.
Worst-case ranking, Pareto selection, or multi-objective down-selection are acceptable decision frameworks.
common_wrong_answers: Selects the Se-containing molecule solely because it produced the highest small-area PCE.
Measures only work function and assumes complete, durable monolayer coverage on textured TCO.
Assumes that identical behavior in perovskite and organic absorbers must follow from the same microscopic passivation mechanism.
Uses shelf storage alone and omits MPP, process-solvent, thermal and large-area uniformity tests.

expected_answer: At low-to-intermediate loading, small, well-dispersed nanocrystals can occupy defective grain-boundary regions without disrupting the perovskite lattice. With favorable band alignment, they form local electron-transport bridges, reduce boundary potential barriers, and passivate or replace poorly conducting defect sites. The expected result is a spatially uniform increase in boundary current, higher electron-only mobility, lower trap density and charge-transfer resistance, larger recombination resistance, reduced dark leakage, and improved fill factor. The response becomes non-monotonic when the loading exceeds the dispersion and interfacial-tolerance window. Agglomerates can create roughness, incomplete perovskite coverage, new oxide/perovskite defect area, field concentration, direct or quasi-direct leakage paths, or blocking islands at the wrong interface. Those effects can lower the PL lifetime through added non-radiative recombination just as easily as through extraction. Therefore TRPL shortening is ambiguous and must be paired with absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting on an inert substrate and with electrical extraction data on selective contacts. The optimum regime should show uniform—not hotspot-dominated—c-AFM contrast, increasing mobility with decreasing trap density, lower series/contact resistance and dark leakage, higher PLQY or preserved QFLS in the absorber, and improved Jsc/FF. The overloaded regime should show agglomeration, broadened device statistics, leakage or shunts, reduced QFLS/PLQY, higher recombination/transfer losses and performance degradation despite short TRPL.
scoring_key_points: Explains the beneficial intermediate-loading regime as dispersed, favorably aligned conductive grain-boundary bridges with reduced barriers/traps.
Explains the high-loading reversal through agglomeration, new interfacial defects, blocking islands, field hot spots or leakage/shunt pathways.
States that TRPL shortening is non-unique and separates extraction from non-radiative decay using PLQY/QFLS plus electrical transport or selective-contact controls.
Predicts a coordinated optimum signature across c-AFM uniformity, SCLC mobility/traps, EIS/contact resistance, dark leakage, optical recombination and device statistics.
accepted_equivalents: Percolation-window, transport-bridge, or grain-boundary band-bending models are acceptable if they explain the non-monotonic dose dependence.
Electroluminescence efficiency, Suns-Voc or transient microwave conductivity may replace PLQY/QFLS where appropriately interpreted.
Recombination resistance and charge-transfer resistance terminology may be adapted to the chosen EIS equivalent circuit if the physical trend is clear.
Local photocurrent, electron-beam-induced current, or scanning Kelvin-probe measurements may substitute for c-AFM in identifying uniform channels versus hot spots.
common_wrong_answers: Concludes that the highest loading is optimal because it gives the shortest TRPL lifetime.
Assumes that any conductive nanoparticle concentration monotonically increases mobility and fill factor.
Uses average c-AFM current without distinguishing uniform boundary conduction from sparse current hot spots or shunts.
Attributes the high-loading loss only to optical absorption even though leakage, agglomeration and resistance changes are provided.

expected_answer: A minimum causal design is a matched 2 x 2 matrix: no oxide/no modifier, bare oxide, free modifier without oxide, and surface-modified oxide at the same effective oxide and modifier doses. Stronger controls include an insulating oxide of similar size to test a purely particulate/passivation effect, a nonfluorinated analogue to separate acid coordination from fluorocarbon hydrophobicity, and an inert hydrophobic additive to separate water exclusion from chemical passivation. Continuous processing should replace the drop antisolvent with a controlled spray, quench bath, gas-knife-assisted secondary ink, or precursor-compatible dispersion, while re-optimizing particle concentration, colloidal stability, wet-film residence time and drying. DLS/TEM before coating and cross-sectional EDS, XPS depth profiling or ToF-SIMS after coating should verify that nanocrystals remain small, dispersed and distributed through relevant grain-boundary regions rather than forming a surface crust or coating-direction gradient. Transport is supported by c-AFM, electron-only mobility, contact/EIS measurements and full-device extraction. Chemical passivation requires lower trap-assisted recombination, higher PLQY/QFLS and defect-state spectroscopy at matched morphology. Hydrophobicity requires contact-angle plus water-sorption or vapor-permeation evidence, not contact angle alone. Ion-migration suppression requires bias- and light-stressed depth profiling, low-frequency ionic impedance or activation-energy measurements, and reduced electrode-side halide accumulation. Separate humidity, dry-heat and illuminated-MPP tests isolate moisture, thermal and operational effects; combined damp-heat-light-bias testing reveals interactions. These experiments can support mechanism-specific contributions and scalable uniformity, but they do not establish module lifetime unless large-area devices, encapsulation, repeatability and long combined-stress tests are also demonstrated.
scoring_key_points: Uses a matched factorial control set that separates oxide transport, free modifier, surface-modified oxide, hydrophobicity and chemical-passivation contributions.
Defines a continuous-coating route and verifies particle size, dispersion and depth/lateral distribution after scale-up.
Assigns distinct diagnostics to transport, defect passivation, moisture exclusion and ion-migration suppression rather than using one proxy for all mechanisms.
Uses orthogonal and combined stress tests and states the boundary between material-level evidence and claims of scalable device or module lifetime.
accepted_equivalents: A 2 x 2 design with oxide and surface modifier as independent factors is acceptable even if additional analogue controls differ.
Slot-die secondary coating, ultrasonic spray quenching, or inline antisolvent misting are acceptable continuous routes if colloidal delivery and drying are controlled.
Quartz-crystal microbalance, gravimetric uptake, dynamic vapor sorption or water-vapor transmission may be used for moisture-barrier evidence.
Operando photoluminescence, Kelvin-probe drift, isotope tracing or transient ion-drift methods may replace ToF-SIMS for ion-migration diagnosis.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only the control and surface-modified oxide, making transport, passivation and hydrophobicity inseparable.
Uses contact angle alone as proof of long-term moisture stability or ion-migration suppression.
Assumes that particles dispersed in the ink remain uniformly distributed through a continuously coated film.
Claims module-scale durability from short shelf tests on small unencapsulated cells.

expected_answer: The hypotheses must be separated with depth-resolved composition and band-structure measurements rather than inferred from morphology or an averaged diffraction pattern. ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved or hard-X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, cross-sectional STEM-EDS/EELS, and depth-sensitive GIWAXS or nano-XRD can map FA/MA and phase evolution. An abrupt bilayer should show a sharp composition step, two distinguishable phase or lattice signatures with limited peak interpolation, and a localized band offset measurable by depth-resolved Kelvin probe, UPS/HAXPES or cross-sectional scanning probe methods. Selective excitation from the top and bottom, wavelength-dependent TRPL, transient absorption or photocurrent should then reveal directional charge transfer or spatial electron-hole separation consistent with a type-II interface. A graded interdiffusion region should instead show a continuous FA/MA profile, continuously shifted or broadened lattice/bandgap signatures, and a smoothly varying surface potential or emission energy rather than a discrete discontinuity. A predominantly single phase with surface passivation should show little sustained compositional gradient or second-phase signature; its main changes would be lower surface-defect density, higher PLQY/QFLS and longer lifetime without a clear depth-dependent band offset or directional transfer. Cross-sectional SEM can show layer thickness and coverage but not cation composition, lattice mixing or band offsets. Conventional out-of-plane XRD averages the film depth, can miss minority or similarly oriented phases, and cannot by itself distinguish a sharp interface from a gradient that produces similar peak shifts.
scoring_key_points: Proposes depth-resolved chemical/structural measurements capable of resolving FA/MA composition and phase as a function of depth.
Predicts a sharp composition and energetic discontinuity plus directional carrier transfer for an abrupt type-II bilayer.
Predicts continuous composition/lattice/bandgap or potential variation for a graded interdiffusion region and primarily defect-related changes for a passivated single phase.
Explains the insufficiency of cross-sectional SEM and conventional out-of-plane XRD for determining composition gradients, band offsets and heterojunction abruptness.
accepted_equivalents: Neutron reflectometry, resonant X-ray scattering, isotope labeling or atom-probe tomography may substitute for other depth-composition methods if resolution is adequate.
Depth-resolved KPFM, HAXPES, cross-sectional electron holography or suitable photoemission may be used to map energetic profiles.
Two-sided selective excitation, time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy or spatially resolved photocurrent may be used to test directional transfer.
A quasi-type-II or graded-band model is acceptable if its predicted signatures are distinguished from an abrupt interface.
common_wrong_answers: Calls the structure a type-II heterojunction solely because PL red-shifts or lifetime increases.
Treats a cross-sectional layer contrast in SEM as proof of a chemically abrupt interface.
Uses only conventional XRD peak shifts without depth resolution to infer interdiffusion or phase identity.
Fails to state different predicted observations for the abrupt, graded and passivated-single-phase hypotheses.

expected_answer: The two functions require orthogonal controls. At minimum, compare no buffer, pristine MXene, functionalized MXene, the quaternary ammonium bromide alone, a non-intercalated physical mixture, and a conventional buffer at matched thickness; an alternative functional group that produces a similar work function but different halide affinity is especially useful. The electronic contribution should be quantified before long aging by UPS or Kelvin probe, PCBM/buffer/metal contact I-V or transfer-length measurements, electron-only devices, EIS and transient extraction. A lower barrier mechanism predicts a reproducible work-function/contact-potential shift, lower specific contact resistance, no S-shaped J-V curve and faster electron extraction even under short tests where substantial ion redistribution has not occurred. The ionic contribution requires bias-, light- and temperature-stressed ToF-SIMS or depth profiling for iodide and metal species, low-frequency ionic impedance or ion-drift measurements, activation-energy analysis, and evidence of reduced Ag-halide formation or electrode corrosion. It is supported if two contacts with similar initial work function and resistance show different iodide accumulation and long-term retention, or if the functionalized layer suppresses migration under an imposed electric field independently of current density. It is falsified if migration scales only with current/temperature and disappears when electrical stress is matched. Conversely, the electronic mechanism is weakened if work function and contact resistance are unchanged despite device gains. PL/TRPL measured through perovskite/PCBM/buffer can shorten because of faster extraction or because of added non-radiative loss; the buffer is not in direct contact with the perovskite, so PL must be combined with PLQY/QFLS, electrical extraction and recombination measurements.
scoring_key_points: Defines orthogonal controls that separate pristine MXene, functionalizer, functionalized MXene, physical mixtures and conventional/matched-work-function buffers.
Assigns UPS/contact-potential and contact-resistance/extraction measurements to the electronic dipole and barrier mechanism, with clear expected signatures.
Assigns bias/light/temperature-dependent ion profiling and ionic-transport or corrosion measurements to the migration-blocking mechanism, including a current-matched falsification test.
Explains the ambiguity of PL/TRPL through PCBM and requires optical recombination metrics plus electrical evidence before claiming improved extraction.
accepted_equivalents: Kelvin-probe mapping, inverse photoemission or contact-potential-difference measurements may replace UPS where appropriate.
Transient ion-drift, thermally stimulated current, isotope labeling or operando XPS may replace ToF-SIMS for ion-migration evidence.
A matched-dipole molecular layer or different quaternary ammonium salt is acceptable as the similar-work-function/different-ion-affinity control.
Metal-halide spectroscopy, cross-sectional TEM-EDS or electrode mass change may be used as corrosion/migration endpoints.
common_wrong_answers: Uses only pristine MXene versus functionalized MXene, leaving the roles of the salt, intercalation and work-function shift confounded.
Treats a shorter TRPL lifetime as conclusive proof of faster extraction.
Infers ion blocking solely from improved shelf stability without measuring ionic redistribution or electrode reaction.
Does not propose matched-current or matched-work-function comparisons capable of falsifying the reviewer's alternative explanation.

expected_answer: The PCBM/buffer/metal stack must be treated as a new contact for each cathode. UPS or Kelvin probe, metal-dependent contact-potential measurements and specific contact resistance must be re-measured because the optimal buffer work function and dipole depend on the PCBM LUMO, metal work function and interface chemistry. Initial J-V should be screened for S-shaped behavior, series resistance and hysteresis. Chemical qualification must determine whether Cu or Al reacts with bromide, MXene terminations or residual water, whether the MXene oxidizes, and whether the quaternary ammonium species desorbs or redistributes under heat and bias; XPS, ToF-SIMS and cross-sectional analysis before and after stress are appropriate. Morphologically, the layer must be continuous enough to block metal and halide migration but thin and oriented enough to avoid excessive vertical or lateral resistance. Concentration/thickness series, sheet and contact resistance, flake-orientation/coverage mapping, pinhole-sensitive leakage and module-scale spatial J-V or electroluminescence maps are required. Flexible devices additionally require adhesion, neutral-axis design and repeated bending with resistance and shunt monitoring. Qualification should combine MPP light soaking, dry heat, damp heat, thermal cycling, bias stress and bending, followed by work-function drift, oxidation, metal/halide depth profiles and delamination analysis. Reject the contact if it develops pinhole shorts, rising series resistance, work-function drift, metal-halide reaction, accelerated ion migration, functionalizer loss, oxidation, delamination or bending-induced shunts, even when the fresh small-area PCE is high.
scoring_key_points: Re-measures energy alignment and specific contact resistance for each PCBM/buffer/Cu or Al contact rather than assuming the Ag optimum transfers.
Evaluates cathode-specific chemical reactions, MXene oxidation and functionalizer retention with pre/post-stress interfacial analysis.
Optimizes thickness, flake orientation, coverage, pinholes and lateral/vertical resistance at module scale and includes mechanical-bending qualification.
Uses combined operational/environmental/mechanical stresses and explicit rejection criteria for resistance, migration, reaction, oxidation, delamination or shunting.
accepted_equivalents: Transmission-line, cross-bridge Kelvin resistor or dedicated electron-only contact structures are acceptable contact-resistance methods.
Grazing-incidence scattering, polarized spectroscopy, AFM or cross-sectional microscopy may be used to assess flake orientation and coverage.
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography or photocurrent mapping may replace spatial J-V mapping for module nonuniformity and shunts.
Cyclic bending, rolling fatigue or torsional tests are acceptable mechanical protocols if electrical degradation is tracked.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that the same work-function shift and buffer concentration optimized for Ag are automatically optimal for Cu and Al.
Considers only vertical extraction and ignores lateral resistance, pinholes and module-scale nonuniformity.
Runs bending tests without simultaneous resistance, shunt or post-bend interfacial analysis.
Accepts high fresh PCE despite evidence of buffer oxidation, cathode reaction, functionalizer loss or accelerated ion/metal migration.

expected_answer:
The most consistent transport mechanism is spectral filtering by repeated absorption and re-emission. The blue side of the quantum-dot emission overlaps most strongly with the absorber's absorption tail, so those photons have the shortest mean free path. During lateral propagation they are preferentially reabsorbed; a fraction is re-emitted after the excited-state lifetime, whereas another fraction is lost nonradiatively or escapes the waveguide. The surviving spectrum therefore becomes progressively enriched in red-tail photons. Once the strongly overlapping wavelengths have been depleted, the spectrum approaches a transport-selected quasi-steady shape, explaining why the apparent overlap or reabsorption penalty changes rapidly at short path length and then saturates. A high PLQY makes repeated re-emission viable but does not make it lossless, because each cycle still carries escape, parasitic absorption, and nonradiative probabilities.

The key experiment must decouple where the material is excited from how far the emitted photons travel. Excite one fixed microscopic region and collect edge spectra at several calibrated path lengths; then move the excitation and collection positions together so that the local material sampled changes but the optical path remains short. Photon recycling predicts a redshift governed primarily by propagation length, not by the absolute sample coordinate. A true size or composition gradient instead produces position-dependent local absorption and front-face PL peaks even at negligible propagation distance, and should be visible by confocal PL, absorption, TEM, or composition mapping. Front-face and edge-excitation spectra measured from opposite directions provide an additional reversal test.

Time-resolved edge emission is especially discriminating. Reabsorption/re-emission should introduce a distance-dependent delayed rise, longer mean arrival time, or an increasing late-time red component because each recycling event adds a radiative waiting time and optical path. Elastic scattering can reduce transmitted intensity, broaden the angular distribution, and increase path length, but wavelength-independent scattering alone should not create a systematic local absorption-edge-correlated redshift or an added excited-state delay. Integrating-sphere measurements and angle-resolved transmission can quantify scattering. Detector or collection artifacts should disappear after response calibration, use of identical numerical aperture, and swapping detector positions; they will not reproduce the coupled distance-dependent spectral and temporal evolution. A final consistency test is to vary the Stokes shift or absorption-tail strength across samples: the magnitude of the propagation redshift should track spectral overlap if photon recycling is dominant.
scoring_key_points: Explains preferential reabsorption of the blue emission wing, red-tail enrichment, and plateau formation after strongly overlapping wavelengths are depleted.
Uses fixed-location/variable-path and variable-location/fixed-path measurements to separate transport effects from a spatial nanocrystal gradient.
Identifies a distance-dependent delayed or late-time red emission component as a photon-recycling signature, while treating scattering as mainly an intensity/angular-path effect.
Includes calibration and orthogonal mapping or overlap-variation controls that can falsify detector artifacts and correlate the redshift with the absorption tail.
accepted_equivalents: Repeated self-absorption and re-emission, radiative transfer, or photon recycling are acceptable equivalent terms.
A distance-dependent increase in effective decay time, delayed rise, or time-gated spectral redshift are acceptable temporal signatures.
Confocal hyperspectral mapping, micro-absorption, cathodoluminescence, TEM/EDS, or equivalent local probes may be used to test a size/composition gradient.
common_wrong_answers: Attributes every redshift to quantum-dot growth even though the shift appears only after lateral propagation.
Claims that near-unity PLQY eliminates all reabsorption losses or guarantees lossless photon recycling.
Uses only steady-state edge spectra and does not include a path-location decoupling experiment or temporal diagnostic.

expected_answer:
The transfer changes the coupled glass chemistry, nucleation thermodynamics, defect chemistry, and photon-transport problem. Iodide-rich perovskites have different precursor solubility, volatility, redox sensitivity, lattice energy, and interfacial reactions with oxide glass formers than bromide perovskites. A heat treatment that produces the desired bromide nanocrystal size can instead cause iodide loss, mixed-halide redistribution, secondary phases, excessive crystal growth, scattering, or nonradiative defects. Raising temperature is particularly unsafe because emission redshift from larger crystallites can be purchased at the cost of lower PLQY and transparency. The relevant process window must be referenced to the new glass transition, viscosity, and crystallization kinetics, not copied from the bromide glass.

Screening should begin with glass-composition and chemical-compatibility maps. Candidate hosts should be assessed for iodide retention, precursor dissolution, melt redox state, corrosion/volatilization, refractive index, and the tendency to form competing lead, cesium, or fluoride/oxide phases. Differential thermal analysis and viscosity measurements should define an annealing/nucleation window. A factorial heat-treatment matrix in temperature and time should then be evaluated by local and bulk probes: XRD and total-scattering/PDF for phase identity, TEM/EDS or atom-scale mapping for nanocrystal size and halide uniformity, and XPS or chemical analysis for halide loss and oxidation. Mixed-halide candidates additionally require light-soaking tests for reversible or irreversible halide segregation.

The optical optimum is not the reddest sample. It must maximize solar-weighted absorption and PLQY while preserving a sufficiently large Stokes shift, narrow parasitic absorption, low haze/scattering, and spectral overlap with the silicon cell's external quantum efficiency. Absolute PLQY should be measured under relevant excitation wavelengths and after thermal processing, and path-length-dependent spectra/ray tracing should use measured—not assumed—quantum yield and absorption coefficients. Refractive index, surface quality, waveguide escape-cone losses, and edge-coupling losses must also be quantified.

Finally, the glass matrix can suppress external moisture ingress but cannot by itself prove photochemical or operational durability. Qualification should include prolonged full-spectrum illumination, elevated-temperature light soaking, thermal cycling, humidity/water exposure, UV stress, and maximum-power-point operation of edge-coupled devices. Failure analysis must track PLQY, spectral segregation, haze, cracks, interfacial delamination, and cell-coupling loss. Large panels require melt-composition and heat-treatment uniformity mapping. Device readiness requires reproducible red emission and high internal quantum efficiency without secondary phases or optical scattering, stable waveguide transport after coupled stresses, and validated electrical output rather than only attractive photoluminescence.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that iodide/mixed-halide transfer changes glass compatibility, volatility, nucleation, defect chemistry, and phase-segregation risk, so the bromide heat schedule cannot simply be copied.
Defines a composition-plus-temperature/time screening matrix with thermal analysis and structural/compositional verification of nanocrystal incorporation and phase purity.
Optimizes solar-weighted absorption, PLQY, Stokes shift, scattering, refractive index, reabsorption, and silicon spectral matching rather than emission wavelength alone.
Requires coupled illumination, heat, moisture/UV, MPP, and large-area uniformity validation with explicit failure criteria before device readiness.
accepted_equivalents: DTA/DSC, hot-stage spectroscopy, viscosity mapping, or crystallization-kinetics measurements are acceptable ways to define the new thermal window.
PDF, solid-state NMR, Raman, synchrotron XRD, TEM-EDS/EELS, or equivalent phase/incorporation probes may be used.
Photoinduced halide segregation may be described as light-driven compositional demixing or emission splitting in mixed-halide nanocrystals.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that a higher annealing temperature is automatically beneficial because it redshifts the emission.
Optimizes only PL peak wavelength and ignores PLQY, reabsorption, haze, index-guiding losses, or silicon spectral response.
Treats water resistance of the glass as proof of outdoor and operational reliability without light-bias and thermal qualification.

expected_answer:
A delayed PL onset by itself only shows slower appearance of an emissive population; it does not establish synchronized conversion. Likewise, a stationary PL peak can be produced by optical filtering, a fixed emitting minority phase, or a thickness-dependent collection effect. The claim of phase-distribution management requires agreement between an optical observable and a structural/compositional observable that separately resolve the film depth.

The decisive structural test is time-resolved GIWAXS or GIXRD collected at at least two penetration depths. True synchronization means that the top-sensitive and bottom-sensitive perovskite reflections appear within the experimental time resolution, follow comparable growth kinetics, and maintain the same scattering-vector position rather than one region converting earlier or continuously changing lattice parameter. A globally slower but still asynchronous process would shift both onset times later while preserving a measurable top-bottom lag or different q evolution. Film-thickness changes can alter absolute intensity but should not make the phase-onset times and q trajectories converge after normalization to illuminated volume. A penetration-depth calibration and an additive-free film of matched thickness are therefore required.

Optical controls should include front-side and substrate-side in situ PL, simultaneous absorption/reflectance, and a thickness series. If the stable PL peak is only due to self-absorption, the apparent peak should depend strongly on collection direction and optical path while the depth-resolved lattice/composition evolution remains asynchronous. True synchronized conversion should give consistent peak energy from both directions after correcting for filtering and should correlate temporally with the structural onset. Time-resolved PL intensity may still rise later because nucleation is retarded, but its spectral position should remain tied to a stable composition.

Post-anneal depth profiling must close the causal chain. TOF-SIMS, angle-resolved or sputter-depth XPS, cross-sectional EDS, or isotope-labeled cation tracing should show a flat A-site composition and no residual nonperovskite phase across the thickness. Exfoliated top/bottom microscopy can test whether grain-size disparity is also reduced. Useful mechanistic controls include a non-coordinating molecular analogue, an additive that coordinates Pb but cannot self-assemble, and a film without the original volatile crystallization additive. If delayed crystallization occurs without elimination of the top-bottom kinetic lag or final composition gradient, the molecule is only a retardant, not a phase-distribution manager.
scoring_key_points: States that delayed or stationary PL alone is non-unique and cannot prove synchronized phase conversion.
Requires time-resolved top- and bottom-sensitive diffraction showing matched onset/growth and stable scattering-vector evolution, not merely later crystallization.
Uses front/back optical collection, thickness/absorption controls, and penetration-depth normalization to exclude self-absorption and geometry artifacts.
Requires final depth-composition uniformity and appropriate molecular/process controls; otherwise the additive is only a crystallization retardant.
accepted_equivalents: Depth-resolved GIWAXS, GIXRD, operando synchrotron diffraction, or equivalent penetration-depth structural measurements are acceptable.
TOF-SIMS, depth-XPS, cross-sectional EDS/EELS, isotope tracing, or another quantitative depth-composition method may be used.
A matched nonbinding analogue, blocked-functional-group molecule, or coordination-strength series is an acceptable mechanistic control.
common_wrong_answers: Treats a delayed PL onset as direct proof of a more homogeneous final film.
Uses only final XRD and cannot determine whether top and bottom phases formed synchronously.
Ignores optical path length and film thickness when interpreting an unchanged PL peak.

expected_answer:
The transferable principle is controlled, spatially uniform precursor anchoring that narrows the distribution of local phase-transition times; the transferable object is not necessarily the original molecule. Blade coating changes solvent evaporation, meniscus flow, shear, wet-film thickness, and top-to-bottom drying gradients, so the molecular concentration and binding strength established in spin coating cannot be copied directly. A useful additive must remain soluble throughout the coating window, avoid premature precipitation at the meniscus, distribute uniformly during solvent loss, and coordinate strongly enough to retard the fastest local conversion without immobilizing lead-halide complexes or leaving an insulating residue. Volatility, diffusion coefficient, acid/base chemistry, and self-association must be evaluated under the actual solvent and drying atmosphere.

The screening stage should use a small library spanning coordination strength, number and geometry of binding groups, aromatic self-assembly, and molecular size. Spectroscopy or calculation can rank binding to Pb-halide complexes, but the candidates must be tested in a coating-speed/temperature/gas-knife/solvent-composition design of experiments. Operando optical imaging, in situ PL, and spatially resolved GIWAXS across and through the moving wet film should determine whether nucleation and phase conversion remain synchronous over the coating width. Final TOF-SIMS or depth-XPS should verify uniform A-site and halide distributions, while hyperspectral PL and KPFM mapping should detect lateral nonuniformity.

A-site phase heterogeneity and mixed-halide photo-segregation are related but distinct failure modes. Uniform FA/Cs distribution after drying does not prove resistance to light-driven I/Br demixing. The wide-bandgap film must therefore be tested under relevant illumination and electrical bias for PL peak splitting, reversible/irreversible band-gap drift, local composition changes, and voltage loss. Candidate additives may improve initial crystallization yet enhance ionic mobility or create halide-rich coordination complexes; temperature-dependent ionic conductivity, bias-stress relaxation, and post-stress compositional mapping are needed.

Tandem transfer requires device-level validation in the intended stack and area. The study should include additive-free and non-coordinating controls, concentration/process windows, and statistics across large-area subcells. Qualification should combine continuous one-sun or spectrum-matched illumination at maximum power point, elevated temperature, thermal cycling, and ambient/encapsulated testing, while monitoring top-cell band gap, current matching, voltage, hysteresis, and spatial electroluminescence/PL uniformity. Success means reproducible phase homogeneity after scalable coating, no light-induced halide-segregation penalty, retained current matching, and slower degradation under coupled operating stresses.
scoring_key_points: Transfers the kinetic-anchoring principle rather than copying molecule or concentration, and accounts for blade-coating flow, evaporation, and vertical drying gradients.
Screens coordination/self-assembly/solubility over a process design space with operando spatial and depth-resolved crystallization measurements.
Separates final A-site homogeneity from photoinduced I/Br segregation and requires light-bias ionic/compositional diagnostics.
Qualifies the additive in tandem-relevant large-area devices under MPP, heat, illumination, and environmental stress with current-matching and spatial-uniformity metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die coating, meniscus coating, or another continuous wet-coating process may replace blade coating if hydrodynamic and drying gradients are addressed.
Gas-quench rate, substrate temperature, solvent-vapor pressure, coating speed, and wet-film thickness are acceptable process variables.
Operando XRD/GIWAXS, optical coherence imaging, hyperspectral PL, or equivalent spatially resolved kinetic tools are acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Copies the spin-coating concentration directly and ignores wet-film residence time and additive redistribution during blade coating.
Assumes that uniform FA/Cs composition automatically prevents photoinduced I/Br segregation in a wide-bandgap film.
Reports only initial single-junction efficiency and omits tandem current matching and coupled light-heat-bias stability.

expected_answer:
PL quenching and a shorter TRPL lifetime report faster disappearance of emissive carriers, but they do not identify the destination of those carriers. The signal can reflect useful hole transfer into the selective contact, interfacial Shockley-Read-Hall recombination, exciton dissociation followed by extraction, or poorer perovskite formation on the substrate. A deeper NiOx valence band can reduce the energetic barrier for hole transfer, while the larger specific surface area of smaller nanocrystals can simultaneously increase reactive Ni3+-rich sites; therefore extraction and loss can increase together.

The first diagnostic axis is charge accounting. Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity, or spectroelectrochemistry should look for the growth of a long-lived charge-separated or oxidized-hole-transport-layer population after perovskite excitation. Beneficial extraction should produce a contact-associated charge signal whose amplitude tracks photocurrent and can be removed or reversed by blocking the hole-transfer pathway. Nonradiative quenching produces rapid PL loss without a corresponding mobile or stored charge population and often increases heat or trap-mediated recombination signatures. Thickness-dependent polymer passivation is useful: an optimum ultrathin layer should suppress direct Ni3+ chemistry while retaining tunneling/transfer; excessive thickness should slow extraction.

The second axis is boundary-condition dependence. Measure absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting under open circuit, short circuit, and with an electron-blocking top layer. Efficient selective extraction may strongly quench PL under extraction conditions but should preserve or increase open-circuit QFLS once interface recombination is passivated. A recombination-active NiOx interface lowers QFLS and electroluminescence efficiency even at open circuit. Comparing perovskite films on inert substrates, on each NiOx type before and after passivation, and on a polymer-only control separates changes in perovskite film quality from contact-induced dynamics.

The third axis is electrical selectivity. Hole-only transport, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, intensity-dependent Voc, impedance, and recombination-resistance measurements should show faster hole collection, lower interfacial accumulation, lower ideality factor, and higher recombination resistance for beneficial extraction. Interfacial loss instead yields lower Voc, stronger nonradiative voltage loss, poorer EL efficiency, and possibly higher leakage despite fast PL decay. UPS/Kelvin probe should confirm the energy-level trend, while XPS/redox probes should quantify whether the polymer actually neutralizes or screens surface Ni3+. The mechanism is established only when faster optical decay is accompanied by detected extracted charge, improved QFLS/Voc/selectivity, and reduced Ni3+-mediated recombination rather than by PL quenching alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains the ambiguity of PL quenching/short TRPL and the coexistence of favorable energy alignment with reactive high-area Ni3+ sites.
Requires direct observation or accounting of transferred/mobile charge rather than inferring extraction solely from PL decay.
Uses open-circuit versus extraction-condition QFLS/PLQY and matched substrate/passivation controls to distinguish recombination from selective transfer.
Links a valid extraction mechanism to improved Voc/EL/selectivity/recombination resistance and verified Ni3+ passivation, with thickness dependence as a control.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, terahertz conductivity, photoinduced absorption, charge-extraction spectroscopy, or another direct contact-charge probe is acceptable.
Absolute PLQY-derived QFLS, electroluminescence EQE, nonradiative voltage loss, or surface-photovoltage measurements may serve as recombination diagnostics.
A tunneling-distance, polymer-thickness, or molecular-coverage series is an acceptable way to separate passivation from transport blockage.
common_wrong_answers: States that shorter TRPL always means better extraction or that longer TRPL always means better passivation.
Uses only UPS alignment and ignores the possibility of interfacial redox or trap-assisted recombination.
Does not include inert-substrate, polymer-only, or boundary-condition controls.

expected_answer:
The replacement must perform several functions simultaneously. It should chemically neutralize or spatially isolate reactive Ni3+-rich surface sites, prevent interfacial redox/deprotonation reactions with the perovskite, and remain electronically compatible with hole extraction. It must form conformal coverage over a high-surface-area nanocrystal film at low thickness, preserve the deep NiOx valence alignment, avoid a large tunneling barrier or series resistance, and not introduce mobile ions, deep states, or unfavorable dipoles. It should also be chemically stable under UV, heat, oxygen, and perovskite-processing solvents and should support uniform perovskite wetting and crystallization over module areas.

Screening should use a chemistry/coverage/thickness matrix rather than a single candidate. XPS or operando photoelectron spectroscopy can quantify changes in Ni3+-related states and interfacial reaction products; UPS/Kelvin probe and conductivity measurements establish whether the valence alignment and transport are retained. Absolute PLQY/QFLS, EL efficiency, transient charge extraction, and impedance distinguish true recombination passivation from a layer that only blocks current. Contact-angle, AFM, cross-sectional microscopy, and large-area mapping verify coatability and pinhole-free coverage. Candidates may include crosslinked polymers, self-assembled molecules, or ultrathin wide-bandgap inorganic layers, but each must be evaluated at the minimum thickness that gives chemical coverage.

Chemical passivation must be separated from UV filtering by optical controls. Measure the interlayer's wavelength-dependent absorption and compare devices under equal absorbed photon flux. Use an external UV-cut filter matched to the candidate's attenuation, and a chemically inert layer with similar UV absorption but no Ni3+ binding. If the candidate improves stability beyond the matched optical filter and suppresses Ni/perovskite reaction products, a chemical contribution is supported. Conversely, stability that disappears after photon-flux matching is primarily shielding. Time-resolved interfacial spectroscopy before and after UV exposure can reveal whether charge-transfer selectivity is preserved.

A thick absorber is inadequate because it sacrifices visible transmission, can generate heat or photoproducts, increases series resistance, and may worsen module current matching and coating nonuniformity. Qualification should therefore combine UV-rich illumination with maximum-power-point operation, elevated temperature, oxygen/humidity, and thermal cycling in the intended encapsulated module stack. Controls should include NiOx-only, interlayer-only, the original bilayer, and matched UV-filter conditions. Track PCE components, leakage, hysteresis, spatial EL/PL, sheet resistance, interconnect degradation, and post-stress interfacial chemistry. A successful transfer retains the NiOx-dependent energy advantage and uniform module performance while reducing chemical degradation under coupled UV-light-bias stress, not merely under a dark or small-cell test.
scoring_key_points: Defines simultaneous requirements of Ni3+ chemical passivation, conformal ultrathin coverage, preserved energy alignment/transport, and process/UV stability.
Uses thickness and chemistry screening with XPS/UPS, QFLS/EL, extraction, morphology, and large-area uniformity measurements.
Separates chemical stabilization from optical shielding through matched photon-flux, external-filter, and inert-absorber controls.
Rejects thick UV absorption as a universal fix and requires coupled UV-MPP-heat-environment module qualification with spatial and chemical failure analysis.
accepted_equivalents: An ultrathin oxide, crosslinked polymer, SAM, 2D layer, or hybrid interlayer is acceptable if the stated functional tests are applied.
XPS, NEXAFS, operando spectroscopy, redox titration, or equivalent methods may quantify Ni3+ passivation and reaction products.
Spatial electroluminescence, photoluminescence, lock-in thermography, or sheet-resistance mapping are acceptable module-uniformity diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Selects the most UV-absorbing coating without considering series resistance, visible loss, heat generation, or interfacial chemistry.
Attributes improved UV lifetime to passivation without a matched optical-filter control.
Qualifies only unencapsulated small cells under UV and ignores MPP bias, temperature, humidity, and module nonuniformity.

expected_answer:
The short darkening assay is a useful perturbation test but not a unique ion-migration measurement. Optical darkening under lateral bias can reflect halide redistribution, electrochemical doping, local field screening, carrier injection, interfacial redox, or field-dependent luminescence. An interlayer can reduce the visible contrast simply by increasing interfacial resistance or redistributing the electric field, even if the bulk mobile-ion population and long-term chemical degradation are unchanged. Therefore, suppression of darkening may indicate a kinetic barrier at the measurement timescale rather than a lower defect concentration or higher migration barrier.

Pristine CsPbI3 nanocrystals can create exactly this false positive. They may physically impede short-range ion passage or alter the field, but their metastable lattice, ligands, surface traps, or energy-level mismatch can increase nonradiative recombination and series resistance. They can also transform, dissolve, or exchange ions under illumination and heat, becoming an additional ionic reservoir. These penalties can reduce Voc or fill factor and accelerate MPP aging even though the early optical proxy looks favorable. A fluoride-interlocked nanocomposite could outperform because its own lattice and interfaces are more chemically stable and provide stronger grain-boundary anchoring without the same electronic penalty, but that mechanism still requires direct evidence.

The diagnostic sequence should first resolve ionic transport directly. Frequency- and temperature-dependent impedance/electrical-modulus spectroscopy, bias-poling/depoling transients, and activation-energy analysis should isolate low-frequency ionic relaxation from electronic conduction. Post-bias TOF-SIMS, isotope tracing, X-ray fluorescence, or depth-resolved XPS should quantify actual I/Br accumulation and depletion. A true suppression mechanism should reduce spatial halide redistribution and history dependence over multiple temperatures and thicknesses, not only reduce optical contrast.

Second, electronic selectivity must be measured independently using QFLS/absolute PLQY, EL efficiency, SCLC or trap spectroscopy, transient extraction, and series-resistance analysis. Temporary blocking predicts less darkening but poorer extraction or lower QFLS. Third, the nanocrystal modifier itself should be tracked by operando XRD/PL and compositional mapping during heat-light-bias exposure to detect phase transformation, ligand loss, or ion exchange. Finally, compare untreated, pristine-nanocrystal, fluoride-interlocked, and an inert barrier control under identical MPP aging. Genuine long-term ion suppression requires concordant direct ion mapping, stable modifier structure, retained electronic transport, and slower device degradation; failure of any of these conditions invalidates the proxy-only conclusion.
scoring_key_points: Explains that bias-induced darkening conflates ion redistribution with field screening, injection, redox, and interfacial resistance, so reduced contrast can be a kinetic false positive.
Identifies plausible penalties of pristine CsPbI3 nanocrystals: metastable phase, traps/ligands, energy barriers, ion exchange, or an added ionic reservoir.
Requires direct ionic relaxation and post-bias compositional mapping rather than relying on the optical proxy alone.
Combines electronic-selectivity and operando modifier-stability measurements with matched MPP controls to define genuine long-term suppression.
accepted_equivalents: Electrochemical polarization, hysteresis relaxation, thermally stimulated current, or bias-stress transients may replace electrical-modulus spectroscopy.
TOF-SIMS, isotope labeling, operando XRF, scanning Kelvin probe after bias, or equivalent ion-distribution measurements are acceptable.
Modifier phase stability may be tracked by operando XRD, Raman, PL, electron microscopy after stress, or another suitable structural probe.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes that less optical darkening automatically proves a higher bulk ion-migration barrier.
Explains the worse MPP lifetime only as measurement noise and ignores electronic or modifier-instability penalties.
Measures only impedance or only PL without direct composition mapping and operational device controls.

expected_answer:
The transfer should preserve functions, not chemical identities or laboratory concentrations. The buried modifier must be compatible with the new coating solvent and hole-contact surface, produce uniform wetting over the moving meniscus, regulate nucleation across lateral and vertical drying gradients, reduce residual stress, and maintain hole extraction. Its adsorption density, solvent, coating speed, substrate temperature, and drying profile must therefore be re-optimized. The top modifier has a different task: it must passivate the specific defects and termination of the finished perovskite, establish favorable band alignment and surface dipole with the new electron-transport layer, and survive deposition of that layer without dissolution or chemical reaction. A treatment that is ideal for C60 can be energetically or chemically wrong for an oxide, polymer, or alternative fullerene.

A two-factor ablation design is essential: no modifier, bottom only, top only, and both, each across relevant concentration/process windows. This matrix separates additive effects and tests synergy rather than assuming it. Bottom-interface diagnostics should include contact-angle and wet-film imaging, in situ GIWAXS/PL during blade coating, film thickness and pinhole maps, grain orientation, residual-stress mapping, buried-interface trap density, and hole extraction. Top-interface diagnostics should include surface XPS/UPS, defect-selective spectroscopy, QFLS/EL, electron extraction, and chemical compatibility with the replacement ETL. An interaction term in device statistics or recombination analysis is needed to claim true synergy. If the dual treatment only equals the sum of independent gains, it is complementary but not necessarily synergistic.

Scale-up must explicitly address spatial uniformity. Coating speed, ink rheology, solvent evaporation, substrate temperature, gas quench, and edge effects should be mapped against thickness, PL/QFLS, sheet resistance, stress, and electroluminescence over the full area. The modifiers must not accumulate at meniscus start/stop regions or migrate between interfaces during drying and annealing. Cross-sectional TOF-SIMS or chemical mapping can verify location retention. Module interconnects and dead-area processing must be checked for chemical incompatibility.

Thermal stability cannot be inferred from dark nitrogen aging of small cells alone. Qualification should use encapsulated large-area cells or modules under maximum-power-point illumination at elevated temperature, thermal cycling, humidity/damp-heat exposure, and UV as appropriate to the intended application. Track Voc, fill factor, series resistance, current matching, spatial hot spots, ion-migration/hysteresis signatures, stress/crack evolution, and post-aging interfacial chemistry. Transfer is successful only if each interface retains its intended function, the combined process is statistically uniform and manufacturable, and the dual-modified large area degrades more slowly under coupled operating stress without creating new transport or coating defects.
scoring_key_points: Separately re-optimizes buried-interface wetting/nucleation/stress/hole extraction and top-interface defect chemistry/band alignment/ETL compatibility.
Uses a no/bottom/top/both factorial design with interface-specific diagnostics and an explicit test for additive versus synergistic effects.
Addresses blade-coating rheology, drying, lateral/vertical uniformity, modifier location, edge effects, and module-patterning compatibility.
Requires encapsulated large-area MPP light-heat-environment qualification with spatial, ionic, mechanical, electrical, and post-mortem interface metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, meniscus, gravure, or another scalable coating method may replace blade coating if the same hydrodynamic and drying controls are considered.
A full or fractional factorial DOE, response-surface design, or orthogonal ablation matrix is acceptable for separating bottom and top effects.
Damp heat, thermal cycling, UV-MPP, hot-light soaking, and outdoor testing may be combined into an equivalent application-relevant qualification plan.
common_wrong_answers: Copies the two laboratory modifier concentrations and assumes the new electron-transport layer has the same surface energetics as C60.
Tests only the dual-modified device and cannot assign gains to bottom, top, or their interaction.
Uses small-cell dark nitrogen storage as sufficient evidence for large-area operational and thermal reliability.

expected_answer: Reduced misorientation makes neighboring grains more crystallographically compatible, which can lower orientation-dependent strain discontinuities and the density or energetic severity of defective grain-boundary configurations. It also reduces spatial variation in band-edge energies and anisotropic transport directions, producing a more homogeneous quasi-Fermi-level landscape and fewer local recombination hot spots. Lower trap-mediated non-radiative recombination and less tortuous carrier transport then increase lifetime, reduce the trap-filled-limit voltage, and preserve a larger quasi-Fermi-level splitting, raising Voc. The ordering interpretation would be weakened or falsified if the apparent device gain persisted when orientation distributions were unchanged but surface chemistry alone was modified, or if the structural treatment increased grain size/removed boundary area while no through-thickness orientation narrowing was detected. Likewise, strong surface-only passivation signatures without bulk-depth structural order, or loss of the electronic advantage after removing a surface overlayer while the orientation remained, would argue against ordering as the dominant mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Links lower misorientation to reduced boundary strain/structural incompatibility and fewer electronically harmful boundary states.
Explains reduced spatial energetic and transport anisotropy, giving more uniform carrier transport and photoluminescence.
Connects lower trap-assisted recombination to longer lifetime, lower trap-filled-limit voltage, larger quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and higher Voc.
Provides two valid falsification tests that separate orientation from surface passivation and grain-size/boundary-area effects.
accepted_equivalents: Reduced mosaicity or texture spread for reduced misorientation
Smaller local band-edge fluctuations or potential disorder for improved energetic homogeneity
Higher quasi-Fermi-level splitting for reduced non-radiative voltage loss
Depth-resolved GIWAXS, rocking-curve, or pole-figure evidence as proof of bulk orientation
common_wrong_answers: Claims that a stronger XRD peak alone proves fewer defects without considering texture, illuminated volume, or grain size.
Attributes all improvements to larger grains even though the premise states similar grain-size distributions.
States that orientation directly increases the bandgap or photocurrent without an intermediate defect/transport mechanism.
Offers no falsifiable control capable of separating structural ordering from chemical passivation.

expected_answer: Wireless transmission is a pulsed load: the relevant constraint is instantaneous power and bus-voltage stability, not only hourly energy. During a radio burst, the photovoltaic source may be unable to supply the peak current, so the storage element must cover the energy and voltage droop while the converters remain inside their input and current limits. First log PV voltage/current, estimated Voc, and MPPT duty or operating voltage during spectral and irradiance changes; operation far from the true maximum-power point indicates MPPT mismatch. Next record capacitor voltage immediately before, during, and after a burst and measure ESR-dependent step droop: a slow excessive discharge indicates insufficient usable capacitance, whereas an abrupt voltage step indicates high ESR. Simultaneously monitor converter input/output voltages, inductor current or current-limit flags, and undervoltage-lockout events to identify dropout or current limiting. Finally power the electronics from a stable laboratory supply and independently interrogate raw sensor resistance and the microcontroller reset log; if apparent failures persist without bus collapse, the problem is sensor cross-sensitivity, calibration, or firmware rather than energy delivery.
scoring_key_points: Explains the distinction between average energy neutrality and instantaneous peak-power/bus-voltage requirements during radio bursts.
Uses PV-side voltage/current and Voc/MPPT logs under spectral change to diagnose maximum-power-point mismatch.
Separates insufficient capacitance from high ESR using the time shape of capacitor-voltage droop during a transmission pulse.
Checks converter limits and uses an external-supply plus raw-sensor/reset-log control to distinguish electrical failure from sensing artifacts.
accepted_equivalents: State-of-charge or energy-buffer headroom for usable capacitor energy
Undervoltage lockout or brownout for reset caused by bus collapse
Supercapacitor internal resistance for ESR
Oscilloscope or high-rate data acquisition traces for time-domain diagnosis
common_wrong_answers: Concludes that positive average harvested power guarantees uninterrupted operation.
Recommends only a larger photovoltaic area without locating the transient bottleneck.
Treats low-lux efficiency measured under one LED spectrum as a universal MPPT calibration.
Does not separate a real microcontroller brownout from sensor cross-talk or calibration drift.

expected_answer: The illumination matrix must span representative correlated color temperatures, spectra, intensities, temporal fluctuations, and incidence angles. Lux must be converted using measured spectral power distributions rather than a universal conversion, and PV current-voltage/MPP behavior must be recorded under each spectrum. System validation should use time-resolved energy accounting: harvested MPP energy, converter losses, storage leakage, sensing/computation energy, and radio-burst energy must be integrated over realistic schedules. The node should demonstrate repeatable energy-neutral cycles, defined state-of-charge margins, and quantified dark autonomy under the worst tested condition. Sensor outputs must be calibrated over the intended temperature/humidity range, tested for cross-sensitivity, drift, hysteresis, response/recovery, and compared with reference instruments while the power system is operating. Reliability should include repeated bending, adhesion/interconnect tests, thermal-humidity/light exposure, storage cycling, and wireless packet-success measurements. 'All-irradiance applicable' is defensible only within a clearly bounded tested envelope; it requires sustained autonomous operation and valid sensing across that envelope, not merely nonzero PV output or high cell efficiency under selected lamps.
scoring_key_points: Uses measured spectra for lux-to-irradiance conversion and maps PV/MPPT performance across realistic spectral and angular conditions.
Performs time-resolved full-system energy accounting and demonstrates energy-neutral cycles plus worst-case dark autonomy.
Validates sensor accuracy, cross-sensitivity, drift/hysteresis, and reference agreement while the complete node is operating.
Includes mechanical/environmental aging and limits the claim to a quantitatively defined irradiance-spectral operating envelope.
accepted_equivalents: Correlated color temperature or spectral power distribution for lamp spectrum
Packet-delivery ratio for wireless reliability
State-of-charge recurrence over a diurnal cycle for energy neutrality
Bending radius/cycle testing for flexible-module durability
common_wrong_answers: Uses lux alone as an optical power unit and ignores spectrum-dependent luminous efficacy.
Equates high photovoltaic PCE with a self-sustaining system without including converters, storage, and radio peaks.
Reports one successful transmission as proof of long-term autonomy.
Uses the phrase 'all irradiance' without specifying a tested lower bound, spectrum, duty cycle, or environmental envelope.

expected_answer: The passivation motifs should be retained but immobilized and used at near-monolayer coverage. Options include a less hygroscopic larger organic framework bearing the same Lewis-base/cationic functions, a zwitterionic or multidentate molecule with lower water activity, covalent or coordination anchoring to the surface, or a bilayer in which the ionic passivant contacts the perovskite and a thin hydrophobic, electronically compatible overlayer blocks water and ion motion. Halide activity must be sufficient to fill vacancies but not create a mobile salt reservoir or an insulating low-dimensional phase. Processing should control concentration, solvent orthogonality, exposure time, annealing, and residual free salt, with coverage quantified rather than inferred from solution concentration. Validation should compare unencapsulated and identically encapsulated treated/control devices under humidity, heat, illumination, and MPP bias; measure contact angle/water uptake, ion migration or bias-induced hysteresis, trap density/QFLS, interfacial energetics, and post-aging chemical redistribution. An intrinsic stability gain is supported when the interface remains chemically localized and electrically passivating, with reduced degradation under unencapsulated or deliberately permeable conditions and no added transport barrier.
scoring_key_points: Retains complementary defect-binding motifs while immobilizing them or shielding them with a hydrophobic, electronically compatible interface.
Limits coverage and free halide/salt to avoid hygroscopic reservoirs, mobile ions, and insulating secondary phases.
Controls solvent, concentration, exposure, annealing, and residual-species/coverage measurements during processing.
Uses matched encapsulation controls and humidity/heat/light/MPP tests with water uptake, ion migration, trap, energetic, and post-aging chemical diagnostics.
accepted_equivalents: Zwitterionic, polymer-bound, crosslinked, or chelating passivant for immobilization
Hydrophobic capping layer or self-assembled monolayer as the moisture barrier
Time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry for ion migration or redistribution
Transient ion-drift, bias-stress hysteresis, or impedance methods for mobile-ion risk
common_wrong_answers: Simply increases passivant concentration because initial PL or PCE improves.
Replaces the ionic passivant with a purely hydrophobic molecule that lacks defect-complementary binding sites.
Claims intrinsic stability from encapsulated shelf storage alone.
Ignores the possibility that a thick passivation layer blocks hole extraction or changes energy alignment.

expected_answer: Energy-alignment/conductivity effects should be tested by UPS or Kelvin-probe work functions and valence levels, hole-only mobility/conductivity, contact resistance, and transport-resistance measurements; the signature is a smaller extraction barrier, higher hole conductivity, and reduced series/transport resistance without necessarily changing interfacial chemistry. Redox and ion-migration suppression requires chemical-state and degradation probes, such as Ni oxidation-state changes, iodide/iodine-loss assays, depth-resolved ion profiles under bias/light, and hysteresis or ionic-transient measurements; the signature is less interfacial chemical conversion and slower ion redistribution. Barrier/morphology effects require AFM/SEM, pinhole and coverage mapping, permeability/contact tests, and thickness-matched inert-polymer controls; the signature is reduced direct perovskite-metal contact and improved uniformity even when energetics are held similar. Composition-series and matched controls—nanoparticle only, polymer only, physical mixture with disrupted ordering, and a morphology-matched but electronically inert polymer—are needed to quantify contributions. PL quenching alone is ambiguous because it can indicate beneficial charge extraction, non-radiative interfacial recombination, optical changes, or differing coverage; TRPL, QFLS, devices, and selective-contact controls are required.
scoring_key_points: Assigns UPS/Kelvin probe, mobility/conductivity, contact resistance, and EIS transport signatures to energy-alignment/electronic improvement.
Assigns chemical-state, iodine-loss, ion-depth-profile, and bias/light transient measurements to redox and ion-migration suppression.
Assigns coverage/pinhole/permeability measurements plus morphology-matched inert controls to the physical-barrier mechanism.
Explains PL-quenching ambiguity and uses composition/matched controls with TRPL/QFLS/device data to separate extraction from recombination.
accepted_equivalents: Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy or surface-potential methods for energy levels
Space-charge-limited current or field-effect mobility for hole transport
ToF-SIMS or operando XPS for ion migration/redox tracking
Conductive AFM or electroluminescence mapping for pinhole/contact uniformity
common_wrong_answers: Interprets stronger PL quenching as proof of lower non-radiative recombination without selective-contact controls.
Attributes higher fill factor only to morphology and ignores energy alignment or conductivity.
Uses no polymer-only, nanoparticle-only, or morphology-matched control.
Infers ion-blocking from shelf stability without bias/light or chemical redistribution measurements.

expected_answer: The replacement polymer must be processable from a solvent that neither dissolves nor chemically attacks the perovskite and must disperse or organize NiOx without aggregation. Its backbone/side chains should promote compact, uniform coverage and preferably mutual ordering with the nanoparticles, while avoiding insulating ligand shells. The HOMO/work function and hole mobility must match the perovskite and electrode, with low contact and sheet resistance at module-relevant thickness. The polymer should not reduce or oxidize the perovskite/NiOx detrimentally, should suppress iodide/metal interdiffusion, and should remain morphologically stable under heat, light, humidity, and repeated bending. Screening should combine structural, energetic, mobility, redox, permeability, and thermal-mechanical metrics before device tests. Module validation must include coating/scribing uniformity, sheet/contact resistance and dead-area losses, spatial PL/EL and thermal maps, MPP tracking under heat/humidity/light, dark 85/85 testing, bending, and post-aging ion/chemical depth profiles. The highest small-cell PCE can fail at module scale if it relies on a narrow thickness window, has high sheet resistance, poor coating uniformity, scribe contamination, polymer creep, pinholes, or weak ion blocking; these losses compound across series-connected subcells and accelerate local hot spots, so T80 can be poor despite an excellent champion pixel.
scoring_key_points: Defines solvent/perovskite compatibility and nanoparticle-polymer dispersion, compactness, and mutual-ordering requirements.
Includes energy-level alignment, mobility, sheet/contact resistance, and avoidance of insulating interfaces at module-relevant thickness.
Includes redox inertness, ion/metal blocking, thermal-humidity-light stability, and mechanical durability in the material rubric.
Uses module-specific uniformity/scribing/resistance mapping and accelerated MPP/85-85/bending tests, explaining how local nonuniformities and series connection decouple champion PCE from T80.
accepted_equivalents: HOMO alignment for valence-band/work-function matching
Slot-die, blade, or spray coating provided module uniformity is evaluated
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, or photoluminescence mapping for local module defects
Metal-diffusion barrier or iodide-blocking layer for interfacial chemical stability
common_wrong_answers: Selects the polymer only by HOMO energy or small-cell champion efficiency.
Assumes thicker polymer always improves ion blocking without considering series resistance or incomplete extraction.
Evaluates only encapsulated shelf storage and omits MPP, heat/humidity, and post-aging ion analysis.
Ignores coating and laser-scribe nonuniformity that accumulates across series-connected subcells.

expected_answer: Use at least a 2 x 2 device matrix containing aligned versus non-aligned PEDOT:PSS and polyurethane versus no polyurethane, with identical layer thicknesses and initial electrical quality. Apply strain parallel to the alignment direction, perpendicular to it, and preferably biaxially; include an unstrained sample receiving the same thermal treatment to separate healing from ordinary thermal annealing. Absorber recovery should be assessed by registered crack maps, absolute photoluminescence quantum yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, spatial lifetime or electroluminescence, and trap/recombination diagnostics. Restoration of the collection network should be assessed independently by direction-resolved sheet resistance, four-point resistance maps, current mapping, series resistance, impedance, contact adhesion, and cross-sectional inspection for delamination. If polyurethane-containing samples recover crack morphology and quasi-Fermi-level splitting regardless of electrode type, but power recovery tracks residual resistance anisotropy, contact loss, or electrode cracking, the dominant irreversibility lies in current collection or interfaces rather than the absorber. Conversely, recovered resistance with persistently depressed quasi-Fermi-level splitting or voltage would identify unrepaired absorber defects. Morphological crack closure alone is not proof of complete electronic recovery.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial comparison that independently varies electrode alignment and polyurethane incorporation, with a thermal-only control.
Separates absorber recovery metrics from electrode, contact, and series-resistance metrics rather than treating crack closure as sufficient.
Includes strain direction or biaxial loading to test whether an aligned network creates anisotropic damage and recovery.
States diagnostic result patterns that distinguish current-collection irreversibility from persistent absorber recombination loss.
accepted_equivalents: Absolute PLQY, calibrated luminescence-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting, or spatially resolved electroluminescence are acceptable absorber electronic-recovery probes.
Conductive AFM, lock-in thermography, light-beam-induced current, or four-probe mapping may substitute for current-collection mapping.
Interfacial delamination, metal-contact cracking, and loss of PEDOT:PSS percolation are acceptable forms of current-collection irreversibility.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that visible crack closure proves complete device self-healing.
Measuring only total PCE before and after heating without independently resolving absorber and electrode losses.
Ignoring loading direction even though the conductive network is intentionally aligned.

expected_answer: The coating window should be defined jointly by ink rheology, wet-film thickness, scraper or slit geometry, web speed, drying rate, and substrate temperature because chain extension requires sufficient shear or extensional flow but excessive alignment can produce high transverse resistance and preferential cracking. Multidirectional robustness can be obtained through cross-hatched sequential alignment, patterned or segmented conductive meshes, locally rotated coating directions, or a controlled balance between aligned load-bearing paths and isotropic percolation. The process should be monitored with full-width thickness and optical-uniformity maps, direction-resolved sheet resistance, resistance anisotropy, transmittance, and a structural alignment surrogate such as polarized spectroscopy or sampled GIWAXS. Polyurethane loading must be optimized at the lowest level that improves defect tolerance and crack recovery, because excess insulating polymer can impede crystallization, carrier transport, or contact formation. Qualification should include uniaxial, transverse, and biaxial cyclic strain; simultaneous maximum-power operation under strain; thermal-healing cycling; damp-heat or controlled humidity; thermal cycling; and full-area current or electroluminescence mapping. A valid process window gives stable electrical uniformity and low local hot-spot formation across web positions and strain directions, not merely a high champion efficiency from one coating lane.
scoring_key_points: Links alignment to a controlled rheology, geometry, coating-speed, and drying window rather than assuming that faster coating is always better.
Introduces a cross-directional or network architecture that prevents excessive resistance and crack sensitivity perpendicular to the main alignment.
Uses in-line spatial and anisotropic electrical metrics, together with structural or optical alignment indicators, to control scale-up uniformity.
Optimizes self-healing additive loading against insulating and crystallization penalties and validates under multidirectional strain plus environmental and operational stress.
accepted_equivalents: Orthogonal double coating, woven or serpentine grids, rotated domains, and hybrid aligned-isotropic networks are acceptable multidirectional designs.
Polarized Raman, polarized absorption, birefringence, or offline GIWAXS sampling may serve as alignment metrics.
Slot-die, blade, gravure, or continuous meniscus coating are acceptable roll-to-roll implementations if the flow and drying controls are explicit.
common_wrong_answers: Maximizing chain alignment without checking transverse resistance or biaxial fatigue.
Scaling only geometric dimensions while keeping coating speed, drying, and rheology unexamined.
Increasing polyurethane concentration indefinitely because it is described as self-healing.
