expected_answer: Use modifiers chosen to decouple fluorination, hydrophobicity, passivation strength, chain length, and grafting density: for example, a fluorinated short-chain silane, a nonfluorinated analogue with similar binding chemistry, a highly hydrophobic long-chain analogue, and an untreated control. Match coverage and initial stabilized power as closely as possible. Age replicated devices under dry inert maximum-power operation, humid dark storage, humid maximum-power operation, elevated temperature in the dark, and electrical bias; include both well-encapsulated and moisture-permeable packages. Measure water sorption or permeation in addition to static contact angle. Track quasi-Fermi-level splitting, transient extraction, impedance and recombination, while depth-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS follows halide displacement, modifier integrity, and Ag or other electrode migration. A moisture-barrier mechanism produces its largest advantage in humid or permeable-package tests and correlates with lower water uptake, but gives little extra benefit in dry inert operation. Migration or reaction suppression produces slower ionic redistribution, core-level change, electrode diffusion, and bias-induced hysteresis even in dry illuminated or biased tests. Improved energetics appears immediately as better extraction or reduced interfacial voltage loss before aging; it explains lifetime only if those parameters deteriorate more slowly rather than merely starting at a better value. More than one contribution may coexist, but the matrix should quantify them separately.
scoring_key_points: Uses chemically matched controls that separate fluorination and passivation from hydrophobicity, chain length, and coverage.
Includes dry versus humid, dark versus illuminated MPP, thermal, bias, and encapsulation-permeability conditions.
Measures water uptake, ionic or metal migration, interfacial chemistry, and electronic extraction over time rather than relying on contact angle or endpoint PCE.
Defines distinct outcome signatures for moisture exclusion, migration/reaction suppression, and a purely initial energetic advantage.
accepted_equivalents: Water-vapor transmission, quartz-crystal microbalance sorption, infrared water uptake, or isotopically labeled moisture tracing are acceptable barrier probes.
Bias-dependent luminescence, impedance, transient ion-drift, or spatial Kelvin-probe measurements may substitute for direct ion-migration imaging.
Copper or gold diffusion may replace silver migration if that is the electrode used in the test stack.
common_wrong_answers: Equating the highest static water contact angle with the longest operational lifetime.
Testing only damp storage and then assigning a mechanism for illuminated maximum-power operation.
Comparing lifetime curves without matching coverage or accounting for different initial device quality.

expected_answer: The detected signal is not a pure voltage observable: it depends exponentially on quasi-Fermi-level splitting but also on the local absorptivity within the passband, the optical collection factor, filter transmission, exposure calibration, and sample temperature. Thickness can move the detected band away from the near-unity-absorptivity regime, while surface tilt changes the angle of incidence and can blue-shift an interference filter or change collection efficiency. First co-register thickness, topography, reflectance or absorptance, and temperature maps with the implied-voltage image. Repeat the measurement with a second nearby high-energy-tail filter, controlled sample tilt or telecentric collection, and the same calibrated source geometry; correct each filter for angle and spectral response. At representative stripe and non-stripe locations, acquire absolute or calibrated spectral PL and derive quasi-Fermi-level splitting independently, preferably supported by PLQY, lifetime, electroluminescence, or local current mapping. A genuine recombination defect should retain a lower derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting across filters and geometry corrections and should co-localize with reduced radiative efficiency or stronger recombination. An optical artifact will scale with thickness, tilt, filter choice, or temperature and shrink or reverse after the appropriate correction without an independent electronic-loss signature.
scoring_key_points: States that filtered PL intensity depends on absorptivity, optical collection, filter transmission, and temperature in addition to quasi-Fermi-level splitting.
Explains how thickness and surface angle can violate the constant-absorptivity and fixed-filter-response assumptions.
Uses co-registered optical, geometric, and thermal maps plus a second filter or independent spectral calibration to test the stripes.
Defines a persistence-and-correlation criterion that separates real recombination loss from a removable imaging artifact.
accepted_equivalents: Hyperspectral PL, absolute PLQY imaging, or calibrated high-energy-tail fitting are acceptable independent quasi-Fermi-level-splitting references.
Telecentric optics, angle-resolved calibration, or flattening the sample may be used to control filter-angle artifacts.
Lock-in thermography, infrared thermometry, or embedded temperature sensors are acceptable temperature corrections.
common_wrong_answers: Interpreting every dark filtered-PL feature as a defect without checking thickness or viewing geometry.
Correcting only exposure time while ignoring filter angle and absorptivity.
Using terminal open-circuit voltage as the sole local validation of a spatial map.

expected_answer: Front/back spectral asymmetry is non-unique because high-energy emission can be reabsorbed by lower-bandgap phases, the two collection geometries sample different optical depths, cavity interference changes out-coupling, and rapid energy transfer can make emission originate from a minority low-bandgap phase far from where carriers were generated. Different surface recombination velocities can further change the apparent spectrum without a composition gradient. Vary excitation wavelength and penetration depth, collect time-resolved spectra from both sides, and repeat on a thickness series or after optical-transfer-matrix correction. A true gradient should also be demonstrated by a depth-sensitive structural or chemical method such as cross-sectional nano-GIWAXS/XRD, cathodoluminescence, STEM/EDS, nano-absorption, or controlled depth profiling. Directional carrier-transfer measurements should agree with the proposed energy funnel and contact polarity. The strongest conclusion requires consistent depth-resolved phase signatures plus front/back optical data that remain after reabsorption, interference, and surface-recombination corrections; front/back PL alone supports only a hypothesis.
scoring_key_points: Identifies reabsorption, escape-depth or interference effects, energy transfer, and surface recombination as non-compositional causes of front/back PL asymmetry.
Uses variable excitation depth, time resolution, thickness variation, or optical modeling to test the optical confounders.
Requires an independent depth-sensitive structural or chemical measurement of n-phase distribution.
Demands consistency between the measured depth profile, carrier-transfer direction, and device-contact architecture before claiming an energy gradient.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional cathodoluminescence, nano-PL, synchrotron depth-resolved GIWAXS, STEM spectroscopy, or secondary-ion profiling are acceptable depth probes.
Transfer-matrix modeling, integrating-sphere collection, or index-matched collection may be used to correct optical out-coupling.
Transient absorption or time-resolved microwave conductivity may replace time-resolved PL for directional transfer analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Treating different front and back PL peaks as direct proof of a vertical phase gradient.
Using only steady-state absorption to infer depth distribution.
Ignoring energy transfer, which can decouple the emission spectrum from the location of carrier generation.

expected_answer: Large-area transfer changes the balance among complexation, nucleation, solvent removal, and solute transport, so the laboratory temperature alone cannot define the process. Use a design of experiments over coordinating-solvent or additive strength, wet-film thickness, blade speed, substrate temperature, gas-knife or drying rate, ambient humidity, and post-annealing profile. These variables control precursor-adduct lifetime, nucleation density, evaporation-driven concentration gradients, and spacer-cation or colloid redistribution; excessive Peclet or Marangoni transport can reverse or laterally pattern the n-phase profile. Select the desired profile for the actual n-i-p or p-i-n stack so that wide-bandgap low-n regions do not form a blocking layer at the wrong extracting contact and the lower-bandgap high-n network remains electrically connected. Monitor full-width wet thickness and drying, then map front/back absorption or PL, spatial PLQY, GIWAXS orientation, and representative cross-sectional phase profiles. Acceptance criteria should include low lateral variance in the intended depth profile, low trap-assisted recombination, balanced carrier extraction, and absence of isolated low-n barriers. Finally, qualify modules under maximum-power illumination, thermal cycling, humidity, and bias while tracking phase redistribution, ion migration, and edge-to-center performance. A stable process window is one whose phase profile and device output remain robust to realistic variations in web speed, temperature, and ambient conditions.
scoring_key_points: Treats coordination, nucleation, evaporation, and spacer transport as coupled scale-dependent variables and proposes a multivariable process window.
Explains that the acceptable gradient is device-polarity-specific and must avoid a wide-bandgap transport barrier at the wrong contact.
Uses spatial and depth-sensitive metrology across the coated area rather than relying on a single front/back spectrum or champion device.
Includes maximum-power, thermal, humidity, and bias qualification with monitoring for phase redistribution and ionic instability.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, meniscus, or spray coating may replace blade coating if wet-film and drying-front controls are specified.
In situ reflectometry, optical coherence, hyperspectral imaging, or drying-front thermography are acceptable in-line process monitors.
A deliberately phase-pure high-n target is acceptable instead of a gradient if the answer explains how the process and acceptance criteria change.
common_wrong_answers: Copying the hot-casting temperature to large-area coating without controlling solvent removal and lateral transport.
Optimizing only the average n value while ignoring depth direction and device polarity.
Using initial efficiency as the sole acceptance criterion without checking phase stability under light, heat, humidity, or bias.

expected_answer: The two lifetime trends refer to different systems. In isolated nanowires, a wide-bandgap secondary phase can passivate surface traps in the emissive nanowire phase, increasing PLQY and lifetime. In the heterostructure, faster decay of absorber PL can instead reflect interfacial charge transfer into the nanowire and then the hole-transport contact; it is not evidence that the nanowires themselves became more defective. However, heterostructure PL quenching is ambiguous because an interfacial recombination center gives the same qualitative decay. Use selective excitation and transient absorption or time-resolved photoinduced absorption to detect the expected charge-separated populations, together with absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, surface photovoltage, transient photocurrent, and device voltage. Vary nanowire coverage and include no-nanowire, single-phase-nanowire, dual-phase-nanowire, and ideally wide-bandgap-phase-only controls. Productive extraction should accelerate absorber quenching while maintaining or increasing quasi-Fermi-level splitting and open-circuit voltage, produce a measurable transferred-hole or long-lived charge-separated signal, and reduce recombination or contact resistance in devices. Parasitic quenching should lower absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting, fail to create a useful charge-separated population, and worsen voltage despite a shorter lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Separates the intrinsic nanowire lifetime from the absorber-to-interlayer transfer lifetime in the heterostructure.
Explains that higher nanowire PLQY and lifetime are consistent with passivation by a wider-bandgap secondary phase.
States that faster absorber PL decay is ambiguous between productive extraction and non-radiative interfacial quenching.
Proposes selective-excitation charge-transfer measurements plus absolute radiative or voltage metrics and defines opposite result patterns.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, terahertz conductivity, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or photoinduced absorption are acceptable charge-transfer probes.
Calibrated PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting, surface photovoltage, or contact-selective transient photocurrent may serve as extraction-quality metrics.
A type-I passivating shell, embedded secondary phase, or trap-inert wide-bandgap domains are acceptable descriptions of the secondary-phase role.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the longer isolated-nanowire lifetime and faster absorber decay mutually inconsistent.
Treating any PL quenching as proof of efficient charge extraction.
Comparing only dual-phase nanowires with a no-nanowire control and omitting single-phase or phase-only controls.

expected_answer: Use orthogonal depth, thickness, substrate, and exposure controls. First, measure a thickness series and compare Au with an electronically and chemically less reactive substrate using angle-resolved or variable-photon-energy XPS. An interfacial Sn0 species should be strongest for the thinnest Au-supported films, attenuate as the film thickens, and change substantially or disappear on the inert substrate; a bulk Sn0 population would not show that interfacial scaling. Second, establish the pristine baseline without breaking vacuum, then dose dry O2, water vapor, and O2 plus water separately while following XPS together with STM/LEED or another surface-structure probe. Surface-initiated oxidation should first alter the outermost chemical states and defect-rich regions, followed by increasing Sn4+ and loss of diffraction order with dose. A genuinely pre-existing bulk oxide would already be detected before exposure and would be less sensitive to surface termination or gas sequence. Third, compare different terminations or controlled vacancy densities: faster oxidation for a particular termination or defect population would support surface-controlled initiation. The absence of a fitted Sn4+ peak is only an upper bound set by XPS sensitivity, sampling depth, and fitting choices, and results from an ultrathin Au-supported model cannot by themselves establish the chemistry of a thick device absorber.
scoring_key_points: Uses film-thickness, substrate, and depth-sensitive XPS controls to test whether Sn0 scales as an interfacial Au-related species.
Uses sequential dry-O2, H2O, and combined exposure with time-resolved chemical and structural probes to test surface-initiated oxidation.
Relates oxidation kinetics to surface termination or controlled defect density rather than treating all observed defects as bulk defect concentrations.
States that non-detection of Sn4+ is sensitivity/fitting limited and that an ultrathin Au model does not prove bulk-device behavior.
accepted_equivalents: Hard-X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or standing-wave XPS may replace variable-angle or variable-energy XPS for depth localization.
An inert conductive substrate, diffusion barrier, or ultrathin decoupling layer may be used instead of changing the metal substrate directly.
Surface-sensitive diffraction or spectroscopy may replace LEED/STM if it resolves the order and chemical-state sequence.
common_wrong_answers: Claims that the absence of Sn4+ proves complete oxidation-free bulk material.
Attributes Sn0 to the perovskite bulk without testing thickness or substrate dependence.
Converts local STM defect counts into a bulk defect density or a device-wide degradation rate.

expected_answer: Prepare nominally identical thick absorbers and devices that are split into at least four handling groups: encapsulated in situ or through a vacuum-connected transfer, encapsulated after controlled inert-atmosphere delay, deliberately pre-exposed before encapsulation, and unencapsulated. Include an inert or device-relevant bottom contact so that Au-specific interfacial chemistry is not mistaken for a general absorber property. Stress matched samples under dry O2, humid inert gas, combined O2/H2O, and operational illumination plus electrical bias, with dark controls. Follow both near-surface and bulk degradation using depth-resolved Sn2+/Sn4+ chemistry, structural probes, spatial composition, carrier density or self-p-doping, dark current/noise, responsivity, and operational drift. The in-vacuum cap is justified only if it reproducibly suppresses oxidation and performance drift relative to delayed or pre-exposed controls, not merely if an initial XPS spectrum looks cleaner. Scale-up acceptance must include barrier permeability and edge-seal limits, pinhole and large-area uniformity mapping, process compatibility, and a defined maximum allowable increase in Sn4+, dark current/noise, and loss of structural or device performance during a specified stress protocol.
scoring_key_points: Includes in-vacuum, inert-delayed, pre-exposed-then-capped, and uncapped controls on thick, device-relevant films or devices.
Separates dry oxygen, moisture, combined atmosphere, and light/bias stress with appropriate dark and substrate controls.
Combines surface/bulk chemical and structural measurements with device metrics such as self-doping, dark current/noise, and responsivity drift.
Defines quantitative scale-up criteria for barrier permeability, edges/pinholes, uniformity, and allowable chemical/device degradation.
accepted_equivalents: A glovebox-integrated encapsulation line with verified sub-ppm exposure may substitute for a fully vacuum-connected cap if exposure is measured and controlled.
Optical or electrical oxidation proxies are acceptable only when calibrated against direct Sn chemical-state measurements.
Water-vapor transmission rate and oxygen-transmission rate may be replaced by an equivalent validated barrier-leak specification.
common_wrong_answers: Simply recommends encapsulation without a delayed-capping or pre-exposure control.
Uses only film XRD or only initial device efficiency and therefore misses chemical oxidation and dark-current drift.
Assumes an ultrathin Au-supported result transfers quantitatively to a thick absorber on a device contact.

expected_answer: Without a separator, the full coupled response should occur: PbI2-rich regions trap holes, iodine accumulates, the perovskite develops red-shifted I-rich emission and structural loss, and organic cation/halide transfer creates new perovskite-like material in the PbI2 compartment. With separator H, the initiating hole flux into PbI2 is removed; therefore light-induced iodine generation and the subsequent red-shift/XRD degradation should be strongly suppressed even though mass transfer is geometrically possible. Adding exogenous iodine should bypass the blocked electronic step and restore the chemical attack, which is a key causal control. With separator M, hole trapping and iodine generation can still occur on the PbI2 side, but the iodine mediator and ionic species cannot reach the perovskite, so iodine may be detected in the PbI2 compartment while perovskite red-shift, cation exchange, and reciprocal XRD loss are strongly reduced. The experiment should include dark thermal aging, isolated-phase photoaging, exogenous-I2 exposure, and matched optical absorption. Spatial PEEM or another hole-trap map, compartment-specific iodine capture, time-resolved PL/XRD, and preferably isotope or tracer analysis should establish the order: hole trapping precedes iodine formation, which precedes compositional and structural degradation.
scoring_key_points: Predicts that blocking hole transfer suppresses light-driven iodine generation and coupled degradation despite allowing mass transfer.
Predicts that permitting holes but blocking mass transfer allows local iodine generation while protecting the adjacent perovskite from the reciprocal chemical loop.
Uses exogenous iodine to bypass the electronic initiation step and includes dark, isolated-phase, and matched-absorption controls.
Requires time-ordered trap, iodine, PL/XRD, and preferably tracer evidence rather than spatial correlation alone.
accepted_equivalents: Carrier-selective contacts in a microfluidic or split-chamber geometry may replace the idealized separators.
Electron-spin, transient absorption, or photocurrent mapping may substitute for PEEM if it localizes the relevant trapped-hole population.
Raman, mass spectrometry, or chemical trapping may replace optical iodine detection.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes PbI2 is harmful solely because it has trap states, without testing iodine-mediated chemistry.
Treats a PL red shift alone as proof of ion transfer and decomposition.
Omits exogenous iodine and dark controls, so electronic initiation cannot be separated from direct chemical attack.

expected_answer: The target is not necessarily mathematically zero PbI2, but the elimination or chemical isolation of electronically coupled, interface-accessible PbI2 inclusions at grain boundaries and transport pathways. Small isolated residues that do not collect holes may be less dangerous than a connected or interfacial population of the same total volume. Process development should therefore vary conversion chemistry and post-treatments while measuring total PbI2 by XRD together with spatially resolved phase/composition maps, grain-boundary PbI2, trap or surface-potential maps, light-induced iodine release, and I-rich PL growth. Candidate films must be tested under illuminated electrical operation or maximum-power-point conditions with dark thermal controls, because dark heat aging does not reproduce a carrier-triggered loop. Track voltage, efficiency retention, spectral segregation, iodine evolution, and the reappearance or growth of PbI2 as both cause and degradation product. Select the process window by a multi-objective criterion: retain the initial voltage/efficiency benefit only if the spatially hazardous PbI2 population and iodine-generation rate remain below a threshold that delivers the required operational lifetime with lot-to-lot and large-area uniformity. Conversion, selective passivation, or a carrier-blocking coating around residual inclusions is preferable to accepting a high total residue for a small initial-performance gain.
scoring_key_points: Controls the connected, grain-boundary, or electronically coupled PbI2 population rather than relying only on total PbI2 amount.
Combines XRD with spatial phase/composition, trap, and light-induced iodine or I-rich-PL diagnostics.
Uses illuminated operating or MPP aging with dark thermal controls and monitors both performance and chemical feedback products.
Defines a multi-objective process window based on initial efficiency, operational lifetime, large-area uniformity, and a threshold for hazardous PbI2/iodine activity.
accepted_equivalents: A selective conversion treatment, chemical sequestration, or carrier-blocking passivation of PbI2 is acceptable if it interrupts electronic coupling or iodine transfer.
Nano-XRF, cathodoluminescence, Raman, PEEM, or correlated microscopy may be used for spatial PbI2 and trap mapping.
A statistically defined iodine-evolution or phase-segregation threshold may substitute for a direct spatial acceptance threshold.
common_wrong_answers: Requires zero PbI2 solely from one XRD scan without considering detection limits or spatial distribution.
Optimizes only initial PCE and assumes any passivating effect guarantees long-term stability.
Uses dark 85 C aging as the only reliability test for a light-triggered carrier-trapping mechanism.

expected_answer: Use a 2 x 2 design with PEA/no-Ge, PEA/Ge, EDA/no-Ge, and EDA/Ge absorbers, fabricated with the same precursor concentration, film thickness, annealing, contacts, active area, and measurement bandwidth. The cation main effect should be assigned from PEA-to-EDA comparisons at fixed Ge content using low-angle and wide-angle XRD or GIWAXS, orientation and phase mapping, grain morphology, shunt-path statistics, and parallel resistance. The Ge main effect should be assigned at fixed cation using Ge-I/Ge-O and Sn4+/Sn2+ XPS, halide binding shifts, SCLC trap density, UPS band alignment, admittance or bias-polarization ion-migration signatures, and air-aging chemistry. Device attribution requires full dark-current noise spectra, operating-noise detectivity, frequency response, transient extraction, and impedance rather than only one reverse-bias current. Synergy is demonstrated by a statistically significant interaction term: the EDA/Ge group outperforms the sum of the independent EDA and Ge effects, accompanied by a coupled mechanism such as a 3D transport geometry that enables Ge passivation to reduce leakage without creating a transport barrier. If the interaction is absent, the result should be described as additive or dominated by one factor, not synergistic.
scoring_key_points: Specifies the complete PEA/no-Ge, PEA/Ge, EDA/no-Ge, and EDA/Ge factorial set with matched processing and device geometry.
Uses phase/dimensionality, orientation, morphology, shunt, and resistance measurements to isolate the organic-cation effect.
Uses Ge chemical-state, oxidation, trap, energy-level, and ion-migration diagnostics to isolate the Ge effect.
Requires noise-resolved device data and a statistical interaction term to claim synergy rather than comparing two confounded endpoints.
accepted_equivalents: A response-surface design with independently varied EDA/PEA ratio and Ge concentration is acceptable if it contains the four factorial corners.
GIWAXS, solid-state NMR, or another validated dimensionality probe may replace conventional XRD.
Mixed-effects or ANOVA analysis may be replaced by an equivalent quantitative interaction analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only the original control and target and assigns every difference to both EDA and Ge.
Uses shorter TRPL lifetime alone as proof of fewer traps or better material quality.
Claims higher shot-noise-limited detectivity without measuring the actual operating noise spectrum.

expected_answer: Build a designed experiment over oxide cycle number or thickness and molecular concentration/coverage, including untreated, bottom-only, top-only, and dual-treated devices. The bottom oxide must be thick and uniform enough to provide fixed charge, dipole, and chemical passivation but thin enough to preserve tunneling or carrier transfer; current-voltage nonlinearity, contact resistance, capacitance, and response time should identify the insulating threshold. The molecular layer must remain fully dissolved and form a continuous sub-monolayer or thin interphase without precipitation, aggregation, or an extraction barrier; verify coverage and chemistry together with work-function direction. Large-area qualification requires maps of thickness, pinholes, surface potential, phase distribution, and contact resistance, plus dark-current density and noise spectra, LDR, responsivity, speed, pixel yield, and cross-wafer variation. The electrostatic polarity must still repel the local minority carrier at each interface after changing substrate, transport layer, or curing process. Finally, apply combined humidity, heat, UV/light, and electrical-bias stresses with edge-seal and encapsulation controls, monitoring PbI2 formation, interface chemistry, field/work-function drift, dark-current noise, and photocurrent retention. The process window is accepted only where performance gain, yield, and stability overlap; an optimum found on one small pixel is not transferable if thickness nonuniformity, molecular precipitation, or field inversion appears at scale.
scoring_key_points: Uses a thickness/concentration DOE with untreated, single-sided, and dual-sided controls to locate both passivation benefit and transport penalties.
Defines oxide tunneling/contact-resistance limits and molecular solubility, coverage, precipitation, and extraction-barrier limits.
Maps large-area uniformity of interlayer thickness, pinholes, surface potential, contact properties, noise, speed, and pixel yield while verifying field polarity.
Qualifies the overlap window under combined humidity, heat, light/UV, and bias stress using chemical, electrostatic, and device-retention criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Sheet-to-sheet or roll-to-roll statistical process control may replace wafer mapping if it measures the same uniformity variables.
Noise-equivalent power or specific detectivity based on measured noise may substitute for separate noise and responsivity reporting.
Accelerated stress may use another validated combined-stressor protocol if it includes environmental exposure and operating bias/light.
common_wrong_answers: Maximizes oxide thickness because more passivation is assumed always better, ignoring tunneling and contact resistance.
Increases molecular concentration beyond solubility and treats a cloudy or aggregated film as greater coverage.
Reports only average dark current from a few pixels and ignores work-function polarity, pinholes, edge leakage, yield, and combined-stress drift.

expected_answer:
The causal variable must be the water activity at the substrate/precursor interface, and it must be perturbed at defined process stages rather than inferred from final spectra. A suitable experiment starts with the same substrate chemistry prepared in several water states: rigorously dried, equilibrated at controlled humidity, and deliberately rehydrated to a measured surface-water loading. Chamber humidity, precursor age, temperature, film thickness and antisolvent timing must be held constant. Surface-water loading should be verified independently, for example by gravimetry/TGA on representative films, quartz-crystal microbalance, infrared/OH spectroscopy, or a calibrated desorption measurement. A chemical-surface control with similar wettability but different water uptake is also needed so that water reservoir and permanent surface chemistry are not conflated.

The process is then divided into perturbation windows. For a nucleation test, the substrate water state is changed before coating while all later steps are identical. For an antisolvent-selection test, the starting substrate is kept dry but a calibrated H2O or D2O pulse is introduced immediately before or with the antisolvent; conversely, a hygroscopic substrate can be rapidly dried or covered by a thin water-blocking interlayer before coating. For a post-crystallization test, films formed under identical dry conditions are exposed to the same water dose only after the small-n/large-n distribution has been established. Isotopically labeled water is especially useful because depth-sensitive vibrational spectroscopy or secondary-ion profiling can confirm that the imposed water reached the buried interface rather than only the free surface.

In-situ PL or absorption should track the appearance and transfer of excitonic states throughout spin coating, antisolvent treatment and annealing; time-resolved GIWAXS/XRD should track nucleation, orientation and phase conversion; synchronized mass or solvent-loss data help separate water effects from drying-rate effects. If water acts mainly during nucleation, changing only the pre-coating substrate water state should alter the earliest excitonic/structural signatures and determine the final phase distribution, whereas post-nucleation water pulses should have little effect. If it acts mainly during antisolvent selection, trajectories should remain similar before the pulse and diverge immediately after antisolvent addition, with the divergence scaling with the interfacial water dose. If it acts mainly after crystallization, initially identical films should red-shift or develop larger-n structural signatures only during annealing or subsequent exposure, and the effect should be reversible or suppressible by a buried water barrier.

The strongest assignment requires a dose-response and a rescue experiment: drying a hygroscopic underlayer or blocking its water release should recover the dry-substrate trajectory, while rehydrating a low-water substrate should reproduce the large-n trajectory. Final PL alone is insufficient because different kinetic histories can converge to similar spectra.
scoring_key_points: Perturbs measured interfacial water independently at pre-coating, antisolvent and post-crystallization stages while controlling substrate chemistry and drying conditions.
Uses synchronized in-situ optical and structural probes to identify when phase trajectories first diverge, with an independent measure or tracer of buried water.
States distinct causal signatures for nucleation control, antisolvent-driven phase selection and post-crystallization redistribution.
Includes dose-response plus rescue/reversal controls and rejects a conclusion based only on endpoint PL or chamber RH.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent humidity-pulse, microfluidic dosing or isotopically labeled D2O protocols that localize water in time and depth.
In-situ absorption, PL, transient absorption, GIWAXS, ellipsometry or Raman measurements that resolve small-n and large-n evolution.
A factorial design crossing substrate water loading with ambient RH and antisolvent timing.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only glass, NiOx and PEDOT:PSS at one humidity, so chemistry, wettability and water uptake change together.
Using final emission wavelength as proof that water acted during nucleation.
Changing chamber RH without measuring the substrate water reservoir or solvent-evaporation rate.
Assuming a post-growth red shift proves new crystallization rather than ion/phase redistribution.

expected_answer:
The manufacturing specification should control substrate water activity and interface passivation as separate critical material attributes. Incoming underlayers should be qualified by a reproducible drying/equilibration protocol, water-uptake or desorption measurement, contact-angle/film-coverage mapping and storage-time limit. Chamber RH alone is not an adequate control because two underlayers can carry different water inventories at the same ambient condition. Web temperature, residence time between cleaning and coating, precursor/antisolvent timing, coating speed, drying rate and annealing history must be mapped against the measured water loading to define a robust process window.

Inline metrology should detect both phase selection and interface quality. Hyperspectral PL or reflectance immediately after coating and after annealing can map the blue peak, spectral width and spatial red-shift tails associated with larger-n domains. A second luminescence measurement after deposition on the actual hole-contact stack, ideally PLQY or time-resolved/photothermal quenching on sampled coupons, should distinguish good blue phase selection from severe interfacial recombination. Optical coherence or scattering, sheet/contact resistance and electroluminescence imaging can identify dewetting, pinholes, shunts and nonuniform injection. Periodic surface-water measurements and reference coupons should be linked statistically to spectral and electrical yield.

The interlayer or additive should be optimized in a two-axis matrix: enough chemical passivation to reduce Pb/halide-related interface traps, but not so much ionic or insulating material that hole injection and series resistance deteriorate. A water-blocking or low-hygroscopic hole contact may be combined with a thin passivating layer, but its coverage, work function and thermal stability must be verified after continuous drying and coating. Champion EQE is less important than area yield and tolerance to water-loading variation.

Qualification must include dark humidity storage, illuminated humidity exposure, electrical operation at constant current or luminance, thermal cycling and bias/light stress. Spectral peak, PLQY/EQE, operating voltage and spatial nonuniformity should be followed together. Post-mortem depth or surface analysis should determine whether failure is caused by water release from the underlayer, phase redistribution, passivator migration, contact corrosion or rising interfacial resistance.

A batch should be rejected even if its initial EL peak is blue when the correct color is obtained only in a narrow substrate-water window, when PLQY or injection uniformity is poor, or when illumination/bias produces rapid red-shift, voltage rise or local dark spots. Acceptance requires reproducible small-n phase selection, low nonradiative loss and stable spectra/electrical resistance across the full coated area and the specified water-loading range.
scoring_key_points: Controls and measures the underlayer water reservoir, drying history and coating/antisolvent/annealing window rather than relying on chamber RH.
Uses spatially resolved inline optical diagnostics for phase distribution plus independent interface-loss/injection diagnostics.
Qualifies the passivation layer for both chemical defect suppression and acceptable hole transport under continuous processing.
Includes combined humidity, light, bias and thermal stresses with a rejection rule based on spectral/electrical instability or narrow process tolerance despite correct initial blue EL.
accepted_equivalents: Karl Fischer, QCM, TGA/desorption, infrared water sensing or another calibrated incoming-substrate moisture metric.
Hyperspectral PL/EL, PLQY mapping, transient luminescence, lock-in thermography or equivalent large-area uniformity measurements.
Statistical process control using reference coupons and a two-dimensional water-loading/passivator-dose process map.
common_wrong_answers: Controlling only room RH and assuming the substrate has equilibrated identically.
Accepting a film because its PL or EL peak is blue without measuring PLQY, injection or spatial uniformity.
Increasing passivator concentration monotonically without checking series resistance or charge imbalance.
Using dark shelf storage alone as evidence of operational stability.

expected_answer:
The cap composition, carrier polarity and contact selectivity must be varied independently. At minimum, the matrix should include bare 3D, 3D/quasi-2D with the same carrier polarity (n-n or p-p), 3D/quasi-2D with opposite polarity (n-p), and a chemically similar but electronically blocking/passivating cap. Each film should be measured both on an inert substrate and in contact-selective device stacks; thickness, optical absorption and excitation density must be matched. Hall or Seebeck measurements should verify carrier polarity, while UPS/KPFM and capacitance-voltage or junction-potential measurements should test whether an electrostatic built-in field exists rather than assuming it from composition.

Defect passivation is supported if the cap lowers trap density and nonradiative recombination even on inert substrates: absolute PLQY should rise, low-fluence lifetime should lengthen, the fast trap-related component or sub-gap absorption should decrease, and SCLC/DLTS or thermal-admittance measurements should show fewer traps. A passivating same-polarity or blocking cap should reproduce much of this behavior without a strong polarity-dependent junction voltage. Lower dark current may then result from reduced trap-assisted generation, but photocurrent extraction need not accelerate.

Field-assisted separation is supported by a response that appears specifically in the verified n-p stack: surface-potential or C-V measurements show a built-in potential, transient absorption or time-resolved microwave/terahertz data show spatially separated carriers or longer-lived charges, the signal depends on illumination direction and junction orientation, and zero-bias photocurrent increases. The apparent PL lifetime can lengthen because electrons and holes are physically separated and recombine more slowly, even while the radiative PL intensity is quenched. Reversing the polarity order should reverse the internal-field direction or alter the extraction asymmetry.

Faster selective extraction is supported when PL quenching becomes much stronger only after adding the appropriate transport contact, while extracted-current transients, time-of-flight or transient photocurrent become faster and contact resistance decreases. On an inert substrate, the same bilayer may show passivation and long lifetime without strong quenching. Selective blocking layers or contact replacement should suppress the fast extraction signature without changing the underlying trap density or built-in voltage.

The dark-current mechanism must also be resolved using bias- and temperature-dependent dark current and noise spectra. A reduction in activation-assisted generation with fewer traps differs from simple injection blocking by a barrier, and both differ from junction depletion. Thus, steady-state PL quenching is ambiguous because it can mean extraction, charge separation or nonradiative loss; a longer multiexponential lifetime is also ambiguous because amplitudes, carrier density and spatial separation change. Only the matched polarity/contact matrix plus absolute quantum yield, junction electrostatics and carrier-collection kinetics can assign causality.
scoring_key_points: Uses bare, same-polarity, opposite-polarity and blocking/passivating controls on both inert and selective-contact substrates.
Defines independent passivation signatures using absolute PLQY/trap measurements that do not require an n-p field or extracting contact.
Defines field-assisted separation signatures using verified polarity, built-in-potential and orientation/zero-bias carrier-separation measurements.
Defines contact-extraction and dark-current signatures and explicitly explains why PL quenching and fitted lifetime are mechanistically non-unique.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent use of transient absorption, terahertz conductivity, surface photovoltage or electron-beam-induced current to track separated carriers.
Equivalent trap probes such as SCLC, DLTS, thermal admittance, sub-gap EQE or photothermal deflection spectroscopy.
A factorial design crossing quasi-2D polarity with contact selectivity and interface passivation.
common_wrong_answers: Calling longer TRPL lifetime proof of fewer defects without measuring PLQY or charge separation.
Calling PL quenching proof of faster extraction without an inert-substrate or blocking-contact control.
Inferring an n-p junction solely from the nominal precursor stoichiometry.
Explaining lower dark current only by a hydrophobic cap without bias, temperature or noise analysis.

expected_answer:
The mechanisms should be distinguished by their different dependence on frequency, temperature, CNT volume fraction, interface density and dc conductivity. A composition series spanning below, near and above the electrical percolation threshold is required, with identical particle size distribution, paraffin fraction, toroid geometry and density. Four-probe/dc conductivity and broadband complex permittivity should be measured on the same specimens. The percolation threshold can be identified from a power-law rise in conductivity and dielectric constant; conduction-dominated loss should increase strongly near/above that threshold and show a low-frequency epsilon-double-prime contribution proportional to sigma/(epsilon0 omega).

Dipolar relaxation intrinsic to the perovskite should persist in a low-conductivity control and show an Arrhenius or non-Debye temperature-dependent relaxation time. Cole-Cole/Havriliak-Negami analysis, modulus formalism and temperature-dependent dielectric spectroscopy can test whether a loss peak shifts systematically with temperature while its characteristic strength follows the number of orientable dipoles or defects. Replacing CNTs with an insulating filler of similar shape/interface area, or changing perovskite defect density without creating a conductive network, helps determine whether the peak is intrinsic dipolar/defect relaxation.

Maxwell-Wagner-Sillars polarization should scale with heterointerface area and conductivity contrast. It is supported if a similar-shape insulating or poorly conducting nanowire control retains an interfacial relaxation but with altered frequency/amplitude, and if changing CNT surface functionalization or dispersion changes the peak without a proportional change in the bulk perovskite phase. Effective-medium modeling and microscopy-derived interface density should correlate with the relaxation strength. Near-percolation conduction is instead supported when the peak/loss broadening tracks network connectivity, dc conductivity and the emergence of long-range CNT paths more strongly than interface area alone.

Magnetic loss must be excluded by measuring complex permeability, magnetic hysteresis and the eddy-current coefficient; permeability near unity and inconsistent eddy-current scaling would indicate dielectric dominance. Fixture and thickness artifacts should be tested by repeating calibrated VNA measurements with multiple specimen thicknesses/densities and, ideally, a free-space or waveguide method. The intrinsic epsilon and mu spectra should be thickness independent even though calculated reflection loss shifts through the quarter-wavelength condition.

Finally, attenuation and impedance matching must be evaluated together. A high-conductivity sample may show large attenuation but poor impedance match, so the composition that gives the largest epsilon-double-prime is not necessarily the best absorber. A mechanistic conclusion should therefore combine dielectric relaxation fits, percolation scaling, interface controls, magnetic exclusion and thickness-independent material parameters.
scoring_key_points: Uses a controlled CNT composition series with matched geometry and simultaneous dc conductivity/broadband complex-permittivity measurements.
Defines distinct temperature/composition signatures and controls for intrinsic dipolar relaxation, Maxwell-Wagner polarization and percolative conduction.
Rules out magnetic loss and fixture/thickness artifacts with permeability tests and independent/calibrated geometry checks.
Separates attenuation from impedance matching and does not equate the largest dielectric loss with the best reflection loss.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent impedance-modulus, electric-modulus, Cole-Cole or distributed-relaxation analysis.
Insulating MoO3/nanowire, functionalized-CNT or morphology-matched controls that vary conductivity contrast independently of interface area.
Free-space, waveguide or resonant-cavity validation of VNA-extracted constitutive parameters.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning both loss peaks to CNT conduction because conductivity rises with CNT loading.
Calling a PL-quenching or XRD-defect trend direct proof of microwave polarization loss.
Using reflection-loss curves at one thickness without extracting intrinsic permittivity/permeability.
Ignoring impedance mismatch and choosing the most conductive composition as the optimum.

expected_answer:
External morphology and a single ensemble PL peak cannot establish homogeneous alloying. The first requirement is spatial and depth-resolved composition. Cross-sectional STEM-EDS/EELS, atom-probe or ToF-SIMS on individual plates should compare the two faces, edge, center and thickness direction. A homogeneous alloy should show a uniform Br:I ratio within experimental resolution; a core-shell or substitution gradient should show systematic depth/edge enrichment even if plan-view EDS appears uniform. Angle-resolved XPS and grazing-incidence versus bulk-sensitive diffraction can provide complementary depth information.

The optical response should then be mapped on the same plate. Confocal hyperspectral PL/absorption and cathodoluminescence can reveal whether different regions emit at different energies. Excitation-wavelength-dependent PL, which changes penetration depth, is especially diagnostic for a vertical gradient. A homogeneous alloy should show one composition-consistent absorption edge and spatially uniform emission apart from strain/defects. A core-shell or gradient structure may show multiple edges, position-dependent PL, energy transfer from wide-gap to narrow-gap regions and excitation-depth-dependent spectra. Time-resolved PL or transient absorption can test directed energy transfer rather than assuming every composition contributes independently.

Light-induced segregation must be tested dynamically. The plate should be monitored under controlled illumination intensity, wavelength and temperature, followed by dark recovery. Reversible growth of low-energy PL, emergence of multiple peaks, local iodine-rich domains or photocurrent spectral drift during illumination supports segregation. A static core-shell gradient should remain after dark recovery and should be visible before illumination in the composition profile. Low-fluence measurements and pulsed excitation help separate intrinsic alloy bandgap from illumination-induced evolution.

To determine which region controls photocurrent, spatially resolved photocurrent/photoconductive AFM or scanning photocurrent microscopy should be correlated with the composition/PL map. Front-side versus back-side illumination and wavelength-dependent penetration can test whether current is generated mainly in a surface shell, buried core or entire plate. Contact geometry and transfer-induced damage must be controlled with four-probe/contact-resistance measurements. If the photocurrent action spectrum follows the absorption edge of only the narrow-gap region despite a broader alloy distribution, energy funneling or preferential contact to that region is implicated.

A convincing conclusion requires concordance among composition, absorption, dynamic PL and spatial photocurrent. Homogeneous composition plus illumination-stable spectra and uniform action response supports a true alloy; a persistent depth-dependent composition with directional energy transfer supports a gradient/core-shell structure; reversible illumination-dependent spectral splitting supports halide segregation.
scoring_key_points: Uses cross-sectional/depth-resolved composition to distinguish homogeneous alloying from a core-shell or substitution gradient.
Uses spatial, excitation-depth and time-resolved optical measurements to identify multiple bandgaps or energy transfer.
Tests illumination-intensity/time dependence and dark recovery to diagnose reversible halide segregation.
Correlates spatial/action-spectrum photocurrent with composition and controls contact/illumination geometry to identify the current-generating region.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent nano-XRF, atom-probe tomography, secondary-ion imaging or cross-sectional electron microscopy for composition profiling.
Cathodoluminescence, near-field optical mapping or transient absorption instead of confocal PL, if spatial/temporal information is retained.
Front/back illumination or wavelength-selective excitation to vary generation depth.
common_wrong_answers: Calling a monotonic ensemble PL shift proof of a homogeneous alloy.
Using plan-view EDS only, which can average a through-thickness gradient.
Assigning multiple PL peaks to composition gradients without testing light-induced segregation and dark recovery.
Assuming the PL-emitting region also dominates photocurrent without spatial/action-spectrum correlation.

expected_answer: Use a factorial control set: untreated, interface-only, precursor-only, and combined treatment, with matched perovskite thickness and annealing. Wetting and heterogeneous nucleation should be assigned primarily from contact angle, in situ optical microscopy or scattering during the first seconds of coating, nucleation density, and early-stage grain statistics. An interface-only sample should change wetting and nucleus density even before any bulk phase redistribution is detectable. Slower bulk crystallization requires a time-resolved crystallization observable, such as in situ GIWAXS, absorption, or PL during drying. The precursor-only sample should show delayed conversion, altered intermediate persistence, and a changed low-n/high-n phase distribution without requiring a change in substrate contact angle. Defect passivation should be supported by higher absolute PLQY, longer fluence-dependent TRPL lifetime, lower trap-filled-limit voltage or reduced nonradiative loss, and chemically specific FTIR/XPS shifts; it cannot be inferred from smooth morphology alone. Energy funneling requires spectrally and temporally resolved evidence: excitation of higher-bandgap low-n domains followed by decay of their bleach or emission and delayed growth of the lower-bandgap high-n population, ideally in transient absorption or time-resolved spectral PL. A static increase in low-n diffraction is insufficient. Complementarity is established if the interface-only treatment mainly changes wetting/nucleation, the precursor-only treatment mainly changes crystallization kinetics and domain distribution, both independently reduce defect-related loss, and only the combined sample achieves the strongest spatial uniformity, funneling efficiency, injection balance, and electroluminescence. Additive or interlayer dose series should show separate optima; a single latent variable would instead cause all observables to track one another monotonically across all controls.
scoring_key_points: Uses untreated, interface-only, precursor-only, and combined controls with matched processing.
Assigns wetting/nucleation and bulk crystallization with distinct time-resolved structural or morphological measurements.
Separates defect passivation from energy funneling using PLQY/trap metrics versus spectrally resolved carrier-transfer evidence.
Defines a result pattern showing independent partial effects and a synergistic combined response rather than simple covariance.
accepted_equivalents: Operando X-ray scattering may replace in situ GIWAXS if it resolves nucleation and phase conversion.
Transient absorption, time-resolved emission spectra, or excitation-dependent PL can support directional energy transfer.
Quasi-Fermi-level splitting or electroluminescence efficiency may substitute for another quantitative nonradiative-loss metric.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing every improvement to smaller grains or a longer PL lifetime.
Using only final-state SEM and steady-state PL, which cannot identify nucleation kinetics or transfer direction.
Claiming that more low-n phase automatically proves efficient energy funneling.

expected_answer: The candidate should not be ranked as superior from binding alone. The four functions are sequential but non-equivalent. First, precursor anti-oxidation concerns the SnI2–anion complex before film formation. A deeper adduct HOMO or higher ionization potential can make electron removal and Sn2+ oxidation less favorable, while coordination may also slow crystallization. This benefit must be assessed independently of what species actually survives in the solid. Second, vacancy binding addresses site occupancy and oxygen competition. The relevant comparison is the free energy of anion incorporation at the iodine vacancy versus O2 adsorption under realistic chemical potentials, including solvation, counterions, entropy, and migration barriers. Stronger binding can block an oxygen/superoxide pathway, but it does not guarantee benign electronic structure. Third, true electronic passivation requires removal—not replacement—of vacancy-derived gap states. Projected density of states, charge localization, transition levels, and local geometry should show that the anion interrupts Sn–Sn orbital coupling without introducing its own shallow or deep trap. The predicted localized occupied state is therefore a major negative result. Fourth, long lifetime requires favorable dynamics as well as static levels. Ab initio molecular dynamics and nonadiabatic calculations should show reduced structural fluctuations, weaker electron–phonon or nonadiabatic coupling, and slower capture/recombination. Large low-frequency fluctuations can enhance dynamic disorder and carrier capture even when the static defect formation energy is favorable. Thus the candidate may be useful as a precursor antioxidant or oxygen blocker but poor as a lifetime-extending passivant. It should be ranked below a candidate that satisfies all four gates. Robust screening should also test charge states, alternative defect sites, competing phases, additive mobility, and sensitivity to the computational functional; otherwise a strong zero-temperature binding energy can produce a false positive.
scoring_key_points: Separates precursor redox regulation from solid-state vacancy occupation.
Explains that stronger-than-O2 binding tests oxygen exclusion but not electronic benignity.
Requires elimination of gap states and rejects a candidate that introduces a localized band-edge trap.
Includes dynamic-disorder/nonadiabatic-coupling criteria and concludes that binding is necessary but insufficient.
accepted_equivalents: Defect transition levels, inverse participation ratio, or charge-density localization may replace projected density of states.
Free-energy or kinetic competition with oxygen is acceptable in place of a simple binding-energy comparison.
Electron–phonon coupling, capture coefficients, or nonadiabatic coupling may be used as the dynamic-loss metric.
common_wrong_answers: Ranking the additive solely by the largest vacancy binding energy.
Assuming that any vacancy-filling species automatically removes traps.
Equating a deeper precursor HOMO with guaranteed device-level carrier-lifetime improvement.

expected_answer: The observables weight the carrier system differently. Under a simple free-carrier picture, PL is proportional to the radiative coefficient times the product np, whereas microwave conductivity is proportional to e(μn n + μp p). Therefore, rapid removal of only one carrier type can collapse np while leaving the majority carrier and hence conductivity relatively large. Selective trapping predicts an early PL loss, a conductivity amplitude or decay that reflects the surviving carrier, trap-filling behavior with increasing fluence, and thermally activated recovery or faster emptying if trapped carriers can escape. A mobility decrease instead reduces conductivity without necessarily causing a proportional PL loss. It is therefore inconsistent with PL decaying much faster than conductivity unless mobility changes in a more complicated, carrier-selective way. Temperature dependence could reveal activated scattering or a structural transition, and a contact-free mobility probe at a different frequency may show dispersion. The key point is that conductivity lifetime conflates density and mobility. Fast nonradiative electron–hole recombination removes both carriers. It should make PL and conductivity populations decay on comparable timescales after accounting for their nonlinear response functions. Its fluence dependence follows the order of the recombination process: first-order trap-assisted loss is weakly fluence dependent, whereas bimolecular or Auger channels accelerate strongly with carrier density. It should not leave a large long-lived single-carrier conductivity population. A coupled rate-equation fit across several fluences and temperatures should therefore be required, not separate exponential lifetimes. Decisive additional measurements include transient absorption with carrier-selective spectral signatures, time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy to constrain mobility, photoinduced absorption of trapped charge, or controlled chemical doping that changes which carrier is minority. If conductivity remains while a trapped-carrier absorption grows and PL vanishes, selective trapping is supported. If an independent mobility measurement falls while carrier-sensitive absorption remains constant, mobility loss is favored.
scoring_key_points: Uses PL proportional to np and conductivity proportional to the mobility-weighted sum of carrier densities.
Derives the characteristic selective-trapping pattern and its trap-filling/thermal-escape predictions.
Distinguishes mobility loss and two-carrier nonradiative recombination using correlated decay and fluence dependence.
Requires global kinetic fitting and proposes a carrier- or mobility-sensitive measurement to break degeneracy.
accepted_equivalents: Optical-pump terahertz probe, Hall-type transient methods, or frequency-dependent conductivity can constrain mobility.
Transient absorption, photoinduced absorption, or EPR can identify trapped or surviving carrier populations.
A selective extraction layer may be used as a perturbation if it clearly changes one carrier population.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that long microwave conductivity directly proves long-lived free electron–hole pairs.
Calling the discrepancy nonradiative recombination without explaining why both carrier densities would not disappear together.
Ignoring mobility and fitting each trace with an unrelated single exponential.

expected_answer: Use a layer-selective control matrix: untreated film; vapor-treated bare film; treated film with the low-dimensional layer partially removed or replaced by an inert spacer of similar thickness; and complete devices with alternative electron contacts. Keep absorber thickness and optical absorption fixed. Bulk-defect reduction should alter properties throughout the film. Test it with excitation-wavelength-dependent or front/back PL, depth-sensitive lifetime measurements, bulk-sensitive defect spectroscopy, and temperature/fluence-dependent PLQY. If improvement persists when excitation and collection emphasize the buried bulk, and trap density falls throughout the thickness, a bulk contribution is supported. If changes are confined to the top few nanometers, the claim should be restricted to surface passivation. Surface chemical passivation should reduce surface recombination velocity and nonradiative loss without requiring a large bulk change. Calibrated absolute PL or quasi-Fermi-level splitting on bare and capped films, surface-sensitive TRPL, XPS chemical shifts, and selective quench experiments can establish this. The strongest test is whether the external electroluminescence efficiency and reciprocity-derived nonradiative voltage loss improve by an amount consistent with the device Voc gain. Band bending/contact selectivity requires energetic and transport evidence. UPS/KPFM depth or thickness series, surface photovoltage, capacitance profiling, and electron-contact-dependent Voc/FF should show that the treatment changes the interfacial field or extraction barrier. A favorable shift should reduce interfacial recombination and contact resistance without creating an insulating transport barrier. Reversing the electron contact or inserting a thin tunneling layer should alter this contribution predictably. A longer PL lifetime alone is ambiguous because it may reflect reduced radiative rate, carrier localization, or blocked extraction; a work-function shift alone can be a surface dipole with no beneficial band bending in the complete stack. The mechanism is established only if calibrated quasi-Fermi-level splitting, chemical/trap evidence, and contact-dependent transport all close the voltage-loss budget and localize where the improvement occurs.
scoring_key_points: Uses depth- or layer-sensitive controls to distinguish bulk from surface effects.
Assigns surface chemical passivation through surface recombination/nonradiative-loss metrics and voltage-loss closure.
Assigns band bending or contact selectivity through energetic profiling and contact-dependent transport tests.
Explains the ambiguity of PL lifetime and work-function shifts when used alone.
accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved two-photon PL or cross-sectional cathodoluminescence may provide depth sensitivity.
Electroluminescence reciprocity, calibrated PLQY, or quasi-Fermi-level splitting can close the nonradiative-voltage budget.
Kelvin probe, UPS, surface photovoltage, or capacitance methods may be combined to infer interfacial electrostatics.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the full Voc increase to the appearance of a low-dimensional diffraction peak.
Treating longer TRPL as direct proof of lower bulk trap density.
Using a single UPS work-function value as proof of favorable band alignment in the finished device.

expected_answer: The process specification should use integrated amine exposure at the surface, not nominal chamber time. Relevant variables are vapor partial pressure, carrier-gas flow, substrate temperature, relative humidity, boundary-layer thickness, web speed, source–substrate distance, exhaust rate, and pre-existing film porosity. Dose uniformity should be modeled and verified across width and along travel direction. The target state is a thin, continuous surface conversion with bounded chemistry and thickness, not maximum uptake. Spatial endpoint detection can combine reflectance or ellipsometry for surface-layer growth, hyperspectral PL/lifetime imaging for passivation uniformity, and Kelvin-probe or contact-potential mapping for the electronic shift. Inline mass spectrometry or quartz-crystal monitoring can constrain delivered vapor. Acceptance criteria should include a narrow distribution of surface-phase optical/structural signature, minimum calibrated PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, no increase in series resistance, no loss of electron-extraction yield, and absence of a new deep-trap or lifetime-decreasing signature. Under-treatment gives patchy passivation and residual nonradiative hotspots; over-treatment gives excessive low-dimensional material, unfavorable alignment, new traps, or reduced transport. To separate stability mechanisms, age untreated and treated bare films, half-stacks, and full devices under controlled light, heat, bias, humidity, and combinations thereof. Surface-recombination suppression should appear immediately as lower nonradiative loss and remain evident without bias. A true ion barrier should reduce field- and temperature-accelerated halide/metal redistribution, hysteresis, and electrode contamination, verified by ToF-SIMS, XPS depth profiles, or cross-sectional microscopy after bias aging. Better initial morphology alone should improve baseline defect metrics but may not change migration activation energy or directional elemental transport. Use matched initial efficiency or defect-density subsets to avoid survivorship bias. Encapsulation controls separate ingress protection from interfacial stabilization. The scaled process is accepted only when dose-state maps predict both initial voltage loss and the specific degradation pathway across the full area.
scoring_key_points: Defines integrated surface dose through vapor pressure, transport, temperature, humidity, flow, and web geometry rather than exposure time alone.
Provides spatial endpoint metrics and bounded acceptance criteria for under- and over-treatment.
Uses bare-film, half-stack, and full-device multi-stress aging to separate recombination, ion-barrier, and initial-quality effects.
Requires direct ion-redistribution evidence and controls for initial performance, morphology, and encapsulation.
accepted_equivalents: Raman, grazing-incidence X-ray scattering, or infrared spectroscopy may supplement optical endpoint detection.
SIMS, electron microscopy/EDS, or isotope tracing can establish ion or metal migration.
A designed exposure chamber with computational fluid dynamics is acceptable for dose-uniformity control.
common_wrong_answers: Specifying only a fixed number of seconds for every substrate size and line speed.
Using average PL from one point as the sole endpoint metric.
Claiming an ion-migration barrier solely because treated devices retain more PCE during storage.

expected_answer: Start with spectral current balance. Measure subcell-resolved EQE using appropriate light and voltage bias, integrate under the target spectrum, and compare the limiting currents. A current-mismatched tandem shows one subcell with lower integrated photocurrent and spectral dependence of tandem current. Selectively changing top-cell thickness, bandgap, texture, or antireflection design should move the limiting current and tandem Jsc without necessarily changing Voc. Next quantify optical losses with transfer-matrix modeling, reflectance/transmittance, and layer-resolved absorption or optical simulations validated by EQE. Parasitic absorption in transparent conductors, transport layers, or recombination layers reduces the photons reaching one or both absorbers. Replacing a lossy layer with a more transparent but electrically similar analogue, or changing optical thickness, should increase EQE in the corresponding wavelength region while leaving dark electrical behavior largely unchanged. Diagnose the recombination contact because the subcells are series connected through it. Measure tandem dark JV, Suns–Voc/pseudo-JV, temperature dependence, series resistance, and luminescence under selective excitation of each subcell. A defective recombination contact can cause S-shaped JV, fill-factor loss, voltage-dependent carrier accumulation, or failure of the tandem voltage to approach the sum of subcell quasi-Fermi-level splittings. Changing only the recombination layer conductivity, band alignment, or sputter buffer should selectively recover FF or voltage. Finally evaluate the top cell's nonradiative and contact losses in the integrated stack using calibrated PL/quasi-Fermi-level splitting, electroluminescence efficiency, ideality factor, and contact-selective half-stacks. If the optical current is adequate but measured Voc is below the radiative/PL-predicted value, interfacial or contact recombination is implicated. Replacing or passivating the top ETL/HTL should change Voc and FF more than Jsc. The hierarchy should be iterated because interventions can couple optics and transport. Standalone efficiencies are insufficient: integration changes spectrum, texture, processing damage, interfaces, and the internal operating point of both series-connected junctions.
scoring_key_points: Uses biased subcell EQE and integrated spectral currents to diagnose series-current mismatch.
Separates parasitic absorption with optical-loss mapping and a selectively transparent layer perturbation.
Diagnoses recombination-contact loss through voltage additivity, pseudo-JV/FF, accumulation, or S-shaped behavior.
Quantifies top-cell nonradiative/contact loss with calibrated luminescence and contact-specific controls while acknowledging integration coupling.
accepted_equivalents: Electroluminescence imaging or luminescence coupling can replace another subcell-selective voltage diagnostic.
Photothermal deflection or spectroscopic ellipsometry may supplement optical-loss analysis.
Impedance spectroscopy or transient photocurrent may identify recombination-contact accumulation and resistance.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the tandem efficiency should equal the sum of standalone subcell efficiencies.
Diagnosing every low fill factor as simple series resistance without testing the recombination junction.
Changing several layers simultaneously and then claiming a unique failure mechanism.

expected_answer: Qualification should begin with a failure-mode map for the actual module stack: perovskite decomposition or phase segregation, ion migration, contact corrosion or diffusion, transparent-electrode damage, encapsulant and edge-seal ingress, interconnect failure, silicon-contact degradation, and thermo-mechanical delamination. Testing only cells omits several dominant module pathways. Use a matrix of single and combined stresses: continuous maximum-power-point light soaking over relevant spectra and temperatures; damp heat; thermal cycling; humidity-free heat; bias plus heat; UV exposure; mechanical load; and outdoor operation at multiple climates. Include encapsulated cells, minimodules, and full-size representative modules, with appropriate controls based on silicon-only and perovskite-only components. Combined tests are essential because light, bias, heat, and moisture can activate coupled chemistry that no single stress reproduces. Track stabilized power, subcell-resolved EQE, Voc and FF, insulation and series resistance, electroluminescence/PL images, spectral shifts, local temperature, leakage current, and spatial degradation. Periodic destructive analysis should measure ion/metal profiles, interfacial chemistry, adhesion, and moisture ingress. A high retained PCE is insufficient if one subcell or interface is accumulating irreversible damage masked by current matching or reversible recovery. Acceleration factors should be derived only when accelerated and field tests share the same rate-controlling failure mode. Use multiple stress levels to fit physically motivated temperature, humidity, light, or bias dependencies, then calibrate against synchronized outdoor datasets with logged irradiance, module temperature, humidity, spectrum, and operating point. Validate predictions prospectively on a second climate or cohort and report uncertainty rather than a single lifetime. Invalidate the model if activation energy changes with stress level, degradation morphology or chemistry differs between accelerated and field samples, ranking reverses across tests, recovery occurs after dark storage, or combined stresses produce a new pathway. Also reject extrapolation when power retention is maintained by compensating subcell changes while adhesion, leakage, corrosion, or ion redistribution crosses a safety or reliability threshold.
scoring_key_points: Builds a module-level failure-mode map and includes encapsulation, interconnects, interfaces, and both subcells.
Uses multiple single and combined stresses with MPP, outdoor, and module-relevant specimens.
Tracks electrical, optical, spatial, chemical, mechanical, and safety observables rather than PCE alone.
Links acceleration to field data only after failure-mode equivalence and states concrete invalidation criteria.
accepted_equivalents: ISOS- or IEC-aligned damp-heat, thermal-cycle, light-soak, and outdoor protocols are acceptable if combined-stress logic is explicit.
Bayesian or physics-of-failure lifetime models may be used if uncertainty and external field validation are included.
Subcell-resolved luminescence or lock-in thermography can substitute for another spatial diagnostic.
common_wrong_answers: Fitting an exponential to one 1000-hour indoor test and multiplying to 25 years.
Reporting only average PCE retention while ignoring module safety, interconnects, and spatial failure.
Assuming identical acceleration factors when the degradation chemistry changes with stress.

expected_answer: The most coherent interpretation begins with the lower chemical and thermal robustness of the MA-containing absorber. Heat and illumination can promote loss or reaction of the volatile organic component and destabilize the alpha-perovskite lattice, producing PbI2, undercoordinated Pb/halide defects, and mobile ionic or molecular products. This bulk chemical change increases the concentration and mobility of charged defects rather than merely reducing the amount of light-absorbing material. Under the built-in field and asymmetric contacts, those species redistribute toward the two interfaces. Their accumulation changes local doping, surface potential, and band bending, so the electron-contact side can acquire an unfavorable p-type shift while the hole-contact side becomes excessively n-type. The two shifts oppose selective extraction at both contacts, increase interfacial recombination and injection/extraction barriers, and therefore reduce quasi-Fermi-level splitting, VOC, and fill factor. The electrical loss can be disproportionate to the remaining alpha-phase fraction because a thin, chemically altered interfacial region can dominate recombination and series/contact resistance. A composition-driven diagnosis requires a factorial control rather than comparing two unrelated devices. Prepare MA-containing and MA-free absorbers with the same transport layers, coating conditions, thickness, and passivator coverage; within each composition include passivated and deliberately unpassivated or uniformly passivated controls. Follow alpha-phase/PbI2 evolution by operando or time-resolved XRD and track interfacial potentials by KPFM or surface-potential mapping at both contacts, ideally supplemented by depth-resolved ToF-SIMS/XPS for cation and halide redistribution. If phase loss and polarity-selective interfacial shifts follow MA content even when passivator coverage is matched, composition instability is causal. If phase stability is unchanged but degradation instead correlates with lateral passivator accumulation, local potential heterogeneity, and spatially localized recombination, the dominant failure is passivation nonuniformity. The strongest test also checks whether the chemical/interfacial signatures precede the VOC and fill-factor decline.
scoring_key_points: Link MA-containing composition to alpha-phase destabilization, PbI2 formation, and creation of mobile charged defects or decomposition products under heat and light.
Explain that field- and contact-directed redistribution changes local doping/band bending at both interfaces rather than acting as a purely uniform bulk loss.
Connect the opposing interfacial potential shifts to reduced selectivity, greater interfacial recombination or barriers, and consequent VOC and fill-factor loss.
Propose a matched composition-by-passivation control with time-resolved phase, spatial potential, and preferably depth-composition measurements that establish temporal causality.
accepted_equivalents: Volatilization, deprotonation, or chemical reaction of the MA-derived component may be used as the initiating instability.
Halide vacancies, A-site vacancies, mobile halides, or charged decomposition products are acceptable mobile-species descriptions if directional interfacial redistribution is explained.
Quasi-Fermi-level-splitting loss, contact barrier growth, or increased surface recombination may be used to explain the VOC decline.
Cross-sectional Kelvin probe, operando XPS, ToF-SIMS, or contact-selective photoluminescence may replace KPFM if both interfaces are resolved.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the entire performance loss only to reduced optical absorption from PbI2 formation.
Treating the opposite interface shifts as harmless because their average potential could remain unchanged.
Claiming that stronger initial Pb-passivator binding proves long-term compositional stability.
Comparing different compositions with different passivators, transport layers, or drying histories and calling the result mechanistically decisive.

expected_answer: Stronger conventional XRD peaks are not sufficient because they can arise from more material, larger grains, lower microstrain, or better overall crystallinity. The structural test must quantify texture.
