GIWAXS or pole-figure measurements should compare azimuthal intensity distributions, orientation factors, and the relative out-of-plane population of the relevant planes after normalization for thickness, illuminated volume, phase fraction, and total scattering. Peak width and integrated intensity should be reported separately so that orientation is not confused with crystallite size or reduced disorder. The bandgap, composition, and film thickness must remain matched. A second set of measurements should separate generic passivation from orientation-enabled transport. PLQY, TRPL, SCLC trap density, Urbach energy, and chemical-state shifts can establish fewer nonradiative defects, but they do not prove directional transport. The orientation hypothesis predicts improved carrier motion or extraction normal to the substrate: shorter extraction transients on a transport layer, higher cross-plane mobility or conductivity, reduced transit time, and lower contact-selective recombination without a corresponding lateral-transport advantage. Comparing additive incorporation with a post-deposition treatment that passivates interfaces but cannot strongly reorganize bulk texture is especially informative. Depth-resolved additive mapping and UPS can verify that interfacial accumulation and energy alignment are not the sole explanations. The stability part requires operando spectral and structural evidence under identical photon flux, temperature, and carrier density. Time-resolved hyperspectral PL should quantify emergence of low-energy I-rich emission, while operando GIWAXS/XRD or compositional mapping tests whether texture loss or halide redistribution accompanies it. If films with stronger normalized orientation show delayed phase-segregation signatures even after trap density and initial PLQY are matched, orientation has an independent role. The causal case is strongest when the orientation metric predicts cross-plane extraction and phase stability across an additive-concentration series, rather than only correlating at one optimum.
scoring_key_points: Quantify texture by normalized GIWAXS/pole-figure azimuthal distributions and separate orientation from thickness, phase fraction, grain size, and peak-width effects.
Use defect-sensitive measurements to quantify passivation but require directional cross-plane transport or extraction evidence for an orientation mechanism.
Use additive-versus-post-treatment or other matched controls plus depth/energy-level measurements to exclude interface passivation as the sole cause.
Test phase segregation operando under matched light and temperature and show that normalized orientation predicts delayed low-energy emission or halide redistribution across a series.
accepted_equivalents: Herman orientation factor, texture coefficient, pole density, or azimuthal FWHM are acceptable quantitative orientation metrics.
Time-of-flight, transient photocurrent, TRMC with directional geometry, space-charge-limited mobility, or charge-extraction transients may establish cross-plane transport.
A structurally inert passivator with similar trap reduction may replace the additive-versus-post-treatment control.
Operando PL, cathodoluminescence, nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS after stress, or operando GIWAXS may be used to track phase segregation.
common_wrong_answers: Equating a higher raw XRD peak with preferred orientation without normalization or azimuthal information.
Using longer TRPL lifetime alone as proof of faster extraction.
Attributing improved VOC entirely to orientation while ignoring trap passivation and energy-level shifts.
Comparing phase segregation under different illumination intensities or film temperatures.

expected_answer: At low loading, a flexible polymer can be excluded from the growing perovskite lattice and concentrate at grain boundaries, crystal edges, and the external surface. Carbonyl or hydroxyl groups can coordinate undercoordinated Pb and hydrogen-bond to organic cations, while the conformal hydrophobic layer reduces water access and immobilizes soluble Pb species. If the polymer also moderates nucleation and strain, trap density and nonradiative recombination fall, so PLQY and lifetime increase and Pb release decreases without necessarily obstructing percolating electronic pathways. The mechanism changes when the amount or molecular coverage exceeds the available defect and boundary area. Polymer-rich domains may become continuous, thicken at the transport-layer interface, fill intergrain necks, or aggregate during drying. Because the polymer is substantially less electronically conductive than the perovskite, this creates tunneling barriers, reduces effective contact area, increases series resistance, and can unbalance extraction. More polymer can therefore continue to improve chemical immobilization and radiative efficiency while decreasing photocurrent and fill factor. Excessive crystallization retardation or altered texture may add a second penalty. PL on glass or another inert substrate mainly reports the competition between radiative and nonradiative recombination within the absorber. It can become brighter when traps are passivated even if carriers cannot leave the film. The decisive comparison is substrate-dependent: on the relevant transport layer, beneficial extraction should cause controlled PL quenching and faster transfer without lowering internal quality. Absolute PLQY, transient absorption, and TRPL should be interpreted together with transient photocurrent/photovoltage, charge-extraction time, mobility, SCLC, impedance, and series resistance. The concentration series should map polymer location and connectivity by cross-sectional TEM, AFM-IR, ToF-SIMS, or chemically specific tomography, while XRD/GIWAXS and strain analysis track lattice incorporation, texture, and crystallization. The optimum is the lowest loading that saturates defect passivation and Pb immobilization while preserving intergrain contact, transport-layer quenching, mobility, and stabilized device output; a monotonic PL or leakage trend alone cannot define it.
scoring_key_points: Describe low-loading polymer localization at boundaries/surfaces as a conformal passivating, Pb-binding, hydrophobic layer that preserves electronic percolation.
Explain that excess polymer can form continuous insulating domains or interfacial barriers, increasing series resistance and reducing extraction despite continued PL and leakage benefits.
State why PL on an inert substrate measures recombination quality but not extraction, and require transport-layer-dependent optical or transfer measurements.
Use a concentration-resolved localization, crystallization/strain, mobility/impedance, and stabilized-device data set to identify the passivation-to-blocking crossover.
accepted_equivalents: A tunneling barrier, reduced grain-neck contact, contact-area loss, or polymer-rich phase percolation are acceptable transport-blocking descriptions.
Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz conductivity, or extraction-sensitive TRPL may replace transient photocurrent measurements.
TEM, nano-IR, ToF-SIMS, neutron reflectometry, or labeled-polymer fluorescence may establish polymer localization.
An optimum defined by a Pareto front of Pb retention, PLQY, mobility, FF, and stabilized PCE is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that the brightest film must give the best device.
Interpreting longer TRPL on every substrate as proof of faster charge extraction.
Increasing polymer loading until Pb release is minimized without checking series resistance or interfacial coverage.
Claiming lattice doping merely because device energetics change, despite no phase/peak shift or localization evidence.

expected_answer: The two substrate geometries probe different rate competitions. On inert glass, there is no efficient electron acceptor, so higher absolute PL or PLQY from the inverse-opal film is consistent with fewer shallow traps, improved crystallization, and a larger fraction of recombination proceeding radiatively. On SnO2, an additional electron-transfer channel is opened. If the absorber remains intrinsically high quality, rapid transfer to SnO2 lowers the steady-state carrier population in the perovskite, producing stronger PL quenching and a shorter apparent lifetime. Thus a high-PL film on glass and a quenched, short-lived film on an extracting substrate can jointly indicate trap reduction and faster extraction. The interpretation is not automatic because photonic structures alter excitation density, scattering, collection angle, and photon outcoupling. Measurements must therefore match absorber volume, thickness or absorbed-photon density, excitation wavelength, spot size, and detection geometry. Absolute integrating-sphere PLQY or front/back calibrated emission should be used on glass to separate internal radiative efficiency from directional outcoupling. A planar film with comparable absorptance and an inverse-opal film on an inert, electronically blocking underlayer are required optical controls. Extraction should be demonstrated independently on SnO2. Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity, transient photocurrent, electron-injection kinetics, or contact-selective quenching can show transfer of carriers into SnO2. PL mapping should verify that quenching is spatially uniform rather than caused by localized damaged regions. Device-level evidence should include improved EQE/photocurrent, reduced interfacial accumulation or recombination, and no loss of VOC that would accompany added nonradiative defects. The competing nonradiative-loss explanation predicts lower PLQY already on glass, stronger sub-gap absorption or trap signatures, and shorter lifetime even without an acceptor, often accompanied by lower VOC. The extraction explanation predicts high intrinsic PLQY on glass, a transfer-associated fast component only when SnO2 is present, and increased collected charge. Only the complete substrate-matched optical and electrical data set resolves the mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Interpret high PL on glass as improved intrinsic radiative quality and strong quenching/shorter lifetime on SnO2 as a possible added extraction channel.
Control absorbed-photon density, absorber amount, scattering, collection geometry, and outcoupling using absolute PLQY and optically matched planar/inert-substrate controls.
Require an independent carrier-transfer or extraction measurement plus spatially uniform quenching and improved collected charge on SnO2.
Reject added nonradiative loss only if the inverse-opal film retains high intrinsic PLQY and VOC and lacks new trap signatures in the absence of SnO2.
accepted_equivalents: An electron-selective quenching layer other than SnO2 may be used if the energy alignment is controlled.
Transient absorption, terahertz conductivity, surface photovoltage, transient photocurrent, or ultrafast interfacial spectroscopy may establish extraction.
Integrating-sphere PLQY, reciprocity-derived nonradiative voltage loss, or calibrated external luminescence efficiency may establish intrinsic radiative quality.
Ray-tracing or electromagnetic correction of the photonic outcoupling is acceptable when combined with experimental controls.
common_wrong_answers: Calling every shorter TRPL lifetime evidence of more defects.
Calling every stronger PL quenching evidence of better extraction without an inert-substrate control.
Comparing raw PL intensities without matching absorbed photons and collection geometry in a strongly scattering photonic structure.
Ignoring device VOC and collected-current data when assigning the recombination mechanism.

expected_answer: The first requirement is dosimetry at the absorber, not nominal lamp power. Measure the spectral irradiance and transmission of glass, FTO, transport layers, encapsulant, and rear electrode, then calculate or directly measure the UV photon flux absorbed by the perovskite. Compare control and additive modules at matched absorbed UV dose and matched device temperature. Either test both illumination directions as separate protocols or adjust exposure time/intensity so that front- and rear-side absorbed doses are equivalent; the two geometries must never be pooled as if they were identical. A severe 310 nm test is useful for acceleration but must be linked to realistic operation. Run full-spectrum one-sun stabilized MPP with a calibrated UV fraction, alongside UV-enhanced and UV-depleted spectra at the same thermal load. Include encapsulated and unencapsulated cells or modules, an optical-filter control matched to the additive's UV absorption, and repeated batches. Report degradation versus cumulative UV dose and time, not only endpoint retention, and check whether downconversion changes current or merely attenuates UV. Mechanistic diagnostics should be acquired during and after stress. Track J-V/MPP, EQE, electroluminescence or PL maps, spectral shifts, impedance, and local heating. Post-mortem XPS/XRD/SEM should quantify Pb0, PbI2, cracking, halide oxidation, film density, and interfacial changes. If protection is durable, chemical-degradation markers and nonradiative-voltage loss should remain lower at the same absorbed dose, not only at the same incident lamp time. The final gate is module-scale reliability. Combine UV with damp heat, thermal cycling, and outdoor or solar-simulator spectral cycling because the framework, ligands, and encapsulant can age or leach and the optical transfer efficiency can change. Measure spatial uniformity, insulation, adhesion, MPP, and post-aging UV-conversion quantum yield. Advance the additive only if benefit persists under glass-encapsulated full-spectrum MPP and multi-stress aging without parasitic absorption, color change, or transport penalty.
scoring_key_points: Normalize comparisons by absorber-level spectral UV dose and matched temperature, treating front/glass and rear illumination as distinct or dose-corrected protocols.
Bridge accelerated 310 nm exposure to full-spectrum stabilized MPP using UV-enhanced/depleted and optical-filter controls with dose-based degradation curves.
Use operando electrical/optical mapping plus post-mortem Pb0, PbI2, cracking, oxidation, and interface diagnostics at equal absorbed dose.
Require glass-encapsulated module performance through combined UV, damp heat, thermal cycling, and realistic spectral aging while tracking conversion efficiency and parasitic losses.
accepted_equivalents: A calibrated reference photodiode plus transfer-matrix optical model is acceptable for absorber-level UV dosimetry.
Dose may be expressed as photons per square centimeter, absorbed UV energy, or equivalent sun-hours if the spectrum is specified.
Outdoor exposure may supplement rather than replace controlled accelerated protocols.
Photoluminescence-excitation action spectra or wavelength-resolved EQE may be used to track whether the conversion pathway survives aging.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing equal lamp time from opposite sides without correcting for glass/FTO absorption.
Claiming operational stability from a short 310 nm test performed at uncontrolled temperature.
Using endpoint PCE retention without chemical degradation markers or cumulative-dose reporting.
Ignoring additive or encapsulant aging because the fresh film initially emits strongly under UV.

expected_answer: The functions should be separated by both when the molecule is introduced and which chemical motif is retained. At minimum, compare precursor incorporation with post-crystallization bulk exposure and a top-interface-only treatment at matched molecular loading. Precursor-only effects should be tested with an analogue that preserves solvent/PbI2 complexation but lacks one defect-binding motif; passivation should be tested with analogues that independently remove the Lewis-basic/halide-coordinating site or the N-H hydrogen-bond donor while retaining molecular size and polarity; an interfacial transport control should retain surface dipole or compatibility with the hole contact but have weak precursor binding. Solution NMR, Raman/IR, and in situ GIWAXS or XRD should quantify DMSO/PbI2 speciation, intermediate lifetime, nucleation, orientation, and film densification. XPS, absolute PLQY or QFLS, SCLC, and defect-sensitive spectroscopy should test metallic Pb, halide vacancies, trap density, and nonradiative recombination. ToF-SIMS should locate the molecule, while hole-only mobility, contact resistivity, transient photocurrent, impedance, or selective-contact PL should test extraction. Crystallization regulation is supported if only precursor incorporation changes the intermediate pathway and facet distribution; chemical passivation is supported if post-crystallization treatment still removes defect signatures and raises QFLS without reproducing the crystallization change; transport assistance is supported if interface-localized material improves extraction or contact resistance without a comparable bulk lifetime change. Genuine synergy requires the complete molecule to outperform the sum or best of the single-function analogues and to improve crystallization, nonradiative loss, and transport without producing an insulating layer.
scoring_key_points: Separates precursor, post-crystallization, and top-interface-only introduction to isolate when each function acts.
Uses matched molecular analogues that independently perturb precursor binding, defect passivation, and contact-facing functionality.
Combines in situ crystallization probes with defect/QFLS measurements and independent extraction or contact-resistance measurements.
Defines multifunctional synergy as orthogonal improvements exceeding single-function controls without a transport-blocking overlayer.
accepted_equivalents: A factorial molecular-design study using protected functional groups or close structural analogues
In situ GIWAXS, XRD, optical interferometry, or spectroscopy for intermediate and nucleation kinetics
PLQY/QFLS, SCLC, deep-level spectroscopy, or XPS for passivation
Transient extraction, impedance, hole-only mobility, conductive AFM, or contact-resistivity testing
common_wrong_answers: Attributes all improvements to passivation because metallic Pb disappears, without testing precursor kinetics.
Uses unrelated molecules whose size, polarity, and solubility change simultaneously, making the ablation uninterpretable.
Treats a preferred XRD orientation as direct proof of lower defect density or faster extraction.
Claims synergy from a champion efficiency alone without orthogonal controls for crystallization, recombination, and transport.

expected_answer: The original additive concentration cannot simply be copied because the relevant quantities are the relative timescales of precursor complexation, solvent removal, PbI2 intermediate formation, conversion, and annealing. A design-of-experiments matrix should vary additive loading, DMSO or coordinating-solvent fraction, solids content, coating speed, wet-film thickness, substrate temperature, gas-knife or drying rate, conversion chemistry, annealing profile, and humidity. Inline or rapid in situ GIWAXS/XRD, optical spectroscopy, and drying-thickness monitoring should define a robust intermediate-to-perovskite process window. Cross-web maps of thickness, roughness, crystallographic orientation, PLQY/QFLS, trap density, composition, and additive distribution should distinguish edge drying or aggregation from uniform crystallization regulation. Module losses require separate P1-P2-P3 scribe-width, dead-area, debris, isolation-resistance, sheet-resistance, contact-resistance, shunt, electroluminescence, and lock-in thermography measurements. High local VOC with low module FF would point toward series resistance, current crowding, or scribe shunts rather than a global recombination problem. Film-level, single-cell, and minimodule controls from the same coating must be aged separately under stabilized MPP, heat, humidity, and combined illumination-temperature stress, followed by encapsulated thermal cycling and damp-heat or outdoor-relevant testing. Manufacturing acceptance requires a wide process window, low spatial variance and defect density, reproducible scribe yield, stable module power, and evidence that the additive remains beneficial rather than migrating or accumulating at boundaries.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes the coupled complexation, drying, conversion, and annealing timescales through a multivariable coating process window.
Uses cross-web structural, compositional, and luminescence mapping to diagnose film-formation nonuniformity.
Separately measures laser-scribe, sheet/contact-resistance, shunt, and current-crowding losses rather than assigning all module loss to the absorber.
Requires film, cell, and module stability under MPP and combined environmental stresses, with process-capability rather than champion-device criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Response-surface or factorial optimization of solvent, additive, coating, drying, humidity, and annealing variables
Inline GIWAXS, hyperspectral PL, optical coherence, XRF, ToF-SIMS, or spatial QFLS mapping
EL imaging, lock-in thermography, four-point sheet resistance, TLM, and scribe-isolation analysis
ISOS-style MPP tests followed by encapsulated thermal cycling, damp heat, and outdoor validation
common_wrong_answers: Uses the small-cell recipe unchanged and treats additive concentration as the only scale-up variable.
Infers uniform crystallization from a few center-of-panel XRD measurements.
Blames low module fill factor on nonradiative recombination despite high local VOC and untested scribe resistance.
Treats unencapsulated laboratory aging as sufficient proof of module manufacturing reliability.

expected_answer: The process should first create a reproducible hydroxylated ITO surface and then define a submonolayer-to-saturation dose window using an orthogonal solvent, controlled coating or vapor exposure, rinsing, and mild annealing compatible with the flexible substrate. Roughness increases the true area and creates valleys, so solution concentration and residence time must be adjusted using surface-density rather than nominal-volume targets. Spatial XPS or ToF-SIMS, ellipsometry where applicable, KPFM, contact-angle, and conductive-AFM maps should verify phosphonate anchoring, molecular orientation, dipole uniformity, and absence of multilayer aggregates. After perovskite deposition, buried-side PL/QFLS, Pb core-level or coordination probes, and cross-sectional chemical mapping should test whether the heteroatom remains coordinated rather than diffusing or reacting. A factorial durability study should compare SAM-coated ITO without perovskite, half stacks, and complete devices under dry heat, humidity, light bias/MPP, and cyclic bending at multiple radii and directions. Anchoring failure produces loss or redistribution of phosphonate/SAM signal and work-function nonuniformity; buried-interface degradation produces preserved ITO/SAM coverage but declining QFLS, increasing trap-assisted recombination, or altered Pb coordination; mechanical electrode cracking produces sheet-resistance and local conductivity loss that follows crack density even if molecular chemistry is intact. Encapsulated and unencapsulated controls are both needed, and acceptance should require stable FF/VOC, low spatial variance, unchanged monolayer chemistry, and preserved electrode continuity after combined bending and damp-heat/MPP stress.
scoring_key_points: Controls ITO surface chemistry and uses surface-density/coverage criteria appropriate for rough large-area substrates.
Maps SAM anchoring, orientation, dipole, and buried Pb coordination before and after perovskite deposition.
Uses isolated ITO/SAM, half-stack, and full-device stresses to distinguish desorption, chemical passivation loss, and electrode cracking.
Requires combined bending, humidity, heat, and MPP testing with both encapsulated and unencapsulated controls.
accepted_equivalents: Meniscus, spray, slot-die, or vapor deposition with rinse and self-limiting monolayer control
XPS/ToF-SIMS, KPFM, NEXAFS, C-AFM, or sheet-resistance mapping
Peel, crack-density, bending-direction, and neutral-axis controls for mechanical failure
Periodic PL/EL/QFLS and contact-resistance mapping during environmental aging
common_wrong_answers: Increases SAM concentration until all roughness is covered, without checking for a multilayer transport barrier.
Attributes every bending-induced FF loss to SAM desorption and ignores ITO cracking.
Uses only contact angle as evidence that molecular orientation and hole selectivity are preserved.
Reports encapsulated stability without separate unencapsulated or half-stack controls.

expected_answer: The initial modifier should contain a distinguishable label, such as a deuterated or 13C/15N bulky cation, and, where feasible, a distinguishable halide tracer. Identically prepared films should be heated in a sealed operando cell while time-resolved GIWAXS/XRD and optical measurements are collected. The total tracer inventory must be measured by calibrated XPS/ToF-SIMS or neutron/ion-beam profiling before and after stress, while a quartz-crystal microbalance, thermal-desorption mass spectrometry, or headspace analysis detects volatile loss. Desorption produces a decrease in total cation tracer, surface depletion without compensating deep accumulation, and labeled volatile species in the headspace. Pure inward diffusion approximately conserves total tracer but broadens the depth profile into the 3D film and increases the deep-to-surface ratio without requiring disappearance of the original phase or formation of new crystalline stoichiometries. Reconstruction by dissolution-reprecipitation or ion exchange can conserve much of the cation tracer yet produces correlated loss/reorientation of the initial RP peaks, new phases or lattice shifts, altered local cation/halide stoichiometry, and spatially heterogeneous tracer redistribution. Separate cation and halide tracers help identify halide exchange rather than simple cation diffusion. Temperature-step experiments, annealing-only controls, solvent-wash controls, different atmospheres, and untreated films are required. A combined outcome is possible, so the conclusion should be based on tracer mass balance plus depth and phase evolution rather than a single surface XPS ratio.
scoring_key_points: Uses a labeled bulky cation and, ideally, a separate halide tracer with operando thermal treatment.
Identifies total tracer loss plus labeled volatile detection as the signature of desorption.
Identifies conserved tracer with depth-profile broadening but no necessary phase change as inward diffusion.
Identifies correlated new phases/lattice or stoichiometric changes with tracer redistribution as dissolution-reprecipitation or ion exchange.
accepted_equivalents: Deuterated, 13C-labeled, 15N-labeled, fluorescent, or mass-spectrometric cation tracers
ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved XPS, neutron reflectometry, ion-beam analysis, or serial-section profiling
TGA-MS, QCM, residual-gas analysis, or sealed-cell headspace spectroscopy
Operando GIWAXS/XRD combined with XRF or nano-XRD mapping
common_wrong_answers: Calls the lower surface cation/Pb ratio proof of desorption without checking total mass or depth redistribution.
Interprets a higher bulk-to-surface RP ratio as pure diffusion even though new phases appear.
Uses only ex situ XRD and cannot determine whether cation material left the film.
Ignores the possibility that cation diffusion and phase reconstruction occur simultaneously.

expected_answer: A controlled series should vary reconstructed-layer thickness while holding the underlying 3D absorber and chemical passivation dose as constant as possible. It should include a predominantly 1D cap, a mixed 1D/3D reconstructed layer, a thin molecular-passivation control, and an untreated 3D surface. Cross-sectional nano-GIWAXS/XRD, TEM, compositional mapping, or tomography should establish whether 3D-connected pathways traverse the layer. Depth-selective excitation or wavelength-dependent TRMC/photoconductivity should compare surface-sensitive and bulk-sensitive carrier dynamics: a genuine bilayer should strongly reduce surface traps while leaving bulk mobility largely unchanged. Vertical conductivity, temperature-dependent current, contact resistivity, transient photocurrent, impedance, and bias-dependent EL should then test extraction through the layer. A continuous insulating cap predicts an approximately exponential or strongly superlinear increase in resistance with thickness, slower extraction, S-shaped J-V, and falling FF/JSC once tunneling becomes limiting. A conductive mixed-dimensional heterojunction predicts a thickness window in which surface QFLS and EQEEL improve while vertical resistance, current, and FF remain nearly unchanged, consistent with percolating 3D channels or favorable band-mediated transfer. The strongest proof correlates local mixed-phase connectivity with local current using conductive AFM, EBIC, or scanning photocurrent and shows that removing the 3D connectivity restores the thickness-dependent transport penalty.
scoring_key_points: Uses a reconstructed-layer thickness series with 1D-rich, mixed 1D/3D, thin-passivation, and untreated controls.
Verifies vertical mixed-phase connectivity structurally and separates surface-sensitive from bulk-sensitive photophysics.
Measures vertical conductivity/contact resistance and predicts strong thickness-dependent transport loss for a continuous insulating cap.
Requires preserved current/FF within a passivating thickness window and local correlation of 3D connectivity with conduction for the bilayer model.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional nano-diffraction, TEM, atom-probe or chemical tomography for phase connectivity
405/600 nm excitation, variable-angle excitation, TRMC, terahertz, or depth-resolved PL
TLM, temperature-dependent current, impedance, transient photocurrent, EBIC, or C-AFM
A percolation or band-alignment explanation for non-tunneling transport through the reconstructed region
common_wrong_answers: Claims the layer is conductive because the final device has high efficiency, without a thickness or phase control.
Uses longer PL lifetime alone, which can also occur for an insulating passivating cap.
Assumes any low-dimensional phase blocks current and ignores mixed-phase percolation.
Measures only lateral film conductivity rather than vertical contact transport.

expected_answer: The three mechanisms require controls that change one property at a time. Alongside the multifunctional modifier, use a passivating analogue that improves QFLS but does not measurably relax strain, an adhesion promoter that changes peel strength without changing perovskite phase or traps, and a mechanically compliant or strain-relieving interlayer with weak chemical passivation. All devices must use the same substrate, electrode, neutral-axis position, absorber thickness, and encapsulation. During monotonic and cyclic bending in both tensile and compressive directions, in situ GIXRD or Raman should track lattice strain and phase evolution, while optical microscopy, SEM, acoustic or electrical crack monitoring, sheet resistance, PL/EL mapping, and J-V measurements track fracture and electrical loss. A strain-relief mechanism predicts lower initial and cyclic lattice strain, reduced strain concentration, delayed crack initiation, and improved durability even when adhesion is matched. An adhesion mechanism predicts higher peel or fracture energy and less buried-interface delamination, but lattice strain and intrinsic crack onset in the absorber may remain similar. A passivation-dominated mechanism predicts higher initial and retained QFLS/VOC at a given crack density, but it should not substantially delay crack formation or electrode-resistance growth. Cross-sectional failure analysis must identify whether cracks are cohesive in the perovskite, adhesive at the buried contact, or electrical in the transparent electrode. The causal claim is strongest when the mechanical outcome follows the strain or adhesion control rather than simply the initial efficiency.
scoring_key_points: Uses orthogonal passivation-only, adhesion-only, and strain-relief controls with identical device mechanics and encapsulation.
Tracks lattice strain/phase, crack initiation, delamination, electrode resistance, and luminescence during controlled bending.
Distinguishes strain relief by delayed cracking, adhesion by higher interfacial fracture resistance, and passivation by better voltage at matched crack density.
Requires cross-sectional failure localization and tensile/compressive or neutral-axis controls.
accepted_equivalents: Four-point bending, mandrel bending, peel, blister, double-cantilever, or fracture-energy tests
In situ Raman, GIXRD, synchrotron diffraction, digital image correlation, or curvature-based strain measurements
PL/EL, sheet-resistance, acoustic-emission, or conductive-mapping measurements during cycling
Matched encapsulated and unencapsulated mechanical stacks
common_wrong_answers: Attributes improved bending retention to lower residual strain solely because both quantities change together.
Uses final PCE after bending without measuring crack density or delamination.
Compares devices with different encapsulation or neutral-axis positions and assigns the difference to interface chemistry.
Calls retained VOC proof of mechanical integrity even when electrode resistance or crack density has increased.

expected_answer: Scale-up should first control the modifier coverage and chemistry on the low-temperature electron-contact surface before the perovskite is coated. A factorial process matrix should vary surface cleaning, modifier dose, web speed, drying temperature, residence time, SnO2 roughness, web tension, and perovskite drying/anneal conditions. Stop-point coupons should be exfoliated or cross-sectioned so that bottom-specific GIWAXS/XRD, Raman strain mapping, PL/QFLS, AFM, and chemical mapping verify photoactive-phase selection, strain distribution, and defect passivation across and along the web. Reliability must use a four-cell logic: unmodified/unencapsulated, modified/unencapsulated, unmodified/encapsulated, and modified/encapsulated. This separates intrinsic buried-interface benefits from barrier effects and their interaction. Tests should include stabilized MPP at elevated temperature and humidity, damp heat, thermal cycling, repeated bending at multiple radii and directions, and combined bend-plus-humidity/light cycling. Periodic EL/PL, sheet/contact resistance, module insulation and scribe tests, water-vapor ingress mapping, and postmortem phase/strain/adhesion analysis should localize the failure. The buried modifier is credited only for differences that persist in unencapsulated matched devices and correspond to retained bottom-phase, lower strain, lower recombination, or delayed cracking; the barrier is credited for moisture-ingress suppression. Qualification requires low spatial variance, no buried-phase reversion or delamination, stable electrical interconnects, controlled water-vapor transmission, and retained module MPP after combined stresses, not only high initial flexible-cell efficiency.
scoring_key_points: Defines a roll-to-roll process matrix for modifier coverage, web mechanics, and low-temperature perovskite formation.
Uses buried-side structural, strain, chemical, and QFLS mapping across the web rather than top-surface averages.
Uses a modified/unmodified by encapsulated/unencapsulated factorial design to separate intrinsic interface and barrier effects.
Requires combined MPP, humidity, thermal cycling, and bending with module-level electrical and failure-localization criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Exfoliated-interface analysis, cross-sectional nano-diffraction, depth-resolved PL, or Raman strain mapping
A 2×2 interface-modifier and encapsulation experimental design
Bending under illumination/humidity, torsion, or dynamic mechanical cycling in addition to standard environmental tests
EL imaging, water-vapor ingress sensors, insulation resistance, scribe continuity, and postmortem adhesion analysis
common_wrong_answers: Attributes all encapsulated durability to the buried modifier without an encapsulation-only control.
Measures only the top surface and assumes the buried phase is uniform across a roll.
Performs mechanical and environmental tests separately and misses synergistic failure.
Uses small-cell bending retention as sufficient evidence for module interconnect and barrier reliability.

expected_answer: The organic absorber must be compared at equal absorbed ultraviolet and visible photon dose, not merely equal lamp time. A standalone organic cell should therefore be tested behind an optical filter that reproduces the measured tandem-front transmittance, while a dummy-front-stack control reproduces interfaces and thermal mass without generating voltage. Complementary tandems should use a more ultraviolet-transparent front absorber or an external ultraviolet filter, with identical encapsulation and interconnecting layers. Sample temperature, absorbed power, current density, voltage per subcell, and maximum-power condition should be independently controlled so that optical shielding is not confused with reduced electrical or thermal load. Subcell EQE, selective PL or EL, Voc loss, organic spectral bleaching, interconnect resistance, and chemical depth profiles should be tracked during aging. Outdoor transfer requires angle- and spectrum-resolved absorbed-dose calculations, thermal cycling, humidity and oxygen controls, and module-scale PL/EL, sheet-resistance, and edge-degradation maps. Filtering is supported if a spectrally matched external filter reproduces the tandem benefit. Interconnect chemistry is supported if protection persists at matched absorbed dose and depends on the recombination layer. Reduced electrical stress is supported if degradation follows subcell voltage or current rather than ultraviolet dose. Each mechanism is falsified when its defining variable is matched but the stability difference remains.
scoring_key_points: Normalizes aging by absorbed spectral dose and separates optical filtering from lamp time, sample heating, and electrical operating point.
Uses a spectrally matched filtered organic control, dummy front stack, altered front-cell ultraviolet transmission, and identical encapsulation or interconnect controls.
Tracks subcell-resolved optoelectronic and chemical degradation together with interconnect resistance and organic photobleaching.
Extends the protocol to angle, spectrum, temperature, humidity, and module-scale spatial mapping with explicit falsification criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Action-spectrum-weighted ultraviolet dose, absorbed photon dose, or absorbed radiant energy as valid exposure normalization
Neutral-density plus spectral filters or a nonfunctional optical stack that reproduces the front-cell transmittance
Subcell electroluminescence, photoluminescence, derivative EQE, or selective-bias JV for locating degradation
Hyperspectral imaging, lock-in thermography, or distributed module IV analysis as alternatives to PL/EL spatial mapping
common_wrong_answers: Comparing tandem and single-junction devices only by elapsed ultraviolet exposure time
Assuming improved tandem retention proves chemical stabilization of the organic layer without a matched optical-filter control
Extrapolating a glovebox ultraviolet test directly to outdoor module lifetime without angle, heat, humidity, and spatial validation

expected_answer: Sharper out-of-plane scattering can indicate improved average slab alignment and therefore better vertical extraction, but it does not establish a favorable phase distribution through the full thickness. Energy funneling can accelerate transfer from small-n to large-n domains and raise fill factor while carriers ultimately accumulate in the lowest-bandgap region. Because the device quasi-Fermi-level splitting is constrained by the lowest-energy recombination-active phase, a buried high-n or nearly 3D pocket, or a defective contact-adjacent region, can reduce Voc even when top-side GIWAXS and front-side PL look improved. The minimum diagnosis should compare front- and rear-excited absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, excitation-depth-dependent PL and transient absorption, angle- or depth-resolved GIWAXS, and cross-sectional cathodoluminescence or nanoscale diffraction. Electroluminescence spectra, Suns-Voc, ideality factor, and contact-selective stacks should test whether the low-energy emission is electronically connected and recombination active. A buried-phase mechanism is supported by depth-localized low-energy structure and EL from that phase; interface recombination is supported by contact dependence without a corresponding structural phase; a misleading orientation metric is exposed when azimuthal narrowing occurs without improved depth-resolved connectivity or extraction.
scoring_key_points: States that average out-of-plane orientation and fast energy transfer can improve extraction without guaranteeing a favorable vertical n-phase distribution.
Explains that the lowest-bandgap, recombination-active region can pin quasi-Fermi-level splitting and reduce open-circuit voltage.
Uses front/rear or excitation-depth-dependent luminescence and transient measurements together with depth-resolved structural probes.
Provides distinct signatures for buried-phase voltage pinning, contact-driven recombination, and a non-diagnostic average orientation metric.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional cathodoluminescence, confocal spectral mapping, or depth-resolved nano-PL for locating low-energy phases
Grazing-incidence angle series, resonant soft X-ray scattering, or cross-sectional nanodiffraction as depth-sensitive structural methods
Electroluminescence, absolute photoluminescence quantum yield, or implied Voc as probes of the recombination-active bandgap
Selective-contact replacement or insertion of an ultrathin passivation layer as interface-recombination controls
common_wrong_answers: Assuming sharper GIWAXS automatically guarantees higher open-circuit voltage
Treating faster energy transfer as proof that no low-bandgap recombination sink exists
Using only front-side steady-state PL to infer the full vertical phase distribution

expected_answer: The transferable quantity is the competition among solvent evaporation, precursor coordination, nucleation, phase conversion, and vertical transport, not the laboratory recipe itself. A process-window design should vary ink and substrate temperature, solvent and coordinating-solvent activity, wet-film thickness, line speed, coating gap and flow, gas-knife or drying rate, ambient humidity, additive concentration, and annealing ramp. These variables should be organized around measurable timescale ratios such as evaporation time relative to nucleation and phase-conversion time. In situ GIWAXS, absorption or reflectance, and spectrally resolved PL should identify the sequence and orientation of low-n and high-n phases during coating and drying. End-of-line acceptance should include orientation distribution or azimuthal width, front/back phase-sensitive PL, depth-resolved composition, PLQY or implied Voc, sheet resistance, shunt and electroluminescence maps, and statistics along and across the coating direction. Stability tests should combine maximum-power operation, heat, humidity, thermal cycling, and bias, followed by repeated GIWAXS and spectral mapping. Phase reorganization is indicated by changing n-phase signatures or orientation before gross moisture ingress; encapsulation failure is indicated by edge-correlated water or oxygen damage with otherwise unchanged internal phase sequence.
scoring_key_points: Transfers crystallization and drying timescale relationships rather than copying the spin-coating recipe or a single temperature.
Controls coating hydrodynamics, solvent activity, wet-film thickness, evaporation rate, humidity, additive level, and annealing history.
Uses in situ structural and optical probes plus along-web, cross-web, and depth-resolved acceptance metrics for phase and orientation uniformity.
Combines operating and environmental stresses with post-aging phase diagnostics that separate intrinsic phase reorganization from encapsulation failure.
accepted_equivalents: Meniscus, blade, spray, or roll-to-roll coating provided wet residence time and drying kinetics are explicitly controlled
In situ Raman, wide-angle scattering, hyperspectral reflectance, or ellipsometry as alternatives to GIWAXS and PL
Peclet-, Damkohler-, or empirically calibrated evaporation-to-crystallization ratios as process-transfer descriptors
Photoluminescence, electroluminescence, dark-lock-in thermography, or local JV mapping as module-uniformity criteria
common_wrong_answers: Copying the spin-coating additive dose and hot-cast temperature directly into slot-die coating
Accepting a similar normal-incidence XRD pattern as proof of the same vertical phase sequence
Using only shelf stability or final PCE without checking phase redistribution during biased illumination and heat

expected_answer: Time-resolved PL alone is ambiguous because both rapid transfer into the HTL and rapid nonradiative loss at the interface reduce the measured decay. The chemical control set should separate the cation and anion functions: a redox-active cation with a different noncoordinating anion, a redox-inactive PF6 salt, pre-oxidized spiro-OMeTAD without the interfacial anion, and the full additive with and without Li-TFSI. An ultrathin inert spacer or placing the additive away from the perovskite can further separate bulk HTL oxidation from direct interface chemistry. Useful extraction should combine faster quenching with higher absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting in the appropriate selective stack, higher electroluminescence efficiency or lower nonradiative Voc loss, faster photocurrent, improved pseudo-FF, and higher mobility without increased dark recombination. Parasitic quenching gives faster decay but lower PLQY, EL efficiency, Voc, or stronger ideality-factor and dark-current losses. UPS or Kelvin-probe shifts establish energetic changes but are non-unique because dipoles and oxidation both move the work function. A mechanism is credible only if the matched controls and placement experiment reproduce the specific conductivity, energetic, and recombination signatures assigned to each function.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that faster PL decay is non-unique and distinguishes transfer-induced quenching from nonradiative interfacial loss.
Uses matched redox-cation, PF6-anion, pre-oxidized-HTL, Li-free, and spatial-placement controls to isolate the proposed functions.
Combines absolute radiative-quality or implied-voltage measurements with EL, photocurrent, pseudo-JV, mobility, dark-current, and ideality diagnostics.
Treats work-function shifts as supportive but non-decisive and defines opposite signatures for beneficial extraction and parasitic recombination.
accepted_equivalents: Quasi-Fermi-level splitting, absolute PLQY, or external luminescence efficiency as radiative-quality metrics
Transient photocurrent, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or charge-extraction measurements as transfer diagnostics
A ferrocene derivative with another anion and an alkali PF6 salt as acceptable function-separating controls
An insulating monolayer, remote-doping geometry, or bilayer HTL as a spatial-separation experiment
common_wrong_answers: Equating shorter TRPL lifetime with better extraction without measuring radiative efficiency or device recombination
Using only conductivity and work-function shifts to claim interfacial passivation
Comparing the full additive only with an untreated device and assigning all changes to one mechanism

expected_answer: The additive should be placed selectively in the Sn precursor, the Pb precursor, both precursors, and a post-deposition treatment, while total ionic strength and solvent composition are matched. Antisolvent timing, drying rate, and annealing duration should be varied, and films should be arrested immediately before antisolvent, just after antisolvent, during early conversion, and after annealing. In situ GIWAXS or XRD, absorption, and scattering should resolve the onset and growth rates of Sn-rich and Pb-rich crystalline intermediates. Stage-resolved cross-sectional ToF-SIMS, EDS, or isotopically labelled A-site or halide tracers should reveal when the vertical Sn/Pb profile becomes uniform. Selective kinetic slowing is supported if the Sn-containing additive changes the initial nucleation sequence, suppresses the early Sn-rich surface before annealing, and loses effectiveness when antisolvent timing bypasses the interaction window. Post-deposition redistribution is supported if early phase formation and gradients are unchanged but flatten progressively with annealing, accompanied by measurable tracer diffusion. Oxygen-free versus controlled-oxygen processing and sulfate or hydrazinium analogues should be included so reduced Sn oxidation is not mistaken for a crystallization-rate effect.
scoring_key_points: Uses selective additive placement in Sn, Pb, both, and post-treatment configurations with matched solvent and ionic-strength controls.
Arrests films at multiple coating and annealing stages while varying antisolvent timing or drying rate.
Combines in situ phase-formation kinetics with stage-resolved depth composition or tracer measurements.
Defines opposite temporal signatures for early kinetic matching and late ion redistribution and controls separately for Sn oxidation.
accepted_equivalents: Rapid thermal quenching, freeze-quenching, or solvent extraction as acceptable methods for arresting intermediate stages
In situ GIWAXS, time-resolved XRD, optical scattering, or synchrotron reflectivity for crystallization kinetics
Isotopic iodide, deuterated organic cations, or element-specific X-ray fluorescence as tracer alternatives
Hydrazinium salt without sulfate and sulfate salt without hydrazinium as acceptable interaction controls
common_wrong_answers: Inferring kinetic regulation only from the uniform composition of the fully annealed film
Using a single post-annealing ToF-SIMS profile without intermediate-time measurements
Ignoring the possibility that lower Sn4+ concentration changes nucleation signals without directly homogenizing Sn/Pb distribution

expected_answer: The dominant pathway is mechanically initiated loss of buried contact rather than wholesale bulk decomposition. Repeated strain concentrates at the weak SnO2/perovskite junction, nucleating interfacial gaps or delamination. The reduced electrically active contact area and longer lateral transport paths raise contact/series resistance and impair extraction, so fill factor and collected current fall even if the absorber's bulk crystal structure remains largely intact. A convincing diagnosis requires three orthogonal classes of evidence: direct mechanical localization of failure by peel/exfoliation, lap-shear, cross-sectional imaging, or fracture-surface analysis; electrical localization by post-bend series/contact resistance and impedance or spatial photocurrent mapping; and bulk-negative controls showing little change in bulk diffraction, absorption, morphology, or composition. Agreement among these measurements separates delamination-driven electrical loss from bulk cracking or new bulk defect chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Identifies strain-driven SnO2/perovskite contact loss or delamination as the dominant failure mode, not bulk decomposition.
Connects lost contact area to higher contact/series resistance, poorer extraction, and preferential losses in fill factor and collected current.
Requires direct mechanical or spatial localization of the failure, such as peel/exfoliation, lap-shear, fracture-surface, cross-sectional, or photocurrent mapping evidence.
Uses unchanged bulk structural/optical/compositional probes as negative controls to rule out bulk cracking or chemically generated bulk defects.
accepted_equivalents: Interfacial debonding, buried-contact separation, or cohesive-versus-adhesive fracture language for delamination.
Contact-resistance growth, current-crowding, extraction-area loss, or transport-path elongation for the electrical consequence.
Any genuinely orthogonal combination of mechanical localization, electrical localization, and bulk-negative controls.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the loss only to bulk perovskite decomposition despite unchanged bulk probes.
Claiming that a change in photoluminescence alone proves mechanical delamination.
Discussing adhesion improvement without explaining the selective current/fill-factor and series-resistance signatures.

expected_answer: The transfer should be treated as a bounded interfacial-coverage problem, not as a simple concentration scale-up. A designed experiment should vary areal dose, solution concentration, solvent, coating speed, wet-film residence time, drying/annealing, oxide surface state, and subsequent precursor contact time. The accepted window should produce a thin, laterally uniform, interfacially localized layer without secondary-phase formation, excess residual precursor, or measurable transport resistance. Qualification must verify both functions: adhesion/fracture mode and residual-stress relief on the mechanical side, and defect density, energy-level alignment, recombination, and extraction/contact resistance on the electronic side. Module-specific checks should map coating thickness, photocurrent, electroluminescence, series resistance, shunts, and P1-P2-P3 scribe damage across the web. Final go/no-go testing should combine maximum-power operation with cyclic bending and then add thermal and humidity stresses, followed by failure localization; a linker that passes isolated bending but fails under simultaneous bias, light, and strain should not be accepted.
scoring_key_points: Defines a multivariable areal-dose/process window rather than directly copying a small-cell solution concentration.
Sets dual-function acceptance criteria covering adhesion/stress and passivation/energy alignment/charge extraction without added resistance or crystallization damage.
Includes area-resolved module uniformity and interconnect/scribe diagnostics, not only champion-cell efficiency.
Requires combined operational-mechanical testing, with thermal/humidity extensions and post-stress failure localization for go/no-go decisions.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, gravure, blade, spray, or other continuous-coating variables may replace roll-to-roll terminology if areal coverage is controlled.
Photoluminescence, electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, LBIC, or impedance mapping are acceptable module-uniformity tools.
Combined bending-under-MPP, light-soak-under-strain, or equivalent coupled-stress protocols.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing the highest linker concentration because it maximizes chemical interaction.
Qualifying the process only by initial PCE or a single adhesion measurement.
Ignoring module scribes, web-scale nonuniformity, or simultaneous light-bias-bending stress.

expected_answer: A scalable window should independently control modifier concentration, pH or acid activity, wet-film thickness, coating speed, residence time before drying, solvent orthogonality, drying rate, and post-treatment temperature. Beneficial treatment should reduce roughness and damaged-grain density only near the top surface, preserve bulk absorption/composition and bulk XRD, and avoid thickness-dependent series resistance. Depth profiling and surface-sensitive diffraction or spectroscopy should confirm that the molecule remains localized at the perovskite/ETL junction and still coordinates the perovskite while interacting with the selected ETL. Large-area qualification should map roughness, composition, work function, PL/EL, contact resistance, shunts, and photovoltaic parameters across coating lanes and interconnect regions. Reliability should compare under-treated, optimal, and over-treated modules under MPP light soaking, humidity, and thermal stress; failure analysis must determine whether degradation begins by chemical etching, loss of the molecular bridge, ETL delamination, or transport-barrier growth.
scoring_key_points: Controls acid activity, areal dose, residence/drying, solvent, and temperature as independent scale-up variables.
Defines surface-localized benefit by smoother/top-surface structural improvement with preserved bulk structure, composition, and optical response.
Verifies interfacial localization, dual-side chemistry, energy alignment, and absence of thickness-induced transport resistance across large area.
Uses under/optimal/over-treatment controls in MPP, humidity, and thermal tests with spatially resolved post-failure diagnosis.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, gravure, spray, or meniscus coating may substitute for slot-die if wet-film residence and areal dose are addressed.
GIWAXS at grazing incidence, XPS depth profiling, ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved spectroscopy, or equivalent surface-localization methods.
EL/PL imaging, LBIC, thermography, or impedance mapping as large-area qualification tools.
common_wrong_answers: Using bulk XRD improvement alone to claim successful surface polishing.
Maximizing acidity to obtain the smoothest AFM image without testing stoichiometry or resistance.
Reporting only average module PCE without lane-to-lane or interconnect spatial mapping.

expected_answer: The fullerene should be redesigned with low-temperature crosslinkable groups, for example photochemical, click, latent-catalyst, or room-temperature network-forming functionality, while retaining the conjugated electron-accepting core and avoiding reagents that attack the substrate or SnO2. Crosslink density and thickness must be optimized rather than maximized. Solvent resistance should be proven before and after exposure to the actual perovskite solvent system using ellipsometry or profilometry, UV-visible absorbance, AFM, and carbon-depth profiling; a noncrosslinked fullerene control is essential. Ion blocking should then be tested under bias and illumination by time-resolved ToF-SIMS or isotope tracing, together with dark-recovery and impedance measurements that track recombination resistance. Electronic selectivity must be checked by UPS/Kelvin probe, electron-only transport, contact resistance, J-V/EQE, and thickness sweeps. Finally, flexible devices should undergo bending while operating at MPP, because a cracked barrier that performs well only when flat would not be a valid transfer.
scoring_key_points: Proposes a credible low-temperature crosslink chemistry that preserves the fullerene's electron-selective core and substrate compatibility.
Demonstrates solvent-wash retention using thickness/morphology/absorbance or depth-profile measurements against a noncrosslinked control.
Validates ion blocking under electrical/optical stress with depth profiling or tracing plus burn-in/dark-recovery and recombination diagnostics.
Optimizes thickness/crosslink density for band alignment and electron transport, then includes bending-under-MPP validation.
accepted_equivalents: UV, visible-light, electron-beam, chemical-click, or catalyst-assisted low-temperature crosslinking.
Ellipsometry, QCM, profilometry, UV-vis, XPS/ToF-SIMS, or AFM evidence of film retention after DMF/DMSO exposure.
Electron mobility, conductivity, SCLC, transfer resistance, or contact-resistivity measurements for transport bottlenecks.
common_wrong_answers: Simply lowering the original cure temperature without demonstrating that crosslinking still occurs.
Using initial PCE as the only proof of ion blocking.
Maximizing barrier thickness without considering electron transport or cracking during bending.

expected_answer: A high contact angle describes surface wetting at one time scale; it does not quantify water-vapor permeation, sorption, pinhole transport, interfacial adhesion, or protection after thermal/light aging. Likewise, champion small-cell efficiency can hide coating nonuniformity and a narrow thickness window. Transfer should begin with coating-rheology and drying studies, followed by area-resolved thickness, pinhole, roughness, PL/EL, sheet/contact resistance, and shunt mapping. A thickness sweep must establish the range over which the undoped polymer maintains adequate hole conductivity, energy-selective extraction, and fill factor without excessive series resistance. Moisture protection should be measured by water uptake or vapor transmission/permeation through realistic stacks, including aged and flexed samples, rather than inferred from contact angle. Reliability should compare dopant-free polymer and doped-spiro modules under MPP illumination, humidity, thermal cycling or heat, and electrode-compatible stress, with statistical yield and postmortem analysis for ion migration, delamination, electrode reaction, and pinhole-driven ingress.
scoring_key_points: Explains that contact angle does not measure water-vapor transport, sorption, pinholes, aged adhesion, or full-stack moisture protection.
Requires large-area coating/yield diagnostics for thickness, pinholes, roughness, shunts, and spatial photo/electroluminescence or resistance.
Defines an electrical thickness-tolerance window using conductivity/mobility, energy selectivity, contact resistance, series resistance, and fill factor.
Uses realistic moisture-permeation and multi-stress MPP/thermal/humidity testing with statistical module yield and postmortem failure analysis.
accepted_equivalents: WVTR, gravimetric sorption, calcium test, impedance moisture sensor, or equivalent permeation/uptake measurements.
LBIC, EL/PL imaging, thermography, sheet-resistance, or contact-resistivity mapping.
Damp heat, thermal cycling, heat plus MPP, or humidity plus illumination as realistic reliability stresses.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the most hydrophobic surface is automatically the best moisture barrier.
Using only champion-cell PCE and a single nominal HTM thickness.
Ignoring pinholes, module yield, electrode reactions, or long-term transport changes.

expected_answer: Holding pyridine fraction constant controls the nominal density of nitrogen coordination sites, so a performance difference between linkage isomers points to connectivity-dependent backbone geometry, segmental regularity, orientation, and accessibility rather than merely more Lewis-base sites. Direct Pb-N passivation should be tested with monomer/oligomer models by NMR, FTIR, or XPS after PbI2 exposure, and with blocked, protonated, or sterically shielded pyridine analogues. A particularly clean test treats an already formed perovskite with the polymers, minimizing changes in nucleation while retaining possible surface coordination. Wetting-mediated crystallization should be isolated using inert surface-energy-matched underlayers or additives that reproduce contact angle and spreading without pyridine coordination, followed by in situ optical/GIWAXS measurements of nucleation and growth. Trap density, defect imaging, PL/extraction, and device metrics should then be compared in a factorial design. The correct conclusion may be that both pathways contribute, but their incremental effects must be experimentally separated.
scoring_key_points: States that equal pyridine content controls coordination-site density, making linkage-dependent conformation/accessibility the key variable.
Tests direct Pb-N interaction with model compounds or coordination-blocked analogues and chemical spectroscopy, ideally on preformed perovskite.
Tests wetting/crystallization with surface-energy-matched noncoordinating controls and time-resolved nucleation/crystallization measurements.
Uses factorial downstream trap, defect, extraction, and device measurements and allows both mechanisms to contribute.
accepted_equivalents: 3,5- versus 2,5-linkage, meta-versus-ortho connectivity, or positional-isomer language.
NMR/FTIR/XPS/Raman or calorimetric binding measurements for Pb-N interaction.
In situ GIWAXS, optical microscopy, interferometry, or precursor-spreading/nucleation kinetics for crystallization control.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming the better polymer simply contains more pyridine when the fraction is fixed.
Using contact angle alone to prove Pb-N passivation.
Using only post-formation XRD, which cannot distinguish nucleation control from later defect passivation.

expected_answer:
The molecular design cannot be transferred by assuming that the same ions will partition identically in a different stack. The cation must have controlled solubility and diffusivity through the chosen fullerene, sufficient affinity for Pb/I defect environments, and a steric size that limits rather than drives destructive low-dimensional conversion. The anion must bind or electronically couple to the new fullerene and electrode, shift the contact work function in the required direction, and remain chemically stable against Cu, ITO, or other cathode species. Hydroxyl density, ion-pair strength, counterion mobility, and molecular dipole should be tuned together; excessive mobility can cause drift, whereas excessive binding can trap the additive at the top surface.

The process window should map solvent activity, dose, coating time, fullerene thickness, drying rate, and temperature. A large-area method must produce spatially uniform infiltration without dissolving the perovskite or roughening the fullerene. Depth-resolved ToF-SIMS or equivalent profiling across multiple module positions should verify cation transport toward the absorber and anion retention near the cathode. GIWAXS should confirm only self-limited low-dimensional phase formation, while UPS/Kelvin-probe mapping and electron-only contact-resistance measurements should show the intended cathode alignment. PLQY/QFLS, trap-density, and ion-migration tests must independently confirm that absorber-side passivation survives the transfer.

Hydrophilicity must be managed as a transport and packaging problem, not denied. The lowest effective hydroxyl content and treatment dose should be used, residual solvent and unbound ionic species should be removed, and a dense top contact or barrier layer should restrict water and metal diffusion without cancelling the electronic dipole. Encapsulation and edge seals should be selected using water-vapor transmission and ion-permeation data. Bias-plus-humidity testing is essential because an ionically mobile, hydrophilic interlayer may behave differently under an electric field than in dark storage.

A go decision requires uniform large-area contact potential, low contact resistance, high QFLS, no S-shaped cells at module scale, and no evidence of additive or metal migration after thermal, damp-heat, and MPP stress. The treatment should be rejected or redesigned if the new electrode does not interact favorably with the anion, if cation penetration becomes nonuniform, if a thick insulating phase forms, or if moisture stability depends entirely on encapsulation while the interlayer itself accelerates water uptake or corrosion.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes cation diffusivity/defect affinity and anion-fullerene/electrode energetics for the new contact rather than assuming unchanged self-separation.
Maps dose, solvent, fullerene thickness, drying, and area uniformity and verifies depth partitioning, limited phase formation, contact energetics, and absorber passivation independently.
Treats hydroxyl-induced hydrophilicity as a moisture/ion-transport risk and uses minimum effective functionality, barrier design, and bias-plus-humidity testing.
Sets go/no-go criteria based on module-uniform contact selectivity, recombination, migration, corrosion, and stressed depth profiles rather than initial PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: C60, PCBM derivatives, or another fullerene acceptor may be used if the answer explicitly re-establishes molecular binding and energy-level alignment.
Cu, Ag, ITO, or another cathode is acceptable provided metal-specific redox and diffusion risks are tested.
A less hydrophilic hydrogen-bond donor or protected hydroxyl that is activated after deposition is an acceptable molecular redesign.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the lower water contact angle is harmless because the original small cells were stable.
Using only surface UPS and concluding that the ions are correctly partitioned through the full stack.
Copying the original treatment concentration to a new fullerene/electrode pair without testing chemical interaction, corrosion, or area uniformity.

expected_answer:
The trigger should be tied to the state of crystallization, not to a fixed number of seconds. A scalable criterion can combine solvent fraction, film temperature, optical-emission trajectory, and the onset of PbI2/perovskite diffraction. The useful window is reached after the primary perovskite network has formed enough to avoid void generation but while PbI2 remains mobile and the film is still capable of grain-boundary reorganization. Dimensionless measures such as treatment time divided by the local solvent-evaporation or crystallization time are more transferable than the one-minute small-cell value. Web speed, substrate temperature, gas flow, wet thickness, and ambient humidity must therefore be used to predict and then verify the local window.

Delivery should be metered against the measured excess-PbI2 inventory. A uniform spray, slot, vapor, or secondary meniscus can be synchronized to the web position, with closed-loop control from in-line reflectance/PL or compact diffraction. The solvent activity must be high enough to mobilize a controlled fraction of PbI2 but low enough to avoid redissolving the primary perovskite. Quantum-dot concentration, droplet or coating mass, residence time, and subsequent annealing must be mapped as a response surface. Edge regions and heater nonuniformity require separate monitoring because the same clock time can correspond to different crystallization states.

Mechanism validation at scale should include a Pb mass balance from coated film and extracted liquid, spatial mapping of residual PbI2 and QD-derived elements, and time-resolved or line-scan evidence of secondary grain coalescence. Too-early treatment should be rejected if it creates voids, compositional gradients, or shunts; too-late treatment should be rejected if QDs remain as a surface layer or PbI2 is unchanged. Excess dose should also be rejected if Cs/Cl/Er incorporation shifts the bandgap, creates insulating residues, or increases ionic conductivity. Module-scale EL/PL and dark-lock-in thermography should demonstrate that improvements are not confined to small regions.

The final qualification must include MPP operation, humidity/heat, UV/visible-light exposure, and bias-driven ion-migration tests because residual PbI2 and incorporated ions can change under illumination. Acceptance requires reproducible module yield, low hysteresis and hot-spot density, uniform residual-PbI2 content, and stability gains that track the correctly timed process window. A process that merely removes PbI2 nonuniformly and raises average PCE while increasing local shunts or compositional drift should fail the transfer.
scoring_key_points: Replaces fixed clock time with a state-based crystallization criterion tied to solvent loss, temperature, optical/diffraction signals, and local process time scales.
Controls reactive dose and solvent activity relative to excess-PbI2 inventory and maps web-speed, thickness, humidity, and thermal nonuniformity.
Uses Pb mass balance, spatial phase/element mapping, secondary-growth evidence, and explicit too-early/too-late/overdose rejection signatures.
Qualifies the module by spatial yield, hot spots, hysteresis, MPP and multi-stress stability, not average initial PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: In-line PL, reflectometry, Raman, XRD/GIWAXS, or another state-sensitive signal is acceptable for triggering the treatment.
Spray, vapor, curtain, slot, or meniscus delivery is acceptable if local dose and solvent exposure are quantitatively controlled.
A kinetic model using Damkohler-, Peclet-, or evaporation-to-crystallization time ratios is acceptable as the scalable process criterion.
common_wrong_answers: Applying the treatment exactly one minute after coating at every web speed and film thickness.
Judging uniformity from a few cut-cell efficiencies while ignoring edge regions, local shunts, and residual-PbI2 maps.
Increasing QD dose until the PbI2 peak disappears without checking compositional drift, lattice incorporation, or solvent damage.

expected_answer:
The four conditions should be: untreated control; rear-perovskite treatment with an anion or analogue that reproduces vacancy/Pb coordination but does not modify carbon; carbon treatment with a cation or analogue that reproduces the carbon work-function shift but does not enter the perovskite; and the complete dual treatment. The two single-component treatments must be dosed so that their respective surface-potential shifts match those produced by the full compound. Morphology, crystallinity, carbon thickness, and optical generation should be held constant, because the claim concerns selectivity and electrostatics rather than light absorption or grain growth.

On the perovskite side, UPS/Kelvin probe and surface-potential mapping should quantify the rear-surface Fermi-level shift; XPS or vibrational spectroscopy should verify vacancy/Pb interaction; and PLQY-derived QFLS or calibrated electroluminescence should quantify non-radiative loss before carbon deposition. On the carbon side, Kelvin probe or ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy should quantify the electrode work-function change, while carbon/perovskite contact-resistance and hole-only measurements should test extraction. Cross-sectional potential profiling under illumination is especially valuable because a back-surface field is an operating electrostatic property, not simply a dark work-function number.

At the device level, Voc and FF should respond most strongly, with little change in EQE-integrated Jsc if optical generation is unchanged. Light-intensity Voc, dark J-V, transient photovoltage/current, and EIS should separate recombination from transport: the perovskite-only treatment should increase QFLS and recombination resistance but may leave a contact barrier; the carbon-only treatment should lower contact resistance and improve FF but leave absorber-side defect loss; the dual treatment should do both. Simulation using the measured energy shifts can test whether the combined field reproduces the observed QFLS and recombination-current reduction.

Synergy means that the dual device exceeds the additive expectation of the two single treatments in a physically linked metric such as rear-interface recombination current, QFLS-to-Voc transfer, or contact selectivity, not merely that it has the highest PCE. The strongest evidence would be restoration of a steep rear potential gradient, simultaneous increase of recombination resistance and decrease of transport resistance, and a Voc/FF gain that cannot be reproduced by either single treatment at matched surface-potential shift. If the full result equals the sum of generic chemical passivation and lower series resistance, the term dual back-surface-field is not necessary.
scoring_key_points: Defines untreated, perovskite-only, carbon-only, and dual conditions with matched electronic shifts and controlled morphology/optics.
Measures rear-perovskite Fermi level, defect interaction, QFLS/recombination and carbon work function/contact resistance separately.
Predicts distinct single-component outcomes and a dual outcome dominated by Voc/FF, higher recombination resistance, and lower transport resistance with little optical-Jsc change.
Defines synergy using a non-additive operating-field/selectivity or recombination metric rather than highest PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Separate salts, covalently tethered analogues, or selective pre-treatments may be used to isolate the anion and cation functions.
Operando Kelvin probe, cross-sectional KPFM, electroabsorption, or another justified potential-profile measurement may establish the rear field.
QFLS, saturation-current density, interface recombination velocity, or selectivity factor are acceptable metrics for non-additive synergy.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the full treatment synergistic simply because its PCE is higher than either single control.
Using only XPS binding-energy shifts and not measuring carbon work function, QFLS, or contact resistance.
Interpreting a Jsc increase as proof of a back-surface field without controlling optical generation and collection.

expected_answer:
The transfer should be built around coupled diffusion, charge-transfer reaction, and film densification. Dopant infiltration length scales approximately with the square root of diffusivity times exposure time, but diffusivity depends strongly on host free volume, temperature, solvent-vapor activity, dopant size, and host-dopant binding. The exposure must swell the HTL enough for the dopant to traverse the target thickness without dissolving the underlying perovskite or leaving a persistent plasticized layer. The following condensation step must remove free volume and residual solvent while preserving the desired oxidation state and preventing dopant back-diffusion or crystallization.

A process map should vary deposited dopant dose, vapor activity, exposure time, temperature, HTL thickness, and condensation conditions. Under-doping is defined by an undoped region near the perovskite, high vertical resistance, and shallow oxidation; over-doping is defined by dopant aggregation, excessive charge-transfer complex formation, optical absorption loss, interfacial quenching, or reduced mobility from Coulombic/energetic disorder. A new host/dopant pair must have sufficient redox driving force for stable p-doping but not so much that it causes irreversible chemical degradation, and both components must be compatible with the perovskite and metal electrode.

In-line controls can include film thickness, solvent-vapor concentration, optical absorption associated with the oxidized host or dopant anion, work-function mapping, and contactless sheet resistance. These are necessary but not sufficient. Periodic depth-resolved audits using ToF-SIMS/XPS, FTIR/Raman, and etched UPS must verify uniform composition and energy levels through the full thickness. Cross-plane hole-only devices and spatial current mapping should be linked statistically to the in-line signals. Large-area acceptance requires low within-web and web-to-web variation, no residual solvent, and no surface-enriched dopant layer that can be hidden by a good sheet-resistance value.

Replacement of conventional ionic dopants requires mechanism-relevant stability evidence: conductivity and depth-profile retention after heat; resistance to humid air and iodide exposure; suppression of metal diffusion; stable morphology under thermal cycling; and long-duration MPP under light and temperature with oxygen/moisture conditions appropriate to the intended package. Post-stress ToF-SIMS, work-function, cross-plane transport, and device-recombination measurements should show that the molecular dopant remains uniformly distributed and that the condensed HTL continues to act as a dense barrier. The process should not pass merely because an unencapsulated cell survives in nitrogen; it should demonstrate a reproducible lifetime and manufacturing-yield advantage over LiTFSI/tBP or another relevant baseline.
