scoring_key_points: Defines the scale-up through coupled infiltration length, redox/doping reaction, solvent swelling, and condensation rather than copying exposure time.
Maps under-doping and over-doping boundaries across dose, vapor activity, temperature, thickness, and host/dopant compatibility.
Combines in-line optical/work-function/resistance controls with periodic depth chemical/energetic and cross-plane transport audits.
Requires post-stress retention of dopant uniformity, conductivity, barrier function, and MPP performance under heat, humidity/iodide, and metal-diffusion stresses versus a conventional baseline.
accepted_equivalents: A Fickian diffusion-reaction model, a swelling-front model, or empirical design-of-experiments map is acceptable if it predicts through-thickness uniformity.
Roll-to-roll vapor, spatial atomic/molecular deposition, controlled solvent annealing, or another continuous implantation method is acceptable.
NiOx, polymeric HTLs, small-molecule HTLs, or other hosts may be proposed if redox compatibility, solvent tolerance, and interfacial stability are revalidated.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling exposure time linearly with HTL thickness without considering diffusivity, swelling, or reaction kinetics.
Using sheet resistance alone as proof of depth-uniform doping.
Claiming superior stability from nitrogen-only operation while omitting humidity, iodide, metal-diffusion, residual-solvent, and post-stress depth-profile tests.

expected_answer:
Strong steady-state PL quenching is mechanistically ambiguous because it only shows that the radiative population is depleted. That depletion may arise from productive electron transfer into SnO2, but it can also arise from faster Shockley-Read-Hall recombination at new interface states, optical interference, different perovskite thickness, or altered grain morphology. The assignment therefore requires a substrate- and timescale-resolved evidence matrix rather than a single PL comparison.

First, separate intrinsic film quality from transport-contact extraction. Perovskite should be deposited under matched thickness and crystallization conditions on an electronically inert substrate, on untreated SnO2, and on hydroxylated SnO2. Absolute PLQY and time-resolved PL on the inert substrate report bulk and surface non-radiative loss without an extracting contact. If hydroxyl chemistry primarily passivates defects or improves morphology, the inert or insulating stack should show a higher PLQY and a longer slow-component lifetime. On the electron-contact stack, productive extraction may shorten the early-time PL decay even while absolute PLQY of the complete film/contact system decreases. The decisive interpretation is therefore not simply 'shorter lifetime equals better' but a combination of improved intrinsic radiative quality on a non-extracting reference and a new fast extraction component only when SnO2 is electronically connected. Front- and back-side excitation, identical optical stacks, and thickness normalization are needed to exclude optical artifacts.

Second, directly measure charge-transfer kinetics and selectivity. Femtosecond or nanosecond transient absorption can track decay of perovskite bleach and appearance or persistence of electrons in the oxide; transient photocurrent, time-of-flight, or impedance measurements should show faster collection and lower interfacial transfer resistance. Electron-only SCLC can support lower electron-trap density, but it must be complemented by dark current and leakage measurements because an apparent trap-filled-limit shift can also reflect mobility or injection-barrier changes. Quasi-Fermi-level splitting or absolute electroluminescence/PL under one-sun-equivalent excitation should increase if non-radiative recombination is genuinely reduced; a quenched PL signal accompanied by lower QFLS or lower Voc would instead implicate parasitic recombination.

Third, verify the electronic and chemical cause. UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements should show a reproducible work-function or conduction-band alignment shift, while XPS/EPR or an oxygen-vacancy-sensitive probe should show lower vacancy-related defect density. Hydroxyl incorporation should be confirmed independently by vibrational spectroscopy or isotopic labeling. To isolate hydrogen-bond-assisted coupling from generic wetting, include controls that reproduce the contact angle without adding hydroxyl coordination, and controls in which hydroxyls are capped, exchanged, or thermally removed while morphology is held as constant as possible. Conversely, prepare morphology-matched films by adjusting solvent or nucleation conditions on untreated SnO2.

Finally, the device-level observables must close the causal loop: higher QFLS/Voc, lower ideality factor or recombination resistance, faster extraction, reduced hysteresis, and improved FF should appear together without increased leakage. If grain size and coverage change, spatial PL/photocurrent mapping and buried-interface microscopy should determine whether performance follows local contact chemistry or merely morphology. A credible assignment to a chemically modified buried interface requires orthogonal evidence for hydroxyl chemistry, defect suppression, favorable energetic alignment, productive transfer kinetics, and recombination reduction, with wetting-only and morphology-only controls failing to reproduce the full signature.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that PL quenching is non-unique and can represent productive extraction, non-radiative recombination, or optical/morphological differences.
Uses inert-substrate versus extracting-contact PLQY/TRPL and direct transient charge-transfer measurements to separate intrinsic passivation from extraction.
Requires orthogonal chemical/energetic evidence and wetting-matched, hydroxyl-blocked, or morphology-matched controls to isolate the interfacial mechanism.
Closes the assignment with consistent QFLS/Voc, recombination, leakage, hysteresis, and collection signatures rather than relying on one spectroscopy result.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, terahertz spectroscopy, surface photovoltage, transient photocurrent, or impedance-based transfer-resistance measurements are acceptable direct extraction probes.
Absolute PLQY-derived QFLS, electroluminescence quantum efficiency, Suns-Voc, or equivalent non-radiative voltage-loss measurements are acceptable recombination diagnostics.
EPR, XPS defect components, positron annihilation, deep-level spectroscopy, or equivalent oxygen-vacancy/trap probes are acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Treats stronger PL quenching or a shorter TRPL lifetime as automatic proof of improved electron extraction.
Uses only device PCE and grain-size data, without a non-extracting reference or direct transfer/recombination diagnostic.
Attributes the result solely to energy-level alignment while ignoring wetting, optical-stack, thickness, leakage, and morphology confounders.

expected_answer:
The transfer cannot be treated as a simple increase in UV dose or as a small-cell recipe copied over a larger area. Hydroxyl coverage is a process variable with a finite optimum. Insufficient treatment leaves oxygen-vacancy-rich, poorly wetting regions; excessive treatment can change surface charge, adsorb water, alter precursor chemistry, increase interfacial ionic reactivity, or create an insulating/hydrophilic layer. Mixed-cation formulations may also respond differently from MAPbI3 because precursor coordination, solvent residence time, and thermal stability change. The process must therefore control dose, surface state, coating response, and subsequent storage between treatment and perovskite deposition.

At the web-processing stage, UV intensity, spectral distribution, exposure time, line speed, oxygen/humidity, substrate temperature, and treatment-to-coating delay should be logged and mapped. In-line or rapid at-line measurements should include contact angle or surface-energy mapping, Kelvin-probe/work-function mapping, optical or XPS-correlated hydroxyl/defect proxies, SnO2 thickness/uniformity, ITO sheet resistance, and web tension/roughness. A dose-response design should identify a plateau where work function, wetting, and defect metrics are uniform without increased water uptake or conductivity loss. The perovskite coating should then be monitored by optical coherence/interferometry, hyperspectral imaging, or machine-vision thickness and drying maps, because a modified surface can shift the nucleation window and create cross-web gradients. Coupon-level buried-interface microscopy, PL/QFLS mapping, and adhesion testing should be tied to web coordinates.

The module experiment needs orthogonal controls. At minimum it should include untreated SnO2, optimally treated SnO2, an overtreated condition, and a wetting-matched chemical control that does not reproduce the electronic modification. Identical P1-P2-P3 geometry and dead area are required. Cell-to-module analysis should separate active-area efficiency from aperture efficiency and quantify subcell Voc, series resistance, shunt resistance, interconnect resistance, current mismatch, and spatial electroluminescence/lock-in thermography. If the treatment is truly scalable, the distribution—not only the champion—of subcell and module metrics should narrow or remain unchanged across web position and production lots.

Mechanical qualification must distinguish cohesive cracking of brittle electrodes/ETLs, interfacial delamination, perovskite fracture, and interconnect failure. Test several bending radii and orientations under cyclic tension and compression, monitor resistance and electroluminescence during cycling rather than only before/after, and use cross-sectional or acoustic/optical failure analysis. A chemically improved interface may preserve Voc but cannot compensate for ITO or scribe cracking; conversely, better adhesion may reduce delamination without proving electronic passivation. Neutral-axis design and encapsulation should be fixed or factorially controlled.

Environmental and operational qualification should combine one-sun MPP tracking with elevated temperature, damp heat or controlled humidity, thermal cycling, UV exposure, and mechanical cycling, because hydroxylated oxides can interact with moisture and heat. Include dark-storage controls to separate photo-bias effects from hydrolysis, and compare sealed versus unsealed samples to identify encapsulation dependence. Failure criteria should include maximum allowed drift in work function/contact resistance, no new shunt hotspots or delamination, bounded PCE and FF loss, stable subcell mismatch, and reproducible retention over multiple modules. A claim of scalable mechanical durability requires uniform surface chemistry and coating over module area, statistically stable module yield, mechanistically assigned failure modes, and retained performance under combined operational-environmental-mechanical stress—not merely a high initial aperture PCE or a single bending-cycle result.
scoring_key_points: Treats hydroxyl coverage as a bounded process window and controls UV dose, atmosphere, delay time, surface energy, work function, and web-scale uniformity.
Uses untreated, optimal, overtreated, and wetting-matched controls plus spatial module diagnostics to separate contact chemistry from coating and interconnect losses.
Separates mechanical failure modes through radius/orientation-dependent in-situ resistance or imaging and controls neutral-axis/encapsulation variables.
Requires combined MPP, thermal, humidity/UV, and bending qualification with statistical module-yield and explicit electrical/physical failure criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Corona/plasma dose mapping may replace UV mapping if the same hydroxylated surface state is the intended scalable treatment.
Electroluminescence, photoluminescence, lock-in thermography, LBIC, or equivalent spatial diagnostics may be used to localize subcell and interconnect loss.
Four-point-probe, transfer-length, impedance, or contact-resistivity measurements are acceptable ways to monitor contact/interconnect degradation.
common_wrong_answers: Proposes simply increasing UV exposure for a larger web without defining an optimum or checking water uptake and spatial uniformity.
Uses only repeated bending at one radius and a final PCE measurement, without distinguishing electrode, scribe, interface, and absorber failure.
Claims scalability from one champion module while ignoring aperture loss, yield distribution, cross-web gradients, and combined environmental operation.

expected_answer:
A three-function molecule requires controls that vary the functions independently or as nearly independently as synthetic chemistry permits. PCBM is a useful baseline but cannot isolate any one contribution. The minimum convincing matrix should include: a non-coordinating analog with similar fullerene core, side-chain volume, and LUMO but phenyl or otherwise Lewis-inactive groups; a coordinating pyridyl analog with reduced steric bulk or different substitution geometry; and, ideally, a sterically matched analog whose hydrophilicity is adjusted without adding a Pb-binding nitrogen site. If possible, mono-, di-, and blocked-pyridine variants provide a coordination-density series. The controls should be compared at matched film thickness, solvent history, molecular purity, and perovskite surface composition.

Steric/cohesion effects should be assigned using GIWAXS, grazing-incidence scattering, AFM, calorimetry or glass-transition measurements, molecular-dynamics/non-bonded interaction calculations, and thermal/photoaging of neat ETL films. The relevant signatures are suppressed large-scale aggregation, stable roughness and conductivity, and preserved lateral/vertical electron transport after aging. Chelation should be demonstrated by binding-energy calculations plus direct spectroscopic perturbation of Pb-rich surfaces: XPS core-level shifts, FTIR/Raman or NMR changes, desorption energetics, and preferably a competition or site-blocking experiment. Chelation should correlate with lower interfacial trap density, higher PLQY/QFLS on a non-extracting reference, lower ideality factor, and improved built-in potential, not merely with a changed contact angle. Hydrophilicity/oxide-nucleation effects require contact-angle and surface-energy measurements, ALD nucleation-delay or mass-uptake data, high-resolution oxide coverage/roughness maps, and pinhole or potential-uniformity measurements after the same number of ALD cycles. A hydrophilic but non-chelating control is essential.

Electronic structure must be treated as a fourth linked but non-equivalent variable. CV/UPS/IPES or equivalent measurements should confirm that analogs do not gain performance simply by shifting the LUMO or interface dipole. Mobility, conductivity, contact resistance, and electron selectivity must be measured before and after aging. Device comparisons should use the same absorber and stack, then test whether the benefit persists when the SnOx overlayer is omitted. If the molecule helps only with SnOx present, oxide nucleation is central; if it helps without SnOx and with a blocked Pb surface, cohesion/transport is more likely; if the benefit disappears when Pb sites are pre-passivated, chelation is implicated.

The difficult mixed result requires a rate-balance interpretation. Improved PL/QFLS and lower trap density indicate reduced recombination, but worse mobility or thermal morphology can raise series resistance, reduce FF, and create delayed instability. The molecule may therefore be an excellent passivator but a poor transport matrix. The correct decision depends on complete-device loss analysis: Voc may rise while FF and MPP stability fall. Dilution in PCBM, altered substitution density, a bilayer, or a thinner ETL could recover percolation while retaining chelation. Conversely, if thermal morphology worsens but device stability remains high because strong interfacial binding anchors the film, the morphology metric may not be performance-limiting. Causality is established only when each molecular perturbation produces the predicted selective change in cohesion, binding, oxide nucleation, and device loss channels.
scoring_key_points: Defines a near-factorial analog set that independently varies coordination, steric bulk/cohesion, hydrophilicity, and preferably pyridine density while matching the fullerene electronic core.
Assigns each function with orthogonal measurements and intervention controls, including a hydrophilic non-chelator and a coordinating steric variant.
Separates LUMO/dipole, mobility, and selectivity from passivation and uses with/without-SnOx or site-blocking device controls to localize the benefit.
Interprets improved recombination but degraded mobility/morphology as a tradeoff requiring device-level Voc-FF-stability analysis rather than a single 'better ETL' conclusion.
accepted_equivalents: A matched fullerene library, protected/deprotected pyridine series, positional isomers, or blend-composition series are acceptable causal control strategies.
QCM/ellipsometric ALD nucleation, TEM, XPS depth profiling, conductive AFM, or KPFM are acceptable oxide-coverage diagnostics.
Space-charge-limited current, field-effect mobility, time-of-flight, conductivity, or impedance/contact-resistance measurements are acceptable transport probes.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only the target molecule with PCBM and assigns all differences to pyridine chelation.
Uses contact angle as proof of better SnOx nucleation or XPS shifts as proof that chelation alone caused the device improvement.
Ignores a mobility/series-resistance penalty because PL and trap-density measurements look favorable.

expected_answer:
The sign of a TRPL lifetime change depends on the boundary condition. On inert glass there is no intended charge-selective sink, so a longer lifetime together with higher absolute PLQY indicates lower bulk/surface non-radiative recombination and improved material quality. On ITO/SnO2, however, electrons can be transferred out of the perovskite. If the film is intrinsically better and the buried contact is more selective, a new fast decay channel can shorten the measured PL lifetime because electrons are productively extracted, not because they recombine. Thus the consistent signature is longer-lived, brighter emission on a non-extracting substrate but faster early-time decay on an extracting contact, accompanied by higher device QFLS/Voc and lower recombination loss.

The minimum optical experiment should use identical perovskite composition, thickness, excitation fluence, and optical geometry on glass, glass/polymer, SnO2, and SnO2/polymer substrates. Absolute PLQY and time-resolved PL should be globally fit rather than reduced to a single average lifetime. A modified film should show reduced non-radiative rate on glass, while the SnO2 stack should exhibit an additional fast component whose amplitude follows contact proximity and electron-transfer driving force. Front/back excitation or thickness variation can test whether the fast component is localized at the buried interface. Quasi-Fermi-level splitting from calibrated PL and electroluminescence efficiency should increase; if lifetime shortens but QFLS and Voc decrease, the decay is parasitic.

Direct extraction evidence should include transient photocurrent or charge extraction, transient absorption/terahertz spectroscopy, and impedance or intensity-dependent measurements. Faster photocurrent rise/decay, lower transfer resistance, longer extracted-carrier lifetime or lower recombination current, and a reduced ideality factor support productive collection. SCLC can quantify trap density, but dark leakage and mobility must be checked. TPC/TPV or Suns-Voc can separate transport from recombination.

To test nucleation control, perform time-resolved UV-vis, GIWAXS/XRD, or optical microscopy during drying and compare nucleation onset, intermediate-phase population, orientation, and vertical crystallization. A contact-angle-only explanation is insufficient; a chemically similar polymer lacking Pb-chelating groups and a surface-energy-matched non-polymer control should be included. Buried-interface exposure and cross-sectional microscopy should quantify void area and contact continuity. A concentration series must demonstrate a nonmonotonic optimum rather than a generic polymer effect.

Strain relief requires depth-sensitive evidence such as 2theta-sin2psi GIXRD, peak-shift mapping, Raman, or nano-diffraction from buried and top regions, linked to lower defect or ion-migration signatures. Vertical energy alignment should be measured by depth-resolved UPS/KPFM or interface-sensitive photoelectron spectroscopy and tested against a control that changes crystallization but not dipole chemistry. Finally, causality is strengthened by intervention: alter polymer functional groups or block chelation/hydrogen bonding, reproduce nucleation with an independent drying protocol, and determine which of nucleation timing, strain, and alignment is necessary for the extraction and QFLS gains. Only the joint pattern—better intrinsic PLQY, faster contact-specific transfer, fewer voids/traps, lower strain, improved band alignment, higher Voc/FF, and lower hysteresis—supports the multifunctional buried-template mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Explains the substrate-dependent lifetime inversion: longer lifetime on inert glass indicates lower non-radiative loss, while a contact-specific fast component can indicate productive extraction.
Requires absolute PLQY/QFLS plus direct extraction and recombination measurements to distinguish collection from non-radiative quenching.
Uses in-situ crystallization, buried-interface imaging, and matched chemical/surface-energy controls to test nucleation and void-reduction causality.
Demands depth-sensitive strain and energy-alignment evidence plus intervention controls linking these mechanisms to device Voc/FF/hysteresis.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, TRMC, THz, surface photovoltage, or time-resolved microwave conductivity are acceptable alternatives for direct carrier-transfer measurements.
Calibrated PL-derived QFLS, electroluminescence EQE, or Suns-Voc are acceptable non-radiative voltage-loss diagnostics.
GIWAXS, GIXRD, micro-Raman, nano-XRD, or equivalent depth-sensitive structural probes are acceptable for strain/orientation analysis.
common_wrong_answers: States that a longer lifetime is always good and a shorter lifetime is always bad, independent of substrate and extraction contact.
Uses only TRPL and SCLC to claim faster extraction without absolute PLQY/QFLS or a direct transport measurement.
Treats improved grain size or contact angle as proof that strain relief and band alignment caused the device improvement.

expected_answer:
Spin coating and meniscus coating impose different mass-transfer fields. In spin coating, rapid radial thinning and evaporation can create a relatively reproducible supersaturation trajectory; in slot-die or blade coating, wet-film thickness, coating speed, substrate temperature, gas flow, solvent boundary layer, and edge effects create position-dependent residence times. A buried template that accelerates heterogeneous nucleation can therefore become too weak in slow-drying regions and too strong in fast-drying regions. The scalable target is not a fixed polymer concentration copied from spin coating but a matched ratio of template-site density to local Pb flux and a synchronized supersaturation/nucleation window across the web.

The process design should vary polymer surface coverage or dry thickness, molecular weight, functional-group density, coating solvent, drying gas, substrate temperature, coating speed, wet-film thickness, precursor concentration, DMF/NMP ratio, and delay before annealing. The polymer must survive precursor solvent exposure, remain laterally uniform, and avoid dissolution or intermixing that produces a thick electronically resistive region. A design-of-experiments should map a lower bound where nucleation remains uncontrolled and an upper bound where preferred orientation, extraction, or conductivity deteriorates. Sheet/contact resistance and electron-only transport should be measured as explicit constraints.

In-situ diagnostics should follow the process at multiple cross-web and down-web positions. Time-resolved reflectance/UV-vis, optical microscopy, or photoluminescence can determine supersaturation and nucleation onset; grazing-incidence X-ray scattering at representative line conditions can track intermediate phases, texture, and conversion. Drying-rate and film-thickness maps should be synchronized with these data. After coating, hyperspectral PL/QFLS, XRD/GIWAXS orientation, profilometry, and machine-vision defect maps should quantify uniformity. Buried-interface peel/exfoliation or cross-sectional tomography/SEM should measure void fraction and contact continuity rather than relying only on top-surface morphology.

Spatial acceptance criteria should include bounded variation in nucleation time, final thickness, orientation, residual PbI2/intermediate phase, strain, PL/QFLS, and contact resistance; no edge-to-center increase in voids or shunts; and a narrow distribution of subcell Voc, FF, and leakage. The process should be challenged at the corners of the manufacturing window—line-speed changes, start/stop transients, solvent-aging time, humidity, and substrate-temperature gradients. A surface-energy-matched non-chelating control and a polymer-free drying-optimized control are needed to show that the template adds robustness rather than simply compensating one laboratory recipe.

Stability testing should target the mechanisms introduced by the polymer. MPP light soaking at controlled temperature should be combined with damp heat, thermal cycling, bias, and storage to reveal polymer swelling, water uptake, ion accumulation, or delamination. Depth-resolved ion profiling and post-aging band/contact measurements should test whether hydrogen bonding truly suppresses iodide redistribution. Mechanical adhesion and thermal-expansion mismatch should be evaluated because a polymer interlayer can relieve stress but also weaken the interface. Module tests should report active and aperture efficiency, scribe/interconnect yield, hotspot formation, and statistics across multiple coatings. The template is scalable only if it broadens or preserves the coating window, maintains a thin electronically transparent buried layer, produces spatially uniform nucleation and low void/trap density, and retains module performance under combined operational and environmental stress.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that meniscus coating changes evaporation and supersaturation fields, so polymer surface coverage must be co-optimized with local drying and Pb flux rather than copied from spin coating.
Defines a process-window DOE with polymer thickness/functionality, solvent, speed, temperature, gas flow, wet thickness, and electronic-resistance constraints.
Uses position-resolved in-situ nucleation/phase diagnostics and buried-interface plus electrical maps with explicit cross-web/down-web acceptance criteria.
Requires mechanism-targeted MPP, humidity, thermal, ion-migration, adhesion, and module-yield tests to prove scalability and rule out an insulating or unstable interlayer.
accepted_equivalents: Meniscus-guided coating, gravure, spray, or inkjet transfer is acceptable if the answer analyzes the changed drying/supersaturation field.
Synchrotron GIWAXS, in-line Raman, interferometry, optical coherence tomography, or equivalent phase/drying diagnostics are acceptable.
Contact resistivity, impedance, electron-only SCLC, or conductive-AFM mapping are acceptable ways to constrain an insulating polymer barrier.
common_wrong_answers: Copies the spin-coated polymer concentration and annealing schedule without considering coating-speed and evaporation gradients.
Judges uniformity only from top-view SEM or average PCE and ignores buried voids, cross-web distributions, and interconnect yield.
Assumes more polymer always gives more nucleation sites and stability, without an upper-bound transport/orientation penalty.

expected_answer:
A coupled redox-to-passivation mechanism makes a stronger prediction than ordinary antioxidant behavior. It predicts that oxidation of the modifier and suppression of Sn2+ oxidation are temporally linked, that the oxidized modifier remains at the relevant interface, that its coordination to Sn/Pb or defect sites increases after conversion, and that this conversion preserves electronic quality rather than merely consuming oxygen. Each alternative explains only part of that sequence.

The redox pathway should first be quantified stoichiometrically and kinetically. Operando or time-resolved FTIR/Raman, UV-vis, NMR on model solutions, and XPS under controlled O2/light/temperature should track loss of catechol/phenol signatures and growth of quinone carbonyl features while simultaneously measuring Sn2+/Sn4+ speciation. Isotopically labeled oxygen or water can establish the oxygen source in the oxidized modifier. Electrochemical redox potentials and radical-scavenging assays should determine whether the molecule is consumed once, reversibly cycled, or regenerated. A mass balance is important: if one molecule is irreversibly oxidized per captured oxidant and then becomes inert, the mechanism is sacrificial, not catalytic or self-regenerating. Self-adapting behavior does not require true catalysis, but it does require that the product contributes a second beneficial function.

The product's coordination must be shown directly. Compare the reduced and independently synthesized oxidized forms at matched coverage using DFT binding energies, XPS/NMR/IR shifts with Sn2+, Pb2+, and representative defect-rich surfaces, and desorption or calorimetric measurements. Spatially resolved XPS, ToF-SIMS, or labeled-molecule imaging should confirm that the oxidized species remains at the buried interface rather than diffusing away. Defect formation or passivation should be tested with SCLC, deep-level or PLQY/QFLS measurements, and surface-specific spectroscopy before and after oxidation. A decisive intervention is to use an analog that retains wetting and steric bulk but cannot undergo the catechol-to-quinone conversion, plus a pre-oxidized quinone analog that lacks antioxidant capacity but retains coordination. The parent should protect early oxidation; the pre-oxidized analog should passivate without scavenging; the redox-inactive analog should fail to reproduce the full time-dependent benefit.

Wetting/crystallization and oxygen-barrier alternatives require matched morphology controls. Adjust contact angle independently with an inert modifier, or fabricate films with matched grain size and density by changing the drying protocol. Measure oxygen permeability/uptake and film density. If protection is solely physical blocking, Sn4+ suppression should track oxygen transmission and remain when redox chemistry is disabled. If it is solely crystallization control, matched-grain films should reproduce the stability and trap-density benefit without formation of the quinone product. In situ GIWAXS/optical microscopy can quantify crystallization delay, but that evidence does not itself prove antioxidant chemistry.

Temporal device signatures should align with the chemical sequence. During controlled aging, formation of the oxidized coordinating product should precede or coincide with stable QFLS, lower trap growth, preserved band alignment, and suppressed I2/SnI4-type degradation products. Operando PL/EL, impedance, and MPP tracking can reveal whether recombination and contact resistance remain low. If antioxidant capacity is exhausted, performance should show a breakpoint that scales with modifier loading and oxidant flux; if the oxidized product continues to passivate, electronic quality may remain superior after the redox reservoir is consumed. Convincing proof therefore requires linked kinetics, product-specific coordination, spatial retention, orthogonal redox-inactive and pre-oxidized controls, and device preservation beyond what matched wetting, morphology, or oxygen permeability can explain.
scoring_key_points: States the unique coupled prediction: stress-driven modifier oxidation must produce a retained, more-coordinating species that continues to suppress defect/recombination growth.
Uses time-resolved redox/speciation measurements, oxygen-source or mass-balance tests, and independently prepared reduced/oxidized forms to distinguish sacrificial from coupled behavior.
Includes redox-inactive, pre-oxidized, wetting-matched, morphology-matched, and oxygen-permeability controls to eliminate simpler alternatives.
Requires synchronized chemical conversion, interfacial localization, defect/QFLS preservation, degradation-product suppression, and MPP/device signatures over time.
accepted_equivalents: Operando XAS, EPR, ambient-pressure XPS, resonance Raman, or equivalent redox/speciation tools are acceptable.
A pre-oxidized quinone analog, electrochemically oxidized film, or chemically locked quinone is an acceptable product-function control.
QFLS, absolute PLQY, EL efficiency, defect spectroscopy, or trap-density growth may be used to quantify ongoing passivation.
common_wrong_answers: Calls any reduction in Sn4+ evidence a self-adaptive mechanism without tracking modifier conversion or product function.
Uses delayed crystallization and larger grains as proof of antioxidant chemistry.
Omits redox-inactive and pre-oxidized controls, so sacrificial scavenging and physical oxygen blocking remain equally plausible.

expected_answer:
Temperature-dependent ionic conductivity is approximately the product of mobile-defect concentration, charge, and mobility. An Arrhenius slope can reflect the migration enthalpy of a dominant defect, but changes in defect formation energy, carrier concentration, phase fraction, interfacial polarization, electrode reaction, or the identity of the migrating species can alter both slope and prefactor. A higher apparent activation energy therefore does not by itself prove that every iodide ion faces a larger bulk migration barrier. A thin secondary phase may instead block injection at one interface, while anion passivation may reduce the number of iodide vacancies available to move.

The causal matrix should separate cation and anion functions. Compare untreated material, excess-PbI2 control, DMA-only treatment capable of forming the DMA-based phase, TFA-only treatment capable of surface passivation, the full salt, and a preformed or deposited DMA-based secondary-phase control with matched coverage. Include a non-coordinating anion salt and a cation that does not convert PbI2. Dose and phase fraction must be quantified. If possible, prepare samples with the same secondary-phase fraction but different anion passivation, and samples with similar defect passivation but no secondary phase.

Mobile-ion concentration should be measured independently from mobility. Methods may include thermally stimulated current, transient ion-drift or capacitance, low-frequency impedance with validated equivalent circuits, ionic charge extraction, bias-induced photoluminescence or potential relaxation, and defect-sensitive spectroscopy. The conductivity prefactor, chemical capacitance, and total displaced ionic charge should be compared. A reduction in mobile-defect concentration should lower the integrated ionic charge or capacitance even if the field-normalized drift mobility is unchanged. Vacancy formation energies from DFT or equilibrium defect chemistry can support, but not replace, experimental concentration estimates.

Migration mobility/barrier should be probed with a known tracer and geometry. Isotopically enriched iodide or halide, lateral devices, or controlled isotope bilayers followed by ToF-SIMS can measure diffusion coefficients versus temperature. Field-dependent drift velocity or time-of-flight gives mobility; an Arrhenius analysis of the independently measured diffusion coefficient is more directly related to the migration barrier. Grain-interior and grain-boundary pathways should be separated by microstructure-controlled samples or spatially resolved mapping.

Interfacial blocking must be distinguished from bulk suppression by varying film thickness and secondary-phase location. A purely interfacial barrier gives a resistance contribution that does not scale with absorber thickness, strong electrode polarization, and protection that depends on which side the phase is placed. Compare surface-treated, buried-interface-treated, and bulk-doped samples; remove or perforate the secondary phase; or insert the same phase at an inert contact. Cross-sectional KPFM, impedance distribution of relaxation times, and operando potential mapping can reveal where voltage drops.

Finally, couple these measurements to direct migration maps under identical bias, light, and heat. Sequential ToF-SIMS/EDS or tracer profiles should show whether the full treatment reduces bulk displacement, electrode accumulation, or both. The full salt demonstrates synergy only if DMA-phase controls mainly increase path resistance, TFA controls mainly reduce mobile-defect population, and the combined treatment produces a quantitatively larger suppression with consistent ionic charge, diffusion coefficient, thickness scaling, and electrode-corrosion results.
scoring_key_points: Explains that apparent ionic activation energy conflates migration barrier, mobile-defect concentration/species, phase fraction, and interfacial polarization.
Defines cation-only, anion-only, full-salt, nonreactive-ion, and matched-secondary-phase controls that isolate phase conversion from passivation.
Separately measures mobile ionic charge/concentration and tracer or field-derived diffusion/mobility rather than inferring both from conductivity.
Uses thickness/location scaling and operando spatial profiles to identify an interfacial blocking contribution and quantify true synergy.
accepted_equivalents: Transient ionic current, DLTS-like ion spectroscopy, Kelvin-probe relaxation, electrochemical strain microscopy, or validated impedance methods may estimate mobile-ion concentration.
Radiotracer, isotope-labeled iodide, bromide tracer, neutron methods, or lateral-drift imaging are acceptable diffusion/mobility probes.
Distribution-of-relaxation-times analysis, blocking/nonblocking electrodes, or thickness-scaling equivalent circuits are acceptable ways to localize interfacial resistance.
common_wrong_answers: Equates a larger Arrhenius slope directly with suppressed ion migration without considering concentration, prefactor, or interfacial effects.
Compares only untreated and full-salt samples, leaving cation-phase and anion-passivation contributions inseparable.
Uses post-aging electrode corrosion alone as proof of a larger bulk iodide migration barrier.

expected_answer:
The original synergy depends on the availability and chemical identity of residual PbI2. In a PbI2-rich Pb perovskite, the cation can consume an unstable lead-halide residue to form a more stable secondary phase while the anion passivates surface Pb and halide-vacancy defects. In a nearly stoichiometric film, the same dose may draw PbI2 out of the perovskite, react with the 3D lattice, or create excessive low-dimensional/secondary material. The treatment should therefore be dosed against measured residual lead-halide surface density, not against substrate area alone. XRD/GIWAXS, XPS, and quantitative surface extraction should define a phase-coverage window; device QFLS, contact resistance, and thickness-dependent transport should set the upper bound.

For the stoichiometric film, compare no treatment, anion-only passivation, low-dose full salt, cation-only treatment, and intentionally PbI2-enriched controls. If the anion-only treatment provides the trap/ion benefit without forming a new phase, the cation function may be unnecessary. A beneficial secondary phase should be sparse, chemically stable, defect-passivating, and electronically thin enough for tunneling or favorable band alignment. It becomes harmful when it is continuous/thick, blocks electron extraction, adds capacitance/hysteresis, creates a band offset, or nucleates nonuniformly at grain boundaries.

Transfer to Sn-Pb absorbers is not chemically neutral. Sn2+ has different Lewis acidity, redox chemistry, defect energetics, and band edges; DMA-containing phases may not form selectively, while TFA or residual acid could alter Sn oxidation, halide balance, or phase segregation. Screen direct binding and redox reactions with SnI2/PbI2 mixtures, quantify Sn4+, and test whether the salt changes crystallization or causes compositional demixing. The optimal cation may need to be replaced by one that stabilizes Sn-related residues without oxidizing Sn2+, and the anion may need different binding strength or lower acidity. Mixed-halide and narrow-bandgap films also require light-bias segregation and band-alignment tests.

Electrode choice changes the failure pathway. Ag readily forms AgI and can migrate bidirectionally; Cu may diffuse or react differently and can be more or less sensitive to halide flux; carbon is less prone to metal-halide formation but may have different contact resistance, porosity, and water ingress. For each electrode, perform identical light/heat/bias aging with depth profiling of halide and electrode species, corrosion-product analysis, and contact-resistance mapping. A salt that mainly blocks AgI formation may show smaller benefits with carbon, while its bulk ion/passivation benefit may remain. Electrode-specific barrier layers should be controlled.

Module transfer requires uniform surface dose and phase formation over coating and scribe regions. Map secondary-phase fraction, work function, PL/QFLS, and contact resistance across subcells; test whether treatment accumulates at edges or P2/P3 scribes and creates shunts. Reliability should include MPP at elevated temperature, damp heat, thermal cycling, reverse-bias or partial-shading stress, and electrode-specific ion profiling. Compare active/aperture efficiency and subcell distributions, not only champion PCE.

The original salt should be retained only when both functions are necessary and the phase/passivation window remains broad. Use anion-only chemistry when little PbI2 exists and no stable phase is needed; redesign the cation for Sn-Pb or other residues; use a separate ultrathin passivator plus electrode diffusion barrier when the combined salt creates an extraction penalty. Replacement is warranted when phase formation is uncontrolled, band alignment worsens, the cation reacts with the host lattice, the anion accelerates Sn oxidation or moisture sensitivity, or electrode-specific degradation is better addressed by a dedicated barrier.
scoring_key_points: Links treatment dose to measured residual PbI2/phase coverage and explains why a stoichiometric film may need anion-only or much lower-dose treatment.
Defines the beneficial-versus-blocking secondary-phase window using phase, QFLS, band alignment, contact resistance, and transport criteria.
Recognizes Sn-Pb-specific redox/defect/bandgap chemistry and electrode-specific Ag, Cu, and carbon degradation pathways requiring separate controls.
Specifies module-uniformity and combined operational/environmental/bias tests and gives clear retain, split-function, redesign, or replace decisions.
accepted_equivalents: Residual PbI2 may be quantified by calibrated XRD, XPS, photothermal deflection, chemical titration, or other quantitative phase/surface methods.
A dedicated electrode diffusion barrier, self-assembled passivator, or low-dimensional capping layer is an acceptable replacement strategy if justified.
Reverse-bias, damp-heat, thermal-cycle, MPP, and partial-shading protocols may be adapted to the electrode/module architecture if failure modes are explicitly monitored.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes the same salt concentration and secondary-phase fraction are optimal for PbI2-rich, stoichiometric, and Sn-Pb absorbers.
Treats carbon electrodes as eliminating the need to test ion migration or contact degradation.
Recommends more secondary phase for stability without checking band offsets, contact resistance, hysteresis, or module-edge accumulation.

expected_answer: The control set should include the fully crosslinked layer, the same molecule before crosslinking or processed below the crosslinking threshold, a noncrosslinkable structural analogue with similar energy levels and wetting, and a conventional inorganic ETL at matched optical thickness. Gate 1 verifies chemistry and solvent resistance: quantify functional-group conversion by FTIR or XPS, then measure retained thickness, absorbance, roughness, and conductivity after repeated exposure to the perovskite solvent. A candidate that only improves wetting but dissolves, swells, or changes energetics fails. Gate 2 tests thermal-electrical integrity using ITO/ETL/metal and electron-only stacks during prolonged heating; sheet/contact resistance, activation behavior, leakage, and spatial current uniformity must remain stable. Gate 3 tests the buried interface by aging perovskite/ETL half-stacks under heat, illumination, and controlled humidity, then measuring PbI2 or phase formation, PLQY/QFLS, trap density, adhesion or acoustic integrity, and cross-sectional morphology. Only after passing these gates should small devices and patterned mini-modules undergo stabilized MPP operation, electroluminescence/PL mapping, series-resistance analysis, and scribe-region inspection. Go requires statistically reproducible retention, limited resistance drift, suppressed interfacial decomposition, and spatially uniform module operation relative to all controls; an initial-PCE gain alone is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Includes crosslinked, uncrosslinked, noncrosslinkable-molecular, and conventional-ETL controls that separate chemistry from wetting and morphology.
Verifies crosslink conversion and solvent resistance before device testing using chemical and film-retention measurements.
Separately evaluates thermal-electrical drift and buried-interface decomposition with appropriate half-stack diagnostics.
Defines module-level go/no-go criteria based on stabilized operation, spatial uniformity, resistance, interfacial integrity, and reproducibility rather than champion PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Gel fraction, ellipsometric thickness retention, or insoluble-mass fraction can substitute for repeated absorbance retention in the solvent-resistance gate.
Ultrasonic or acoustic-resonance tracking may substitute for adhesion testing if it is correlated with independently measured interfacial damage.
Thermal cycling can complement or replace isothermal aging if equivalent resistance and interface-failure criteria are defined.
common_wrong_answers: Tests only complete devices and never verifies that crosslinking actually occurred.
Uses a single short MPP test as proof of long-term stability.
Attributes all improvement to better precursor wetting without controlling molecular chemistry, energy alignment, or film insolubility.

expected_answer: No single surface spectrum can distinguish these structures because persistent FA can arise either from exposed 3D regions or from FA incorporated into the deposited layer. First, combine angle-resolved or variable-energy XPS with minimally destructive depth profiling such as ToF-SIMS. Incomplete coverage should produce lateral patches with surface FA but abrupt PEA-rich composition inside covered regions; true interdiffusion should produce a continuous FA-to-PEA depth gradient beneath an otherwise closed film; a pure thick cap should show little surface FA and an abrupt interface. Second, use variable-incidence GIWAXS and cross-sectional electron diffraction to locate and orient phases. A gradient should show surface-confined, mixed-n or n greater than 1 signatures without a dominant thick n = 1 slab, whereas the blocking cap should show intense, horizontally oriented n = 1 scattering. Third, hyperspectral PL, cathodoluminescence, or nanoscale PL mapping should test lateral continuity. Islands should generate spatially segregated 3D-only and low-dimensional emitters; a gradient should yield co-located 3D and quasi-2D emission with relatively homogeneous passivation; the pure cap should dominate low-dimensional emission and attenuate the 3D signal. Finally, correlate these maps with vertical conductivity or charge-extraction measurements: intermediate gradients should reduce recombination while preserving extraction, whereas a continuous parallel n = 1 cap should raise transport resistance.
scoring_key_points: Explains why persistent surface FA alone cannot distinguish exposed 3D islands from FA interdiffusion.
Uses depth- and angle-resolved chemical/structural probes to identify lateral coverage, composition gradients, phase identity, and orientation.
Predicts distinct spatial luminescence signatures for islands, a quasi-2D gradient, and a pure n = 1 cap.
Correlates structural assignments with vertical transport and the passivation-to-blocking transition.
accepted_equivalents: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or standing-wave XPS may replace angle-resolved XPS for depth sensitivity.
Cross-sectional STEM-EELS/EDS may replace ToF-SIMS if it resolves FA/PEA-related chemistry and phase continuity.
Conductive AFM, impedance, or selective-contact transient measurements may replace direct vertical conductivity measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Concludes that FA detected by XPS necessarily proves cation interdiffusion.
Uses only conventional XRD and ignores its limited sensitivity to thin or poorly crystalline quasi-2D phases.
Treats stronger low-dimensional emission as automatically beneficial without considering orientation and out-of-plane transport.

expected_answer: At minimum, the precursor matrix should compare rare-earth chloride, a chemically compatible nonchloride salt of the same cation, a chloride-only control without the rare-earth cation, and interface-only rare-earth treatment at otherwise fixed absorber composition. A dose series is required because the onset of a secondary phase defines the solubility/strain limit. True lattice substitution should be supported by a systematic lattice-parameter or local-coordination change from Rietveld analysis, solid-state NMR, EXAFS, or atomically resolved spectroscopy that persists when chloride is removed as the counterion. Transient chloride-assisted crystallization should instead be reproduced by the chloride-only control and appear mainly in in situ GIWAXS nucleation kinetics, grain formation, and reduced residual strain, despite little final Cl. Interfacial passivation should scale with depth-resolved rare-earth enrichment and should be reproduced by surface- or buried-interface-selective treatment, with reduced interface recombination but limited bulk lattice change. Finally, raw Voc must be normalized to optical gap: improved quasi-Fermi-level splitting or a smaller Eg/q minus Voc deficit, rather than a higher Voc alone, is required to claim lower nonradiative loss. The strongest causal conclusion would come from a full factorial analysis linking each controlled variable to phase, depth distribution, recombination, and Voc deficit.
scoring_key_points: Constructs chloride-only, rare-earth-without-chloride, interface-only, and dose-series controls.
Assigns lattice substitution to persistent crystallographic or local-coordination evidence rather than surface detection alone.
Separates transient crystallization effects from interfacial passivation using in situ growth and depth-selective diagnostics.
Evaluates recombination using quasi-Fermi-level splitting or bandgap-normalized voltage deficit rather than raw Voc.
accepted_equivalents: Pair-distribution-function analysis or synchrotron X-ray absorption may replace EXAFS/Rietveld for local lattice incorporation.
Time-resolved PL combined with selective-contact structures may replace some interface-recombination measurements if bandgap changes are explicitly corrected.
A rare-earth iodide, nitrate, or acetate precursor is acceptable as the nonchloride control if its own chemistry is accounted for.
common_wrong_answers: Treats absence of chlorine in the final film as proof that chloride had no role during crystallization.
Treats rare-earth detection by XPS or ToF-SIMS as sufficient proof of lattice substitution.
Uses higher Voc alone to claim defect passivation despite a simultaneous increase in bandgap.

expected_answer: Changing the I/Br ratio changes lattice parameter, defect chemistry, phase stability, bandgap, and rare-earth solubility, so the original dopant fraction cannot be assumed to remain below the secondary-phase threshold. The first gate is a composition-specific dose-phase map using diffraction, local structure, strain, and optical-gap measurements; performance should be assessed by voltage deficit, not only raw Voc. The quantum dots should be composition- and lattice-matched closely enough to avoid uncontrolled halide exchange, local band offsets, or phase-segregation seeds. Their bulk-incorporation and surface-passivation doses should be optimized independently because one affects crystallization and internal defects while the other affects pinholes, grain boundaries, and contact energetics. For scale-up, deposition and hot-air/annealing uniformity must be mapped across the module using PL/QFLS, phase, thickness, and electroluminescence imaging. Mandatory controls are dopant-only, bulk-QD-only, surface-QD-only, combined treatment, and deliberately overdoped or overcoated samples. Go requires no detectable nonperovskite phase, a reduced voltage deficit, rapid selective extraction, spatially uniform module output, and retention under combined humidity, high temperature, continuous illumination, and stabilized MPP operation. A strategy that succeeds only in dry storage or only at small area is not transferable.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes dopant loading through a composition-specific solubility, strain, phase, and voltage-deficit map.
Requires quantum-dot composition/lattice matching and independent optimization of bulk and surface doses.
Uses factorial controls and spatially resolved scale-up diagnostics rather than a single combined treatment.
Defines go/no-go criteria under coupled humidity, heat, illumination, and MPP stress at module scale.
accepted_equivalents: Low-dimensional or nanocrystal passivants other than QDs are acceptable if lattice matching, ion exchange, and transport barriers are treated explicitly.
Photoluminescence, electroluminescence, or lock-in thermography may be used for spatial process mapping if their failure signatures are justified.
A sequential Bayesian or design-of-experiments optimization is equivalent to a full grid if interaction terms are captured.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes the same rare-earth percentage is universally optimal for all halide compositions.
Uses QD-only stability as a substitute for testing the coupled bulk-and-surface strategy.
Accepts black-phase retention in storage as sufficient proof of operational module stability.

expected_answer: The blend ratio is only a formulation coordinate; changing solvent evaporation, coating shear, drying rate, and substrate temperature can alter vertical segregation, molecular exposure, roughness, and conductivity even at the same nominal composition. The invariant targets are a continuous pinhole-free HTL, sufficient surface exposure of the active coordinating molecule, an appropriate surface-energy window for uniform perovskite nucleation, selective hole energetics, and low lateral and contact resistance. Co-optimized variables should include small-molecule fraction, total solids, solvent and cosolvent activity, coating speed, wet-film thickness, drying-gas flux, substrate temperature, and post-annealing. Surface composition and segregation should be measured by angle-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS; thickness, roughness, and wetting should be mapped across the web; and four-point, transfer-length, or conductive-AFM measurements should track electrical uniformity. After perovskite deposition, spatial GIWAXS, PLQY/QFLS, lifetime, and electroluminescence maps should verify uniform crystallization and low nonradiative loss. The accepted window is not a fixed weight fraction but the region in which these functional metrics and stabilized device output remain within tolerance across the full area and after photothermal operation. A formulation that reproduces average PCE but creates local dry spots, compositional segregation, or resistance gradients fails transfer.
scoring_key_points: Explains why identical blend fraction does not guarantee identical vertical segregation, surface exposure, or film function under a new coating history.
Defines invariant interfacial targets covering continuity, active-molecule exposure, wetting/nucleation, energetics, and resistance.
Co-optimizes formulation, coating, drying, and thermal variables rather than changing one factor at a time.
Uses spatial chemical, structural, optical, electrical, and stabilized-device maps to define the acceptable process window.
accepted_equivalents: Kelvin-probe or ultraviolet-photoelectron maps may substitute for some energy-level measurements.
Roll-to-roll blade coating or spray coating may replace slot-die coating if the same segregation and drying arguments are addressed.
Photoluminescence imaging plus local J-V or electroluminescence is acceptable when GIWAXS mapping is unavailable.
common_wrong_answers: Copies the laboratory blend ratio and changes only coating speed.
Optimizes average contact angle or average PCE while ignoring spatial segregation and local resistance.
Assumes the polymer fraction controls only film formation and cannot alter active-molecule exposure at the buried interface.

expected_answer: Increasing iodine-vacancy formation energy is a preventive mechanism: hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interaction, or local lattice stabilization lowers the rate and equilibrium population of vacancy generation before iodine is oxidized. I2 scavenging is a remedial redox mechanism that acts after iodide oxidation has occurred; it consumes a degradation product and is therefore potentially sacrificial and capacity-limited. The two contributions should be separated with a molecular analogue matrix: a full modifier, an analogue retaining ammonium/N-H interactions but lacking the redox-active sulfur motif, an analogue retaining sulfur/Pb affinity but lacking the iodide-binding N-H group, and an untreated control. Before stress, compare vacancy-related trap density, ion-migration activation, and nonradiative loss using SCLC or thermal admittance, bias-dependent impedance, PLQY/QFLS, and, where possible, defect-sensitive spectroscopy. During calibrated light/heat exposure, quantify I2 evolution operando by optical absorption, headspace mass spectrometry, or periodic solvent extraction, while tracking sulfur oxidation states by XPS, FTIR, or mass spectrometry. Scavenger capacity is obtained from I2 consumed per modifier dose and should show a dose-dependent induction period. Exhaustion is identified when oxidized sulfur products plateau, I2 begins to accumulate, and Voc, PL, phase purity, or MPP output deteriorates. Pb-chelation effects must be held constant or measured separately to avoid assigning all stabilization to iodine chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes preventive vacancy suppression from post-formation, potentially sacrificial I2 scavenging.
Uses functional-group analogues that independently remove iodide binding and sulfur redox activity.
Combines pre-stress vacancy/ion-migration measurements with operando I2 and sulfur-oxidation measurements.
Defines finite capacity and exhaustion through dose-time stoichiometry and correlated onset of I2 accumulation and device degradation.
accepted_equivalents: Iodine-selective electrochemical sensing or quartz-crystal microbalance detection may replace optical/headspace I2 quantification.
Deep-level transient spectroscopy or thermally stimulated current may replace SCLC/admittance for vacancy-related defect tracking.
A kinetic isotope or isotopically labeled iodide experiment is acceptable if it separates generated iodine from background contamination.
common_wrong_answers: Treats vacancy suppression and I2 scavenging as the same passivation reaction.
Measures only end-point device efficiency and never quantifies I2 or sulfur oxidation.
Assumes scavenging is catalytic and unlimited without testing stoichiometric capacity or reaction products.

expected_answer: The transfer must begin by treating precursor quality and solution history as controlled variables rather than background details. SnI2, SnF2, organic iodides, and additives should be compared across supplier lots and purity levels, with water, oxygen, Sn(IV), and iodine impurities quantified before mixing. Fresh and deliberately aged solutions should be prepared under defined oxygen, light, temperature, and DMSO residence conditions. The yellowing should be tracked by UV-visible or Raman spectroscopy, iodometric or electrochemical assays, XPS or mass spectrometry on dried aliquots, and carrier-density measurements on films; DLS or scattering should also identify colloid formation or precipitation. The formulation study should use a fractional or full factorial matrix that varies the vacancy compensator, antioxidant, crystallization regulator, and contact independently and in selected combinations. Additive ratios, precursor concentration, solution age, coating speed, wet-film residence time, gas-knife strength, substrate temperature, and annealing profile should be co-optimized because a combination that is chemically compatible in a vial can still segregate during drying. GIWAXS, optical interferometry, rheology, and in situ absorption or scattering should follow nucleation and phase formation. Spatial diagnostics must compare the leading edge, trailing edge, module centre, perimeter, and laser-scribed regions. Useful maps include thickness, XRD/GIWAXS orientation, PLQY or QFLS, hyperspectral PL, Sn(IV)/iodine and additive distributions by XPS or ToF-SIMS, EL/LBIC, dark leakage, local series resistance, and subcell-resolved J-V. Edge VOC loss should be assigned to nonradiative recombination, chemical oxidation, thickness variation, or contact damage rather than assumed to be a generic scale effect. Qualification should use stabilized maximum-power-point operation under defined spectrum, temperature, humidity, atmosphere, encapsulation, and electrical bias, together with periodic chemical and ionic diagnostics. Shelf storage, thermal aging, damp heat, and light-bias stress should remain separate protocols. A go condition is a formulation and coating window that remains chemically stable during the allowable reservoir time, produces no additive-rich or secondary-phase regions, gives uniform QFLS and resistance across the module, and suppresses Sn oxidation and output loss during reproducible MPP testing. A formulation should be rejected even if its best small cell is efficient when it has narrow timing tolerance, solution yellowing, edge-selective recombination, rising series resistance, or unstable ion/redox signatures.
scoring_key_points: Controls precursor supplier, purity, oxygen/water exposure, solvent residence time, and fresh-versus-aged solution chemistry, with direct Sn(IV)/iodine measurements.
Uses a factorial additive-and-process matrix that captures compatibility, segregation, coating kinetics, and drying-dependent crystallization rather than transferring one spin-coated recipe.
Requires spatial chemical, structural, luminescence, leakage, resistance, and subcell mapping across edges, centre, coating direction, and interconnects.
Defines go/no-go by a reproducible process window and stabilized MPP durability under explicitly normalized stress protocols, not by champion-cell PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Iodometric titration, UV-visible iodine signatures, Raman, electrochemistry, or calibrated XPS may be used to quantify redox aging.
Hyperspectral PL/QFLS, EL, LBIC, thermography, scanning photocurrent, or local impedance are acceptable module-uniformity probes.
A statistically designed response surface or sequential design-of-experiments campaign is acceptable in place of a complete full factorial if interactions remain identifiable.
common_wrong_answers: Uses a single supplier lot and assumes stated reagent purity is sufficient.
Optimizes all four interventions together without single-component or pair controls.
Attributes edge VOC loss only to thickness variation without chemical or recombination mapping.
Combines glovebox shelf storage, ambient MPP, and damp-heat results into one undifferentiated stability claim.

expected_answer: The experiment must separate the additive's particulate or pre-nucleated state from its dissolved molecular state and from its action after crystallization. First, the precursor should be fractionated by controlled filtration, centrifugation, or size-exclusion methods. The colloid-rich fraction, colloid-depleted supernatant, and recombined material should be characterized by DLS plus an orthogonal method such as SAXS, cryo-TEM, or analytical centrifugation. If nucleation benefits disappear when the colloidal fraction is removed and return when isolated seed material is added back at matched dissolved-additive concentration, the evidence favours a seed mechanism. Second, chemically matched controls are required: an analogue with similar charge, hydrogen-bonding, ionic strength, and rheological effect but unable to form a layered Pb-halide lattice; a viscosity or solvent-coordination control; and preformed low-dimensional seeds added without free additive. Third, timing should be varied. Addition after 3D nucleation or as a post-treatment can test passivation: improved PLQY or stability without a change in induction time, orientation, or early nucleation would indicate a post-crystallization role rather than seeding. Conversely, a seed mechanism should alter the induction period and the number or spatial distribution of nuclei before most of the 3D phase forms. In situ GIWAXS, time-resolved UV-visible absorption, scattering, and optical microscopy should track the appearance of the low-dimensional phase, the onset of 3D crystallization, orientation, and conversion rate. Isotopic labelling or ToF-SIMS can determine whether the low-dimensional component remains at the surface or grain boundaries, but final distribution alone does not prove that it nucleated the film. The strongest support is a convergent pattern: a structurally verified pre-existing low-dimensional seed population, preferential formation before 3D crystallization, loss of the kinetic and orientation benefit after seed removal despite unchanged dissolved chemistry, restoration by seed add-back, and failure of matched non-seeding analogues to reproduce the effect. Longer lifetime or lower trap density alone is insufficient because both can arise from conventional passivation.
scoring_key_points: Separates colloid-rich and colloid-depleted precursor fractions and uses seed-removal/add-back experiments at matched dissolved-additive concentration.
Includes chemically and rheologically matched non-seeding controls plus preformed-seed controls.
Uses addition timing and in situ crystallization measurements to distinguish altered nucleation kinetics from post-crystallization passivation.
Requires the nucleation benefit to track a structurally verified seed population rather than relying on final PL, lifetime, or trap-density improvements alone.
accepted_equivalents: SAXS, cryo-TEM, nanoparticle tracking analysis, or analytical ultracentrifugation may complement DLS.
In situ GIWAXS, optical absorption, Raman, interferometry, or synchrotron scattering are acceptable crystallization-kinetics probes.
Delayed addition, surface post-treatment, or a two-reservoir mixing experiment may be used to separate seeding from passivation.
common_wrong_answers: Treats a larger DLS hydrodynamic diameter as direct proof of crystalline 2D seeds.
Uses only longer TRPL lifetime to claim heterogeneous nucleation.
Compares the additive with no-additive control but does not match viscosity, ionic strength, or solvent coordination.
Uses ToF-SIMS enrichment in the final film as proof that the enriched species initiated nucleation.

expected_answer: The precursor must be treated as an evolving dispersion whose age and shear history are process variables. Seed or colloid size distribution, number density, structure, and chemical state should be measured versus reservoir residence time, temperature, light exposure, oxygen/water content, pump recirculation, shear, and batch size using DLS with an orthogonal scattering or imaging method. The study should compare no filter, several defined pore sizes, and bypass or staged filtration, while analysing material retained on each filter. The goal is to determine whether the filter removes beneficial seeds, harmful aggregates, or both. Fresh, aged, seed-depleted, and seed-add-back precursors should be coated in the same campaign. Coating speed, wet-film thickness, substrate temperature, gas-knife strength, solvent evaporation rate, delay to annealing, and web direction should be varied because the useful seed density may depend on drying kinetics. In situ optical spectroscopy or GIWAXS on a moving or representative coating should track nucleation and phase conversion. Across the module, thickness, grain orientation, low-dimensional-phase distribution, PLQY/QFLS, residual stress, and defect density should be mapped at the leading and trailing edges, centre, perimeter, and near interconnects. Indoor qualification must use the intended LED spectrum and illuminance and should emphasize dark leakage, shunt resistance, ideality factor, VOC deficit, local series resistance, subcell uniformity, and stabilized output, because shunts and nonradiative recombination are especially damaging at low photon flux. EL/PL imaging, LBIC, dark-current maps, and subcell J-V can identify rare defective regions hidden by average film characterization. The stable process window is not simply the residence time that gives the largest mean colloid size. It is the range in which seed population and coating response remain reproducible, filters do not remove the active fraction, no large aggregates or coating streaks appear, and low-light output remains spatially uniform. Qualification should include repeated start-stop cycles, allowable precursor hold time, multiple batches, and MPP aging under the indoor spectrum, together with separate humidity and thermal storage tests. Post-stress chemical, stress, and luminescence mapping should verify that the low-dimensional component does not create insulating accumulation or accelerated interfacial degradation. A process should be rejected if performance is highly sensitive to minute-scale precursor age, filter lot, or coating position even when one champion module is efficient.
scoring_key_points: Controls precursor age, temperature, shear, recirculation, atmosphere, seed size/number, and filter pore size, including analysis of the retained fraction and seed add-back.
Co-optimizes seed population with slot-die wet-film residence, drying, substrate temperature, coating speed, and annealing rather than transferring spin-coating conditions directly.
Maps phase distribution, film quality, residual stress, luminescence, leakage, resistance, and subcell output across the module under the intended indoor spectrum.
Defines a robust allowable hold/filter/process window and qualifies stabilized indoor MPP durability across batches and start-stop cycles, not a champion module.
accepted_equivalents: SAXS, nanoparticle tracking, turbidity with calibration, or cryogenic microscopy may replace one of the colloid measurements.
Hyperspectral PL/QFLS, EL, LBIC, dark-current imaging, scanning photocurrent, or local impedance are acceptable spatial electrical probes.
An accelerated precursor-aging model is acceptable if it is validated against real reservoir residence and recirculation conditions.
common_wrong_answers: Specifies a single filter pore size without determining whether it removes beneficial seeds.
Optimizes only one-sun J-V performance and ignores low-light leakage and VOC loss.
Uses average XRD from a module coupon and misses coating-direction or interconnect defects.
Accepts a process whose optimum changes sharply with precursor age or pump history.

expected_answer: The four materials should be deposited at matched surface coverage and thickness on the same ITO or recombination-electrode substrate, with solvent, annealing, and surface cleaning held constant. Before perovskite deposition, UPS/Kelvin probe should compare work function and energy alignment, while metal-insulator-metal conductivity, conductive AFM, transfer-length structures, or SCLC should assess lateral and vertical hole transport. If the full molecule and the core-only or ester-protected analogues retain favourable energetics and conductivity while the anchor-only acid does not, those functions can be assigned mainly to the silole conjugated core. Anchoring must be tested independently by wash resistance, angle-resolved XPS, infrared or NMR binding signatures, desorption measurements, and, where useful, DFT. If the full molecule and anchor-only acid bind strongly or remain after rinsing while the core-only and protected ester do not, the COOH group is responsible for substrate/perovskite coordination. Perovskite growth must then be characterized by contact angle, in situ nucleation or GIWAXS, XRD orientation and FWHM, SEM/AFM, KPFM potential variance, and composition or Sn2+/Sn4+ analysis. Similar morphology across controls is ideal for isolating direct passivation; if morphology differs, it must be treated as a mediator rather than ignored. Direct interfacial benefit requires higher absolute PLQY or QFLS, lower surface-recombination velocity, longer contact-appropriate lifetime, lower trap-filled voltage or ideality factor, and reduced Sn oxidation at matched film morphology. An anchor-only acid may passivate or improve Sn2+ retention but still produce poor fill factor because it lacks a continuous hole-transport pathway. A core-only or ester-protected material may conduct well yet fail to passivate or remain bound. The full molecule is genuinely multifunctional only if it combines the core-derived conductivity and energy selectivity with COOH-derived anchoring/passivation and produces an interaction benefit beyond either fragment alone, without adding series resistance. The study should not assign all improvements to molecular binding from one DFT energy or to transport from one champion J-V curve.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched full, core-only, anchor-only, and protected-anchor controls at comparable coverage and processing conditions.
Assigns core-derived transport and energetic functions using pre-perovskite work-function, conductivity, mobility, and contact-resistance measurements.
Assigns COOH-derived anchoring/passivation using binding/wash-resistance chemistry plus Sn-oxidation and recombination diagnostics, while accounting for morphology as a mediator.
Defines multifunctionality as the combination or interaction of selective transport, durable anchoring, passivation, and low resistance rather than any single characterization result.
accepted_equivalents: A non-acidic amide or phosphonate analogue may replace the ester-protected control if it cleanly changes anchoring while preserving the transport core.
UPS, Kelvin probe, PESA, conductive AFM, SCLC, or transfer-length measurements are acceptable transport/energy diagnostics.
Absolute PLQY/QFLS, surface-recombination velocity, TRPL with appropriate boundary conditions, ideality factor, or electroluminescence efficiency are acceptable recombination diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Compares only the full molecule with PEDOT:PSS and calls the difference proof of both core and COOH functions.
Uses stronger XRD intensity as sufficient evidence of direct chemical passivation.
Interprets faster contacted-stack PL decay as necessarily higher recombination without checking extraction.
Ignores surface coverage and morphology differences among the molecular controls.

expected_answer: The comparison must keep the wide-bandgap subcell, recombination junction, optical stack, active area, and all processing after the bottom HTL identical while changing only PEDOT:PSS versus Silole-COOH at the narrow-bandgap buried contact. Parallel narrow-bandgap single junctions on both the model ITO substrate and the actual recombination electrode are required because binding, wetting, work function, and coverage can change on sputtered ITO or another recombination layer. Partial stacks should stop after the HTL, after Sn-Pb crystallization, after C60, and after ALD oxide or top-electrode deposition. At each stage, surface composition, Sn2+/Sn4+, molecular coverage, work function, contact resistance, PLQY/QFLS, and morphology should be checked to identify solvent, plasma, sputter, or ALD damage. In the complete two-terminal tandem, total J-V alone cannot localize the benefit. Subcell EQE under bias light, spectrally resolved EL or PL, luminescence coupling analysis, voltage additivity, impedance or transient measurements, and temperature/light-intensity dependence should determine whether the narrow-bandgap subcell has lower nonradiative voltage loss and whether the recombination junction remains low resistance. Optical modelling and EQE-integrated currents should verify current matching; otherwise an apparent fill-factor or PCE change could be produced by altered absorption or current limitation rather than better passivation. Stabilized two-terminal MPP, not the sum of independent subcell efficiencies, is the relevant performance test. Operational aging should combine continuous illumination, heat, and controlled ambient conditions with periodic subcell-resolved EQE/EL or luminescence measurements. Post-mortem XPS/ToF-SIMS, microscopy, adhesion analysis, and resistance mapping should distinguish renewed Sn oxidation or buried-interface recombination from recombination-junction degradation, current mismatch, electrode diffusion, or delamination. The causal claim is supported only if the Silole contact remains chemically intact through the full process, selectively lowers the narrow-bandgap subcell's nonradiative loss without increasing contact or recombination-layer resistance, and delays the same narrow-bandgap failure signature during tandem MPP operation.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched tandems and parallel single-junction/partial-stack controls on the actual recombination electrode, changing only the narrow-bandgap buried HTL.
Checks molecular coverage, Sn oxidation, energetics, morphology, recombination, and resistance after each subsequent deposition step to verify process survival.
Uses subcell-resolved EQE/luminescence, voltage-loss, current-matching, and recombination-junction diagnostics rather than relying on total tandem J-V.
Localizes operational failure during stabilized two-terminal MPP and requires a persistent narrow-bandgap interfacial benefit without new transport or junction penalties.
accepted_equivalents: Bias-light EQE, electroluminescence deconvolution, spectrally resolved PL, or voltage-dependent luminescence may be used for subcell localization.
