Transfers the test to aged precursor and operando MPP devices with realistic spectrum, temperature, atmosphere, depth distribution, ion-migration, and performance readouts.

Defines go/no-go criteria based on repeated capacity recovery and limited irreversible depletion, including rejection if regeneration needs unrealistic conditions or causes transport/migration penalties.
accepted_equivalents: Ellman's reagent, electrochemical thiol quantification, LC-MS, GC-MS, quantitative NMR, sulfur K-edge XAS, Raman, or XPS may be used to quantify sulfur redox states.
Photochemical action spectra, intermittent illumination, or controlled photon-dose experiments are acceptable ways to identify the regeneration trigger.
A redox-cycling turnover number, retained scavenging capacity per cycle, or sulfur mass-balance closure is an acceptable quantitative regeneration metric.
White-LED, AM1.5G, UV-filtered, and dark-bias MPP comparisons are acceptable realistic-operation controls.
common_wrong_answers: Calls the mechanism self-healing because the precursor becomes colourless once.
Measures only device PCE retention and never quantifies thiol, disulfide, iodine species, or irreversible sulfur products.
Shows regeneration under intense UV in oxygen-free solution and assumes it will occur in an encapsulated device under the operating spectrum.
Ignores finite scavenging capacity and additive migration or depletion during repeated stress.

expected_answer:
At low loading, the assistant should improve C60 solubility and interrupt uncontrolled fullerene aggregation, producing continuous coverage with fewer pinholes and local shunts. This improves extraction even if the intrinsic conductivity of pristine C60 is high. At excessive loading, however, the non-fullerene component can dilute or spatially separate the C60 hopping network, increase the mean intermolecular tunnelling distance, or create resistive assistant-rich domains. Thus a visually smooth film can become electronically less connected. The simultaneous fall in mobility, local current, and FF, together with little change in Voc, points primarily to a transport/percolation penalty rather than a large change in recombination energetics.

A decisive electrical experiment is thickness-normalized vertical and lateral transport measurement across the loading series, such as SCLC plus temperature-dependent conductivity or frequency-dependent impedance. A percolation-limited film should show a loading-dependent mobility/conductivity collapse and larger transport activation energy even when thickness and roughness are matched. A second, orthogonal experiment should map structure and energetics independently: GIWAXS or nano-IR/ToF-SIMS can test for assistant-rich phase separation, while UPS/KPFM and selective-contact PL or transient absorption can test energy-level shifts and extraction. If morphology and energy levels remain nearly unchanged above the optimum but transport connectivity collapses, the percolation/dilution interpretation is supported; if roughness-independent composition domains or a work-function/extraction shift appears, those mechanisms must be included.
scoring_key_points: Explains the low-loading benefit as suppression of C60 aggregation and formation of continuous, pinhole-poor coverage.
Explains the high-loading penalty as dilution/disruption of the C60 hopping or percolation network despite a smooth surface.
Uses the mobility-current-FF decline with nearly unchanged Voc to prioritize transport loss over a dominant energetic or recombination shift.
Proposes two orthogonal diagnostics with predictions: matched-film electrical transport plus independent structural/compositional and energetic/extraction measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Electronic dilution, broken fullerene connectivity, increased hopping distance, or resistive assistant-rich domains are equivalent descriptions of the high-loading penalty.
Temperature-dependent conductivity, SCLC, impedance, or lateral four-probe transport may serve as the transport diagnostic if thickness and contact effects are controlled.
GIWAXS, resonant scattering, nano-IR, ToF-SIMS, or composition-sensitive microscopy may serve as the independent phase-distribution diagnostic.
UPS, Kelvin probe, KPFM, PLQY/QFLS, transient absorption, or contact-selective TRPL may serve as the energetic/extraction diagnostic.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that the smoothest film must have the best device performance.
Attributing the optimum only to higher C60 solubility without discussing electrical connectivity at high assistant loading.
Interpreting lower PL lifetime alone as proof of lower recombination without separating extraction from recombination.
Proposing only AFM or SEM, which cannot distinguish a smooth but electrically diluted film from a well-connected ETL.

expected_answer:
The control set must separate binding functionality, orientation, and dipole while holding surface coverage as constant as possible. At minimum it should include: the intact bifunctional molecule; a thiol-blocked analogue that retains the ammonium/dipole but cannot coordinate undercoordinated Pb; an ammonium-neutralized or replaced analogue that retains the sulfur donor but removes the cationic hydrogen-bonding site; and a nonbinding dipolar analogue with a similar molecular dipole and spacer geometry. An orientation-locked pair, or short- versus long-spacer homologues whose adsorption geometry is independently verified, strengthens the test. Coverage should be checked by quantitative XPS, QCM, or calibrated elemental analysis so that lower performance cannot be assigned to lower uptake.

Chemical engagement should be measured independently of energetics: S-H/Pb and N-H/iodide or organic-cation interactions can be probed by FTIR, XPS core-level shifts, solid-state NMR, or model-surface spectroscopy. UPS/Kelvin probe/KPFM measures the dipole-induced work-function shift, while PLQY/QFLS, SCLC trap density, recombination kinetics, and temperature-dependent ion conductivity measure defect and ion-migration consequences.

If simultaneous dual-site passivation is dominant, blocking either group should preserve much of the work-function shift when the molecular dipole is retained but should markedly weaken binding signatures, trap-density reduction, QFLS gain, and ion-migration activation-energy increase. The intact, correctly oriented bifunctional molecule should show a superadditive response relative to the two single-function controls. If a surface dipole is dominant, the nonbinding dipolar analogue should reproduce the work-function and Voc/QFLS changes without corresponding chemical-binding, trap, or ion-migration improvements, and orientation should matter mainly through dipole projection rather than dual defect neutralization.
scoring_key_points: Proposes intact, thiol-blocked, ammonium-disabled, and nonbinding dipolar controls, preferably with an orientation-locked or spacer-control pair.
Requires surface-coverage normalization so orientation/functionality is not confounded by adsorption amount.
Separates chemical binding, work-function/dipole, defect-recombination, and ion-migration measurements with orthogonal probes.

States contrasting predictions: dual-site passivation loses trap/ion benefits when either group is blocked, whereas a dipole-only analogue preserves energetic shifts without chemical/defect improvements.
accepted_equivalents: A thioether, protected thiol, or sterically inaccessible sulfur group is acceptable as the thiol-disabled control.
An amine, quaternary ammonium lacking hydrogen-bond geometry, neutral amide, or matched nonionic head group may serve as the ammonium-disabled control if the dipole consequence is discussed.
DFT adsorption geometries may support, but not replace, experimental orientation and coverage measurements.
PLQY-derived QFLS, absolute PL, ideality-factor analysis, or interface-selective recombination measurements may be used to quantify nonradiative loss.
common_wrong_answers: Using only UPS or KPFM and inferring chemical passivation from a work-function shift.
Comparing molecules with different surface coverage without normalization.
Treating longer PL lifetime as unambiguous proof of better extraction or lower recombination without device-stack context.
Claiming dual passivation merely because both functional groups are present, without blocked controls or evidence of simultaneous engagement.

expected_answer:
A minimal library should vary three factors independently. First, use at least two aromatic-core sizes bearing the same directly conjugated aldehyde or ketone group. Second, include aldehyde-free analogues of each aromatic core to measure any direct pi-only interaction. Third, break conjugation by inserting a saturated methylene spacer between the aromatic ring and carbonyl while retaining similar size and polarity. An even stronger factorial design adds electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents on the same aromatic core, allowing carbonyl electron density to change without changing aromatic area. A nonaromatic aldehyde can provide a baseline carbonyl control.

The causal chain should be measured before film morphology is considered. DFT/ESP or calibrated carbonyl basicity should predict donor strength; carbonyl stretching frequency, model PbI2 binding, NMR, and Pb 4f XPS shifts should quantify coordination. Post-deposition surface treatment or matched crystallization conditions should then test whether trap-density, PLQY/QFLS, and recombination changes persist when grain growth is held constant. Morphology, XRD, and local-current data are downstream consequences, not the primary proof.

The mediation model is validated if carbonyl-Pb binding and defect reduction track carbonyl electron density: larger conjugated cores or electron-donating substituents strengthen the carbonyl interaction; aldehyde-free aromatics remain weak; and the conjugation-broken aryl-CH2-carbonyl analogue loses the large-core advantage. It is falsified if aldehyde-free large aromatics passivate as strongly as carbonyl compounds, if the conjugation-broken analogue retains the full trend without a carbonyl-electronic change, or if device improvements occur only with morphology changes and no corresponding binding/defect signatures.
scoring_key_points: Builds a factorial library containing conjugated carbonyl aromatics, aldehyde-free pi-only analogues, and a saturated-spacer conjugation-break control.
Optionally strengthens causality with donor/withdrawer substituents at fixed aromatic size or a nonaromatic carbonyl baseline.
Orders evidence from carbonyl electronic structure and Pb binding to defect/recombination metrics, while controlling or bypassing crystallization changes.
States validating and falsifying trends that distinguish carbonyl-mediated electronic tuning from direct pi binding and morphology-only effects.
accepted_equivalents: A ketone, amide, or ester series is acceptable if the same carbonyl functionality is held constant and its donor strength is independently quantified.
Hammett constants, computed lone-pair energy, carbonyl proton affinity, or vibrational shifts may represent carbonyl electron density.
Post-treatment, vapor treatment, or identical seeded crystallization may be used to decouple passivation from nucleation and grain-growth effects.
PbI2 adduct spectroscopy, single-crystal model surfaces, or undercoordinated-Pb molecular complexes may substitute for direct film binding measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only three different aromatic aldehydes and treating correlation with ring size as proof of causation.
Omitting aldehyde-free or conjugation-broken controls.
Using larger grain size or stronger XRD peaks as the sole evidence for defect passivation.
Claiming that pi electrons directly coordinate Pb2+ without testing whether carbonyl electron density mediates the effect.

expected_answer:
The two tests expose different failure modes. Dark thermal storage stresses adhesion, thermal-expansion mismatch, and buried-contact continuity, so a substrate-selective nucleation layer can prevent peeling and preserve hole collection. One-sun MPP operation generates carriers and electric fields that drive halide vacancies and ions toward the top electron-contact/electrode interface, where they can change band alignment, create interfacial recombination, or react with the metal. Improving the buried contact therefore need not improve the top-interface ionic failure.

A rational device retains the buried nucleation/adhesion layer and adds a top-side intervention: low-defect crystal termination, halide-vacancy passivation, an ion-blocking but electronically selective interlayer, a chemically robust ETL, and/or an electrode diffusion barrier. The top treatment must be thin enough to preserve electron extraction and should not introduce a new delamination plane.

The stress matrix should include dark 85 degrees C storage, thermal cycling, one-sun open circuit, one-sun MPP, forward-bias dark stress, and combined light-bias-temperature testing. Buried failure is diagnosed by adhesion/peel tests, optical or tomographic air-gap maps, contact resistance, and loss of hole collection without halide redistribution. Top-interface ionic failure is diagnosed by time-resolved PL/EL shifts, ToF-SIMS or XPS depth profiles, electrode discoloration/corrosion, interfacial impedance, and spatial recombination maps. Combination is justified when the buried treatment uniquely preserves adhesion and dark-heat performance, the top treatment uniquely suppresses ionic/electrode signatures and MPP decay, and the combined device exhibits both benefits without added resistance or optical loss.
scoring_key_points: Separates dark-heat buried delamination/contact loss from carrier- and field-driven top-interface ion migration/electrode chemistry.
Combines the buried nucleation/adhesion strategy with a selective top-surface vacancy/ion-blocking and electrode-protection intervention.
Defines a stress matrix spanning dark heat, thermal cycling, light-only, MPP, bias-only, and coupled stress.
Specifies orthogonal failure diagnostics and an additive-benefit criterion showing why both interventions are needed.
accepted_equivalents: A robust fullerene/oxide electron contact, self-assembled ion barrier, 2D cap, or metal-diffusion barrier is acceptable if extraction and new-interface risks are addressed.
Acoustic microscopy, scanning laser-beam-induced current, electroluminescence imaging, or cross-sectional microscopy may diagnose contact loss.
Secondary-ion mass spectrometry, isotope tracing, operando XPS, or ion-sensitive impedance may diagnose top-interface migration.
A factorial 2x2 device experiment with buried treatment, top treatment, both, and neither is an acceptable proof of complementarity.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the buried-contact strategy failed because it did not improve MPP aging.
Replacing the buried treatment with a top passivator and ignoring thermal peeling.
Using only total PCE retention without assigning the physical failure mode.
Claiming operational stability from dark thermal storage.

expected_answer:
At least four matched compositions or processes are required. The baseline is the original mixed-halide film without the cation. A Br-reduced control without the cation tests whether lower Br fraction alone is sufficient, with bandgap matched as closely as possible through A-site composition or optical-thickness design. A cation-containing composition at the original Br fraction tests cation effects independent of Br reduction. A nonincorporating crystallization retarder or solvent additive should be tuned to reproduce grain size, residual PbX2, trap density, and roughness without changing the lattice. A useful additional control is a post-treatment that exposes the surface to the cation but prevents A-site incorporation, or a size/dipole-matched A-site analogue that changes crystallization but not the same bond/strain state.

The control set must verify where the cation resides and whether the intended lattice change occurred. Composition and incorporation can be checked by NMR/mass spectrometry, XPS/ToF-SIMS, and diffraction. Residual strain, octahedral distortion, bond lengths, vacancy formation energy, trap density, Urbach energy, and morphology should be measured independently. Ionic transport then needs temperature-dependent conductivity or transient ion-drift measurements for activation energy and mobile-ion density.

The decisive test is operando coupled illumination plus forward bias, ideally with temperature control. Intrinsic lattice reinforcement is supported if the A-site-incorporated samples retain stable PL/EL spectra and diffraction/composition, show higher migration activation energy and lower mobile-ion density, and do so even when Br fraction and morphology are matched. If the Br-reduced control or morphology-matched retarder suppresses segregation equally without the strain/bond/vacancy-energy signature, the lattice-reinforcement claim is not unique. If only initial PLQY or trap density improves while spectra red-shift under coupled stress, defect reduction alone is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Includes baseline, Br-reduced/no-cation, cation-at-matched-Br, and morphology/crystallization-matched nonincorporating controls.
Verifies cation incorporation and independently measures lattice strain/bonding/vacancy energetics, morphology/traps, and ionic transport.
Uses coupled light-plus-forward-bias operando testing rather than relying on dark, light-only, or initial-device metrics.
Defines the decisive pattern: only true A-site incorporation gives stable spectra/composition and higher ion-migration barriers after Br and morphology are controlled.
accepted_equivalents: A matched-bandgap rather than exactly matched-Br control is acceptable if the compositional tradeoff is explicitly handled.
A different A-site cation with similar crystallization effect but different lattice bonding may serve as the morphology/process control.
Operando absorption, hyperspectral imaging, nano-XRD, or cathodoluminescence may replace PL/EL if segregation is directly resolved.
Transient ion drift, dielectric relaxation, impedance spectroscopy, or isotope migration may replace temperature-dependent conductivity.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only baseline and cation-treated films, which conflates Br content, crystallization, traps, and lattice effects.
Using lower trap density as sufficient proof of phase-segregation suppression.
Testing only under illumination without the tandem-relevant bias component.
Assuming reduced Br content automatically eliminates phase segregation.

expected_answer:
The cation cannot be selected only for phase stability because it changes octahedral tilting, lattice strain, crystallization, and often the bandgap. The first constraint is optical/electrical current matching to silicon: the absorber composition and thickness must retain the target approximately 1.75 eV absorption edge, adequate near-band-edge absorption, and current density compatible with the silicon bottom cell. Any reduced-Br benefit must be balanced against bandgap shift and parasitic absorption in transport or recombination layers.

Materials validation must confirm true A-site incorporation, single perovskite phase, acceptable tolerance factor, no low-dimensional or nonperovskite inclusions, uniform strain, low trap/Urbach energy, and unchanged or improved carrier mobility and selective-contact extraction. The cation must not create a persistent insulating intermediate, excessive residual stress, or incompatibility with textured silicon, recombination-junction processing, and subsequent thermal steps.

The stress sequence should progress from films to single-junction front cells and then full two-terminal tandems. It must include dark, light-only, bias-only, temperature, and combined light-bias-temperature testing at the actual front-cell operating voltage/current and MPP, because a tandem redistributes voltage and carrier density differently from an isolated film. Operando PL/EL/absorption, QFLS/Voc, ion-migration activation energy/mobile-ion density, diffraction, and depth-resolved halide profiles should be coupled to tandem current matching and stabilized power. Finally, large-area coating must demonstrate uniform cation incorporation, bandgap, strain, PL spectrum, and module/tandem current across textured substrates.

Reject the strategy if it causes current mismatch or optical loss that outweighs voltage/stability gains; introduces secondary phases, low mobility, contact barriers, FF or QFLS loss; suppresses segregation only in light-only tests but not under coupled tandem stress; or cannot maintain composition and performance uniformity at scale.
scoring_key_points: Requires preservation of the target bandgap, absorption and current matching to silicon, not stability optimization in isolation.
Requires phase-pure A-site incorporation with acceptable strain, defects, mobility, contact extraction, and process compatibility with the tandem stack.
Defines staged film-front-cell-full-tandem validation under dark, light, bias, temperature, and coupled MPP-relevant stress with direct ionic/segregation diagnostics.
Provides explicit rejection criteria for current mismatch, secondary phases, transport/QFLS/FF losses, coupled-stress failure, or scale-up nonuniformity.
accepted_equivalents: Optical transfer-matrix/current-matching simulation plus measured EQE is acceptable for the bandgap/current constraint.
Perovskite-silicon tandem stress may be specified through the measured front-cell quasi-Fermi splitting or subcell-resolved bias rather than a fixed external voltage.
Nano-XRD, hyperspectral PL, ellipsometry, or spatial EQE may be used for large-area uniformity mapping.
A three-terminal diagnostic tandem may be used during development if final validation is performed in the intended two-terminal architecture.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a cation that stabilizes a perovskite/organic tandem will transfer unchanged to a silicon tandem.
Ignoring bandgap and current-matching penalties caused by lattice or halide-composition changes.
Testing only isolated films or single-junction cells under light soaking.
Accepting improved T90 despite secondary phases, FF loss, or large-area bandgap nonuniformity.

expected_answer: Longer PL lifetime is not sufficient because both reduced recombination and inhibited extraction can prolong carrier residence. The minimum design should include untreated, bulk-network-only, surface-layer-only, combined-network, noncoordinating-polymer, and nitrile-monomer controls, plus a surface-layer thickness or pre-polymerization-time series. Absolute PLQY under calibrated excitation should be converted to implied quasi-Fermi-level splitting and compared with device Voc; front- and rear-side excitation and an optical-cavity-matched inert overlayer should test photon-recycling and outcoupling artifacts. Fluence-dependent PLQY/TRPL and temperature-dependent recombination should separate trap-assisted from bimolecular channels. Chemical coordination should be supported by Pb-sensitive spectroscopy and a change in electrically measured trap density, not spectroscopy alone. Extraction must be measured in complete selective-contact stacks using transient photocurrent, charge-extraction time, impedance, field-dependent PL quenching, and pseudo-JV or Suns-Voc. True passivation gives higher PLQY/QFLS, lower trap density and ideality factor, and equal or faster extraction with improved Voc and pseudo-FF. An optical effect changes detected PL without a consistent QFLS or electrical recombination benefit and depends strongly on observation geometry. A transport barrier gives long TRPL but slower photocurrent, charge accumulation, S-shaped or illumination-dependent JV, and a thickness-dependent FF penalty. The optimal layer must therefore maximize nonradiative-loss reduction before extraction resistance appears.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that stronger PL and longer TRPL can result from passivation, optical outcoupling/photon recycling, or inhibited extraction.
Uses bulk-only, surface-only, combined, noncoordinating-polymer, monomer, and thickness/pre-polymerization controls to vary coordination and transport independently.
Requires absolute PLQY-derived QFLS, fluence/geometry dependence, Pb coordination and electrical trap measurements, plus device-level extraction diagnostics.
Provides distinct passivation, optical-artifact, and transport-barrier signatures, including the possibility of a thickness-dependent fill-factor penalty.
accepted_equivalents: Implied Voc from absolute luminescence, calibrated external PL efficiency, or quasi-Fermi-level splitting as equivalent nonradiative-loss metrics
Transient photocurrent, time-of-flight, charge-extraction, or frequency-resolved photoconductivity as extraction diagnostics
An optically matched inert polymer, dielectric overlayer, or cavity simulation as an outcoupling/photon-recycling control
Ideality factor, Suns-Voc, electroluminescence efficiency, or recombination resistance as device-level recombination probes
common_wrong_answers: Declaring passivation solely because TRPL becomes longer
Using only XPS or FTIR coordination evidence without an electrical or quasi-Fermi-level-splitting measurement
Ignoring that an overthick polymer layer can improve PL while reducing charge extraction and fill factor

expected_answer: The process must be parameterized by polymerization, drying, crystallization, and phase-conversion times rather than by nominal additive concentration alone. A factorial study should vary monomer and initiator ratios, inhibitor content, ink age, solvent coordination strength, temperature, wet thickness, coating speed, gas-knife intensity, substrate temperature, surface-treatment molecular weight, and secondary-cure time. In-situ Raman or FTIR should track vinyl conversion, while GPC/DLS or rheology tracks pre-polymer growth; in-situ GIWAXS and optical spectra should show whether perovskite nucleation and halide-phase formation remain controlled. Depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS and cross-sectional microscopy should verify a continuous but ultrathin surface layer and a distributed grain-boundary network without polymer-rich insulating domains. Bulk-only, surface-only, noncoordinating-polymer, and no-initiator controls are required. Under illumination and bias, spatially resolved PL/EQE should monitor mixed-halide phase segregation, while transient ion-drift, low-frequency impedance, and halide depth profiles test migration. Module acceptance should include cross-web conversion, thickness, PLQY, sheet resistance, EL/PL, local shunt, and series-resistance maps. The strategy should be rejected if polymer conversion and perovskite crystallization cannot be independently controlled, if phase segregation is accelerated, if local extraction resistance grows with surface coverage, or if module uniformity requires a process window narrower than manufacturing capability.
scoring_key_points: Defines and independently varies polymerization, solvent-drying, perovskite-nucleation, and secondary-cure timescales for scalable coating.
Uses conversion, molecular-weight/rheology, in-situ crystallization, and depth-resolved network diagnostics with bulk-only, surface-only, noncoordinating, and no-initiator controls.
Tests mixed-halide phase segregation and ion migration under coupled illumination, bias, and heat rather than relying only on initial PCE.
Sets module-scale spatial acceptance and explicit rejection criteria for extraction barriers, accelerated segregation, uncontrolled crystallization, or an impractically narrow process window.
accepted_equivalents: Real-time NIR, Raman, calorimetry, or dielectric spectroscopy for monitoring polymer conversion
GIWAXS, XRD, optical reflectance, or spectroscopic ellipsometry for tracking perovskite crystallization during coating
Bias-dependent PL mapping, hyperspectral imaging, or operando absorption as mixed-halide phase-segregation diagnostics
Residence-time distribution and dimensionless reaction-to-drying ratios as equivalent process-transfer descriptors
common_wrong_answers: Copying the small-cell monomer dose and cure time directly into slot-die coating
Assuming more polymer always improves stability without measuring extraction resistance or phase segregation
Using only final module PCE and no chemical conversion, depth distribution, or spatial-uniformity criteria

expected_answer: The layer changes at least three variables, so a single treated-versus-control comparison is underdetermined. Chemical passivation should be isolated with a molecular or ionic treatment that supplies the same vacancy-binding groups but does not form the low-dimensional lattice. Ionic blocking should be isolated with a chemically inert, high-ion-migration-barrier interlayer having similar thickness and band alignment, while electronic effects should be varied through a thickness series and low-dimensional compositions with different band offsets but comparable surface coverage. PLQY/QFLS, TRPL, trap-filled-limit voltage, surface-potential mapping, and ideality factor test passivation. Temperature-dependent ionic conductivity, hysteresis relaxation, transient ion-drift, and operando or post-bias ToF-SIMS/EDS quantify iodide blocking and extract activation energies. UPS/KPFM, band-offset measurements, transient photocurrent, charge extraction, impedance, intensity-dependent JV, and Suns-Voc separate contact selectivity from series resistance. Passivation is supported when QFLS and trap metrics improve even in the nonblocking treatment. Ionic blocking is supported when iodine redistribution and hysteresis slow without a corresponding change in electronic extraction. Contact modification is supported by systematic thickness- and band-offset-dependent extraction. Hidden resistance is present if thicker layers or low temperature produce S-shaped JV, slower photocurrent, reduced high-flux collection, or a larger gap between pseudo-FF and measured FF even though ion migration and aging improve.
scoring_key_points: Uses passivation-only, ion-barrier-only, and band-offset/thickness controls to decouple the three functions of the interlayer.
Assigns vacancy passivation using QFLS/PL, SCLC or trap metrics, surface potential, and recombination measurements.
Assigns ionic blocking using temperature- and bias-dependent migration kinetics, activation energy, hysteresis relaxation, and halide depth profiling.
Diagnoses electronic contact resistance with extraction/pseudo-JV methods and identifies S-shaped, low-temperature, high-flux, or thickness-dependent penalties as hidden resistance.
accepted_equivalents: A noncrystallizing diammonium treatment, vacancy-binding monolayer, or passivating salt as a passivation-only control
An ultrathin oxide, wide-gap 2D material, or isostructural high-barrier perovskitoid as an ion-barrier control if band alignment is measured
Bias-stress recovery, low-frequency impedance, isotope tracing, or Kelvin-probe relaxation as ionic-kinetic alternatives
Suns-Voc/pseudo-FF, transient extraction, temperature-dependent JV, or contact-resistivity measurements for hidden electronic resistance
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the unchanged Voc to absence of passivation even though recombination and fill factor may change without a champion Voc shift
Claiming that less iodine at the electrode proves the layer has no electronic transport penalty
Using only one interlayer thickness and no passivation-only or barrier-only control

expected_answer: The transferred layer must combine a high migration barrier for halide vacancies with low electronic trap density, chemical compatibility, conformal coverage, and band offsets that remain selective rather than blocking the collected carrier. Its thickness must be below the carrier tunneling or transport limit yet continuous enough to eliminate pinholes; an orthogonal solvent and low-temperature process should preserve the single crystal. Controls should include the untreated detector, a passivation-only treatment, an inert insulating layer of matched thickness, and a composition or thickness series that changes ionic barrier and electronic offset separately. Under sustained electric field and X-ray dose, the study should track dark-current drift, baseline recovery, sensitivity, charge-collection efficiency, mobility-lifetime product, temporal response, energy resolution, polarization time, and spatial response uniformity. Operando current transients, impedance, Kelvin-potential mapping, and depth-resolved halide/electrode profiles after bias should quantify ionic redistribution; temperature dependence should yield activation energies. Genuine ion blocking gives slower polarization, less electrode contamination, stable dark current, and preserved or improved charge collection and response speed. An insulating contact merely lowers both dark and signal current, increases collection time or trapping, worsens the mobility-lifetime product or energy resolution, and produces thickness-dependent field loss. A design fails if stability improves only by reducing internal field or detector gain, if pinholes cause local breakdown, or if the process damages the crystal surface.
scoring_key_points: Specifies simultaneous ionic-barrier, low-trap, conformal, chemically compatible, and carrier-selective energetic requirements for the interlayer.
Uses untreated, passivation-only, inert-insulator, and thickness/composition controls to separate ion blocking from current suppression.

Measures polarization, dark-current drift, sensitivity, charge-collection efficiency, mobility-lifetime product, response speed, spatial uniformity, and ion/electrode redistribution under dose and bias.
Defines genuine blocking as ionic stabilization with preserved signal collection, and rejects designs that reduce both dark and photocurrent through an insulating or field-screening contact.
accepted_equivalents: Gamma-ray, beta-particle, or photoconductor detector transfer if high-field polarization and charge collection are evaluated
Hecht analysis, time-of-flight mobility, transient current technique, or charge-sensitive pulse analysis for carrier collection
Operando X-ray fluorescence, isotope-resolved SIMS, cross-sectional EDS, or XPS depth profiling for electrode/halide migration
Guard-ring mapping, scanning microbeam response, or pixel-to-pixel gain mapping as spatial uniformity diagnostics
common_wrong_answers: Judging success only from a lower dark current without measuring signal charge collection or response time
Assuming a thicker blocking layer is always better for stability
Transferring the solar-cell interlayer without measuring detector-specific band offsets, high-field polarization, or radiation-induced damage

expected_answer: The diagnosis requires observing both disappearance of the donor carrier and appearance of the acceptor or product-forming state. Optical controls should first correct absorption, scattering, inner-filter effects, and catalyst loading using integrating-sphere absorptance and front/back or diluted-powder measurements. Material controls should include pristine perovskite, MoS2 alone, a physical mixture, an electronically decoupled interface with an ultrathin spacer, a stoichiometry series that changes Pb-S bonding, and a conventional cocatalyst benchmark. A global kinetic model should contain perovskite radiative and trap-assisted recombination, interfacial electron-transfer rate, back-transfer rate, MoS2 trapping/catalytic consumption, and fluence-dependent multicarrier terms. Selective excitation and spectrally resolved fs-TA or time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity should seek a MoS2 electron or reduced-state rise that is temporally correlated with perovskite bleach decay, followed by a long-lived separated-charge population. Time-resolved EPR, radical trapping, isotope labeling, photocurrent, AQE, and hydrogen rate should scale with the extracted transfer yield. Productive transfer gives matched donor-decay/acceptor-rise kinetics, suppressed recombination, long-lived charges, and higher quantum yield. Trap quenching gives faster PL/bleach loss without an acceptor-state rise, strong fluence dependence, heat generation, or low AQE. Optical reabsorption changes detected PL but not carrier conductivity, acceptor-state population, or chemical quantum yield.
scoring_key_points: Requires direct observation of an acceptor-side electron or reduced catalytic state in addition to donor PL/bleach decay.
Uses absorption/scattering corrections and pristine, physical-mixture, spacer-decoupled, stoichiometry, and cocatalyst controls.
Builds a kinetic model containing transfer, back-transfer, trapping, radiative/nonradiative recombination, catalytic consumption, and fluence-dependent channels.
Links transfer yield to long-lived separated charges, photocurrent/AQE, radicals, and hydrogen production, with distinct signatures for trap quenching and optical artifacts.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved X-ray absorption, EPR, microwave conductivity, or terahertz conductivity for observing acceptor-side charge
An insulating ligand, oxide spacer, or chemically blocked sulfur interface as an electronically decoupled control
Apparent quantum yield, incident-photon-to-hydrogen efficiency, or action-spectrum-normalized product yield as chemical transfer validation
Global target analysis, kinetic Monte Carlo, or coupled rate equations if donor, acceptor, trapping, and back-transfer channels are explicit
common_wrong_answers: Treating shorter PL lifetime as automatic evidence of beneficial charge transfer
Using only steady-state hydrogen rate without correcting absorption, scattering, or catalyst loading
Omitting an acceptor-state or long-lived-charge measurement and relying solely on perovskite-side signals

expected_answer: Manufacturing should use mix-on-demand preparation with metered precursor and additive feeds, a short static or microfluidic mixer, minimal dead volume, and a defined residence-time distribution before the coating head. Tank recirculation that repeatedly ages the ink should be avoided or separated from a small controlled hold-up loop. Temperature, oxygen, water content, solvent ratio, concentration, shear history, and filtration must be fixed because they alter coordination and aggregation rates. Inline Raman or NIR spectra, optical turbidity, multi-angle scattering, viscosity, density, conductivity, and temperature should be calibrated against offline metal NMR/SAXS and film performance. Acceptance limits should define a multivariate precursor-state window rather than a clock time alone; out-of-window ink should be automatically diverted, diluted, cooled, remixed, or discarded. Residence-time-distribution tracers and periodic samples at mixer, manifold, coating edges, and web center should detect local aging and cross-web nonuniformity. Validation should link precursor state to in-situ crystallization, film roughness/orientation, QFLS, sheet resistance, module EL/PL and local JV, followed by MPP aging at room and elevated temperature. Residence-time control is insufficient if identically measured inline states still yield batch-dependent films, if turbidity nucleates unpredictably in dead zones, if the acceptable window is shorter than equipment response, or if oxygen/water and concentration sensitivity dominate. Then donor strengths, counterion, additive loading, solvent coordination, or a less aggregation-prone bifunctional molecule must be redesigned.
scoring_key_points: Uses mix-on-demand equipment with controlled residence-time distribution, minimal dead volume, and explicit control of temperature, water, oxygen, solvent, concentration, and shear.
Defines a calibrated multivariate inline precursor-state window using spectroscopy, scattering/turbidity, rheology, and physical-property sensors rather than elapsed time alone.
Implements diversion or corrective feedback and samples the mixer, manifold, coating width, and run time to detect local aging and nonuniformity.
Links precursor state to film/module quality and MPP stability and states when stochastic nucleation, excessive sensitivity, or an unmanufacturably narrow window requires molecular reformulation.
accepted_equivalents: Inline static mixing, impinging-jet mixing, microfluidic mixing, or point-of-use additive injection with a measured residence-time distribution
Raman, NIR, UV-visible, fluorescence, dielectric, acoustic, or small-angle optical scattering as inline state sensors after calibration
Model-predictive control, statistical process control, or digital-twin residence-time control as feedback frameworks
Web-resolved PL/EL, hyperspectral reflectance, sheet-resistance, lock-in thermography, or local JV mapping for module validation
common_wrong_answers: Preparing a large batch and merely instructing operators to coat it quickly
Using a fixed 30-minute timer without monitoring temperature, water, oxygen, aggregation, or residence-time distribution
Claiming scale-up success from one small-area champion device without cross-web statistics and operational stability

expected_answer: The b-axis anomaly cannot be assigned from the photocurrent alone. Incomplete switching or domain-wall pinning would preserve the bulk polar phase but reduce the switched b-axis polarization; it should appear as a degraded b-axis PUND or polarization-electric-field response and as incomplete domain reversal, while the c-axis response remains intact. Mobile ions or contact polarization can create a slowly relaxing internal field, higher dark conductance, and apparent photovoltaic memory without true polarization reversal; this contribution should depend strongly on dwell time, frequency, temperature, bias history, and electrode configuration, and should relax in the dark. Loss of the bulk polar phase would suppress the intrinsic switching response and should be accompanied by a symmetry or dielectric change rather than only a contact-dependent drift. A decisive sequence is therefore: axis-resolved PUND or switching-current measurements before and after cycling; domain-sensitive imaging where applicable; dark-relaxation, frequency, temperature, and electrode-reversal tests with symmetric contacts; and variable-temperature diffraction or dielectric measurements correlated with axis-resolved zero-bias photocurrent and poling reversal.
scoring_key_points: Identifies incomplete domain switching or domain-wall pinning as a mechanism that selectively suppresses the switched b-axis polarization while the bulk may remain ferroelectric.
Identifies mobile-ion redistribution or contact polarization as a slow, history-dependent source of apparent zero-bias signal and increased dark conductance.
Distinguishes loss of the bulk polar phase by requiring collapse of intrinsic switching plus a symmetry or dielectric signature, not merely photocurrent drift.

Proposes an axis-resolved sequence combining PUND/P-E or switching current, domain or surface-potential imaging, relaxation/frequency/temperature/contact controls, and structural or dielectric verification.
accepted_equivalents: Domain pinning, incomplete ferroelastic variant switching, or an unfavorable domain population may be treated as equivalent domain-switching failures.
Halide-vacancy drift, ionic space charge, electrochemical contact modification, or electrode-barrier polarization are acceptable mobile-field mechanisms.
Variable-temperature single-crystal XRD, second-harmonic generation, pyroelectric response, or dielectric anomalies may serve as bulk-polar-phase checks when interpreted correctly.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the failure only to lower b-axis optical absorption without addressing loss of poling reversibility and slow dark relaxation.
Treating any persistent zero-bias photocurrent as proof of ferroelectric bulk photovoltaic behavior.
Using only post-cycling XRD and ignoring axis-resolved switching and contact or ionic controls.

expected_answer: Layer number changes crystallographic symmetry, octahedral distortion, organic-cation ordering, and the number and orientation of allowed polarization states; multiaxial ferroelectricity is therefore not guaranteed to evolve monotonically with increasing inorganic thickness. Higher conductivity and a narrower bandgap can improve absorption and carrier collection, but excess free carriers can screen ferroelectric polarization, increase dark current and noise, and reduce the useful zero-bias voltage or detectivity. A higher-n member may also place the operating temperature closer to a polar-to-nonpolar transition or make domain states less stable under field, heat, or strain. Candidate selection should combine variable-temperature structural symmetry and dielectric classification, axis-resolved PUND or P-E switching, axis-resolved zero-bias voltage/current with reversible poling, and detector metrics that include dark noise, response stability, phase-transition margin, and cycling. Device geometry should use well-defined crystallographic axes and symmetric, nonreactive contacts so that contact fields are not mistaken for a bulk photovoltaic effect.
scoring_key_points: States that ferroelectric dimensionality and allowed polarization directions are symmetry-controlled and need not increase monotonically with inorganic-layer number.
Explains the absorption/conductivity benefit versus polarization screening, dark-current, and noise trade-off.
Recognizes operating-temperature, phase-transition, domain-stability, or strain margins as reliability constraints.
Requires joint structural, dielectric/switching, axis-resolved poling-reversible photovoltaic, and noise/cycling validation with controlled contacts and crystal orientation.
accepted_equivalents: Free-carrier screening, depolarization-field compensation, and leakage-current masking are equivalent descriptions of the conductivity penalty.
Second-harmonic generation or pyroelectric measurements can complement diffraction and dielectric tests for polar-symmetry validation.
Signal-to-noise ratio, specific detectivity, or noise-equivalent power may be used instead of dark current alone as the practical detector criterion.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a narrower bandgap or larger photocurrent necessarily means a larger bulk photovoltaic voltage.
Assuming every higher-n Ruddlesden-Popper phase remains polar and multiaxial.
Selecting a material from room-temperature conductivity alone without checking phase stability, switching, dark noise, and contact artifacts.

expected_answer: Unchanged bulk diffraction only shows retention of the average crystalline phase and can miss reconstruction of the outermost, catalytically active layers. Likewise, detecting *CO and *CHO proves that intermediates exist somewhere on the electrode but not that they occupy chemically nonequivalent neighboring sites or undergo the productive cross-coupling step. Surface reduction, vacancy redistribution, cation segregation, or conversion of distinct Cu coordination environments into more similar sites could redirect *CHO toward hydrogenation and methane even while the bulk lattice survives. A second explanation is a change in local CO2 activity, pH, water activity, ionomer wetting, flooding, or gas transport, which changes *CO coverage and proton delivery without destroying the motif. The two causes should be separated by correlating selectivity with surface-sensitive operando structure/valence probes such as XAS/EXAFS, Raman, or ambient-pressure XPS; time-resolved or isotopic vibrational measurements that test productive C-C coupling rather than intermediate presence alone; and matched hydrodynamic, gas-flow, pressure, electrolyte, and electrode-wetting controls. Recovery after restoring mass transport would support an environmental cause, whereas persistent selectivity loss coupled to altered local Cu coordination would support reconstruction.
scoring_key_points: Explains that bulk XRD cannot establish retention of the catalytically active surface coordination or ordered adjacent-site motif.
Explains that simultaneous *CO and *CHO detection does not establish spatial adjacency or productive asymmetric C-C coupling.
Contrasts surface reconstruction/valence-vacancy changes with local pH, CO2 activity, wetting, flooding, proton supply, or other mass-transport changes.
Proposes correlated surface-sensitive operando structure/valence measurements, transient or isotope-sensitive intermediate tests, and matched transport/environment controls with a recovery criterion.
accepted_equivalents: Surface amorphization, reduction to Cu-like phases, oxygen-vacancy reorganization, or coordination homogenization are acceptable reconstruction mechanisms.
Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry, isotope labeling, or potential-step kinetics can substitute for transient infrared tests if they directly probe coupling pathways.
Operando total scattering, grazing-incidence XAS, Raman, or surface-sensitive electron spectroscopy are acceptable alternatives to the named structural probes.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that unchanged bulk XRD proves the active surface is unchanged.
Treating the presence of *CO and *CHO peaks as direct proof that a C-C bond is being formed between them.
Assigning the selectivity shift only to catalyst deactivation without controlling local pH, flooding, gas delivery, or ionomer state.

expected_answer: The initial PL and voltage gain is consistent with passivation of interfacial traps and reduced Shockley-Read-Hall recombination, but it does not establish that the interface is dynamically stable. An ionic passivant, a weakly bound counterion, or a passivant-induced interfacial dipole can become mobile under heat, illumination, and field. Its redistribution, together with native halide or A-site ions, can alter band bending, accumulate charge at selective contacts, and create time-dependent extraction barriers, producing hysteresis and enhanced low-frequency capacitance. Irreversible reactions with the transport layer, electrode, or perovskite, loss of adhesion, or contact corrosion can then cause permanent efficiency loss. Mobile accumulation is supported by strong bias-, temperature-, frequency-, and dwell-time dependence and partial recovery after dark or zero-bias rest; irreversible degradation is supported by persistent loss and new chemical, structural, or contact-resistance signatures. The diagnosis should combine bias/temperature-dependent impedance and transient current-voltage measurements with dark-recovery tests, spatial surface-potential or ion-distribution mapping, and before/after interface-sensitive chemical and structural analysis. Neutral, covalently anchored, or immobile-passivant controls are needed to separate trap passivation from ionic mobility.
scoring_key_points: Reconciles the initial PL/Voc gain with reduced interfacial non-radiative recombination rather than assuming global stability.
Explains how mobile passivant species or native ions can alter band bending and extraction, producing hysteresis and low-frequency capacitance.
Distinguishes reversible ionic accumulation by history dependence and dark/zero-bias recovery from persistent chemical, mechanical, or contact degradation.
Proposes coupled transient/impedance, recovery, spatial ion or potential mapping, interface chemistry/structure, and immobile-passivant control experiments.
accepted_equivalents: Slow interfacial polarization, ionic double-layer formation, or field-driven space charge are equivalent to mobile-ion accumulation when tied to dynamic band bending.
ToF-SIMS, Kelvin probe force microscopy, operando XPS, depth-resolved XPS, or isotope labeling may be used to track ionic redistribution.
Suns-Voc, transient photovoltage/current, intensity-dependent Voc, or stabilized MPP measurements may complement impedance for separating recombination and extraction losses.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that higher initial PL automatically guarantees better operational stability.
Explaining low-frequency capacitance only as an electronic dielectric response while ignoring slow ionic processes.
Using a single post-aging J-V curve without recovery, bias-history, temperature, or chemical controls.

expected_answer: The chemistry cannot be transferred by copying solution concentration alone. Slot-die coating changes wet-film thickness, drying rate, solvent history, meniscus flow, and substrate residence time, while flexible substrates add roughness and surface-energy variability. These factors can produce incomplete or multilayer SAM coverage, poor perovskite wetting, pinholes, and spatially variable interface dipoles. The module also introduces long lateral current paths, interconnects, dead area, barrier edges, and larger defect statistics, so fill-factor loss may arise from series resistance or local shunts even if small-area interface recombination is improved. Bending can delaminate a weakly bound monolayer or crack electrodes, and damp heat can accelerate desorption, hydrolysis, and ion or metal migration. Transfer should therefore establish a coating-process window using contact angle, thickness/coverage, surface-potential, PL/EL, and defect maps across web position and speed; redesign the chemistry for robust low-temperature deposition, solvent compatibility, and preferably crosslinking or stronger anchoring; and co-optimize electrodes, interconnects, encapsulation, and mechanical neutral-axis placement. Qualification must use statistically meaningful module yield, spatially resolved resistance and luminescence, stabilized MPP under light/heat/humidity, thermal cycling, bending, and post-stress failure localization.
scoring_key_points: Explains how slot-die wetting, rheology, drying, substrate roughness, and residence time can change SAM coverage and perovskite nucleation relative to spin coating.
Identifies module-specific series resistance, shunts, interconnect/dead-area, and defect-statistics losses rather than attributing all fill-factor loss to recombination.
Addresses mechanical adhesion/cracking and damp-heat-driven desorption, hydrolysis, ion migration, or electrode reactions with chemistry/process redesign.
Requires spatial process mapping, statistically meaningful yield, stabilized MPP, environmental and bending tests, and post-stress failure localization before adoption.
accepted_equivalents: Blade coating, gravure, or roll-to-roll transfer considerations are acceptable analogues to slot-die coating when the altered drying and wetting physics are addressed.
Crosslinking, polymerizable anchors, multidentate binding, or an ultrathin protective overlayer are acceptable strategies for immobilizing the interface.
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, LBIC, hyperspectral PL, or sheet/contact-resistance mapping may be used for spatial module diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the module will match the cell if the same molar concentration and annealing temperature are used.
Attributing the lower fill factor only to larger area without identifying resistance, shunt, coating, or interconnect mechanisms.
Reporting only initial module efficiency without spatial mapping, stabilized MPP, humidity, thermal, and mechanical reliability tests.

expected_answer: The absence of a new GIWAXS phase rules out only sufficiently abundant, crystalline, long-range decomposition products; it does not exclude interfacial ion accumulation, amorphous products, nanoscale halide segregation, strain changes, or defect creation. A PL decrease together with increased low-frequency capacitance is consistent with slow ionic redistribution that changes local band bending and non-radiative recombination. Reversible ion redistribution or light-induced segregation should show systematic dependence on bias polarity, illumination, temperature, and time and should substantially recover during dark, open-circuit, or zero-bias relaxation. Irreversible decomposition should produce persistent optical/electrical loss and eventually chemical, mass, gas-evolution, or local structural signatures even if the average diffraction pattern changes little. The experiment should use programmed light/bias on-off and polarity steps with synchronized PL or hyperspectral imaging, impedance or transient current/voltage, and structure-sensitive scattering; add surface-potential or ion-distribution measurements and chemical spectroscopy at selected states. Spatially resolved data and an unilluminated or unprobed control are necessary to distinguish intrinsic device evolution from beam, laser, or thermal damage.
scoring_key_points: States that unchanged GIWAXS does not exclude ionic accumulation, amorphous/interfacial change, nanoscale segregation, strain, or defect evolution.
Links PL loss plus low-frequency capacitance to slow ionic redistribution and altered band bending/recombination without treating the signature as unique.
Uses reversibility, bias polarity, illumination, temperature, and rest behavior to distinguish ionic/segregation processes from persistent decomposition.
Designs synchronized light/bias perturbations with optical, electrical, structural, chemical/spatial measurements and probe-damage controls.
accepted_equivalents: Electroluminescence, absorption-edge mapping, cathodoluminescence, or Raman mapping may substitute for PL when used to resolve spatial/compositional evolution.
KPFM, ToF-SIMS, X-ray fluorescence, or isotope tracing may be used to detect ion redistribution.
Dark recovery, thermal recovery, polarity reversal, or compositional remixing are equivalent reversibility tests when kinetics are explicitly analyzed.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the device is chemically stable solely because GIWAXS shows no new diffraction peak.
Calling every PL decrease phase segregation without considering extraction, field, defects, heating, or contact changes.
Collecting the structural, optical, and electrical data in unrelated samples or at unrelated times and inferring causality from correlation alone.

expected_answer: A defensible pair is a fast structure-sensitive method such as grazing-incidence X-ray scattering or diffraction and a spatially scalable optical method such as hyperspectral reflectance/absorbance, photoluminescence imaging, or spectroscopic ellipsometry. The structural channel should identify nucleation, intermediate-phase conversion, orientation, and crystallization completion, while the optical channel should map solvent removal, band-edge evolution, thickness or composition uniformity, and emerging non-radiative regions. Both channels must be synchronized to web position, wet-film age, substrate temperature, gas flow, and coating speed so that a signal is assigned to the correct point in the drying trajectory. Calibration requires designed process perturbations and correlation with offline thickness, composition, morphology, defect maps, and final device yield or stabilized performance; multivariate thresholds should be validated across batches rather than fitted to one champion run. Closed-loop actions may adjust ink flow, web speed, substrate temperature, gas-knife intensity, or solvent-vapor environment. Probe dose, illumination heating, incidence-angle footprint, spatial aliasing, and sampling gaps must be measured with probe-off controls, duplicate tracks, and independent reference sensors before the system is allowed to reject material or alter the process.
scoring_key_points: Chooses complementary structure-sensitive and scalable optical/optoelectronic modalities and assigns each to distinct film-formation observables.
Synchronizes signals to web position, wet-film age, temperature, gas flow, and coating speed so kinetic states are not mixed.
Calibrates in situ features against designed perturbations, offline film properties, spatial defects, and final device yield or stabilized performance across batches.
Defines actionable process variables and controls for beam/light heating, dose, footprint, aliasing, and sparse sampling before closed-loop deployment.
accepted_equivalents: Fast XRD, GISAXS, total scattering, or Raman may serve as the structure-sensitive channel if phase and crystallization information is demonstrated.
Reflectometry, optical coherence tomography, IR thermography, machine-vision interference, or PL/hyperspectral imaging may serve as the scalable channel when linked to relevant process states.
Statistical process control or model-predictive control is acceptable in place of simple thresholds if trained and validated on independent production runs.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing two modalities that report essentially the same observable while leaving crystallization kinetics or spatial uniformity unmeasured.
Triggering process changes from uncalibrated signal intensity without aligning data to wet-film age and web position.
Ignoring X-ray or optical probe heating, limited footprint, and sampling aliasing when interpreting local defects.

expected_answer: High PL quantum yield or PeLED efficiency does not guarantee low loss under photovoltaic conditions because the carrier-density and field regimes differ. At the high carrier densities used for PL or LED operation, traps may be filled and bimolecular radiative recombination can dominate, whereas one-sun operation can remain sensitive to low-density Shockley-Read-Hall recombination. A PeLED architecture may deliberately confine electrons and holes and use injection barriers to balance carriers; the same barriers, dipoles, or low-mobility layers can impede extraction in a solar cell, increase series resistance, and reduce fill factor. External LED efficiency also includes optical outcoupling and charge-balance effects and therefore is not a direct measure of absorber quasi-Fermi-level splitting. The diagnosis should compare absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting versus carrier density, intensity-dependent Voc and Suns-Voc, electroluminescence-based reciprocity or non-radiative voltage loss, mobility and contact-resistance measurements, and transient extraction/recombination data. Interface-selective measurements and optical modeling should separate material radiative quality from contact losses and outcoupling.
scoring_key_points: Explains that high-injection PL/PeLED operation can fill traps and favor radiative recombination while one-sun photovoltaics probe a lower-carrier-density loss regime.
Contrasts carrier confinement/injection balance useful for PeLEDs with extraction barriers, series resistance, and fill-factor losses in PSCs.
States that external LED efficiency contains charge-balance and optical-outcoupling factors and is not identical to absorber quasi-Fermi-level splitting.
Proposes carrier-density-resolved PL/QFLS, Suns-Voc or intensity-dependent Voc, EL reciprocity, transport/contact-resistance, transient, and optical analyses.
accepted_equivalents: Trap saturation, state filling, or a change from SRH-dominated to bimolecular recombination are equivalent carrier-density explanations.
Space-charge-limited current, time-of-flight, impedance, or field-effect mobility may be used to diagnose transport when contact effects are separated.
Internal quantum efficiency plus optical modeling may substitute for external quantum efficiency in separating radiative and outcoupling contributions.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that high PLQY at one excitation density proves the solar cell must have a high Voc and fill factor.
Treating PeLED EQE as a direct measurement of perovskite internal radiative efficiency without charge-balance and outcoupling corrections.
Explaining the poor solar cell only by bulk traps while ignoring extraction barriers, contact resistance, and operating-carrier-density differences.

expected_answer:
The laboratory additive concentration and annealing recipe cannot be copied directly because large-area coating changes solvent residence time, nucleation density, thermal gradients, and additive segregation. A scale-up map should vary cesium/lead/iodide stoichiometry, additive and spacer-cation loading, solvent coordination strength, wet-film thickness, coating speed, substrate temperature, gas-knife or antisolvent timing, drying rate, and annealing profile. The acceptable window must produce the black phase across the entire web while avoiding residual solvent, yellow-phase nuclei, excessive low-dimensional material, and vertical segregation of additive or spacer toward one contact. The process should be robust to realistic precursor age and humidity rather than optimized at one ideal laboratory condition.

Near-line or in-line measurements should follow the formation pathway. Wet-film interferometry, reflectance, temperature, and mass-loss or solvent-vapor signals can control drying. Spatially resolved absorption/reflectance and photoluminescence should identify regions with incorrect phase, bandgap, or recombination. Representative strips should be examined by GIWAXS/XRD for black-phase fraction and orientation, and by cross-sectional chemical analysis for vertical additive and low-dimensional-phase distribution. Hyperspectral PL or contactless photoconductance maps should be correlated with local sheet resistance and finished-module electroluminescence. A stable black phase is necessary but not sufficient: the surface phase must also be thin and oriented enough to pass carriers.

Transport penalties require explicit dose and thickness controls. Devices should be fabricated with the additive alone, surface treatment alone, both together, and chemically similar but nonpassivating or nonforming controls. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy or Kelvin-probe measurements should check contact energetics; temperature-dependent current, impedance, transient photocurrent, and intensity-dependent current-voltage measurements should detect a tunneling or extraction barrier. If increasing the low-dimensional fraction raises photoluminescence but also raises series resistance, reduces short-wavelength or long-wavelength EQE according to its location, or causes current crowding in electroluminescence maps, the treatment has crossed from passivation into insulation. Carbon contact adhesion, wetting, contact resistivity, and laser-scribe cleanliness must be included because surface organics can interfere with carbon deposition and module interconnection.

Module qualification should stress the failure modes that are weakly represented by small cells: maximum-power-point light soaking at elevated temperature, thermal cycling through the phase-stability range, damp heat and edge ingress, UV exposure, reverse bias and partial shading, and repeated start-stop operation. Spatial maps should track local phase reversion, shunts, series resistance, hot spots, and mismatch among series-connected cells. Go criteria should include high coating and module yield, narrow performance distribution, stable subcell current collection, and retained power under defined stress; a high champion-cell PCE is insufficient. A no-go decision is warranted if phase stabilization depends on an unscalable drying transient, if additive/spacer segregation produces local transport barriers, if carbon contact or scribe resistance rises, or if the module energy yield is worse despite improved shelf stability.
scoring_key_points: Defines a large-area composition, coating, drying, annealing, humidity, and precursor-age window rather than copying the small-cell recipe.
Uses spatial phase, optical, photoconductive, and depth-composition controls to verify uniform black-phase stabilization and additive/2D-layer distribution.
Separates passivation from extraction blockage using dose controls, energy-level and transport diagnostics, carbon-contact resistance, and scribe compatibility.
Requires module-level MPP, thermal, damp-heat, UV, reverse-bias, ingress, hot-spot, yield, and energy-retention evidence with explicit no-go criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, gravure, spray, or another scalable coating route is acceptable if wet-film formation, drying, and spatial uniformity are controlled.
Hyperspectral PL, electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, microwave photoconductance, or equivalent large-area mapping methods are acceptable.
A graded 2D/3D interface or ultrathin oriented low-dimensional phase is acceptable if transport and contact compatibility are demonstrated.
Energy yield, stabilized module power, or a reliability-adjusted output metric may be used as the final scale-up criterion.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only the additive mass in proportion to coated area while keeping all drying and annealing assumptions unchanged.
Using black-phase XRD and shelf storage as the sole evidence of scalable operational stability.
Assuming that a higher PL intensity always indicates a better module even when the surface layer blocks extraction.
Ignoring carbon-electrode contact resistance, laser-scribe contamination, cell-to-cell mismatch, and partial-shading stress.

expected_answer:
Surface XPS, a longer decay, and brighter PL are not by themselves proof of a larger device quasi-Fermi-level splitting. XPS samples only a shallow region and may miss buried Sn4+, tin-vacancy-related acceptors, or gradients created during annealing. A reductive additive may suppress one oxidation product while leaving deep defects, changing stoichiometry, or introducing a new interfacial species. A longer PL lifetime can also arise because carriers are no longer extracted efficiently: an insulating additive-rich layer or unfavorable dipole can confine carriers in the absorber, increase PL, and simultaneously reduce device fill factor. The unchanged voltage indicates either that the bulk improvement is too small, that recombination has moved to a buried interface, or that contact energetics and self-doping still pin the achievable quasi-Fermi-level splitting.

The first step is to quantify the absorber's intrinsic radiative and nonradiative voltage loss independently of extraction. Absolute PLQY under calibrated one-sun-equivalent excitation should be converted to quasi-Fermi-level splitting and compared for bare films, films on each transport layer, and full stacks. Time-resolved PL must be interpreted together with PLQY; lifetime without emission yield is ambiguous. Spatial and depth-sensitive chemical measurements, including cross-sectional XPS or TOF-SIMS, should establish whether the additive and Sn4+ are uniformly distributed or concentrated at the top surface or buried interface. Tin-vacancy concentration, carrier density, and Fermi level should be assessed by Hall effect, Kelvin probe, capacitance, or other doping-sensitive methods.

Device diagnostics should separate voltage recombination from transport loss. Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV gives a series-resistance-free voltage and pseudo-fill factor; a high pseudo-fill factor but low measured fill factor indicates extraction or resistive loss. Electroluminescence quantum efficiency and voltage-dependent ideality factor test whether nonradiative recombination remains dominant in the complete stack. Transient photocurrent, transient photovoltage, impedance spectroscopy, temperature-dependent JV, and light-intensity dependence can distinguish slow extraction, a contact barrier, trap-assisted recombination, and ionic screening. Selective-contact stacks and electron-only or hole-only devices can localize the problematic interface.

Energy-level and chemical-contact tests are then required. UPS, Kelvin-probe measurements, and contact-potential profiling should determine whether the additive shifts the valence band, work function, or interfacial dipole. If bare-film quasi-Fermi-level splitting improves but drops sharply when one transport layer is added, and the loss is accompanied by stronger ideality or lower electroluminescence efficiency, that interface is recombination-active. If QFLS remains high in the stack but current extraction is slow, pseudo-FF exceeds measured FF, and temperature-dependent transport reveals an activation barrier, the additive is blocking extraction. If both QFLS and conductivity deteriorate during air or bias exposure while Sn4+ or contact-reaction products grow at a buried interface, the apparent initial reduction is chemically unstable. Only an improvement that persists in depth, raises stack QFLS and electroluminescence efficiency, preserves doping control, and does not create an extraction barrier can be assigned to useful passivation.
scoring_key_points: Explains the ambiguity of surface Sn4+ XPS, PL lifetime, and PL intensity, including the possibility that brighter/longer PL reflects blocked extraction.
Uses absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting and depth-resolved chemistry/doping measurements on bare films and selective-contact stacks.
Separates recombination from resistive or barrier loss using Suns-Voc/pseudo-JV, electroluminescence, ideality, transients, impedance, and temperature dependence.
Defines distinct evidence patterns for bulk passivation, buried-interface recombination, altered self-doping, extraction blockage, and chemically unstable contacts.
accepted_equivalents: Calibrated generalized-Planck-law QFLS, absolute PLQY, or an equivalent radiative-voltage-loss analysis is acceptable.
Hall, Seebeck, Mott-Schottky, Kelvin probe, or another justified carrier-density/Fermi-level method may be used to assess self-doping.
Electron-only/hole-only devices, selective-contact stacks, surface photovoltage, or interface-specific spectroscopy are acceptable localization methods.
An additive-rich insulating layer, interfacial dipole, unfavorable band offset, or contact reaction are acceptable extraction/contact mechanisms.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that lower surface Sn4+ and longer TRPL automatically guarantee a higher device open-circuit voltage.
Treating all fill-factor loss as series resistance without testing interfacial recombination, barriers, or ionic effects.
Measuring only the neat perovskite film and assuming the result transfers unchanged to buried device interfaces.
Ignoring that a reducing additive can alter stoichiometry, self-doping, energy levels, or chemical compatibility even if it initially suppresses oxidation.

expected_answer:
The transfer target is not the best isolated narrow-bandgap cell but the highest stable tandem power after optical, electrical, and processing coupling. The Sn-Pb composition and thickness should first be chosen with the realizable wide-bandgap top cell, transparent contacts, recombination junction, and parasitic absorption included. Subcell-resolved EQE must demonstrate current matching under the intended spectrum and temperature; a bottom-cell bandgap or thickness that maximizes single-junction current can overdrive the series tandem or require an optically lossy interlayer. Optical modeling should be validated by measured reflectance, absorption, and EQE, including the additive/2D layer and all transparent electrodes.

Voltage preservation should be checked through subcell quasi-Fermi-level splitting and electroluminescence rather than tandem Voc alone. Absolute PL or electroluminescence from each subcell, luminescence coupling analysis, Suns-Voc, and tandem ideality can reveal whether the recombination junction or a buried interface consumes the bottom-cell voltage gain. The 2D interlayer must be thin and energetically aligned enough to suppress recombination without adding series resistance. The recombination contact should provide efficient majority-carrier recombination while preventing direct solvent, redox, and ion exchange between subcells. Contact resistivity, optical loss, and chemical stability must be measured before and after the next deposition step.

Processing compatibility is a central go/no condition. The solvent, antisolvent, anneal, plasma, sputter, or lamination used for the upper stack must not extract the reducing additive, oxidize Sn2+, dissolve the 2D phase, or introduce pinholes and shunts. Sequential half-stack controls should be characterized after every later process step by depth-resolved Sn4+/Sn2+, composition, QFLS, morphology, and conductivity. An inert transfer or barrier layer may be necessary, but its optical and resistive cost must be counted. Additive diffusion into the recombination junction or wide-bandgap subcell should be checked by TOF-SIMS or equivalent profiling.

Stability testing should combine oxygen/moisture control with electrical and ionic stress. Encapsulated tandems should be operated at maximum power under heat and realistic spectral conditions, with periodic subcell EQE, luminescence, impedance, and composition mapping. Light-dark cycling, reverse bias, thermal cycling, and oxygen-leak or edge-ingress challenges should identify Sn oxidation, halide migration, and recombination-junction degradation. The design passes only if the additive and 2D layer preserve bottom-cell QFLS and low doping after complete-stack processing, maintain matched subcell currents and low junction resistance, and deliver a replicated stabilized tandem efficiency and energy yield advantage over a simpler control. It fails if the isolated bottom cell improves but tandem current mismatch, parasitic absorption, processing damage, additive diffusion, or junction resistance erases the gain.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes the Sn-Pb composition/thickness within the full tandem optical stack and verifies subcell current matching by EQE rather than isolated bottom-cell PCE.
Tracks subcell QFLS, electroluminescence, recombination-junction voltage loss, contact resistance, and 2D-layer transport penalties.
Uses stepwise processing-compatibility and depth-profile controls to detect solvent, thermal, plasma, redox, or additive-diffusion damage during tandem fabrication.
Requires complete-stack MPP, heat, spectral, light-dark, ingress, oxidation, ion-migration, and subcell-resolved stability evidence with explicit go/no criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Four-terminal optical validation may be used as a diagnostic control, but the go/no decision must address the monolithic two-terminal series constraint.
A tunnel junction, recombination layer, interconnecting layer, or equivalent contact architecture is acceptable if optical loss, resistance, and chemical isolation are quantified.
Subcell-selective PL/EL, electroreflectance, EQE biasing, or another justified method may be used to resolve tandem subcell voltage and current losses.
Inert processing, lamination, vapor deposition, or barrier-mediated deposition are acceptable routes if they protect the Sn-Pb layer without excessive loss.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the bottom-cell recipe with the highest standalone PCE and assuming it will maximize monolithic tandem efficiency.
Checking only total tandem Voc and total JV without resolving which subcell or interconnection loses voltage and current.
Ignoring damage from later solvent, plasma, sputtering, annealing, or additive diffusion steps.
Reporting encapsulated shelf stability without maximum-power-point operation, subcell-resolved diagnostics, or oxidation and ion-migration tracking.

expected_answer:
A photovoltaic interface is optimized to extract photocarriers with minimal loss, whereas an LED must inject electrons and holes at comparable rates, confine them in an emissive region, and favor radiative recombination. A 2D cap that is acceptable as a moisture barrier in a solar cell may be too insulating for injection, create a large turn-on voltage, or force recombination at a damaging contact.
