Claiming scalability from crystal area alone without thickness uniformity, yield, contact deposition, throughput, and operational stability.

expected_answer:
Scale-up must begin with a coupled redox-crystallization process map. Relevant variables include precursor oxygen and water content, Sn2+/Sn4+ ratio, reducing additive and excess-tin concentration, ligand or spacer stoichiometry, solvent coordination, wet-film thickness, coating speed, drying-gas composition, substrate temperature, annealing history, and time before encapsulation. These variables jointly control oxidation, nucleation rate, low-n/high-n quasi-2D phase distribution, grain coverage, and residual insulating ligand content. The transport layers and electrodes must then be adjusted to balance electron and hole current at the intended radiance, because current crowding can erase gains from bulk passivation.

A panel cannot be represented by a central coupon. Across-web and along-web maps should include thickness, GIWAXS/XRD phase and orientation, absorption and photoluminescence quantum yield, lifetime, Sn valence or oxide content, sub-gap defect response, sheet/contact resistance, leakage, and spatial electroluminescence. Batch-to-batch distributions and edge regions are as important as the best pixel.

Qualification should operate encapsulated devices at fixed luminance or current density while recording EQE, voltage, spectral centroid/linewidth, dark recovery, and thermal maps. Use separate oxygen/moisture, thermal, electrical, and on-off cycling stresses, followed by failure analysis for Sn4+ growth, halide redistribution, ligand loss, electrode reactions, and transport-layer degradation. A transferable solution retains phase/redox uniformity, balanced injection, spectral stability, and a narrow lifetime distribution across area and batches. A high champion EQE accompanied by broad spatial variation, rising series resistance, current crowding, or rapid spectral drift indicates a small-area processing artifact.
scoring_key_points: Maps redox, additive, solvent, coating, drying, annealing, and encapsulation variables that jointly control Sn oxidation, crystallization, quasi-2D phase distribution, and ligand retention.
Includes spatially resolved structural, optical, chemical, and electrical diagnostics across the full coated area rather than relying on one coupon or champion pixel.
Qualifies devices under controlled radiance/current, atmosphere, temperature, and cycling while tracking efficiency, voltage, spectrum, heat, and post-mortem failure chemistry.
Defines successful transfer by reproducible area- and batch-level uniformity, balanced injection, spectral stability, and lifetime distribution, not by peak EQE alone.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, blade, spray, or other continuous coating methods with an explicit drying and redox-control window
Operando XPS alternatives such as XANES, optical redox proxies, or destructive sampled chemical mapping
A fixed-radiance lifetime protocol instead of fixed current, provided electrical and thermal conditions are reported
common_wrong_answers: Copying the spin-coating recipe without mapping drying and oxygen exposure at larger scale
Optimizing only the emissive film while ignoring current balance and transport-layer-induced heating
Using average panel photoluminescence without spatial maps of phase, defects, resistance, and electroluminescence
Claiming commercial stability from a single short inert-atmosphere T50 measurement

expected_answer:
A decisive design should independently vary grain-contact topology and iodine-defect chemistry. Prepare films with matched composition, grain size, thickness, texture, absorbed photon flux, and average photostriction, but with either densely contacted boundaries or mechanically separated/compliant boundaries. Contact topology can be tuned by a soft intergrain phase, controlled porosity, or patterned confinement. In a second axis, vary iodine-vacancy chemistry with a halide chemical-potential or defect-passivation treatment while matching modulus and boundary spacing. This produces a contact-high/contact-low crossed with vacancy-easy/vacancy-hard matrix.

Operando XRD establishes equal bulk expansion. Local Raman or nano-XRD strain mapping, AFM modulus/contact mapping, and finite-element reconstruction quantify stress concentration. Nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS, STEM/EDS, or another spatial chemical probe should then follow iodine loss and PbI2 at the same boundaries; scanning photocurrent or cathodoluminescence links chemistry to optoelectronic damage. Time-resolved sampling must show local crowding or compressive stress first, iodine deficiency or vacancy-related trapping second, PbI2 formation third, and photocurrent loss last.

The contact-mechanics model predicts an interaction: at equal bulk expansion and composition, degradation localizes and accelerates where contact density and local compressive stress are high; soft separation suppresses it even if photostriction remains. A uniform-strain model predicts degradation from average expansion independent of contact topology. A chemical-passivation-only model predicts that vacancy-control chemistry dominates even when local stress is unchanged and does not require boundary-contact localization. The mechanical model is falsified if local stress fails to precede or spatially predict iodine loss, or if changing contact topology does not alter degradation after chemistry and bulk expansion are matched.
scoring_key_points: Uses a crossed design that independently varies grain-contact topology or compliance and iodine-vacancy chemistry while matching average photostriction and other film variables.
Measures local stress/contact mechanics, local iodine or PbI2 chemistry, and local optoelectronic damage at the same boundaries.
Requires the temporal sequence stress concentration to iodine loss/trapping to PbI2 to photocurrent loss rather than relying on end-point correlation.
States distinct predictions for contact-mechanics, uniform-strain, and chemical-passivation models and gives falsification criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Patterned mechanical confinement, compliant substrates, or controlled grain-boundary gaps as the contact-topology perturbation
Nano-beam diffraction, Brillouin/Raman mapping, or calibrated AFM nanomechanics for local stress reconstruction
Scanning photocurrent, cathodoluminescence, Kelvin-probe mapping, or local photoluminescence as the damage readout
common_wrong_answers: Comparing additives that simultaneously change grain size, chemistry, modulus, and photostriction without orthogonal controls
Using only average XRD strain and bulk PbI2 content to claim a local grain-boundary mechanism
Assuming all grain boundaries are mechanically equivalent
Inferring causality when PbI2 is observed before any time-resolved stress or iodine-loss measurement

expected_answer:
The process window should treat the polymer as a mechanically functional grain-boundary phase, not simply maximize its concentration. Map polymer chemistry and molecular weight, precursor concentration, polymer loading, solvent selectivity, coating speed, wet thickness, antisolvent or gas-drying history, substrate temperature, and annealing. These variables control whether the polymer forms discontinuous boundary buffers, a continuous insulating network, surface segregation, or altered grain nucleation. A chemically similar but rigid additive and a passivating small molecule with little mechanical compliance are useful controls.

Across coated areas, combine GIWAXS/XRD and microscopy for crystallization and texture with ToF-SIMS or spectroscopic mapping for polymer location. AFM nanomechanics, Raman/nano-XRD strain mapping, and boundary-gap statistics should quantify compliance and contact density. Electrical maps must include photoluminescence lifetime/quantum yield, local photocurrent or electroluminescence, contact resistance, mobility, series resistance, shunts, and current crowding. The optimum should reduce stress hotspots and iodine-loss/PbI2 formation without sacrificing out-of-plane transport or fill factor.

Qualification must include open-circuit light soaking to maximize photocarrier-driven expansion, maximum-power operation, thermal aging, thermal cycling, and combined illumination-temperature tests on encapsulated mini-modules. Monitor power, voltage, current, thermal images, hysteresis, and spatial degradation, followed by chemical and mechanical post-mortem analysis. Adoption requires reproducible area and batch distributions, retained transport and fill factor, reduced local stress and iodine loss, and slower degradation under both open-circuit and operating conditions. A champion cell with lower stress but rising series resistance, broad polymer segregation, or unstable edge regions fails the transfer test.
scoring_key_points: Maps polymer loading, chemistry, coating, drying, and annealing variables that determine boundary localization, mechanical compliance, crystallization, and insulating-network formation.
Uses spatial mechanical, chemical, structural, and electrical maps to locate the compliance/transport optimum rather than relying on average film data.
Qualifies encapsulated large-area devices under open-circuit light soaking, maximum-power operation, heat, and thermal cycling with spatial failure analysis.
Requires reproducible stress reduction and suppressed iodine-loss/PbI2 degradation without increased series resistance, current crowding, or fill-factor loss.
accepted_equivalents: Another soft intergrain phase or elastomeric molecular buffer, provided its distribution and transport penalty are explicitly tested
Nanoindentation, Brillouin microscopy, or Raman strain mapping as alternatives to AFM nanomechanics
Slot-die, blade, spray, or other scalable coating platforms with a defined drying window
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the highest polymer concentration because it gives the lowest measured modulus
Using photoluminescence improvement alone to conclude that mechanical buffering survives scale-up
Testing only dark heat or humidity while omitting illuminated open-circuit and operating stresses
Ignoring polymer segregation, edge effects, contact resistance, or current-crowding penalties

expected_answer:
The ALD sequence must be deconvoluted into chemistry and film formation. Compare precursor-only pulses, water-only pulses, complete alternating cycles, an inert-gas/thermal exposure control, and a nonreactive barrier deposited by another method. Repeat these controls over substrate temperature, precursor dose, purge time, and cycle number. Saturation curves for each half-reaction are essential; isotopically labeled water or an alternative oxidant can help trace oxygen incorporation and volatile products.

In situ quartz-crystal microbalance, ellipsometry, infrared spectroscopy, ambient-pressure XPS, and mass spectrometry of desorbing species should determine whether growth is self-limiting and whether methylammonium-, formamidinium-, iodine-, or nitrogen-containing products leave the surface. GIWAXS/XRD and depth-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS should quantify PbI2, lattice change, and oxide continuity. Electronic consequences must be separated using absolute photoluminescence/QFLS, surface recombination velocity, band alignment, transient carrier transfer, contact resistivity, tunneling current, and moisture/ion permeation.

True passivation predicts saturating ALD growth, reduced interfacial trap recombination and higher QFLS without progressive stoichiometric loss, with an optimum ultrathin thickness that preserves tunneling. Controlled reconstruction predicts a limited precursor dose that removes or converts defective surface species, correlated volatile products and PbI2/reconstructed chemistry, and no requirement for a continuous oxide. A physical barrier predicts improved environmental or ion-blocking stability but little immediate reduction in interfacial recombination; performance should depend mainly on continuity and permeability. The passivation claim is falsified by non-self-limiting decomposition or by voltage gains that disappear when chemical etching is reproduced without oxide growth. The barrier claim is falsified if incomplete, noncontinuous films give the same benefit through trap reduction.
scoring_key_points: Separates precursor, co-reactant, complete-cycle, thermal, and independently deposited barrier effects across dose, temperature, and cycle number.
Uses in situ mass, optical, vibrational, chemical, and evolved-gas measurements to test self-limiting growth and perovskite decomposition.
Connects the reaction pathway to QFLS, recombination, band alignment, contact resistance, tunneling, and barrier function rather than Voc alone.
States different predictions and falsification tests for genuine passivation, controlled reconstruction/etching, and physical barrier mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: QCM, in situ ellipsometry, AP-XPS, DRIFTS, or another surface-reaction-sensitive combination
Plasma or ozone co-reactant controls if ion/radical damage and temperature are separately matched
A molecular-layer-deposited or sputtered reference barrier as the non-ALD physical-barrier control
common_wrong_answers: Calling any Voc increase passivation without checking stoichiometric loss or transport resistance
Comparing only zero cycles with one optimized ALD recipe and omitting half-cycle controls
Assuming ALD is chemically inert because the growth is conformal
Using ex situ XPS alone without tracking volatile products, growth saturation, or thickness dependence

expected_answer:
The spatial-ALD process must reproduce functional film properties, not merely nominal thickness. Map precursor partial pressure and dose, gas-zone separation, purge efficiency, substrate speed, substrate temperature, plasma use if any, nucleation delay, and total cycles/passes. The window must be compatible with the perovskite's thermal and chemical sensitivity while giving complete coverage over texture and interconnect topography. A temporal-ALD reference, no-buffer control, and matched-thickness films deposited at different speeds are required.

Inline or rapid mapping should measure thickness and refractive index, sheet and contact resistance, optical loss, stoichiometry, work function/conduction-band position, pinhole density, and conformality at cell edges and laser-scribed regions. Before and after transparent-electrode sputtering, compare photoluminescence/QFLS, sub-gap defects, leakage, shunt density, and local photocurrent to quantify damage protection. Cross-sectional microscopy and electrical tomography can test whether the layer isolates subcells while maintaining low out-of-plane resistance; excessive lateral conductivity or discontinuities can create recombination losses or shunts.

Scale from coupons to mini-modules while tracking PCE distribution, series resistance, current matching, interconnect loss, and yield rather than only champion efficiency. Reliability should include illuminated maximum-power operation, heat, humidity, thermal cycling, light-soak/sputter-induced defect evolution, and adhesion/flex testing where relevant. Post-mortem analysis should distinguish SnO2 chemical change, perovskite damage, electrode diffusion, pinhole growth, and delamination. Transfer is successful only if high-speed films match the reference in band alignment, contact resistivity, sputter-damage suppression, conformality, module yield, and degradation rate across width and batches.
scoring_key_points: Maps spatial-ALD dose, gas separation, speed, temperature, nucleation, and pass count while respecting perovskite thermal and chemical limits.
Uses inline spatial metrology for thickness, stoichiometry, band alignment, resistance, pinholes, conformality, and optical loss, especially at interconnects.
Directly verifies sputter protection and subcell isolation using pre/post-deposition optical, defect, leakage, and local-current measurements.
Qualifies mini-modules for yield, current matching, resistance, and combined operational/environmental reliability, with explicit functional equivalence to temporal ALD.
accepted_equivalents: Atmospheric-pressure spatial ALD or another continuous ALD architecture with separated precursor zones
Kelvin probe/UPS alternatives for band alignment and conductive-AFM or transfer-length methods for contact resistance
Perovskite-silicon, all-perovskite, or perovskite-CIGSe tandems provided the buffer and recombination-contact functions are explicitly tested
common_wrong_answers: Matching only average SnO2 thickness while ignoring nucleation, pinholes, band alignment, and contact resistance
Using small-area PCE as the sole evidence that sputter protection survives high-speed processing
Ignoring laser-scribed interconnects, edge coverage, lateral shunts, or subcell current mismatch
Qualifying storage stability without maximum-power, thermal-cycle, and post-sputter damage tests

expected_answer:
Use a molecular control matrix that separates coordination from volatility. The key set is: the target molecule with both a coordinating carbonyl and suitable volatility; a nonvolatile carbonyl analogue that coordinates but remains; a volatile, weakly coordinating analogue; a structurally similar noncarbonyl molecule; and no additive. Binding strength, vapor pressure, size, and concentration should be measured rather than assumed. Process all films across annealing temperature and residence time, and repeat on substrates with different thermal-expansion coefficients. Morphology should either be matched by adjusting nucleation conditions or included as an explicit independent factor.

In situ ATR-IR or Raman should track coordination and its disappearance, while TGA/QMS or mass-loss measurements verify sublimation timing. Time-resolved GIWAXS/XRD and in situ photoluminescence should separate nucleation, crystal growth, lattice expansion, and stress relaxation. Final residual strain must be measured by tilt-dependent diffraction or wafer-curvature methods; XPS, ToF-SIMS, and IR should test for retained additive. Microscopy, trap-density measurements, and absolute luminescence then connect morphology and passivation to electronic quality.

The transient thermodynamic mechanism predicts that only the molecule combining coordination and correctly timed sublimation produces a temporary lattice response followed by low residual strain with no residue; the effect should shift with annealing rate and substrate mismatch. Permanent passivation predicts retained chemical signatures and defect reduction even when residual strain is not relieved. A nucleation-only mechanism predicts that strain and lifetime differences disappear once grain size, texture, and phase distribution are matched. Transient stress release is falsified if a noncoordinating volatile gives the same strain response, if the additive remains in the final film, or if stress reduction does not follow the measured coordination-desorption sequence.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched molecular analogues that independently provide coordination, volatility, both functions, or neither, plus no-additive controls.
Tracks coordination, sublimation, crystallization, lattice evolution, residual strain, and final chemical residue with time-resolved and ex situ measurements.
Separates morphology from chemistry by matching or independently varying nucleation, grain size, texture, and substrate thermal-expansion mismatch.
States distinct predictions and falsification criteria for transient stress release, permanent passivation, and nucleation-only mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: A nonvolatile Lewis-base analogue and a volatile hydrocarbon/weak Lewis base as the two orthogonal molecular controls
In situ mass spectrometry, thermogravimetry, ellipsometry, or optical mass-loss tracking for additive departure
Wafer curvature, Raman stress calibration, or sin2psi diffraction as the residual-stress measurement
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only the target additive with a no-additive film
Treating improved photoluminescence lifetime as direct proof of stress release
Assuming no visible residue means no persistent chemical passivation
Failing to control morphology or substrate thermal-expansion mismatch when interpreting strain

expected_answer:
The manufacturing window must synchronize solvent removal, perovskite nucleation, additive coordination, additive sublimation, crystal growth, and substrate cooling. Map additive concentration, precursor age, solvent coordination, wet-film thickness, coating speed, antisolvent or gas-quench timing, dryer-zone temperatures, gas flow, residence time, web tension, cooling rate, and PET/PEN substrate thermal-expansion behavior. A narrow laboratory anneal cannot simply be converted to one dryer temperature; the sequence and time-temperature history must be preserved.

Inline FTIR/Raman or another chemical probe should track coordinated carbonyl signatures, while exhaust mass spectrometry or calibrated mass-loss monitoring confirms additive departure. In-line or near-line GIWAXS, photoluminescence imaging, film-thickness mapping, and optical inspection should follow crystallization and defects. Across-web and along-web maps of residual strain, texture, carrier lifetime, sheet/contact resistance, pinholes, and residual additive are required, including edge and splice regions. Statistical process control should link these maps to local cell performance and yield.

Qualification should compare no-additive and molecular-control modules under repeated bending at several radii, thermal cycling, illuminated maximum-power tracking, continuous light, heat/humidity, and combined bend-plus-operation protocols. Monitor power, voltage, resistance, electroluminescence uniformity, crack formation, delamination, and strain redistribution, followed by chemical residue and phase analysis. Scale-up is successful only if the additive leaves completely, residual strain is uniformly reduced, electrical extraction is not impaired, and mechanical and operational lifetime improve across batches. Local high efficiency with across-web strain gradients, incomplete sublimation, edge cracking, or unstable resistance indicates an uncontrolled residence-time artifact.
scoring_key_points: Defines a time-temperature-process window that synchronizes coordination, nucleation, sublimation, growth, cooling, and substrate thermal-expansion mismatch.
Uses inline chemical, exhaust, structural, optical, and thickness measurements to verify additive departure and crystallization during continuous coating.
Requires across-web and along-web statistical maps of residual strain, residue, texture, electronic quality, resistance, defects, and yield.
Qualifies modules under coupled bending, maximum-power operation, light, heat/humidity, and thermal cycling, with acceptance based on uniform stress release and durable electrical performance.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, slot-die, gravure, or another continuous web process with an explicit residence-time and dryer-zone map
Inline IR, Raman, ellipsometry, QMS, or equivalent chemical/mass-loss sensors for coordination and sublimation
Digital image correlation, curvature mapping, Raman, or diffraction-based strain mapping across the web
common_wrong_answers: Using only the final dryer temperature and ignoring residence time, cooling rate, and web tension
Assuming complete sublimation from bulk TGA without measuring the coated web or exhaust
Testing bending and operational stability separately while omitting combined mechanical-electrical stress
Reporting average module efficiency without mapping strain, residue, resistance, and edge defects

expected_answer:
The observations are consistent with an orientation-controlled transport effect, but they do not prove it by themselves. Matching salt dose, surface Br content, roughness, trap-filled-limit voltage, and absolute PLQY removes several common explanations: a larger chemical passivation dose, a larger band-gap shift from Br incorporation, a smoother contact, or simply a lower trap density. In a layered Ruddlesden-Popper phase, transport is strongly anisotropic. Domains with inorganic sheets oriented approximately normal to the substrate can provide a continuous out-of-plane pathway to the electron contact, whereas face-on domains place insulating organic spacers across the extraction direction. A faster decay only after the electron contact is deposited is therefore compatible with a larger extraction rate rather than with poorer passivation. The absence of a conventional low-angle XRD peak is not decisive because an ultrathin, surface-localized layer can fall below bulk XRD sensitivity.

The decisive experiment must vary orientation while holding thickness, composition, coverage, and defect passivation constant. At minimum, prepare a deposition-rate or post-treatment series that changes texture but is matched by quartz-crystal-microbalance dose, ellipsometric or cross-sectional thickness, XPS/ToF-SIMS Br and spacer-cation loading, AFM roughness, and nanoscale coverage mapping. Use surface-sensitive GIWAXS at several incidence angles, preferably with pole-figure or azimuthal analysis, and cross-sectional HRTEM to quantify the fraction of edge-on or vertically aligned RP domains. Measure both in-plane and cross-plane conductivity or mobility, cross-plane conductive-AFM current, contact resistance, and contact-selective TRPL or transient absorption on otherwise identical stacks. A thickness series is needed to exclude the possibility that V is merely less continuous or thinner.

The orientation hypothesis is supported only if the texture metric, not total RP amount or Br loading, tracks the cross-plane/in-plane transport anisotropy, extraction rate, and fill factor. Samples with more vertical texture should show higher cross-plane conductance and faster contact-induced carrier removal while retaining similar PLQY, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and trap density. A face-on sample of the same thickness and chemistry should preserve passivation but exhibit slower extraction and a larger series-resistance or fill-factor penalty. Conversely, the claim fails if the performance advantage disappears after matching thickness and coverage, follows Br content or pinhole fraction rather than texture, or is reproduced by an equally thin non-oriented layer.
scoring_key_points: Explains that layered-perovskite transport is anisotropic and that vertical inorganic-slab orientation can improve out-of-plane extraction without requiring stronger chemical passivation.
Recognizes that contact-induced faster PL decay can signify faster extraction and that the absence of a conventional XRD peak does not exclude an ultrathin surface RP layer.
Proposes an orientation-controlled, thickness/composition/coverage-matched experiment using surface-sensitive texture measurements plus cross-plane and in-plane transport diagnostics.
States a falsifiable pattern: transport and FF must track quantified texture at matched chemistry; correlation with thickness, pinholes, or Br loading instead would reject the orientation claim.
accepted_equivalents: Edge-on RP domains, c-axis texture, or inorganic slabs aligned along the extraction direction may be used instead of vertically oriented RP domains.

Contact-selective transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity with directional geometry, or impedance-derived contact resistance may replace one of the proposed extraction measurements.
Grazing-incidence diffraction with azimuthal integration or cross-sectional electron diffraction is acceptable in place of a formal pole figure if orientation is quantitatively resolved.
common_wrong_answers: Treating any faster PL decay as proof of increased non-radiative recombination without considering contact extraction.
Claiming that no low-angle theta-2theta XRD peak proves that no layered phase is present.
Comparing treatments with different salt dose or thickness and attributing all performance differences to orientation.

expected_answer:
The observation in dry nitrogen argues against a fast, spontaneous Cu-perovskite reaction under the tested thermal condition. It does not prove universal inertness, but it makes a different causal sequence plausible in air: oxygen and/or water first destabilize the perovskite or its organic iodide chemistry, generating PbI2 together with mobile or volatile iodine-containing species such as I2, HI, or iodide-rich intermediates; Cu then reacts with those products to form CuI. In that sequence, CuI is a marker and possibly an accelerator or sink, not necessarily the initiating event. The experiment must independently vary oxygen and water rather than treating 'air' as one variable.

A minimum atmosphere matrix is dry N2, humid N2, dry O2 or dry synthetic air, and humid O2/synthetic air at identical temperature, illumination, pressure, and gas flow. Water activity and oxygen partial pressure should be measured, not inferred. Each condition should include: perovskite/Cu direct-contact stacks; the same perovskite without Cu; a stack with a chemically inert or diffusion-blocking interlayer between perovskite and Cu; and, where practical, a non-Cu electrode control with comparable morphology and work function. A Cu film exposed to the same gases without perovskite distinguishes direct Cu oxidation from halidation supplied by the absorber. Pinhole density and Cu thickness must be matched.

Time-resolved or interrupted aging should track absorber decomposition and CuI formation separately. Suitable measurements include in situ or sequential GIWAXS/XRD for PbI2 and CuI, XPS or hard-XPS depth profiles for Cu oxidation state and iodine chemistry, optical absorption/PL for perovskite loss, ToF-SIMS for halide and Cu profiles, and gas-phase mass spectrometry or an iodine-selective optical sensor. Isotopically labelled water or oxygen can be used to identify incorporation into oxygen-containing products, although the core decision does not depend on isotopic labelling. Electrical resistance, dark leakage, and trap-density measurements establish whether electronic failure precedes or follows phase formation.

The primary-Cu-initiation model is supported if degradation occurs in dry N2 only when Cu is in direct contact, Cu-containing reaction products appear before PbI2 or absorber decomposition, and a chemically inert interlayer suppresses the initial absorber changes. The environment-first/secondary-sink model is supported if the no-Cu perovskite begins to form PbI2 or release iodine species under humid N2 and/or dry O2, if those signals precede CuI in the Cu stack, and if CuI formation follows the availability of iodine products. The four-atmosphere result also identifies whether water, oxygen, or their synergy is the dominant trigger. A mixed mechanism remains possible if Cu lowers the activation barrier after environmental initiation; the answer should not force a single reagent without the matrix data.
scoring_key_points: Uses dry N2 stability to argue against rapid intrinsic Cu/perovskite reaction while allowing an environment-first pathway in which CuI can be a secondary product.
Specifies an independent dry/humid and N2/O2 atmosphere matrix with matched perovskite/Cu, no-Cu, inert-interlayer, and electrode controls.
Uses time-resolved phase, chemical-depth, gas-phase, and electrical measurements to determine event order rather than relying on endpoint CuI detection.
Provides explicit decision rules distinguishing Cu-first, absorber-first, and mixed catalytic mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Controlled relative humidity in argon may replace humid nitrogen.
Operando Raman, synchrotron diffraction, or near-ambient-pressure XPS may replace one of the proposed time-resolved methods.
An ultrathin carbon or chemically inert barrier electrode may be used as the nonreactive control if its transport effect is separately calibrated.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that detection of CuI alone proves Cu diffusion through the perovskite or proves that Cu initiated degradation.
Comparing only air with nitrogen and failing to separate oxygen from water.
Using only endpoint XRD without determining whether PbI2, volatile iodine, CuI, or electrical failure appeared first.

expected_answer:
The edge-localized pattern makes package ingress or edge/scribe defects the first hypothesis, not proof that Cu is intrinsically unsuitable. Water and oxygen can enter through an imperfect edge seal, destabilize the perovskite, generate iodine-containing products, and then corrode Cu. Rare pinholes or damaged transport layers can create direct Cu/perovskite contact and local shunts without requiring long-range Cu diffusion. The central cells serve as an internal low-ingress control, but the module must be redesigned and tested so that electrode chemistry, transport-layer integrity, and encapsulation are varied independently.

Architectural mitigation should combine a low-water-vapor and low-oxygen barrier, a chemically resistant edge seal with adequate overlap around scribes, and a continuous electron-selective or diffusion-blocking interlayer between perovskite and Cu. The interlayer must block halide/metal exchange without creating an extraction barrier. Pinhole density, step coverage at textured or laser-scribed regions, Cu adhesion, and galvanic coupling to grids or busbars must be controlled. A thin corrosion-resistant Cu cap or bilayer may be considered, but it cannot substitute for a defective edge seal. Water/oxygen getters can be useful only if capacity and reaction products are qualified.

A discriminating factorial matrix should compare Cu with a reference electrode, with and without the blocking/electron-transport layer, across at least two encapsulation and edge-seal designs. Add deliberate pinhole-density or scribe-quality levels and test both open-circuit and maximum-power-point bias because field-assisted ion movement and local heating may alter the failure path. Expose modules and matched coupons to illuminated damp heat, dry heat, humidity without light, thermal cycling, and bias-humidity. Spatially resolved humidity/oxygen indicators or permeation witness sensors should be placed from edge to center.

Diagnostics must be more sensitive and spatially resolved than a bulk CuI XRD threshold alone. Use EL/PL and lock-in thermography to locate shunts, cross-sectional SEM/TEM and ToF-SIMS or XPS to distinguish Cu penetration from iodine migration, micro-XRD/Raman to map CuI and PbI2, four-point or local resistance measurements to track series resistance, and trap/dark-current measurements to detect electronic damage. If CuI/PbI2 and shunts follow the ingress gradient and are suppressed by a better edge seal even with the same Cu, packaging is limiting. If failures track intentional pinholes and disappear with a continuous barrier, direct-contact defects are limiting. If Cu penetrates intact layers and appears ahead of absorber decomposition even in dry conditions, Cu transport or intrinsic chemistry is implicated.

The lifetime criterion should be tied to the earliest functionally relevant, mechanism-specific event: for example, a specified increase in local leakage or series resistance, mapped Cu or iodine penetration beyond a defined depth, or a statistically bounded onset of CuI/PbI2 at edges under a validated acceleration model. It should be calibrated against multiple sensitive diagnostics and operational MPP data, not extrapolated solely from the time at which a bulk diffraction peak becomes visible.
scoring_key_points: Interprets edge-localized failure as a package/pinhole hypothesis and separates it from intrinsic Cu incompatibility or long-range Cu diffusion.
Proposes edge-seal/barrier improvements and a continuous transport or diffusion-blocking interlayer while controlling pinholes, scribes, adhesion, and galvanic contacts.
Defines a factorial Cu/reference-electrode, barrier/no-barrier, encapsulation, pinhole, bias, and coupled-stress matrix with spatial diagnostics.
Uses an early, sensitive, mechanism-specific operational failure criterion rather than a bulk XRD threshold or dark-storage retention alone.
accepted_equivalents: Atomic-layer-deposited oxide, dense organic-inorganic nanolaminate, or a robust fullerene/buffer bilayer may serve as the diffusion-blocking contact if electrical compatibility is demonstrated.
Laser-beam-induced current, electroluminescence, photoluminescence, or dark lock-in thermography may be used for spatial shunt localization.
A probabilistic time-to-failure distribution is acceptable in place of a single threshold if it is tied to the same mechanism-specific observables.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring Cu unsuitable solely because corrosion occurs near a failed edge seal.
Improving only the bulk encapsulant while ignoring scribes, pinholes, step coverage, and direct-contact defects.
Using unilluminated storage retention or the first bulk CuI XRD peak as the sole module lifetime endpoint.

expected_answer:
The immediate appearance of the black phase at low coating temperature is primarily kinetic evidence: Cs may lower the nucleation barrier, create room-temperature black-phase nuclei, alter precursor association, or otherwise accelerate conversion before the thermal anneal. The more persistent suppression of yellow-phase and PbI2 signatures after extended annealing is more consistent with a change in phase stability or conversion completeness, although a kinetic history can also be frozen into the final film. The optical blue shift supports actual Cs incorporation and a changed lattice/composition rather than a purely morphological effect, but it is not by itself a direct free-energy measurement. Thus the observations suggest coupled kinetics and thermodynamics, not a clean proof of either branch.

A decisive study must hold MA/FA ratio, I/Br ratio, precursor concentration, solvent, substrate, drying history, and annealing schedule fixed while independently varying Cs and nucleation seeding. Use at least four branches: Cs-free/unseeded, Cs-free with preformed black-phase seeds or an equivalent heterogeneous nucleation treatment, Cs-containing/unseeded, and Cs-containing with the same seeding treatment. A Cs-free seed control tests whether the early blackening and grain uniformity can be reproduced without changing equilibrium composition. A composition control in which halide content is fixed is essential so that Br-induced stability or band-gap changes are not misassigned to Cs.

Time-resolved GIWAXS or XRD, in situ absorption/reflectance, and PL during coating and annealing should quantify induction time, nucleation rate, phase-conversion rate, and transient intermediate phases. Long isothermal holds and repeated heating-cooling cycles should test whether the final phase fraction and transition boundary remain different after kinetic memory has largely relaxed. Calorimetry or variable-temperature diffraction can provide additional equilibrium or hysteresis information. Final composition and spatial homogeneity should be checked by XPS/ToF-SIMS or elemental mapping, and grain morphology should be treated as an outcome rather than a surrogate for phase thermodynamics.

For a purely kinetic mechanism, seeding the Cs-free formulation should reproduce the early black phase and, after sufficient annealing, erase most differences in phase fraction and device yield; Cs should not shift the long-time phase boundary once composition-related band-gap changes are accounted for. For a purely thermodynamic mechanism, Cs-free seeding may shorten induction time but will not reproduce the long-time suppression of yellow phase, the shifted transition/hysteresis behavior, or the compositional optical shift. For a coupled mechanism, seeding partially rescues the Cs-free induction time and morphology, while Cs-containing films still show a more stable black phase and wider process window after long holds and thermal cycling.
scoring_key_points: Assigns immediate low-temperature black-phase formation mainly to nucleation/conversion kinetics and persistent impurity suppression plus compositional blue shift to a possible thermodynamic/compositional contribution.
Notes that final phase purity can retain kinetic history and that a blue shift is not by itself a free-energy measurement.
Proposes a Cs/no-Cs by seeded/unseeded matrix with fixed MA/FA and I/Br composition and time-resolved crystallization measurements.
Gives distinct predicted patterns for purely kinetic, purely thermodynamic, and coupled mechanisms after long anneals or thermal cycling.
accepted_equivalents: Heterogeneous nucleation on a pretreated substrate or addition of black-phase nanocrystal seeds is acceptable as the seeding control.
Operando optical scattering or synchrotron GIWAXS may replace conventional in situ XRD.
Tolerance-factor or lattice-free-energy language is acceptable for the thermodynamic branch if fixed-halide controls are maintained.
common_wrong_answers: Calling early blackening alone proof that Cs thermodynamically stabilizes the final phase.
Calling the optical blue shift a morphology effect while ignoring compositional incorporation.
Changing Br content together with Cs and then assigning all thermal or phase stability differences to Cs.

expected_answer:
The appropriate objective is a robust composition-process window, not the Cs level that gives the best single device. Moderate Cs can reduce sensitivity to early crystallization temperature and suppress undesirable phases, whereas excessive Cs can shift composition, widen the band gap, disturb the optimal A-site balance, or create new crystallization and transport penalties. The line should therefore optimize both the mean and variance of yield-relevant responses over the expected environmental distribution.

Use a response-surface or factorial design spanning Cs fraction, MA/FA ratio, halide ratio, substrate and ink temperature, coating speed or wet-film residence time, antisolvent/drying timing, solvent-vapor activity, humidity, annealing temperature, and ink age. The core attribution experiment must include fixed-I/Br branches when Cs is varied, because Br changes band gap and thermal stability. Separate branches can deliberately co-optimize Br later, but the first-stage Cs effect cannot be inferred from compositions in which both vary. Include low, moderate, and overdoped Cs levels and repeat complete batches on different days, tools, and operators.

In-line or near-line observables should detect crystallization before final device testing: time to black-phase formation from reflectance or colorimetry, in situ PL/absorption, optical scattering, wet-film thickness, drying rate, and a calibrated diffraction or spectroscopic phase-purity surrogate. Distributed witness coupons should verify final yellow-phase/PbI2 content, elemental homogeneity, grain continuity, and band gap. These measurements should be linked to batch-level Jsc, Voc, FF, PCE, shunt rate, and device-to-device distributions.

The statistical objective should penalize variance and catastrophic failures. A suitable criterion is high lower-quantile PCE or high probability of exceeding minimum Jsc/FF/PCE and phase-purity thresholds across the full 15-30 degrees C and vapor-history envelope, with constraints on band gap and current loss. Hierarchical or mixed-effects analysis should separate composition, day, tool, and operator effects. The selected moderate-Cs window is one whose worst-case yield and reproducibility outperform the Cs-free and high-Cs branches, even if its champion is not the highest.

Stability qualification must use the same fixed-halide controls and track which metric decays. Perform MPP illumination under inert and realistic encapsulated heat/humidity conditions, thermal cycling, and storage of multiple lots. Early FF loss, phase reappearance, or current loss should be correlated with phase and interface diagnostics. A short nitrogen MPP plateau is useful screening evidence but cannot be extrapolated to outdoor or IEC lifetime. The process window is accepted only if it improves both batch robustness and protocol-defined operational stability without relying on a Br increase or a band-gap penalty to create the apparent gain.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes a moderate Cs composition-process window for mean, variance, and failure probability rather than selecting the highest champion PCE or highest Cs fraction.
Uses a multivariable DOE over Cs, A-site/halide composition, temperature, vapor/drying history, coating, annealing, and ink age with fixed-halide controls for Cs attribution.
Connects in-line crystallization and phase-purity observables to batch distributions of photovoltaic metrics and uses a lower-quantile or yield-based statistical objective.
Requires multi-lot MPP and coupled environmental stability qualification and rejects apparent stability obtained only from higher Br content or a widened band gap.
accepted_equivalents: Taguchi robust design, Bayesian optimization with variance constraints, or response-surface methodology is acceptable if environmental noise factors are explicitly included.
Inline hyperspectral imaging or Raman mapping may replace reflectance/PL if calibrated to phase formation and band gap.
A process-capability index or probability-of-specification objective is acceptable in place of lower-quantile PCE.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the Cs concentration that produced the single highest PCE without analyzing batch variance or cold-process failures.
Varying Cs and Br together and attributing band-gap or thermal-stability changes solely to Cs.
Qualifying the process from a single short nitrogen storage or MPP trace without multi-lot environmental testing.

expected_answer:
The key discriminator is whether degradation can propagate without physical or electrical continuity. A volatile-I2 mechanism predicts gas-phase communication: a degraded source can release iodine species into a shared headspace, attack a physically separated fresh receiver, and convert the receiver into a secondary source. Purely solid-state ion migration requires a continuous perovskite or interfacial path and usually responds strongly to the electric field and microstructural connectivity. Local thermal runaway requires a local temperature excess and should not remotely damage an isothermal receiver once radiation and heat transfer are controlled.

Construct paired microreactors containing an aged or deliberately initiated iodide-perovskite source and a fresh receiver coupon. In the decisive branch, source and receiver share a sealed gas volume but are separated by an inert, nonporous physical gap and have no common electrode, substrate, or perovskite film. In a matched control, they are held at the same temperature and illumination in separate gas volumes. Add further branches with an iodine-selective scavenger or getter between source and receiver, a gas-permeable but ion/electron-blocking membrane, different headspace volumes, and top covers of different iodine permeability. Include a receiver exposed to a calibrated I2 dose as a positive control and a source made from a lower-iodide or low-defect composition as an initiation control.

Monitor the headspace with an iodine-sensitive optical cell, electrochemical sensor, or mass spectrometry. Map receiver color, absorption/PL, micro-XRD or Raman PbI2 formation, XPS/ToF-SIMS iodine chemistry, EL activity, and lesion position versus time. Infrared thermography and embedded temperature sensors must show that source and receiver are isothermal; electrical bias can be applied independently to test field dependence. A spatially compartmentalized receiver can determine whether degradation begins on the face exposed to the headspace rather than along a buried contact.

Volatile propagation is supported if a receiver in the shared headspace degrades despite the inert gap, if iodine is detected in the gas phase before receiver failure, if a getter or smaller source-receiver conductance suppresses or delays the event, and if the receiver later emits iodine or produces secondary lesions. The rate should depend on source area, headspace volume, ventilation/permeability, and scavenger capacity. A solid-state migration mechanism is supported if remote receivers remain intact and propagation occurs only across a continuous film or contact, follows grain boundaries or field direction, and is insensitive to a headspace scavenger. An electric-field front should reverse or change strongly with bias polarity but cannot cross an inert gap. Thermal runaway is supported only if lesion advance correlates with a local temperature rise and can be reproduced by matched heating without iodine; it is rejected if remote isothermal receivers fail only in the shared iodine-containing headspace. A mixed mechanism is plausible: solid-state or defect chemistry can initiate the first source, while volatile iodine controls long-range autocatalytic propagation.
scoring_key_points: Identifies noncontact gas-phase transfer as the decisive discriminator between volatile propagation and solid-state or field-driven mechanisms.
Designs shared-headspace versus separate-headspace source-receiver controls with an inert gap, iodine getter/permeability variations, and a calibrated I2 positive control.
Combines gas-phase iodine detection, spatial phase/optical/electrical mapping, bias variation, and isothermal thermal controls.
States distinct outcome patterns for volatile autocatalysis, continuous-path ion migration, electric-field propagation, thermal runaway, and a mixed initiation-propagation model.
accepted_equivalents: A divided operando cell with a gas-permeable, ion-impermeable membrane is acceptable as the source-receiver geometry.
UV-visible iodine absorption, quartz-crystal sensing, or colorimetric iodine dosimetry may replace mass spectrometry.
A microfluidic headspace or controlled carrier-gas transfer experiment is acceptable if no solid or electrical path connects source and receiver.
common_wrong_answers: Using only a continuous device and inferring vapor transport from circular lesion shape.
Calling any halide redistribution proof of volatile I2 without measuring or functionally intercepting the gas phase.
Ignoring local temperature and bias controls, so thermal or field-driven fronts remain viable explanations.

expected_answer:
The result shows why hermetic sealing alone is not sufficient. A highly impermeable top stack reduces external ingress but can also retain internally generated I2, HI, or other volatile products and increase their local chemical activity and pressure. The design must address three stages separately: generation at defective absorber sites, chemical propagation through volatile iodine, and mechanical/electrical damage at the transparent contact.

Initiation should be reduced by lowering deep-defect and iodine-interstitial populations, controlling iodide stoichiometry, minimizing harmful residual PbI2, and using a composition with less volatile MA and, where the tandem band-gap requirement permits, a moderated iodide fraction through FA/Cs/Br engineering. These changes must be evaluated at fixed band gap or with current-matching penalties explicitly included. Surface and buried-interface passivation should reduce hole accumulation and non-radiative hot spots without introducing unstable organic salts. Local heating and reverse-bias sensitivity at shunts should also be minimized through uniform contacts and robust scribe design.

Propagation should be interrupted by a thin, transparent, electrically compatible interlayer that is resistant to iodine and either blocks I2 transport or binds it reversibly/irreversibly into a nonvolatile, nonconductive product. A distributed iodine getter can be placed outside the primary carrier-transport path or at module dead zones so that reaction products do not create recombination centres. Lateral compartmentalization or chemically resistant barriers around sub-cells can limit the radius over which one seed contaminates neighboring active area. The electron-selective layer and transparent conductor must be screened for iodine reactivity.

Volatile management requires a controlled sink rather than indiscriminate trapping. Options include a finite-capacity getter coupled to a designed diffusion path from the active stack, a peripheral scavenging reservoir, or a pressure-tolerant headspace that directs species away from the active junction while preserving the external moisture barrier. Simply making the top electrode more permeable could release iodine but may admit oxygen or water and is therefore not a complete solution. Mechanical compliance, adhesion, and pressure tolerance of the transparent electrode should be improved so that local gas generation does not delaminate or rupture the contact. Getter capacity, saturation products, optical absorption, and electrical contamination must be quantified.

Validation should use spatially resolved MPP heat-light soaking at tandem-relevant current and temperature, with matched cells that independently vary absorber composition/passivation, iodine barrier/getter, top-electrode permeability, and mechanical design. Monitor gas-phase iodine, lesion nucleation density and radial growth rate, EL/PL active-area maps, micro-XRD/Raman PbI2, top-contact displacement or acoustic events, series resistance, shunts, EQE/current matching, and optical transmission. Deliberate I2 dosing tests propagation resistance; defect-seeding tests whether the architecture contains a known initiation event. A successful design lowers seed density, prevents remote lesion growth, avoids electrode bulging, and retains optical/electrical performance after the getter is partly loaded. Failure modes include getter saturation, iodine-reactive transport layers, new interfacial recombination, ion accumulation at a blocking layer, optical parasitic loss, and pressure relocation to another weak interface.
scoring_key_points: Explains that hermetic sealing can suppress ingress yet trap internally generated iodine and pressure, so initiation, propagation, and mechanical failure require separate controls.
Reduces initiation through defect/stoichiometry/residual-PbI2 and composition engineering while respecting tandem band-gap and current-matching constraints.

Uses an electrically and optically compatible iodine-resistant barrier or getter plus a controlled volatile sink or compartmentalization strategy rather than simple impermeability or ventilation alone.
Defines spatial MPP heat-light, I2-dosing, defect-seeding, gas/phase/mechanical/electrical validation and monitors getter saturation and interface penalties.
accepted_equivalents: A peripheral iodine-reactive metal-organic framework, activated sorbent, or redox-stable molecular getter is acceptable if its products and capacity are qualified.
Microencapsulated getter islands or patterned dead-zone scavengers may replace a continuous getter layer.
A mechanically compliant transparent conductor or buffer layer may be used to manage pressure if it does not replace chemical mitigation.
common_wrong_answers: Recommending only stronger hermetic encapsulation even though the failure is driven by internally generated and trapped volatiles.
Making the electrode freely permeable without addressing moisture/oxygen ingress or iodine propagation.
Adding an iodine scavenger directly in the carrier path without testing recombination, conductivity, optical loss, or saturation products.

expected_answer:
The molecular requirement is not merely a deep HOMO and high mobility. The polymer must maintain intrinsic conductivity without hygroscopic ionic dopants, form the preferred packing/orientation under the slower drying history of slot-die coating, wet and conformally cover a rough perovskite without dissolving it, adhere to both absorber and electrode, resist thermal softening or reorganization, and avoid redox reactions, mobile ionic species, or metal-ion complexation. Its solvent system must be orthogonal to the perovskite and compatible with web speed, rheology, filtration, and downstream electrode deposition.

The process window should jointly map solids concentration, molecular weight distribution, solvent blend, coating speed, wet thickness, substrate temperature, drying gradient, and final anneal. The target is a continuous, compositionally uniform HTL with stable face-on or otherwise favorable transport order, no pinholes at grains or scribes, low residual solvent, and a thickness that is above the coverage threshold but below the resistance-limited regime. Center-to-edge variation suggests nonuniform drying, orientation, thickness, or contact formation rather than a change in the molecular HOMO.

Validation should progress from ink to film to cell to module. Ink tests include rheology, aggregation and shelf life. Coated films require thickness and residual-solvent maps, GIWAXS/orientation maps, microscopy, adhesion, conductive-AFM or sheet/vertical transport, and transfer-length contact resistance. Small cells and submodules require stabilized J-V statistics, EL/PL imaging, series/shunt maps, and scribe-line inspection. Reliability must include dark humidity, damp heat, thermal cycling, light plus bias/MPP, and post-mortem depth profiling for water, mobile ions, and metal diffusion, with appropriate encapsulation and edge-seal controls.

Mobility and HOMO are bulk equilibrium properties and do not establish module-scale coverage, contact resistance, or drying-induced order. Contact angle measures only an initial surface wetting proxy; it does not prove low water-vapor transmission, edge protection, chemical inertness, or resistance to ion and metal migration. The formulation advances only if it gives spatially uniform electrical contact and stable MPP operation, not merely a hydrophobic neat film or a champion small cell.
scoring_key_points: Defines a molecular window including intrinsic dopant-free transport, packing/orientation, adhesion, chemical inertness, thermal stability, and solvent orthogonality.
Defines a slot-die process window that controls rheology, wet thickness, drying gradients, residual solvent, coverage threshold, and resistance-limited thickness.
Provides a staged ink-film-cell-module validation plan with spatial transport/contact and scribe-line diagnostics plus coupled reliability testing.
Explains why mobility, HOMO, and contact angle do not establish module-scale coverage, water-vapor/edge protection, ion migration, or MPP stability.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, gravure, meniscus, or slot-die coating is acceptable if slow and spatially nonuniform drying are explicitly addressed.
GIWAXS, polarized spectroscopy, grazing-incidence scattering, or mobility anisotropy may be used to track molecular orientation.
EL imaging, PL imaging, dark lock-in thermography, or spatial J-V mapping may be used as module-uniformity diagnostics.
Water-vapor transmission, calcium tests, ToF-SIMS, or isotopic-water tracing may be used to distinguish hydrophobicity from true barrier performance.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the spin-coated thickness and formulation transfer unchanged to slot-die coating.
Selecting the polymer solely from HOMO and neat-film mobility.
Equating high water contact angle with complete humidity and edge-seal protection.
Using only champion-cell PCE and dark shelf storage without spatial module mapping or MPP stress.

expected_answer:
The delayed nucleation, larger grains, and gains in Jsc and fill factor indicate that the crystallization-regulation function is operating. A basic nitrogen-containing gas can interact with the wet/intermediate film, slow nucleation, extend mass mobility, and improve film formation. The missing Voc, QFLS, and deep-trap improvement, together with weak and spatially nonuniform sulfur coordination, indicate that complementary passivation of undercoordinated metal sites is incomplete. Thus the process has reproduced the crystallization role but not the full dual-defect passivation role.

The minimum chemical controls are nitrogen-containing gas only during annealing, sulfur-containing gas only, the combined gases, and temporally separated or post-annealing exposures at matched partial pressure and thermal history. These controls distinguish a gas that changes nucleation only while the film is wet from one that passivates the final surface. In situ UV-vis/PL/XRD or mass-loss measurements should quantify nucleation time, intermediate persistence and grain formation, while XPS/Raman, surface-sensitive spectroscopy, trap spectroscopy, PLQY/QFLS and defect-depth profiling should quantify chemical coordination and non-radiative loss.

Mass transfer must be tested independently by placing witness samples along and across the flow direction, measuring gas concentration or using an inert tracer, reversing the flow, changing source distance/residence time, and mapping N/S signals, PLQY, trap density and local Voc/EL. If reactor transport is responsible, the sulfur, QFLS and Voc gradient should follow the inlet and change or flatten when flow direction, mixing, pressure or residence time is altered, while the nitrogen-related nucleation delay may remain more uniform. If intrinsic sulfur chemistry is ineffective at the chosen temperature or film state, sulfur uptake and Voc gains will remain weak everywhere even after the reactor concentration is homogenized. If crystallization alone is responsible for performance, Jsc/FF and grain metrics will track nitrogen exposure, whereas Voc/QFLS and deep-trap metrics will track successful dual-site surface coordination.
scoring_key_points: Diagnoses successful crystallization regulation from delayed nucleation, larger grains, and Jsc/FF gains, but failed or incomplete complementary surface passivation from unchanged Voc/QFLS/deep traps.
Uses gas-only, combined, and timing/post-treatment controls to separate wet-film crystallization effects from final-surface passivation.
Uses spatial gas/tracer and N/S chemical maps with flow reversal or mixing changes to distinguish reactor mass transfer from intrinsic chemistry.
Predicts that crystallization metrics track the nitrogen-containing gas, whereas uniform sulfur coordination, QFLS/Voc, and deep-trap reduction track successful complementary passivation.
accepted_equivalents: NH3 and CS2 may be named explicitly, but generic nitrogen- and sulfur-containing annealing species are acceptable if their roles are correctly separated.
Thermal admittance, DLCP, SCLC, deep-level spectroscopy, or surface photovoltage may be used to quantify defect populations.
PL/EL mapping, local Kelvin probe, or spatially resolved Voc may substitute for other maps of non-radiative loss.
Computational fluid dynamics is acceptable as support but must be paired with an experimental concentration or spatial-response test.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that larger grains automatically imply lower deep-trap density and higher Voc.
Attributing the result only to insufficient annealing temperature without testing spatial gas delivery.
Using a single combined-gas control, which cannot separate crystallization timing from passivation chemistry.
Treating XPS nitrogen and sulfur signals as proof of uniform functional passivation without QFLS/trap or spatial correlation.

expected_answer:
Improved conductivity does not guarantee a more selective contact. At low or intermediate loading, dispersed graphene can provide faster electron pathways, improve oxide connectivity and lower series resistance. At excessive loading, flakes can agglomerate, protrude through a thin oxide, create locally graphene-rich domains, or directly contact the perovskite. Those sites may introduce energetic disorder, nonselective extraction, interfacial traps or microshunts. They can shorten PL decay by extracting carriers or by non-radiative quenching, while simultaneously increasing dark recombination, ionic-field concentration and hysteresis. Thus the falling Voc and hotspot formation are consistent with loss of selectivity rather than a reversal of the conductivity improvement.

The experiment should vary graphene loading, flake size and ETL thickness independently. Cross-sectional TEM or tomography, depth-resolved ToF-SIMS/Raman mapping, conductive AFM and composition-sensitive microscopy should determine whether graphene reaches the perovskite interface and whether hotspots coincide with agglomerates. UPS/Kelvin probe/KPFM should measure uniform or local work-function shifts. Sheet/vertical conductivity, SCLC or impedance should quantify bulk transport, while PLQY-derived QFLS, external EL efficiency, dark J-V, ideality factor and light-intensity-dependent Voc quantify selectivity and non-radiative loss.

If the limitation is bulk ETL transport, increasing graphene should mainly reduce series resistance and improve fill factor; Voc and EL efficiency should remain approximately stable, and no interface-correlated hotspots should appear. If direct contact or agglomeration is responsible, high-loading devices should show graphene-rich protrusions or domains spatially coincident with dark-current/low-PL or low-EL hotspots, rising leakage and ideality factor, and lower QFLS/Voc despite lower sheet resistance. If a work-function mismatch dominates, KPFM/UPS should show a comparatively uniform energetic shift and extraction barrier or nonselective alignment without requiring discrete agglomerate hotspots. A thin oxide spacer that prevents direct contact while retaining the graphene-assisted bulk conductivity is a decisive rescue control.
scoring_key_points: Explains that conductivity can improve while contact selectivity worsens, and that fast PL decay may include non-radiative quenching.
Identifies excessive-loading mechanisms such as direct graphene-perovskite contact, agglomeration, energetic disorder or local shunts that lower Voc and increase hysteresis.
Uses an independent loading-flake-size-ETL-thickness design with depth/spatial composition, work-function, transport and recombination measurements.
States decisive predictions for bulk transport, direct-contact/agglomeration and uniform work-function-shift hypotheses, including an insulating-spacer rescue control.
accepted_equivalents: Graphene oxide, graphene nanoplatelets, GQDs or other GRMs are acceptable if the answer treats concentration, location and selectivity explicitly.
Cross-sectional TEM, tomography, nano-IR, Raman, ToF-SIMS or labeled-flake imaging may be used to locate carbon domains.
EL efficiency, QFLS, ideality factor, dark saturation current or surface photovoltage may be used to diagnose non-radiative/selectivity loss.
A conformal TiO2 overcoat or insulating ultrathin barrier is equivalent to the stated direct-contact rescue control.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming lower sheet resistance must monotonically improve all photovoltaic metrics.
Treating faster PL decay as unambiguous proof of beneficial extraction.
Attributing the high-loading loss only to optical absorption without testing leakage or interface location.
Using only average AFM roughness, which can miss buried protrusions and sparse recombination hotspots.

expected_answer:
Bending retention and dark shelf survival establish only two limited functions: mechanical compliance and some passive environmental tolerance. They do not prove that the graphene interface remains electrically selective or chemically inert under illumination, current flow and heat. Voc loss near the metal grid suggests locally enhanced non-radiative recombination from metal-ion migration, corrosion products, interfacial redox chemistry or heat-accelerated contact damage. Rising series resistance can arise from poor graphene sheet conductivity, high graphene/transport-layer or graphene/metal contact resistance, discontinuities, delamination, oxidation/reduction-state drift, or current crowding and Joule heating.

The stress matrix should separate bending-only, dark heat, humidity, light-only, bias/current-only and combined light-heat-MPP conditions, with and without edge encapsulation. Spatial EL/PL, dark-current and infrared thermography should locate voltage loss, current crowding and hot spots. Four-probe sheet resistance and transfer-length contact resistance should be tracked during stress. ToF-SIMS or cross-sectional chemical mapping should measure metal-ion and halide migration; XPS/Raman should track graphene oxidation, doping and defects; microscopy and adhesion tests should detect delamination or cracks; water/oxygen tracer or barrier measurements should test whether protection is real or only apparent in shelf storage.

A useful redesign may require continuous low-defect multilayer graphene, controlled reduction/functionalization and work function, an ion-blocking or chemically inert spacer at the metal interface, lower contact resistance, redesigned grid spacing/current collection, and robust edge sealing. Increasing graphene loading is not automatically beneficial because it may reduce transparency, alter energetics, create lateral resistance gradients or introduce catalytic defect sites.

A stability claim requires stabilized MPP retention under relevant light, temperature and humidity, spatially uniform Voc/EL, stable sheet and contact resistance, absence of metal/halide intrusion, and post-stress chemical/structural integrity relative to a matched non-graphene control. Mechanical cycles and dark shelf tests alone are insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Separates mechanical compliance and passive barrier behavior from illuminated, current-carrying electrical selectivity and chemical stability.
Connects grid-localized Voc loss and rising series resistance to testable metal-ion, Joule-heating, contact-resistance, delamination and graphene-chemistry mechanisms.
Proposes a decomposed stress matrix with spatial electrical/thermal maps, resistance tracking, depth chemistry and barrier/adhesion measurements.
Defines a redesign and operational go/no-go claim based on MPP retention, spatial uniformity, stable contacts and absence of ion/metal intrusion, not bending or shelf life alone.
accepted_equivalents: Raman D/G evolution, XPS, Kelvin probe, or conductivity measurements may be used to track graphene chemical/doping drift.
Time-of-flight SIMS, X-ray fluorescence, electron microscopy/EDS, or isotopically labeled metal tracing may be used to detect electrode intrusion.
Dark lock-in thermography, infrared imaging, electroluminescence or local voltage mapping may be used to identify current crowding and hot spots.
A chemically inert 2D spacer, oxide barrier or carbon multilayer is acceptable as the ion-blocking redesign if contact resistance and selectivity are verified.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming operational stability from bending retention and dark shelf storage alone.
Attributing all degradation to moisture without testing metal migration, current crowding or contact resistance.
Adding more graphene without considering sheet resistance, work function, defects, transparency and contact interfaces.
Using only average module PCE and missing the grid-localized failure pattern.

expected_answer:
The evidence is insufficient and the contact-stack kinetics are unfavorable. New low-q peaks establish a low-dimensional or ordered product but do not prove the intended phase, orientation, thickness or depth location. A longer bare-film lifetime can indicate lower non-radiative recombination, but the desired electron-selective surface layer should normally preserve or increase QFLS while allowing faster transfer after PCBM is added. A longer lifetime in the perovskite/PCBM stack together with slower transient photocurrent and unchanged Voc suggests an extraction barrier, excessive 2D thickness, unfavorable band alignment, insulating side products or bulk conversion rather than a properly functioning ultrathin heterostructure.

The structural test must identify phase and orientation, not just peak presence. Angle-dependent or depth-sensitive GIWAXS, grazing-incidence XRD, cross-sectional TEM and optical signatures should determine the low-dimensional n value and whether it lies parallel at the surface. ToF-SIMS/XPS depth profiling, isotope labeling and profilometry should show that the spacer is confined to an ultrathin top region without a large bulk-thickness or composition change. NMR, FTIR or mass spectrometry on model mixtures should rule out a spacer-host cyclization or other side reaction.

UPS/KPFM and photoelectron spectroscopy should determine whether the surface becomes appropriately electron selective rather than forming a large barrier. Absolute PLQY/QFLS and EL efficiency should show reduced non-radiative loss. Contact-selective TRPL or transient absorption must be interpreted in stack context: the desired pattern is a longer lifetime or higher PLQY for the passivated bare film but a faster extraction component after PCBM deposition, together with faster photocurrent, lower interfacial resistance and higher Voc.

A thick/blocking 2D layer gives strong low-q intensity, surface accumulation, slow PCBM extraction and high interfacial resistance. Bulk conversion gives depth-distributed spacer, significant low-dimensional optical emission and altered absorption/thickness. A side product may give chemical signatures without the expected crystallographic orientation, band alignment or extraction rescue. The treatment should not be accepted until these alternatives are excluded.
scoring_key_points: States that low-q peaks plus longer bare-film TRPL do not prove the intended ultrathin, surface-localized and electronically selective heterostructure.
Uses the longer PCBM-stack lifetime, slower photocurrent and unchanged Voc to diagnose an extraction barrier, excessive thickness, bulk conversion or side product.
Requires phase/orientation and depth-localization measurements plus chemical controls that rule out unintended spacer-host reactions.
Defines the desired kinetic/energetic signature: improved QFLS with faster extraction after ETL contact, lower interfacial resistance and higher Voc.
accepted_equivalents: GIWAXS incidence-angle variation, standing-wave XPS, neutron/X-ray reflectometry or cross-sectional microscopy may be used for depth localization.
Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, photocurrent transients or impedance may substitute for contact-selective TRPL if extraction and recombination are separated.
Solution NMR, solid-state NMR, FTIR, LC-MS or model-reactant analysis may be used to detect side reactions.
An unfavorable conduction-band offset, tunneling barrier or insulating low-n layer are equivalent transport-blocking interpretations.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring success from the appearance of any low-q GIWAXS peak.
Treating a longer TRPL lifetime in the PCBM stack as automatically beneficial.
Ignoring phase orientation, thickness and depth localization.
Attributing unchanged Voc only to bulk defects without testing whether the post-treatment blocks electron extraction.

expected_answer:
The original recipe cannot be assumed to transfer because the driving force for the spacer-host side reaction changes with FA fraction, halide activity, surface termination, solvent and annealing history. With less FA, the unwanted reaction may be weaker, so the additional small cation may provide little benefit or may instead alter halide stoichiometry, promote a different low-dimensional phase, change surface doping, or create an extraction barrier. The different ETL also changes the acceptable band offset and interfacial chemistry.

The minimum factorial contains untreated, diammonium spacer only, small-cation salt only and combined treatment, with a concentration/ratio series and matched solvent/thermal controls. Model-solution NMR, FTIR or mass spectrometry, supported by adsorption or molecular simulations, should quantify whether the spacer-host product is suppressed. Halide-balanced controls are required to distinguish a cation effect from extra iodide/bromide or halide exchange.

GIWAXS/XRD and optical spectroscopy should identify the low-dimensional n value, phase purity and orientation. XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiles, isotope labeling and thickness measurements should verify an ultrathin surface-localized layer rather than bulk conversion or composition drift. UPS/KPFM, PLQY/QFLS, contact-selective transients, interfacial impedance and device Voc/FF should establish electron selectivity with the new ETL.

Stability must be tested under dark, light-only, bias-only and combined light plus forward-bias/MPP conditions at relevant temperature. Time-resolved PL/EL spectra and maps, in situ XRD and depth composition should track I/Br segregation, PbI2 formation and ion migration. The transfer is rejected if the combined treatment does not uniquely suppress the side product, causes bulk halide/composition shift, produces an uncontrolled or blocking low-n phase, slows ETL extraction, fails to improve QFLS/Voc, or leaves phase segregation and MPP lifetime no better than the best single-component control.
scoring_key_points: Explains why lower FA, higher Br and a different ETL change side-reaction driving force, phase selection, halide exchange and band-alignment constraints.
Uses untreated, spacer-only, small-cation-only and combined treatments with ratio and halide-balanced controls to isolate the chemical mechanism.
Validates side-reaction suppression, low-dimensional phase/orientation, surface localization, composition and ETL selectivity with orthogonal chemistry, structure, depth and kinetic measurements.
Requires coupled light-bias/MPP phase-stability tests and gives explicit rejection criteria for wrong phase, bulk exchange, blocked extraction or no stability gain.
accepted_equivalents: A full factorial design of experiments is equivalent to the four-arm minimum if cation, spacer, halide and concentration effects are independently estimable.
Operando absorption, cathodoluminescence, nano-XRD or hyperspectral PL may be used to track phase segregation.
Transient ion drift, impedance, temperature-dependent conductivity or ToF-SIMS after bias may be used to assess ion migration.
A different small cation is acceptable if the answer re-establishes side-reaction inhibition and phase selectivity rather than assuming chemical equivalence.
common_wrong_answers: Using the original spacer-to-small-cation ratio without re-testing the altered absorber chemistry.
Interpreting improved initial PL as proof that halide segregation and side reactions are suppressed.
Omitting the small-cation-only and halide-balanced controls.
Accepting any 2D signal without verifying n value, surface localization and compatibility with the new ETL.

expected_answer:
The inference confuses absence of a diffraction peak with absence of a chemical intermediate. Immediate XRD can miss an amorphous, nanoscale, low-volume-fraction or poorly oriented solvent-rich phase. Residual-solvent FTIR at the initial time already proves that solvent-containing material remains. Peaks appearing during room-temperature aging may therefore reflect increased ordering or crystallization of a pre-existing solvent-coordinated species as molecular mobility rises, followed by peak disappearance when the solvent leaves. They do not require new solvent uptake or prove that the species was absent during pump-down. In addition, a surface delta-phase or solvent-rich capping layer can control diffusion without producing the same crystalline adduct peaks.
