The experiment should combine high-time-resolution in situ or rapid-transfer GIWAXS/XRD during pump-down, cold hold, warm-up and annealing with an independent chemical/mass probe such as ATR-FTIR/Raman, quartz-crystal microbalance or gravimetry, ellipsometry and temperature/pressure logging. Cryogenic or sealed transfer at selected times should arrest the structure. Isotopically labeled solvent or vapor-free aging can verify that later peaks arise from retained solvent rather than environmental uptake. A matrix of coldplate temperature, pressure, pump time and controlled aging time should determine whether the same solvent signal exists before diffraction peaks become visible.

The ordering hypothesis predicts measurable residual-solvent or coordination signatures and mass before the XRD peaks, followed by peak growth during warm aging without an increase in solvent mass, then loss of both peaks and solvent signal. De novo formation would require a new chemical or mass uptake coincident with peak appearance.

Buried voids should be correlated with the solvent-flux history and capping-layer function, not simply with whether an adduct peak is observed. Excessively high flux can create a rapidly solidified surface and violent solvent escape or voids; insufficient flux can leave a poorly consolidated, pinholed film. An optimal window can be void-free even if the crystalline adduct peaks are transient or initially invisible. Cross-sectional microscopy and spatial residual-solvent mapping must therefore be linked to the measured flux trajectory.
scoring_key_points: States that absence of immediate XRD peaks does not exclude an amorphous, nanoscale, low-fraction or poorly oriented solvent-rich intermediate.
Interprets later peak appearance as possible ordering of pre-existing retained-solvent species rather than necessarily de novo formation.
Proposes time-resolved diffraction plus independent solvent/mass/coordination measurements, arrest controls and a temperature-pressure-time matrix with predicted outcomes.
Relates buried voids to the evaporation-flux/capping history rather than using adduct-peak presence alone as the causal variable.
accepted_equivalents: Synchrotron GIWAXS, rapid laboratory XRD, electron diffraction or cryo-TEM may be used to observe short-lived ordering if temporal resolution is adequate.
FTIR, Raman, NMR, QCM, thermogravimetry, ellipsometry or residual-solvent mass spectrometry may be used as the independent chemical/mass probe.
A sealed dry transfer or isotopically labeled solvent is equivalent to the vapor-free control for excluding external uptake.
A delta-phase cap, amorphous skin or solvent-rich diffusion barrier are acceptable descriptions if their kinetic function is distinguished from the crystalline adduct peaks.
common_wrong_answers: Equating no XRD peak with no intermediate or no residual solvent.
Assuming the later peaks require solvent absorption from the environment without a mass or isotope test.
Using only ex situ XRD snapshots and no independent solvent-sensitive measurement.
Claiming that adduct peaks alone determine whether buried voids form.

expected_answer:
Identical equipment settings do not produce identical solvent flux because vapor pressure, latent heat, gas-phase transport, viscosity, film diffusivity, coordination and phase behavior are solvent specific. The candidate should coordinate strongly enough to maintain a coherent wet/intermediate film during rapid pressure reduction, but weakly enough that the coordinated solvent or adduct can be removed during controlled warming/annealing. A high boiling point or very strong metal coordination can create persistent residual solvent and stable adducts; a very volatile or weakly coordinating solvent can solidify the surface or deplete the film too rapidly. Freezing point and viscosity determine flow and diffusion on the coldplate, while hygroscopicity affects storage, residual-water uptake and later stability.

The process map should measure actual solvent mass flux rather than copy temperature and pressure. A design of experiments should vary coldplate temperature, absolute pressure, pump-down rate, hold time, wet-film thickness, substrate thermal mass and web speed. In situ gravimetry/QCM or exhaust mass spectrometry, temperature logging, FTIR/Raman and GIWAXS/XRD should track evaporation, residual coordination and phase formation. Cross-sectional microscopy, profilometry and PL mapping should evaluate both the top and buried interfaces. Each solvent requires its own window and may require a different pressure-temperature pair.

At excessive flux, rapid surface solidification and steep concentration gradients can trap or expel solvent violently, generating buried voids, whitening, delamination or a dense crust over a defective interior. At insufficient flux, the film may remain mobile too long, dewet, retain excess solvent, form pinholes or convert nonuniformly. The optimum gives a temporary diffusion-regulating cap, limited removable residual solvent, compact buried contact and reproducible conversion to the black phase.

Go/no-go tests include residual-solvent/adduct disappearance after annealing, phase purity, void- and pinhole-free morphology across the web, low trap-assisted recombination, high QFLS and stabilized cell/module output. Reliability must include heat aging and continuous MPP under air/humidity, with post-mortem PbI2, composition and residual-solvent analysis. The solvent is rejected if it needs an impractically narrow window, retains a stable adduct, produces spatial flux gradients or buried defects, or shows accelerated thermal/MPP degradation despite high initial PCE.
scoring_key_points: Explains why temperature, pressure and time cannot be copied across solvents and identifies vapor/transport, coordination, phase, viscosity and hygroscopicity variables.
Defines a solvent-specific temperature-pressure-time-thickness-web-speed process map based on measured evaporation flux and in situ solvent/phase diagnostics.
Predicts high-flux buried-void/crust failures and low-flux pinhole/dewetting/residual-solvent failures, with an intermediate capping-state optimum.
Provides film, device and operational MPP/thermal go/no-go criteria, including rejection for persistent adducts, spatial nonuniformity or accelerated degradation.
accepted_equivalents: DMAC, GVL or another single solvent may be used as an example, but the answer must re-optimize rather than copy DMF settings.
A semi-empirical mass-transfer model, dimensionless transport analysis or calibrated evaporation-rate map is acceptable if validated experimentally.
FTIR, Raman, TGA-MS, NMR or XRD may be used to quantify residual solvent and adduct persistence.
Module EL/PL imaging, dark thermography or spatial J-V may be used to evaluate web-scale uniformity.
common_wrong_answers: Copying the DMF coldplate temperature and pressure because the solvents have similar boiling points.
Selecting the strongest-coordinating solvent to maximize intermediate stability.
Inspecting only the top surface and ignoring buried voids or residual solvent.
Accepting a solvent from initial PCE without thermal and continuous-MPP testing.

expected_answer: Keep absorber thickness and both selective contacts fixed, then measure a broad scan-rate matrix after controlled forward and reverse pre-bias, in dark and under several light intensities and temperatures. Extract the hysteresis peak or characteristic relaxation time rather than comparing one scan rate. Low-frequency impedance, IMPS, transient capacitance, Kelvin-probe relaxation, or time-resolved surface-potential measurements should quantify the ionic time constant and the integrated charge displaced. A lower mobile-ion density gives a smaller integrated ionic capacitance or transferred charge across conditions, not merely a shifted response frequency. Faster equilibration gives a similar ionic charge magnitude but a shorter relaxation time and lower activation barrier or higher effective ionic conductivity; hysteresis reappears when the scan becomes faster than that time scale. Reduced electronic recombination should be supported independently by absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, intensity-dependent open-circuit voltage, TRPL, and transient photovoltage, together with higher stabilized voltage, but it need not shift the ionic relaxation frequency by orders of magnitude. Contact capacitance should be tested with electron-only, hole-only, and symmetric stacks, altered contact thickness, and at least one alternative electron-contact morphology; a contact-controlled time constant will track the contact architecture more strongly than absorber composition. Contactless THz mobility should be distinguished from device extraction by transient photocurrent and pseudo-JV. A defensible conclusion may assign separate fractions to faster ionic response and lower recombination, but cannot equate reduced hysteresis with elimination of ion migration.
scoring_key_points: Uses scan-rate, pre-bias, illumination, and temperature dependence to extract a characteristic hysteresis or relaxation time rather than relying on one JV scan.
Separates mobile-ion density from ion mobility/equilibration using integrated ionic charge or capacitance and relaxation/activation-energy measurements.
Requires independent quasi-Fermi-level, recombination, mobility, and extraction diagnostics to test an electronic-quality contribution.
Uses half-device or alternative-contact controls to identify contact capacitance and states explicit signatures for all four candidate mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Transient ion-drift, thermally stimulated current, bias-stress recovery, or isotope-tracer relaxation as ionic diagnostics
Suns-Voc, electroluminescence efficiency, or ideality-factor analysis as alternatives for recombination loss
Time-of-flight, microwave conductivity, or optical-pump terahertz conductivity as contactless mobility probes
A drift-diffusion model fitted simultaneously to scan-rate and impedance data, provided fitted ion density and ion mobility are independently constrained
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that ion migration is absent because hysteresis is small at a conventional scan rate
Treating longer TRPL as direct proof of faster ionic equilibration
Using only impedance fitting without contact controls or independent constraints on ionic charge and electronic recombination

expected_answer: Average visible transmittance is a photopic integral, so very different spectral shapes can be metameric in AVT while producing different color rendering, tint, occupant response, and lighting demand. Measure hemispherical and specular transmittance and reflectance across the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared range, not only 400-700 nm. From the visible spectrum calculate CIE chromaticity, correlated color temperature, color-rendering index or a modern fidelity/gamut metric, luminous transmittance, and color difference relative to a neutral reference. Include haze, polarization, and incidence-angle dependence because thin-metal or dielectric cavities can change color with angle. For thermal performance, determine solar heat-gain coefficient or an equivalent calorimetric quantity, near-infrared rejection, absorbed heat, interior surface temperature, and heat transfer to the building. For electrical performance, measure spectral EQE, stabilized PCE, and annual energy yield under location-specific spectra, temperature, angle, and shading. Use transfer-matrix or optical-device modeling, validated by measured optical constants, to partition absorber, electrode, and interference losses and to predict changes with thickness and angle. Finally couple the measured window spectra to a building-energy model that includes daylight-driven lighting savings and HVAC loads. Device A may fail color-quality criteria despite adequate AVT; Device B may look neutral but impose a cooling penalty. Rank candidates using a Pareto front with minimum thresholds for color, thermal load, transparency, and energy yield rather than one scalar AVT-PCE score.
scoring_key_points: Explains that identical AVT can conceal different visible spectra, chromaticity, color rendering, tint, and angular appearance.
Requires full spectral and angular optical measurements with CIE/CCT/CRI-type metrics, haze, and a neutral-reference color criterion.
Separately quantifies near-infrared heat gain, absorbed heat, and building HVAC effects alongside spectral EQE and annual photovoltaic yield.
Uses validated optical and building-energy models and ranks designs by Pareto constraints rather than reducing all performance to AVT or PCE.
accepted_equivalents: TM-30 fidelity/gamut, daylight glare probability, melanopic daylight efficacy, or equivalent advanced daylight-quality metrics in addition to basic CIE descriptors
Solar heat-gain coefficient, g-value, calorimetric heat flux, or spectrally integrated NIR rejection as thermal metrics
Finite-difference optical simulation or rigorous coupled-wave analysis instead of transfer-matrix modeling when scattering or patterning is important
Multi-criteria decision analysis instead of a Pareto front, provided hard minimum criteria prevent compensation of unacceptable color or heat gain
common_wrong_answers: Ranking the devices as equivalent because PCE and AVT are identical
Using a single transmittance value at 550 nm as a substitute for color and daylight quality
Counting NIR transmission as harmless because it lies outside the visible range

expected_answer: Start by mapping the entire window, because acceptable averages can hide unacceptable local appearance and electrical loss. Measure transparent-electrode sheet resistance, contact resistance, line resistance, film thickness, optical constants, spectral transmittance/reflectance, haze, and color coordinates on a two-dimensional grid. Compare these with electroluminescence, photoluminescence, LBIC or photocurrent maps, lock-in thermography, and distributed JV measurements. A busbar-related loss will follow current path length and sheet resistance, improve with grid redesign, and appear as an electrical gradient without the same spectral color pattern. Optical-thickness or cavity nonuniformity will correlate with interference fringes, angular color shift, and measured layer-thickness variation; transfer-matrix reconstruction should reproduce it. Coating defects will create localized shunts, dead zones, or haze features. Package failure should be edge-correlated and accompanied by moisture tracers, delamination, corrosion, or compositional change. Qualification must combine stabilized MPP operation, damp heat, UV exposure, thermal cycling, mechanical load, freeze-thaw where relevant, partial shading, and repeated angle/temperature optical measurements, using matched unencapsulated, edge-seal, and full-laminate controls. Include building-specific tests for safety glazing, visible distortion, color uniformity, and solar heat gain. Pass/fail rules should limit local sheet resistance and voltage drop, color difference and AVT variation, shunt density, hotspot temperature, edge-ingress distance, and post-stress power retention. Reject a design whose average PCE or AVT masks visible banding, local reverse bias, or package-driven degradation.
scoring_key_points: Uses full-area spatial maps of sheet/contact resistance, thickness, spectra, color, haze, luminescence, current, and temperature rather than average metrics.
Provides discriminating signatures for busbar resistance, optical-cavity/thickness variation, coating defects, and edge/package failure.
Combines MPP, damp heat, UV, thermal cycling, mechanical, shading, and package-control tests with repeated optical as well as electrical assessment.
Defines building-product pass/fail limits for spatial color/AVT, voltage drop, shunts, hotspots, edge ingress, safety, and retained power.
accepted_equivalents: Electroluminescence, photoluminescence, dark lock-in thermography, or magnetic-field imaging as current-distribution diagnostics
Inline spectroscopic ellipsometry, hyperspectral imaging, or interferometric thickness mapping for optical-cavity control
IEC photovoltaic-module and architectural-glazing tests adapted to the semitransparent window function
Distributed circuit modeling or finite-element current-flow analysis for busbar and sheet-resistance optimization
common_wrong_answers: Approving the window because its area-averaged PCE and AVT meet specification
Attributing every color band to absorber thickness without checking electrode cavities or incidence-angle effects
Testing only damp heat and ignoring current distribution, thermal cycling, partial shading, and glazing-specific optical criteria

expected_answer: Translate the functions, not the original thermal recipe. Deposit a low-temperature compact hole-selective layer by nanoparticle NiOx, combustion chemistry with low-temperature activation, sputtering, plasma-assisted deposition, or a robust self-assembled/contact bilayer. Verify that it is continuous at the valleys of the flexible transparent electrode and has suitable work function, low electron leakage, and no acidic or mobile dopant residue. Add a low-temperature inert porous overlayer from preformed Al2O3 or SiO2 nanoparticles, a crosslinked nanocomposite, or a patterned dielectric that fills roughness without forming an extraction barrier. Optimize compact-layer thickness, scaffold thickness, pore size, porosity, surface energy, drying, and perovskite wetting/infiltration under the substrate thermal budget. Use AFM/profilometry, cross-sectional microscopy, conductive-AFM, sheet resistance, optical spectra and haze, UPS/KPFM, dark leakage, shunt/series resistance, PL/QFLS, and local module maps. Mechanical qualification should include repeated bending at multiple radii, tension/compression orientation, cyclic adhesion, and post-bend mapping of cracks, shunts, and contact resistance. Couple these with MPP light soaking, heat within the polymer limit, humidity, UV, and thermal cycling, using barrier-film and edge-seal controls. Reject a process if conformality is achieved only by an optically absorbing layer, if the porous layer causes incomplete infiltration or moisture uptake, if work-function/selectivity drift creates voltage loss, or if bending opens recurrent shunt paths. Acceptance should specify maximum exposed-electrode fraction, leakage density, optical loss, spatial FF variation, bend-cycle degradation, and retained output.
scoring_key_points: Replaces the high-temperature recipe with low-temperature compact selective and inert roughness-filling layers while preserving their separate functions.
Optimizes thickness, porosity, pore size, surface energy, drying, and infiltration within the flexible-substrate thermal and solvent budget.
Combines conformality, leakage, energetics, optical, luminescence, and spatial module diagnostics with bending and environmental/MPP stresses.
Defines explicit rejection limits for optical absorption, incomplete infiltration, moisture uptake, selectivity drift, mechanically reopened shunts, and output loss.
accepted_equivalents: Low-temperature CuOx, polymeric hole-selective contacts, or SAM-based contacts if electron blocking and long-term chemical stability are demonstrated
Atomic-layer-deposited, sol-gel nanoparticle, printed dielectric, or crosslinked porous scaffold routes compatible with the substrate budget
Roll-to-roll flex testing, mandrel bending, or cyclic tensile testing as equivalent mechanical qualification
Barrier-film water-vapor transmission and calcium tests as additional package controls
common_wrong_answers: Lowering the original sintering temperature without proving continuity, selectivity, or scaffold integrity
Replacing the scaffold with a thick dense insulator that blocks both shunts and useful hole extraction
Reporting initial flexible-cell efficiency without bend-cycle, leakage-map, moisture, or adhesion qualification

expected_answer: Begin with subcell-resolved EQE using appropriate electrical and optical bias so the limiting photocurrent of each junction is measured independently. Compare integrated currents before and after stress and repeat under spectrally selective excitation. Wide-bandgap segregation is supported by reversible red-shifted or split PL, spatial PL heterogeneity, altered high-energy EQE, and recovery in the dark or after mild thermal reset; operando diffraction or composition mapping can confirm halide redistribution. Narrow-bandgap degradation should preferentially reduce near-infrared EQE and lifetime, increase background p-doping or dark conductivity, and produce persistent Sn4+, Sn-vacancy-related chemistry, or morphology changes by XPS/Mossbauer-like chemical-state probes, capacitance, Hall/Seebeck, or depth profiling. The interconnecting layer should be tested by Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV, intensity-dependent FF, temperature-dependent series resistance, impedance, transient recombination, and electroluminescence coupling between subcells. An ICL resistance increase can lower FF and voltage-dependent collection while subcell generation and luminescence remain largely intact; poor recombination selectivity may create charge accumulation, nonideal electroluminescence, or an S-shaped response. Selective half-stacks and witness ICL films exposed to the same solvents, heat, and light should identify metal diffusion, barrier failure, or contact damage. Total tandem Voc alone is insufficient because compensating subcell changes can mask loss. Assign the dominant subsystem only when spectral, chemical, and electrical signatures converge and the reconstructed series tandem JV reproduces the measured degradation.
scoring_key_points: Uses optically and electrically biased subcell EQE and spectrally selective excitation to localize current loss in the WBG or NBG junction.
Identifies WBG segregation by reversible spectral/PL heterogeneity and NBG Sn degradation by persistent NIR, doping, and Sn-chemical-state changes.
Tests ICL resistance and recombination with pseudo-JV/Suns-Voc, temperature/intensity dependence, impedance, luminescence coupling, and witness structures.
Rejects total Voc as a unique locator and requires convergent subcell reconstruction, chemical evidence, and electrical signatures.
accepted_equivalents: Two-color lock-in EQE, luminescence imaging under selective excitation, or subcell-resolved electroluminescence as junction-localization methods
Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, XANES, Mossbauer spectroscopy, or chemical titration for Sn2+/Sn4+ analysis
Dark recovery kinetics, operando absorption, or hyperspectral imaging for halide-segregation diagnosis
Four-terminal test coupons, buried-contact resistance structures, or transfer-length methods for ICL resistance isolation
common_wrong_answers: Assigning the loss to the current-limiting top cell from tandem JV alone
Using a stable total open-circuit voltage to rule out subcell recombination or chemical degradation
Calling every fill-factor loss an ICL series-resistance problem without subcell EQE, chemical-state, or selective-stack controls

expected_answer: Control each subcell and the interconnecting layer as linked process windows. Map WBG and NBG bandgap, thickness, absorption, PL peak, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and integrated subcell EQE across the coating width, then use optical-electrical modeling to set tolerances that keep local series current matched over realistic spectra, temperatures, and incidence angles. The ICL process must protect the lower subcell from upper-cell solvents, sputter or plasma damage, heat, and metal diffusion while remaining transparent and low resistance; use witness stacks, solvent-soak controls, transfer-length structures, and depth profiling. Design module stripes, dead-area geometry, busbars, and possibly smaller electrically isolated segments or bypass elements to limit reverse voltage and hotspot energy under shade. Use EL/PL, LBIC, lock-in thermography, distributed voltage sensing, and subcell-biased EQE to detect local mismatch before lamination. Qualification should combine stabilized MPP, spectral cycling, temperature cycling, damp heat, UV, partial-shading and reverse-bias sequences, with operando thermal imaging and post-stress analysis of WBG segregation, NBG Sn oxidation, ICL delamination/resistance, and metal/halide migration. Test both uniform and patterned shade because current-matched tandems can become locally reverse biased even when global JV appears normal. Reject modules with local subcell-current mismatch beyond the modeled safe window, hotspot temperature or reverse voltage above material limits, ICL resistance/nonuniformity above specification, or degradation that propagates between stripes. Average PCE and a single standard spectrum are insufficient acceptance metrics.
scoring_key_points: Controls and spatially maps WBG/NBG bandgap, thickness, luminescence, and subcell EQE to maintain local current matching across spectrum, temperature, and angle.
Qualifies the ICL for solvent, thermal, plasma/sputter, optical, resistance, delamination, and diffusion protection using witness and depth-resolved structures.
Uses module segmentation/interconnect design plus EL/PL/LBIC/thermal/voltage maps and coupled MPP, climate, shading, and reverse-bias stresses.
Defines rejection limits for local mismatch, hotspot temperature, reverse voltage, ICL nonuniformity, and propagation of damage rather than relying on average PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Distributed bypass diodes, current-limiting interconnects, smaller stripe segmentation, or other reverse-bias protection architectures
Hyperspectral PL, luminescence tomography, or two-color photocurrent mapping as local subcell-mismatch diagnostics
IEC 61215-derived sequences augmented with tandem-specific spectral mismatch and reverse-bias testing
Digital-twin or probabilistic yield models that translate spatial process distributions into hotspot and lifetime risk
common_wrong_answers: Optimizing only the globally current-matched champion cell under one AM1.5G spectrum
Assuming encapsulation alone prevents reverse-bias or hotspot damage
Testing the ICL only by initial tandem efficiency and omitting solvent resistance, metal diffusion, local resistance, and shading stress

expected_answer: The observations are compatible with several coupled mechanisms and therefore cannot, by themselves, establish which one is causal. A minimal matrix should include an untreated control, a molecule with comparable near-UV optical density but negligible Pb-binding ability, a Pb-binding ligand with little absorption at the aging wavelength, and the dual-function additive; loading and film thickness should be adjusted so that optical attenuation and ligand concentration can be compared independently. Chemical passivation should be evaluated before UV aging under excitation that the additive does not appreciably absorb. It is supported by direct coordination evidence, reduced deep-trap signatures, higher quasi-Fermi-level splitting or electroluminescence efficiency, a lower ideality factor or light-intensity slope, and lower trap density without requiring a change in incident UV dose. Optical protection should be tested by measuring the transmitted and absorbed UV flux, using an external optical filter or placing the absorber on the illumination side without chemical contact, illuminating from opposite sides, and comparing wavelengths inside and outside the additive absorption band at matched absorbed photon flux and temperature. A benefit that follows spectral overlap and can be reproduced by an external layer, while initial electronic defect metrics remain unchanged, indicates optical screening or conversion. Phase or crystallization stabilization requires operando or time-resolved GIWAXS/XRD during film formation and during thermal or light stress, ideally with matched UV dose. Earlier formation or longer retention of the photoactive phase, altered nucleation kinetics, reduced strain, or a changed phase-transition endpoint that persists when optical filtering is removed supports a thermodynamic or kinetic structural contribution. Metallic-Pb XPS after aging is an important outcome but is not diagnostic by itself, because less Pb0 can result from fewer reactive Pb defects, fewer absorbed UV photons, or a more stable lattice. A credible conclusion therefore assigns relative contributions only when the optical, chemical, electronic, and structural signatures are mutually consistent across the orthogonal controls.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that the reported optical, electronic, structural, and Pb0-aging observations are mechanistically non-unique and may arise from coupled effects.
Uses orthogonal controls that independently vary UV absorption and Pb coordination, including untreated, optical-only, ligand-only, and dual-function cases.
Defines discriminating optical tests such as matched absorbed photon flux, wavelength dependence, illumination geometry, or an external-filter control.
Defines independent passivation and phase-stability signatures using direct coordination/deep-trap diagnostics and operando structural or crystallization measurements.
accepted_equivalents: A nonabsorbing chelator and a nonchelating chromophore may be implemented as close structural analogues, externally deposited layers, or otherwise well-matched controls.

Quasi-Fermi-level splitting, absolute PLQY, EQEEL, thermal-admittance spectroscopy, deep-level spectroscopy, or credible trap-sensitive alternatives may replace specific named recombination measurements.
Operando GIWAXS, temperature-dependent XRD, calorimetry, strain-resolved diffraction, or another phase-sensitive kinetic method is acceptable for testing structural stabilization.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all improvement to Pb passivation solely because PL and TRPL increase.
Calling reduced metallic Pb after UV aging proof of chemical stabilization without measuring the UV dose absorbed by the perovskite.
Using additives at unmatched optical density or concentration and then comparing aging directly.
Treating a larger grain size or weaker secondary-phase peak as sufficient evidence of thermodynamic phase stabilization without kinetic or stress-dependent controls.

expected_answer: Comparable PLQY establishes that both molecules can emit efficiently, but it does not show that emitted photons reach the absorber, that the spectral conversion produces a useful current gain, or that either molecule forms a favorable electronic contact. The control set should vary photophysics and interface chemistry independently. Useful controls include an emissive analogue lacking the coordinating group, a nonemissive or weakly emissive analogue retaining the same coordinating group and dipole, an external optical layer containing the emitter but not contacting the buried interface, and interface molecules with similar absorption/PLQY but different dipole moments or energy levels. Optical conversion is supported if the benefit follows excitation wavelengths absorbed by the emitter, can be reproduced by an external optical layer, produces a measurable photon-balance or short-wavelength EQE gain, and largely disappears under visible-only stress while dark electronic defect metrics remain unchanged. Chemical passivation requires interface-specific evidence such as core-level or vibrational shifts of the coordinating group, reduced Pb- or iodide-vacancy trap signatures, higher quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and lower trap-assisted recombination even under excitation outside the emitter absorption band. Electrostatic or band-alignment control is identified by UPS/KPFM or contact-potential changes, improved selective extraction and reduced interfacial charge accumulation, and a response that correlates with molecular dipole or energy levels rather than PLQY. Crystallization and void suppression should be resolved by in situ GIWAXS or optical crystallization kinetics, peel-off cross-sectional imaging, and spatial luminescence or composition mapping; it is supported when early conversion kinetics and buried morphology change before device operation. Molecule A can therefore outperform molecule B despite similar PLQY because its coordination geometry, local electrostatic field, energy alignment, and film-growth consequences are more favorable. A strong conclusion requires that the chemical, energetic, morphological, and optical controls converge rather than using PLQY as a universal descriptor.
scoring_key_points: Explains that near-unity PLQY is a photophysical property and does not by itself prove interfacial passivation, useful photon conversion, or favorable contact energetics.
Uses controls that independently vary emission, coordinating functionality, molecular dipole/energy level, and physical location at or away from the interface.
Defines wavelength-resolved and external-layer signatures that would specifically support optical conversion rather than chemical interface effects.
Separates coordination, band alignment, and crystallization/void mechanisms using direct chemical, energetic, trap, kinetic, and buried-morphology measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Absolute external quantum efficiency, spectral responsivity, integrating-sphere photon balance, or wavelength-dependent stability may be used to test the optical contribution.
XPS/FTIR, solid-state NMR, ToF-SIMS-supported coordination analysis, or another direct chemical-interaction probe is acceptable.
Cross-sectional SEM after delamination, tomography, confocal PL of the peeled interface, or another credible buried-void mapping method may be used.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that molecule A works because its PLQY is near unity even though molecule B has comparable PLQY.
Using only steady-state PL from the complete film to claim both down-conversion and defect passivation.
Ignoring that an unfavorable conduction-band offset or molecular dipole can negate otherwise good photophysics.
Assigning improved crystallization from final XRD alone without resolving conversion kinetics or buried-interface morphology.

expected_answer: The primary requirement is a factorial comparison in which the buried-interface treatment, hole-transport material, electrode or contact stack, and encapsulation are varied independently rather than changing several at once. At minimum, treated and untreated cells and modules should be fabricated with the identical champion stack and with the identical stability stack, each in encapsulated and unencapsulated form where safe and meaningful. Replicates should be aged under controlled MPP with measured device temperature and equal incident and absorbed photon dose. Spectral stress should include UV-rich illumination, UV-filtered or visible-only illumination, and a matched external fluorescent/UV-absorbing layer that provides optical protection without contacting the interface. If the buried treatment remains beneficial under visible-only, thermal, or bias stress and is accompanied by persistent reductions in trap-assisted recombination or interfacial void evolution, the evidence favors chemical/electronic stabilization. If the advantage scales strongly with spectral overlap, is reproduced by the external optical layer, and vanishes when UV is removed while interface electronic metrics are unchanged, optical protection is dominant. Scale-up qualification must map treatment coverage and interface quality across the module using spatial PL or electroluminescence, light-beam-induced current or photocurrent mapping, KPFM/work-function sampling, thermography, and subcell or scribe-resolved electrical analysis. Nonuniform coating can create local shunts, series-resistance losses, or hot spots that average small-area measurements miss. Stability should be reported with aperture area, module geometry, bypass or interconnect details, and identical ISOS-style conditions, followed by post-mortem mapping of traps, delamination, voids, phase change, and contact degradation. The claim is attributable to the treatment only if the effect survives stack-matched controls, is statistically reproducible over module area, and has a mechanism-specific spectral and post-mortem signature.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial, stack-matched design that independently controls the interface treatment, HTL/contact stack, and encapsulation in both cells and modules.
Controls spectral dose and temperature and includes UV-rich, UV-filtered/visible-only, and external-optical-layer comparisons to separate optical from chemical protection.
Requires spatial module diagnostics for coverage, local recombination, current collection, interconnect losses, and hot spots rather than relying only on total-area J-V data.
Defines attribution criteria based on reproducible MPP durability plus mechanism-consistent electronic and post-mortem evidence under documented module conditions.
accepted_equivalents: A split-module design or matched module coupon array may replace a full factorial module set if processing and illumination are demonstrably equivalent.
EL, PL, LBIC, lock-in thermography, spatially resolved impedance, or equivalent mapping techniques are acceptable spatial diagnostics.
Visible-light MPP, dark-bias thermal aging, or wavelength-selective accelerated tests may be used to probe non-optical stabilization.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing a treated encapsulated stability device with an untreated unencapsulated champion-stack device.
Attributing module stability to the emitter while changing the HTL, electrode, and encapsulation simultaneously.
Using only average module PCE retention without checking local coating defects, interconnects, or hot spots.
Calling the effect down-conversion solely because the molecule fluoresces, without wavelength-dependent or external-layer controls.

expected_answer: The experiment must observe the film during formation rather than infer causality from the completed device. A suitable molecular series contains an anchor-only control that interacts with the oxide but weakly with the perovskite, a head-group control that can interact with the perovskite but lacks robust oxide anchoring, the full bidirectional molecule, and an untreated substrate. Surface coverage, solvent, ionic strength, and wetting should be matched as closely as possible. In situ GIWAXS during coating and annealing should track the first appearance, orientation distribution, conversion rate, lattice parameter, and intermediate phases. Time-resolved optical reflectance or PL can track bandgap and conversion, while films quenched at selected stages can be examined by depth-resolved GIXRD, Raman or strain mapping, cross-sectional microscopy, interface-sensitive XPS, and trap or quasi-Fermi-level measurements. If templated nucleation is primary, the full coordinator should show a different orientation distribution at the earliest detectable nuclei, before a measurable strain or trap-density divergence; reduced strain and fewer defects would emerge later as consequences of oriented, conformal growth. If strain relief is primary, a lattice-parameter or stress difference should appear at or before the orientation divergence, and an independent strain-modifying control without strong trap passivation should reproduce much of the orientation effect. If chemical passivation is primary, the earliest measurable difference should be reduced interface trap occupation or altered surface electronic states, while initial nucleation orientation and strain remain similar; crystallization and strain should diverge only later. Depth-resolved measurements are essential because a buried-interface mechanism may be diluted in bulk averages. The causal assignment should require reproducibility of the temporal ordering and should not treat a final narrow rocking curve, longer lifetime, or lower trap density as proof of which event initiated the chain.
scoring_key_points: Explains why final orientation, strain, and trap correlations cannot establish causal direction and requires observation during nucleation and growth.
Uses anchor-only, head-only, full bidirectional, and untreated controls with matched processing to isolate the two coordination directions.
Combines in situ crystallization/orientation measurements with depth-resolved strain, interface chemistry, and electronic-defect measurements at quenched stages.
States distinct temporal predictions for templating-first, strain-first, and passivation-first mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Fast GIWAXS, synchrotron XRD, electron diffraction with appropriate beam-damage controls, or another credible in situ orientation probe is acceptable.
Depth-resolved strain may be measured by angle-dependent GIXRD, Raman mapping, nanobeam diffraction, or thickness-dependent bandgap spectroscopy.
Trap passivation may be tracked by transient PL/QFLS, surface photovoltage, deep-level spectroscopy, or quenched-stage SCLC devices if temporal resolution is justified.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that reduced strain causes orientation merely because both are observed in the final film.
Using only final SEM grain size and XRD intensity to infer the first event in crystallization.
Comparing molecules with different coverage or wetting without controlling those variables.
Relying on bulk-averaged measurements that cannot resolve a buried-interface gradient.

expected_answer: TRPL on a perovskite/contact stack measures an effective decay that contains both recombination and charge-transfer or extraction channels. A well-coupled hole-selective contact can shorten PL decay because carriers leave the perovskite rapidly; if aging blocks transfer, delaminates the contact, or converts part of the interface into an insulating wide-bandgap material, the remaining carriers can emit for longer even while the solar cell performs worse. Spatially averaged TRPL can also be dominated by intact, poorly extracted regions while small pinholes create local perovskite/metal shunts that lower Voc and shunt resistance. The first diagnostic is to compare the aged and fresh perovskite without the HTL, the perovskite with the HTL, and complete devices. Absolute PLQY or calibrated quasi-Fermi-level splitting on the bare absorber should increase and independent trap measurements should improve if genuine passivation occurred. In contrast, a lifetime increase only after adding the aged contact, accompanied by reduced photocurrent extraction, carrier accumulation in transient absorption, slower transient photocurrent, or a larger interfacial transfer resistance indicates blocked extraction. Spectrally resolved PL and absorption/XPS/XRD can test for a new wide-bandgap or decomposition product; such a product may suppress transfer and shift or add emission without reducing the underlying defect density. Cross-sectional and plan-view microscopy, conductive AFM, PL/EL mapping, and contact-adhesion measurements should correlate long-lived regions with delamination or transport-layer rupture and correlate dark or shunted regions with pinholes. Genuine passivation should raise quasi-Fermi-level splitting and Voc, reduce trap-assisted recombination, and preserve or improve extraction and resistance. Extraction blockage should lengthen PL while reducing charge-transfer yield and fill factor or increasing series resistance, whereas pinhole-mediated shunting should reduce shunt resistance and create localized nonradiative or metal-contact pathways. Only this combined evidence can interpret the paradoxical lifetime increase.
scoring_key_points: States that TRPL in a contact stack convolves recombination with carrier extraction, so blocked extraction can lengthen PL while device performance worsens.
Separates bare-perovskite, perovskite/HTL, and complete-device measurements and requires absolute PLQY/QFLS or independent trap diagnostics for genuine passivation.
Uses charge-transfer and electrical measurements to identify extraction barriers, carrier accumulation, series-resistance growth, or shunting.
Correlates spatial optical signals with microscopy or conductive mapping and considers wide-bandgap interfacial products and HTL rupture as alternative causes.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz spectroscopy, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, or impedance may be used to assess extraction and carrier accumulation.
Conductive AFM, electron-beam-induced current, lock-in thermography, cross-sectional tomography, or other spatially resolved contact diagnostics are acceptable.
Quasi-Fermi-level splitting may be inferred from absolute PLQY or electroluminescence under appropriate calibration.
common_wrong_answers: Equating a longer TRPL lifetime with lower defect density in every device geometry.
Ignoring the fact that efficient selective-contact extraction can shorten PL decay.
Explaining the Voc and fill-factor loss only by bulk degradation while disregarding HTL pinholes and delamination.
Using a single spatially averaged TRPL trace without morphology, charge-transfer, or electrical measurements.

expected_answer: Contact angle and initial coverage are not sufficient because a hydrophilic surface can spread the SAM solution uniformly without creating a durable chemical bond. The experiment should generate surfaces in which wettability and reactive hydroxyl density are decoupled. For example, one control can be made hydrophilic with a physically adsorbed or nonreactive polar layer while oxide hydroxyls are blocked or capped; another can retain reactive surface hydroxyls while its macroscopic wetting is adjusted through processing. The same surface series should be coated with the normal phosphonic-acid molecule and with a close analogue whose phosphonic acid is ester-protected or otherwise unable to condense to P-O-Sn but has similar size, dipole, and solution wetting. Initial uptake and post-DMF-wash retention should be quantified separately using XPS P/Sn ratios, ellipsometry, radiolabeling, quartz-crystal methods, or ToF-SIMS. Direct or near-direct bond evidence can come from isotope-labeled surface hydroxyl oxygen followed by ToF-SIMS or solid-state NMR, characteristic vibrational changes, angle-resolved XPS, or another method that distinguishes a bridging P-O-Sn species from physisorbed phosphonate. Work-function maps should be repeated after solvent challenge, not only before it. Chemical anchoring is established if durable SAM mass, phosphorus signal, and work-function uniformity track the presence of reactive oxide hydroxyls and an unprotected phosphonic-acid group, even when initial contact angle or initial coverage is matched. A hydrophilic but nonreactive surface should show good initial spreading but substantial loss after DMF, while an OH-rich reactive surface should retain the SAM. Conversely, if retention follows contact angle independent of hydroxyl reactivity and condensation capability, the covalent-bond interpretation is not supported.
scoring_key_points: Explains why contact angle and initial SAM coverage cannot distinguish wetting-assisted deposition from durable chemical anchoring.
Decouples reactive surface-OH density from macroscopic wettability using matched hydrophilic/nonreactive and OH-reactive controls.
Uses a phosphonic-acid versus condensation-disabled molecular analogue and quantifies both initial uptake and post-solvent retention.
Requires bond-specific or isotope-supported evidence and states that retention must track reactive OH plus condensable phosphonic acid, not contact angle alone.
accepted_equivalents: Surface hydroxyls may be blocked by silylation or another selective capping reaction, provided the answer addresses changes in surface energy and includes matched controls.
An isotopically labeled oxygen bridge, solid-state 31P NMR, high-resolution XPS/IR, or a chemically justified desorption-energy measurement may provide direct or near-direct bonding evidence.
A methylphosphonate, phosphonate ester, or otherwise protected anchor is acceptable as the condensation-disabled molecular control if its photophysical and wetting properties are reasonably matched.
common_wrong_answers: Using lower contact angle as proof that P-O-Sn bonds formed.
Measuring phosphorus only before DMF washing and equating greater initial adsorption with stronger bonding.
Comparing chemically unrelated SAM molecules whose different solubility or dipole prevents mechanistic interpretation.
Failing to include a hydrophilic but nonreactive surface control.

expected_answer: The interlayer should be accepted only if the initial voltage gain survives a hierarchical validation. At absorber and buried-interface level, absolute PLQY, TRPL and QFLS should be measured before and after contact formation to verify that recombination is reduced rather than transferred to another interface. At the junction level, UPS/Kelvin-probe or equivalent energetics, contact-selective PL/EL, dark-current and ideality-factor measurements should show improved alignment and selectivity without a new tunnelling barrier or shunt pathway. Ion-related behavior must be tested under controlled bias, illumination and temperature using stabilized J-V/MPP tracking, scan-rate and pre-bias protocols, transient VOC or current, and impedance or ionic-capacitance analysis; increasing hysteresis or a growing ionic time constant would indicate that the treatment has not solved the coupled recombination-stability problem. Contact reliability must also include thermal cycling, adhesion/delamination inspection, leakage mapping and morphological/chemical analysis after aging, because defective or thermally unstable molecular layers can create nonuniform coverage and local shunts. The treatment is rejected if the PLQY gain is accompanied by a persistent QFLS-VOC mismatch, increasing dark leakage, field-screening/hysteresis, interlayer desorption or redistribution, loss of contact selectivity, or poor stabilized MPP retention even when the initial reverse-scan PCE remains high.
scoring_key_points: Requires absorber- and contact-resolved PLQY/QFLS measurements to verify that non-radiative recombination is actually reduced across the assembled junction.
Requires energy-alignment, carrier-selectivity, dark-current and recombination diagnostics to exclude an insulating barrier, back-transfer, or shunting.
Includes bias/light/temperature-dependent ionic and hysteresis testing under stabilized operation rather than relying on a single J-V scan.
Includes thermal/mechanical contact reliability and explicit rejection criteria based on leakage, QFLS-VOC mismatch, ionic instability, or poor MPP retention.
accepted_equivalents: Stabilized power output, stabilized current-voltage operation, or maximum-power-point tracking are acceptable operational tests.
Ion-migration diagnostics may include transient ion-drift, temperature-dependent impedance, capacitance-frequency analysis, or spatial ion profiling after bias stress.
Contact reliability may be expressed through adhesion, coverage uniformity, molecular desorption, chemical interdiffusion, or shunt-resistance retention.
common_wrong_answers: Accepting the interlayer solely because initial VOC, PLQY, or reverse-scan PCE improves.
Treating hysteresis as an irrelevant measurement artifact rather than a warning of ionic field redistribution or interfacial charging.
Testing only the bare film and not the completed contact stack.
Using shelf storage alone while omitting heat, illumination, electrical bias, leakage and stabilized MPP operation.

expected_answer: The two PL results probe different processes. In the bare film, stronger PL and a longer lifetime indicate that the treatment passivates non-radiative surface defects, for example under-coordinated lead sites. Once PCBM is added, stronger quenching can be beneficial because the surface Fermi-level shift toward the conduction band creates n-type band bending and removes or reduces the electron-extraction barrier at the CsPbI3/PCBM junction. Carriers that would radiatively recombine in the bare film are then rapidly transferred into PCBM, so quenching in the bilayer is consistent with improved extraction rather than renewed trap loss. Surface-confined chemical signals support a local electronic junction modification rather than homogeneous bulk doping. A successful treatment should therefore increase VOC through lower non-radiative recombination, increase fill factor through reduced extraction resistance and improved selectivity, lower dark leakage/current, lower the light-intensity-derived ideality factor, increase built-in potential, and reduce scan-direction hysteresis by weakening interfacial charge accumulation and recombination. These predictions should be checked together; PL quenching alone is not sufficient because it can also arise from interfacial traps.
scoring_key_points: Interprets stronger bare-film PL and longer lifetime as surface-defect passivation and reduced non-radiative recombination.
Interprets stronger PL quenching in the CsPbI3/PCBM stack as faster electron extraction enabled by surface n-type band bending and improved conduction-band alignment.
Uses surface-confined depth profiles to distinguish a local junction modification from bulk doping.
Predicts higher VOC/FF/built-in potential and lower dark current/ideality factor/hysteresis, while noting that PL quenching alone is not uniquely diagnostic.
accepted_equivalents: The Fermi-level movement may be described as upward band bending, a p-to-n surface transition, or formation of an electron-selective surface region.
Lower ideality factor may be described as reduced trap-assisted or interface-mediated recombination.
Higher built-in potential may be described as a stronger junction field or improved charge-separation driving force.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the bare-film PL enhancement and bilayer PL quenching contradictory measurements.
Assuming every instance of PL quenching proves defect passivation rather than distinguishing extraction from recombination.
Inferring homogeneous bulk doping despite the surface-confined depth profile.
Predicting higher dark current or lower fill factor for an interface whose extraction barrier and recombination are both reduced.

expected_answer: Because the wet thickness is initially uniform, the dominant defect most likely develops during drying rather than during meniscus formation or fluid delivery. Faster edge evaporation, stronger edge gas exchange, or a lateral temperature gradient raises supersaturation earlier at the perimeter, causing a dense nucleation burst and rapid formation of a continuous fine-grained film. The center loses solvent more slowly and remains in a coordinated Pb2+-solvent intermediate. If that intermediate persists nonuniformly and converts only during later annealing, nucleation density is lower, growth continues for longer, and isolated large grains leave uncovered regions or pinholes. The intermediate itself is not intrinsically harmful; the problem is spatially nonuniform formation and conversion. A hydrodynamic origin would instead appear as a nonuniform wet-film thickness, ribbing, dewetting or meniscus instability before crystallization. Discrimination requires spatially resolved wet-thickness/meniscus imaging, thermography and local evaporation or solvent-content mapping, combined with time-resolved spatial GIWAXS, optical scattering/reflectance or spectroscopy to follow intermediate and perovskite phases. Corrective variables include gas-flow or vacuum-field uniformity, substrate temperature, coating speed, solvent/additive coordination and the timing between coating, quenching and annealing.
scoring_key_points: Explains edge-first crystallization by faster local solvent removal or heating, earlier supersaturation and a higher nucleation density.
Explains center pinholes by delayed, spatially nonuniform intermediate retention/conversion, lower nucleation density and prolonged growth into sparse large grains.
Distinguishes drying/crystallization kinetics from coating hydrodynamics by using the stated initially uniform wet thickness and identifying hydrodynamic signatures.
Proposes spatially and temporally resolved thickness/flow, temperature/solvent and phase-evolution measurements, with relevant process-control variables.
accepted_equivalents: Edge effects may be described as enhanced convective mass transfer, contact-line evaporation, gas-boundary-layer differences, or lateral thermal gradients.
Time-resolved phase tracking may use GIWAXS, XRD, optical interferometry, Raman/IR, absorption, photoluminescence or another spatially resolved in situ method.
A retained intermediate may be described as a solvent adduct, Lewis-base-Pb2+ complex, or precursor coordination phase.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the center defect solely to nonuniform blade gap despite the explicitly uniform initial wet thickness.
Assuming that any intermediate phase is necessarily beneficial or necessarily detrimental independent of its spatial conversion kinetics.
Claiming that larger grains automatically imply a higher-quality film while ignoring sparse nucleation and pinholes.
Proposing only ex situ SEM, which cannot locate when the nonuniformity first develops.

expected_answer: A work-function decrease can contain two physically distinct contributions: a shift of the vacuum level produced by an oriented interfacial dipole, and a movement of the surface Fermi level relative to the perovskite bands caused by charge transfer or n-type band bending. A pure dipole can change the secondary-electron cutoff and therefore the work function without shifting semiconductor core levels or the valence-band onset relative to EF. Here, the approximately rigid 0.20 eV shift of perovskite core levels together with the valence-onset change supports an EF upshift or n-type band bending in addition to any molecular dipole. The larger 0.58 eV work-function change can therefore be decomposed qualitatively into an electronic band-bending component plus a vacuum-level/dipole component. Surface confinement to about 1 nm explains why the junction can be strongly modified without bulk doping, and the resulting alignment should reduce the electron barrier to C60. The most direct separation would use angle-resolved or controlled-depth XPS/UPS, ideally with gentle cluster-ion sputtering or standing-wave photoemission, to track whether core-level/band-edge shifts decay into the bulk while the vacuum-level shift remains interfacial; depth-resolved Kelvin-probe or cross-sectional potential mapping can provide complementary evidence.
scoring_key_points: Explains that the measured work-function decrease can combine a vacuum-level shift from a molecular/interface dipole with an EF/band-edge shift from surface band bending.
Uses the core-level and valence-onset shifts relative to EF as evidence for n-type surface band bending, which a pure dipole would not produce.
Uses the approximately 1 nm confinement to distinguish a surface electronic junction from homogeneous bulk doping and links it to the near-zero C60 electron barrier.
Proposes angle- or depth-resolved photoemission/potential profiling to separate the spatial decay of band bending from the interfacial dipole.
accepted_equivalents: N-type band bending may be described as an upward Fermi-level shift, downward band bending in electron-energy convention, or surface electron accumulation.
Depth-resolved methods may include angle-resolved XPS, GCIB-XPS/UPS, standing-wave photoemission, hard-X-ray photoemission, or cross-sectional Kelvin-probe mapping.
The work-function dipole term may be described as a vacuum-level offset or interface dipole.
common_wrong_answers: Treating the entire work-function change as proof of bulk n-type doping.
Claiming that a pure interface dipole must rigidly shift all perovskite core levels relative to the Fermi level.
Ignoring the depth confinement and describing the effect as uniform throughout the absorber.
Using only conventional XRD to distinguish a vacuum-level dipole from electronic band bending.

expected_answer: Chemically, annealing should remove or cleave the halogen-containing part while retaining an intact organic cation framework that binds to the perovskite; controls must exclude simple vacuum desorption, ligand destruction and perovskite decomposition. The residual layer should be approximately monolayer-scale and surface-confined, with no evidence for a thick insulating film or conversion of a substantial absorber volume into a low-dimensional phase. Thermally, the activation window must be high enough to drive anchoring but below the temperature that damages the absorber, substrate or adjacent contact, and it should be tolerant to realistic process-time variations. Electronically, core-level/band-edge and work-function measurements should show useful surface n-type character and a near-zero electron-extraction barrier to C60 without excessive dipole or tunnelling resistance. Device acceptance requires recovery or improvement of JSC and fill factor together with VOC, reduced hysteresis, low dark leakage and stable maximum-power output. Stability testing must compare sub-activated, optimally activated and over-annealed controls under one-sun MPP, heat and storage. Reject the ligand if halogen is removed only by wholesale decomposition, the organic layer remains thick, the perovskite phase is altered, the electron barrier persists or reverses, JSC/FF collapse, or burn-in merely shifts to later operation.
scoring_key_points: Requires selective halogen loss/cleavage with retention and surface anchoring of the organic framework, supported by controls against vacuum loss and decomposition.
Requires a narrow thermal/process window that yields a monolayer-scale surface layer without damaging or converting the 3D perovskite.
Requires favorable work-function/band-edge alignment and a low electron barrier to C60 without a thick tunnelling barrier or excessive interface dipole.
Requires device and MPP-stability validation across under-, optimally- and over-activated controls, with explicit rejection for JSC/FF loss, burn-in or phase damage.
accepted_equivalents: Anchoring may be described as chemisorption, covalent/ionic binding, or a strongly bound surface-confined cation layer.
Preserving the 3D absorber may be demonstrated by XRD/absorption null results plus depth-resolved chemistry; direct structural imaging is advantageous but not mandatory.
Burn-in may be evaluated by stabilized power output, continuous MPP, or time-resolved photocurrent/voltage under one sun.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the ligand solely because it produces the largest initial VOC increase.
Assuming that a thicker bulky-organic layer always gives better passivation and stability.
Interpreting disappearance of the halogen signal as sufficient proof of controlled anchoring without checking organic-framework retention or perovskite damage.
Claiming long-term durability from a short initial stabilized-power trace while omitting heat and over-annealing controls.

expected_answer: The fast process is the formation of sparse, iodide-rich terminal domains near the illuminated surface or extraction interface. Their lower bandgap produces the red-shifted PL shoulder and makes them efficient carrier-funnelling sites. Even if their volume fraction is too small to measurably move the bulk absorption edge, their strategic location at the carrier-extraction surface allows them to intercept a large fraction of photocarriers, create local traps or potential barriers, and reduce collected current. The slower process is conventional iodide accumulation or compositional segregation along grain boundaries, enabled by extended ion migration; this progressively changes internal fields and increases hysteresis. The two observations therefore represent distinct spatial and temporal modes of halide migration rather than one uniform bulk phase transition. A falsifying result would be a reproducible JSC loss that remains unchanged when the surface red-shifted domains are eliminated or spatially absent, or operando mapping showing that the 1.60 eV emission originates only in the bulk and does not correlate temporally or spatially with extraction loss. Likewise, recovery of JSC without changing the terminal-domain signal would weaken the causal assignment.
scoring_key_points: Assigns the rapid red-shifted surface PL to sparse I-rich terminal domains formed on a seconds-scale.
Explains large JSC loss through low-bandgap carrier funneling, trapping or extraction barriers at a strategically located surface/interface despite a small optical volume fraction.
Assigns hour-scale grain-boundary iodide enrichment and increasing hysteresis to slower extended halide migration and ionic field redistribution.
Provides a genuine falsification criterion based on loss of temporal/spatial correlation or unchanged JSC after suppressing the proposed terminal domains.
accepted_equivalents: Terminal domains may be called sporadic I-rich islands, surface I-rich nanodomains, or low-bandgap extraction-blocking domains.
The slow mode may be described as grain-boundary segregation, iodide accumulation, or extended ionic redistribution.
Carrier loss may be described as funneling to recombination centers, interfacial trapping, local band-offset formation, or blocked extraction.
common_wrong_answers: Treating the weak red-shifted PL feature as irrelevant because it represents only a small material volume.
Assigning both the seconds-scale surface signal and hour-scale grain-boundary enrichment to one homogeneous bulk phase transition.
Claiming that the unchanged absorption edge disproves any phase segregation.
Offering a confirmatory measurement rather than a result that could actually falsify the causal hypothesis.

expected_answer: The thicker film should not be selected merely because one bulk impedance metric suggests less ionic motion. Thickness changes strain, crystallographic stacking, optical generation, transport distance and the probability of forming surface terminal domains. A strained thick film can therefore show a small average ionic response yet still create a highly damaging low-bandgap phase at the extraction interface, where it disproportionately reduces JSC. The thinner film may permit more detectable ionic redistribution but maintain shorter transport paths, lower extraction resistance and fewer harmful terminal domains, giving better operational output. Optimization should co-design absorber thickness with strain management, composition/additive control, grain-boundary defect reduction and selective surface/contact passivation; tandem current matching sets the lower optical-thickness bound. Validation must combine spatially resolved operando PL or CL for terminal domains, absorption/Urbach and PLQY/QFLS for radiative and non-radiative losses, JSC/VOC/FF and stabilized MPP tracking, ionic impedance or drift measurements, and structural/strain mapping. Light, electrical bias and temperature should be varied independently and jointly. The winning design is the one with stable current-matched MPP and suppressed harmful interfacial domains, not necessarily the lowest apparent ion mobility.
scoring_key_points: Rejects optimization by a single bulk ion-migration metric and explains why a small average ionic response can coexist with harmful surface terminal domains.
Balances optical current generation/current matching against strain, transport distance, extraction resistance and terminal-domain formation when selecting thickness.
Co-designs thickness with strain/composition, grain-boundary and interface/contact engineering rather than treating thickness as an isolated variable.
Proposes operando spatial phase mapping, recombination/energetic diagnostics, ionic measurements and stabilized MPP aging with light/bias/temperature decoupling.
accepted_equivalents: Bulk ionic response may be measured by impedance, transient ion drift, capacitance, conductivity or another migration proxy.
Terminal-domain mapping may use operando PL, cathodoluminescence, hyperspectral imaging, nanoscale X-ray methods or another spatially resolved composition-sensitive technique.
Current matching may be expressed as maintaining the required tandem top-cell photocurrent while minimizing transport and stability penalties.
common_wrong_answers: Automatically choosing the thick film because it has the smaller impedance-derived ionic response.
Automatically choosing the thinnest film without considering tandem current matching and optical absorption.
Using only ex situ composition maps or only transient J-V scans instead of operando stabilized testing.
Assuming that all halide migration affects VOC and JSC through the same pathway and spatial location.

expected_answer:
J-V hysteresis is a kinetic convolution of electronic extraction, recombination, interfacial capacitance, mobile ionic charge, trap filling, and the measurement history. Nearly overlapping forward and reverse scans at one speed can occur because the scan is much slower than all relevant relaxations, because it is too fast for ions to respond, because prebias has placed both scans in similar states, or because capacitive currents happen to compensate the underlying losses. Faster PL decay and higher contact conductivity support faster electron transfer, but a shorter optical lifetime can also indicate interfacial non-radiative recombination. Neither observation proves the absence of mobile ions.

The first requirement is a complete history-dependent J-V matrix. Forward and reverse scans should be acquired over several orders of magnitude in scan rate, with controlled start voltage, dwell time, light-soaking time, dark rest, and positive and negative prebias. The delay time per voltage step must be long enough to test convergence rather than chosen to minimize visible hysteresis. The device should also be held at the maximum-power point and at selected fixed voltages until the current stabilizes. A genuinely low-hysteresis device should give the same stabilized power and nearly the same steady-state current regardless of scan direction and reasonable preconditioning; an apparent overlap that disappears when scan rate or prebias changes is dynamic masking.

The second requirement is to separate ionic and electronic time constants. Transient photocurrent, transient photovoltage, intensity-modulated photocurrent/photovoltage, impedance or admittance spectroscopy, and bias-step current relaxation can identify fast extraction and slower capacitive or ionic modes. Low-frequency capacitance, temperature-dependent relaxation, and activation-energy analysis can reveal mobile-ion redistribution even when J-V curves overlap. Kelvin-probe or photovoltage mapping after opposite biases, time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry after bias stress, or reversible contact-potential changes can provide spatial evidence of ionic accumulation. A device may be operationally hysteresis-free over a useful timescale while still containing mobile ions; the claim should be phrased accordingly.

The third requirement is to verify that the fullerene layer improves selective extraction rather than adding quenching sites. Absolute PLQY and TRPL should be compared for perovskite on an inert substrate, on the fullerene layer, and on the control contact under matched optical conditions. Productive extraction should create a fast decay component only with an extracting contact and should be accompanied by faster photocurrent rise, lower transfer resistance, higher EQE or collection efficiency, and no loss of quasi-Fermi-level splitting or open-circuit voltage. If PL is quenched while QFLS, Voc, or electroluminescence efficiency falls, the contact is introducing non-radiative loss rather than useful extraction.

The mechanistic conclusion is defensible when three signatures coincide: electronic extraction is faster and more balanced between the two contacts; slow ionic/capacitive relaxation has a smaller amplitude or weaker coupling to the internal field and recombination; and stabilized MPP output is independent of scan history. Structural or chemical evidence may show that the contact passivates surface traps or blocks ion accumulation, but complete elimination of ion migration requires direct ionic measurements. The scientifically precise conclusion may therefore be that the inverted architecture suppresses measurable hysteresis by reducing carrier accumulation and recombination under the tested operating conditions, not that the absorber contains no mobile ions.
scoring_key_points: Explains that one forward/reverse scan and fast PL decay are kinetically ambiguous and do not prove absence of ion migration.
Requires scan-rate, step-delay, prebias, light-soaking, rest, and stabilized-MPP measurements that test history independence and convergence.
Separates fast electronic extraction from slow ionic/capacitive modes using transient, impedance/admittance, temperature, or spatial ion/potential diagnostics.
Accepts the mechanism only when selective extraction, preserved QFLS/Voc, reduced slow relaxation, and history-independent stabilized output are mutually consistent.
accepted_equivalents: Bias-stress recovery, open-circuit voltage relaxation, charge extraction by linearly increasing voltage, or transient ion-drift measurements may replace some impedance diagnostics.
KPFM, surface photovoltage, electroabsorption, or bias-dependent photoluminescence mapping may be used to detect field redistribution.
ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, thermal admittance, or activation-energy analysis are acceptable evidence for mobile-ion motion.
Steady-state current at fixed voltage or long-duration maximum-power tracking is equivalent to a stabilized power measurement.
Operationally hysteresis-free, negligible hysteresis over a specified timescale, or weak coupling of ion redistribution to recombination are acceptable bounded conclusions.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring the device ion-migration-free because forward and reverse scans overlap at a single scan rate.
Treating shorter TRPL lifetime as unambiguous proof of better extraction.
Comparing scans without controlling start voltage, prebias, illumination history, or dwell time.
Using only a hysteresis index from non-stabilized curves and omitting maximum-power-point tracking.
Assuming a more conductive electron layer automatically balances hole and electron flux without testing both contacts.

expected_answer:
The claim has two separable components: a technology-specific scale effect and a location-specific cost effect. The technology-specific component is the weaker diseconomy of small scale expected for coating, printing, and lower-temperature module assembly relative to purified-wafer and cell manufacturing. The location component includes labour, tariffs, logistics, energy price, financing, taxes, and local demand. A valid analysis must separate these contributions and compare equivalent products at equivalent factory gates and quality levels.

The first step is to define boundaries. Perovskite and silicon options must include the same functional output: a saleable, warranted module at a specified efficiency, area, degradation rate, and lifetime. Imported inputs, depreciation, working capital, yield loss, quality control, encapsulation, frame, junction box, waste treatment, recycling obligations, and distribution must be included consistently. If the perovskite case begins with coated glass while the silicon case begins with polysilicon, or if one includes module assembly and the other includes cell production, the scale comparison is not causal. Separate scenarios should therefore be reported for local module assembly, local cell fabrication with imported specialty materials, and deeper upstream integration.

The cost model should decompose cost per watt into annualized capital cost, fixed labour and overhead, variable materials and utilities, maintenance, scrap, financing, and logistics. Capacity utilization, line yield, module efficiency, and downtime convert nameplate capacity into saleable watts and are often more important than nominal factory size. The scale exponent or learning curve for each unit operation should be estimated from analogous coating and PV manufacturing data, with uncertainty ranges rather than a single curve. Technology-specific advantage exists only if the perovskite route retains a lower break-even capacity after labour, tariff, and finance assumptions are set equal.

Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis should be global rather than one-variable-at-a-time. Monte Carlo or probabilistic sensitivity analysis should vary yield ramp, utilization, efficiency, lifetime, degradation, cost of capital, exchange rate, imported-material fraction, tariff policy, energy price, labour productivity, environmental compliance, and recycling cost. Break-even capacity and probability of cost competitiveness should be reported, along with tornado or variance-decomposition results identifying the dominant drivers. Correlated uncertainties matter: a low-volume factory may simultaneously have lower yield, higher material purchasing cost, and higher financing risk.

Counterfactuals should include importing finished silicon modules, importing silicon cells for local module assembly, importing perovskite subcomponents, regional rather than national manufacturing, and a local perovskite pilot that shares infrastructure with other coated products. Demand should be treated as bankable annual offtake, not merely national electricity need. Scenarios should test whether the factory can maintain utilization under seasonal demand, policy change, and module price decline. Cost per watt should be complemented by levelized cost of electricity or present value per delivered kilowatt-hour so that shorter lifetime or faster degradation cannot be hidden by low factory cost.

A defensible conclusion would state the region of parameter space in which local perovskite production is competitive, the probability of that outcome, and the variables requiring pilot evidence. If competitiveness disappears when lifetime, yield, financing, and imported inputs are treated realistically, the result is an optimistic scenario rather than a demonstrated technology advantage. If the lower break-even capacity persists under matched location assumptions and equal product requirements, then the small-scale process architecture is the causal advantage.
scoring_key_points: Separates technology-specific economies of scale from country-specific labour, tariff, logistics, demand, and finance assumptions and requires matched factory/product boundaries.
Builds cost per saleable watt from capex, fixed and variable costs, utilization, yield, efficiency, imported inputs, compliance, and financing rather than nameplate capacity alone.
Uses probabilistic/global sensitivity analysis including lifetime and degradation, correlated uncertainties, and reports break-even distributions and dominant drivers.
Tests counterfactual local-assembly/import/regional options and accepts a true perovskite scale advantage only if it persists under equalized location assumptions and equivalent warranted output.
accepted_equivalents: Monte Carlo simulation, Latin hypercube sampling, Bayesian uncertainty propagation, or scenario ensembles are acceptable uncertainty methods.
Sobol indices, variance decomposition, probabilistic tornado plots, or elasticity analysis may identify key drivers.
Cost per warranted watt, levelized module cost, LCOE, or present cost per delivered lifetime energy are acceptable normalized outputs if boundaries are explicit.
