Local module assembly, local coating with imported specialty materials, regional hub manufacturing, and finished-module import are acceptable counterfactuals.
A matched-gate or cradle-to-gate comparison is acceptable provided both technologies have equivalent scope and product quality.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the lower break-even capacity entirely to cheap labour or avoided tariffs.
Comparing a perovskite module-assembly plant with an integrated silicon wafer-to-module factory.
Using national electricity demand as if it were guaranteed factory offtake and utilization.
Reporting only module manufacturing cost while ignoring yield ramp, lifetime, degradation, financing, compliance, and imported material exposure.
Presenting a single deterministic threshold without uncertainty, counterfactuals, or sensitivity to correlated risks.

expected_answer:
Lifetime is not an intrinsic quality label; it is the decay time of a population under a specific boundary condition. In a bare or electronically blocking perovskite film, a longer PL lifetime can indicate fewer non-radiative recombination centres. In a perovskite/contact stack, a shorter PL lifetime can indicate productive charge transfer out of the emissive layer, but it can also indicate additional interface recombination. Conversely, an extremely long PL decay in an aged contacted stack may arise because the contact no longer extracts carriers, leaving a weak, isolated population to recombine slowly. TPC and TPV also measure different processes: TPC is dominated by collection and circuit extraction, whereas TPV at open circuit reflects recombination and capacitance. Their times should not be compared as if they were the same lifetime.

The fresh-device data therefore describe a mixed electronic picture rather than universal superiority. Faster TPC and a longer TPV decay for the alloy are consistent with lower transport resistance and slower open-circuit recombination in that specific device. However, lower Jsc and a higher trap density indicate that some carriers are still lost or that the contact/transport layer has injection, optical, coverage, or trap limitations. The result can be internally consistent if the alloy contact is chemically benign and has good macroscopic extraction while the underlying electron-contact stack contains more traps or less favourable optical/electrical coupling than Cu. It is also possible that the SCLC trap estimate is affected by injection barriers; this must be checked rather than ignored.

The decision tree begins with matched optical controls. Absolute PLQY and TRPL should be measured on bare perovskite, perovskite/electron-transport layer, and complete perovskite/electron-transport/electrode stacks with identical thickness, excitation direction, and optical interference. A contact-induced shorter lifetime is productive only if it coincides with an increased extracted charge, faster photocurrent, preserved or higher QFLS/Voc, and no increase in non-radiative voltage loss. If PL shortens while Voc, PLQY, or electroluminescence efficiency decreases, interface recombination is more likely.

The next branch tests transport and trapping. TPC, charge extraction, impedance, frequency-dependent capacitance, dark J-V, temperature-dependent contact resistance, EQE, and mobility/trap measurements with more than one electrode geometry should be combined. A genuine extraction advantage gives shorter TPC, lower transport/contact resistance, higher collection efficiency, and little dependence on injection electrode. A trap-rich or injection-limited stack may show an apparent SCLC threshold shift, dispersive transients, light-intensity dependence, and lower EQE or Jsc. Optical reflectance and parasitic absorption should be measured because a different metal/alloy morphology can change Jsc without changing carrier physics.

Aging interpretation requires time-matched post-mortem evidence. If Cu develops a huge TRPL lifetime while TPC slows, series/contact resistance rises, EQE and device current collapse, and the electron-transport/electrode interface shows cracks, corrosion, iodide reaction, or metal diffusion, the long PL is evidence of blocked extraction, not improved passivation. Spatial PL may increase or persist because carriers are no longer quenched by the contact. Chemical depth profiling, XPS after iodide exposure, ToF-SIMS, microscopy, and adhesion measurements should identify whether the electrode, buffer layer, or perovskite has changed. Recovery after removing or replacing the electrode is a powerful causal test.

The final assignment should be conditional: fresh alloy devices may combine acceptable extraction and slower recombination with residual trap/Jsc penalties; their primary advantage may be chemical and processing stability. Cu can quench PL rapidly when fresh but become an electronically blocking, corroded contact when aged. No single lifetime, whether longer or shorter, establishes the mechanism without the direction of charge flow, circuit condition, QFLS, extracted charge, optical controls, and post-aging chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Explains that PL, TPC, and TPV lifetimes have stack- and boundary-condition-dependent meanings and that very long aged-stack PL can indicate blocked extraction.

Reconciles the fresh alloy data as a mixed picture—faster macroscopic extraction/slower recombination but residual Jsc, trap, injection, or optical losses—rather than universal electronic superiority.
Builds a matched-control decision tree combining PLQY/TRPL, QFLS/Voc, extracted charge, TPC/TPV, impedance, EQE, dark current, and trap/contact checks.
Uses time-matched chemical, morphological, and depth-profile evidence and electrode-removal/replacement logic to attribute aged Cu failure to corrosion, diffusion, cracks, or contact blocking.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz spectroscopy, or surface photovoltage may replace or complement PL-based extraction diagnostics.
Electrochemical impedance, intensity-modulated photocurrent/photovoltage, charge extraction, or time-of-flight methods may diagnose transport and recombination.
ToF-SIMS, XPS, XRF, cross-sectional microscopy, nano-IR, or elemental mapping are acceptable post-aging chemical methods.
Optical transfer-matrix modelling, reflectance/EQE decomposition, or integrating-sphere absorption may test electrode-induced optical Jsc losses.
Contact replacement, peel-off analysis, or a barrier-layer rescue experiment is an acceptable causal intervention.
common_wrong_answers: Calling every longer lifetime better and every shorter lifetime worse, independent of stack and circuit condition.
Interpreting the aged Cu stack's extremely long PL decay as superior passivation despite slow extraction and device failure.
Ignoring lower Jsc and higher trap density because TPC and TPV appear favourable.
Comparing TRPL values from different optical stacks without controlling thickness, excitation side, interference, or signal amplitude.
Using one SCLC trap-density value as definitive without checking injection barriers and contact dependence.

expected_answer:
A fusible electrode creates a coupled processing–service tradeoff. Its melting point must be low enough to print without damaging the perovskite, fullerene, buffer layer, substrate, or encapsulant, but high enough to remain mechanically and dimensionally stable at the highest module operating temperature. Melting point alone is insufficient because solid-state creep, phase segregation, grain-boundary diffusion, oxidation, and cyclic thermal expansion can occur well below complete melting. The selected alloy therefore needs a quantified service-temperature margin and mechanical data under sustained stress.

The process specification should define alloy composition and purity, liquidus/solidus range, viscosity and surface tension at printing temperature, oxide-skin management, wetting on the buffer layer, line-edge fidelity, thickness, porosity, adhesion, and solidification rate. Printing temperature and dwell time should remain below the damage threshold of the absorber/contact stack. The blade, mask, chuck temperature, atmosphere, and web speed should be controlled so that the alloy does not penetrate pinholes or scratch the underlying layers. Patterned module electrodes must have low sheet resistance and reliable overlap with interconnects without bridging laser scribes or producing edge beads that cause shunts.

Electronic compatibility requires a stable effective work function and a selective, low-resistance contact after solidification and aging. UPS/Kelvin probe, contact-resistance structures, dark J-V, impedance, TPC, EQE, and temperature-dependent measurements should be used. A barrier or dipolar interlayer may be required if the bare alloy work function is mismatched or composition dependent. The buffer layer must prevent metal/alloy diffusion and halide reaction while remaining pinhole-free and mechanically tolerant. The electrode should not be selected solely because one fresh transient metric is favourable; Jsc, trap density, recombination loss, and module series resistance must all meet specifications.

Chemical and mechanical stability must be engineered together. Iodide exposure and bias-assisted corrosion tests, XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiles, oxidation tests, adhesion and peel measurements, and cross-sectional microscopy should verify that alloy components do not migrate into the fullerene/perovskite and that halides do not enter the alloy. Coefficients of thermal expansion and elastic/creep behaviour should be matched or accommodated by compliant layers. If the alloy softens near normal rooftop temperatures, it may flow, delaminate, or bridge interconnects even without melting. Encapsulation must limit oxygen and moisture but should not trap corrosive volatiles at the electrode.

Validation must reproduce operation, not only storage. Modules should be run at maximum power under one-sun-equivalent illumination at elevated temperature, including a temperature near the expected field maximum but below the specified safety margin. Tests should include damp heat, thermal cycling across the alloy phase-stability range, humidity-freeze if relevant, UV exposure, mechanical flex or vibration for flexible products, reverse-bias and partial-shading stress, and sustained current through interconnects. Electroluminescence, infrared thermography, sheet resistance, contact resistance, adhesion, local thickness, and chemical depth profiles should be monitored during aging. Current crowding or local softening should appear as hot spots before average PCE fails.

Controls should include evaporated Cu or Ag with and without diffusion barriers, a higher-melting alloy, and the same fusible alloy with alternative buffer layers. Failure analysis must distinguish absorber decomposition, buffer cracking, alloy oxidation, interdiffusion, creep, and encapsulation leakage. A commercial claim requires reproducible module yield, stabilized power retention under loaded aging, no scribe bridging or electrode flow, and a quantified acceleration model. Long unencapsulated dark-storage retention is useful evidence of chemical compatibility but cannot establish certified outdoor operational durability.
scoring_key_points: Balances printability against field-temperature margin and explicitly includes solid-state creep, phase segregation, thermal expansion, adhesion, and dimensional stability below the melting point.
Specifies rheology/wetting/patterning, sheet resistance, interconnect geometry, work-function/selectivity, buffer integrity, and damage limits for module integration.
Requires chemical and mechanical diagnostics for iodide reaction, oxidation, diffusion, corrosion, softening, and interfacial failure with suitable metal/alloy and barrier controls.
Validates under loaded illumination, elevated temperature, damp heat, thermal cycling, UV, bias/shading, and module-level hot-spot/interconnect monitoring rather than shelf storage alone.
accepted_equivalents: A liquidus/solidus safety margin, homologous-temperature creep criterion, softening-point criterion, or empirically validated maximum service temperature is acceptable.
A dipolar molecule, BCP modification, oxide barrier, fullerene cross-linking, carbon interlayer, or other selective diffusion barrier is acceptable.
Screen printing, slot coating, doctor blading, or patterned transfer is acceptable if molten-alloy rheology and scribe fidelity are controlled.
ToF-SIMS, XPS, glow-discharge profiling, electron microscopy/EDS, X-ray tomography, or isotope tracing may diagnose migration and corrosion.
ISOS/IEC-style MPP aging, damp heat, thermal cycle, hot-spot, reverse-bias, and outdoor validation are acceptable qualification frameworks.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the alloy with the lowest melting point without considering rooftop temperature, creep, or scribe bridging.
Assuming iodide inertness in a short immersion test guarantees long-term biased operational stability.
Optimizing only fresh PCE and ignoring lower Jsc, trap density, work-function uncertainty, or contact resistance.
Using room-temperature dark shelf storage as the primary commercial durability proof.
Testing only isolated cells and omitting module interconnect current, thermal hot spots, pattern fidelity, adhesion, and thermal-expansion mismatch.

expected_answer: Scale-up should be treated as a coupled coating-imprinting-conversion problem, not as geometric enlargement of the small-cell recipe. A designed experiment should scan wet-film thickness, additive loading, imprint pressure, temperature, dwell time, stamp release, coating speed, organic-salt dose, drying time, humidity, and annealing profile. The process window must include fresh and deliberately aged PbI2 and organic-salt solutions because precursor aging can change viscosity, coordination, nucleation, and conversion. Inline or high-throughput maps should quantify PbI2-scaffold thickness, imprint depth, roughness, pore/array fidelity, and sheet-scale drying gradients. After conversion, spatial GIXRD/XRD or Raman mapping should measure residual PbI2 and phase uniformity; PLQY or hyperspectral PL maps should identify non-radiative regions; XRF/XPS-type compositional mapping should test I/Pb uniformity; profilometry and cross-sectional sampling should detect local thinning; and electroluminescence, dark lock-in thermography, and subcell-resolved J-V should localize shunts and series-resistance losses. Acceptance limits should be based on distribution tails, not only area averages. A useful residual-PbI2 level must be distinguished from random, connected, or deeply buried residue that becomes a degradation nucleus. Reliability qualification should include encapsulated maximum-power-point tracking under one-sun heat, and damp-heat or humidity-bias testing; thermal cycling and light-soaking with periodic EL/PL imaging are also appropriate. Shelf retention is insufficient because it does not stress ion migration, contacts, interconnects, or local Joule heating. The mechanism is considered transferred only if conversion-front uniformity, stoichiometry, shunt yield, and MPP stability remain statistically linked across multiple module lots, while the unmodified and non-imprinted controls fail in the predicted manner.
scoring_key_points: Defines a multivariable coating, imprinting, drying, and conversion process window rather than copying the small-cell recipe.
Uses spatially resolved structural, compositional, optical, and electrical maps with tail-based acceptance criteria to identify residues and shunts.
Includes fresh-versus-aged precursor controls and distinguishes benign average PbI2 from harmful local or buried residue.
Requires operational MPP plus damp-heat/thermal-cycle/light-soak qualification, not shelf storage alone.
accepted_equivalents: Meniscus, slot-die, or blade coating may be used if the same process variables and uniformity logic are addressed.
LBIC, photoluminescence imaging, or current-density mapping may complement or replace electroluminescence for spatial electrical diagnosis.
An IEC-style damp-heat or a rigorously defined ISOS operational protocol is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling pressure, additive concentration, and annealing time linearly with module area.
Judging module transfer only from average PCE or average residual-PbI2 intensity.
Assuming all residual PbI2 is either universally beneficial or universally harmful.
Citing dark shelf storage as proof of operational durability.

expected_answer: The first step is to decouple deposition rate from the variables that usually change with it. Films should be grown at several rates while independently matching substrate temperature, total thickness, source history, chamber pressure, and post-annealing; a complementary series should vary temperature at fixed rate. Organic-source behavior must be measured with residual-gas analysis or mass spectrometry, source-temperature-dependent decomposition tests, calibrated flux transients, and post-growth chemical-state/depth analysis. A correct bulk elemental ratio does not exclude loss of volatile fragments, wrong molecular incorporation, compensating off-stoichiometry, or vertical gradients. XPS, solid-state vibrational spectroscopy, and ToF-SIMS can test these possibilities. Kinetically frozen bulk defects are supported if high-rate bare films show lower absolute PLQY/QFLS, more sub-gap absorption or trap emission, and poorer mobility even on passivating substrates and after identical contacts; partial recovery after a controlled low-temperature anneal would strengthen this assignment. Interface limitation is supported if bare-film QFLS remains high but falls sharply only after contact deposition, if changing the selective contact or adding an ultrathin passivation layer restores Voc, or if surface-sensitive lifetime differs from bulk-sensitive photoconductivity. Optical artifacts must be excluded with integrating-sphere PLQY, matched absorption, roughness/scattering measurements, and thickness-normalized excitation. Smaller grains are a correlation, not a sufficient cause. Bulk XRF averages over depth and chemical state, while conventional XRD is insensitive to many point defects, amorphous fractions, surface reactions, and electronically active interfaces. The mechanism is resolved only by a coherent correlation among precursor chemistry, depth-resolved composition, bare-film QFLS, transport, and contact-specific voltage loss.
scoring_key_points: Decouples rate from substrate temperature, thickness, source history, pressure, and post-annealing using matched control series.
Tests organic precursor decomposition/incorporation with gas-phase diagnostics and chemical-state/depth-resolved analysis.
Separates bulk defects from interface recombination by comparing bare-film QFLS/transport with full-stack and passivated/contact-swapped devices.
Explains the averaging and sensitivity limits of XRF and XRD and excludes PL/scattering/thickness artifacts.
accepted_equivalents: Quadrupole mass spectrometry, FTIR of the vapor stream, or isotope tracing may substitute for residual-gas analysis.
Time-resolved microwave conductivity or optical-pump terahertz spectroscopy may substitute for bulk photoconductivity.
Absolute electroluminescence efficiency and voltage-loss analysis may substitute for direct QFLS measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that smaller grains alone prove grain-boundary recombination.
Accepting bulk XRF stoichiometry as proof that organic precursors did not decompose.
Using relative PL intensity without correcting for absorption, thickness, and scattering.
Attributing all Voc loss to an intrinsic disadvantage of vapor deposition.

expected_answer: The routes should pass common gates before economic comparison: conformal coverage on the actual texture, high-rate absorber quality, composition and thickness uniformity across production dimensions, bottom-cell preservation, module-relevant yield, uptime, material utilization, and operational stability. Co-evaporation offers one-step formation and compositional flexibility but carries the highest simultaneous-flux-control burden; organic precursor decomposition, adsorption memory, delayed reaction, and source drift can create hidden stoichiometric gradients. Sequential vapor reduces simultaneous flux coupling, but incomplete conversion, diffusion-limited reaction, volume expansion, and residual precursor can become the dominant defects. A hybrid route adds solvent, drying, and contamination risks, yet it may be preferred when a vapor inorganic scaffold provides conformality and solvent protection while a mild solution step supplies conversion completion, surface passivation, or wide-bandgap composition control that cannot yet be achieved at high vapor rate. The wet step is acceptable only if it does not attack the silicon stack, textured interface, recombination junction, or previously deposited transport layers, and if its yield and solvent-recovery burden are quantified. Before CAPEX commitment, the manufacturer needs high-rate QFLS and device distributions, in-line flux and gas-phase chemistry control, wafer/module-scale thickness-composition maps, texture-specific coverage and pinhole statistics, bottom-cell before/after diagnostics, source refill and cleaning data, run-to-run drift, material utilization, and lot-level yield. Accelerated MPP testing must be performed on devices made at target throughput. A pilot line should compare total cost per good watt, not absorber deposition cost alone, and should include downtime, consumables, environmental controls, rework, and yield sensitivity. The winning route is the one that maintains a statistically stable process window at required rate and area; it need not be the chemically purest route.
scoring_key_points: Uses common stage gates for conformality, high-rate optoelectronic quality, bottom-cell preservation, uniformity, yield, uptime, and stability.
Identifies co-evaporation flux/decomposition risk, sequential-conversion risk, and hybrid solvent/integration risk.
Explains when a hybrid route is justified by conformal vapor formation plus wet conversion/passivation benefits.
Requires pilot-line distributions and total cost per good watt, including drift, downtime, utilization, and yield before CAPEX.
accepted_equivalents: A close-space sublimation or single-source route may be added if its precursor-decomposition and composition-control risks are analyzed.
Texture coverage may be assessed by cross-sectional tomography, conformality ratios, or electrically active pinhole maps.
Cost per passing module or levelized manufacturing cost may substitute for cost per good watt.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting vapor solely because it is solvent-free or already used in CdTe/CIGS manufacturing.
Selecting the route with the highest small-area record PCE without target-rate and yield data.
Rejecting all hybrid routes as non-scalable because they contain a solution step.
Comparing only nominal deposition cost while holding industrial yield and uptime implicit.

expected_answer: Qualification should be organized by process stage and mapped over the full substrate. After substrate preparation, after epitaxial growth, after each thermal treatment, and after each contact, the program should measure orientation and mosaicity by wafer-scale XRD/GIWAXS, local strain by reciprocal-space mapping or Raman, thickness and roughness by ellipsometry/profilometry, and defect/recombination distributions by hyperspectral PLQY, lifetime, or contactless photoconductivity. Sparse cross-sectional TEM should validate interface coherence, but it cannot replace statistical mapping. Band edges and work functions should be measured at center and edge locations before and after contact deposition; test structures with alternative contacts should identify chemical reaction, sputter/evaporation damage, and extraction barriers. Thermal-expansion mismatch and perovskite phase transitions require controlled heating-cooling cycles with in-situ diffraction and optical monitoring, followed by crack, delamination, and QFLS maps. The substrate choice follows the dominant constraint. A lattice-matched rigid substrate is preferred when coherent strain can be kept within a validated beneficial window and the thermal-expansion mismatch is small. A compliant buffer is preferred when modest mismatch or contact processing would otherwise generate dislocations, provided the buffer does not introduce transport barriers or contamination. A van der Waals template is preferred when large lattice mismatch, flexible integration, or thermal-mismatch relaxation dominates, but its weaker registry and transfer/contact resistance must be quantified. The route passes only if distributions of strain, orientation, QFLS, and contact resistance remain within predefined limits after full-stack processing and thermal cycling, and if device-area scaling follows the mapped material quality. A high-quality as-grown coupon is insufficient evidence of manufacturable epitaxy.
scoring_key_points: Requires full-area, stage-by-stage maps of orientation, strain, thickness, recombination, and band alignment rather than isolated microscopy.
Tests thermal-expansion mismatch and perovskite phase transitions through in-situ thermal cycling and post-cycle integrity maps.
Qualifies contact chemistry, deposition damage, and extraction barriers with partial stacks and alternative contacts.
Provides a conditional decision rule for lattice-matched, compliant-buffer, and van der Waals templates with quantitative pass limits.
accepted_equivalents: Micro-LED, photodetector, or photovoltaic test arrays are acceptable full-stack vehicles if the same epitaxy-survival logic is applied.
Scanning XRD, synchrotron mapping, or electron backscatter-style orientation mapping may serve as the spatial crystallographic method.
Remote epitaxy or 2D interlayers may be treated as a van der Waals/compliant-template strategy.
common_wrong_answers: Using one TEM cross-section as proof of wafer-scale epitaxial uniformity.
Choosing the substrate solely from room-temperature lattice mismatch.
Ignoring phase transitions and thermal-expansion mismatch during contact processing or operation.
Assuming low trap density in the as-grown film survives chemically reactive or energetic contact deposition.

expected_answer: The transferable object is the top-to-bottom nucleation-rate asymmetry and solvent-removal trajectory, not the nominal additive concentrations. The blade process should therefore scan bottom-seed density and coverage, top-inhibitor surface concentration and residence time, wet-film thickness, coating speed, solvent activity, gas-knife or drying rate, substrate temperature, antisolvent-free extraction conditions, and annealing ramp while respecting the SAM thermal budget. Measurable descriptors should include the time difference between bottom and top nucleation onset, the velocity and direction of the crystallization front, residual-solvent concentration versus depth, final through-film grain continuity, buried-void fraction, and axial trap-density/charge-accumulation profiles. In-situ reflectance/absorption and PL across the coating width, depth-sensitive diffraction at selected process times, and post-process NMR or mass-spectrometric solvent analysis should define the process window. Seed and inhibitor distributions should be mapped to ensure that the apparent asymmetry is not merely local. Device gates should include full-area QFLS/PLQY, cross-sectional KPFM or equivalent axial potential mapping, DLCP/TAS, subcell-resolved J-V, and electroluminescence/shunt maps. A surface-treated control that receives the inhibitor only after crystallization is essential: if it improves PL but retains internal charge planes or residual solvent, the scaled process has not eliminated high-dimensional defects. Stability gates should include encapsulated damp heat and MPP light-soaking at elevated temperature, with periodic structural and spatial electrical mapping. Transfer is accepted only if the directionality descriptors and buried-defect metrics remain uniform across lots and correlate with long-term stability; matching initial PCE or surface trap density alone is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Defines nucleation asymmetry and solvent-removal trajectory as the transferable mechanism, not fixed seed/inhibitor concentrations.
Scans coating/drying/thermal variables and measures top-bottom nucleation timing, front direction, residual solvent, and buried-defect descriptors.
Uses internal electrical/structural diagnostics and a post-growth surface-treatment control to distinguish high-dimensional-defect elimination from passivation.
Requires area-uniform, lot-reproducible results plus damp-heat and elevated-temperature MPP stability gates.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die or meniscus coating is acceptable if its drying and nucleation fields are treated explicitly.
A dimensionless competition between nucleation time, drying time, and crystal-growth time may replace direct concentration matching.
Scanning photocurrent or EBIC may complement cross-sectional KPFM for buried charge-collection defects.
common_wrong_answers: Keeping the same molar additive concentrations while ignoring wet-film thickness and drying kinetics.
Using only top-surface PL or XPS to claim full-thickness defect elimination.
Increasing annealing temperature beyond the SAM thermal budget to force conversion.
Accepting matched initial PCE without depth-resolved defect evidence or operational stability.

expected_answer: The diagnosis should begin with the generation step and then proceed through separation, transport, and extraction. Absolute absorption strength must be distinguished from transition usefulness: temperature-dependent absorption/PL, Tauc-model comparison, photothermal deflection, and radiative-lifetime analysis can reveal indirect or weakly allowed band-edge transitions. Field- and temperature-dependent PL, electroabsorption, or excitonic absorption features can estimate exciton binding and determine whether free carriers are generated at operating fields. Contactless mobility and lifetime measurements such as TRMC, terahertz conductivity, or time-of-flight should test intrinsic transport, while thickness-dependent EQE and intensity-dependent collection reveal diffusion-length or connectivity limits. Hall measurements, Seebeck response, XPS chemical states, and air/light exposure series should test oxidation-driven self-doping; very high background carrier density can narrow depletion widths, increase recombination, and distort SCLC-derived trap estimates. UPS/Kelvin probe, selective-contact swaps, interface PLQY, and impedance or transient extraction measurements should identify barriers and interfacial recombination. Finally, SEM/AFM, cross-sectional imaging, phase mapping, and conductive mapping should test pinholes, disconnected grains, secondary phases, and poor coverage. A nominal band gap says little about transition directness, oscillator strength, or carrier extraction. Strong absorption at higher photon energy can coexist with a weak band edge. SCLC trap density is model-dependent and can be invalidated by injection barriers, mobile ions, doping, nonuniform thickness, or incorrect dielectric assumptions; it also does not measure mobility, oxidation stability, or interface selectivity. Photovoltaic suitability requires a consistent chain from absorbed photons to long-lived free carriers, percolative transport, and selective extraction under device operating conditions.
scoring_key_points: Orders diagnostics across optical transition character, exciton dissociation, bulk transport/connectivity, doping/oxidation, interfaces, and morphology.
Names discriminating measurements for indirect/forbidden transitions and exciton binding rather than relying on a single Tauc plot.
Tests oxidation/self-doping and interface barriers with chemical-state, carrier-density, band-alignment, and contact-swap experiments.
Explains the limitations of nominal band gap, high-energy absorption, and model-dependent SCLC trap density.
accepted_equivalents: Magneto-optical spectroscopy or first-principles symmetry analysis may support the transition-directness diagnosis.
Photo-CELIV, space-charge-limited mobility with validated contacts, or field-effect mobility may complement contactless transport methods.
Light-intensity-dependent Voc and EQE may supplement the recombination and collection analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that an optimal band gap and strong absorption guarantee high Jsc.
Treating one SCLC fit as definitive proof of low electrically active defect density.
Ignoring self-doping because the absorber is nominally stoichiometric.
Attributing low FF only to series resistance without checking morphology, transport, and interfaces.

expected_answer:
The direct transfer fails because the optical objective and the electrical penalty are not separable when a deep texture is placed in the emissive semiconductor. In a solar cell, increased path length can compensate for some surface or morphology penalty. In an LED, however, increased perovskite surface area, thickness nonuniformity, exposed grain boundaries and rough contacts can increase non-radiative recombination, leakage and local electric-field concentration. Conformal deposition over a high-aspect-ratio pattern can also create current crowding, incomplete transport-layer coverage and Joule-heating hot spots. More extracted photons at the beginning therefore do not prove a net outcoupling gain if the internal quantum efficiency has fallen.

The preferred first transfer is to move the photonic function out of the active perovskite. A patterned substrate, transparent electrode, transport layer, external microlens array or low-loss dielectric grating can couple substrate/waveguide modes to the escape cone while leaving the emissive film planar. If active-layer patterning is unavoidable, the relief should be shallow, retain a continuous residual perovskite layer, use rounded features and receive conformal chemical passivation before the next contact. The optical structure should be located where the modal field overlaps the trapped optical mode but where added surface area does not create a high-density recombination interface.

The optical design must target the LED emission spectrum and stack, not copy the solar-cell dimensions. Period, depth, duty cycle, refractive-index contrast and distance from the emissive zone should be optimized with measured n and k to maximize power radiated into useful angles while minimizing absorption in metal or doped transport layers. Angular color shift, polarization dependence and narrow resonances should be limited unless directional emission is explicitly required. Fabrication tolerances and refractive-index drift during aging should be included in the optimization.

A matched control matrix should separate extraction from internal efficiency: planar and patterned devices with identical perovskite thickness/composition; an external optical replica that changes outcoupling without changing film growth; and patterned stacks measured before and after perovskite deposition. Absolute PLQY, transient PL and optical modeling can estimate internal radiative efficiency and extraction efficiency. Electrical qualification should include current-voltage-luminance behavior, leakage, ideality, spatial electroluminescence, contact resistance and temperature mapping. Cross-sectional microscopy should verify conformal layers and absence of field-concentrating cusps.

The design is accepted only when the EQE gain remains after normalization for internal radiative efficiency, the voltage and leakage are not worsened, the emission remains spatially uniform, and the benefit survives constant-current or constant-luminance operation, thermal cycling and humidity/light stress. A structure that gives a brighter initial image but causes faster voltage rise, spectral drift, hot spots or shortened lifetime should be rejected even if its instantaneous outcoupling is higher.
scoring_key_points: Explains why active-layer texture can improve optical extraction yet reduce LED IQE through added surfaces, nonuniform contacts, current crowding and heat generation.
Moves the primary structure to a substrate/electrode/transport layer or uses a shallow passivated residual-layer design that decouples optics from film and contact quality.
Re-optimizes period, depth, index contrast and modal overlap for the emission stack and verifies extraction separately from PLQY/IQE and electrical injection.
Defines acceptance by retained EQE, voltage, leakage, uniformity and operational lifetime, not by initial brightness or simulated extraction alone.
accepted_equivalents: External scattering films, dielectric metasurfaces, microlens arrays or corrugated transparent contacts that preserve a planar emissive layer.
Optical extraction estimated by integrating-sphere electroluminescence plus absolute PLQY and a calibrated optical model.
A shallow unpenetrated imprint with conformal passivation and transport layers as an alternative to fully external patterning.
common_wrong_answers: Copying the solar-cell period and relief depth without recalculating the LED modal distribution.
Equating higher outcoupled intensity with higher extraction efficiency while ignoring reduced internal quantum efficiency.
Optimizing only the optical field and ignoring contact coverage, leakage, current crowding and local heating.
Accepting a narrow directional resonance that causes severe angular color shift or disappears after refractive-index drift.

expected_answer:
A stable total photocurrent argues against catastrophic loss of photovoltage or electrode area, but it does not identify where the electrons go. The central quantity is the electron-resolved product balance: time-dependent CO and H2 rates, faradaic efficiencies, total faradaic closure and any liquid products must be measured together. A falling CO fraction with rising H2 at nearly constant current is consistent with a selectivity change at the cathode, but the same pattern can also result from CO2 depletion or a local pH increase that suppresses CO2 reduction and favors hydrogen evolution.

Catalyst reconstruction is tested by holding the cathode potential and electrolyte composition constant in a separate three-electrode or dark electrolysis experiment. Operando or time-resolved surface-sensitive measurements should track Cu/In ratio, oxidation state and local structure; suitable methods include X-ray absorption, operando Raman, quasi-in-situ XPS and post-test microscopy/elemental mapping. If the selectivity drift is intrinsic to reconstruction, it should recur at the same accumulated charge under fixed CO2 activity, correlate with a reproducible surface-composition change, and persist when the aged cathode is transferred into fresh, pH-controlled electrolyte. Replacing the aged cathode with a fresh one while retaining the same photovoltaic/photoanode components should restore the initial product ratio.

CO2 and pH effects require direct reactor measurements rather than bulk assumptions. Dissolved CO2, gas flow and pressure, carbonate accumulation, electrolyte pH and preferably near-electrode pH should be monitored. The gas-liquid mass-transfer coefficient and bubble coverage should be checked. If CO2 depletion or alkalization is dominant, increasing CO2 flow or pressure, refreshing electrolyte, buffering pH or improving mixing should rapidly and reversibly restore CO selectivity without replacing the catalyst. A 13CO2 test can verify that measured CO is generated from the fed carbon source rather than contamination.

Photovoltaic or photoanode degradation is diagnosed by resolving the tandem electrically. Reference electrodes can measure the operating potentials of the cathode and BiVO4 photoanode while the leaf remains at zero external bias. Periodic light and dark J-V curves, open-circuit photovoltage, spectral response and photoanode oxygen evolution/faradaic efficiency should be recorded. A declining photovoltage, a shifted cathode operating potential, loss of photoanode current or oxygen imbalance would implicate the light absorber, conductive encapsulation or photoanode even if total current initially appears stable. A solar-simulator control at fixed irradiance and a potentiostatically driven cathode control separate illumination variability from catalyst chemistry.

The strongest conclusion comes from orthogonal rescue and swap experiments: fresh electrolyte versus fresh catalyst, fresh PV/photoanode versus aged catalyst, and fixed-potential electrolysis versus the integrated leaf. Stable current alone is insufficient because it can conceal a redistribution of current among products or compensating losses within the tandem.
scoring_key_points: Uses time-resolved product rates and complete faradaic/electron balance, recognizing that constant photocurrent does not imply constant selectivity or component health.
Tests catalyst reconstruction with fixed-potential controls, operando/quasi-in-situ composition measurements and aged/fresh cathode swap or accumulated-charge comparisons.
Tests CO2/pH/mass-transfer drift by measuring dissolved CO2, local or bulk pH, flow/pressure and reversibility after gas, mixing or electrolyte restoration.
Separates PV/photoanode degradation using component potentials, photovoltage/J-V and oxygen-side diagnostics plus orthogonal rescue controls.
accepted_equivalents: Operando XAS, Raman, XPS, XRD or electrochemical fingerprints that track Cu-In reconstruction at equal charge throughput.
Buffering, rotating-electrode, flow-cell or membrane-separated controls that stabilize CO2 transport and interfacial pH.
Reference-electrode monitoring or intermittent component I-V/EQE measurements that resolve the operating point of the tandem.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the photovoltaic component is stable solely because the total photocurrent is stable.
Assigning the H2 increase to catalyst reconstruction without measuring CO2 activity, pH or gas-transfer conditions.
Reporting product concentration without gas-flow calibration or faradaic closure.
Using only post-mortem catalyst composition, which cannot establish that reconstruction preceded the selectivity change.

expected_answer:
A champion device samples the best local overlap of coating thickness, solvent content and plasma exposure; it does not measure process capability. A lower mean with a wider distribution indicates that the plasma-spray route can reach a high-quality state but does so over only part of the substrate or process window. In a millisecond crystallization process, small variations in spray flux, precursor age, nozzle overlap, plasma-substrate distance, scan speed, ambient humidity, gas flow or substrate temperature can create large changes in supersaturation and nucleation density. Thus high peak performance and poor yield are exactly the pattern expected from a narrow, spatially nonuniform process window.

The experiment should generate a common coordinate map from wet deposition through completed device. Immediately after spraying, film thickness, solvent mass or optical interference should be mapped; high-speed imaging or laser reflectometry can capture wet-film breakup. During plasma passage, spatially resolved optical-emission intensity, UV dose, gas temperature, substrate temperature and scan trajectory should be recorded. The local residence time between spray and plasma must also be known. After processing, hyperspectral PL, PL lifetime, absorption/reflectance, XRD or GIWAXS peak intensity/width, residual-solvent spectroscopy and surface topography should be measured on the same grid. Completed devices should be divided into many small pixels or mapped by electroluminescence, lock-in thermography and local J-V so that material maps can be correlated with shunts, voltage loss and series resistance.

A factorial perturbation should vary spray flow or pass overlap independently of plasma power, nozzle distance and scan speed. If wet-film nonuniformity dominates, final performance should correlate primarily with initial thickness or dewetting maps even when plasma dose is spatially uniform. If plasma nonuniformity dominates, equal-thickness regions should show performance gradients that track optical-emission/UV/temperature dose. If the crystallization window is intrinsically narrow, a small change in delay or dose should produce a steep, reproducible transition from incomplete conversion to damaged film even on uniform coupons. If downstream contacts dominate, the perovskite optical/structural maps should be uniform while electroluminescence, sheet resistance or contact-resistance maps explain the device spread.

Under-processing should leave residual solvent or precursor/intermediate, incomplete conversion, pinholes or weakly connected grains, giving low PL, short lifetime, low shunt resistance and possibly delayed structural growth. Over-processing can cause excessive solvent flash-off before coalescence, rough or discontinuous films, thermal/plasma decomposition, volatile loss or damaged underlying layers, producing broadened or secondary-phase diffraction, surface roughness, reduced absorption/PL and local leakage. The optimum region should show complete conversion with continuous coverage and minimal electrical hot spots.

The process should then be expressed as a dose-response window and a capability metric, not a single best recipe. Replicated maps across time and nozzle positions are required to distinguish random device noise from systematic process nonuniformity.
scoring_key_points: Interprets champion parity plus poor mean/variance as evidence of achievable quality but inadequate process-window width or spatial uniformity.
Maps wet-film thickness, plasma/thermal/UV dose, crystallization/PL/morphology and local device response on a common spatial coordinate system.
Uses independent perturbations and correlation patterns to separate spray, plasma, intrinsic kinetic-window and downstream-contact causes.
States physically distinct under-processing and over-processing signatures and converts the result into a reproducible process-capability window.
accepted_equivalents: Equivalent inline ellipsometry, reflectometry, pyrometry, optical emission, high-speed imaging or mass-loss diagnostics synchronized to web position.
Pixelated devices, PL/EQE maps, electroluminescence, thermography or conductive-AFM as local device-yield diagnostics.
A response-surface or Bayesian process map linking local energy dose and wet-film state to conversion and device yield.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming scalability from the best device while ignoring the lower batch mean and larger variance.
Changing spray and plasma conditions simultaneously, so the source of nonuniformity cannot be assigned.
Mapping only final morphology without recording the wet-film and plasma history at the same position.
Assuming every low-efficiency pixel reflects perovskite crystallization rather than electrode or contact fabrication.

expected_answer:
The original plasma dose cannot be copied because the new ink and substrate have different intermediate chemistry, solvent absorption, volatility and thermal tolerance. FA/Cs compositions form different precursor-solvate and halide/cation distributions from MAPbI3, so the balance among solvent removal, charged/radical chemistry, UV absorption, nucleation and grain coalescence must be re-established. The flexible electrode, transport layer and polymer substrate may also be oxidized, embrittled or heated by the air plasma even when the perovskite converts successfully.

A factorial transfer study should vary precursor solvent/additive system, wet-film thickness, spray or coating rate, delay between coating and plasma, plasma power and gas composition, nozzle distance, web speed, substrate preheating and ambient water/oxygen. Plasma optical emission and gas-phase analysis should verify the radical/UV environment, while fast pyrometry or embedded sensors measure actual web temperature rather than gas temperature. Time-resolved or stroboscopic GIWAXS/WAXS, reflectance and PL should identify the onset and completion of phase formation and whether growth continues during cooling. The target is a broad region of complete conversion and low defect density, not simply the shortest exposure.

The moving-web system needs closed-loop control. Inline thickness or wet-film reflectometry, optical-emission/UV-dose monitoring, web-position tracking, temperature mapping and post-cure hyperspectral PL/reflectance should be synchronized. Edge-to-center and start-stop transients must be included. The process should automatically adjust plasma power or web speed when wet thickness or temperature drifts, and reject regions outside the validated dose window. Patterned module areas require additional checks for coating over scribe lines and for electrode resistance.

Chemical compatibility controls should expose bare substrate/electrode/transport-layer stacks to the plasma without perovskite, and expose the new ink to matched heat, UV-only and plasma-species controls. Changes in work function, sheet resistance, adhesion and surface chemistry should be measured. Encapsulation should be integrated early because a composition processed rapidly in air may still be intrinsically moisture- or thermally sensitive.

Mechanical fracture energy of a free film or specimen is not equivalent to operational stability. Qualification must include repeated bending at relevant radius, adhesion/peel, thermal cycling, damp heat, light soaking and maximum-power-point operation on full interconnects. Voltage, fill factor, leakage, electroluminescence nonuniformity, scribe resistance and local temperature should be tracked. The transferred process is accepted only if it has a statistically capable web-speed/dose window, no plasma-induced contact degradation, retained module performance after combined flexing and environmental/MPP stress, and failure analysis showing no systematic edge or hot-spot mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Re-derives plasma, UV, radical, thermal and drying conditions for the new precursor/intermediate chemistry instead of copying the MAPbI3 dose.
Uses synchronized inline wet-thickness, plasma-emission/UV, temperature and post-cure optical/structural feedback with closed-loop web control.
Includes bare-stack and heat/UV/species controls to detect plasma damage to flexible substrates, electrodes and transport layers.
Separates film toughness from durability and requires flex, adhesion, environmental and MPP module qualification over a statistically capable process window.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, gravure or ultrasonic spray coating on a web, provided the coating-to-plasma delay and local dose are explicitly controlled.
Stroboscopic GIWAXS, fast optical reflectometry or in-line PL as equivalent crystallization-completion diagnostics.
Nitrogen, argon/oxygen or tailored plasma chemistry if it is revalidated for radical composition, substrate damage and perovskite conversion.
common_wrong_answers: Using the same scan speed and plasma power because the target perovskite has a similar final bandgap.
Treating low web temperature as proof that UV/radicals did not damage the transport layers or polymer substrate.
Using bending survival alone as proof of moisture, thermal or operational stability.
Reporting one flexible champion without edge-to-center yield, start-stop transients or module interconnect tests.

expected_answer: The peak shift must be referenced to a chloride-free MAPbI3 film measured with the same temperature program, an internal diffraction standard, and preferably a calibrated high-temperature stage. Sequential Rietveld or whole-pattern analysis should track lattice parameters, peak asymmetry, phase fractions, and microstrain rather than using a single peak position. Isothermal holds and several heating rates should separate equilibrium composition changes from kinetic strain relaxation; cooling-reheating cycles can test reversibility. Simultaneous TGA/DSC and temperature-programmed desorption mass spectrometry, ideally with isotopically labelled MACl or a chlorine tracer, should correlate lattice contraction with loss of chloride-containing volatile species. A consistent interpretation is that an early chloride-rich precursor/intermediate loses MACl-derived species and promotes accompanying MAI loss, producing a progressively chloride-poor perovskite; once little chloride remains, the lattice shift is dominated by normal thermal expansion. The later stage is degradation of this chloride-depleted perovskite through volatile organic-halide products, with products that may remain amorphous, nanocrystalline, or chemically different from bulk PbI2, explaining the weak PbI2 diffraction signature. The model is falsified if the anomalous peak shift occurs without any chloride mass loss, if total chlorine is conserved while a reversible stress change explains the shift, if resolved phase mixing rather than continuous composition change accounts for the peak motion, or if volatile evolution is temporally uncorrelated with structural degradation.
scoring_key_points: Uses a chloride-free thermal-expansion reference, internal calibration, and whole-pattern analysis to separate composition, strain, phase coexistence, and drift.
Requires heating-rate/isothermal/reversibility tests plus simultaneous mass-loss and evolved-gas measurements.
Infers early chloride-containing volatile loss followed by a chloride-depleted perovskite whose peak shift is mainly thermal expansion.
Explains the weak PbI2 peak through noncrystalline or alternative products and gives explicit falsification conditions.
accepted_equivalents: In situ GIWAXS or synchrotron XRD with Rietveld, pair-distribution-function, or lattice-parameter analysis
13C-, deuterium-, or chlorine-isotope labelling of methylammonium chloride for evolved-gas assignment
A two-population phase model if peak splitting or asymmetric broadening is explicitly tested
Operando XRD-TGA-MS or separate experiments synchronized by an identical thermal protocol
common_wrong_answers: Treats every diffraction-peak shift as direct proof of chloride loss without a thermal-expansion or strain control.
Assumes absence of crystalline PbI2 means that no degradation has occurred.
Infers the mechanism only from TGA mass loss without identifying the evolved species or structural transition.
Calls the pathway two-stage but does not define distinct compositions, reactions, or diagnostic signatures.

expected_answer: The process should be optimized around the sequence of precursor complexation, intermediate conversion, chloride removal, and perovskite crystallization rather than around a nominal chloride concentration alone. A factorial study should vary chloride dose and source, DMF/DMSO or other coordinating-solvent content, wet-film thickness, drying rate, substrate temperature, annealing ramp, dwell time, and atmosphere. In situ GIWAXS/XRD, mass-loss or evolved-gas monitoring, and residual-halide depth profiling should identify the lowest thermal budget that completes conversion without entering the temperature-time region where MACl-assisted MAI loss accelerates. Because thick coated films retain solvent and volatile species differently from thin spin-coated films, the process should be validated at realistic thickness and gas-flow conditions, with center-to-edge mapping. Residual chloride must be quantified spatially and related to lattice parameter, composition, electronic disorder, and ion migration; neither zero residual chloride nor maximum chloride retention should be assumed optimal. Process-exposed witness films should be compared with complete devices to separate intrinsic absorber decomposition from contact reactions, encapsulation, electrode diffusion, and electrical bias effects. Qualification should include stabilized maximum-power-point operation at several temperatures, thermal cycling, damp heat, light-dark and bias cycles, and post-stress volatile/compositional analysis. Acceptance requires a wide conversion window, reproducible phase completion, low residual-solvent/halide gradients, no early volatile release within the module operating envelope, and stable device power; a high TGA onset or a short annealed-film test alone is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes chloride chemistry together with solvent coordination, thickness, drying, heating ramp, dwell, and atmosphere.
Uses in situ phase/evolved-gas measurements and residual-halide depth mapping to define a safe temperature-time conversion window.
Validates the process at manufacturing-relevant thickness and spatial scale rather than extrapolating from drop-cast or thin films.
Separates film decomposition from full-device operational failure through MPP, thermal, humidity, bias, and post-stress analyses.
accepted_equivalents: A time-temperature-transformation or process-of-record map for precursor, intermediate, perovskite, and degradation regimes
Inline GIWAXS, FTIR, residual-gas analysis, ion chromatography, XRF, XPS, or ToF-SIMS for phase and chloride control
Accelerated aging below and above the anticipated module temperature with Arrhenius analysis used cautiously
Witness films, half stacks, and complete-device controls from the same coating run
common_wrong_answers: Selects the highest annealing temperature that gives the fastest crystallization.
Assumes that the final average chlorine concentration fully determines stability.
Uses a thick drop-cast TGA result as a direct lifetime prediction for an encapsulated operating device.
Ignores solvent retention and film-thickness effects when transferring the chloride recipe to coating.

expected_answer: The sample should be examined with synchronized, time-resolved spectroscopy and nanoscale composition or structure probes. Pre-existing iodide-rich minority domains should produce the low-energy emission immediately at the lowest nonperturbative excitation, remain spatially correlated with I-rich regions in nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS, cathodoluminescence, or hyperspectral PL, and persist in the dark; their volume fraction may be below bulk-XRD detection. Light-induced segregation should show an induction period, fluence- and temperature-dependent growth of the red band under illumination, spatial nucleation of low-energy emissive domains, and partial or full recovery after dark storage or bias removal. Operando nano-XRD, absorption, or compositional mapping may reveal emerging I-rich/Br-rich populations even when average XRD remains unchanged. Deep-trap emission should correlate with trap density and defect passivation, often show sublinear or saturating power dependence, thermally activated quenching or detrapping, and a characteristic delayed lifetime, but it need not create a reversible halide-composition redistribution. Passivation that removes the red band without changing local I/Br composition supports the trap model. Measurements must use calibrated low-fluence controls because the probe light can create the phenomenon being diagnosed. A steady-state PL peak is nonunique: minority phases, carrier funneling, traps, and photoinduced segregation can all dominate emission while contributing little to absorption or diffraction.
scoring_key_points: Identifies immediate, dark-persistent, composition-correlated emission as evidence for pre-existing iodide-rich minority domains.
Identifies illumination-time/fluence dependence and dark reversibility with emerging compositional contrast as evidence for light-induced segregation.
Identifies trap-saturation, thermal detrapping/quenching, delayed dynamics, and passivation response without composition change as evidence for localized traps.
Requires low-perturbation time-resolved and spatially resolved structural/compositional controls and explains PL nonuniqueness.
accepted_equivalents: Hyperspectral PL, cathodoluminescence, nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS, atom-probe, or scanning nano-XRD
Light-on/light-off cycling, excitation-dose dependence, and temperature-dependent PL
Transient absorption, time-resolved PL, thermally stimulated current, or deep-level spectroscopy for traps
An iodide-rich minority phase below the detection limit of conventional XRD
common_wrong_answers: Calls the red band phase segregation solely because it lies below the nominal band gap.
Uses high-intensity PL mapping without testing whether the measurement itself induces segregation.
Rules out minority phases because conventional XRD and absorption appear single-phase.
Uses a longer PL lifetime as unambiguous proof of fewer traps without considering carrier funneling.

expected_answer: The search should treat band gap as one constraint rather than the objective. A design-of-experiments matrix should vary Br fraction around the optical target together with FA/MA ratio and, if allowed, a stabilizing third cation, while crossing composition with lead-halide excess, solvent coordination, antisolvent timing or gas quench, annealing, and film thickness. Each formulation should be mapped for absorption edge and EQE-derived band gap, absolute PLQY/QFLS, sub-bandgap PL and Urbach energy, phase purity and nanoscale I/Br uniformity, residual PbI2/PbBr2, morphology, and contact energetics. Time- and fluence-dependent PL under illumination must screen for segregation rather than relying on initial XRD. Complete devices should be compared by stabilized VOC, JSC, FF, hysteresis, ideality factor, pseudo-JV versus electrical J-V, and EQE-integrated current. Tandem evaluation must include optical/current matching to silicon and recombination-layer compatibility; a wider gap that raises VOC but loses current or QFLS is not optimal. Manufacturing transfer requires replacing an artisanal antisolvent step with a controlled coating/drying window and testing spatial uniformity. Selection should be based on the center of a robust process window that retains composition, QFLS, current matching, and FF during MPP illumination, elevated temperature, light-dark cycling, and humidity/encapsulation tests, with no growing low-energy emission or halide redistribution.
scoring_key_points: Jointly varies halide and cation composition with crystallization variables instead of optimizing Br fraction alone.
Screens sub-bandgap recombination, nanoscale halide uniformity, residual precursor phases, QFLS, and contact energetics in addition to band gap.
Evaluates stabilized device and tandem current/voltage matching, hysteresis, pseudo-FF, and interconnect compatibility.
Selects a robust coating and operational-stability window with no light-induced segregation rather than a champion composition.
accepted_equivalents: Response-surface, Bayesian, or active-learning optimization with phase-stability and device constraints
Hyperspectral PL, nano-XRF, GIWAXS, ToF-SIMS, Urbach-energy, and absolute-QFLS screening
A small Cs/Rb-type stabilizing cation or alternative cation strategy if justified and independently controlled
MPP aging with spectrally resolved PL/EL and post-stress composition mapping
common_wrong_answers: Chooses the composition whose absorption edge is closest to the target tandem band gap.
Optimizes only VOC and ignores the JSC penalty and current matching to silicon.
Treats initial single-phase XRD as proof against later light-induced halide segregation.
Transfers a timing-sensitive antisolvent recipe to large-area coating without defining a process window.

expected_answer: The deposition process should be mapped in two dimensions for the individual source fluxes, substrate temperature, thickness, composition, and chloride/iodide or organic/lead ratio. Quartz-crystal monitors and witness substrates at multiple positions should be calibrated against XRF, XPS/ToF-SIMS, profilometry, XRD, and morphology. Annealing time, temperature, and vapor loss must be controlled locally because stoichiometric and grain-boundary gradients can preserve average absorption while changing transport and recombination. Spatially resolved optical-pump THz or microwave conductivity, combined with TRPL/QFLS and temperature-dependent kinetics before and after aging, can show whether local mobility, lifetime, or bimolecular loss changes in the absorber. These contactless measurements should be performed on process-matched witness films, not interpreted as direct module collection efficiency. Complete devices require EL/PL maps, Suns-VOC or pseudo-JV versus electrical J-V, sheet/contact resistance, TLM, impedance, lock-in thermography, and scribe-isolation tests. Preserved pseudo-FF with reduced electrical FF implicates contact or interconnect resistance; degraded QFLS and THz mobility-lifetime product implicate the absorber; a spatial correlation with source-flux composition implicates deposition nonuniformity. Qualification should include stabilized MPP, thermal cycling, elevated-temperature operation, and post-stress spatial remapping. Acceptance requires uniform stoichiometry and μτ, low resistive loss, and stable module power over a defined process window.
scoring_key_points: Maps source flux, substrate temperature, thickness, stoichiometry, structure, and morphology across the deposition area.
Uses spatial contactless transport/recombination measurements on matched witness films before and after aging.
Separates absorber and resistive module losses with pseudo-JV/EL, contact/sheet resistance, thermal imaging, and scribe diagnostics.
Requires spatially resolved operational and thermal-aging qualification and explicitly limits what film-level THz can prove.
accepted_equivalents: Rotating substrates, source baffling, closed-loop rate control, or combinatorial witness arrays
THz, TRMC, transient absorption, PLQY/QFLS, or Hall mapping for absorber properties
Suns-VOC, impedance, TLM, four-point probe, EL, LBIC, or lock-in thermography for device losses
Half-stack and full-device controls fabricated from the same spatial positions
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the edge failure to poor absorption despite unchanged optical density.
Uses one central THz measurement to certify the entire module.
Assumes a high local mobility guarantees high fill factor without testing contacts and interconnections.
Changes both source rates simultaneously without spatial composition calibration or witness samples.

expected_answer: The intrinsic radiative coefficient should be remeasured on the aged absorber or a process-matched witness by radiometrically calibrated, early-time PL at independently known injected carrier density, using the same temperature and optical model before and after aging. Unchanged B with shorter lifetime identifies increased nonradiative k1 or nonradiative k2; fluence-dependent global kinetics, PLQY/QFLS, ideality factor, and defect spectroscopy can locate the order and origin of the loss. External PL or EL must be converted cautiously because roughness, refractive index, electrode absorption, scattering, waveguiding, and photon recycling can change the escape probability without changing internal radiative physics. An integrating sphere, angle-resolved or front/back emission, reflectance/ellipsometry, and transfer-matrix/outcoupling model should test this. Contacts and injection are separated by comparing contactless PL/QFLS with device EL, Suns-VOC or pseudo-JV, impedance, transient extraction, contact resistance, and dark-JV behavior. If contactless QFLS is retained but EL and electrical FF fall, injection/contact degradation is likely; if both PLQY/QFLS and lifetime fall while B is constant, absorber or interface nonradiative recombination increased; if internal PL remains stable but external emission changes with optical-stack parameters, outcoupling changed. The aging protocol should control temperature, carrier density, prebias, ion-distribution history, and measurement geometry. Luminescence loss is a valid stability metric only after these optical, radiative, nonradiative, and electrical contributions are separated.
scoring_key_points: Remeasures the intrinsic radiative coefficient with calibrated instantaneous PL and known carrier density under matched conditions.
Uses fluence-dependent lifetime, PLQY/QFLS, and recombination-order diagnostics to identify increased nonradiative loss.
Corrects or tests optical escape, waveguiding, electrode absorption, and photon recycling with independent optical measurements.
Separates contact/injection degradation from absorber loss using contactless versus device luminescence and electrical pseudo-JV/resistance diagnostics.
accepted_equivalents: Suns-PLQY, calibrated absolute PL, or radiometric TRPL for contactless QFLS and recombination analysis
Integrating-sphere, angle-resolved, front/back EL/PL, ellipsometry, or optical transfer-matrix modelling
Suns-VOC, impedance, TLM, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, or selective-contact lifetime measurements
Process-matched capped films and half stacks aged alongside complete devices
common_wrong_answers: Interprets lower external EL efficiency directly as a lower intrinsic radiative coefficient.
Uses unchanged absorption to rule out defect formation or interfacial nonradiative recombination.
Compares TRPL lifetimes before and after aging at different injection densities.
Attributes all luminescence loss to the absorber without checking contact injection and optical outcoupling.

expected_answer:
The transfer should be treated as a coupled chemistry-localization-transport optimization, not as a direct copy of the concentration used in MAPbI3. The molecular hypothesis is that a fully alkylated, aprotic onium lacks labile N-H bonds and is therefore less susceptible to water-assisted proton abstraction than a protic ammonium. That hypothesis must be separated from generic hydrophobicity by using matched controls: a protic cation with comparable size and hydrophobic surface area, a hydrophobic but non-coordinating barrier molecule, and the untreated absorber. Water contact angle alone is insufficient; water uptake, headspace products, organic-cation retention, Pb-O formation, and dry-recovery behavior must be compared under identical humidity, light, temperature, and bias.

Dose and location must then be mapped. At low loading, the desired additive should enrich surfaces, grain boundaries, or a deliberately thin top interphase while preserving the 3D bulk lattice. XPS angle/depth profiling, ToF-SIMS, GIWAXS/XRD, solid-state NMR where practical, and cross-sectional microscopy should establish whether the species remains interfacial or produces a continuous low-dimensional phase. A dose series must include the onset of new low-n diffraction or excitonic features, changes in orientation, and any increase in interfacial thickness. The optimum is not the concentration with the highest water contact angle; it is the lowest loading that suppresses irreversible chemical products and ion accumulation without creating a percolating insulating organic layer.

Transport and recombination must be evaluated in selective-contact stacks and full devices. Absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting, electroluminescence efficiency, Suns-Voc/pseudo-JV, transient extraction, mobility or local conductivity, impedance, temperature-dependent JV, and measured versus pseudo fill factor distinguish true passivation from extraction blockage. If voltage and non-radiative loss improve while measured FF, current, or temperature-activated resistance deteriorates, the additive is over-thick, poorly oriented, energetically misaligned, or forming too much low-dimensional material. Spatial PL/current mapping on large areas should detect additive gradients and local blocking regions.

Scale-up qualification should reproduce coating, drying, precursor-age, humidity, and thermal windows on representative textured or module substrates, with depth-composition and electrical-uniformity maps across the area. Stability must be tested at MPP under simultaneous light, heat, humidity, and bias, because a molecule that performs in humid-dark storage may fail through ion accumulation or contact reactions during operation. A go decision requires reproducible surface/grain-boundary localization, chemically specific suppression of proton-transfer/Pb-O products versus matched hydrophobic controls, no meaningful current or FF penalty, and improved energy retention under operational stress. Bulk low-dimensional conversion, large area gradients, or stability gains explainable only by a thick water barrier are no-go outcomes.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched protic, hydrophobic-barrier, and untreated controls to distinguish aprotic molecular chemistry from simple water exclusion.
Maps dose-dependent surface/grain-boundary localization and the onset of low-dimensional phases with depth, structural, and spectroscopic measurements.
Separates passivation from extraction blockage using QFLS/recombination, pseudo-JV versus JV, transport, resistance, and spatial-uniformity diagnostics.
Defines scale-up and operational-stability go/no criteria rather than relying on humid-dark film retention or contact angle.
accepted_equivalents: Aprotic onium may be described as fully substituted sulfonium, phosphonium, or ammonium chemistry provided the absence of labile heteroatom-bound hydrogen is central.
Surface or grain-boundary localization may be established by angle-resolved XPS, ToF-SIMS, neutron methods, cross-sectional spectroscopy, or equivalent depth-sensitive tools.
Transport blockage may be diagnosed through mobility, conductivity, extraction time, series resistance, pseudo-FF, temperature activation, or local current mapping.
Operational stability may use IEC-relevant or equivalent MPP light-heat-humidity-bias protocols with energy-yield retention.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the highest additive dose because it gives the largest contact angle.
Assuming any new 2D phase is beneficial and cannot reduce vertical transport.
Claiming molecular suppression of deprotonation without a protic, hydrophobicity-matched control.
Using dark shelf stability of a small film as sufficient evidence for module-scale operational stability.

expected_answer:
The structural observations show that the additive has modified nucleation and conversion, but they do not prove that either selective contact is electronically benign. In a textured tandem, voltage and fill factor depend on the entire loss chain: bulk non-radiative recombination, the buried hole-selective contact, the exposed perovskite surface, the C60 interface, energy offsets, mobile ions, and series resistance. Larger grains or complete alpha-phase conversion can coexist with a defective buried interface or a surface residue that blocks electron extraction.

The first branch tests bulk and buried-interface quality before C60. Absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting should be measured on the perovskite half-stack, together with depth-sensitive GI-XRD or composition analysis near the hole-selective layer and transient surface photovoltage or equivalent hole-extraction measurements. If the half-stack QFLS is low, residual trap signatures remain near the buried interface, or hole extraction is slow, then low-temperature conversion has not produced a good bottom contact even if the top-view morphology is improved. A bottom-interface-specific treatment or altered wetting/annealing should recover the loss without changing the top surface.

The second branch compares the half-stack with the same sample after C60 and with a controlled post-growth surface treatment. A large C60-induced QFLS/Voc loss, short C60-stack PL lifetime, strong interfacial recombination in transient spectroscopy, and recovery after an independent surface interlayer identify the top contact as the failure. XPS depth/angle analysis should determine whether additive-derived species remain at the surface, while UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements test whether the valence/conduction energetics have shifted unfavorably. A voltage loss that follows an unfavorable contact potential or extraction barrier, but not a rise in non-radiative recombination, points to energy-level mismatch.

The final branch separates recombination from resistive blocking. Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV, PL-derived implied FF, electroluminescence, measured JV, transient extraction, impedance, and temperature-dependent resistance should be compared. If pseudo-FF and QFLS are high but measured FF and current are low, the dominant problem is series resistance or an extraction barrier. Surface-enriched additive, increasing resistance with dose, thermally activated current, and local current nonuniformity would support an insulating residue or poorly oriented low-dimensional interphase. If both pseudo-FF and measured FF are poor, recombination remains dominant. The diagnostic conclusion must therefore assign the missing function rather than assuming that any additive that improves crystallization will automatically passivate and align the C60 contact.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that crystallization, buried-interface quality, top-contact recombination, energy alignment, and series resistance are separable functions.
Uses half-stack QFLS/PL plus buried-interface structural and extraction diagnostics to test the hole-selective interface.
Uses pre/post-C60 comparisons, independent surface treatment, XPS/UPS, and stack-dependent recombination measurements to test the top interface and energetics.
Separates recombination from insulating-residue or extraction-barrier loss using pseudo-JV versus JV, implied FF, transients, resistance, dose, and spatial-current signatures.
accepted_equivalents: Transient surface photovoltage may be replaced by time-resolved microwave conductivity with selective contacts, transient photocurrent, or another interface-specific extraction probe.
Absolute PLQY/QFLS, electroluminescence, or calibrated Suns-PL may be used to quantify non-radiative voltage loss.
UPS, Kelvin probe, photoelectron spectroscopy, or temperature-dependent JV may be used to diagnose energy barriers.
An insulating residue may be described as excessive additive, a thick organic interlayer, or an unfavorably oriented low-dimensional phase.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that larger grains and lower PbI2 necessarily imply higher device voltage and fill factor.
Attributing every FF loss to bulk traps without comparing pseudo-FF and measured FF.
Using only bare-film PL to infer the quality of the perovskite/C60 contact.
Assuming surface additive enrichment is always passivating and cannot create an extraction barrier.

expected_answer:
Scale-up must preserve both functions of the additive over a much larger and more heterogeneous surface. A design-of-experiments window should vary precursor loading, additive concentration, coating speed, solvent evaporation, gas or antisolvent quench, substrate temperature, ambient humidity, and anneal time. Because textured pyramids create local thickness and drying differences, conformality must be mapped at pyramid tops, sidewalls, valleys, and module edges. Cross-sectional SEM/TEM, spatial GIWAXS/XRD, reflectance/PL imaging, and compositional mapping should verify complete alpha-phase conversion, limited residual PbI2, and absence of local shunts or unconverted pockets.

The additive window must be defined by function, not nominal concentration. Depth-sensitive XPS/ToF-SIMS and surface spectroscopy should quantify whether additive-derived species are consistently enriched at the intended interface rather than trapped throughout the absorber.
