A concentration series must identify the point at which a passivating residue becomes an insulating layer, changes wetting, or produces nonuniform low-dimensional material. Large-area QFLS/PL maps before and after C60, local conductivity/current maps, contact resistance, pseudo-JV versus measured JV, and temperature-dependent extraction are required. The module process is a no-go if the dose that gives low-temperature conversion also creates spatially variable C60 barriers or high series resistance.

Optical and electrical integration must be optimized in the complete tandem. Perovskite thickness/composition, front electrode, antireflection layer, and texture must be tuned using subcell EQE so that current matching is maintained after scaling; a small decrease in top-cell current cannot be hidden by a voltage/FF improvement if it makes the tandem current-limited. Sheet resistance, grid design, transparent-electrode damage, ALD/sputter compatibility, interconnect and scribe losses, edge shunts, and area-dependent Voc/FF must be included. Statistical yield and spatial standard deviation are as important as the champion cell.

Qualification must go beyond dark nitrogen or half-stack aging. Representative minimodules should be encapsulated with module-relevant edges and tested under MPP with simultaneous one-sun-equivalent illumination, elevated temperature, humidity, and realistic spectral/thermal cycling. Light-soaking transients, mobile-ion density, series resistance, subcell-resolved electroluminescence/EQE, and local hot spots should be tracked. Damp heat, thermal cycling, UV exposure, reverse bias/shading, and adhesion tests are needed because low-temperature chemistry can alter interfaces and mechanical reliability. A go decision requires a reproducible large-area process window, uniform phase and interface passivation, no meaningful current-matching or resistance penalty, acceptable module yield, and improved retained energy output. Small-cell PCE, lower annealing temperature, or short half-stack stability alone are insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Defines a large-area coating, drying, humidity, and annealing process window and verifies conformal conversion across textured features and module edges.
Controls additive localization and the transition from passivating residue to insulating or nonuniform interphase using depth, optical, and transport mapping.
Includes full-tandem current matching, transparent-contact/interconnect resistance, area scaling, spatial statistics, and module yield.
Requires module-relevant MPP light-heat-humidity and mechanical/electrical stress qualification with explicit go/no criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Spatial GIWAXS, hyperspectral PL, EL, LBIC, lock-in thermography, or equivalent imaging may be used for large-area uniformity.
Current matching may be established by subcell EQE, optical modeling validated by EQE, or spectrally resolved tandem diagnostics.
Module-specific risks may include scribe damage, edge ingress, sheet resistance, hot spots, reverse bias, and encapsulation adhesion.
Operational stability may follow IEC-like or equivalent MPP protocols if simultaneous stress and retained energy are measured.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only the substrate area while keeping the small-cell recipe and nominal concentration unchanged.
Using average XRD or one JV curve to claim uniform conversion and passivation across a module.
Ignoring current matching because the additive improves Voc and FF.
Claiming scalability from reduced annealing temperature and dark half-stack aging without module MPP testing.

expected_answer:
At low loading, a chemically compatible DJ phase can act as a sparse nucleation skeleton or template, reduce lattice strain and voids, passivate defects, and create localized low-n domains that transfer excitation or carriers into the 3D matrix. If the low-n domains are discontinuous, favorably oriented, and energetically coupled to the 3D phase, they need not interrupt vertical transport. At high loading, the same chemistry can cross a percolation threshold: thicker or more continuous organic-separated layers, unfavorable orientation, and deeper energy barriers can confine carriers or block extraction even while suppressing local non-radiative recombination.

The increasing PL lifetime is therefore ambiguous. True passivation should increase absolute PLQY and QFLS while preserving carrier collection and conductivity. Extraction blockage can also lengthen PL because carriers remain in the absorber instead of being transferred to a contact. The distinction requires measurements on the neat film, selective-contact half-stacks, and complete devices. Absolute PLQY/QFLS, electroluminescence, light-intensity Voc, and pseudo-JV assess recombination; transient photocurrent, time-resolved extraction, mobility/local conductivity, temperature-dependent JV, and measured versus pseudo FF assess transport barriers. High pseudo-FF with low measured FF is a classic blocking or resistance signature.

Depth and orientation are central. ToF-SIMS or cross-sectional chemical mapping should determine whether the amidino phase is uniformly dispersed, enriched at one interface, or forms a continuous vertical band. GIWAXS/XRD with incidence-angle or depth sensitivity should measure low-n phase fraction and whether inorganic slabs are oriented to permit vertical transport. AFM/conductive AFM and cross-sectional microscopy can reveal insulating patches or percolating organic-rich regions. UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements should map dose-dependent band offsets.

Ultrafast spectroscopy should test the proposed funnel. At beneficial dose, low-n bleach or exciton signatures should decay as the 3D population rises, with transfer faster than trapping and with high mobile-carrier yield. At excessive dose, long-lived low-n populations, stronger excitation-wavelength dependence, reduced terahertz/TRMC mobility, or delayed/inefficient 3D population would indicate confinement or interrupted connectivity. A dose-dependent optimum is established only when structural distribution, transfer kinetics, QFLS, transport, and device FF all agree. The high-dose state should not be labeled 'more passivated' solely because TRPL is longer; it may be electronically isolated.
scoring_key_points: Explains a non-monotonic transition from sparse, compatible low-n domains that template/passivate and funnel carriers to a continuous or misoriented blocking network.
Recognizes that longer PL lifetime can arise from either reduced recombination or suppressed extraction and requires absolute QFLS/PLQY plus stack-dependent tests.
Uses depth and orientation measurements to determine low-n phase location, continuity, fraction, and vertical transport connectivity.
Uses ultrafast transfer, mobility/extraction, pseudo-FF versus measured FF, energetics, and dose trends to distinguish passivation from confinement/blockage.
accepted_equivalents: The blocking transition may be described as a percolation threshold, excessive quantum-well fraction, insulating organic-layer continuity, or unfavorable 2D orientation.
Energy transfer may be evaluated by transient absorption, time-resolved PL excitation dependence, terahertz spectroscopy, TRMC, or equivalent carrier-population methods.
Depth distribution may be measured by ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved photoemission, cross-sectional spectroscopy, neutron methods, or chemical tomography.
Transport loss may be diagnosed by reduced mobility, slow extraction, increased activation energy/resistance, low measured FF relative to pseudo-FF, or local-current discontinuity.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that stronger low-n absorption and longer TRPL always mean better passivation and device performance.
Ignoring the orientation and continuity of the low-dimensional phase.
Using only XRD preservation of the 3D phase to claim that vertical transport is unaffected.
Attributing the high-dose current loss solely to optical absorption without testing extraction and resistance.

expected_answer:
The minimum design is a crossed additive × PEAI experiment rather than a comparison of only the final optimized devices. On each compatible architecture, fabricate four matched groups: no additive/no PEAI, additive/no PEAI, no additive/PEAI, and additive/PEAI. Film thickness, 3D precursor stoichiometry, solvent history, electrode area, and measurement protocol must be held constant. An amidino-free or conventional amino-spacer analogue and an additive-dose series provide additional chemical controls. The same matrix should be repeated on rigid TiO2 and flexible SnO2 stacks, with annealing temperature crossed where substrate limits permit or with matched thermal-budget controls.

Mechanistically, depth-sensitive composition and phase measurements must establish what each treatment changes. ToF-SIMS/cross-sectional spectroscopy, XRD/GIWAXS, low-n optical signatures, XPS, and morphology should determine whether the amidino phase is distributed through the film while PEAI is primarily surface-localized. In situ PL or crystallization measurements should test whether the amidino additive alters nucleation before PEAI is applied. Absolute PLQY/QFLS on bare films and selective-contact stacks, TRPL, transient absorption, mobility/extraction, hysteresis, light-intensity Voc, and electroluminescence should determine whether the two treatments independently or synergistically reduce traps and recombination. A statistical interaction term in the factorial analysis is necessary: an additive benefit only in the PEAI group is synergy, not an additive-only effect.

The temperature/substrate branch should distinguish chemistry from process. If the additive still forms the intended low-n/3D distribution and improves QFLS on both contacts at matched phase fraction, the mechanism is relatively transferable. If low-temperature flexible processing changes 2D phase fraction, orientation, residual solvent, or interfacial segregation, the rigid result cannot be assumed to apply. Contact-specific extraction and band alignment should be measured because TiO2 and SnO2 impose different buried-interface energetics. Mechanical strain may also redistribute or fracture a low-dimensional phase even when the rigid device is stable.

Stability claims must remain condition specific. Ambient storage should track moisture ingress and phase/composition; light soaking and MPP should track voltage, hysteresis, spectral drift, and ion redistribution; 85 °C stress should be run on the same factorial groups with the same transport layer and encapsulation; flexible devices should undergo bending at defined radius while operated or periodically measured, with EL/PL imaging for crack and interconnect localization. The additive can be credited with intrinsic stabilization only if additive/no-PEAI groups outperform no-additive/no-PEAI under matched processing and the effect survives architecture transfer. If the gain appears only with PEAI, it should be reported as synergy. If it disappears at low temperature or on SnO2, it is process/contact dependent. Small-area rigid performance, universal PEAI use, or separate flexible processing cannot by themselves establish a general additive mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Uses a crossed additive × PEAI matrix with matched controls, dose/chemistry controls, and replication on rigid TiO2 and flexible SnO2 architectures.
Separates bulk/distributed amidino effects from surface PEAI effects using depth, phase, crystallization, QFLS/recombination, and transport diagnostics.
Crosses or matches thermal budget and contact/substrate conditions to identify process-dependent phase distribution, energetics, and extraction.
Applies ambient, operational light/MPP, thermal, and bending tests to the same factorial groups and states intrinsic, synergistic, and process-dependent conclusions.
accepted_equivalents: A 2×2 factorial design, response-surface model, or ANOVA interaction analysis is acceptable if additive and PEAI main/interaction effects are isolated.
Rigid/flexible transfer may be evaluated with TiO2/SnO2 contact swaps, matched-temperature model substrates, or another controlled architecture crossover.
Depth distribution may use ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved XPS, cross-sectional microscopy/spectroscopy, or equivalent methods.
Mechanical stability may include cyclic bending under or between MPP measurements with crack, EL, PL, resistance, and retained-energy mapping.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only optimized 4AP+PEAI rigid devices with untreated controls and attributing the entire difference to 4AP.
Using separate rigid and flexible recipes without controlling annealing, contact, thickness, or phase fraction.
Combining ambient, thermal, light, and bending retention into one generic stability claim.
Assuming a surface PEAI treatment cannot interact with a bulk 2D/3D additive.

expected_answer:
Operational modules require interfaces that resist humidity, heat, ultraviolet exposure, electrical bias, thermal cycling, mechanical stress, and ion migration. Recycling, in contrast, benefits from interfaces that debond rapidly and selectively. A weak interface that is continuously susceptible to water, heat, or common solvents may therefore improve laboratory disassembly while accelerating delamination, ingress, corrosion, and lead escape in service. The interface must be conditionally labile rather than simply weak.

A credible design places a thin triggerable layer at an interface whose separation releases a recoverable sub-stack without exposing the absorber during normal use. Examples include a cleavage layer activated only by a narrowly defined solvent or pH outside environmental conditions, a thermally switchable layer triggered above the module's validated service and fire-safety envelope, or an electrically/chemically addressable bond activated after removal of the encapsulant. The trigger chemistry must be orthogonal to the perovskite, TCO, transport layers, electrode, edge seal, and lead-sequestration components. Encapsulation and on-device lead capture should remain intact until the module is inside a controlled recycling line, and the stack order should be chosen so that high-value coated glass, electrodes, and transport layers can be recovered with minimal cross-contamination.

Validation requires side-by-side modules with and without the trigger layer. Operational qualification should include damp heat, thermal cycling, ultraviolet exposure, mechanical loading, potential-induced degradation or bias stress, and maximum-power tracking, with adhesion, water-vapor ingress, interfacial chemistry, performance, and lead-release measurements. End-of-life tests should quantify activation selectivity, disassembly time and energy, component purity, solvent or reagent recovery, worker exposure, lead capture, and retained performance over multiple reuse cycles. A cradle-to-cradle TEA/LCA must include synthesis of the trigger layer, its recovery or disposal, solvent regeneration, and any reduction in module lifetime. The design succeeds only if it preserves service reliability and lead containment while increasing functional recovery and lowering total cost and environmental impact.
scoring_key_points: Identifies the stability-versus-delamination conflict and requires a conditionally labile interface rather than a generally weak or water-soluble bond.
Proposes a trigger, interface location, and encapsulation/lead-containment sequence that are orthogonal to normal outdoor stresses and compatible with architecture-specific recovery.
Defines operational qualification under coupled environmental, electrical, and mechanical stresses with adhesion, performance, ingress, and lead-release measurements.
Requires end-of-life functional-recovery metrics and full TEA/LCA including trigger manufacture, solvent/reagent regeneration, reuse cycles, and any lifetime penalty.
accepted_equivalents: Thermal, chemical, electrochemical, photochemical, or reversible supramolecular triggers are acceptable if their activation window is demonstrably outside service conditions.
A sacrificial release layer, reversible adhesive, or self-dismantling interlayer is acceptable terminology.
Extended-producer-responsibility logistics may be included as part of the controlled activation and collection system.
common_wrong_answers: Using a permanently weak adhesive and assuming encapsulation alone prevents premature delamination.
Choosing water as the trigger without demonstrating immunity to humidity, condensation, and damaged-module exposure.
Measuring only disassembly speed while omitting operational reliability, lead release, component purity, and reagent recovery.
Claiming improved sustainability without accounting for trigger-layer manufacture, solvent energy, or shortened module lifetime.

expected_answer:
The measured photoconductivity is proportional to the product of mobile-carrier density and mobility. Its decay therefore need not be a population lifetime: in a disordered CQD solid, carriers can remain present while their mobility changes as they cool, localize, redistribute among dots, or enter slower hopping states. Conversely, a smaller steady-state PL signal can reflect faster exciton dissociation or transfer into a conductive network rather than more non-radiative recombination. The simultaneous changes do not uniquely establish passivation, and a single exponential fit cannot separate density from mobility.

Carrier population should be measured independently with a calibrated population-sensitive probe such as transient absorption, fluence-dependent TRPL with an optical model, or charge extraction. Time-resolved terahertz or microwave conductivity can then be divided by the independently determined carrier density to estimate mobility evolution. Measurements over excitation density and temperature are needed to distinguish trap filling, bimolecular recombination, thermally activated hopping, and static doping. Field-effect or space-charge-limited-current measurements, dark conductivity, Seebeck/Hall measurements where feasible, and capacitance or Kelvin-probe measurements can test whether the treatment changes equilibrium carrier density rather than only interdot transfer.

Stronger coupling should produce consistent changes in activation energy, spectral overlap or excitonic features, thickness tolerance, and transport, while retaining surface passivation. The same active layer must also be tested in identical contact stacks. Contact-selective devices and half-stacks should determine whether the apparent fill-factor and current gains arise from the CQD network or from modified energy alignment, chemical doping, or extraction at the interfaces. In particular, oxygen-dependent doping of an EDT-PbS hole-transport layer must be controlled because insufficient or variable doping can alter JSC, FF, and stability independently of the bridge chemistry. Only a joint fit of population, mobility, equilibrium doping, and contact extraction can justify the proposed mechanism.
scoring_key_points: States that photoconductivity is the product of carrier density and mobility, so a slower decay is not automatically a longer recombination lifetime in a hopping CQD solid.
Uses an independent carrier-population measurement together with time-resolved conductivity, fluence, and temperature dependence to separate recombination from mobility evolution and trap filling.
Includes equilibrium-doping and interdot-coupling diagnostics rather than assigning all conductivity improvement to passivation.
Controls the device contacts and EDT-PbS oxygen-doping state with matched stacks or half-devices before attributing JSC/FF gains to the treated active layer.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, calibrated TRPL, charge extraction, or photoinduced absorption are acceptable population probes.
Time-resolved microwave conductivity may replace terahertz conductivity.
FET mobility, temperature-dependent conductivity, SCLC, or mobility-edge analysis are acceptable coupling/hopping tests.
common_wrong_answers: Equating a longer photoconductivity decay directly with a longer carrier lifetime.
Interpreting lower PL intensity as proof of increased non-radiative recombination without testing exciton dissociation or extraction.
Using only dark conductivity to claim stronger quantum coupling.
Ignoring changes in equilibrium doping, energy alignment, active-layer thickness, or EDT-PbS oxygen exposure.

expected_answer:
Scale-up must control reaction and transport, not only the nominal salt concentration. Critical variables include quantum-dot size and facet distribution, initial ligand coverage, film porosity and thickness, formamidinium-halide concentration and water content, solvent penetration, treatment time, temperature, coating speed, and the strength and duration of the acetonitrile wash. In a thick film, the top surface can be over-reacted while the interior remains under-treated; an aggressive wash can remove desired species or restructure the film, whereas an insufficient wash can leave bulk perovskite or PbI2 that falsely improves optical signatures but destabilizes the device. A process window should therefore be mapped against depth and not optimized from top-surface measurements alone.

Lot release should combine compositional stoichiometry with phase and transport tests. Depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS or cross-sectional elemental analysis can verify formamidinium and halide penetration; RBS or calibrated elemental analysis can constrain average stoichiometry. GIWAXS/XRD should confirm the intended strained interfacial environment while placing a detection limit on bulk perovskite/PbI2. Absorption/PL signatures, temperature-dependent conductivity or mobility, and thickness-dependent device performance should demonstrate coupling without excessive recombination. Spatial mapping of sheet conductance, PL, and film thickness is needed across module dimensions. A wash-control sample, an intentionally under-treated sample, and a deliberately bulk-perovskite-contaminated sample provide essential reference signatures.

Integration tests must use the final transport layers and contacts because the active-layer benefit can be masked or mimicked by contact doping. The oxygen exposure and doping state of EDT-PbS should be fixed or replaced with a contact that has a controlled activation protocol. Accelerated testing should include thermal aging across the intended process and service range, continuous illumination at maximum power, inert and oxygen-containing storage, humidity exposure appropriate to the encapsulation, and thermal cycling. Periodic structural, depth-profile, mobility, J-V, stabilized-output, and luminescence measurements should determine whether bridges remain chemically intact or convert into segregated phases. Acceptance requires uniform bridge chemistry through thickness, absence of detectable bulk residue, reproducible transport gain, and retention of performance without a new contact- or thermal-instability mode.
scoring_key_points: Controls reaction-diffusion and washing variables, including QD/facet/ligand variability and through-thickness uniformity, rather than transferring only the laboratory concentration.
Uses depth-resolved composition plus diffraction controls to verify the bridge regime and set a detection limit for residual bulk perovskite or PbI2.
Requires spatially resolved transport, optical, thickness, and device tests with under-treated, wash, and bulk-residue controls.
Validates final-contact integration and bridge persistence under thermal, illumination, atmosphere, and cycling stresses with stabilized device output.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional SIMS, angle-resolved XPS, sputter depth profiling, RBS, or micro-XRF may be used for depth and composition control.
GIWAXS, XRD, Raman, or another phase-sensitive method is acceptable if a quantitative residue-detection limit is stated.
Slot-die, blade, spray, or immersion treatment is acceptable provided mass transport and solvent recovery are addressed.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the same treatment time and concentration work at all film thicknesses.
Using only top-surface XPS or a single XRD scan to certify a micrometre-thick module film.
Treating any detectable perovskite phase as evidence of successful monolayer bridging.
Ignoring the oxygen-dependent contact-layer doping and testing only isolated films under inert storage.

expected_answer:
The experiment must treat illumination history, residual-PbI2 content, and X-ray dose as independent variables. First, the XPS measurement itself should be dose-calibrated using fresh, spatially separated spots, short acquisitions, beam-off intervals, and a time series at constant illumination. If the metallic-Pb peak grows with accumulated X-ray dose in the dark, especially on a PbI2 reference, the probe is creating at least part of the signal. Low-dose or hard-X-ray conditions and post-measurement comparison of exposed and unexposed areas can quantify this artifact.

Second, stoichiometric perovskite, deliberately PbI2-rich perovskite, isolated PbI2, and a PbI2-consuming A-site-cation-treated film should undergo identical external light aging in an inert atmosphere before any XPS exposure. Samples should be transferred without air exposure. If light-generated Pb0 scales with residual PbI2 and disappears when PbI2 is consumed, the feedstock is residual PbI2 rather than the stoichiometric lattice. If a truly stoichiometric film produces Pb0 under external light before meaningful X-ray dose, intrinsic lattice photoreduction remains plausible.

Third, a beam-independent chemical and structural signature is required. Light-aged samples should be examined by methods such as XRD for a metallic-Pb reflection, electron diffraction or HRTEM lattice spacing, iodine-loss mapping by EDS, or X-ray absorption methods run with a documented dose limit. Optical darkening, pinhole formation, and carrier-lifetime collapse can support degradation but are not specific enough alone. The complete factorial matrix—light on/off, low/high X-ray dose, and low/high residual PbI2—yields distinct predictions: pre-existing Pb0 appears at the first low-dose spectrum and is corroborated independently; PbI2-mediated photoreduction appears after external light only in PbI2-containing samples; beam damage increases with X-ray dose even without prior illumination. The claim of intrinsic perovskite photoreduction is valid only after the latter two pathways are excluded.
scoring_key_points: Treats external illumination, residual PbI2, and X-ray dose as independent variables and uses fresh-spot/dose-series controls to identify beam-induced Pb0.
Compares stoichiometric, PbI2-rich, isolated-PbI2, and PbI2-consuming-treated samples under identical inert light aging.
Requires a beam-independent Pb0 or iodine-loss signature rather than relying solely on XPS, optical darkening, or lifetime changes.
States distinct predicted outcomes for pre-existing Pb0, residual-PbI2 photodecomposition, and X-ray-induced formation, and reserves intrinsic-lattice attribution until both artifacts are excluded.
accepted_equivalents: Low-dose XPS, HAXPES, synchrotron dose extrapolation, or repeated fresh-spot measurements are acceptable beam-damage controls.
XRD, selected-area electron diffraction, HRTEM/EDS, XANES/EXAFS, or another independently dose-qualified method may corroborate metallic Pb.
MAI, GAI, DMAI, PEAI, BABr, or another demonstrably PbI2-consuming treatment is acceptable as the feedstock-removal control.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that an operando signal cannot be generated by the probe.
Using only one nominally stoichiometric film without measuring residual PbI2.
Calling PL quenching or film darkening a unique fingerprint of metallic Pb.
Comparing spectra acquired with different X-ray doses and attributing peak growth solely to illumination time.

expected_answer:
The production strategy should control both the amount of residual PbI2 and its photon history. PbI2 precursor, coated intermediate films, and partially processed modules should be stored and transported in dark, inert, temperature-controlled conditions with defined maximum exposure time. Lot genealogy should record light dose, water/oxygen exposure, and storage age. Fresh and deliberately light-aged precursor lots should be processed in parallel during qualification so that the line is sensitive to precursor-history effects rather than only final stoichiometry.

A useful small PbI2 excess need not be eliminated before crystallization, but residual PbI2 left in the final film should be consumed or converted after it has served its processing/passivation role. A calibrated A-site or bulky-ammonium-halide treatment can convert the residue into a stable mixed-dimensional or passivating phase while removing the feedstock for Pb0 formation. The dose must be optimized: insufficient treatment leaves PbI2, whereas excess treatment can create transport barriers, phase inhomogeneity, or ionic instability. Stoichiometric, excess-PbI2, and excess-PbI2-plus-treatment controls are required on every process transfer.

Release diagnostics should quantify residual PbI2 and Pb0 with low-dose, artifact-aware methods; phase-sensitive XRD/GIWAXS, surface/depth composition, optical or luminescence mapping, and calibrated electrical metrics can be combined. A stable optical bandgap and integrated photocurrent, together with declining VOC/FF, QFLS, built-in potential, or depletion width and increasing trap density/depth, indicate recombination/electrostatic degradation rather than loss of spectral absorption. The stress matrix should include fresh versus aged precursor, dark storage versus one-sun illumination, temperature, electrical bias or maximum-power operation, and encapsulated versus unencapsulated conditions. Periodic XPS must use dose controls to avoid creating the defect being measured. Acceptance should be based on stabilized MPP retention, low non-radiative voltage loss, stable Vbi/trap energetics, and absence of Pb0 growth, not only initial PCE.
scoring_key_points: Controls and records PbI2 precursor/intermediate light, atmosphere, temperature, and storage history, with fresh-versus-aged lot qualification.
Uses an optimized post-crystallization PbI2-consuming treatment that retains passivation but removes the Pb0 feedstock, with stoichiometric and untreated controls.
Implements artifact-aware phase/composition and optoelectronic release tests that separate unchanged bandgap/JSC from VOC/FF, Vbi, depletion-width, and trap degradation.
Uses coupled illumination, temperature, bias/MPP, atmosphere, and encapsulation stresses with stabilized-output and Pb0-growth acceptance criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Bulky ammonium bromide/iodide, A-site cation salts, or another treatment is acceptable if it demonstrably consumes residual PbI2 without blocking transport.
QFLS, electroluminescence efficiency, Suns-VOC, or absolute PLQY are acceptable non-radiative-voltage metrics.
Admittance spectroscopy, DLCP, thermally stimulated current, or another trap-energetics method may replace a specific trap measurement.
common_wrong_answers: Removing all PbI2 indiscriminately without testing whether it was needed for film formation or interface passivation.
Qualifying precursor lots only by nominal composition and ignoring storage/light history.
Attributing degradation to a bandgap shift despite stable EQE-integrated current and optical gap.
Using repeated high-dose XPS as the sole release test for metallic Pb.

expected_answer:
The result is consistent with a selective trade-off: the low-dimensional phase may passivate defects and block mobile ions or moisture, increasing QFLS and VOC, while its larger exciton binding energy, insulating organic spacing, poor out-of-plane orientation, or unfavorable energy alignment slows charge transfer and lowers JSC and FF. The design should therefore keep the highly transporting three-dimensional absorber as the bulk and confine the quasi-2D material to an ultrathin surface, grain-boundary, or contact-adjacent region where it can passivate and impede ion exchange without becoming a series transport layer.

Optimization variables include the organic spacer length and dipole, n-value distribution, halide composition, orientation, coverage, energetic offset, and thickness. A composition or thickness gradient can provide a chemically robust outer surface while preserving a 3D percolation path. The treatment should be compared on both electron- and hole-extraction sides because the same energetic barrier may be benign at one contact and harmful at the other. A dose series with a deliberately over-thick control is needed to identify the onset of transport limitation.

Electronic validation requires absolute PL/QFLS and electroluminescence for non-radiative loss, contact-selective TRPL or transient absorption for transfer, TPC/TPV and charge extraction for collection/recombination, and mobility or contact-resistance measurements for the transport penalty. Ionic validation should include prebias/scan-rate dependence, low-frequency impedance or ion-drift measurements, temperature-dependent activation behavior, and dark recovery. Chemical stability should be tested under damp heat, illumination, oxygen, and thermal cycling, while complete devices operate at maximum power. The treatment is beneficial only if stabilized energy yield and lifetime improve: reduced ionic response and better chemical durability must coexist with preserved current collection and fill factor, rather than being inferred from lower hysteresis or higher VOC alone.
scoring_key_points: Identifies the passivation/ion-blocking benefit and the excitonic, energetic, orientation, or resistive mechanism that can reduce JSC and FF.
Confines or grades the low-dimensional phase at a targeted interface/grain boundary while retaining a continuous 3D transport network.
Optimizes spacer, n-value, orientation, coverage, band alignment, and thickness with dose and contact-side controls that expose the transport threshold.
Requires agreement among electronic-transfer, ionic-response, coupled-stress, maximum-power, and lifetime/energy-yield measurements before claiming a net benefit.
accepted_equivalents: A 2D/3D gradient, self-assembled monolayer-like spacer, grain-boundary decoration, or ultrathin capping layer is acceptable if a 3D percolation path remains.
Time-of-flight, impedance, transient absorption, TPC, charge extraction, or contact-resistance measurements may be used to quantify transport.
Ion-drift, bias-stress recovery, ToF-SIMS under bias, or low-frequency capacitance may be used to quantify ionic stabilization.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing the low-dimensional layer thickness until hysteresis disappears without checking current or series resistance.
Using a higher VOC alone to claim that the treatment improves overall carrier dynamics.
Assuming humidity stability proves suppression of electrically driven ion migration.
Testing only isolated films and omitting maximum-power operation and contact-specific extraction measurements.

expected_answer:
A flat witness film does not reproduce capillary filling, local thickness, curvature, or drying at a textured buried interface, so its PL and TRPL cannot exclude voids or incomplete contact in the tandem. Buried voiding or premature crystallization should be tested by cross-sectional FIB-SEM, tomography, or serial sectioning at electrically hot and cold locations, combined with lock-in thermography, electroluminescence, and dark-current mapping. If the defect originates from hot-substrate or overly rapid gas-knife crystallization, void density and shunting should increase with substrate temperature or early/strong drying and should fall when coating and crystallization are temporally separated.

Wetting and planarization should be varied through solvent coordination, DMSO/Pb ratio, wet-film thickness, coating speed, gas-knife timing, substrate surface energy, and texture statistics. Contact-angle or meniscus imaging, in-line thickness mapping, and cross-sections should show whether valleys remain unfilled. A successful wetting correction should reduce spatial shunts without materially changing bulk QFLS or flat-film lifetime. Flat, textured, and texture-depth-series substrates coated in the same run provide the essential geometry control.

PTAA and contact resistance require a separate thickness series, sheet/contact-resistance measurements, and hole-only or selective-contact devices. Excessively thick or nonuniform PTAA should raise series resistance and reduce FF broadly, but need not create buried voids or localized leakage. Bulk perovskite defects should instead appear in absolute PL/QFLS, electroluminescence efficiency, absorption or XRD uniformity, and recombination maps on both flat and textured samples. A crossover matrix—optimized bulk ink on altered texture/wetting, and altered ink on a verified interface—should identify whether the causal variable is chemistry, geometry, or contact. The assignment is accepted only when the predicted structural and electrical signatures co-localize and the targeted process change rescues stabilized tandem performance.
scoring_key_points: Explains why flat-film PL/TRPL cannot rule out texture-specific buried voids, wetting failure, or contact defects.

Uses cross-sectional imaging and spatial electrical/optical mapping with substrate-temperature, drying, solvent-coordination, coating, and texture controls to test interfacial voiding and planarization.
Separates PTAA/contact resistance using thickness and contact-resistivity controls from bulk recombination using absolute PL/QFLS and matched flat/textured films.
Requires geometry/chemistry/contact crossover controls, predicted co-localized signatures, and rescue of stabilized device performance for causal assignment.
accepted_equivalents: X-ray nano-tomography, acoustic microscopy, cross-sectional TEM, or destructive serial polishing may replace FIB-SEM if buried voids are resolved.
PL, EL, LBIC, lock-in thermography, dark-current, or photocurrent mapping are acceptable spatial diagnostics when interpreted with structure.
Surface-energy modification, solvent/additive tuning, or gas-knife timing may be used as the wetting/planarization intervention.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that good flat-film TRPL proves the textured buried interface is defect-free.
Attributing all low FF to bulk traps without imaging the interface or measuring series/contact resistance.
Changing several coating variables simultaneously and treating any performance improvement as mechanistic proof.
Using only top-view SEM, which can miss voids beneath a planarized surface.

expected_answer:
A square-metre module introduces distributions that are nearly absent in a small cell. The sub-micrometre pyramid height, angle and density, PTAA thickness, wet-film thickness, DMSO coordination, coating speed, gas-knife flow, and annealing temperature must be mapped across the web or panel. In-line reflectometry, imaging, thickness/roughness metrology, PL/EL mapping, and statistical cross-sections should define a process-capability window for complete planarization without buried voids. Coating qualification should include start/stop regions, edges, drying gradients, and solvent recovery, not only a central coupon.

Because the tandem is two-terminal, local current mismatch limits the entire series-connected area. Spectrally resolved subcell EQE, angle- and temperature-dependent optical modelling, and outdoor spectral monitoring are needed to verify current matching across the module. PDMS light-scattering or antireflection structures must be integrated with an encapsulant and front sheet that retain refractive index, texture, adhesion, UV stability, and cleanliness; an optical gain measured on an exposed laboratory layer may disappear after lamination or aging. Transparent electrodes, recombination layers, metal grids, laser-scribed interconnects, and busbars require sheet/contact-resistance, dead-area, and thermal-hotspot optimization as lateral current paths increase.

Reliability testing should combine maximum-power operation with damp heat, humidity-freeze, thermal cycling, UV exposure, mechanical load, hail or abrasion as relevant, and repeated temperature/spectral changes. Edge seals and lead-sequestration layers must be tested after mechanical damage and water ingress. Failure analysis should separate perovskite photochemical/ionic degradation, contact corrosion, delamination, PDMS/encapsulant optical change, interconnect resistance, and current-mismatch drift through spatially resolved electrical and optical measurements. The 100 h laboratory result is short, uses a small unencapsulated or laboratory-configured device under controlled illumination, and does not sample outdoor spectra, temperature cycles, moisture ingress, mechanical stress, large-area defects, or interconnection losses. Qualification must therefore be based on stabilized module energy yield and failure-mode-resolved lifetime, not retention of one cell under one stress.
scoring_key_points: Defines large-area process-capability and spatial metrology for texture, PTAA, wet/dry film thickness, solvent coordination, drying, planarization, and buried-void control.
Addresses two-terminal subcell current matching under spectral, angular, temperature, and spatial variation together with module-scale interconnection and resistive losses.
Integrates the PDMS/optical concept with encapsulation, UV/thermal/adhesion durability, edge sealing, and lead containment rather than treating the laboratory optical layer as module-ready.
Requires maximum-power coupled-stress qualification and failure-mode-resolved spatial diagnostics, and explains why 100 h laboratory retention does not represent outdoor module durability.
accepted_equivalents: IEC-style damp heat, thermal cycling, humidity-freeze, UV, mechanical-load, and MPP protocols are acceptable even if exact standard numbers are not cited.
An alternative durable textured front sheet or antireflection structure may replace PDMS if its optical function is preserved after lamination.
LBIC, EL, PL, thermography, distributed I-V, or submodule segmentation may be used for spatial failure localization.
common_wrong_answers: Extrapolating 100 h cell retention linearly to a multi-year module lifetime.
Assuming uniform current matching from one central EQE measurement.
Ignoring series resistance, scribe/interconnect dead area, and hotspot formation during area scaling.
Testing optical performance before encapsulation but not after UV, heat, moisture, and mechanical aging.

expected_answer: LCOE is governed by both the discounted cost numerator and the discounted lifetime-energy denominator, so a higher initial efficiency is not sufficient. The tandem gains annual energy per area, but a short service life and faster degradation reduce the cumulative energy sold, especially after discounting. Costly transport, contact, and recombination layers, poor material utilization in evaporation, and lower production yield raise the cost per saleable module; these penalties can exceed the cost of the perovskite absorber itself and can dominate even when facility cost is similar. The diagnosis should first build a harmonized bill of materials and process-flow model, converting scrap and yield loss into cost per delivered watt or square metre. It should then vary efficiency, lifetime, degradation rate, layer cost, utilization, yield, throughput, and capital cost independently and jointly, reporting elasticities or LCOE changes and break-even thresholds. A global uncertainty or Monte Carlo analysis is preferable after one-at-a-time screening because lifetime, yield, and process choice are correlated. The dominant penalty is the variable whose realistic improvement most reduces LCOE, not necessarily the variable with the largest laboratory performance effect.
scoring_key_points: Explains LCOE as a balance between discounted total cost and discounted lifetime energy, so initial efficiency alone cannot determine competitiveness.
Identifies short lifetime and faster degradation as reductions in cumulative energy yield that can erase the tandem efficiency advantage.

Identifies expensive functional layers, poor evaporation utilization, and lower production yield as potentially dominant cost-per-saleable-module penalties, while similar facility cost need not dominate.

Proposes harmonized one-at-a-time and joint sensitivity or uncertainty analysis with break-even thresholds for efficiency, lifetime, degradation, material cost, utilization, yield, throughput, and capital cost.
accepted_equivalents: Net present cost divided by net present electricity generation is equivalent to the numerator-denominator explanation of LCOE.
Scrap rate, line yield, uptime, and rework may be grouped as manufacturing-yield penalties.
Elasticity analysis, tornado plots, Sobol analysis, or Monte Carlo break-even analysis are acceptable sensitivity methods when inputs are normalized consistently.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that the 30% tandem must have lower LCOE because efficiency is the only relevant variable.
Blaming the perovskite absorber price while ignoring expensive transport, contact, and recombination layers and process utilization.
Comparing cell PCE and nominal module cost without including degradation, lifetime, production yield, and discounting.

expected_answer: The two designs must be compared on a common commercial functional unit, not on champion-cell efficiency. Stage 1 should create a process-resolved bill of materials and cost model that includes material price, utilization, deposition rate, throughput, equipment depreciation, energy use, labor, yield, rework, and module interconnection losses. High-cost gold or organic layers and low-utilization vacuum processing should be treated as explicit redesign targets because the absorber itself is unlikely to be the main cost bottleneck. Stage 2 should demonstrate scalable coating uniformity and reproducible module efficiency, including geometric fill factor, subcell current matching, recombination-layer yield, and defect tolerance. Stage 3 should measure degradation and failure modes under light, heat, humidity, thermal cycling, and partial-shading or reverse-bias stress, then translate the observed lifetime and annual degradation into discounted lifetime energy. Stage 4 should couple the validated inputs to LCOE sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, define break-even combinations of efficiency, lifetime, yield, and layer cost, and reject a design whose advantage depends on implausible assumptions. Design B can be superior despite lower PCE if its materials, utilization, yield, and durability produce lower cost per delivered lifetime kilowatt-hour.
scoring_key_points: Requires a harmonized process-resolved cost and LCOE comparison rather than ranking designs by champion-cell efficiency.
Prioritizes replacement or minimization of expensive electrodes, transport layers, recombination layers, and low-utilization vacuum steps while accounting for throughput and yield.
Requires scalable module evidence and quantified reliability under relevant environmental and fault stresses, with degradation converted into lifetime energy yield.
Uses sensitivity, uncertainty, and break-even analysis to set go/no-go thresholds for efficiency, lifetime, degradation, yield, utilization, and layer cost.
accepted_equivalents: Printed, coated, or otherwise high-throughput solution processing may replace the named printing route if utilization and yield are quantified.
Bankability or warranty evidence may substitute for some accelerated tests when the field-to-acceleration relationship is justified.
Cost per watt, minimum sustainable price, and LCOE may all be used, but the final decision must include lifetime electricity generation.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting Design A solely because its certified cell efficiency is higher.
Assuming abundant materials guarantee low cost without measuring utilization, throughput, uniformity, and production yield.
Using a 1000-hour stability result as a direct commercial lifetime without a degradation model or validated acceleration factor.

expected_answer: At minimum, the study needs four thickness-matched conditions: an untreated abrupt bilayer; quantum dots treated before deposition so their ligand shell and interdot transport are improved without allowing interfacial halide exchange; a stacked bilayer exposed to the gradient-forming treatment; and an independently fabricated composition-gradient or mixed-halide interfacial control that reproduces the depth profile without the same ligand treatment. Single-layer and absorption-matched controls are also needed. Quantum-dot transport or passivation should primarily lower film resistance, raise mobility, reduce trap-assisted recombination, and improve fill factor or voltage even when depth composition remains abrupt. A genuine bandgap gradient should produce a reproducible halide and band-edge profile, altered depth-dependent absorption or luminescence, and improved collection of long-wavelength carriers without requiring a thicker absorber. Extra thickness alone should raise absorption and possibly photocurrent but usually increases series resistance and may lower fill factor. Composition must be verified with at least one orthogonal depth method that controls sputter broadening, such as calibrated XPS or ToF-SIMS plus cross-sectional nano-XRF, EDS/EELS, or optical-bandgap mapping. Transport and recombination should be measured by impedance, mobility or SCLC, transient spectroscopy, and PL, while wavelength-resolved EQE, bias-dependent EQE, and J-V/MPP tests identify where the current gain originates.
scoring_key_points: Defines controls that independently vary quantum-dot surface treatment, interfacial halide grading, and absorber thickness or optical density.
Predicts that ligand/passivation improvement mainly changes resistance, mobility, traps, fill factor, or voltage without requiring a composition gradient.

Predicts that a true gradient requires a depth-resolved composition and band-edge profile plus improved long-wavelength carrier collection, whereas thickness alone can increase absorption but worsen series resistance.
Requires orthogonal composition profiling with sputter-artifact controls and complementary transport, recombination, spectral-EQE, and stabilized-output measurements.
accepted_equivalents: A factorial design with ligand chemistry and interdiffusion time as independent variables is equivalent to the four-arm matrix.
Cross-sectional cathodoluminescence, Kelvin probe mapping, nano-FTIR, or photothermal-deflection spectroscopy may support the bandgap-gradient assignment.
Time-resolved microwave conductivity, field-effect mobility, or impedance-derived transport may substitute for SCLC.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all improvement to the graded bandgap because a broadened absorption edge is observed.
Using only sputter-depth XPS without assessing ion mixing, preferential sputtering, or depth-calibration artifacts.
Comparing films of different thickness and treating higher absorption as proof of improved charge collection.

expected_answer: The scale-up must preserve solvent orthogonality so that the second coating does not dissolve or roughen the first, while still allowing a controlled amount of interdiffusion. The gradient should be set by post-treatment activity, wet-film residence time, temperature, drying rate, and web speed; too little exchange leaves an abrupt barrier, whereas excessive exchange can erase the designed bandgap profile or destabilize the wide-bandgap layer. Quantum-dot ligand removal or crosslinking and final thickness must be controlled because thicker films add absorption but increase interdot and vertical resistance. A continuous process should therefore use thickness and spectral-absorption mapping, sheet resistance or contactless conductivity, PL or hyperspectral imaging, and defect inspection across the web; calibrated depth composition and band-edge measurements can be performed at-line on sampled coupons to correlate with the in-line signals. Process capability should be judged by module-scale EQE uniformity, fill factor, stabilized power, and yield, not small-cell champion PCE. Because the all-inorganic label does not confer moisture immunity, low-water processing, rapid encapsulation, edge seals, and water-vapor transmission control are mandatory. Qualification should include damp heat or controlled-humidity exposure, thermal cycling, light soaking, and monitoring for phase yellowing, gradient relaxation, resistance growth, and delamination.
scoring_key_points: Controls solvent orthogonality and interdiffusion through treatment activity, residence time, temperature, drying rate, and web speed to maintain a finite composition gradient.
Controls quantum-dot ligand state, crosslinking, and thickness to balance added absorption against interdot and vertical series resistance.
Defines cross-web optical, electrical, defect, and sampled depth-profile quality controls tied to module EQE, fill factor, stabilized power, and yield.

Includes moisture-exclusion processing, rapid encapsulation and edge sealing, plus humidity, thermal, and illumination qualification for phase change, gradient relaxation, resistance growth, and delamination.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, blade, spray, gravure, or other continuous coating methods are acceptable if solvent and residence-time control are specified.
Inline XRF, ellipsometry, reflectance, photoluminescence, terahertz conductivity, or machine-vision metrics may serve as process-control observables.
Barrier laminates, atomic-layer-deposited barriers, or multilayer encapsulation are acceptable moisture safeguards.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that the same spin speed and dip time can be directly converted to web speed without a mass-transfer or drying model.
Maximizing QD-layer thickness to increase absorption while ignoring series resistance and fill-factor loss.
Claiming that an all-inorganic absorber removes the need for humidity control or encapsulation.

expected_answer: TRPL lifetime is not an intrinsic defect count unless the device boundary conditions are fixed. On inert glass, where there is no selective extraction pathway, a longer lifetime together with higher PL yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting indicates reduced bulk or surface non-radiative recombination. On SnO2, a shorter decay can result from rapid electron transfer out of the perovskite, which is beneficial, but the same signature could also arise from interfacial recombination. The distinction requires correlated measurements. Beneficial extraction should be accompanied by improved energy-level or work-function alignment, stronger but controlled PL quenching at the contact, faster photocurrent or transient-absorption transfer, lower interfacial resistance, reduced ideality factor, and improved voltage or fill factor without a loss of radiative efficiency in the isolated film. Interfacial recombination would instead reduce PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, increase voltage deficit, and often increase trap-assisted signatures. Measurements must use matched thickness, absorption, excitation density, and surface treatment, and should compare glass/perovskite, glass/modifier/perovskite, SnO2/perovskite, and SnO2/modifier/perovskite structures. Work-function mapping and stability tracking can further test whether the modifier removes the buried electrical discontinuity rather than merely accelerating a lossy decay channel.
scoring_key_points: Explains that longer TRPL on inert glass can indicate lower non-radiative recombination or trap density when no extraction contact is present.
Explains that shorter TRPL on SnO2 can indicate faster electron transfer, but recognizes that interfacial recombination can produce the same raw decay trend.

Distinguishes beneficial extraction from lossy quenching using PLQY or QFLS, transient extraction, impedance or resistance, ideality factor, work-function alignment, and device voltage or fill factor.
Requires matched optical and structural controls across inert-substrate and selective-contact half stacks rather than comparing lifetimes in different boundary conditions directly.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption, time-resolved microwave conductivity, transient photocurrent, or terahertz spectroscopy may replace the named extraction probes.
Electroluminescence efficiency or non-radiative voltage loss may replace PLQY/QFLS when measured and interpreted consistently.
Lower interfacial recombination velocity plus higher transfer rate is an acceptable formal description of the desired outcome.
common_wrong_answers: Treating every shorter photoluminescence lifetime as evidence of higher defect density.
Calling every strong PL quench efficient extraction without checking voltage loss, PLQY/QFLS, or trap-assisted recombination.
Comparing lifetimes from different substrates without matching thickness, excitation density, absorption, and interface chemistry.

expected_answer: The process variables should include molecule concentration, solvent water content, immersion or coating time, rinse, drying or curing temperature, substrate age, and line speed. Coverage and chemical attachment should be mapped by XPS or ToF-SIMS, contact angle, and preferably spatial work-function mapping or UPS/KPFM; a uniform amount of molecule is not sufficient if its dipole gives the wrong energy shift. Mechanical performance should be measured by peel or fracture testing and by adhesion mapping before and after light, heat, humidity, and thermal cycling. Electrical qualification should correlate local work function with contact resistance, ideality factor, PLQY/QFLS, extraction dynamics, fill factor, and spatial electroluminescence. Negative controls should include the same anchoring chemistry with an opposite or weak terminal dipole, a strong-binding analogue that does not correct the work function, and a process blank, allowing adhesion and electronic alignment to be separated. Downstream controls should vary perovskite annealing and solvent exposure to test SAM displacement or decomposition. Go/no-go limits should require bounded cross-web work-function mismatch, minimum interfacial fracture energy, no systematic work-function drift or local PbI2 growth during MPP aging, stable module fill factor and yield, and no persistent delamination after combined environmental and operational stress.
scoring_key_points: Defines process variables and spatial chemical or coverage measurements, including direct work-function mapping rather than assuming nominal SAM deposition is uniform.
Separates mechanical adhesion from electronic dipole alignment using peel or fracture tests and electrical or optical contact diagnostics.
Uses negative controls with matched anchoring but opposite or weak dipoles, plus strong-binding or process-blank controls, and tests downstream solvent or annealing compatibility.

Sets go/no-go criteria for work-function uniformity and drift, adhesion, recombination or extraction, fill factor and yield, PbI2 or chemical evolution, and delamination under combined MPP and environmental aging.
accepted_equivalents: Scanning Kelvin probe, photoelectron spectroscopy, or contact-potential mapping may substitute for KPFM when spatial resolution is adequate.
Four-point bend, double-cantilever-beam, scratch, blister, or peel testing are acceptable interfacial-adhesion methods.
An amine-terminated or otherwise opposite-dipole analogue is an acceptable negative control if anchoring and coverage are comparable.
common_wrong_answers: Measuring only average XPS coverage and assuming that correct work-function tuning and adhesion follow automatically.
Using a no-SAM control only, which cannot separate terminal-group dipole effects from generic surface coverage.
Qualifying the process from initial small-cell PCE without spatial mapping or post-stress work-function, adhesion, and chemical checks.

expected_answer: The minimum analogue set should include the untreated control; an ammonium-containing analogue that preserves facet interaction but lacks the sulfur or Lewis-base group needed for strong SnO2/Pb passivation; a sulfur- or Lewis-base-containing analogue that can passivate the interface but lacks the cationic head responsible for facet-selective binding; the bifunctional molecule; and ideally a physical mixture of the two monofunctional analogues or a separately deposited interfacial passivator. In situ GIWAXS or GIXRD should quantify nucleation time, alpha-phase formation, azimuthal texture, and growth kinetics, while ToF-SIMS and XPS should establish where each molecule accumulates and whether SnO2 oxygen-vacancy/hydroxyl and perovskite Pb defects are reduced. PLQY or QFLS on glass and on SnO2, SCLC, transient transfer, and device voltage, fill factor, and stability should separate bulk orientation effects from buried-contact losses. An orientation-only analogue should reproduce texture with limited buried-interface chemical improvement; a passivation-only analogue should improve interfacial recombination or extraction without reproducing strong texture; the bifunctional molecule should combine both signatures and outperform either arm. If the physical mixture matches the bifunctional molecule, covalent role integration is not essential; if it does not, coupled spatial delivery or intramolecular geometry is part of the mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Defines monofunctional facet-binding and interface-passivating analogues, the bifunctional molecule, an untreated control, and preferably a two-molecule mixture or separate-interface control.
Uses in situ diffraction to isolate nucleation and orientation, and depth-resolved chemical analysis to verify buried enrichment and defect coordination.
Uses substrate-dependent PLQY/QFLS, trap or transport measurements, and device metrics to separate orientation-driven bulk effects from buried-interface recombination and extraction.
Specifies the predicted outcome pattern for orientation-only, passivation-only, bifunctional, and mixture controls, including what would demonstrate coupled spatial delivery.
accepted_equivalents: A head-group-swapped homologous molecular series is acceptable if steric size and concentration are controlled.
GIWAXS, pole figures, or azimuthal diffraction may replace GIXRD for texture analysis.
Surface photovoltage, transient absorption, impedance, or electroluminescence-derived voltage loss may complement or replace individual electronic probes.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only the bifunctional additive with an untreated film and attributing every improvement to both proposed functions.
Using ex situ XRD texture alone to claim that orientation caused the voltage and stability gains.
Assuming buried sulfur enrichment proves defect passivation without chemical-state and recombination evidence.

expected_answer: Buried enrichment is a kinetic and interfacial-partitioning outcome, not an inherent property of adding the molecule to the ink. Slot-die coating changes wet-film thickness, solvent evaporation, convection, residence time, antisolvent history, and crystallization rate, so the additive may remain in the bulk, accumulate at the top surface, or form an insulating or low-dimensional phase. A different electron-transport layer may not provide the same oxygen-vacancy, hydroxyl, Lewis-acid, or surface-energy interactions that attract the original sulfur-containing group. The plan should map additive concentration, solvent coordination, substrate surface chemistry, drying temperature, gas-knife or quench conditions, coating speed, and annealing using in situ GIWAXS and cross-sectional chemical profiling. Molecular analogues or modified terminal groups should be screened when the new ETL requires different binding chemistry. Cross-web texture, PL or QFLS, contact extraction, sheet or vertical conductivity, thickness, and defect maps should be correlated with module voltage, fill factor, yield, and stabilized power. The process must also verify that no detectable 2D or impurity phase forms and that residual additive does not impede transport. Finally, module qualification should use a thermally stable transport stack and combined light, heat, humidity, and thermal-cycling tests, with post-stress depth profiles and orientation measurements to determine whether additive segregation, interface passivation, and texture remain intact.
scoring_key_points: Explains that buried enrichment depends on drying, diffusion, crystallization, wet-film thickness, and substrate affinity, all of which change in slot-die coating.
Recognizes that a different electron-transport layer may require different terminal-group chemistry because its defects, hydroxylation, Lewis acidity, and surface energy differ from SnO2.

Defines a process map using in situ texture measurements, cross-sectional additive localization, and cross-web optical, electrical, thickness, and defect controls tied to module performance and yield.
Requires checks against insulating or low-dimensional phases and verifies retention of segregation, passivation, orientation, and transport after combined operational and environmental aging.
accepted_equivalents: Blade, meniscus, gravure, or other scalable coating can substitute for slot-die if the altered drying and segregation kinetics are addressed.
ToF-SIMS, neutron or X-ray reflectometry, angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy, or labeled-molecule profiling may establish additive location.
Terminal-group redesign, ETL surface functionalization, or a controlled pre-deposited anchor layer are acceptable ways to restore selective buried localization.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that the same additive concentration will produce the same depth distribution in every coating method and on every ETL.
Optimizing only XRD texture while ignoring additive location, buried-interface recombination, and vertical transport.
Interpreting any new low-angle diffraction peak or thicker organic-rich interface as beneficial passivation without checking transport and phase identity.

expected_answer: The shorter TRPL lifetime does not, by itself, indicate poorer material quality. In a perovskite/charge-selective-contact bilayer, TRPL quenching can become faster because carriers are extracted more rapidly across the buried interface. That interpretation is consistent with the independent device-level evidence: a lower Voc-light-intensity slope indicates less trap-assisted recombination, a longer transient-photovoltage lifetime indicates slower recombination of photogenerated carriers under device-like conditions, and the lower SCLC-derived trap density is consistent with fewer electrically active traps. The UPS shift supports a reduced energetic barrier or improved selectivity, while the reduced tensile strain can lower defect formation and ion-migration propensity. The defensible conclusion is therefore a coupled mechanism involving improved extraction/energy alignment, interfacial passivation, and strain regulation. It is not defensible to claim that the shorter TRPL proves lower bulk lifetime, that SCLC directly counts all defects, or that any one mechanism has been quantitatively isolated as the sole cause of the efficiency gain.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes contact-induced TRPL quenching from device recombination and explains why a shorter TRPL lifetime can indicate faster extraction.
Uses the lower Voc-light slope, longer TPV lifetime, and lower SCLC-derived trap density as convergent evidence for suppressed trap-assisted recombination.
Connects UPS energy-level changes and reduced tensile strain to improved selectivity/extraction and lower defect or ion-migration propensity.
States the causal limits: SCLC is model dependent, the lifetime measurements probe different physics, and the individual mechanisms are not quantitatively deconvolved.
accepted_equivalents: Interfacial charge-transfer quenching instead of bulk nonradiative quenching
Reduced ideality factor or reduced Shockley-Read-Hall recombination
Multifunctional buried-interface engineering rather than single-cause passivation
Trap-filled-limit analysis as an indirect estimate rather than a direct defect census
common_wrong_answers: Interpreting the shorter TRPL lifetime as conclusive evidence of more traps or faster recombination.
Treating TPV and TRPL lifetimes as interchangeable measurements of the same process.
Attributing all improvements solely to trap passivation while ignoring extraction, energy alignment, and strain.
Claiming that the SCLC number is a direct and complete count of microscopic defects.

expected_answer: A minimal design must separate photon-energy effects from atmospheric effects and from ordinary operational stress. At minimum, matched devices should be aged under (i) monochromatic near-UV light in nitrogen, which probes UV-driven photochemistry without oxygen or moisture; (ii) the same UV dose in air, which adds oxygen/moisture-assisted degradation; and (iii) white-light maximum-power-point operation at matched temperature, which tests normal carrier, field, and ion-migration stress. The control set should include the untreated interface, the active interlayer, an optically matched but chemically inert UV-filter control, and preferably a chemically similar non-photoactive analogue or an independently strain-modified control. Spectral transmission must verify equal absorbed UV dose. Before, during, and after aging, the study should track stabilized PCE/T90, Voc/FF and hysteresis, PLQY or QFLS, interfacial recombination transients, XRD/GIWAXS strain and phase evolution, and chemical changes by XPS or related spectroscopy. Module transfer additionally requires spatial maps of coating thickness, strain, PL/electroluminescence, shunts, and series resistance, plus statistically meaningful aperture-efficiency and encapsulated damp-heat/operational tests. A single retention curve cannot assign the protection mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Separates UV-in-inert, UV-in-air, and white-light operational aging instead of collapsing them into one stability test.
Uses controls that decouple optical filtering from chemical passivation and strain modification, with matched UV dose or transmission.
Combines device metrics with structural, optical/recombination, and chemical readouts to identify the dominant degradation pathway.
Adds large-area uniformity, yield, shunt/resistance mapping, encapsulation, and module-relevant aging as transfer criteria.
accepted_equivalents: A factorial light-atmosphere-control design
An inert chromophore or external UV-filter control with matched optical density
Operando diffraction or Raman strain mapping instead of ex situ GIWAXS
Electroluminescence or lock-in thermography for module nonuniformity and shunt mapping
common_wrong_answers: Using only one white-light shelf or MPP test and assigning all improvement to UV protection.
Comparing unmatched light doses, temperatures, or encapsulation conditions.
Reporting only champion PCE retention without structural or interfacial diagnostics.
Assuming a small-area spin-coated result transfers to modules without spatial-uniformity and yield measurements.

expected_answer: At fixed electronic band gap, a moderate increase in exciton binding energy can move or strengthen bound-exciton absorption below the continuum edge and thereby add near-band-edge absorbed photons. This raises Jsc only if those excitons dissociate efficiently into free carriers at the operating temperature and internal field, and if the intervention does not introduce traps, energetic disorder, transport barriers, or parasitic recombination. If the binding energy becomes too large relative to thermal energy and interfacial dissociation driving force, the free-carrier yield can fall; any gain in absorptance can then be offset by lower EQE, Voc, or FF. The transfer decision must therefore be composition specific because dielectric screening, vacancy chemistry, phase segregation, and band alignment all change with band gap and halide ratio. A go decision requires: a reproducible increase in excitonic oscillator strength/Elliott-fitted binding energy; field- and temperature-dependent EQE or ultrafast free-carrier-yield measurements showing efficient dissociation; an integrated near-edge current gain that matches stabilized Jsc; and no loss in QFLS/Voc, FF, ion-migration resistance, or operational stability. Failure of any of these device-level closure tests is a no-go even if the optical binding energy increases.
scoring_key_points: Explains how stronger bound-exciton absorption can add near-edge photons at fixed electronic band gap.
States that the benefit requires efficient exciton dissociation and collection under operating temperature, field, and interface conditions.
Identifies the failure mode of excessive binding or new disorder/traps causing lower free-carrier yield, Voc, or FF.
Defines composition-specific go/no-go tests that close optical spectroscopy to EQE/Jsc, QFLS/transport, ion migration, and stabilized operation.
accepted_equivalents: Comparing binding energy with kBT and interfacial charge-transfer driving force
Field-dependent photoluminescence quenching or time-resolved microwave conductivity for dissociation yield
External quantum efficiency plus optical modeling as the collection test
Rejecting the strategy when optical gain is not converted into stabilized electrical output
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a larger exciton binding energy is always beneficial.
Considering only absorption and ignoring exciton dissociation and free-carrier collection.
Transferring the same precursor recipe without re-evaluating dielectric screening and halide-vacancy chemistry.
Using a higher peak Jsc alone as the go criterion while ignoring Voc, FF, hysteresis, and stability.

expected_answer: Bulk HTM mobility is only one part of contact performance. The relevant device descriptors also include valence-band/HOMO alignment, electron blocking, interfacial contact resistance, film continuity, chemical passivation, and whether the solvent or dopants damage the nanocrystal solid. Likewise, a shorter PL lifetime can arise from desired interfacial hole transfer or from undesired nonradiative quenching. Uniform lifetime shortening combined with higher photocurrent, faster transient photocurrent, low contact resistance, and preserved or improved QFLS supports extraction; XPS shifts and reduced trap signatures support chemical passivation. Dark spatial patches, reduced PLQY/QFLS, and local electrical loss indicate damage even if the topography is smooth. Essential controls include the same solvent/dopant treatment without the HTM, doped versus undoped material C, an inert polymer or insulating spacer with matched thickness, and bilayers with a hole-blocking contact. Spatially resolved PL/FastFLIM should be combined with PLQY/QFLS, transient extraction, energy-level measurements, XPS, GIWAXS, and device resistance/hysteresis. Smooth AFM rules out gross crystallization or roughness, but not chemical ligand stripping, surface decomposition, or sub-surface damage.
scoring_key_points: States that bulk mobility is insufficient because band alignment, selectivity, contact resistance, passivation, and process compatibility govern the complete contact.
Explains that shorter PL lifetime is non-unique and must be separated into charge-transfer quenching versus nonradiative damage.
Proposes solvent/dopant-only, doped-versus-undoped, inert-layer, or hole-blocking controls with spatial and transient measurements.
Interprets smooth AFM plus dark PL patches as evidence against gross topographic crystallization but not against chemical or sub-surface processing damage.
accepted_equivalents: Interfacial transfer rate rather than isolated-film mobility as the relevant kinetic descriptor
PLQY or QFLS preservation as a discriminator between extraction and damage
Time-resolved photocurrent, terahertz conductivity, or impedance as extraction/contact tests
Ligand stripping or dopant/solvent attack as processing-damage mechanisms
common_wrong_answers: Selecting material A solely because it has the highest hole mobility.
Treating every shorter PL lifetime as proof of faster extraction.
Concluding that smooth AFM excludes all film damage.
Using XPS shifts alone as proof that chemical passivation improves device operation.

expected_answer: The HTM must be re-qualified rather than treated as universally optimal because nanocrystal surface treatment changes ligand density, surface dipoles, defect chemistry, valence-band position, and Fermi level. The transfer protocol should first remeasure the treated absorber and polymer energy levels, then verify hole-transfer driving force, electron blocking, contact resistance, and conductivity at the thickness required for the larger area. Chemical compatibility must be tested with XPS or vibrational spectroscopy, trap/QFLS measurements, and solvent-only controls to ensure that the polymer solution does not strip ligands, dissolve the multilayer, or create new surface defects. Coating transfer requires wetting, pinhole density, thickness uniformity, sheet/contact resistance, shunt mapping, and device-yield statistics across the full area, not only a champion cell. The polymer is rejected if energy-level changes create a Voc penalty, if thicker films produce excessive series resistance, if extraction becomes spatially nonuniform, or if the process damages the QD solid. Stability qualification should include inert storage, air/light exposure, thermal stress, and stabilized MPP with matched encapsulation, tracking Voc/FF, hysteresis, PL/QFLS, and chemical changes. A low initial voltage loss is insufficient if the contact oxidizes, delaminates, or loses selectivity during aging.
scoring_key_points: Re-measures absorber and HTM energy levels/selectivity because surface treatment can shift band edges, Fermi level, and surface dipoles.
Tests interfacial chemistry, ligand preservation, passivation, extraction, and thickness-dependent contact resistance rather than relying on mobility alone.
Requires large-area wetting, uniformity, shunt/resistance mapping, and statistically meaningful yield and reproducibility.
Defines thermal, light, atmosphere, and MPP stability stop criteria and rejects contacts that trade initial voltage loss for degradation or nonuniformity.
accepted_equivalents: UPS/Kelvin-probe requalification of energy alignment
Electroluminescence, photoluminescence, or lock-in thermography for area-uniformity diagnostics
Four-point-probe plus transfer-length measurements for sheet and contact resistance
A no-go criterion based on stabilized rather than reverse-scan performance
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the same polymer remains optimal after the QD surface chemistry changes.
Screening only hole mobility and HOMO level while ignoring solvent damage and passivation.
Scaling thickness or area without checking series resistance, wetting, shunts, and yield.
Using short inert-storage stability as proof of operational or ambient durability.

expected_answer: The molecular additive primarily passivates Pb-related defects and suppresses nonradiative recombination, especially near the perovskite/electron-contact side, which explains the Voc gain. If pseudo-FF remains nearly unchanged while measured FF improves, the FF gain is dominated by lower transport or series-resistance loss rather than a large change in the recombination-limited ideal FF.
