The orientation claim is sustained if the face-on population gives higher cross-plane transport, faster contact-induced hole transfer, lower interfacial recombination, and higher FF at matched coverage, work function, and chemical composition, while any in-plane advantage of the edge-on state does not translate into vertical extraction. It fails if performance follows coverage, phosphorus loading, work function, pinhole fraction, or multilayer thickness rather than the independently quantified tilt angle.
scoring_key_points: Creates a counterfactual that changes tilt/orientation while matching conjugated core, anchor chemistry, areal coverage, work function, and energy levels.
Quantifies orientation with an angular surface-sensitive method and independently measures coverage, thickness, and monolayer versus multilayer formation.
Measures cross-plane transport and contact-induced extraction separately from in-plane conductivity and from nonradiative recombination.
Requires performance and vertical transport to track quantified face-on fraction at matched coverage and energetics; correlation with coverage or dipole instead rejects the orientation claim.
accepted_equivalents: Polarized NEXAFS, angle-resolved photoemission, sum-frequency generation, or polarized IR may serve as the primary orientation measurement.
A matched three-anchor positional isomer or spacer-length pair is acceptable if calculated and measured HOMO/work function remain comparable.
Transient surface photovoltage or time-resolved microwave conductivity in directional geometry may substitute for one vertical-extraction diagnostic.
common_wrong_answers: Using stronger PL quenching alone as proof of favorable face-on orientation.
Comparing a dense tripodal monolayer with a patchy monopodal layer and assigning the entire FF gain to molecular tilt.
Treating average phosphorus loading or contact angle as a direct orientation measurement.

expected_answer:
Average phosphorus loading and work function can hide the defects that dominate a large-area device. Rough FTO presents a distribution of local curvature, oxide crystal facets, hydroxyl density, and shadowed regions. A tripodal molecule may bind with all three anchors on some sites, with only one or two anchors on others, or form aggregates and multilayers where solvent dries nonuniformly. Those states can have similar average P content but very different conjugated-core orientation, local dipole, tunneling distance, adhesion, and uncovered-area fraction. Rare bare patches or thick aggregates can dominate recombination and series resistance even when the mean signal looks acceptable.

Process control should therefore begin with the oxide surface: cleaning, UV-ozone or plasma hydroxylation, water content, and storage time must be controlled. Coating concentration, solvent identity and dryness, web speed, wet-film thickness, drying rate, and annealing temperature should be mapped because they determine adsorption kinetics and aggregation. The process window must enforce a true monolayer rather than simply maximizing molecular loading. Rough-FTO-specific solvent and wetting optimization is required; a recipe transferred from flat ITO is not automatically valid.

Quality assurance should be hierarchical. Fast in-line measurements can include spatial contact-angle or surface-energy mapping, calibrated work-function mapping, and spectroscopic thickness or fluorescence from a trace label. Statistical sampling should add XPS/P mapping, angle-sensitive orientation spectroscopy, and ellipsometry or AFM to detect multilayers. KPFM and conductive-AFM should quantify the low-percentile local work function and conductance, not only their averages. After a small perovskite witness layer is deposited, PL/QFLS maps and wetting/crystallization maps should expose uncovered or poorly extracting regions.

Operational stability requires proof that anchors do not hydrolyze or desorb and that the monolayer does not reorganize under heat, light, bias, or humidity. Adhesion/desorption analysis, post-aging orientation/coverage measurements, encapsulated MPP tracking, thermal cycling, and humidity stress should be correlated with spatial FF loss. Acceptance should be based on defect-tail thresholds—maximum uncovered fraction, maximum local contact resistance, and minimum orientation/coverage uniformity—rather than average P loading alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains that rough-FTO facet, hydroxyl, curvature, and drying heterogeneity can create partially anchored molecules, bare patches, aggregates, or multilayers despite matched average P and work function.
Controls surface preparation and coating/drying variables that determine monolayer adsorption, orientation, and aggregation rather than merely maximizing loading.
Uses spatial and low-percentile QC—coverage/orientation mapping, KPFM, conductive-AFM, and witness-layer PL/QFLS—rather than relying on averages.
Verifies anchor retention and orientation under heat, light, bias, and humidity with operational MPP and post-aging surface analysis, using tail-based acceptance criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Scanning photoelectron microscopy, fluorescence lifetime mapping, or patterned witness electrodes may replace one nanoscale coverage or conductance method.
FTO may be replaced by another rough TCO if local hydroxylation and orientation heterogeneity are explicitly addressed.
A statistical process-control limit on local contact resistance or implied Voc is acceptable as a low-tail acceptance criterion.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming equal average phosphorus automatically means equal monolayer coverage and orientation.
Using only a single macroscopic work-function measurement to qualify square-meter-scale coating.
Testing dark shelf life without checking anchor desorption, orientation change, and MPP behavior under heat and bias.

expected_answer:
The two lifetimes probe different kinetic boundary conditions. In a perovskite/HTM bilayer, the observed PL decay contains both recombination and carrier removal into the HTM. A shorter decay can therefore result from a larger hole-transfer rate even if the interface is less recombination-active. In a completed device near open circuit, TPV primarily probes how long separated excess carriers survive before recombination; a longer TPV decay is consistent with lower interfacial or bulk recombination. Thus, efficient extraction under an extracting condition and slow recombination under open-circuit conditions can coexist.

The first step is to establish the radiative quality of the absorber and interface. Absolute PLQY and implied Voc should be measured for bare perovskite and both bilayers at matched excitation density. A blocking-layer or energetically mismatched HTM control should show what the decay looks like when hole transfer is suppressed. The second step is to measure transfer directly with contact-selective transient absorption, time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy, or a calibrated PL-quenching/charge-yield experiment. The number of extracted holes or the interfacial transfer rate must be quantified, not inferred only from a shorter lifetime. TPC or charge-extraction measurements in complete devices should confirm rapid collection and low contact resistance.

The third step is to assess recombination independently. Injection-dependent PLQY/QFLS, light-intensity-dependent Voc, EIS recombination resistance, TPV, thermal-admittance tDOS, or SCLC should determine whether trap-assisted recombination is reduced. Optical absorption, perovskite thickness, and excitation profile must be matched so that a lifetime difference is not caused by generation or reabsorption.

Simultaneous extraction and passivation are established if the planar contact produces a larger and faster extracted-charge yield, shorter contact-induced bilayer decay, and faster TPC, while retaining or increasing bilayer QFLS and showing longer TPV, lower ideality factor, higher recombination resistance, and fewer deep traps in the full device. Harmful quenching is indicated if PLQY/QFLS falls, no extracted charge appears, or the short decay is reproduced by a nonextracting trap-rich control. A longer TPV alone is also insufficient if it results from slow transport or capacitive artifacts, so it must be paired with rapid TPC and low contact resistance.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes bilayer TRPL, which includes extraction, from open-circuit TPV, which mainly probes recombination of separated carriers.
Requires direct extracted-charge or transfer-rate measurement plus absolute PLQY/QFLS, rather than interpreting shorter PL lifetime alone.
Separately evaluates collection/contact resistance and trap-assisted recombination with TPC/charge extraction and device recombination diagnostics.
States the joint signature: faster extraction with preserved or higher QFLS and lower device recombination; PL loss without collected charge or slow transport falsifies the claim.
accepted_equivalents: Contact-selective transient absorption, terahertz spectroscopy with interfacial modeling, or time-resolved photoemission may substitute for a direct transfer-rate measurement.
Small-signal IMPS/IMVS may replace TPC/TPV if transport and recombination time constants are cleanly separated.
Quasi-Fermi-level splitting from calibrated electroluminescence is acceptable instead of absolute PLQY.
common_wrong_answers: Calling every shorter TRPL lifetime evidence of more nonradiative recombination.
Calling every longer TPV lifetime evidence of better passivation without excluding slow extraction or capacitive storage.
Comparing films with different absorption, thickness, or excitation density and interpreting the raw lifetimes mechanistically.

expected_answer:
Planarity is useful only if the resulting packing remains uniform, vertically conductive, and morphologically stable. Increasing planarity raises the driving force for π-stacking and can improve mobility, but it can also lower solubility, accelerate nucleation, produce anisotropic crystallites, or cause dewetting and grain coarsening. The molecular screen must therefore evaluate not only HOMO and mobility but also glass-transition or melting behavior, decomposition temperature, solubility, aggregation tendency, and the free-energy difference between amorphous and crystalline states. Variable-temperature GIWAXS, DSC, TGA, and optical/AFM imaging should determine whether the film reorganizes within the processing and operating temperature range.

The molecular redesign should preserve a planar transport core while frustrating uncontrolled three-dimensional crystallization. Options include a spiro or other noncoplanar junction outside the transport core, asymmetric or branched side groups, steric shielding at selected positions, or stronger but spatially directed interfacial binding. The design should maintain a high glass-transition temperature and an amorphous or finely textured film while retaining short π-stacking distances and appropriate vertical orientation. The reaction product and synthesis cost should remain compatible with dopant-free processing.

Process development should map solvent blend, concentration, substrate surface energy, wet-film thickness, coating speed, drying gradient, and annealing temperature. In-line optical scattering, thickness, and drying-front imaging can detect early crystallization. Large-area GIWAXS, AFM/optical maps, vertical mobility, sheet and contact resistance, work function, and thickness uniformity should be measured statistically. The overlying perovskite must also show uniform nucleation, morphology, QFLS, and buried-interface recombination across the area.

A go decision requires that the mobility and energy-alignment advantage survive the blade-coating window and thermal history without crystallite growth, pinholes, or local contact-resistance tails. Encapsulated MPP tracking at elevated temperature, thermal cycling, and post-aging GIWAXS/AFM/ToF-SIMS should demonstrate stable packing, interface composition, trap density, and FF uniformity. The candidate is rejected if high fresh mobility is obtained only in small areas, if crystallization produces spatial FF loss or perovskite nonuniformity, or if the process window is too narrow for manufacturing control.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes the planarity tradeoff: stronger π-stacking and mobility can be offset by crystallization, dewetting, anisotropy, or low amorphous stability.
Defines molecular screening and redesign around Tg/melting, thermal and morphological stability, solubility, directed packing, and steric frustration while preserving the planar transport core.
Maps scalable coating variables and requires spatial measurements of crystallinity, morphology, vertical transport, contact resistance, work function, and perovskite growth.
Uses elevated-temperature MPP and thermal cycling with post-aging structural/interface diagnostics as the go/no-go criterion, rejecting narrow or small-area-only process windows.
accepted_equivalents: Dynamic mechanical analysis or fast-scanning calorimetry may supplement DSC for amorphous-stability assessment.
Slot-die or meniscus coating may replace blade coating if the same drying and crystallization controls are addressed.
A polymer-tethered or cross-linkable derivative is acceptable if it remains dopant-free and preserves energy alignment and vertical charge transport.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing the most planar molecule solely because it has the highest small-area SCLC mobility.
Treating a high decomposition temperature as proof that the amorphous film will not crystallize or dewet at 85 °C.
Qualifying only average large-area PCE while ignoring local contact-resistance and crystallinity tails that dominate module yield.

expected_answer:
The assignment requires a linked donor-loss/acceptor-growth experiment rather than the acceptor triplet signal alone. Under donor-selective excitation, the Mn-state population and lifetime should be measured together with the rise of the dye triplet. For a sequential exciton-to-Mn-to-dye pathway, increasing dye concentration should quench the Mn emission or Mn excited-state signal, and the dye-triplet rise should follow the loss of the Mn population with the same concentration- and distance-dependent rate. The prompt dye singlet kinetics should remain tied to the nanocrystal excitonic channel and should not acquire the Mn-state time constant. An undoped donor must retain singlet transfer but lose the Mn-correlated triplet channel.

Transient absorption or time-resolved EPR should then distinguish a neutral dye triplet from charge-separated intermediates. Charge transfer requires dye radical-ion and/or nanocrystal carrier signatures, charge-balance kinetics, and sensitivity to donor or acceptor redox potentials. A series of acceptors that changes redox driving force while approximately preserving triplet energy, together with a second series that changes triplet energy while approximately preserving redox potential, can separate electron transfer from triplet energy transfer. Triplet transfer should show an energetic threshold set by the Mn donor state and acceptor T1 level, whereas charge transfer should follow the redox free energy.

A controlled insulating-spacer or ligand-length series is also required. Dexter-type transfer should decrease approximately exponentially with donor-acceptor separation and be rescued by restoring short-range contact. Mn-enhanced intersystem crossing within the dye would instead require prior population of the dye singlet and would make triplet growth track the dye-singlet decay rather than Mn-state quenching; an external Mn salt or a noninteracting Mn-doped nanocrystal control can test whether a generic heavy-atom or paramagnetic effect is sufficient. Oxygen quenching of the long-lived acceptor state, triplet-triplet absorption or phosphorescence assignment, and triplet-sensitizer/triplet-quencher controls should verify triplet identity. The decisive pattern is stoichiometric Mn-state quenching coupled to dye-triplet growth, no radical-ion intermediates, a triplet-energy threshold, and strong short-range distance dependence.
scoring_key_points: Requires matched Mn-state decay and dye-triplet rise kinetics under donor-selective excitation, with the undoped donor retaining only the singlet channel.
Uses transient spectroscopy or spin-sensitive measurements to distinguish a neutral dye triplet from dye/nanocrystal radical-ion charge-transfer intermediates.
Separates triplet-energy and redox driving-force dependence and includes a controlled donor-acceptor distance or ligand-shell test.

States the sequential-pathway signature: Mn-correlated triplet growth, no radical pair, triplet-energy threshold, short-range dependence, and prompt singlet kinetics largely independent of Mn loading.
accepted_equivalents: Nanosecond transient absorption, time-resolved EPR, transient microwave conductivity, or spectroelectrochemical radical references are acceptable for radical-versus-triplet assignment.
A rigid molecular spacer, ligand-length series, silica shell of controlled thickness, or covalent linker series is acceptable for the distance test.

Magnetic-field effects, triplet quenchers, triplet-triplet energy transfer to a secondary reporter, or sensitized singlet-oxygen generation may support triplet identity if radical controls are also included.
An acceptor homolog series or pressure/solvent tuning is acceptable for separating T1 energetics from redox energetics.
common_wrong_answers: Treating the appearance of a long-lived dye signal as sufficient proof of Mn-to-dye triplet energy transfer.
Using only oxygen quenching, which cannot by itself exclude charge separation followed by recombination.
Claiming that unchanged absorption edge proves the absence of charge transfer.
Failing to correlate the dye-triplet rise with depletion of the Mn excited state or to include an undoped donor control.

expected_answer:
The minimum experiment is a crossed isotope matrix under otherwise identical temperature, flow, humidity and dark conditions: H2-16O/16O2, H2-18O/16O2, H2-16O/18O2, H2-18O/18O2, plus H2O/N2 and dry O2 controls. A light/dark duplicate can determine whether illumination accelerates the same chemistry or creates a distinct superoxide route. The film should be followed continuously or repeatedly from the first minutes of exposure rather than only after complete decomposition.

Surface and bulk phase evolution should be measured separately by grazing-incidence diffraction at incidence angles above and below the critical angle, while ambient-pressure XPS, isotope-sensitive ToF-SIMS, Raman/IR of iodate, and, where possible, O K-edge or iodine X-ray absorption identify oxygenated surface products and their isotope composition. Cryogenic or rapid-transfer quenching can preserve transient species. Online mass spectrometry or trapping followed by NMR/ion chromatography should quantify volatile or soluble FA-, ammonia-, HI-, I2- or iodine-containing products. Depth profiles should track N/I depletion, oxygen incorporation and vacancy propagation from the surface inward.

If the proposed sequence is correct, humid nitrogen should permit some surface solvation or FAI loss but little iodate accumulation and much slower structural conversion; dry oxygen should show little reaction because iodide is not sufficiently exposed or mobilized. Humid oxygen should show early surface N/I loss, oxygenated iodine/Pb species, then surface-first nonperovskite nucleation and later bulk conversion. If O2 supplies the iodate oxygen, the iodate isotope should follow 18O2 rather than H2-18O. If water supplies the oxygen atoms while O2 acts only as the electron acceptor, the opposite labeling pattern will appear; either result is mechanistically decisive and must be separated from mere atmospheric correlation.

A hydrate-only mechanism would produce water-isotope-containing hydrated intermediates and phase conversion in humid nitrogen without requiring O2-derived iodate. A superoxide-dominant mechanism should be strongly light/electron dependent, show O2-derived reactive-oxygen signatures before substantial FAI loss, and be suppressed by electron scavenging or dark conditions. The sequential surface-to-bulk model is supported only when FAI/N loss precedes or accompanies O2-dependent iodate formation, oxygenated products originate at the surface, and the front of vacancy/phase conversion moves inward with time.
scoring_key_points: Uses crossed H2-18O and 18O2 exposures with humid-N2, dry-O2, and light/dark controls under matched conditions.
Combines surface-versus-bulk operando diffraction with isotope-sensitive chemical depth profiling and volatile-product analysis.
States isotope predictions that distinguish O2-derived iodate oxygen from water-derived oxygen and separates both from hydrate-only and light-driven superoxide alternatives.
Requires temporal ordering of surface FAI/N-I loss, iodate/Pb-oxygen species, vacancy propagation, and inward nonperovskite phase growth for the sequential mechanism.
accepted_equivalents: Near-ambient-pressure XPS, isotope-resolved SIMS, atom-probe methods, isotope-sensitive vibrational spectroscopy, or X-ray absorption are acceptable for oxygen-source assignment.
Quartz-crystal microbalance, effluent ion chromatography, cold-trap NMR, or online mass spectrometry may be used for FA/iodine loss if species are identified.
A radical spin trap, EPR, electron scavenger, or controlled illumination/bias experiment is acceptable for testing a superoxide pathway.
Neutron or isotope-sensitive scattering may substitute for vibrational identification of hydrated intermediates.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only humid air with dry air, which cannot identify the source of oxygen atoms in iodate.
Using only ex situ XPS after complete degradation and inferring temporal order from endpoint composition.
Assuming that any 18O signal proves an oxygen-driven mechanism without locating the isotope in iodate and separating water from O2 labels.
Calling the pathway superoxide-driven solely because oxygen is required, despite dark degradation and no radical evidence.

expected_answer:
The design must break more than one step of the loop. A hydrophobic, electronically benign surface treatment can reduce water adsorption and FAI dissolution, but it must also remain selective and chemically stable under bias. A dense ion-blocking passivation layer or low-dimensional surface phase should cover pinholes and exposed grain boundaries without creating a transport barrier. Edges and laser scribes require dedicated sealant or conformal inorganic/organic barrier coverage because they provide short diffusion paths that a planar top encapsulant does not protect. The package should combine low water-vapor transmission, low oxygen transmission, strong adhesion, and chemical compatibility with the perovskite and metal contacts.

A second design layer may reduce the consequences of local A-site loss, for example by suppressing volatile-FA escape, providing a chemically compatible FA/iodide reservoir, or using an interface that does not catalyze iodide oxidation. Oxygen getters alone are not sufficient if water continues to dissolve FAI, and hydrophobicity alone is not sufficient if oxygen reaches exposed iodide through defects. The contact stack and encapsulant must also prevent metal- or electrode-catalyzed redox reactions under illumination.

Validation requires a factorial stress matrix: dry N2, humid N2, dry O2/air, humid O2/air, each in dark and under MPP illumination, with matched temperature and water activity. Coupon, mini-module and full-module stages should include intentionally patterned scribes and controlled pinhole defects. Spatial PL/QFLS or electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, and local J-V should locate the earliest electrical loss. Surface- and depth-sensitive GIWAXS, XPS/SIMS or XRF should track nonperovskite phases, N/I loss, oxygenated iodine species and the inward degradation front from scribes and edges. Water/oxygen tracer permeation and cross-sectional microscopy should verify the barrier path rather than relying on contact angle.

A go decision requires no accelerated surface or edge phase conversion under humid oxygen, no progressive N/I depletion or iodate/Pb-oxygen accumulation, no inward-moving vacancy/phase front, and stable spatial QFLS, leakage and MPP output relative to a matched untreated module. Failure under the combined stress despite success in humid nitrogen or dry oxygen means the coupled loop has not been interrupted.
scoring_key_points: Breaks multiple steps using a hydrophobic/selective surface treatment, conformal defect coverage, and dedicated edge/scribe barriers rather than relying on a planar moisture barrier alone.
Requires both water and oxygen exclusion or chemical interception and considers volatile-FA/iodide retention and contact-catalyzed redox compatibility.
Uses a matched water/oxygen x light/dark stress matrix with intentional edge/scribe defects and spatial electrical, structural, and chemical depth diagnostics.
Defines go/no-go criteria that directly test suppression of FAI/N-I loss, iodate formation, inward phase propagation, and operational voltage/output loss.
accepted_equivalents: Atomic-layer-deposited oxides, 2D capping phases, polymer/inorganic nanolaminates, self-assembled monolayers, or cross-linked surface layers are acceptable if selectivity and coverage are verified.
Desiccants, oxygen getters, redox buffers, or volatile-cation reservoirs may be included, but their capacity and byproducts must be tested under operation.
Spatial XRF, nano-XRD, Raman mapping, cathodoluminescence, PL imaging, or EL imaging may be used to locate the degradation front.
A calcium test or isotope-tracer permeability measurement is acceptable for package characterization if module-specific edge leakage is also assessed.
common_wrong_answers: Specifying only a lower water-vapor transmission rate and ignoring oxygen, exposed scribes, and surface redox chemistry.
Using water contact angle as proof of module protection without testing pinholes, edges, adhesion, or gas permeation.
Testing only dark damp heat and claiming protection under illuminated MPP operation.
Accepting stable average PCE while spatial voltage loss and edge-localized phase conversion are already developing.

expected_answer:
A simple correlation between gap and corner-sharing fraction is not causal because every cation substitution changes several variables. The first requirement is a matrix of all-iodide compounds that spans connectivity while controlling composition as far as possible: isostructural cation analogues with different dipoles or polarizabilities, and different-connectivity phases made from closely related cations. Single-crystal XRD, total-scattering/PDF and temperature-dependent diffraction should quantify corner-/edge-/face-sharing fractions, Pb-I-Pb angles, bond lengths, strain, static disorder and thermal motion. Optical absorption, photothermal deflection or ellipsometry should determine the true absorption edge separately from broad PL or defect emission.

A lattice-only perturbation can be produced by hydrostatic pressure, epitaxial strain, temperature, or controlled halide-free mechanical compression that changes Pb-I-Pb geometry without changing the organic cation. A cation-only perturbation can use an isostructural solid solution or cation analogue that preserves the inorganic framework while changing dipole, mass, polarizability or hydrogen bonding. Frozen-lattice DFT calculations should compare the same inorganic coordinates with different cation charge distributions, and the same cation with experimentally observed alternative inorganic connectivities. Wannier/band-decomposed calculations should identify whether band-edge dispersion and orbital overlap increase specifically along corner-sharing paths.

If connectivity is the mediator, the bandgap and carrier effective masses should track the corner-sharing network and Pb-I-Pb geometry across the lattice-only perturbations, while cation swaps that leave the framework unchanged should have smaller effects after electrostatic alignment is accounted for. Directions dominated by face-sharing linkages should retain flatter bands or heavier masses than corner-sharing directions. Transport anisotropy, polarization-resolved absorption, and single-crystal mobility should follow the same structural directions. Mediation analysis or multivariate regression can test whether cation size loses predictive power after measured connectivity and distortion are included.

If isostructural cation substitutions produce large gap shifts without changes in the inorganic lattice, or if pressure changes connectivity without the predicted electronic response, then cation electrostatics, dynamic disorder or strain is not a secondary variable. Temperature-dependent Raman and electron-phonon coupling measurements are needed to test whether the broad optical edge arises from dynamic disorder rather than the static connectivity itself.
scoring_key_points: Rejects simple correlation and constructs matched all-iodide/isostructural controls that independently vary connectivity and organic-cation properties.
Quantifies connectivity, distortion, strain and disorder using crystallography/PDF and separates the absorption edge from defect or broad PL features.
Uses lattice-only and cation-only perturbations plus frozen-lattice electronic-structure calculations and anisotropic transport/optical tests.
States the causal signature: gap, dispersion and effective mass follow corner-sharing geometry after cation effects are controlled, with face-sharing directions remaining electronically flat.
accepted_equivalents: Pressure, epitaxial strain, temperature, chemical pressure within an isostructural solid solution, or reversible phase control are acceptable lattice-only perturbations.
DFT cation removal with a compensating background, electrostatic embedding, constrained-geometry calculations, or Wannier analysis may be used to separate framework and cation effects.
Single-crystal field-effect mobility, time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz conductivity, or polarization-resolved spectroscopy may test transport anisotropy.
Partial least squares, causal mediation, or multivariate structure-property regression is acceptable if based on independently measured structural descriptors.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring corner-sharing causal because the lowest-gap sample has the highest corner-sharing fraction.
Comparing mixed-halide and all-iodide samples, which reintroduces halide chemistry as a dominant confounder.
Using only PL peak position despite broad emission, Stokes shift, and possible trap or disorder contributions.
Performing DFT on relaxed structures only, so cation and lattice effects remain inseparable.

expected_answer:
Avoiding halide segregation removes one failure mode but does not guarantee a useful top cell. The inorganic network must be oriented so that the most dispersive corner-sharing pathways connect the two selective contacts; random texture can force vertical transport through flat face-sharing directions and create a low fill factor even when Voc is high. Processing should therefore optimize nucleation, grain orientation, phase purity and continuity, with GIWAXS pole figures and cross-sectional diffraction tied to vertical and lateral mobility. Film thickness must balance complete absorption against the carrier collection length in the slow direction.

The broad luminescence must be decomposed into band-edge, dynamic-disorder and defect/sink-state components. Absolute PLQY/QFLS, temperature- and fluence-dependent PL, transient absorption, terahertz or microwave conductivity and spatial PL imaging should determine whether the low fill factor is caused by bulk trapping, anisotropic transport, grain boundaries or interfaces. Contacts must be selected using measured ionization energy/electron affinity and interfacial QFLS rather than transferred blindly from a conventional perovskite. Interlayers should suppress recombination without forming barriers to the unusually anisotropic absorber.

The decisive comparison is a matched 2.0 eV mixed-halide top cell fabricated at similar thickness, optical density, contact stack and area. Both should be tested as single junctions and in tandem-relevant optical/electrical conditions. Stress testing must include continuous one-sun or tandem-spectrum MPP, elevated temperature, humidity, bias, and thermal cycling, with simultaneous PL/EL imaging, impedance, series resistance, phase-sensitive XRD/GIWAXS, and contact/electrode chemical analysis. An all-iodide film that remains crystalline while the device loses fill factor from contact reaction or current crowding has not demonstrated a technology-level stability advantage.

A go decision requires reproducible vertical texture or demonstrably sufficient isotropic collection, low non-radiative voltage loss, collection length exceeding the chosen thickness, stable series/contact resistance, no growth of broad sink-state emission, and superior stabilized energy yield or T80/T90 to the matched mixed-halide control under the same operational stress. Stable PL peak position and unchanged XRD alone are insufficient because they do not test carrier collection, interfaces or tandem current matching.
scoring_key_points: Links the low fill factor to possible transport along flat face-sharing directions and requires texture that connects dispersive corner-sharing pathways to the contacts.
Optimizes thickness, phase purity and contacts using QFLS, trap/disorder, anisotropic mobility and collection-length measurements rather than light-stable XRD alone.
Uses a matched 2.0 eV mixed-halide control and separates absorber, interface, contact and electrode failures under tandem-relevant MPP stress.
Defines go/no-go criteria based on reproducible collection, low non-radiative loss, stable resistance and superior operational energy yield, not only absence of halide segregation.
accepted_equivalents: GIWAXS pole figures, grazing-incidence diffraction tomography, polarized spectroscopy, or cross-sectional electron diffraction may establish texture.
TRMC, terahertz conductivity, field-effect mobility, time-of-flight, or space-charge-limited current may quantify anisotropic transport if contact effects are controlled.
A semi-transparent top-cell stack or optically filtered single-junction stress is acceptable for tandem-relevant validation.
T80, integrated energy yield, stabilized PCE retention, or voltage/FF retention may serve as operational criteria if measured under matched stress and area.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming an all-iodide composition is automatically stable and efficient because it cannot segregate Br and I.
Improving absorption by making the film thicker without measuring collection length in the slow crystallographic direction.
Using only unchanged XRD and PL peak position as proof of operational stability.
Comparing with a mixed-halide literature record made in a different stack, thickness, area, or stress condition.

expected_answer:
The variables must be separated chemically rather than inferred from a single MACl series. A minimum additive matrix includes MACl; a methylamine source without chloride, such as a matched MAI or controlled methylamine treatment; a chloride source that cannot generate methylamine under the process conditions; and no additive. The exact surrogate chloride must be screened for its own A-site or templating effects. Solvent, temperature, water content, additive concentration and residence time should be varied independently because the amine-FA reaction is thermally and solvent activated.

Isotope tracing can assign product origin. For example, 13C- or 15N-labeled methylammonium together with 13C/15N-labeled FA can identify whether the methyl group and formamidine skeleton in MFA/DMFA products originate from MA and FA. Time-resolved solution NMR, LC-MS and evolved-gas MS should quantify methylamine, MFA and DMFA during ink aging and heating. Rapidly quenched films should be followed by in situ GIWAXS/XRD, solid-state NMR and chemical mapping. XPS/SIMS or ion chromatography should measure residual chloride after annealing, while absorption and composition-controlled single crystals or films test the cubic-phase bandgap.

A transient crystallization-aid mechanism is supported if morphology/nucleation changes occur during processing but the labeled methylammonium, methylated FA products and chloride are absent from the final cubic film; the benefit should follow evaporation kinetics and be reproduced by another volatile templating additive. A chloride contribution is supported if the cubic bandgap shift and lattice/electronic changes scale with measured residual Cl and are reproduced by the non-methylamine chloride control even when MFA/DMFA are absent.

Irreversible side-reaction chemistry is supported if labeled methyl groups appear in MFA/DMFA with a thermal-dose- and solvent-dependent growth law, and if the yellow 2H phase tracks MFA concentration, low solubility and the characteristic low-angle diffraction rather than total chloride. The decisive result is therefore a three-way mass balance linking morphology to transient species, cubic bandgap to residual Cl, and persistent 2H phase formation to methylated FA products.
scoring_key_points: Uses independent methylamine-without-chloride and chloride-without-methylamine controls, plus no-additive and MACl conditions, across solvent/time/temperature variables.
Uses isotopically labeled MA and/or FA with time-resolved NMR/MS and quenched-film structural/chemical analysis to trace MFA/DMFA formation.
Assigns a residual-chloride mechanism only when cubic-phase bandgap changes follow measured Cl and are reproduced without methylamine side products.

Assigns transient templating to species that disappear after processing and the yellow 2H phase to thermally generated methylated FA products rather than to MACl as a single undifferentiated additive.
accepted_equivalents: NH4Cl, a bulky ammonium chloride, metal chloride, or another non-methylamine chloride may be used if its own incorporation and templating effects are explicitly controlled.
13C, 15N, deuterium, or position-specific isotope labeling is acceptable if it uniquely traces the methyl and formamidine fragments.
In situ IR/Raman, capillary NMR, HPLC, or quantitative mass spectrometry may replace LC-MS if MFA/DMFA and methylamine are resolved.
Composition-controlled single crystals, epitaxial films, or phase-pure thin films are acceptable for isolating the residual-Cl bandgap effect.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only 0 and 35 mol% MACl, which cannot separate chloride, methylamine, and methylated-FA chemistry.
Attributing the yellow phase to chloride incorporation solely from the presence of MACl in the recipe.
Using final-film XPS alone and missing transient solution products and volatile species.
Calling MACl fully volatile because the parent salt is absent, while ignoring irreversible MFA/DMFA products.

expected_answer:
The first control variable is cumulative chemical age, not simply additive molar fraction. The reservoir temperature, residence-time distribution, solvent composition, water content, amine partial pressure and local thermal history must be logged and bounded. The ink should be stored cold or prepared on demand, with minimized hot hold-up volume, inert transfer lines and a defined discard time. A plug-flow or recirculation design should avoid a broad age distribution, and the dryer should be mapped for temperature and solvent-removal uniformity across and along the web.

Critical material attributes include concentrations of MACl, free methylamine, MFA/DMFA products, FA/MA ratio, Pb/halide stoichiometry, residual chloride after annealing, and propensity to nucleate 2H material. Rapid quantitative NMR or LC-MS on reservoir samples, headspace/evolved-gas MS, viscosity/conductivity or spectroscopic fingerprints, and periodic water analysis can monitor the ink. Inline optical/Raman/IR measurements may serve as calibrated proxies but cannot replace product-specific validation. Coated films should be sampled center-to-edge and at early/middle/late roll positions for GIWAXS/XRD, solid-state NMR or SIMS/XPS, absorption edge, PL/QFLS, morphology and device statistics.

Reformulation should separate desired chloride chemistry from methylamine chemistry. If residual Cl is beneficial, a chloride source with lower propensity to generate nucleophilic methylamine should be screened in a factorial design. If transient volatile templating is desired, it should be supplied by a species whose byproducts are demonstrably volatile and nonreactive toward FA. Lower-temperature or shorter-residence processing, a less reactive solvent, staged additive mixing immediately before coating, or removal of MACl may be preferable to accepting uncontrolled MFA formation. Any alternative must be checked for A-site incorporation, new low-dimensional phases and contact compatibility.

Rejection criteria should include a validated upper limit for MFA/DMFA in the ink, no growth of the characteristic yellow/2H diffraction feature during the allowed thermal budget, bounded residual Cl and bandgap, stable FA/MA composition, and no statistically significant center-edge or roll-age drift in phase fraction, QFLS, Voc and yield. A film with attractive grain size but uncontrolled side-product chemistry is a reject because the thermally stable 2H product can persist through downstream annealing.
scoring_key_points: Controls cumulative ink age, temperature, solvent/water state and residence-time distribution through cold/on-demand mixing and mapped thermal zones.
Defines product-specific assays for methylamine, MFA/DMFA, residual Cl and 2H nucleation, with calibrated inline proxies and cross-web/roll-age sampling.
Reformulates by separating desired chloride or transient templating functions from methylamine-generating chemistry and validates alternative-additive side effects.
Sets explicit rejection thresholds for side products, 2H phase, residual Cl/bandgap and spatial/time drift, rather than accepting morphology alone.
accepted_equivalents: At-line benchtop NMR, automated HPLC, Raman chemometrics, or mass-spectrometric sampling may be used if quantitatively calibrated to MFA/DMFA.
Single-use mixing, static mixers immediately before the coating head, or a low-volume chilled day tank are acceptable residence-time controls.
A non-MA chloride, gas-phase chloride treatment, or post-deposition chloride step is acceptable if chloride and cation side effects are independently measured.
Statistical process control, design-of-experiments limits, or multivariate release specifications may define the rejection window.
common_wrong_answers: Monitoring only ink viscosity and assuming chemical composition is unchanged.
Increasing annealing temperature to drive off MACl even though methylated FA products and the 2H phase are not simply volatile.
Sampling only the beginning of the roll and missing reservoir-age and center-edge thermal gradients.
Approving batches based on grain size or average PCE while bandgap and phase chemistry drift.

expected_answer:
The process must decide whether spacer conversion is prohibited or deliberately used. For a fixed-composition product, AA and IdPA salts should be synthesized, purified and quantified separately, and the film precursor should avoid concentrated HI heating or any solvent/temperature history that hydroiodinates the allyl group. Low-temperature, short-residence, nonreactive solvent processing and mixing immediately before coating reduce conversion. If in situ conversion is intentionally used, it must be treated as a reaction step with a controlled temperature-time-acid window and an endpoint assay, not as an unmeasured additive transformation.

Quantitative solution NMR, chromatography or mass spectrometry should measure AA/IdPA ratio and byproducts before coating and after every thermal step. A phase map must span spacer ratio, nominal n, Pb/MA/iodide stoichiometry, solvent, water activity, temperature and residence time because the same nominal formula can yield RP, non-RP, 0D or 1D products. SCXRD-derived fingerprints, GIWAXS/PXRD, solid-state NMR and compositional analysis should be combined; PXRD peak matching alone may not distinguish AA from IdPA solid solutions or reveal reactive-cation identity.

The coating window must also control texture and thickness. GIWAXS pole figures and cross-sectional microscopy should verify that inorganic slabs support the intended transport direction and that no low-n surface skin or insulating byproduct interrupts contacts. PLQY, fluence/temperature-dependent PL, transient absorption and charge-sensitive measurements should quantify band-edge loss and sink-state population as a function of spacer ratio. Mechanical modulus, adhesion, thermal cycling, humidity and illuminated-bias aging should be measured because the short spacer can stiffen interlayers while iodine functionality and reactive organic groups may alter chemical stability.

A go decision requires a bounded AA/IdPA ratio before and after annealing, a single intended n=3 structural family without growing 0D/1D or nonperovskite fractions, reproducible orientation and transport, a controlled sink-state fraction rather than batch-dependent broad emission, and stable composition/phase under processing and operation. Nominal stoichiometry is not proof of final dimensionality, and PXRD alone cannot identify cation conversion or mixed-spacer occupancy.
scoring_key_points: Chooses either preformed, purified spacers with suppressed conversion or a deliberately controlled hydroiodination step with quantified kinetics and endpoint.
Builds a multidimensional phase map and uses NMR/MS plus structural and compositional methods because nominal n and PXRD cannot uniquely identify spacer chemistry or dimensionality.
Controls film texture, low-n/byproduct distribution and trap/sink-state population with GIWAXS, microscopy and time-resolved photophysics.
Defines go/no-go criteria for spacer-ratio stability, n=3 phase purity, orientation/transport, trap reproducibility and mechanical/thermal/operational reliability.
accepted_equivalents: A protected allyl spacer, alternative acid/counterion route, vapor conversion, or pre-synthesized IdPA-only process is acceptable if final spacer identity and phase are measured.
Quantitative NMR, HPLC, capillary electrophoresis, or calibrated mass spectrometry may be used to assay AA/IdPA conversion.
Solid-state NMR, neutron scattering, single-crystal references, or isotope labeling may complement PXRD for mixed-spacer occupancy.
Nanoindentation, dynamic mechanical analysis, bend tests, adhesion tests, or thermal-mechanical cycling may assess mechanical reliability.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the weighed AA/IdPA precursor ratio remains unchanged during heated acidic processing.
Using PXRD alone to assign mixed organic-cation occupancy and phase purity.
Optimizing broad trap emission as a performance metric without identifying whether it represents useful self-trapping or non-radiative defects.
Ignoring low-n 0D/1D byproducts because the nominal inorganic stoichiometry is n=3.

expected_answer:
The experiment must vary electronic hole population and ionic redistribution independently rather than comparing only biased and unbiased samples. Use a device or gated film with selective hole injection, an electron-injection control, and a field-only dark control. Repeat the hole-injection experiment at temperatures where ionic motion is strongly slowed, with an ion-blocking/passivating treatment, or with short pulses that end before measurable halide redistribution. In the complementary arm, deliberately pre-pole or compositionally redistribute the halides, then remove the large field and compare recombination at the same low hole density as an unmigrated control. Match current density, lattice temperature, illumination, and contact geometry, and include a resistive dummy structure to quantify Joule heating.

Measure the electronic response with time-resolved PL or transient absorption, absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and, where possible, injection-dependent electroluminescence. Track ionic motion simultaneously or on the same time axis using spectrally resolved PL mapping, Kelvin-probe or surface-potential mapping, impedance/low-frequency capacitance, and post-stress compositional depth profiling. A direct hole effect is supported if the lifetime or quasi-Fermi-level splitting changes essentially as soon as the hole population changes, scales with hole density, is reversible when holes are extracted, and persists when ions are immobilized. Such a response may occur without a significant band-gap shift and is consistent with stronger coupling of the valence-band states to soft lattice modes, increased electronic-state overlap or nonadiabatic coupling, and altered dephasing.

A migration-mediated contribution is supported if the recombination loss appears only after the ionic redistribution time, follows the growth of the halide/vacancy profile or hysteresis, remains partly after the external hole population is removed, is suppressed by ion immobilization, and can be reproduced in a pre-migrated sample at matched carrier density. Both channels may coexist: an immediate reversible component can be assigned to direct hole-lattice coupling, while a delayed persistent component can be assigned to the migrated defect configuration. Field-only and temperature-matched controls must show that neither electric field nor heating alone reproduces the coupled signatures.
scoring_key_points: Independently varies hole population and ionic mobility using selective injection, ion-immobilized or short-pulse conditions, and pre-migrated controls.
Uses synchronized electronic and ionic diagnostics rather than inferring migration solely from a PL-lifetime change.
Identifies an immediate, hole-density-dependent, reversible response in ion-frozen samples as evidence for direct hole-assisted recombination.
Identifies a delayed, composition-correlated, persistent response reproduced by pre-migration as evidence for migration-mediated recombination, with matched field and heating controls.
accepted_equivalents: Low-temperature, polymer-crosslinked, grain-boundary-passivated, or 2D-capped samples as ways to suppress ionic motion while preserving carrier injection
Transient photocurrent, time-resolved microwave conductivity, or terahertz spectroscopy as alternatives for tracking the fast electronic response
Operando X-ray fluorescence, nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS, or isotope-labeled halide mapping as alternatives for tracking ionic redistribution
A two-component kinetic model that assigns a prompt reversible term to holes and a delayed memory term to ionic rearrangement
common_wrong_answers: Assigning the faster recombination to ion migration merely because both occur under bias, without separating their timescales
Using a higher sample temperature as the only migration accelerator and failing to control its direct effect on recombination
Treating a PL spectral shift alone as proof that the changed ionic distribution caused the lifetime decrease

expected_answer:
A thicker or poorly aligned hole contact can block ionic species yet simultaneously create an electronic extraction barrier. The resulting increase in hole residence time and interfacial hole density can strengthen local electric fields, populate hole traps, and enhance coupling to the soft Pb-halide lattice. It can therefore accelerate the same ionic motion and nonradiative recombination that the contact was intended to suppress. Extra thickness also raises series resistance and may reduce fill factor, so a lower ionic permeability is not sufficient evidence of a better device. A very deep contact ionization energy is not automatically more selective; excessive energetic offset can reduce interfacial charge transfer or produce carrier pile-up.

The safer design separates the electronic and ionic functions. Use a thin, conformal, chemically stable hole-selective contact with high hole mobility or conductivity and a small extraction barrier, combined with defect passivation that removes hole-trapping sites. If an ion barrier is required, make it ultrathin, electronically transparent by tunneling or suitable band alignment, and free of mobile dopants or reactive species. A graded or dipole-modified interface can maintain selectivity without a large energetic cliff. The design should minimize local current crowding, pinholes, and contact roughness, because these generate both charge accumulation and enhanced ionic fields.

Qualification must measure carrier accumulation under operating conditions, not only ex situ ion permeability. Compare matched devices using bias- and illumination-dependent PL or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, transient extraction or charge-extraction time, surface-potential mapping, and injection-dependent EL. Quantify voltage-dependent series resistance, contact selectivity loss, ideality factor, fill factor, and hysteresis. Track ionic behavior with low-frequency impedance, transient current, bias-dependent compositional or spectral mapping, and activation-energy analysis under equal temperature. Perform maximum-power-point, open-circuit light-soaking, and polarity-reversal stresses, because hole density and field distribution differ strongly among these states. A successful contact lowers the steady-state interfacial hole population, ionic-memory signal, and recombination loss while preserving or improving quasi-Fermi-level splitting, stabilized voltage, and fill factor. A design that reduces a migration marker but increases extraction time, series resistance, or voltage loss fails the transfer test.
scoring_key_points: Explains that excessive thickness or energetic offset can create an extraction barrier, hole pile-up, series resistance, and stronger hole-lattice-driven ionic/recombination losses.
Separates hole-selective transport, defect passivation, and ion blocking into compatible functions rather than maximizing barrier thickness.
Measures hole accumulation, extraction, selectivity, recombination, voltage-dependent resistance, and ionic memory under matched operating conditions.
Requires coupled MPP, open-circuit, polarity, and thermal controls and rejects designs that trade lower ion motion for lower voltage or fill factor.
accepted_equivalents: A self-assembled monolayer, conductive oxide, dopant-free organic semiconductor, or ultrathin 2D interlayer as the selective contact, provided extraction and ion blocking are independently verified
Transient surface photovoltage, charge-extraction-by-linearly-increasing-voltage, or time-resolved photocurrent as alternatives for carrier-accumulation and extraction diagnostics
A thin wide-gap interlayer with demonstrated tunneling transport instead of a graded interface
Device operation or control logic that avoids prolonged high-hole-density open circuit, provided energy yield and protection tradeoffs are quantified
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a thicker transport layer always improves stability because it is a better physical diffusion barrier
Optimizing only the contact HOMO or ionization energy without measuring extraction kinetics or carrier accumulation
Claiming success from reduced hysteresis while ignoring voltage, fill factor, series resistance, and operational ion-migration measurements

expected_answer:
First define and reproduce the device state. Control temperature, spectral distribution, illumination history, electrical bias, rest time, and scan direction. Precondition every device to a stated operating point, then verify state repeatability with two or more identical low-dose reference measurements. Use a randomized or mirrored measurement order across replicate devices so that a systematic drift caused by the protocol can be distinguished from aging. Between diagnostic blocks, return the tandem to a defined MPP, open-circuit, short-circuit, or dark-rest condition and record the relaxation. A stable reference tandem or silicon cell should be measured in parallel to track calibration and lamp drift.

At each aging interval, acquire a rapid terminal IV or stabilized MPP point, subcell-resolved Suns-VOC to obtain pseudo-IV, pseudo FF and pseudo voltage, and calibrated Suns-PLI to obtain implied voltage, implied IV and spatial maps. Use spectrally selective excitation and carefully measured subcell photocurrents so that the injection levels of the perovskite and silicon cells are known and current mismatch is not mistaken for a real FF gain or loss. Add injection-dependent EL or PL-versus-EL comparison to test whether electrical injection encounters an extra barrier that optical excitation does not. Calculate transport loss from the terminal-to-pseudo voltage difference at matched current, selectivity loss from implied-to-pseudo voltage, and recombination evolution from the implied-voltage/ideality behavior. Do not force the transport loss into a fixed resistance if it varies with voltage.

Use full-area PL/EL or implied-FF maps to separate uniform degradation from local extraction barriers, shunts, edge damage, or interconnect defects. Confirm that PL-to-voltage calibration remains valid by checking absorptance, phase segregation, optical thickness, and temperature; otherwise an apparent implied-voltage change may be optical rather than electronic. The silicon subcell provides an internal spatial comparison.

The protocol is nonperturbative only if repeated diagnostic loops at the same aging state reproduce the same pFF, iFF, pVOC, iVOC, spectra and maps within predefined tolerances and if swapping measurement order does not change the result. Significant drift during Suns-VOC or Suns-PLI, scan hysteresis, recovery during dark rest, or dependence on diagnostic dose must be reported as metastability rather than averaged away. Qualification should store the complete time sequence and state metadata, not a single post-aging terminal IV curve.
scoring_key_points: Defines reproducible preconditioning, state metadata, mirrored or randomized measurement order, repeated loops, and recovery checks to detect diagnostic-induced metastability.
Combines terminal IV/MPP, subcell Suns-VOC, calibrated Suns-PLI, and PL/EL methods to separate transport, selectivity, and recombination losses.
Controls spectral current matching, voltage-dependent resistance, absorptance, phase segregation, temperature, and calibration artifacts.
Uses spatial subcell maps and explicit repeatability tolerances to localize aging and prove that the measurement sequence has not altered the device.
accepted_equivalents: jSC-VOC or other validated pseudo-IV methods instead of Suns-VOC
Absolute PLQY or calibrated hyperspectral luminescence imaging instead of Suns-PLI, provided subcell voltage is recovered
Separate sacrificial devices for each diagnostic dose as an alternative to randomized order on the same device
Three-terminal or electrically accessible subcell structures as stronger subcell-localization controls
common_wrong_answers: Running a long sequence of bright-light measurements once and assuming the final curve represents the pre-measurement aged state
Using terminal IV alone to assign degradation to one subcell
Treating a change in PL intensity as a voltage loss without checking absorptance, temperature, phase segregation, and calibration

expected_answer:
Mitigation should reduce both the electrostatic driving force and the chemical sink for mobile perovskite species. At the system level, choose grounding, string polarity, frame insulation, and power-electronics architecture so that no cell region remains at a large negative potential relative to the frame for long periods. Use field grading, controlled leakage paths where safe, and continuous leakage-current monitoring. These measures must be evaluated over the full string and edge geometry because local potentials can differ from the nominal module voltage.

At the package level, screen encapsulants for low uptake, low solubility and low diffusivity of halides and perovskite-derived cations, not only high bulk resistivity. Add a thin, optically transparent, chemically inert ion-blocking layer between the perovskite-side stack and the encapsulant or at vulnerable edges. Improve edge seals and prevent electrode/encapsulant reactions. Alkali-free glass can remain a control, but it does not address a mechanism dominated by material leaving the perovskite. Barrier thickness must be limited by optical loss, lamination stress, thermal expansion, adhesion, water-vapor transport, outgassing, and added series or contact resistance. A thicker high-resistivity polymer can also store charge, intensify local fields, or become a stronger chemical reservoir, so insulation resistance alone is an incomplete design metric.

Qualification should use module-relevant positive and negative system voltages, high temperature and humidity, light and dark conditions, MPP and open-circuit states, thermal cycling, and sufficiently long exposure to reveal delayed diffusion. Include heat-only, zero-bias, polarity-reversal, encapsulant-swap, barrier/no-barrier, and glass controls. Track leakage current, stabilized power, FF and voltage continuously. At intervals, acquire subcell-resolved PL/EL or three-terminal data to determine whether the perovskite or silicon cell is failing, plus full-area thermal and luminescence maps for edge initiation. Pre- and post-stress depth profiles and cross-sectional microscopy should quantify elemental depletion, encapsulant enrichment, contact chemistry, voiding and delamination.

Acceptance criteria should include maximum negative leakage current, no growing perovskite-element inventory in the encapsulant above analytical uncertainty, limited subcell voltage/FF loss, absence of edge-localized hotspots, and recovery-independent retained power. A design that passes a short insulation test but later shows perovskite-element transfer or subcell-selective damage is not PID resistant.
scoring_key_points: Reduces cell-to-frame negative potential through grounding, string/power-electronics design, field grading, and leakage monitoring.
Selects encapsulants and ion barriers by chemical uptake and diffusivity as well as resistivity, with edge sealing and compatibility tradeoffs.
Uses bidirectional high-voltage, heat/humidity, light/dark, operating-state, polarity, and materials controls at module scale.
Defines subcell-resolved electrical/luminescence diagnostics and quantitative elemental-transfer acceptance criteria rather than relying on a thicker insulator.
accepted_equivalents: A conductive or semiconductive field-relief layer instead of field grading, provided safety and optical/electrical losses are addressed
Inorganic-organic multilayer barriers, atomic-layer-deposited oxides, or chemically resistant interlayers as ion-blocking concepts
Bipolar strings or center grounding as acceptable system-level potential-management approaches
IEC-derived PID protocols extended with subcell-resolved and chemical diagnostics
common_wrong_answers: Specifying alkali-free glass as the sole mitigation despite evidence that Na ingress is not the dominant pathway
Equating higher encapsulant resistivity with lower PID risk without measuring ion uptake or field distribution
Qualifying only at positive bias or only with terminal IV, thereby missing polarity asymmetry and perovskite-localized damage

expected_answer:
The architecture should make the migration path intentional. Use a sharp lateral heterojunction with the junction normal aligned to the programming field and lithographically controlled channel length, electrode separation and edge geometry. Because edges can dominate transport, either define one reproducible edge channel or passivate all but the intended channel. Use chemically inert contacts, a moisture/oxygen barrier, and a current-compliance circuit. A reference device with the junction parallel to the field and a single-composition sheet should be fabricated on the same substrate.

Programming should use calibrated voltage or current pulses shorter and weaker than those that cause irreversible PL loss, contact reaction or crystal damage. Read the state at a much lower, nonperturbative bias using rectification ratio, conductance, or a spectrally selected PL signal. The read pulse must be shown not to move ions. Use incremental pulse amplitude/duration maps to define a reversible operating window and separate state-setting energy from catastrophic breakdown. Polarity should set distinguishable states, and field-off relaxation should be quantified rather than described qualitatively.

Qualification must include retention at multiple temperatures, humidity levels and illumination conditions; endurance over many bipolar write/erase cycles; device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variation; switching energy and speed; read-disturb; state drift; and recovery after rest. Full spatial PL/composition maps should verify that the same ionic front is written repeatedly rather than a different damaged region forming each cycle. Electrical tests should monitor leakage, rectification, contact resistance and noise. Thermal-only controls, infrared temperature mapping, parallel-junction controls and identical pulses on homogeneous crystals must show that the state is field- and junction-dependent.

Useful ionic memory requires bounded, mass-conserving composition changes with retained crystallinity and reproducible reversibility. Operando or post-cycle Raman/XPS, microscopy and elemental mapping should show no increasing I2/Br2 signature, electrode corrosion, voiding, delamination, irreversible edge recession, or net halide loss. Progressive PL quenching, monotonically increasing leakage, a one-way composition shift, rising programming voltage, or a state that survives only because the crystal decomposed are failure signatures. Acceptance criteria should specify minimum rectification or optical contrast, retention time, endurance cycles, maximum drift, maximum read disturbance and maximum irreversible chemical change.
scoring_key_points: Defines field-aligned heterojunction geometry, controlled edge channels, inert contacts, encapsulation, current compliance, and matched geometric controls.
Separates strong programming pulses from low-disturb readout and establishes a reversible operating window below degradation.
Qualifies retention, endurance, variability, temperature/light dependence, read disturb, spatial repeatability, and electrical drift.
Requires chemical and structural evidence excluding oxidation, corrosion, halide loss, and progressive decomposition as the origin of nonvolatility.
accepted_equivalents: A multi-terminal geometry that independently writes and reads the ionic state
Optical absorption, Raman, or photocurrent contrast instead of PL as the nonperturbative readout
A deliberately engineered edge notch or encapsulated one-dimensional edge channel as an edge-management strategy
Neuromorphic analog states instead of binary memory, provided linearity, retention, endurance and degradation are quantified
common_wrong_answers: Calling any persistent post-bias PL pattern a memory state without write/erase endurance or chemical analysis
Using the same high voltage for programming and reading, thereby continuously moving ions
Ignoring edge variability even though the migration pathway is edge localized

expected_answer:
Use a component-resolved factorial matrix. Compare the complete salt with: the same anion paired with a weakly coordinating or non-metal counterion; the same metal paired with a redox-inactive, chemically similar anion; a physical mixture of the separate anion and metal controls at matched molar activity; a chelated-metal control that preserves ionic strength but suppresses iodide coordination; and a redox-disabled or pre-oxidized anion control. Keep Pb/halide stoichiometry, solvent, water, ionic strength, total additive concentration, coating thickness and drying history matched. Include a morphology-only control that reproduces nucleation or grain size through processing rather than the proposed chemistry.

In solution, quantify I2/I3- or other oxidized iodine species by calibrated UV-visible spectroscopy, iodometric titration, electrochemistry or mass spectrometry. Measure free iodide activity and material balance, identify metal-amine or metal-iodide complexes by NMR/FTIR/Raman/X-ray methods, and quantify precipitate composition by XRD, ICP or elemental analysis. Two challenge series are decisive: add a controlled amount of molecular iodine at constant total iodide, and separately add excess iodide without iodine. A redox-active anion should rescue the iodine challenge even without the coordinating metal, whereas the metal branch should preferentially respond to excess iodide and generate a measurable complex or precipitate.

In films, map metal and anion depth distributions, residual complexes, stoichiometry, grain size, orientation, coverage and roughness using XPS/ToF-SIMS, GIWAXS/XRD and microscopy. Measure absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, TRPL, trap-density spectra, ideality behavior and local luminescence. In devices, compare stabilized VOC, FF, shunt/series resistance, hysteresis and operational degradation. If a matched morphology-only film has the same grain size but lacks the chemical signatures and voltage gain, morphology is not sufficient. If anion-only and metal-only controls produce separable challenge-specific benefits and the complete salt equals their sum, the pathways are additive; a benefit larger than the independent branches, accompanied by both lower iodine and lower excess-iodide/trap signatures, supports synergy.

The experiment should not claim a specific grain-boundary location for a complex from bulk XRD or trap spectroscopy alone. Spatial coordination claims require depth- or interface-resolved evidence.
scoring_key_points: Creates matched full-salt, anion-only, metal-only, mixed-component, coordination-disabled, redox-disabled, and morphology controls.
Uses separate iodine and excess-iodide challenge experiments with quantitative redox, free-iodide, complex, precipitate, and mass-balance measurements.
Connects chemical outcomes to spatial film composition, morphology, absolute luminescence/trap metrics, and stabilized device voltage/fill factor.
States falsifiable patterns for redox, coordination/precipitation, morphology, additive effects, and super-additive synergy without overlocating the complex.
accepted_equivalents: A non-zinc divalent cation series or ligand-blocking series as an alternative way to tune coordination independently
Ion chromatography, iodine-selective electrodes, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, or EPR as alternative iodine/complex diagnostics
A seeded-crystallization or antisolvent control that reproduces grain size without adding the reactive ions
A response-surface interaction term as a quantitative definition of chemical synergy
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the gain to passivation because PL lifetime increases, without separating anion and cation chemistry
Concluding that smaller grains cause the voltage gain without a matched morphology control
Using only the complete salt and one untreated control, which cannot identify either mechanistic branch

expected_answer: Qualification should proceed through nested gates so that losses are assigned before the next device level is added. At the precursor gate, symmetric p-type lifetime structures should be mapped over full wafers and across representative texture regions rather than measured at one central point. The process should meet targets for median and lower-tail lifetime or J0, spatial variation, oxide continuity and dopant-profile uniformity, with replicate lots used to quantify sensitivity to oxidation time, furnace loading and hydrogenation. A high central iVOC with poor edge or pyramid-orientation uniformity is a no-go because large-area cells are governed by local recombination shunts and the low-performance tail. At the contact gate, the same wafers must be completed with the intended ITO/metal or equivalent contact sequence. Actual Voc should be compared with implied Voc; TLM/contact resistivity, sheet resistance, Suns-Voc or pseudo-fill-factor analysis, dark J-V and series-resistance mapping should determine whether tunnelling, dopant activation, physical contact or metallization has consumed the passivation gain. A recipe that improves J0 but requires contact resistivity or series resistance incompatible with the fill-factor budget should be rejected or re-optimized. Front p-type and rear n-type contributions should be separated with one-sided or matched-contact controls so that a gain is not incorrectly assigned to the wrong surface. At the wafer and manufacturing gate, thickness, texture, oxide and dopant uniformity should be measured over industrial dimensions, including repeatability after cleaning, handling and thermal cycling. Statistical criteria should include yield and lower-percentile performance, not only champion cells. At the tandem-integration gate, optimized and control bottom cells should receive the same top-cell process. The analysis should track bottom-cell Voc before and after ALD, sputtering, annealing and metallization; current matching, optical reflection/texture, recombination-junction resistance and top-cell film conformity should be measured. This distinguishes a silicon-contact problem from top-cell damage, optical mismatch or interconnection loss. Finally, reliability testing should include hydrogen-retention/thermal-budget sensitivity of the TOPCon contact and MPP aging of the complete tandem under defined temperature and atmosphere. Silicon-contact stability must be separated from perovskite ion migration, selective-contact degradation and burn-in by using bottom-cell-only controls and post-stress recombination/contact measurements. Go/no-go criteria should therefore impose simultaneous limits on area-uniform J0/iVOC, actual-to-implied voltage loss, contact resistivity and series resistance, tandem current mismatch, process yield and post-stress drift. The production objective is a robust Pareto optimum that survives all downstream steps; maximum coupon iVOC alone ignores transport, area defects, integration damage and reliability.
scoring_key_points: Uses staged gates that begin with full-wafer spatial and lot-to-lot mapping of precursor passivation rather than a single champion coupon.
Compares implied and completed-cell behavior with contact-resistivity, series-resistance and pseudo-FF diagnostics, including separation of front and rear contact contributions.
Adds controlled tandem-integration experiments that isolate optical/current-matching, recombination-junction and top-cell-processing losses from the silicon contact itself.
Defines multi-metric statistical and stability go/no-go criteria and rejects champion iVOC as a sufficient scale-up objective.
accepted_equivalents: Photoluminescence imaging, microwave photoconductance, QSSPC mapping or another spatially resolved lifetime/J0 method may be used at the precursor gate.
Contact-resistance transfer-length methods, Cox-Strack structures, contact-end resistance or equivalent calibrated contact diagnostics are acceptable.
A split-lot or paired-wafer design may replace one-sided controls if it independently assigns p-type, n-type and tandem-process contributions.
common_wrong_answers: Repeating the coupon measurement on more samples without completing contacts or tandem process steps.
Attributing low fill factor to recombination alone while omitting contact resistivity and series resistance.
Treating all tandem degradation as failure of the silicon TOPCon contact without bottom-cell-only controls.
Using only average efficiency or a champion tandem as the scale-up criterion and ignoring spatial yield and lower-tail performance.

expected_answer: The controls must vary coordination chemistry, polymer topology and hydrophobicity independently. A minimal set includes the target coordinating polymer; a non-coordinating polymer with similar molecular weight, viscosity and water contact angle; a low-molecular-weight or monomeric analogue with comparable carbonyl Lewis basicity but little post-anneal retention; and, if feasible, a coordinating polymer of different molecular weight or a polymeric acid control. Additive concentration and solution viscosity should be matched or explicitly measured so that slower drying is not confused with chemical coordination. In-situ optical microscopy, GIWAXS/XRD, calorimetry or scattering during spin coating and annealing should quantify induction time, intermediate-phase ordering, nucleation density and grain-growth kinetics. A response that follows viscosity or molecular weight even for the non-coordinating polymer indicates a rheological/nucleation contribution; a response that follows Lewis basicity and precursor vibrational shifts indicates adduct-mediated crystallization. Post-anneal retention and bridging require direct evidence that the polymer remains at or across grain boundaries and is chemically associated with the lead-halide lattice. Appropriate evidence includes temperature-dependent mass retention, FTIR/XPS coordination shifts after annealing, ToF-SIMS or nanoscale chemical mapping, and lattice-resolved imaging or diffraction of the bridge. A selective wash, thermal desorption, controlled depolymerization or ligand-competition perturbation is especially valuable: if removing or disrupting the retained polymer leaves grain size unchanged but reverses passivation, inter-grain conduction or ion-migration resistance, the persistent bridge is causal rather than merely a crystallization history marker. Lewis-base passivation should improve absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, reduce deep-trap or ideality-factor signatures and lower nonradiative recombination under dry conditions, including in samples with similar morphology. A generic hydrophobic coating should mainly improve water ingress and humidity aging, with much weaker effects on dry thermal ion migration or trap-sensitive electronic metrics. A retained cross-linked composite should combine continued inter-grain electrical connectivity with a higher ion-migration activation energy, lower bias-induced ionic polarization/hysteresis, reduced halide redistribution and improved dry-light or thermal operational stability. The conclusion should therefore rest on a chain from precursor coordination and altered crystallization to verified post-anneal retention, electronically benign grain-boundary localization and persistent suppression of ion motion. Larger grains, higher contact angle or longer TRPL alone cannot identify that chain.
scoring_key_points: Uses orthogonal controls that independently vary Lewis basicity, molecular weight/retention, viscosity and hydrophobicity rather than comparing only treated and untreated films.
Specifies in-situ crystallization measurements that distinguish rheological/nucleation effects from chemically coordinated intermediate-phase control.
Requires direct post-anneal localization/coordination evidence and a removal or disruption perturbation to establish a persistent macromolecular bridge.
Separates dry electronic passivation and ion-migration signatures from generic moisture-barrier behavior and states why morphology or TRPL alone is insufficient.
