accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved GIWAXS, in-situ XRD, optical interferometry, light scattering or another credible crystallization-kinetics method may be used.
Nano-FTIR, solid-state NMR, STEM-EELS, isotope-labelled ToF-SIMS or another spatially resolved chemical method may demonstrate polymer retention and localization.
Bias-dependent transient current, impedance, Kelvin-probe relaxation, isotope tracing or temperature-dependent conductivity may substitute for a named ion-migration measurement.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that a polymer bridge exists solely because grains are larger or moisture stability is better.
Using a non-coordinating polymer control with unmatched viscosity or molecular weight and treating the comparison as chemically orthogonal.
Using longer TRPL as proof of reduced ion migration without a bias-, temperature- or species-sensitive ionic measurement.
Ignoring the possibility that the polymer affects crystallization transiently but is absent from the final grain boundary.

expected_answer: The transfer should begin with a property window rather than the original additive concentration. Coordination density must be high enough to form a useful precursor intermediate and passivate undercoordinated lead, but not so high or so strongly binding that conversion is incomplete, residual intermediate phase remains, or halide/cation incorporation is kinetically frozen. Molecular weight can improve retention and grain-boundary bridging, yet it also increases solution viscosity, slows diffusion and solvent removal, promotes polymer segregation or agglomeration, and can create an insulating boundary if chain density is excessive. A factorial or response-surface design should therefore vary coordination-site density, molecular weight, loading, solvent/antisolvent or gas-quench conditions, wet-film thickness, line speed and drying temperature/humidity. Rheology, coating-window stability and drying profiles must be measured so that chemistry is not confounded with slot-die flow. Structural qualification should include in-situ or time-resolved diffraction during coating, final phase purity, grain-boundary polymer distribution, thickness uniformity and composition maps across large areas. Wide-bandgap mixed-halide absorbers require additional tests for light-induced halide segregation: spatially and temporally resolved PL under operating carrier density, composition-sensitive diffraction or mass spectrometry, and recovery kinetics in the dark. The polymer should reduce ionic redistribution without trapping a non-equilibrium halide distribution or introducing local bandgap fluctuations. Electrical tests should determine whether grain-boundary bridging remains conductive at module-relevant thickness. Absolute PLQY/quasi-Fermi-level splitting, lateral and vertical conductivity, mobility, contact selectivity, ideality factor, hysteresis and impedance should be combined; an apparent lifetime gain accompanied by lower extraction or higher series resistance is not acceptable. Module-scale tests should include coating defects, thickness gradients, scribe compatibility, edge regions and cell-to-cell current mismatch, with replicate mini-modules rather than only small cells. Stability qualification must use encapsulated and unencapsulated controls under continuous MPP, thermal cycling, damp heat, UV-rich illumination and, for a tandem, current-matched operation with the bottom cell. Open-circuit stress can exaggerate charge accumulation and differs from MPP in electric field, carrier density and ion distribution; shelf tests omit photochemical and bias-driven degradation. Extrapolated T80 from a short open-circuit trace is therefore not a substitute for directly measured MPP retention. Selection should use a Pareto criterion that simultaneously meets coating yield, phase homogeneity, low nonradiative loss, low ionic drift, acceptable series resistance and statistically robust module stability.
scoring_key_points: Defines a multivariable process/property window that jointly varies coordination chemistry, molecular weight, loading and slot-die drying/rheology conditions.
Explains the trade-off between stronger retained cross-linking and risks of incomplete conversion, polymer segregation, insulating boundaries or coating nonuniformity.
Requires mixed-halide phase-segregation and inter-grain transport diagnostics under operating carrier density, not just morphology or initial efficiency.
Uses large-area/module and continuous-MPP stability qualification and explains why open-circuit, shelf or short extrapolated tests are not equivalent.
accepted_equivalents: Blade coating, inkjet printing or another scalable meniscus coating method is acceptable if the answer explicitly treats rheology, drying and area uniformity.
Operando PL spectral mapping, GIWAXS, XRF/XRD composition mapping or another validated phase-segregation method may be used.
A Bayesian or sequential design-of-experiments strategy is acceptable in place of a full factorial design if interactions and process confounding are addressed.
common_wrong_answers: Keeping the small-cell polymer weight percentage fixed and scaling only the coated area.
Assuming that higher molecular weight and stronger binding always improve stability without transport or conversion penalties.
Evaluating mixed-halide stability only by initial XRD or a single-area PL spectrum.
Claiming long operational lifetime from dark storage or open-circuit aging without MPP, module-area and encapsulation controls.

expected_answer: The comparison should deliberately match the initial electrostatic and passivation response so that long-term differences cannot be attributed simply to a larger dipole or a larger starting quasi-Fermi-level splitting. Besides untreated, monodentate and bidentate samples, useful controls include a bidentate analogue with sterically blocked chelation, a molecule with similar dipole/basicity but poor geometric access to Pb, and, where possible, a hydrophobic non-coordinating layer of comparable thickness. Surface coverage and optical absorption should be matched. A chelated skeleton requires direct structural evidence beyond N 1s or C 1s detection: a distinct lead-ligand coordination environment from single-crystal or local-structure analysis, a phase-specific diffraction or vibrational signature, and cross-sectional evidence of a compact, finite-depth converted layer. Ligand-exchange competition, thermal cycling, solvent rinsing or controlled cleavage should test persistence. If the bidentate layer is truly a reconstructed surface phase, its coordination and morphology should survive perturbations that remove weakly adsorbed monodentate species; disrupting chelation should specifically eliminate the long-term benefit. The dipole contribution should be quantified by UPS/KPFM and band-bending measurements before and after stress, preferably across hole contacts of different work function. If both treatments initially produce the same energy shift but only the chelated layer retains it and suppresses ionic redistribution, dipole magnitude alone is insufficient. Generic defect passivation should be assessed with absolute PLQY, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, trap-sensitive spectroscopy, ideality factor and carrier-selective-contact measurements. Similar initial values for both ligands establish that the later divergence is not merely a starting recombination difference. Skeleton stabilization and ion blocking should then be tested by temperature-dependent ionic conductivity, isotope or ToF-SIMS depth profiling after bias, vacancy-sensitive measurements, and post-stress Pb0/secondary-phase/pinhole analysis. The expected signature of a dipole-only treatment is an initial Voc or extraction improvement that decays as the molecule redistributes or desorbs, with little increase in ion-migration activation energy. A true chelated surface phase should show a higher migration barrier, lower iodide penetration into the transport layer/electrode, less Pb reduction or skeleton collapse, and better MPP retention even when initial electronic metrics are matched. Hydrophobicity may improve short water exposure but cannot by itself explain dry-bias ion suppression. The strongest inference is therefore an interaction: bidentate geometry creates a persistent lead-coordination network whose structural survival predicts ionic and operational stability independently of the initial dipole/passivation gain.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched monodentate, bidentate, chelation-disabled and hydrophobic/dipole controls so that initial work-function and passivation effects are not confounded.
Requires phase- and coordination-specific structural evidence plus a perturbation that tests whether the reconstructed layer persists or can be selectively disrupted.
Separates initial dipole and defect-passivation contributions with energy-level and recombination measurements before and after stress.
Defines ion-migration and skeleton-failure signatures whose stress dependence uniquely supports persistent chelation rather than hydrophobicity or an initial dipole.
accepted_equivalents: X-ray absorption, solid-state NMR, pair-distribution-function analysis or another local-coordination technique may replace single-crystal structural evidence.
Operando Kelvin probe, surface photovoltage, UPS, photoelectron spectroscopy or another calibrated band-bending method may quantify the dipole contribution.
ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, temperature-dependent conductivity, bias-relaxation spectroscopy or another species-sensitive ionic diagnostic is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Calling a work-function shift proof of a chelated surface skeleton.
Comparing unmatched ligands whose initial PLQY, coverage or dipole differs substantially and assigning the stability difference to denticity.
Using only short water-contact tests to claim suppression of dry operational ion migration.
Treating lower iodide signal after aging as conclusive without verifying that the chelated phase formed and remained structurally intact.

expected_answer: The original selectivity cannot be assumed to transfer across polarity. The first gate is to determine the electronic structure of the reconstructed surface on the actual wide-bandgap composition, because ligand dipoles, Fermi-level position and band bending may change with halide ratio and underlying defect chemistry. UPS/KPFM or equivalent measurements should be combined with absolute band-edge estimates and contact-specific photoemission after deposition of the intended electron transport layer. Electron-only devices, contact-selective PL/TRPL and transient extraction should determine whether the layer blocks holes while still allowing electron transfer. If the reconstructed layer produces a large electron barrier, S-shaped J-V, slow electron extraction or contact-dependent recombination despite good bare-film PL, the chemistry or interfacial dipole must be redesigned rather than merely copied. The second gate is a dose-time-conversion map. Ligand concentration, exposure time, solvent activity and post-treatment should be varied to control conversion depth. Cross-sectional structural/chemical profiling should verify a compact ultrathin layer rather than deep dissolution-reprecipitation, roughening or residual insulating ligand. Performance should be plotted against converted-layer thickness, contact resistance and recombination so that the optimum is not chosen solely by surface PL. The third gate addresses mixed-halide stability. Operando spectral PL, composition mapping, bias/light ion profiling and temperature-dependent ionic response should test whether chelation raises halide-vacancy formation/migration barriers without creating local Br/I partitioning, strain or a low-dimensional phase that seeds segregation. Because a wide-bandgap top cell operates at high quasi-Fermi-level splitting, tests must be performed under MPP-relevant illumination and electric field. The fourth gate is contact formation: the treatment solvent must not damage the underlying film, and subsequent C60/SnOx or other electron-contact deposition must not destroy or chemically react with the chelated phase. Interface resistance, adhesion and thermal/plasma tolerance should be measured through the complete process sequence. Tandem qualification should compare treated and untreated top cells on identical bottom cells, tracking top-cell Voc, fill factor, current matching, recombination-junction loss and spectral response before and after aging. Large-area uniformity and MPP stability under heat and illumination are required. Transfer is justified only if the layer remains structurally defined, lowers nonradiative loss and ionic migration, preserves or improves electron-selective contact resistance, avoids mixed-halide segregation, and produces a statistically robust tandem gain. Persistent extraction barriers, polarity-inappropriate band bending, deep conversion, phase segregation or degradation during contact deposition are redesign triggers; reducing concentration alone may not correct an intrinsically wrong dipole or band alignment.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that hole-side band bending/selectivity cannot be assumed to work at an electron-extraction interface and requires composition- and contact-specific band-alignment tests.
Defines a conversion-depth/thickness process window with cross-sectional verification and joint evaluation of passivation, extraction and contact resistance.
Requires mixed-halide phase-segregation and ion-migration measurements under bias and illumination, not only initial film characterization.
Qualifies the complete electron contact and monolithic tandem for current matching, process compatibility, large-area uniformity and MPP stability, with clear redesign triggers.
accepted_equivalents: C60, SnO2, fullerene derivatives or another justified electron-selective contact may be used in the transfer protocol.
Hard X-ray photoemission, surface photovoltage, contact-potential measurements or device-based band-offset extraction may replace specific UPS/KPFM measurements.
A graded or mixed interlayer, ligand redesign or reversed dipole is an acceptable redesign response if the answer identifies the polarity mismatch.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a layer beneficial for hole extraction must also improve electron extraction because it is wide bandgap.
Optimizing treatment only by PL lifetime while ignoring S-shaped J-V, contact resistance or extraction kinetics.
Testing a single-halide film and extrapolating directly to a wide-bandgap mixed-halide tandem top cell.
Reducing ligand concentration in response to an intrinsically unfavorable dipole without re-measuring band alignment.

expected_answer: The design variable is a permeability-conductivity Pareto front, not maximum thickness or filler loading. A matrix should vary fullerene thickness and graphene fraction while independently varying the contact modifier. For each condition, ionic/water permeability or crossover flux should be measured on dedicated coupons, and vertical electronic conductivity, mobility, contact resistance, series resistance and recombination should be measured on matched devices. Increasing tortuosity is beneficial only while the layer remains continuous and the added electronic resistance stays within the module fill-factor budget. Filler loading also has a percolation/aggregation window: too little may not lengthen the diffusion path, whereas too much can create rough domains, shunts, poor fullerene packing or nonuniform drying. Scalable coating studies should include solvent compatibility, wet-film rheology, low-temperature drying and interaction with the perovskite and subsequent electrode. Rare defects dominate large-area barriers, so average thickness is insufficient. Optical/fluorescence inspection, conductive-AFM sampling, electroluminescence or photoluminescence imaging, lock-in thermography, voltage-biased leakage maps and cross-sectional microscopy should identify pinholes, graphene agglomerates and edge/scribe defects. Barrier validation should use area-normalized defect statistics and intentionally introduced defect controls to establish sensitivity. The contact modifier should be selected through work-function alignment, contact linearity, adhesion and thermal/chemical stability with the chosen electrode. It should recover an ohmic contact without adding mobile ions or a chemically fragile low-work-function layer. Fresh-device fill factor, transient extraction and contact resistance should be separated from long-term diffusion results. Stability qualification should cross bare/interlayer-only films, unencapsulated cells, identically encapsulated controls and complete modules. Species-resolved depth profiles after dry heat, damp heat and biased illumination should verify reduced iodide/water crossover and metal reaction. MPP tests should include thermal cycling, humidity, UV and reverse-bias or partial-shading conditions relevant to modules, with repeated measurements of contact resistance and barrier integrity. If only encapsulated target devices survive, or if lifetime tracks initial contact quality but not measured species flux, the barrier claim is unproven. A scalable design is accepted when the selected thickness/loading remains uniform over the module, suppresses crossover relative to a same-thickness neat-fullerene control, preserves fill factor and extraction, and retains those properties after realistic stress with statistically meaningful module yield.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes a quantified permeability-conductivity/contact-resistance Pareto front across layer thickness, graphene loading and contact-modifier variables.
Addresses filler aggregation, coating/drying compatibility and rare module-scale pinholes or scribe/edge defects with spatial diagnostics and defect statistics.
Separates contact-modifier effects on initial extraction and fill factor from species-resolved ion/water barrier performance.
Uses matched encapsulation controls, unencapsulated coupons and realistic module MPP stress to demonstrate durable barrier function rather than packaging or initial-contact artifacts.
accepted_equivalents: Roll-to-roll slot-die, blade, spray or another low-temperature scalable coating method is acceptable if uniformity and solvent/process compatibility are treated.
Helium/water-vapor permeation analogues, isotope diffusion cells or accelerated ion-crossover structures may complement device depth profiling.
A multilayer or graded fullerene/carbon architecture is acceptable if the answer preserves separate transport and barrier optimization.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the thickest, highest-graphene layer without quantifying electronic resistance or aggregation.
Using only average film thickness or a few SEM images to certify a module-scale diffusion barrier.
Comparing target encapsulated modules with unencapsulated controls and attributing all lifetime gain to the interlayer.
Using fresh fill factor as the sole evidence that the contact modifier and barrier will remain stable.

expected_answer: The perturbations should be applied to a spatially decoupled architecture while monitoring the photovoltaic subcell and catalyst separately. Catalyst-side NIR or local resistive heating should be square-wave or pseudo-randomly modulated, with the perovskite temperature independently measured. Mechanical stirring or controlled flow should alter bubble residence without directly changing catalyst surface temperature, while electrical load and solar intensity should vary the balance between carrier generation and consumption. Fast electrochemical charge-transfer effects should appear on the millisecond-to-second scale as a lower catalyst overpotential, smaller interfacial charge-transfer resistance, changed Tafel response and an immediate photocurrent increase synchronized with catalyst heating. These signatures should occur before large changes in bubble population. A catalyst with poor photothermal response or a temperature-matched non-NIR control should remove the spectral ambiguity. Bubble-detachment effects should occur on slower seconds-to-minutes time scales and correlate with high-speed video measurements of nucleation density, residence time, departure diameter, surface coverage and local flow. Stirring should reproduce the bubble-coverage component; if it improves bubble removal but does not reproduce the full electrochemical or stability response, hydrodynamics is contributory but not sufficient. Direct perovskite heating would produce a measurable absorber-temperature rise, bandgap/PL spectral shift, altered PV dark current or Voc and a response when NIR is directed at the encapsulated PV subcell even without changing HER kinetics. The absence of those signatures under catalyst-only excitation argues against direct absorber heating. Charge-accumulation-driven degradation acts over minutes to hours rather than as the immediate current transient. It should track the operating point of the PV: near-open-circuit or high generation/slow consumption should increase PL or potential accumulation and accelerate performance loss, whereas short-circuit-like extraction, lower sun or faster HER consumption should reduce it. Operando PL, contact potential or voltage of the PV subcell, together with post-stress KPFM/ToF-SIMS/XRD, can link accumulated holes to iodide redistribution and lattice degradation. Load-step experiments are particularly discriminating because they change carrier accumulation without requiring thermal or hydrodynamic changes. A system-identification analysis should therefore decompose an immediate electrochemical component, a delayed bubble-coverage component and a much slower degradation-rate component. If stability follows perovskite temperature rather than load/charge balance, the proposed charge-accumulation mechanism is falsified; if stirring alone reproduces all effects, catalyst kinetics are not uniquely required; and if local heating changes overpotential without altering later ion-migration signatures, the large lifetime gain needs another explanation.
scoring_key_points: Independently modulates catalyst temperature/NIR, hydrodynamics, electrical load and light intensity in a spatially decoupled architecture.
Assigns fast electrochemical and slower bubble responses using catalyst potential/EIS/Tafel and high-speed bubble observables with explicit time-scale logic.
Defines direct-perovskite-heating controls using absorber temperature, PL/bandgap and PV electrical signatures under catalyst-side versus absorber-side excitation.
Links slow stability changes to carrier accumulation through load/low-light controls and operando/postmortem ion-migration evidence, including falsification criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Frequency-response, lock-in, step-response or randomized perturbation analysis is acceptable in place of square-wave modulation.
Surface potential, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, subcell voltage, electrochemical potential or another calibrated charge-accumulation observable may be used.
Particle-image velocimetry, acoustic bubble sensing or electrochemical bubble-coverage proxies may supplement high-speed video.
common_wrong_answers: Using only steady-state photocurrent and assigning the entire effect to faster HER.
Treating stirring and catalyst heating as equivalent perturbations without measuring bubble and charge-transfer responses separately.
Calling unchanged bulk solution temperature proof that the perovskite subcell is not locally heated.
Inferring reduced ion migration directly from a short current increase without load-dependent or post-stress ionic evidence.

expected_answer: The process must control the two steps separately. Host concentration, alkali-to-crown ratio, coating volume, wet-film residence time, solvent orthogonality, drying/annealing history, humidity and the delay before guest coating should be fixed and monitored; the guest dose must be sufficient to complex the host-rich surface without dissolving the perovskite or leaving a thick ammonium salt layer. Coupons spanning the coating direction should be analyzed by XPS or another surface-composition method and, where available, TOF-SIMS or spectroscopic ellipsometry to verify surface-confined and spatially uniform loading. Host-guest complexation should be checked by solid-state NMR or an appropriate vibrational/spectroscopic signature, while GIWAXS/GIXRD must confirm retention of the photoactive 3D phase and absence of a layered 2D phase. Spatial acceptance should include large-area PLQY or calibrated PL/QFLS mapping, work-function or contact-potential mapping, and morphology/coverage inspection; isolated high-PL regions are not sufficient if work function or thickness is nonuniform. Electronic acceptance requires a narrowed QFLS-VOC deficit, reduced surface recombination, uniform contact energetics, low dark leakage, no increase in series resistance, minimal pseudo-FF-to-FF loss and negligible scan-rate/pre-bias hysteresis. Small module sections should undergo stabilized output and MPP tests under light, heat and controlled humidity before full qualification. The coating is rejected if the average PLQY rises but spatial tails remain poor, if diffraction reveals 2D phase, if crown-rich regions cause extraction barriers or FF loss, or if treatment uniformity drifts with coating position. Hydrophobicity may support stability, but it cannot replace direct recombination, transport and phase validation.
scoring_key_points: Controls the sequential chemistry through host/guest dose, stoichiometry, solvent, drying, annealing and timing rather than treating it as one undifferentiated coating.
Requires composition/complexation and GIWAXS/GIXRD-type phase checks that distinguish a supramolecular surface from an insulating residue or 2D perovskite.
Uses spatial mapping of PL/QFLS, work function, morphology or thickness to detect module-scale nonuniformity and bad distribution tails.
Defines electrical and operational acceptance through QFLS-VOC transfer, FF/series resistance, leakage, hysteresis and stabilized light/heat/humidity performance.
accepted_equivalents: Surface-composition mapping may use XPS mapping, TOF-SIMS, infrared/Raman mapping, fluorescence labeling or another calibrated chemical imaging method.
A 2D phase may be excluded by GIWAXS, GIXRD, solid-state NMR or another phase-sensitive structural method.
Pseudo-FF-to-FF loss may be expressed as transport-induced FF loss, series-resistance loss or a gap between Suns-QFLS and measured J-V performance.
common_wrong_answers: Using only average module PCE and ignoring spatially nonuniform host or guest coverage.
Assuming any ammonium-iodide surface signal proves host-guest complexation rather than unreacted salt or a 2D phase.
Accepting a large PLQY increase despite new series resistance or a reduced fill factor.
Relying on contact angle alone to claim operational stability.

expected_answer: A fixed mass loading is not a transferable design rule because the relevant variables are geometric and kinetic. The process should preserve a particle diameter small relative to the local texture radius and film thickness, a facet-distributed nucleation-site spacing short enough that every tip and sidewall lies within the solute diffusion/capture length of a nucleus, and a coverage fraction high enough to seed all facets but below the level that blocks the hole-selective contact or creates a continuous parasitic layer. The perovskite wet thickness relative to pyramid height must remain sufficient for conformal filling. Kinetically, particle immobilization or solvent evaporation must be faster than particle migration to valleys, and the crystallization time must allow distributed nuclei to form before valley nuclei monopolize solute. The scale-up window should therefore vary particle size, coverage, spray/coating flux, substrate temperature, line speed, solvent evaporation and subsequent perovskite drying while mapping the actual facet-resolved distribution. Acceptance requires uniform particle and wetting maps across the substrate, time-resolved or dilute-precursor confirmation of distributed nucleation, and statistically sampled cross-sections showing tip/sidewall/valley coverage without voids. Optical parasitics must be checked by reflectance/EQE and tandem current matching; electrical penalties by contact resistance, dark leakage, FF, recombination and shunt yield; and chemical compatibility by surface spectroscopy. The process should be rejected if higher loading improves coverage but reduces transmission, blocks charge transfer, increases shunts or creates nonuniform local thickness. Final qualification requires stabilized tandem output and MPP aging under relevant illumination and temperature, with post-aging phase and composition analysis because residual precursor phases or PbI2 can dominate long-term degradation.
scoring_key_points: Uses transferable ratios involving particle size, texture geometry, film thickness, site spacing/diffusion length and facet coverage instead of one absolute loading.
Includes a kinetic requirement that particles be immobilized before valley migration and that distributed nucleation precede valley-dominated solute capture.
Defines wafer-scale distribution, nucleation and cross-sectional coverage measurements with statistical yield rather than a single local image.
Requires optical, contact/electrical and stabilized MPP-stability acceptance, including rejection of overcoverage and residual-phase penalties.
accepted_equivalents: Particle redistribution time versus solvent-drying time may be expressed through a Peclet-type competition between advection/diffusion and evaporation.
Nucleation-site spacing relative to solute diffusion length may be described as ensuring each texture facet has a local nucleus before valley growth depletes it.
Electrical blocking may be identified through contact resistivity, reduced FF, extraction delay, increased series resistance or lower external quantum efficiency.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling particle mass directly with wafer area while ignoring texture height, facet coverage and particle migration.
Increasing coverage to nearly 100% without considering optical loss or blockage of the charge-selective contact.
Using one cross-sectional micrograph as proof of production-scale conformality and yield.
Qualifying the process only by initial PCE while omitting stabilized operation and residual-phase analysis.

expected_answer: Rapid initial removal is consistent with efficient liquid access, external mass transfer and capillary delivery through a porous network, followed by occupation of high-affinity amine/amide sites. A pseudo-second-order fit is compatible with site-limited uptake and is often associated with chemisorption, but a high R-squared value alone does not prove a unique chemical rate-limiting step; several diffusion-plus-binding mechanisms can mimic the same empirical kinetics. The later approach to equilibrium can include intraparticle diffusion, depletion of accessible sites and slower chelation in confined pores. Lower sequestration in river water is expected when competing cations, dissolved organic matter, anions, pH-dependent Pb speciation or pore fouling reduce free Pb activity, block ligands or change transport. The minimum control set is a porous but ungrafted carbon network to measure physical/capillary adsorption, a ligand-functionalized low-porosity or nonporous support to isolate chelation, the full porous functionalized trap, and an unmodified blank, all normalized by mass, accessible area and ligand density. Kinetics should be measured across stirring rate, particle thickness, ionic strength, pH and Pb concentration, then analyzed with film-transfer and intraparticle-diffusion models in addition to pseudo-second-order fitting. Equilibrium isotherms, breakthrough tests and desorption behavior should quantify capacity and reversibility. XPS/FTIR or another coordination-sensitive method before and after Pb exposure can verify ligand binding, while ICP-based Pb mass balance and speciation measurements in synthetic river-water matrices can identify competition and fouling. Synergy is established only if the full trap outperforms the sum or expected limits of the physical-only and chemical-only controls under matched conditions.
scoring_key_points: Interprets rapid uptake as compatible with porous/capillary mass transfer plus high-affinity sites, not as proof of chelation alone.
States that pseudo-second-order goodness of fit is empirical and cannot uniquely establish chemisorption or the rate-limiting step.
Explains river-water loss through competing ions, Pb speciation, dissolved organics, ionic strength or pore/ligand fouling.
Proposes matched physical-only, chemical-only, full-trap and blank controls with kinetic, isotherm, spectroscopy and Pb-mass-balance measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Capillary capture may be described as wicking, convective pore filling, external film transfer or rapid delivery to internal sites.
Chemical binding may be described as chelation, coordination, complexation or ligand-site adsorption by amine/amide groups.
Matrix interference may include carbonate/chloride complexation, Ca/Mg competition, natural organic matter adsorption, pH effects or suspended-solid fouling.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that pseudo-second-order R-squared greater than 0.99 conclusively proves chemisorption is the sole rate-limiting process.
Attributing the entire 5-minute uptake to equilibrium ligand binding while ignoring transport through the porous network.
Treating lower river-water performance as random experimental error rather than testing speciation and competition.
Comparing controls with different surface area or ligand density without normalization.

expected_answer: The experiment should independently vary head compliance and linker rigidity while keeping the phosphonic-acid anchor, approximate molecular length, head-group redox energy/dipole as closely matched as synthesis permits, deposition solvent, concentration, co-adsorbed wetting additive and perovskite recipe constant. The four classes are: rigid head/rigid conjugated linker, flexible head/rigid conjugated linker, rigid head/flexible nonconjugated linker, and flexible head/flexible nonconjugated linker. Anchoring and packing should be measured by XPS elemental ratios and binding signatures, electrochemical surface density, AFM and KPFM uniformity, and an orientation-sensitive method or molecular dynamics. Electronic continuity and alignment should be tested by UPS/CV, conductivity or contact resistance, charge-transfer dynamics and calculations such as electron-localization or coupling analysis. Interfacial compliance should be assessed through wetting/contact, adhesion, perovskite nucleation and morphology, operando or post-growth strain/GIWAXS, and bending or thermal-stress response. PLQY/TRPL/FLIM, trap-density spectroscopy, dark current, EIS and complete-device VOC/FF then connect molecular properties to recombination and extraction. Synergy is supported by a statistically significant interaction term: a flexible head improves wetting, contact, passivation and strain mainly when the rigid conjugated linker preserves dense packing and electronic coupling, so the flexible-head/rigid-linker combination exceeds the additive expectation from changing either factor alone. A flexible head with an alkyl linker should lose charge continuity or packing, while a rigid head with a rigid linker may transport well but retain poorer adaptive contact or stress relief. Merely finding one best molecule without the fourth factorial control does not prove synergy.
scoring_key_points: Defines all four head-flexibility by linker-rigidity combinations with a common phosphonic-acid anchoring framework.
Holds anchor, size/dipole, formulation, co-additive and perovskite processing constant enough to isolate the two molecular factors.
Measures packing/orientation, energy alignment/electronic continuity, interfacial compliance/strain and optoelectronic loss using orthogonal methods.
Defines synergy as a non-additive factorial interaction in which head flexibility is beneficial only when rigid-linker packing and transport are retained.
accepted_equivalents: A rigid conjugated linker may be aromatic or another electronically continuous spacer; a flexible linker may be alkyl or another torsionally disordered nonconjugated spacer.
Surface density may be measured by cyclic voltammetry, quartz-crystal methods, calibrated XPS ratios or another quantitative coverage technique.
Interfacial compliance may be described as conformational adaptation, improved wetting/adhesion, stress accommodation or reduced residual microstrain.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only three molecules and claiming synergy without the missing rigid-head/flexible-linker or equivalent factorial control.
Changing anchor group, molecular length, dipole and processing simultaneously with head/linker structure.
Using device PCE alone without separately measuring packing, electronic continuity and interfacial stress/contact.
Assuming maximum molecular flexibility always improves a SAM even when it disrupts conjugation and dense packing.

expected_answer: The comparison must use identical perovskite composition, SAM formulation including any co-adsorbate, contact stack, active area and encapsulation so that mechanical and thermal differences are not confused with architecture changes. Devices and witness substrates should be subjected to a matrix of bend radius, cycle number, temperature and illumination/MPP bias, including bend-only, heat/light-only and combined-stress controls. Operando or interval measurements should map stabilized PCE, VOC, FF, series resistance, leakage, electroluminescence/PL or QFLS, impedance and spatial nonuniformity; GIWAXS or another strain-sensitive method should track perovskite microstrain, while microscopy and adhesion tests identify cracking or delamination. Reversible conformational reorientation is supported when optical/electronic shifts recover after unloading or thermal relaxation and when molecular identity and anchor chemistry remain unchanged. Irreversible chemical degradation or desorption is indicated by new or lost FTIR/Raman, XPS or 1H/31P NMR signatures, reduced surface coverage, altered phosphonate bonding, decomposition products, persistent work-function drift or increasing contact resistance after recovery. KPFM/UPS and contact-resistance measurements should determine whether a nominally intact but highly flexible alkyl linker has lost electronic continuity or packing. An overly rigid head/linker system is rejected if it preserves initial conductivity but concentrates strain, worsens adhesion, produces cracks, delamination or irreversible recombination growth under bending. An overly flexible nonconjugated linker is rejected if mechanical survival is good but surface density, energy alignment, hole-transfer rate or FF deteriorates through conformational disorder. The preferred design maintains anchor coverage and conjugated charge continuity while allowing enough head-group motion to relieve stress, and it must retain uniform stabilized output through the combined-stress test, not only recover a single J-V scan after resting.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched stacks and separate bend-only, heat/light-only and combined-stress controls over radius, cycles and MPP conditions.
Combines device/optoelectronic mapping with strain, adhesion and morphology measurements to locate mechanical versus electrical failure.
Distinguishes reversible conformation from irreversible chemistry/anchor loss using recovery tests plus XPS, vibrational/NMR and surface-coverage evidence.
Defines opposite rejection signatures for excessive rigidity and excessive flexible-linker disorder while requiring retained conjugated transport and stabilized output.
accepted_equivalents: Chemical integrity may be assessed by XPS, FTIR, Raman, solid-state or solution NMR of recovered material, mass spectrometry or another bond-specific method.
Mechanical failure may be identified by crack density, delamination, peel/adhesion strength, sheet-resistance mapping or spatial electroluminescence loss.
Electronic discontinuity may be expressed as work-function disorder, reduced tunnelling/coupling, increased contact resistivity, lower FF or slower hole transfer.
common_wrong_answers: Using only post-bending J-V scans without chemical, strain, adhesion or spatial diagnostics.
Calling every thermally induced spectral change chemical decomposition without testing reversibility or molecular identity.
Selecting the most flexible molecule solely because it survives bending while ignoring loss of conjugation, packing and charge transfer.
Comparing efficiency and stability data obtained from different device stacks without matched controls.

expected_answer: The first step is to build a directional photon budget. Front- and rear-illumination EQE should be measured together with wavelength-resolved reflectance and transmittance of the complete stack, and a transfer-matrix or equivalent optical model should predict the absorption profile and integrated current for both directions. If the penalty is optical, the missing current should be spectrally localized where the rear electrode, buffer or transport layer absorbs or where interference reduces absorber generation. After normalizing for absorbed photon flux, open-circuit voltage, fill factor, ideality and collection efficiency should remain similar. Electrical damage should instead produce signatures that cannot be explained by the optical model: lower voltage or fill factor, increased series resistance or shunting, stronger non-radiative recombination, bias-dependent collection, spatially localized dark or weak-current regions, and altered PL/EL near the rear interface. Useful controls include changing buffer thickness, using a lower-damage TCO deposition condition, comparing otherwise identical opaque and transparent rear contacts, and illuminating both directions at matched absorbed-photon flux. Spatial PL/EL or photocurrent imaging and impedance/Suns-Voc measurements can then separate deposition-induced electrical damage from a purely directional optical loss.
scoring_key_points: Constructs a directional optical budget using front/rear EQE, reflectance/transmittance and optical-field modelling with integrated-current closure.
Predicts that a primarily optical loss changes the spectral Jsc while leaving normalized Voc, FF and collection/selectivity largely unchanged.
Identifies electrical-damage signatures such as recombination, resistance, shunting, bias dependence and spatial non-uniformity beyond optical-model predictions.
Includes controlled changes to buffer/TCO deposition and matched absorbed-photon-flux or spatial diagnostics to establish causality.
accepted_equivalents: Rigorous coupled-wave analysis or finite-difference optical simulation may replace transfer-matrix modelling.
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography or light-beam-induced current mapping may replace spatial PL if they identify rear-contact damage.
Suns-Voc, quasi-steady-state photovoltage or intensity-dependent J-V are acceptable recombination diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that rear illumination must create a different photovoltaic junction.
Calling the loss optical solely because the rear electrode is transparent.
Comparing only total Jsc without wavelength-resolved EQE or absorbed-photon normalization.
Using a lower rear current as proof of sputter damage without checking voltage, fill factor, resistance or spatial uniformity.

expected_answer: Qualification should use a factorial sequence of process controls and stress tests. Thermal-budget compatibility must be verified on the actual flexible substrate by monitoring dimensional stability, adhesion, perovskite phase and device performance after each deposition and annealing step; a low peak temperature alone does not prove compatibility. Sputter damage should be isolated with witness films and devices that vary plasma energy, deposition time and buffer thickness while tracking PL/QFLS, surface chemistry, shunts and spatial uniformity. Moisture and oxygen sensitivity should be separated using encapsulated and unencapsulated devices under controlled damp-heat and light-soaking conditions. Transparent-electrode degradation requires four-point sheet resistance, contact resistance, adhesion and optical-transmission measurements during thermal cycling, bending and MPP operation. Full devices should undergo continuous one-sun MPP tracking, thermal cycling, humidity, UV and, for flexible claims, repeated bending at specified radius; EQE, transmittance and front/rear response should be remeasured to detect optical drift. Flexible readiness requires an actually fabricated flexible device with statistically reproducible area-scaled performance and mechanical durability. Tandem readiness requires filtered bottom-cell or complete four-terminal power measurements, spectral/current matching analysis, optical-loss accounting and stability of both subcells under the combined operating spectrum. A short ambient MPP trace is only a preliminary screen.
scoring_key_points: Separates thermal-budget, plasma/sputter, environmental, electrode-resistance and optical-coupling variables with controlled process splits.
Specifies relevant stress tests and tracked observables, including MPP, damp heat, thermal cycling, UV, bending, sheet/contact resistance, adhesion, EQE and transmittance.
Requires actual flexible-device demonstrations and statistically reproducible mechanical durability before making a flexible claim.
Requires filtered-bottom-cell or full four-terminal tandem power and optical/current-matching validation rather than extrapolating from semitransparency alone.
accepted_equivalents: Sequential coupon testing or design-of-experiments matrices are acceptable alternatives to a full factorial study.
Equivalent standardized stress protocols may be used if temperature, humidity, illumination, bias, encapsulation and sample number are specified.
Sheet-resistance mapping or eddy-current mapping may replace point four-probe measurements for large areas.
common_wrong_answers: Equating a sub-50-degree process with proven flexible-substrate compatibility.
Treating a short unstandardized MPP trace as an operational-stability claim.
Claiming tandem readiness from high near-infrared transmittance without measuring combined power output.
Ignoring transparent-electrode resistance and adhesion during bending or thermal cycling.

expected_answer: A diffraction shift is not unique to elastic strain: it can also arise from changes in cation or halide composition, lattice phase, texture, grain population or calibration geometry. Likewise, a depth-dependent PL shift can reflect composition, defect-state emission, optical filtering or reabsorption, not only deformation-potential coupling. The variables must therefore be measured and perturbed independently. Composition should be mapped by depth-resolved mass spectrometry or cross-sectional chemical microscopy, while residual strain should be quantified using a stress-sensitive method such as sin-squared-psi diffraction, nano-beam diffraction or calibrated Raman analysis. PL should be corrected for excitation and escape-depth effects and compared with absorption or cathodoluminescence. Most importantly, strain should be changed at approximately fixed composition, for example by controlled mechanical bending, substrate thermal-expansion mismatch, reversible thermal cycling or a post-crystallization relaxation treatment that minimizes mass transport. Conversely, composition should be varied while holding the mechanical boundary condition constant. A strain-causal model is supported if local band-edge/PL shifts follow the measured strain reversibly and with the sign and magnitude expected from deformation potentials, and if carrier-extraction/recombination changes follow strain after composition and optical artifacts are controlled. If the PL gradient persists after strain is relaxed, or instead follows the cation/halide profile, strain is not the dominant cause.
scoring_key_points: Explains the non-uniqueness of both diffraction and PL depth shifts, including composition, phase/texture, defects and optical reabsorption confounds.
Uses independent depth-resolved measurements for composition, residual strain and optical band-edge/emission behavior.
Introduces orthogonal perturbations that change strain at nearly fixed composition and/or composition at fixed mechanical boundary conditions.

Defines a falsifiable decisive result: reversible, quantitatively consistent band-edge and carrier-dynamics tracking with strain after confound control, or rejection if the gradient persists independently of strain.
accepted_equivalents: Nano-XRD, grazing-incidence diffraction tomography or electron diffraction may replace sin-squared-psi analysis if true elastic strain is extracted.
Cathodoluminescence, hyperspectral confocal PL or depth-resolved absorption may be used if reabsorption and collection-depth artifacts are corrected.
Piezoelectric bending, external pressure or a lattice-matched substrate series are acceptable fixed-composition strain perturbations.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a lower diffraction angle automatically proves tensile strain without excluding composition or phase changes.
Using correlated XRD and PL shifts as causal proof with no independent perturbation.
Ignoring photon reabsorption and depth-dependent excitation/collection in confocal PL.
Claiming that DFT alone proves the experimental vertical bandgap mechanism.

expected_answer: The vertical strain profile is set by coupled crystallization and mechanics: solvent-removal direction, nucleation and crystallization front, film thickness, composition segregation, temperature gradient through the wet film and substrate, annealing ramp and dwell, cooling rate, substrate coefficient of thermal expansion, substrate modulus and interfacial adhesion. A scaled process therefore needs a window in these variables rather than a single annealing time. Acceptance should map strain versus depth and lateral position together with composition, phase purity, PL/QFLS, grain morphology, pinholes/voids, interface contact, local photocurrent or EL and module resistance. The area average can hide tensile hot spots at the free surface, compressive over-correction at the buried interface and edge-to-centre gradients that dominate recombination or fracture. Reorienting a still-wet film can trap solvent, disrupt the crystallization front and create buried voids or pinholes. Excessive temperature or dwell can volatilize organics and generate PbI2 or other decomposition products. Thermal-expansion mismatch during cooling can recreate strain, delamination or cracking even if the film is nearly strain-free at the annealing temperature. The process should therefore be optimized against depth-resolved extremes, defect formation, electronic performance and cycling stability, not against minimum mean strain alone.
scoring_key_points: Identifies crystallization, solvent-flow, thermal-gradient, cooling, film-thickness, substrate CTE/modulus and adhesion variables controlling vertical strain.
Defines a spatial and depth-resolved acceptance map that combines strain, composition/phase, morphology, interfaces and optoelectronic/module metrics.
Explains why local tensile/compressive extremes and lateral gradients matter more than an area-averaged strain value.
Correctly predicts wet-film void/pinhole formation, thermal decomposition and CTE-mismatch-induced cracking/delamination or residual stress.
accepted_equivalents: Roll-to-roll drying direction, gas-knife profile or substrate heating-zone design may be included as scale-specific controls.
Raman/XRD/PL mapping, curvature methods or digital image correlation are acceptable strain/process maps when depth and local extremes are addressed.
A statistical process-control envelope may replace a deterministic acceptance map if the same variables and failure modes are monitored.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the laboratory annealing time and temperature can be copied directly to a larger coating area.
Optimizing only the average XRD peak position while ignoring buried-interface strain and pinholes.
Treating more aggressive annealing as universally beneficial for strain relief.
Ignoring stress generated during cooling by flexible-substrate thermal-expansion mismatch.

expected_answer: Förster transfer is non-radiative dipole-dipole coupling. It requires donor-emission/acceptor-absorption overlap and an emissive donor, causes donor-lifetime shortening and sensitized acceptor population, and falls strongly with donor-acceptor separation on the nanometre scale. A thin electrically insulating spacer can preserve Förster transfer over a few nanometres while suppressing direct charge transfer; a thickness series should follow an approximately R0- and distance-controlled trend. Radiative reabsorption instead involves emitted photons: it depends on optical path length, collection geometry and acceptor absorption, but it should not shorten the intrinsic donor lifetime. Dexter transfer requires wavefunction overlap, decays exponentially over sub-nanometre distances and should disappear with even a very thin insulating spacer. Charge transfer is governed primarily by interfacial electronic coupling and energy-level offsets; it can occur without strong spectral overlap, is sensitive to electric field or contact selectivity, produces polarons or separated-charge signatures in transient absorption and may yield photocurrent. It should be strongly suppressed by an insulating spacer. A convincing matrix therefore combines spacer-thickness dependence, spectral-overlap or donor-PLQE controls, time-resolved donor and acceptor signals, geometry-dependent photon-reabsorption controls, field/bias dependence and transient spectroscopic detection of charges.
scoring_key_points: Identifies Förster transfer by spectral overlap, donor lifetime shortening, sensitized acceptor excitation and nanometre-scale distance dependence that can survive a thin insulating spacer.
Distinguishes radiative reabsorption by optical-path/geometry dependence and the absence of an intrinsic donor-lifetime change.
Distinguishes Dexter transfer by sub-nanometre exponential distance dependence and immediate suppression by a very thin spacer.
Distinguishes charge transfer by energy-level/field dependence, charge or polaron signatures and spacer-sensitive electrical coupling rather than spectral overlap alone.
accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved emission, transient absorption, upconversion or streak-camera measurements are acceptable kinetic probes.
A non-emissive but spectrally similar donor, an overlap-mismatched acceptor or controlled PLQE series are acceptable Förster controls.
An optical cavity or front/back collection geometry series may be used to diagnose radiative reabsorption.
common_wrong_answers: Calling any PL quenching energy transfer without measuring donor lifetime or charge formation.
Assuming spectral overlap alone proves Förster transfer.
Confusing Dexter and Förster transfer as having the same distance range.
Using increased perovskite PL intensity as proof while ignoring photon reabsorption and optical interference.

expected_answer: Shorter PL lifetime and stronger quenching can arise from beneficial transfer of holes into the transport layer, but they can also arise from new interfacial traps or non-radiative recombination. The optical result must therefore be interpreted with independent measures of charge generation, selectivity and recombination. Selective-contact stacks and ultrafast or transient-absorption measurements should show faster formation of long-lived extracted-hole or charge-separated populations, while insulating-spacer or non-binding-molecule controls should suppress the effect. PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting measured under comparable excitation should not decrease; ideally they increase in the absorber or complete selective stack. Device-level evidence should include higher voltage, lower dark saturation current, an ideality factor closer to radiative/transport-limited behaviour, lower trap density, larger recombination resistance, reduced low-frequency charge accumulation and reduced hysteresis. Hole-only transport or conductivity measurements should show that the bridge does not merely increase bulk resistance or create an injection barrier. The beneficial interpretation is strongest when extraction becomes faster while quasi-Fermi-level splitting and voltage rise and recombination indicators fall. If the lifetime shortens but PLQY/QFLS, voltage or charge lifetime decreases, the bridge is acting as a non-radiative quencher rather than a selective extraction/passivation element.
scoring_key_points: States that PL quenching and shorter TRPL can represent either beneficial extraction or harmful non-radiative recombination.
Requires direct charge-separation/extraction evidence with selective-contact and molecular/spacer controls rather than optical quenching alone.
Uses PLQY/QFLS, voltage, dark current/ideality, trap density, impedance/capacitance and hysteresis to demonstrate passivation and reduced recombination.
Defines the decisive cross-validation: faster extraction accompanied by higher QFLS/Voc and lower recombination, not merely a shorter optical lifetime.
accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved microwave conductivity, terahertz spectroscopy or photocurrent transients may replace transient absorption if extracted-charge formation is measured.
Suns-Voc or electroluminescence-derived non-radiative voltage loss may replace direct QFLS measurements.
Transient photovoltage/photocurrent or charge-extraction measurements are acceptable full-device cross-checks.
common_wrong_answers: Equating a shorter TRPL lifetime automatically with fewer traps.
Using PL quenching alone as proof of faster hole extraction.
Ignoring the possibility that the bridge creates an energy barrier or bulk P3HT transport penalty.
Citing only a higher champion efficiency without recombination or charge-selectivity diagnostics.

expected_answer:
The three hypotheses are coupled in the as-fabricated device and cannot be separated by comparing only pristine and modified SnO2. The experiment must orthogonalize contact transport from absorber morphology. One branch should produce perovskite films with closely matched grain size, crystallinity, thickness, and trap density on the two contacts by independently tuning nucleation and annealing. A complementary branch should vary perovskite morphology on the same modified contact while keeping contact chemistry and thickness fixed. A transport series should then change electron conductance without changing the surface chemistry, for example through a controlled ETL-thickness series, electrostatic carrier-density tuning, or a matched SnO2 doping series. Hole-contact conductance should also be varied so that the electron-to-hole extraction-time ratio is swept through unity.

Hysteresis must be measured as a dynamic phenomenon rather than as one reverse/forward scan pair. Required measurements include scan-rate- and pre-bias-dependent J-V curves, stabilized maximum-power output, transient photocurrent and photovoltage, charge-extraction or time-of-flight measurements, and impedance/admittance spectroscopy that resolves fast electronic transport from slow low-frequency capacitance. Bias- and time-resolved KPFM, transient ion-drift measurements, or depth-resolved ion profiling after electrical poling can directly test whether mobile-ion redistribution and interfacial polarization are reduced. Absolute photoluminescence or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, electroluminescence efficiency, trap-filled-limit measurements, and ideality analysis should quantify morphology- and recombination-related changes independently of contact conductivity.

A flux-matching mechanism is supported if hysteresis reaches a minimum when electron and hole extraction times or conductances are balanced, even for morphology-matched absorbers, and if interfacial stored charge falls without a comparable change in ion-migration activation energy or mobile-ion redistribution. A trap/ionic-polarization mechanism is supported if the modified interface suppresses slow capacitance, bias-induced potential or ion redistribution, and pre-bias memory even after electronic conductance is matched. A morphology-mediated mechanism is supported if hysteresis tracks absorber trap density, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and grain-boundary metrics across both contacts, and is reproduced by changing crystallization while contact transport is held constant. A decisive conclusion requires a crossover or rescue experiment in which selectively restoring the proposed limiting variable restores the hysteresis behavior.
scoring_key_points: Constructs orthogonal or crossover controls that independently vary ETL transport, hole-contact transport, and perovskite morphology/trap density instead of relying on a two-device comparison.

Uses dynamic hysteresis diagnostics—scan rate, pre-bias, stabilized MPP, electronic transients, low-frequency impedance, and a direct ion/potential-redistribution probe—rather than only reverse/forward J-V curves.
States distinct predicted signatures for flux matching, trap-assisted ionic polarization, and morphology-mediated recombination.
Requires a selective perturbation or rescue experiment that links the limiting variable to hysteresis while controlling energy alignment, thickness, and absorber quality.
accepted_equivalents: Electron-hole flux balance may be expressed as matched extraction times, conductances, mobilities, or interfacial transfer rates.
Bias-dependent ToF-SIMS, Kelvin-probe mapping, transient ion-drift, thermally stimulated current, or low-frequency capacitance may serve as the slow ionic-polarization diagnostic.
Absolute PLQY, QFLS, electroluminescence efficiency, or non-radiative voltage loss are acceptable recombination diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that higher electron mobility alone proves flux matching without varying the hole-contact transport or measuring extraction times.
Using only smaller J-V scan hysteresis as both the observation and the mechanistic proof.
Attributing all improvement to larger grains while leaving ETL conductance and energy alignment uncontrolled.
Interpreting low-frequency capacitance as uniquely ionic without scan-rate, temperature, or bias-history controls.

expected_answer:
The stability claim requires decoupling absorber microstructure from contact chemistry. A minimum factorial design contains: modified and unmodified SnO2 with absorber films deliberately processed to have matched grain-size distributions and trap densities; one contact with at least two controlled grain-size states; and, where feasible, a transferred-film or seeded-crystallization control that preserves absorber morphology while changing the buried contact. Film thickness, composition, encapsulation, top contact, and initial stabilized efficiency must be matched. Replicated devices and spatially resolved measurements are necessary because grain-boundary distributions and edge defects are statistical.

The stress matrix should separate and then combine humidity, temperature, illumination spectrum, and electrical bias. Dark humidity tests probe passive water ingress; dry heat tests probe chelate desorption, colloid-derived residues, and contact reconstruction; light-only and UV-controlled tests probe photo-induced interfacial chemistry; and maximum-power bias under damp heat probes coupled ion migration, redox, and moisture. Edge-seal and full-area module coupons should be included because water ingress and current crowding are geometry dependent. Periodic dark recovery should be recorded so that reversible redistribution is not mistaken for durable stabilization.

Diagnostics must connect degradation location to mechanism. Isotopically labelled water with ToF-SIMS or depth profiling can map ingress; cross-sectional microscopy and water-vapour or fluorescence tracing can locate grain-boundary and edge pathways. XPS/FTIR or related spectroscopy should test whether the chelated contact remains chemically intact, while KPFM, impedance, electroluminescence/PL mapping, ion profiling, and contact-resistance measurements distinguish interfacial recombination, mobile-ion accumulation, and resistive loss. Grain-boundary chemistry, phase evolution, electrode corrosion, delamination, and shunt formation should be tracked separately.

Grain size is sufficient only if stability follows grain-boundary density across both contacts and remains similar when morphology is matched. An interface-dominated mechanism is supported if modified SnO2 remains more stable at matched morphology and the divergence co-localizes with preserved chelation, lower interfacial ion accumulation, or better extraction. Module selection should therefore require not just large initial grains, but reproducible contact composition, chemically durable chelation, uniform wetting across large areas, low contact resistance, compatibility with encapsulants and edge seals, and retained performance under combined MPP/damp-heat stress. Flexible translation must additionally separate ETL chemistry from transparent-electrode cracking and substrate-barrier failure.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial or crossover design that independently varies buried-contact chemistry and perovskite grain size/trap density while matching the rest of the stack.
Includes separated and combined humidity, heat, illumination/UV, and maximum-power bias stresses with edge-seal or module-relevant geometry controls.
Specifies spatial and chemical diagnostics that distinguish moisture pathways, chelate/contact degradation, ion accumulation, recombination, resistance, delamination, and electrode failure.
Derives module criteria from the causal result and rejects grain size alone as a qualification metric unless matched-morphology controls support it.
accepted_equivalents: A two-by-two contact × morphology design, split-lot seeded crystallization, or absorber-transfer experiment is acceptable.
D2O tracing, fluorescent moisture indicators, neutron methods, or calibrated water-ingress mapping may replace isotope ToF-SIMS.
Combined light-humidity-bias testing may be described as MPP damp heat or coupled-stress operational aging.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that larger grains necessarily cause all stability improvement without a matched-grain contact control.
Using only dark shelf storage to infer operational module stability.
Measuring PCE retention without locating degradation chemically or spatially.
Ignoring encapsulation, module edges, electrode corrosion, and flexible-substrate failure because the ETL itself is low temperature.

expected_answer:
The central requirement is to vary the putative dispersion function independently from surfactant chemistry. The control series should include the phosphonic-acid SAM alone, surfactant alone, their mixture, a bromide salt without the long alkyl chain, a chloride or other counter-ion analogue with a similar cation, a nonionic or zwitterionic dispersant, and at least one homologous cationic surfactant with a different chain length. A pre-anchored SAM followed by a surfactant rinse and a mixed solution followed by rigorous solvent washing separate solution-phase dispersion from persistent interlayer effects. A concentration series must include both the beneficial regime and excess surfactant, because an inert residue should eventually increase contact resistance.

Solution aggregation should be quantified by DLS, small-angle scattering, or concentration-dependent spectroscopy. On the substrate, anchored phosphonate coverage and uniformity should be measured before and after a standardized wash using phosphorus mapping, quantitative XPS, infrared spectroscopy, ellipsometry, and nanoscale potential or adhesion mapping. Depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS after perovskite deposition should test whether the surfactant cation or bromide remains at the buried interface or enters the absorber. UPS/KPFM on coverage-matched samples, hole-only devices, contact-resistivity measurements, and temperature-dependent transport distinguish a direct dipole or insulating interlayer from improved SAM coverage.

Perovskite nucleation and bulk quality should be measured separately through contact angle, in-situ crystallization, GIWAXS/XRD, morphology, absolute PL/QFLS, and spatial PL. The anti-aggregation hypothesis is supported if chemically different dispersion regulators improve device performance in proportion to the amount and uniformity of wash-resistant anchored SAM, while bromide-only and surfactant-only controls do not reproduce the effect. It is further strengthened if the work function and hole extraction improve only when SAM coverage improves, if little surfactant remains after washing or within the perovskite, and if excess surfactant worsens contact resistance despite continued dispersion. A direct bromide-passivation or dipole mechanism would instead track retained bromide/cation dose or work-function shift even when anchored SAM coverage is held constant. A nucleation-only explanation would improve bulk-film metrics without the corresponding wash-resistant coverage and contact-selectivity signatures.
scoring_key_points: Uses chemically informative controls—SAM alone, surfactant alone, counter-ion and chain-length analogues, bromide-only/nonionic controls, washing, and a concentration series—to isolate anti-aggregation from direct additive effects.
Quantifies solution aggregation and wash-resistant anchored SAM coverage/uniformity with complementary solution, surface, and spatial measurements.
Checks surfactant/bromide residue, work function, contact resistivity, and hole-selective transport separately from perovskite nucleation and bulk quality.
States the causal result pattern: performance follows durable SAM coverage across regulators, not retained surfactant or bromide dose, and excess inert surfactant creates an upper process limit.
accepted_equivalents: CTAC or another halide-swapped analogue may be used as the counter-ion control.
QCM, AFM-IR, NEXAFS, fluorescence-labelled surrogate mapping, or sum-frequency spectroscopy may replace one of the listed SAM-coverage methods.
Contact selectivity may be assessed using hole-only devices, Suns-VOC, ideality factor, electroluminescence, or contact-resistivity structures.
common_wrong_answers: Calling the surfactant an additional hole-transport layer without demonstrating conductivity or selective transport.
Using a single surfactant concentration and no counter-ion or surfactant-only control.
Inferring stronger anchoring solely from higher phosphorus signal before washing.
Claiming anti-aggregation because grains become larger, while ignoring possible bromide incorporation, dipole shifts, or insulating residue.

expected_answer:
The protocol must measure the bare TiO2 contact and the complete device under identical optical histories. Required optical conditions are ultraviolet-only, visible-only with a UV-blocking filter, full spectrum, and dark recovery. Each condition should be applied for times long enough to reach a defined steady state, followed by chopped illumination with multiple pulse lengths and repetition periods. A less-defective or post-annealed TiO2 contact, an inert electron contact, and a TiO2 photoconductor without perovskite provide controls for contact-generated and displacement currents. Irradiance and temperature series are needed because trap filling, release, and photoconductive gain have characteristic nonlinearities and activation energies.

The electrical protocol should avoid relying on swept J-V curves. Continuous maximum-power tracking, steady short-circuit current, stabilized open-circuit voltage, and steady-state EQE should be recorded before, during, and after UV activation. Transient photocurrent, transient photovoltage, charge extraction, impedance/admittance spectroscopy, and dark-current relaxation should resolve fast collected carriers from slow trap charging and capacitance. Current integrated over a light pulse should be compared with the absorbed-photon flux and with the bare-TiO2 signal. Open-circuit and blocking-contact measurements can identify displacement current that flows during potential redistribution but does not deliver sustained external power.

True extraction enhancement is supported if UV activation lowers transport resistance or extraction time, raises steady-state EQE and MPP power, and the increase persists at constant bias after transient charging has decayed. The gain should be absent or much smaller in the bare contact's contribution to the complete-device spectral response, and collected charge must be consistent with perovskite photogeneration rather than an unaccounted TiO2 photochemical current. A capacitive or scan artefact would scale strongly with scan rate, pulse edge, pre-bias, or dwell time, produce large transient current without corresponding steady MPP gain, and relax in the dark. A TiO2-only photocurrent would appear in the contact control or at wavelengths where the perovskite does not account for absorption. A causal conclusion requires the less-defective control to lose the slow-gain signature and the stabilized extraction advantage under the same spectrum.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched bare-contact and complete-device controls under UV-only, visible-only, full-spectrum, and dark-recovery histories, including a less-defective TiO2 reference.
Replaces scan-only evidence with continuous MPP, steady EQE/current/voltage, transient charge, impedance/admittance, and dark-relaxation measurements.

Distinguishes sustained extraction from capacitive displacement, scan memory, and TiO2-only photocurrent using time integration, spectral attribution, pre-bias/scan-rate dependence, and pulse-duration tests.
States a falsifiable result pattern in which the stabilized power/extraction benefit co-varies with TiO2 trap-controlled photoconductivity and disappears in the defect-suppressed control.
accepted_equivalents: Intensity-modulated photocurrent/photovoltage spectroscopy, frequency-domain transfer functions, or time-of-flight extraction may replace individual transient methods.
A UV-transparent versus UV-blocking spectral pair is acceptable instead of monochromatic UV and visible illumination.
An electron-blocking stack or isolated FTO/TiO2 photoconductor may be used to quantify the TiO2-only contribution.
common_wrong_answers: Using a faster reverse J-V scan after light soaking as proof of higher steady-state efficiency.
Calling all persistent current photoconductive gain without subtracting capacitive or TiO2-only contributions.
Comparing UV-on and UV-off states without equal dwell times or dark-recovery histories.
Ignoring that a large transient current can deliver little stabilized power.

expected_answer:
The design target is not the maximum vacancy or trap density. Too few deep hole traps may give insufficient photoconductive activation and leave photogenerated holes available for oxidative surface chemistry; too many defects can create electronic recombination centres, sub-gap absorption, unstable stoichiometry, ion adsorption sites, or long recovery times that worsen hysteresis after darkness. A controlled defect-density and defect-depth series is therefore required, ideally with a chemically passivated outer surface so that bulk or subsurface traps provide gain while reactive surface sites are minimized. TiO2 thickness, band alignment, and dark conductivity must be co-optimized so that the module can start efficiently after night without relying on a long UV preconditioning step.

Qualification should use realistic spectral sequences rather than continuous one-sun illumination alone: UV-rich sunlight, UV-filtered visible light, indoor light, partial shade, dawn ramp, full dark, and repeated day-night cycles. These sequences should be combined with oxygen, controlled humidity, temperature cycling, and maximum-power bias. Separate dry-inert, humid-inert, dry-oxygen, and humid-oxygen conditions distinguish photocatalytic oxidation from moisture-driven interface reactions. MPP output, start-up time, hysteresis, dark recovery, and spectral EQE should be tracked throughout.

The defect population and surface chemistry must be measured before and after aging by EPR, XPS, sub-gap spectroscopy or defect PL, conductivity relaxation, and temperature-dependent detrapping. Perovskite decomposition, interfacial ion accumulation, and TiO2 photocatalytic activity require complementary chemical analysis, depth profiling, PL/EL mapping, and a calibrated oxidation assay. Surface passivation, a selective UV-management layer, or controlled doping can be tested as design interventions, but a UV filter is acceptable only if it does not remove the photons required to activate the contact or reduce energy yield more than it improves stability.

Acceptance requires stable MPP energy yield over repeated spectral and dark cycles, short and reproducible start-up, low photocatalytic decomposition, limited defect evolution, low interfacial recombination, and no progressive increase in scan-history dependence. The optimized contact must outperform a less-defective reference under combined humidity/oxygen/temperature/bias stress, not only after laboratory UV pre-soaking. Module encapsulation and edge seals should limit oxygen and water while preserving the intended optical spectrum.
scoring_key_points: Explains the non-monotonic defect-density trade-off between photoconductive gain/photocatalysis suppression and recombination, instability, sub-gap absorption, or slow memory.
Proposes a controlled defect-depth/density series with surface-passivation, thickness, alignment, and dark-start considerations rather than maximizing oxygen deficiency.
Uses realistic UV/visible/indoor/day-night sequences combined with oxygen, humidity, temperature and MPP bias, with defect and degradation diagnostics.
Defines acceptance by stable energy yield, start-up, low photocatalysis, limited defect evolution and low memory under coupled outdoor-relevant stresses.
accepted_equivalents: Intentional doping, plasma treatment, reducing anneals, or vacancy control may be used to create the defect series.
EPR, thermally stimulated current, conductivity-decay activation energy, sub-gap absorption, or XPS may be used to quantify defect evolution.
A down-conversion or spectral-management layer is acceptable if the energy-yield and activation trade-off is explicitly evaluated.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that more oxygen vacancies always improve both efficiency and stability.
Qualifying the contact only under continuous UV-rich illumination and never testing dark recovery or visible/indoor conditions.
Using a UV-blocking layer without checking whether the beneficial photoconductive mechanism is lost.
Measuring only device PCE retention and not TiO2 defect chemistry, photocatalysis, or interfacial decomposition.

expected_answer:
Sacrificial half-reactions demonstrate that the semiconductor can perform one interfacial redox reaction when the complementary charge is rapidly consumed; they do not prove simultaneous overall water splitting, compatible band energetics, balanced surface kinetics, or stability without a scavenger.
