The translated system needs an H2-evolution photocatalyst and an O2-evolution partner, or spatially separated reduction and oxidation sites, with energetics that support both water redox potentials after overpotential and pH losses. In a Z-scheme, the redox mediator and solid contacts must selectively transfer the intended carriers while avoiding optical shielding, mediator decomposition, and short-circuit recombination.

Cocatalyst architecture must be optimized for selectivity as well as rate. The reduction alloy should collect electrons and catalyse H2, while the oxide shell must suppress hole attack on the metal and reverse reduction of oxidized mediator or O2. The O2 cocatalyst must collect holes without accelerating nitrogen loss or surface oxidation of the oxynitride. Spatial mapping and transient spectroscopy should verify that electrons and holes reach the intended sites. Control experiments that omit each cocatalyst, shell, mediator, or partner establish which back reaction is suppressed.

Validation requires closed-system gas chromatography or mass spectrometry with H2:O2 approaching 2:1, isotope tests where needed, blank and dark controls, and carbon/contaminant analysis to rule out sacrificial or organic decomposition. Apparent quantum yield and solar-to-hydrogen efficiency must be measured under defined spectra using absorbed-photon and illuminated-area accounting. Long runs and repeated start-stop cycles should track induction, gas crossover, mediator balance, and pressure effects rather than reporting only an initial rate.

Durability analysis must test nitrogen loss, oxidation-state and phase changes, surface reconstruction, dissolution, cocatalyst alloy segregation, Cr2O3-shell cracking or permeability, and CoOx leaching/agglomeration. XRD, XPS/XAS, elemental mass balance, microscopy, and post-reaction carrier dynamics should be linked to activity decay. Scale-up additionally requires reproducible nanocrystal synthesis and washing, control of residual chloride or alkaline-earth substitution, cocatalyst deposition uniformity, catalyst immobilization or recovery, light penetration, slurry mixing, gas disengagement, mass transfer, and safe H2/O2 separation. The result qualifies as overall water splitting only when stoichiometric gases, stable quantum efficiency, and material mass balance persist without sacrificial donors under reactor-relevant conditions.
scoring_key_points: Explains why sacrificial half-reaction rates do not prove simultaneous water splitting, compatible energetics, balanced kinetics, or stability without scavengers.
Designs selective reduction/oxidation sites or a Z-scheme with mediator/contact controls, cocatalyst-shell functions, charge-routing evidence, and back-reaction tests.
Requires stoichiometric H2/O2, blank/isotope controls, AQY/STH accounting, and long start-stop operation without sacrificial reagents.
Addresses oxynitride photocorrosion and nitrogen loss, cocatalyst/shell durability, mediator stability, reproducible synthesis, reactor mass/light transfer, catalyst recovery, and gas safety.
accepted_equivalents: A particulate-sheet, tandem photoelectrochemical, suspension Z-scheme, or immobilized flow-reactor design is acceptable if both half-reactions and charge transfer are closed.
Redox-mediator-free solid-state electron transfer is acceptable in place of a soluble mediator if recombination and contact selectivity are validated.
Photodeposition mapping, selective scavenger tests, transient absorption, surface photovoltage, or operando spectroscopy may verify charge routing.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming overall water splitting because separate H2 and O2 sacrificial tests are both fast.
Reporting H2 evolution without measuring O2 stoichiometry or excluding decomposition products.
Assuming the Cr2O3 shell and alloy remain intact because the initial activity is high.
Ignoring light attenuation, slurry transport, catalyst recovery, residual flux, and explosive H2/O2 handling during scale-up.

expected_answer:
A homogeneous energy landscape and efficient energy funneling are different physical states. Homogeneity means that the population of quantum-well thicknesses is narrow and that the energetic offsets between the remaining phases are small, so carriers do not repeatedly encounter large downhill steps, band tails, or isolated low-gap sinks. Funneling instead requires energetic heterogeneity: carriers created in higher-gap, lower-n domains transfer into a minority population of lower-gap, higher-n or three-dimensional-like domains. Faster disappearance of a high-energy bleach and stronger low-energy photoluminescence can therefore indicate more efficient transfer without demonstrating that the starting phase distribution has narrowed. A longer photoluminescence lifetime is also ambiguous because it may reflect storage of carriers in low-gap domains, reduced extraction, photon recycling, or a changed radiative coefficient rather than reduced nonradiative disorder.

The first diagnostic block must establish the phase and energy census independently of emission intensity. Linear absorption and excitation spectroscopy should resolve the number and relative oscillator strengths of phase-specific excitonic features. GIWAXS or another structural phase probe should determine whether low-n, high-n, and three-dimensional-like signatures have actually disappeared rather than merely becoming weak emitters. Transient absorption should be globally fitted using the positions, amplitudes, and temporal evolution of all phase-specific bleaches; a genuinely narrower distribution should show fewer distinct bleach energies and a smaller total energy span, not only a faster transfer time. Front-side and substrate-side excitation/detection, angle-dependent measurements, or cross-sectional nano-optical mapping should test whether a vertical low-n/high-n gradient persists. Depth-resolved compositional or structural measurements are needed because a film can have an apparently narrow surface spectrum while retaining a broad buried distribution.

The second block should separate transfer from transport. Fluence-dependent and temperature-dependent transient absorption and time-resolved photoluminescence should measure spectral relaxation, transfer rates, and the population lifetime of each phase. Strongly activated or fluence-dependent downhill transfer, delayed rise of the low-energy population, and persistent spectral relaxation are signatures of a heterogeneous funnel. In a homogeneous film, the phase-selective transfer amplitude and spectral red-shifting should be reduced because fewer large offsets exist. Minority-carrier mobility and diffusion length should be measured in device-relevant geometries using more than one method, such as time-resolved microwave conductivity or optical-pump terahertz conductivity together with photocurrent or diffusion measurements. A genuine reduction in energetic disorder should improve long-range minority-carrier transport and reduce its thermal activation; rapid local funneling alone may increase low-energy emission while trapping minority carriers in isolated domains and leaving vertical transport poor.

The third block should connect the microscopic landscape to recombination and voltage. Absolute photoluminescence quantum yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting under calibrated one-sun-equivalent excitation, electroluminescence external quantum efficiency, Urbach energy, sub-gap absorption, ideality factor, and impedance or temperature-dependent disorder metrics should be compared at matched carrier density. Contact-selective controls are essential so that a voltage gain caused only by improved extraction or a work-function shift is not misassigned to the absorber. A homogeneous landscape should reduce band-tail absorption and spatial potential fluctuations, suppress trap-assisted recombination, increase quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and decrease the nonradiative voltage loss. If the low-energy photoluminescence becomes stronger but the Urbach tail, phase-resolved energy span, minority mobility, or quasi-Fermi-level splitting does not improve, the result is better funneling rather than true homogenization.

The homogeneous-landscape interpretation is accepted only when orthogonal evidence closes the causal loop: the number and energetic span of phase signatures decrease throughout the film; delayed low-energy population growth and spectral relaxation diminish rather than merely accelerate; minority-carrier transport becomes less activated and more spatially uniform; and calibrated radiative-efficiency measurements show a smaller nonradiative voltage loss at matched carrier density. Persistence of broad phase signatures, a strong depth gradient, pronounced downhill-transfer kinetics, or localized low-gap emission falsifies the claim even if the device voltage and photoluminescence lifetime improve.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes a genuinely narrow n-value/energy distribution from rapid downhill funneling and explains why low-energy PL, bleach decay, and lifetime alone are non-unique.
Requires an independent phase and depth census using phase-resolved absorption/TA plus structural or cross-sectional measurements, not emission intensity alone.
Uses fluence/temperature-resolved kinetics and device-relevant minority-carrier transport to test for persistent spectral relaxation, trapping, and activated transport.
Accepts homogenization only if reduced phase-energy span coincides with lower band tails/nonradiative voltage loss and improved spatially uniform transport at matched carrier density.
accepted_equivalents: Narrower quantum-well-width distribution for narrower n-value distribution
Energy cascade or downhill carrier migration for carrier funneling
Absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting or EQEEL-derived voltage loss as a radiative-efficiency diagnostic
Front/back excitation, angle-resolved probing, or cross-sectional hyperspectral mapping as depth-sensitive tests
Urbach tail, sub-gap EQE, or spatial potential variance as measures of energetic disorder

Using only GIWAXS orientation or average crystallinity without quantifying the n-phase energy distribution
Equating faster energy transfer with better long-range minority-carrier transport
Attributing a higher open-circuit voltage to absorber homogenization without controlling contact energetics and calibrated quasi-Fermi-level splitting

expected_answer:
The absence of large precursor colloids is only an initial-state constraint. It reduces heterogeneous nucleation sites present before coating, but the final n-value distribution is created during solvent evaporation, supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, organic-spacer redistribution, and annealing. Slot-die coating changes all of these rates relative to spin coating: the wet film is thicker, solvent removal is slower and spatially nonuniform, the coating bead and edges experience different mass transfer, substrate temperature can vary along the web, and the residence time before crystallization is much longer. Even a molecularly uniform ink can therefore develop local organic-cation depletion, edge-first nucleation, vertical segregation, or high-n domains if the local evaporation-to-crystallization balance is not controlled.

The scale-up strategy should first define a process window around the relevant kinetic ratios rather than copy spin speed or annealing time. Ink solids content, spacer and additive concentration, solvent/coordination strength, wet-film thickness, coating speed, substrate temperature, ambient humidity, drying-gas velocity and direction, solvent-vapour partial pressure, and the time between coating and thermal treatment must be co-optimized. A staged drying sequence is preferable: an initial uniform levelling/coordination period, controlled solvent extraction that avoids edge-first supersaturation, and a subsequent anneal that completes conversion without allowing prolonged phase coarsening. Gas knives, enclosed solvent-rich drying zones, zoned substrate heating, edge shields, or recirculated vapour can be used to reduce transverse evaporation gradients. The additive dose may need to be re-optimized because the additive-to-nucleation-site ratio and its diffusion time change with wet-film thickness. Spacer chemistry must still provide small intrinsic band offsets; process control cannot compensate for a strongly stepped intrinsic band ladder.

Closed-loop diagnostics should monitor both kinetics and the final energy landscape. During coating and drying, spatially resolved reflectance/absorption or hyperspectral imaging can track the appearance and growth of phase-specific excitonic bands. In-situ or rapid-scan GIWAXS can map crystallization onset, orientation, and phase evolution across the web. Wet-film thickness, temperature, and solvent-vapour concentration should be logged so that phase maps can be linked to local process history. End-point acceptance should include transverse and longitudinal mapping of phase-resolved absorption, photoluminescence peak and linewidth, absolute photoluminescence quantum yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and sheet/device voltage. Front/back spectroscopy or cross-sectional mapping should verify that the narrow phase distribution extends through the thickness. GIWAXS, transient absorption, and sub-gap/Urbach measurements on representative regions should confirm that the apparent uniform colour is not masking a buried low-gap population. Module-scale electroluminescence and photoluminescence imaging should show small spatial variance, while stabilized maximum-power operation—not only local reverse-scan curves—should verify uniform extraction.

The low-n stability advantage must be tested after the process window is established. Encapsulated and unencapsulated samples should undergo separate humidity, elevated-temperature, continuous-illumination, and combined light/heat tests, with repeated phase-resolved optical and structural mapping. The key degradation modes are spacer migration, phase-width coarsening, formation of high-n or three-dimensional-like sinks, loss of vertical orientation, and additive redistribution or chemical decomposition. Bias or maximum-power tracking should be included because electric fields and mobile ions can drive redistribution not visible in dark storage. Thermal cycling and damp-heat testing are especially important for a large coated film because transverse stress and solvent-residue gradients can amplify phase segregation.

Scale-up is accepted only if the same narrow energy span, low band-tail absorption, high quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and minority-carrier transport are reproduced with low spatial variance over the full coated area and remain stable under stress. A colloid-free DLS trace without uniform crystallization kinetics, depth-resolved phase control, and post-ageing phase stability is not sufficient evidence of successful transfer.
scoring_key_points: Explains that colloid suppression controls the precursor state but not the spatially varying evaporation, supersaturation, segregation, and crystallization kinetics of a large wet film.
Defines a coupled process window for wet thickness, solvent coordination, coating speed, substrate temperature, gas/vapour management, additive dose, and staged drying/annealing.
Requires spatially and depth-resolved in-line/end-point phase, optical, structural, quasi-Fermi-level-splitting, and module-uniformity measurements.
Qualifies transfer with light/heat/humidity/bias ageing that checks phase redistribution, spacer/additive migration, stabilized output, and retention of the narrow energy landscape.
accepted_equivalents: Blade coating, meniscus coating, or roll-to-roll coating for slot-die scale-up
Drying Damkohler-type balance or nucleation-versus-evaporation timescale for the kinetic process window
Hyperspectral reflectance/PL, in-line absorption, or rapid GIWAXS for phase-evolution mapping
Quasi-Fermi-level-splitting maps, electroluminescence maps, or stabilized local Voc maps for voltage uniformity
Combined damp-heat/light/bias testing for post-fabrication phase redistribution
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that an unchanged ink recipe and a colloid-free DLS trace guarantee the same solid-state phase distribution
Copying spin-coating time and temperature without controlling wet-film mass transfer and transverse drying gradients
Using only average XRD or a few local J-V curves to claim large-area uniformity
Improving initial efficiency by allowing high-n domains to form while ignoring loss of low-n stability and later phase redistribution

expected_answer:
The purpose of the chloride-containing intermediate is to decouple rapid solvent loss from immediate perovskite crystallization. A scalable process should preserve that temporal buffering: first create the same crystalline precursor uniformly across the wet film, then remove the disordered volatile salt in a controlled manner, and finally complete precursor-to-perovskite conversion while avoiding local depletion fronts. Maximizing temperature, vacuum, or dry-gas flow from the start would defeat the mechanism by collapsing the induction period and reintroducing uncontrolled burst nucleation.

A practical line can be divided into at least three zones. In the levelling/precursor-formation zone, substrate temperature and solvent-vapour activity should be high enough to prevent edge skinning yet low enough to allow the chloride-containing crystalline intermediate to form uniformly. Wet thickness, blade gap, coating speed, ink temperature, and solids concentration must be tightly controlled because they set both the solvent-diffusion length and the volatile-salt inventory per area. In a second conditioning zone, solvent is removed under a spatially uniform, moderate gas-transfer coefficient while MACl vapour is allowed to accumulate to a controlled partial pressure. Enclosed or recirculating gas, transverse flow balancing, edge masks, and zoned heating can prevent the edges from losing MACl far earlier than the centre. In the final conversion zone, the MACl partial pressure is lowered progressively or the sweep flow is increased so that the gate is released across the web within a narrow time window. Temperature should be ramped rather than stepped abruptly, and residence time should be chosen from phase/element kinetics rather than copied from a spin-coated film.

The process variables are coupled. A thicker wet film requires longer solvent and MACl transport times; raising temperature accelerates both evaporation and precursor conversion; stronger gas flow reduces the boundary-layer resistance; and a high MACl back-pressure suppresses net volatilization. The control objective is therefore a narrow spatial distribution of the local sequence 'precursor formed—solvent substantially removed—MACl threshold crossed—perovskite conversion completed.' Computational mass-transfer modelling or simple tracer experiments can be used to design gas manifolds and residence times, but the model must be calibrated against in-line data.

Useful in-line measurements include hyperspectral reflectance or absorption to detect precursor and perovskite optical signatures, grazing-incidence diffraction at representative line positions to track precursor decay and perovskite growth, and X-ray fluorescence or another chlorine-sensitive method to follow the residual halide inventory. Exhaust mass spectrometry, infrared analysis, or salt trapping should quantify solvent and MACl release separately. Thermal imaging, wet-thickness interferometry, and gas-vapour sensors should map the process boundary conditions. End-point mapping must cover edge, centre, coating direction, and multiple production runs: phase fraction and orientation, residual chlorine and its depth profile, grain morphology/void density, thickness, local photoluminescence quantum yield or carrier lifetime, and sheet/device uniformity. A single centre coupon is inadequate.

Removal that is too rapid produces a steep supersaturation front, simultaneous nucleation of many small or misoriented grains, incomplete lateral coalescence, pinholes or voids from volatile release, and strong edge-to-centre phase differences. It may also strand composition gradients because the surface converts before the interior. Removal that is too slow leaves residual precursor or chloride-rich domains, prolongs exposure to hot solvent, encourages coarsening or decomposition, and can create insulating salt at grain boundaries or interfaces. A long induction period is not intrinsically beneficial if it is spatially nonuniform or if the final film is incompletely converted.

The transfer claim requires more than a shifted conversion time. At matched final thickness and composition, the staged process should narrow the spatial distribution of conversion onset, residual chlorine, grain structure, optical quality, and device parameters relative to an uncontrolled rapid-drying process. Stabilized power output, voltage, fill factor, hysteresis, and batch yield should improve, with no hidden penalty from residual chloride or volatile-induced voids. Operational light/heat testing should verify that any residual chloride-containing regions do not evolve during use. Because precursor-controlled crystallization can plausibly improve morphology but does not guarantee device performance, the mechanism and the photovoltaic outcome must be validated as separate links.
scoring_key_points: Preserves the precursor's kinetic-buffer role through staged levelling/precursor formation, controlled solvent and MACl removal, and synchronized final conversion rather than immediate aggressive drying.
Controls the coupled gas-flow, MACl partial-pressure, temperature, wet-thickness, and residence-time fields to minimize edge-centre and along-web conversion gradients.
Uses in-line phase/chlorine/effluent/thermal/thickness measurements plus large-area end-point maps of residual chloride, morphology, optoelectronic quality, and device uniformity.

Identifies burst nucleation/voids for overfast removal and residual precursor/salt or prolonged hot-solvent damage for overslow removal, and requires stabilized device-quality evidence beyond conversion time.
accepted_equivalents: Zoned oven, enclosed drying tunnel, or recirculating vapour chamber for staged annealing
Controlled MACl back-pressure, chloride activity, or volatile-salt atmosphere for regulating the gate
In-line XRF, laser-induced fluorescence, or calibrated halide-sensitive spectroscopy for chlorine mapping
Exhaust mass spectrometry, vapour trapping, or thermogravimetric calibration for separating solvent and MACl flux
Blade, slot-die, or meniscus coating as equivalent scalable wet-film processes
common_wrong_answers: Using the highest possible temperature or vacuum to remove chloride immediately
Assuming that a longer induction time automatically produces larger grains and better devices
Monitoring only final XRD at the centre of the substrate without mapping residual chlorine or conversion timing
Ignoring wet-film thickness and gas-boundary-layer differences between edges and centre
Claiming improved photovoltaic quality from morphology or lifetime alone without stabilized device statistics

expected_answer:
A distributed bulk-barrier mechanism and a contact barrier can produce similar S-shaped or field-dependent current-voltage curves, but they scale differently. A contact barrier is localized at a fixed interface: changing the contact energetics, interlayer chemistry, or device polarity should strongly change the loss, whereas increasing absorber thickness at otherwise fixed contacts should add comparatively little activation beyond ordinary transport distance. Distributed barriers are repeated throughout the absorber: the probability of collection decreases with the number of barriers traversed, so thickness, temperature, and internal field should interact even when the contacts are optimized.

The first experiment is a thickness series fabricated with matched composition, orientation, roughness, and defect density. The normalized photocurrent or collection efficiency should be analysed over the full operating-voltage range, not only at short circuit. For distributed barriers, the low-field collection loss and apparent activation should grow systematically with thickness, and the field needed to recover collection should increase with the transport path or barrier count. A contact-limited device should show a similar extraction threshold or interfacial voltage loss across thicknesses after optical-generation differences are accounted for. Three-dimensional perovskite or composition controls with the same contacts can determine whether the contacts themselves support thickness-insensitive collection.

The second block deliberately changes the contacts while keeping the absorber unchanged. The suspected electron and hole contacts should be varied independently using interlayers or electrode work functions that span the relevant band edges, and their conductivity/doping should be changed to alter built-in field without changing absorber morphology. Normal and inverted polarities, selective-contact-free or symmetric test structures, and electron-only/hole-only devices can identify carrier asymmetry. If one interface is dominant, an energetically better-aligned or more heavily doped contact should collapse the activation and restore thick-film collection; reversing the architecture should transfer the loss to the opposite polarity. If the barriers are distributed in the RP stack, contact optimization can raise the field and partially improve collection, but a thickness-dependent, thermally activated residual should remain.

Temperature, illumination, and bias supply orthogonal signatures. Temperature-dependent photocurrent, time-of-flight or transient extraction should yield an effective activation energy for carrier escape. In the bulk-barrier model, lower temperature increases residence in quantum wells, lengthens transit tails, and increases field dependence throughout the device. Light-intensity data should be interpreted by voltage region: near short circuit, current may remain nearly linear if the field rapidly removes carriers, while near maximum power or open circuit, accumulated carriers in wells enhance recombination. A contact barrier instead often produces interfacial accumulation, capacitance, and recombination whose magnitude depends strongly on injection direction and contact occupancy; its activation may not grow with absorber thickness. Care is required because ideality factors alone do not locate recombination.

Transient and spatial measurements should locate where carriers wait. Bias-dependent transient photocurrent, photo-CELIV, time-of-flight, impedance/admittance spectroscopy, and intensity-modulated photocurrent can reveal a broad distribution of transit or detrapping times. Cross-sectional Kelvin-probe, electroabsorption, or operando potential mapping can test whether voltage drops gradually or in repeated regions through the absorber versus abruptly at a contact. Depth-selective excitation from opposite sides is especially useful: a contact-limited cell should be sensitive to which contact carriers must approach, while a distributed-barrier loss should depend primarily on total path length through the layered stack. Temperature-dependent luminescence or spatially resolved recombination can test whether low-temperature carriers remain in quantum wells across the bulk.

Modelling must compare, rather than assume, the two topologies. Drift-diffusion simulations should fit the complete thickness-temperature-intensity-voltage data with either repeated well/barrier elements or a single interfacial barrier, using the same optical generation profile and independently measured contact parameters. A distributed model is credible only if one physically consistent barrier height/density reproduces the coupled trends and predicts new thickness or contact data. Excessive free parameters can make either model fit one curve.

The distributed-barrier mechanism is accepted if the activated, field-assisted loss scales with absorber thickness, persists after both contacts are energetically optimized, produces bulk transit/detrapping signatures, and is reproduced by a repeated-barrier model. The contact hypothesis is accepted if changing one interface removes the loss across all thicknesses, the voltage drop and carrier accumulation localize at that interface, and a single-barrier model predicts temperature and illumination behaviour. If contact engineering only increases the built-in field but leaves a thickness-dependent residual, it has mitigated rather than located the root cause.
scoring_key_points: Uses absorber-thickness scaling to distinguish a repeated path-length/barrier-count penalty from a fixed interfacial extraction penalty while controlling morphology and optics.
Independently perturbs electron and hole contact energetics, doping, and polarity and states that a true contact barrier should collapse when the responsible interface is corrected.
Combines temperature, illumination, bias-dependent transients, and spatial/depth-selective measurements to locate activated waiting and voltage drop in the bulk versus at an interface.
Requires competing bulk-barrier and single-contact models to predict the full coupled data and accepts a distributed mechanism only if a thickness-dependent residual survives contact optimization.
accepted_equivalents: Repeated quantum-well escape barriers, distributed hopping barriers, or serial internal barriers
Interfacial band offset, extraction barrier, Schottky-like barrier, or selective-contact barrier
Transient photocurrent, time-of-flight, photo-CELIV, or intensity-modulated photocurrent for transit/detrapping
Cross-sectional Kelvin probe, electroabsorption, or operando potential mapping for voltage-drop localization
Normal/inverted architecture or selective contact swapping as a contact-localization test
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the loss to poor vertical orientation without comparing matched-thickness structural data
Assuming a low-temperature activation energy automatically identifies where the barrier is located
Changing contact conductivity only and treating a partial field-induced recovery as proof of a contact barrier
Using a single current-voltage curve or ideality factor without thickness, polarity, and spatial/transient tests
Fitting a repeated-barrier model with many free parameters but not comparing a single-contact alternative

expected_answer:
A low g²(0) is an output metric, not a unique mechanism marker. Single-photon purity improves whenever two-photon or biexciton emission is suppressed relative to the exciton channel. Benign phonon-driven localization is a selective mechanism: thermally activated soft-lattice distortions transiently compress the electron-hole wavefunctions into a smaller effective volume, increasing the biexciton Auger-Meitner rate while preserving a bright, high-yield exciton. A static surface trap can also quench biexcitons, but it usually opens nonradiative loss for the exciton, produces blinking or dark states, and may create spectral jumps. Charging produces trions with strong Auger decay and can lower apparent multiphoton probability, but it is associated with discrete charge-state spectra, intermittency, and excitation-history dependence. Photobleaching or detector thresholding can make g²(0) look favourable simply because the emitter becomes dim.

The decisive experiment should perturb lattice dynamics reversibly while holding size, excitation, and surface chemistry constant. Temperature is the first axis: photon statistics, spectra, and state-resolved lifetimes should be measured on the same dot from low temperature to room temperature and back. Hydrostatic pressure, mechanical confinement, ligand-induced lattice stiffening, or an A-site cation series with different lattice softness can provide independent perturbations. Isotopic substitution of the molecular cation, where experimentally feasible, is valuable because it shifts vibrational frequencies with smaller changes in static electronic composition. All composition comparisons should be matched by physical size and by size normalized to the exciton Bohr diameter; otherwise stronger geometric confinement can masquerade as phonon localization. Surface-passivation and ligand-density controls are required because frontier-state localization in a finite dot can be dominated by surface states.

Heralded single-particle photoluminescence should separate exciton and biexciton photon windows rather than infer the mechanism from conventional ensemble decay. For each perturbation, one should measure g²(0) as a function of excitation probability, exciton and biexciton lifetimes, exciton quantum yield, saturation count rate, ON fraction, blinking dwell-time distributions, spectral centroid/linewidth, and spectral diffusion. Pump-power dependence is essential: a true single-emitter mechanism should retain the expected exciton and biexciton population scaling, whereas bleaching or state switching may change during acquisition. Charge-state assignment can be strengthened by identifying trion spectral shifts, altered exciton lifetime, photon-energy correlations, or changes under electrostatic gating. Surface traps can be tested by controlled passivation, ligand exchange, and oxygen/moisture exposure; if purity improves only when exciton yield and ON fraction deteriorate, the result is trap-assisted quenching rather than benign localization.

The dynamic-localization hypothesis predicts a specific covariance. As thermally active lattice disorder increases, the biexciton lifetime should shorten and g²(0) should decrease while the exciton quantum yield, exciton lifetime within its radiative regime, saturation brightness, and ON fraction remain high. Cooling or stiffening the lattice should weaken this selectivity, enlarge the effective wavefunction volume, lengthen the biexciton lifetime, and worsen antibunching in physically large dots; the changes should be reversible on reheating or pressure release. The effect should correlate with independent vibrational or electron-phonon-coupling observables such as Raman linewidths, temperature-dependent PL redshift/broadening, or lattice-displacement metrics. A cation series should follow lattice softness more closely than surface-trap density.

Static traps predict a different pattern: reduced exciton quantum yield and brightness, longer dark periods, nonreversible spectral changes, sensitivity to ligand/passivation treatment, and no clean reversible scaling with lattice-softness perturbations. Trion-mediated purity should correlate with charge-state switching, trion spectral/lifetime signatures, and gate or excitation-history dependence. Bleaching predicts declining count rate and ON fraction during the same trace. AIMD or electronic-structure calculations can support the localization picture by showing temperature-dependent frontier-state contraction, but they cannot substitute for the single-dot covariance because finite models and surface termination may bias localization.

The phonon-localization mechanism is accepted only if reversible lattice-softness perturbations selectively modulate biexciton lifetime and photon purity while preserving exciton yield and brightness, and if trap, charging, bleaching, size, and surface explanations are experimentally excluded. Low g²(0) alone, even with a short biexciton lifetime, is insufficient.
scoring_key_points: Explains that dynamic localization should selectively enhance biexciton Auger quenching while preserving the bright exciton, unlike traps, trions, or bleaching.
Uses reversible temperature plus independent lattice-stiffness/softness perturbations with physical-size, Bohr-diameter, and surface-passivation controls.
Requires heralded single-dot exciton/biexciton lifetimes and g²(0) together with exciton QY, brightness, ON fraction, blinking, spectra, and charge-state diagnostics.
Accepts phonon localization only when biexciton quenching covaries reversibly with lattice softness while exciton performance remains high and parasitic mechanisms show their expected signatures.
accepted_equivalents: Auger recombination or Auger-Meitner recombination for biexciton quenching
Pressure, rigid matrix confinement, ligand-induced stiffening, isotope substitution, or A-site cation substitution as lattice-dynamics perturbations
Photon-arrival heralding, photon-cascade spectroscopy, or state-resolved correlation spectroscopy
Trion spectral shift, electrostatic gating response, or charge-state blinking as charging diagnostics
Bohr-diameter-normalized size or confinement-regime matching for cross-composition controls
common_wrong_answers: Treating any mechanism that lowers g²(0) as equivalent to a high-quality single-photon source
Using ensemble photoluminescence lifetime alone without separating exciton and biexciton channels
Comparing dots only by nanometre size while ignoring different Bohr diameters and geometric confinement
Calling reduced brightness or increased blinking evidence for beneficial localization
Using a small finite-dot simulation as conclusive proof without surface and single-particle controls

expected_answer:
The proposed chain is physically possible because conductivity is sigma = q n mu. Compressive strain may increase the equilibrium or metastable electron concentration through changes in defect energetics, band-edge position, or charge compensation even while it makes the conduction band less dispersive and lowers mobility. Relaxation can therefore raise mu but lower n by a larger factor, reducing conductivity and fill factor. However, a thickness series alone cannot assign causality: thickness changes nucleation, grain structure, residual precursor, vertical composition, buried-contact chemistry, current path, and capacitance. Strain could be only a marker for one of these variables.

The strongest test changes strain on the same completed film or device while leaving thickness, composition, and morphology approximately fixed. A perovskite can be deposited on a bendable substrate, a piezoelectric actuator, or a substrate with a calibrated thermal-expansion mismatch. Small compressive and tensile strains should be applied reversibly while in-situ GIWAXS, X-ray diffraction, or Raman peak shifts quantify the actual lattice response. The strain range must remain below cracking, plastic relaxation, phase transition, and irreversible ion-migration thresholds. Measurements should be performed in a sequence such as zero strain—compression—zero—tension—zero to test reversibility and hysteresis. Temperature-based strain actuation requires a compositionally identical strain-relieved control because temperature also changes mobility, ion motion, and defect occupation.

At each strain state, conductivity, mobility, and carrier density must be determined independently. Four-probe or appropriately de-embedded vertical conductivity avoids mistaking contact resistance for bulk conductivity. Contactless optical-pump terahertz or microwave conductivity can provide a mobility-sensitive measure, while time-of-flight or space-charge-limited measurements with verified injection conditions can supply a second mobility estimate. Carrier density should be cross-checked using methods with different sensitivities, such as frequency- and scan-rate-dependent Mott-Schottky/DLCP, Hall or magnetotransport where signal permits, Seebeck coefficient, Kelvin-probe/Fermi-level shifts, charge extraction, or calibrated conductivity divided by independently measured mobility. In an ionically mobile perovskite, a single low-frequency capacitance slope is not sufficient because mobile ions and interfacial capacitance can mimic doping. Agreement over a frequency/time window where ionic response is suppressed, plus a non-capacitive method, is required.

A spatial causality test should co-map the same regions. Nanobeam GIWAXS or micro-Raman can map local strain; conductive AFM, Kelvin-probe force microscopy, microwave impedance microscopy, or patterned microelectrodes can map conductivity and potential. If strain controls electron concentration, regions with greater compressive strain should show a reproducible Fermi-level/carrier-density shift and higher conductivity after mobility differences are accounted for. Depth-resolved GIWAXS and cross-sectional electrical probing are important because the relevant strain may be concentrated near the substrate. Correlation must be evaluated within a single film and across repeated films, not by comparing unrelated points.

Matched controls should separate strain from process history. Films of the same thickness and composition should be prepared with different substrate lattice/thermal-expansion conditions or with inserted strain-pinning layers, while annealing, grain size, roughness, additive content, and contact stack are matched. XPS/ToF-SIMS or equivalent depth profiling should exclude cation/halide/additive gradients; microscopy should exclude cracks, porosity, and grain-size changes; and contact-resistance measurements should exclude a strain-dependent interface barrier. A chemically identical strain-relaxed reference made by controlled post-annealing can test whether the effect follows strain rather than the deposition sequence. DFT can predict the signs of effective-mass and defect-formation-energy changes, but it supports rather than establishes the experimental causal chain.

The device-level rescue should manipulate strain without simultaneously introducing a new passivating chemistry. Reversible compression of a poor thick device, or a strain-retaining intermediate layer with a chemically matched inactive control, should increase carrier density and bulk conductivity, lower series resistance, and restore fill factor while diffusion length, optical absorption, and composition remain essentially unchanged. Releasing the imposed strain should reverse the electrical change. The mechanism is accepted if same-sample strain produces the predicted reversible n and conductivity changes, local strain/electrical maps covary, independently measured mu and n close the sigma = q n mu balance, and device Rs/FF respond accordingly. It is rejected if only capacitance-derived 'doping' changes, if the effect follows interface chemistry or morphology rather than strain, or if conductivity recovery occurs without the predicted carrier-density response.
scoring_key_points: Explains the sigma = q n mu decomposition and why higher mobility can coexist with lower conductivity when strain relaxation lowers carrier density more strongly.
Uses a reversible same-sample compressive/tensile strain cycle with in-situ strain measurement and safeguards against cracking, phase change, temperature, and ionic hysteresis.
Separates mobility, carrier density, bulk conductivity, and contact resistance with orthogonal methods and rejects a single low-frequency capacitance estimate in an ionically mobile film.
Requires local strain-electrical co-mapping, matched composition/morphology/interface controls, and reversible device rescue of carrier density, Rs, and FF to establish causality.
accepted_equivalents: Bending stage, piezoelectric actuator, pressure cell, or thermal-expansion-mismatch substrate for reversible strain control
Hall, Seebeck, Kelvin-probe/Fermi-level, charge-extraction, or frequency-resolved capacitance methods for carrier-density cross-checking
THz, microwave, time-of-flight, or carefully validated SCLC for mobility
Nanobeam XRD/GIWAXS or micro-Raman paired with c-AFM, KPFM, or microwave impedance microscopy for local co-mapping
Defect-formation-energy or Fermi-level shift as the microscopic link between strain and electron concentration
common_wrong_answers: Claiming causality from a monotonic thickness series without independently changing strain
Using only Mott-Schottky slope as carrier density despite mobile-ion and interfacial-capacitance artefacts
Assuming higher mobility must always produce higher conductivity
Treating conductivity changes as bulk effects without de-embedding contact resistance
Using a chemically different passivation layer as the only strain rescue, so that strain and chemistry remain confounded

expected_answer:
The design target is a controlled through-thickness strain profile that preserves the electronic benefit of compressive strain without storing enough elastic energy to cause mechanical or chemical failure. Maximum compression is not automatically optimal. Compressive strain may increase electron concentration and conductivity, but it can also increase effective mass, alter defect and ion-migration energetics, and generate cracking or delamination during thermal cycling. The process window must therefore be defined jointly by carrier transport, device output, mechanical integrity, and operational stability.

A scalable architecture can divide the thick absorber into sequentially converted sublayers. Each intermediate converted surface acts as a quasi-substrate that limits complete relaxation of the next layer. The sublayer thickness and number of interfaces should be optimized: interfaces must be frequent enough to retain a reproducible compressive profile but sparse and chemically clean enough not to form insulating low-dimensional sheets, trap-rich boundaries, solvent barriers, or optical discontinuities. A graded scheme may be preferable to identical repeated layers, with stronger strain pinning near the buried electron contact and progressively more relaxed upper layers to reduce surface stress. The precursor/additive inventory, conversion completeness, and solvent exposure at every step must be controlled so that later coating does not redissolve or chemically alter earlier interfaces.

Mechanical boundary conditions are as important as chemistry. The substrate and transport layers should have compatible thermal-expansion coefficients and stiffness; otherwise cooling from the anneal can create uncontrolled transverse and edge stress. Zoned heating, controlled ramp and cooling rates, substrate support, film thickness, web tension, and humidity during conversion should be specified. On textured substrates, local curvature and thickness variation can concentrate stress, so conformal deposition and finite-element thermo-mechanical modelling are needed. Edge termination may require a strain-relief design because module edges often crack first. The optimized process should produce the target residual strain after full cooling, not only at the annealing temperature.

In-line mapping should measure process history and final structure across the entire area. Spectroscopic ellipsometry or interferometry can map sublayer and total thickness; thermal imaging records annealing and cooling uniformity; hyperspectral imaging detects incomplete conversion or compositional domains. Rapid or scanning GIWAXS/XRD and Raman mapping should quantify lattice parameter, strain sign/magnitude, depth dependence, and transverse/longitudinal variance. Wafer or web curvature can estimate integrated stress. Representative cross-sections should be examined for interface continuity, voids, cracks, and low-dimensional blocking phases. Composition and additive depth profiles should verify that a strain gradient is not actually a chemical gradient.

Electrical acceptance must close the transport balance. Carrier density, mobility, and conductivity should be mapped or statistically sampled, with contact resistance separated from bulk resistance. Module electroluminescence, photoluminescence, and dark-lock-in or impedance imaging can locate high-series-resistance regions. The desired strain profile should give low and spatially uniform sheet/vertical resistance, recovered fill factor, low series resistance, high stabilized power, and no loss of quasi-Fermi-level splitting or diffusion length. Coupons from centre, edge, and process-direction positions should be compared. A process that raises average efficiency but creates a long tail of low-FF cells is not scalable.

The harmful-stress threshold must be found experimentally through a strain/interface-density matrix. As compression or the number of quasi-substrate interfaces increases, one should track mobility and carrier concentration, crack density, adhesion energy, residual curvature, ionic conductivity, bias-induced hysteresis, and nonradiative recombination. Beneficial strain ends where additional compression no longer improves conductivity/FF or where mechanical and ionic degradation rates accelerate. Operando XRD/Raman during light soaking and temperature cycling can reveal relaxation; acoustic, optical, or resistance monitoring can detect crack initiation. Bias-dependent ion-migration tests and depth profiling after ageing should determine whether high strain drives halide/cation redistribution.

Qualification should combine stresses rather than rely only on dark storage. Encapsulated modules should undergo stabilized maximum-power illumination, damp heat or controlled humidity, thermal cycling, mechanical bending or vibration appropriate to the substrate, and combined light-heat-bias tests. Performance maps and strain maps should be repeated during and after stress to see whether strain relaxation precedes series-resistance or voltage loss. Delamination and crack propagation should be assessed at interfaces and edges. A chemically identical, strain-relaxed thick-film control and a conventional thin-film control are needed to separate strain retention from generic multilayer passivation.

Successful transfer is demonstrated when a reproducible strain window—not the highest strain—produces uniform carrier concentration and conductivity, low series resistance, high fill factor and stabilized module output, while retaining adhesion, phase/composition uniformity, and performance through combined ageing. If the initial FF gain disappears as strain relaxes, or if stronger compression increases cracks, hysteresis, ion redistribution, or voltage loss, the process has exceeded the beneficial strain regime.
scoring_key_points: Targets an optimum through-thickness compressive-strain profile using controlled sublayer thickness/interface density while avoiding insulating or trap-rich repeated interfaces.
Controls substrate mechanics, thermal-expansion mismatch, annealing/cooling ramps, texture/edge stress, and uses structural/mechanical modelling for large-area transfer.
Requires large-area strain/thickness/composition maps plus carrier-density, mobility, conductivity, contact-resistance, Rs, FF, quasi-Fermi-level-splitting, and stabilized-power acceptance.

Locates the harmful-stress threshold with strain/interface matrices and combined light-humidity-thermal-bias-mechanical ageing that tracks cracking, delamination, strain relaxation, and ion migration.
accepted_equivalents: Sequential sublayers, multilayer strain pinning, quasi-substrate interfaces, or graded strain-retaining architecture
GIWAXS/XRD lattice mapping, Raman strain mapping, or curvature-based residual-stress measurement
Finite-element thermo-mechanical modelling or calibrated substrate-curvature analysis
Electroluminescence/photoluminescence, impedance, lock-in thermography, or resistance mapping for module electrical uniformity
Damp heat plus thermal cycling and maximum-power bias for combined operational qualification
common_wrong_answers: Maximizing compressive strain without checking mobility, crack formation, adhesion, or ion migration
Adding as many interfaces as possible while ignoring insulating low-dimensional phases and recombination at repeated boundaries
Measuring strain and efficiency only at the module centre
Using dark shelf storage alone and omitting bias, illumination, humidity, and thermo-mechanical cycling
Claiming scale-up from a high initial average PCE despite large spatial variance or a poor-yield tail

expected_answer:
The transfer cannot be decided from the n=1 crystal descriptor alone. The single-crystal result establishes an intrinsic local structure-function tendency, whereas the n=4 device adds phase distribution, vertical orientation, grain boundaries, interfaces, solvent-dependent assembly, and contact energetics. The first task is therefore to verify that the same supramolecular motif and ammonium/inorganic geometry survive in the multi-n film rather than assuming that a crystal trend automatically transfers to a device.

A spacer and process matrix should compare a non-interacting control, a discrete point-interaction spacer, and a strongly associating or zipper-forming spacer under identical precursor stoichiometry. Solvent, concentration, coating speed, drying rate, substrate temperature, and solvent-vapour or thermal annealing should be varied around a controlled window. GIWAXS with incidence-angle dependence, absorption/PL phase mapping, solid-state NMR or vibrational probes, and cross-sectional microscopy/ToF-SIMS should establish low-n/high-n phase fractions, vertical distribution, inorganic-slab orientation, spacer segregation, and whether a continuous organic-rich layer forms at either contact. A useful spacer should reproduce the favorable local geometry while giving a narrow and reproducible phase/orientation distribution.

The electrical diagnosis should separate recombination from vertical extraction. Absolute PLQY-derived quasi-Fermi-level splitting, electroluminescence efficiency, Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV, and transient photovoltage assess non-radiative loss. Vertical mobility, transient photocurrent, impedance, temperature-dependent JV, contact-resistance analysis, and measured versus pseudo fill factor test extraction. If local structure and QFLS improve but measured FF and vertical conductivity deteriorate, the failure is likely horizontal slab orientation, an insulating spacer-rich interphase, unfavorable low-n phase placement, or contact misalignment rather than failure of the local supramolecular concept.

Association strength must remain in a processable window. Discrete, reversible point interactions may template the inorganic layer without causing excessive precursor aggregation, poor solubility, kinetic trapping, or mechanically brittle organic networks. An extended zipper or overly strong association may lock an unfavorable phase, broaden nucleation, generate insoluble aggregates, or impede stress relaxation. Rheology, solution spectroscopy/scattering, nucleation kinetics, coating-uniformity maps, thermal cycling, humidity exposure, and MPP operation should therefore be included. The go decision is the lowest-complexity spacer/process combination that preserves the local angle/transport benefit, produces vertically connected high-n domains and clean contacts, and improves retained energy under operational stress. A no-go result is a benefit confined to n=1 crystals, a narrow irreproducible coating window, persistent vertical-transport loss, or stability that depends on a transport-blocking organic network.
scoring_key_points: Separates intrinsic n=1 local structure-function chemistry from n=4 film phase distribution, depth profile, orientation, interfaces, and vertical transport.
Defines a spacer/process matrix and structural metrology that verifies survival and spatial placement of the supramolecular motif in coated multi-n films.
Uses recombination-versus-extraction diagnostics to explain improved local/QFLS properties but reduced measured fill factor.
Identifies a bounded association-strength and manufacturing window, with operational stability and reproducibility as go/no-go criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Blade coating may be replaced by slot-die, meniscus, spray, or another scalable coating method if drying and orientation are explicitly controlled.
Phase/orientation mapping may use GIWAXS, XRD, hyperspectral PL, absorption, microscopy, NMR, Raman, or equivalent depth-sensitive combinations.
Pseudo-JV may be replaced by Suns-Voc, electroluminescence-derived non-radiative loss, or another method that separates recombination from series/transport losses.
Over-association may be described as precursor aggregation, kinetic trapping, insoluble supramolecular networking, brittle packing, or formation of an insulating spacer-rich interphase.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the spacer solely because it gives the largest bond angle or smallest bandgap in an n=1 crystal.
Assuming that stronger hydrogen bonding is always better and ignoring solubility, nucleation, orientation, and stress relaxation.
Using longer PL lifetime as proof of better device transport without testing vertical extraction and contact resistance.
Declaring scale-up success from one champion small-area device without phase-uniformity, process-window, yield, and MPP stability evidence.

expected_answer:
Trap passivation can explain higher PLQY, longer PL lifetime, reduced monomolecular non-radiative loss, and lower trap-filled-limit voltage, but it is not by itself a complete explanation for scan-rate-dependent hysteresis, current overshoot, voltage undershoot/recovery, or long-time drift under constant electrical stress. Those signatures require a slow state variable. In halide perovskites the leading candidate is field-driven ion redistribution and interfacial ionic space charge, although thermal drift and dielectric/electronic trapping must be excluded. The low-dimensional grain-boundary phase can contribute separately by passivating electronic defects and by increasing migration barriers or tortuosity.

The optical branch should quantify recombination without a large electric field. Absolute PLQY, excitation-density-dependent TRPL, temperature-dependent PL, and SCLC trap-density/mobility measurements should determine whether H has a lower non-radiative coefficient while retaining similar electronic mobility. These measurements establish passivation but do not prove ionic suppression. The decisive ionic branch should use constant-voltage current transients, stepwise constant-current voltage transients, forward/reverse sweeps over several scan rates, low-frequency impedance or capacitance, and temperature-dependent activation analysis. Ion-sensitive spatial measurements such as bias-conditioned ToF-SIMS, Kelvin-probe mapping, or operando PL at interfaces can provide direct corroboration.

Ordinary electronic RC charging should scale with device capacitance and series resistance, occur on short and nearly temperature-insensitive time scales, and be reproducible without progressive history dependence. Ionic redistribution should be much slower, strongly dependent on temperature, field, dwell time, sweep rate, and polarity, and should alter interfacial potential or composition. In P, migration saturation time should shorten as current or field increases, overshoot/hysteresis should grow with pre-bias history, and low-frequency impedance should show a large ionic contribution. In H, those slow components, spatial ion accumulation, and activation-controlled drift should be strongly reduced even after electronic RC constants are matched.

A useful causal control is a film that receives comparable electronic passivation but no continuous low-dimensional boundary phase, together with a low-dimensional-phase sample whose trap density is matched to P by a separate treatment. If two samples have similar PLQY and trap density but only the boundary-phase sample suppresses slow electrical transients and bias-induced ion profiles, ion blocking is independently supported. Conversely, if all differences disappear after recombination and capacitance are matched and no slow temperature/field-dependent ionic signature remains, passivation plus RC effects may suffice. The strongest conclusion is dual: H reduces non-radiative recombination and independently suppresses ionic redistribution.
scoring_key_points: Explains why PL lifetime and trap-density improvements establish electronic passivation but do not by themselves explain slow overshoot, hysteresis, and voltage drift.
Uses orthogonal optical/SCLC and electrical transient, scan-rate, frequency, temperature, or spatial-ion measurements to separate recombination from migration.
States distinct predictions for fast electronic RC charging versus slow field-, polarity-, history-, and temperature-dependent ionic redistribution.
Proposes matched-passivation or matched-trap controls that isolate the ion-blocking contribution of the low-dimensional grain-boundary phase.
accepted_equivalents: Ion migration may be described as vacancy-mediated halide/cation motion, ionic space-charge formation, or field-driven compositional redistribution.
Operando PL, KPFM, ToF-SIMS, impedance, transient ion-drift, or equivalent techniques are acceptable when their time-scale and field dependence are interpreted correctly.
An electronic passivation control may use a molecular passivant, defect-healing treatment, or another route that matches PLQY/trap density without forming the same boundary phase.
RC exclusion may use impedance-derived capacitance/resistance, device-area scaling, pulse-width scaling, or high-frequency measurements.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that longer PL lifetime alone proves slower ion migration.
Calling every current transient ionic without checking RC, thermal, capacitance, and trap-filling time scales.
Using a single forward/reverse JV or EL scan at one rate as decisive evidence for ion blocking.
Treating trap passivation and ion blocking as mutually exclusive rather than potentially coexisting mechanisms.

expected_answer:
The defining prediction of a confinement/nucleation mechanism is a thermodynamic or nucleation-barrier threshold, not merely slower ion motion. Forming an iodide-rich nucleus inside a small mixed-halide domain costs bulk free energy plus interfacial and elastic energy. When the domain radius approaches the critical nucleus size, the interface penalty and limited volume can remove or greatly raise the free-energy minimum for a segregated phase. Increased photocarrier density changes the light-induced driving force, and temperature/composition change the mixing free energy and strain terms, so the stability boundary should move systematically with all four variables.

A decisive experiment should fabricate a domain-size series at fixed Br/I composition, matrix chemistry, matrix fraction, film thickness, absorption, and defect-passivation treatment. Size should be measured by TEM, scattering, or diffraction rather than inferred only from PL linewidth. A second series should vary matrix/domain interfacial chemistry or coherency while keeping domain size similar. Operando PL/absorption and GIWAXS under controlled excitation and temperature should map the onset time, segregated peak energy, reversibility, and critical intensity. If possible, nanoscale composition mapping after illumination should verify whether a new iodide-rich domain actually nucleates.

The confinement hypothesis is supported by a sharp or strongly nonlinear stability improvement below a critical radius, a systematic shift of critical intensity/temperature/composition with radius and interface coherency, and agreement with a free-energy model using independently estimated mixing and interface energies. Halide diffusivity may remain comparable within the guest domains; ions can be mobile without a stable segregated nucleus. A coherent matrix with higher interface penalty should stabilize more strongly than an incoherent or chemically mismatched host at equal size. Br-richer compositions or lower temperature may cross the stability boundary first if their light-modified free energy favours segregation more strongly.

Alternative explanations require different signatures. Lower defect density should correlate stability with trap density or non-radiative rate even after domain size is matched; deliberate defect creation/passivation should shift the onset without a critical-size law. Reduced diffusivity should appear as a higher activation energy or lower tracer/ionic conductivity and mainly change kinetics, whereas a purely thermodynamic confinement effect can eliminate segregation within the observation window despite measurable ion motion. Optical dilution would lower the apparent segregated-PL amplitude but should not prevent new diffraction/composition features or preserve the original band-edge absorption. Controls must normalize absorbed photon density and collection geometry. The strongest conclusion uses both kinetic ion measurements and structural/compositional evidence: mobility may affect how fast segregation develops, but finite size and interface energy determine whether a segregated nucleus is stable.
scoring_key_points: Frames confinement as a critical-nucleus/interface-energy problem whose stability boundary depends on radius, composition, temperature, and photocarrier density.
Requires matched domain-size and interface-coherency series with operando spectral, structural, and nanoscale compositional measurements at normalized absorbed excitation.
Distinguishes thermodynamic suppression from lower diffusivity by separating whether segregation is energetically allowed from how rapidly ions move.
Provides discriminating predictions for defect passivation and optical dilution rather than attributing all stability to confinement.
accepted_equivalents: The finite-size explanation may be formulated with classical nucleation, Cahn-Hilliard, phase-field, or another model that includes bulk, interfacial, and elastic/light-induced terms.
Halide mobility may be measured by tracer diffusion, ionic conductivity, transient ion drift, ToF-SIMS, impedance, or bias/temperature-dependent methods.
Operando structural evidence may use GIWAXS, XRD, electron diffraction, absorption, Raman, or nanoscale composition mapping.
A critical radius need not be perfectly sharp in a polydisperse film; a systematic size-dependent transition or probability is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that smaller domains necessarily have fewer defects and therefore proving confinement without matched-defect controls.
Equating slow spectral change with thermodynamic stability while never measuring ionic kinetics or structural/compositional segregation.
Comparing incident rather than absorbed photon density when the matrix changes absorption and optical collection.
Treating reduced segregated PL intensity as proof that no iodide-rich phase formed.

expected_answer:
The architecture must decouple the length scale required for phase stability from the length scale required for electronic conduction. One option is a dense, vertically connected network of subcritical mixed-halide guest domains separated by an ultrathin, crystallographically compatible matrix; another is vertically oriented guest columns or a graded matrix fraction that provides lateral confinement but continuous transport toward the contacts. The matrix should have a wider gap and band offsets small enough for the required carrier or should contain designed tunnelling distances. A thick, electronically insulating host that produces isolated bright dots is unsuitable for a solar absorber and may also cause charge accumulation in an LED.

A morphology matrix should vary guest radius, host volume fraction, interface coherency, and connectivity independently as far as possible. Co-evaporation, sequential vapour conversion, or another scalable method should be controlled with in-line rate/stoichiometry monitoring. GISAXS/GIWAXS, cross-sectional TEM, tomography, and composition mapping should quantify radius distribution, connected pathways, matrix thickness between guests, and stability after thermal processing. The selected point must keep essentially all guest domains below the critical size while remaining above the electronic percolation or tunnelling threshold.

Electronic qualification should start before full devices. UPS/inverse photoemission or Kelvin-probe measurements determine offsets; time-resolved microwave/terahertz conductivity, Hall or FET measurements, temperature-dependent conductivity, and vertical space-charge-limited current test mobility and activation barriers. Selective-contact half-stacks and transient photocurrent/photovoltage reveal whether carriers cross the matrix or accumulate at guest-host interfaces. In LEDs, excitation-zone location, turn-on voltage, EL spectral uniformity, efficiency roll-off, and bias-induced red-shift are critical. In tandem absorbers, EQE, collection length, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, pseudo- versus measured fill factor, and current matching are required.

Stability must be tested under electrical operation, not inferred from optical pumping. Operando EL/PL spectra, GIWAXS, impedance, and spatial current/temperature mapping should track phase segregation, ion accumulation, and hot spots under realistic current or MPP, heat, and illumination. A successful transfer preserves the confinement-derived critical-intensity margin while maintaining low transport activation, acceptable contact resistance, and uniform current. No-go outcomes include high PLQY but orders-of-magnitude lower vertical mobility, large turn-on or series resistance, strong thermally activated hopping, severe charge accumulation at host-guest interfaces, loss of guest connectivity during scale-up, or spectral stability only because carriers cannot reach or populate much of the absorber. Device-area yield and composition/radius uniformity must be demonstrated before the matrix concept is considered scalable.
scoring_key_points: Proposes a morphology that keeps guest domains below the segregation-critical radius while providing vertically connected percolation or short tunnelling paths.
Treats matrix band offsets, interface coherency, guest fraction, radius distribution, and connectivity as independent design and manufacturing variables.
Requires transport, contact, half-stack, and full-device measurements that reveal barriers or charge accumulation rather than relying on PL stability.
Defines electrical-operational stress tests and explicit no-go outcomes where optical stability is caused by isolation or poor carrier access.
accepted_equivalents: Connected guests may be arranged as columns, a bicontinuous network, graded volume fraction, thin-shell particles, or another architecture satisfying subcritical radius and transport continuity.
Transport may proceed by percolation, resonant/tunnelling coupling, or through a semiconducting matrix if energy offsets and mobility are adequate.
Scalable fabrication may use dual-source evaporation, co-sputtering, printing followed by conversion, vapour deposition, or another process with independent stoichiometry control.
Operational stability may be tested in an LED, solar cell, or suitable charge-injection/extraction stack if the stress and spectral/compositional diagnostics are device-relevant.
common_wrong_answers: Maximizing matrix fraction to suppress segregation without checking electronic connectivity.
Claiming device readiness from five-hour PL stability in an optically pumped film.
Using high PLQY as evidence of good extraction even when carriers may be trapped or isolated.
Ignoring domain-size broadening and connectivity changes during large-area deposition or thermal processing.

expected_answer:
The absorber program must first create a low-background-doping, low-trap, oxidation-controlled material without eliminating the phonon bottleneck or introducing deep localized states. SnF2 or related Sn-rich chemistry, reducing processing, oxygen exclusion, Lewis-base passivation, and composition control should be screened by Hall/Seebeck measurements, Sn2+/Sn4+ spectroscopy, vacancy-sensitive calculations or composition analysis, Urbach energy, PLQY, mobility, and carrier-temperature dynamics. The optimum is not simply the film with the longest PL lifetime: excessive additives, insulating residues, or very high doping can reduce conductivity, alter absorption, and obscure hot-carrier populations.

The contact architecture must extract carriers over a narrow energy window above the relaxed band edges and do so faster than the measured cooling time. Candidate concepts include resonant tunnelling layers, quantum wells/dots, energy-filtering heterojunctions, or molecular/2D interlayers with sharp density-of-states features. Electron and hole filters must be energy-aligned, thin enough for rapid transfer, and selective enough to suppress cold-carrier leakage and interfacial recombination. The absorber thickness and optical design should maintain generation without making transit slower than cooling. Interface chemistry must also block Sn oxidation and ion migration under the contact.

The extraction claim requires time-resolved and steady-state evidence. Ultrafast transient absorption or energy-resolved PL should measure the carrier-temperature decay in the finished contact stack and compare it with interfacial transfer kinetics. Energy-resolved photocurrent, photoemission, or spectrally selective extraction should show that collected carriers originate above the band edge. A contact that rapidly quenches hot PL is useful only if the quenching corresponds to extracted charge rather than interfacial non-radiative loss; charge yield, external quantum efficiency, and interfacial recombination must be measured simultaneously. Controls should include broadband nonselective contacts with similar chemistry and contact resistance.

The decisive device tests must move toward one-sun continuous operation and realistic temperature. Measure stabilized power, voltage, and EQE versus illumination while modelling the conventional bandgap-limited reference. Evidence for a hot-carrier benefit would include energy-selective photocurrent, an output voltage or retained carrier energy exceeding the value expected from a fully cooled population at the same absorber quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and a power advantage that follows the hot-carrier lifetime/contact bandwidth rather than pulsed-fluence artefacts. Thermal balance and lattice heating must be monitored. Long-term bias/light testing should track Sn oxidation, doping drift, contact broadening, ion migration, and loss of selectivity. No-go outcomes are hot PL only at many-sun pulsed excitation, extraction slower than cooling, voltage gain explainable by ordinary passivation, contact quenching without charge yield, or rapid loss of selectivity under operation.
scoring_key_points: Couples Sn-vacancy, oxidation, background-doping, disorder, mobility, and carrier-temperature control rather than optimizing PL lifetime alone.
Designs narrow-band energy-selective electron and hole contacts with transfer faster than cooling and with cold-carrier/recombination suppression.
Requires finished-stack measurements linking hot-population quenching to energy-resolved extracted charge and charge yield, with nonselective-contact controls.
Defines near-one-sun stabilized device evidence and no-go outcomes that exclude pulsed-heating, ordinary passivation, or non-radiative contact quenching.
accepted_equivalents: Energy-selective contacts may use resonant tunnelling, quantum-confined layers, molecular filters, 2D semiconductors, or other narrow-transmission architectures.
Hot-carrier extraction may be demonstrated by energy-resolved photocurrent, ultrafast charge transfer, selective photoemission, or equivalent carrier-energy accounting.
Conventional-reference modelling may use detailed balance, drift-diffusion with thermalized carriers, or an experimentally matched nonselective-contact device.
Oxidation/doping control may use Sn-rich additives, reducing agents, encapsulation, vacancy compensation, passivation, or composition engineering if transport remains acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming a hot-carrier solar cell from a blue-shifted PL spectrum or long PL lifetime alone.
Using contacts that quench PL without proving charge extraction or energy selectivity.
Testing only high-fluence pulsed excitation and ignoring one-sun steady-state carrier temperature and thermal heating.
Suppressing Sn vacancies with an insulating additive layer that destroys transport but improves optical lifetime.

expected_answer:
The fast-sweep two-terminal value is only an apparent mobility until several artefacts are excluded. Tin-vacancy self-p-doping raises the equilibrium hole density and conductivity, producing high off current and weak gate modulation; it can also make contact injection look favourable while reducing the on/off ratio. Mobile ions or dipolar polarization change the interfacial electrostatic potential during a sweep, creating history-, rate-, polarity-, and temperature-dependent transconductance that can be mistaken for electronic field effect. Contact resistance inflates or suppresses the extracted mobility depending on regime, and an incorrect or frequency-dependent gate capacitance directly rescales the calculated value.

The minimum matrix should combine forward/reverse sweeps over several rates and temperatures, pulsed-gate measurements with variable pulse width/duty cycle, constant-bias stress/recovery, output curves, gate-current monitoring, and capacitance-frequency/voltage characterization of the exact dielectric stack. Electronic channel current should respond on the fast pulse time scale and be reproducible after ionic motion is frozen or minimized; ionic contributions should grow with dwell time, show activation with temperature, depend on sweep direction and pre-bias, and relax after bias removal. Gate leakage must remain far below drain current and must not track the apparent transconductance.

Contacts require independent analysis. Channel-length scaling, transfer-length method, gated four-probe measurements, or Kelvin-probe potential mapping should separate channel resistance from source/drain injection. If the two-terminal mobility falls toward the four-terminal value after contact correction, the original number was contact dominated. Nonlinear output curves, strong length dependence of apparent mobility, and temperature-activated contact resistance are warning signs. The gate capacitance should be measured at the frequency/time scale relevant to the electronic pulse; using a low-frequency capacitance containing ionic polarization can substantially over- or underestimate electronic charge density.

Self-doping should be quantified independently by Hall/Seebeck, conductivity, photoelectron spectroscopy, or chemical/defect analysis. A credible transistor must show gate-controlled charge density substantially larger than uncontrolled background carriers, low off current, and a stable threshold. Intrinsic field-effect mobility should be reported only when two- and four-terminal/contact-corrected values agree within uncertainty, the value is stable across a fast electronic pulse window, hysteresis and threshold drift are small, gate leakage is negligible, capacitance is appropriate, and channel-length/temperature trends are physically consistent with electronic scattering rather than ion motion. Long bias holds should retain current and threshold, not merely recover after a fast sweep. The result should include device statistics, because a single high-mobility trace may reflect a rare contact or local filament.
scoring_key_points: Separates electronic channel transport from Sn-vacancy self-doping, ionic/polarization transients, capacitance/leakage error, and contact resistance.
Defines sweep-rate/temperature, pulsed-gate, bias-stress, leakage, and frequency-dependent capacitance tests with distinct ionic versus electronic signatures.
