The second gate is chemical cleanliness. XPS, FTIR, NMR, thermal desorption and ToF-SIMS should identify residual cations, anions, solvents and volatile by-products in fresh and aged HTLs. Ion mobility must be tested in HTL-only stacks, half stacks and complete devices under field, light, heat and humidity using depth profiling, impedance, bias-stress, displacement-current or isotope-tracer methods. A dopant that provides high conductivity by leaving a mobile ionic reservoir is not acceptable. The third gate is device physics: selective-contact PL, transient extraction, contact resistance, dark J-V, ideality factor and stabilized J-V should confirm that the dopant does not trade conductivity for interfacial recombination or hysteresis. Stability must include dark storage and continuous light, but also programmed light-dark and voltage on-off cycling with controlled dwell times, temperature and bias amplitude, because transition periods can activate migration, reduction or reaction chemistry. Periodic GIWAXS/XRD, EL/PL, depth profiles and chemical analysis should identify phase conversion or new products. Acceptance requires competitive transport and PCE, no persistent mobile cation or reactive residue, stable HTL/perovskite composition, and retained MPP power under cycling. Rejection is warranted if cycling reveals ion accumulation, irreversible reaction products, phase instability or performance loss even when continuous-light lifetime is long.
scoring_key_points: Separates dose-dependent p-doping/transport performance from chemical-residue and mobile-ion characterization.
Uses HTL-only, half-stack and full-device bias/light/thermal migration tests with depth or tracer measurements.
Requires extraction, contact-resistance and recombination controls so conductivity gains are not confused with device selectivity.
Includes light-dark and voltage cycling as mandatory gates and rejects dopants that fail through mobile or reactive residues.
accepted_equivalents: ESR, UV-vis/NIR polaron absorption, conductivity, Kelvin probe or UPS for spiro oxidation and work function
ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, impedance, transient ion-drift or operando XPS for mobility and residue
Cycling matrices that vary dwell time, voltage amplitude, temperature and illumination spectrum
A no-residue dopant, immobilized dopant or covalently bound redox system if transport is retained
common_wrong_answers: Approves the dopant solely because its fresh HTL conductivity exceeds that of LiTFSI.
Uses only continuous-light aging and therefore misses transition-driven ion chemistry.
Assumes a nominally lithium-free dopant is stable without measuring its own mobile counterion or by-products.
Ignores the possibility that stronger oxidation raises conductivity while worsening interfacial recombination.

expected_answer: The control set must keep total chloride, total ammonium concentration, solvent composition and solids content constant. It should include each single additive, binary mixtures, the full ternary mixture, an equimolar chloride supplied by a common small cation, and mixtures in which chain-length distribution is changed while total carbon content or ionic strength is approximately matched. A Lewis-base-free control is required because the alkylammonium chloride alone may not maintain soluble iodoplumbate complexes. Solution NMR, FTIR, Raman and UV-vis should quantify Lewis-base coordination, acid-base or HCl-transfer chemistry and precursor speciation. Time-resolved GIWAXS/XRD, optical absorption and PL during coating and annealing should determine nucleation onset, intermediate identity and lifetime, alpha-phase conversion and orientation. High-speed imaging, contact angle and drying-front analysis should test wetting and pinhole suppression, while SEM and grain-size statistics should quantify growth. Residual organic/chloride depth profiles and evolved-gas or thermal analysis should test whether longer-chain species remain or depart during annealing. A time-separated-role mechanism is supported if short-chain components advance alpha-phase nucleation, medium-chain components extend a beneficial growth intermediate, and long-chain components improve wetting/coverage, with the full mixture producing a phase-kinetic and morphology combination not reproduced by equal total chloride. Non-additive synergy requires the complete mixture to outperform the weighted or best single/binary controls in QFLS, grain-boundary recombination and device distribution without a persistent low-dimensional insulating phase.
scoring_key_points: Uses equal-total-chloride, equal-ionic-strength and Lewis-base controls in addition to single, binary and full mixtures.
Measures precursor speciation and time-resolved nucleation/intermediate/alpha-phase conversion.
Separately quantifies wetting, pinholes, grain growth, orientation and residual additive distribution.
Defines synergy as a unique combined kinetic/morphological and recombination benefit not reproduced by total chloride or additive averaging.
accepted_equivalents: A factorial or mixture-design experiment over alkyl-chain fractions at constant total additive
In situ GIWAXS, XRD, PL, reflectometry, interferometry or drying-front imaging
Mass spectrometry, TGA, ToF-SIMS or XPS for additive removal and residual chloride
Bliss-type, response-surface or other non-additivity analysis if scientifically justified
common_wrong_answers: Compares the ternary mixture only with one single additive and calls the difference synergy.
Changes total chloride concentration while changing chain-length distribution.
Uses final SEM and XRD only and cannot assign time-separated molecular roles.
Assumes better coverage necessarily means lower recombination despite possible smaller grains or insulating residues.

expected_answer: A near-surface bandgap gradient can produce band bending that depletes minority electrons from a defective, hole-rich surface. The resulting reduction in electron-hole overlap lowers the measured surface recombination and the apparent second-order coefficient even if the intrinsic radiative coefficient and some defect-capture cross-sections are unchanged. A field-dominated sample should therefore show directional depth sensitivity: excitation from the modified surface should produce carrier redistribution, spectral evolution and decay kinetics different from excitation through the substrate, whereas uniform chemical passivation should be much less sensitive to excitation direction after absorption-profile corrections. Raising injection or applying a bias that screens or flattens the band bending should restore carrier overlap, increase the apparent bimolecular term and shorten the field-extended decay; ordinary trap filling alone should not reproduce the full directional and bias-dependent response. Finally, a control that preserves the ligand and quasi-2D surface chemistry but removes the halide/compositional gradient should retain only the passivation contribution. Loss of the directional, screening-sensitive lifetime enhancement in that control, together with depth-resolved confirmation of the changed band profile, would identify the surface field as the dominant cause.
scoring_key_points: Explains that band bending reduces minority-carrier density and electron-hole overlap near the defective surface, so the measured k2,eff and lifetime need not equal intrinsic recombination constants.
Predicts a corrected front/back-excitation asymmetry for a field-driven mechanism and substantially weaker directional dependence for uniform chemical passivation.
Predicts partial collapse of the lifetime/k2,eff benefit when high injection or forward bias screens the field, while distinguishing this from simple trap filling.
Uses a chemistry-matched, gradient-flattened control plus depth-resolved energetic/compositional verification to separate field and passivation contributions.
accepted_equivalents: Minority-carrier exclusion, carrier depletion or reduced wavefunction/charge-density overlap may be used instead of electron repulsion.
Surface-potential modulation by electrostatic gating, ionic screening or controlled contact bias is acceptable instead of forward-bias screening.
UPS depth profiling, Kelvin-probe profiling or another validated depth-sensitive band-edge measurement is acceptable for confirming field removal.
common_wrong_answers: Treating every longer TRPL decay as proof that all defect densities and capture cross-sections decreased.
Using PL intensity alone without excitation-direction, injection-level or field-flattening tests.
Changing the ligand chemistry and the gradient simultaneously, which prevents causal separation.

expected_answer: Additive-only treatment can reduce non-radiative surface traps, so the perovskite stores carriers longer and has higher PLQE or a longer decay. Once a functional electron-selective layer is added, a shorter interfacial decay can instead mean faster transfer of electrons out of the perovskite; it must be interpreted with PL quenching, extracted charge and transport measurements rather than labeled as increased recombination. The minimum stack series is bare perovskite, perovskite/additive, perovskite/PCBM and perovskite/PCBM-plus-additive with matched optical density and ETL thickness. The first pair quantifies passivation, while the second pair combines time-resolved spectroscopy with photocurrent, conductivity or electron-only transport to quantify extraction. PCBM or PCBM-plus-additive films/solutions must then be aged under matched light/heat and examined directly for dimer products, molecular orientation, spatial coverage and conductivity. A causal claim requires all three links: improved perovskite-only radiative quality, faster and less trap-limited interfacial extraction, and a lower dimer fraction with more uniform/oriented PCBM whose transport advantage persists after stress. PL decay alone cannot establish the mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes longer additive-only lifetime from faster complete-ETL quenching: the former can be passivation, the latter efficient electron extraction.
Uses the four essential stacks with matched thickness/absorption to isolate additive passivation from PCBM extraction.
Directly measures dimer products and PCBM orientation/coverage/transport before and after matched light-heat stress.
Requires convergence of passivation, extraction and dimer/packing evidence; rejects a causal claim based on PL/TRPL alone.
accepted_equivalents: Time-resolved microwave conductivity, transient photocurrent or electron-only SCLC may substitute for one another as extraction/transport evidence.
Mass spectrometry, a validated dimer-specific spectroscopic marker or chromatographic analysis is acceptable for direct dimer quantification.
Polarized Raman, SFG, GIWAXS or another orientation-sensitive method is acceptable when linked to vertical transport.
common_wrong_answers: Calling every shorter TRPL decay greater non-radiative recombination without considering charge extraction.
Using only bare-film passivation data to claim improved PCBM transport or dimer suppression.
Inferring suppression of a chemical dimer solely from better device stability or smoother morphology.

expected_answer: Scale-up must control additive-to-PCBM ratio, solution complexation time and age, solvent composition, coating shear and speed, substrate temperature, wet-film drying/vacuum history and final ETL thickness. These variables determine whether the additive segregates to the buried interface, whether PCBM stands up or aggregates, and whether an over-rich insulating layer forms. Before completing the module, the coated area should be mapped for additive depth/enrichment, PCBM carbonyl or fullerene distribution, orientation, film thickness, local potential and electron conductivity, including grain-boundary regions and positions adjacent to scribe lanes. Additive-free modules and a chemically related control that lacks the key complexing/organizing interaction should be fabricated with identical perovskite coating, drying, electrode deposition and P1/P2/P3 geometry. Reliability testing should combine standardized light/heat/bias and humidity stresses with direct post-ageing measurements of PCBM dimer fraction, ETL transport, ion/electrode corrosion and spatial failure maps. The mechanism transfers only if uniform orientation/enrichment predicts higher FF and slower chemical/transport degradation across the module; a gain caused only by altered wetting, scribe resistance or active-area definition is not sufficient.
scoring_key_points: Controls additive ratio, solution ageing/complexation, solvent/drying history, coating shear/temperature and ETL thickness, including an over-addition boundary.
Maps interfacial enrichment, molecular distribution/orientation, thickness, potential and electron transport across the active area and scribe-adjacent regions.
Uses additive-free and interaction-deficient molecular controls with identical coating, electrode and P1/P2/P3 processing.
Combines standardized module ageing with direct dimer/transport/ion-electrode failure analysis and rejects gains attributable only to coating or scribing artifacts.
accepted_equivalents: Angle-resolved spectroscopy, polarized Raman, SFG or GIWAXS may be used for orientation if spatial sampling is adequate.
ToF-SIMS, AR-XPS on witness samples, cross-sectional microscopy or calibrated fluorescence/X-ray mapping may be used for additive enrichment.
A non-iodinated or weaker-binding benzoic-acid analogue is acceptable as an interaction-deficient control.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a small-cell additive concentration can be copied directly to a different coating hydrodynamic regime.
Reporting only module PCE without mapping ETL chemistry, orientation or scribe-related losses.
Attributing all ageing improvement to suppressed PCBM dimerization while ignoring ion migration and electrode corrosion.

expected_answer: The three variables must be separated rather than changed together. Useful groups include hydroxylation without appreciable etching; etching followed by controlled re-oxidation or vacancy passivation while retaining high OH; etching that exposes the underlying surface but is subsequently dehydroxylated; the full hydroxylation-etching treatment; and untreated or OH-depleted controls. Work function, roughness, sheet resistance and surface area should be matched or included as covariates. Before SAM deposition, O 1s chemistry/contact angle should quantify hydroxyls, EPR or a validated proxy should quantify oxygen vacancies, and structural/thickness measurements should quantify removal of the weak layer. After deposition and after DMF rinsing, sonication, storage and heat/light stress, SAM density, phosphorus distribution, desorption and local conduction/pinhole density should be measured. High OH with good initial adsorption but poor retention would show that hydroxyls are necessary but insufficient. If vacancy-passivated/re-oxidized ITO retains the SAM as well as the full treatment, the uncoordinated-In coordination model is not required; if retention collapses despite high OH, it supports that model. If an etched but OH-poor surface anchors poorly, removal alone is insufficient. The full mechanism is supported only when initial adsorption follows OH while long-term retention additionally follows stable exposed coordination sites and removal of the weak layer.
scoring_key_points: Creates treatment groups that independently vary hydroxylation, etching/weak-layer removal and vacancy/uncoordinated-In density while controlling roughness and conductivity.
Quantifies OH chemistry, vacancy sites and removed-layer structure before SAM deposition rather than using contact angle alone.
Measures SAM density/uniformity and desorption after solvent, storage and thermal/photochemical challenges, including local pinhole/conduction mapping.
States falsifiable outcome patterns: OH governs initial adsorption, removal alone is insufficient, and vacancy-associated coordination is supported only if retention tracks it at matched OH.
accepted_equivalents: Chemical vacancy passivation, oxygen annealing or plasma re-oxidation is acceptable for suppressing vacancy-associated In sites if OH is re-established and verified.
XPS/ToF-SIMS phosphorus mapping, ellipsometry, radiolabeling or another quantitative SAM-coverage method is acceptable.
Conductive AFM, local work-function mapping or selective electrochemical probes may be used to quantify pinholes/direct ITO exposure.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only untreated ITO with the full treatment, which leaves all three variables confounded.
Using superhydrophilicity as proof of strong multidentate SAM bonding.
Ignoring changes in sheet resistance, roughness or surface area caused by etching.

expected_answer: Orientation must be varied while the chemical passivation groups and energy levels are held as constant as possible. One route is to use the same polymer with substrate treatments, solvent additives or annealing conditions that tune face-on order without changing composition; a complementary route is a close structural analogue with matched LUMO and binding groups but deliberately disrupted backbone planarity or packing. GIWAXS azimuthal analysis and orientation-sensitive spectroscopy should quantify face-on fraction, while both out-of-plane and in-plane conductivity/SCLC and thickness-dependent electron-only transport establish anisotropy. UPS/CV, interfacial PLQE/TRPL, trap density and surface-potential measurements must show that energy alignment and passivation remain comparable. Orientation is assigned a dominant role only if increased face-on order systematically improves vertical conductivity, extraction time, series resistance and device FF across thickness while Voc, trap density and band offsets remain approximately unchanged. If FF instead follows LUMO shifts, PLQE/trap changes or film-coverage defects, orientation is correlated but not proven causal.
scoring_key_points: Varies molecular orientation using the same polymer or matched analogues while holding LUMO alignment and passivating chemistry approximately constant.
Quantifies face-on order and anisotropic out-of-plane versus in-plane transport, including ETM-thickness dependence.
Demonstrates matched energy levels, interfacial trap/passivation metrics and morphology across the orientation series.
Requires FF/series-resistance/extraction improvements to track vertical order and conductivity independently of Voc, traps and band offsets.
accepted_equivalents: Grazing-incidence diffraction, near-edge X-ray absorption or polarized spectroscopy is acceptable for orientation quantification.
Vertical organic transistor structures, cross-plane impedance or electron-only diodes are acceptable alternatives to SCLC for cross-plane transport.
A multivariate mediation analysis is acceptable if the experimental perturbations provide independent variation of orientation, passivation and energy alignment.
common_wrong_answers: Using only high OTFT mobility, which is usually an in-plane metric and may not predict cross-plane device transport.
Comparing chemically different ETMs whose energy levels, passivation and morphology all change with orientation.
Assigning causality from GIWAXS and FF correlation without vertical-transport or matched-interface controls.

expected_answer: The absorber, contacts, active area and electrode must be fixed while ETM identity, buffer layer and encapsulation are varied factorially: for example polymer versus PCBM crossed with the same organic buffer and ALD-SnOx, with encapsulated and unencapsulated subsets. Replicates should be tested under identical maximum-power-point light/temperature conditions, dark heat, damp heat or humidity, and thermal cycling; T80 and retention must be reported only within the same protocol, not merged across different buffers or stress modes. During ageing, the analysis should track ETM chemical/spectral change, aggregation or packing, hydrophobic-barrier integrity, interfacial trap/recombination growth, series resistance, ion/electrode migration and moisture ingress. An intrinsic ETM advantage is supported when the polymer outperforms PCBM across buffer and encapsulation levels with mechanism-consistent slower ETM/interface degradation. A strong ETM-by-buffer interaction, such as benefit only with SnOx, indicates stack-specific stabilization and must not be presented as a universal polymer property. Large-area coating uniformity and thickness sensitivity should be added before claiming manufacturing transfer.
scoring_key_points: Uses a factorial ETM x buffer-layer x encapsulation matrix with the same absorber, electrode, geometry and processing controls.
Compares T80/retention only under matched MPP, heat, humidity and cycling protocols and does not merge distinct stress tests.
Tracks ETM chemistry/packing, moisture barrier, interface traps/recombination, resistance and ion/electrode degradation during ageing.
Distinguishes a consistent ETM main effect from an ETM-by-buffer or ETM-by-encapsulation interaction and limits scale-up claims accordingly.
accepted_equivalents: A mixed-effects or survival-analysis framework is acceptable for separating ETM, buffer and encapsulation effects.
In situ UV-visible/IR/Raman, GIWAXS, XPS on aged replicas or validated electrical degradation proxies are acceptable for ETM chemical/packing tracking.
ISOS-aligned stress categories or equivalently documented light, temperature, humidity, bias and encapsulation metadata are acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing polymer/BCP MPP T80 directly with polymer/SnOx dark-heat retention as if they were the same stability metric.
Changing buffer, encapsulation and ETM simultaneously and attributing all improvement to the ETM.
Using hydrophobic contact angle or TGA alone as proof of operational device stability.

expected_answer: PL intensity and lifetime primarily report radiative yield and recombination kinetics; neither uniquely fixes a transport coefficient, so regions with similar or even longer lifetime can still have very different vertical diffusivity. A genuine depth-redistribution signal should be encoded through wavelength-dependent self-absorption and should show the expected complementary or symmetric evolution in reflection and transmission geometries. Its inferred transport rate should also remain consistent in a low-fluence regime where bimolecular recombination, band filling, bandgap renormalization and density-dependent photon recycling are minimized. The optical forward model must use the measured absorption and collection/filter response and must be tested against excitation-depth, surface-recombination and carrier-profile assumptions; the result is generally an effective ambipolar electron-hole transport coefficient rather than an isolated electron or hole mobility. If these checks are satisfied, the most plausible origin is anisotropic grain-boundary topology: vertically or obliquely connected grains form fast percolating columns, whereas disconnected or tortuous boundaries create slow regions.
scoring_key_points: Explains that PL intensity and recombination lifetime are non-unique proxies for diffusivity and cannot by themselves identify vertical transport.
Requires reflection/transmission spectral consistency plus low-fluence controls to reject intrinsic spectral shifts, nonlinear recombination and photon-recycling artefacts.
Identifies sensitivity to absorption/outcoupling calibration, excitation profile, surface recombination and the effective ambipolar nature of the extracted diffusivity.
Attributes validated heterogeneity to vertical/oblique grain connectivity and percolating versus disconnected transport paths.
accepted_equivalents: Complementary front-side and back-side spectral evolution
Depth-dependent reabsorption or optical self-filtering
Effective bipolar or ambipolar diffusion coefficient
Columnar-grain percolation or anisotropic grain-boundary connectivity
common_wrong_answers: Calculating diffusivity directly from PL lifetime or brightness without an independent transport observable
Treating every transient red shift as carrier motion without reflection/transmission and fluence controls
Claiming that larger grains alone prove fast vertical transport, without considering connectivity and boundary orientation

expected_answer: The even-in-field, second-harmonic response establishes an electrostrictive symmetry rather than a dominant linear piezoelectric response. However, the millisecond-to-subsecond kinetics and low-frequency cutoff are too slow for ordinary electronic or dipolar electrostriction, while the reversible field-dependent ionic activation energy indicates that the field changes the population of mobile, lattice-distorting defects. The most consistent interpretation is reversible formation and annihilation of iodide-related point-defect pairs, such as iodine Frenkel pairs, whose anisotropic local strain sums to a macroscopic contraction along the field. To distinguish this from simple electrode polarization, use blocking and non-blocking contacts, vary crystal thickness, and spatially resolve lattice strain or composition: a bulk defect-mediated strain should occur through the crystal and recover after removing the field, whereas net ionic accumulation should produce contact-localized concentration gradients and stronger electrode/thickness dependence. Simultaneous pulse-resolved XRD or interferometry and conductivity/activation-energy measurements over frequency and temperature should show matched defect-kinetic time constants; a conventional intrinsic electrostrictive response would persist to much higher frequency and would not track reversible ionic-activation changes.
scoring_key_points: Uses the E-squared, polarity-independent second-harmonic response to identify electrostrictive symmetry rather than dominant piezoelectricity.
Uses the slow frequency response and reversible field-dependent ionic activation energy to support field-induced formation/annihilation of lattice-distorting iodide defects.
Distinguishes bulk reversible defect strain from electrode-localized ion accumulation using contact type, thickness dependence, spatial strain/composition and recovery tests.
Proposes synchronized frequency-, temperature- or pulse-dependent structural and conductivity measurements; notes that intrinsic electrostriction should be much faster.
accepted_equivalents: Reversible iodine Frenkel-pair population
Field-induced point-defect chemical expansion or contraction
Second-harmonic electromechanical response
Blocking-electrode and thickness-scaling test
common_wrong_answers: Calling the response piezoelectric solely because an electric field causes strain
Attributing the bulk shape change to ion migration without any defect-formation or lattice-strain mechanism
Claiming that a low-frequency response proves ferroelectric domain switching despite the even-in-field, hysteresis-free behavior

expected_answer: PL quenching is mechanistically ambiguous because both rapid transfer of electrons into a selective contact and rapid nonradiative recombination at new interface defects reduce PL intensity and lifetime. Beneficial extraction first requires energetically downhill electron transfer, a hole-blocking offset and sufficiently higher electron than hole conductivity or mobility; thickness must be low enough that the interlayer does not add series resistance. The optical evidence should therefore include absolute PL quantum yield or quasi-Fermi-level splitting together with time-resolved transfer measurements: extraction may shorten the interfacial transient, but it should not produce a loss of quasi-Fermi splitting inconsistent with the device voltage. Selective-contact or electron-only/hole-only measurements, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, and control interlayers that remove the conductive or thiol functionality should isolate charge selectivity. At the device level, higher Voc and FF, reduced light-intensity ideality or Shockley-Read-Hall signature, near-linear Jsc with intensity, low series resistance and stable maximum-power output must converge; quenching accompanied by lower Voc or increased ideality would instead indicate an interfacial recombination sink.
scoring_key_points: States that PL quenching can arise from either useful charge transfer or harmful nonradiative recombination.
Requires favorable electron-energy alignment, hole blocking, electron-selective transport and controlled interlayer resistance/thickness.
Combines absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi splitting with time-resolved/selective-contact measurements to distinguish extraction from voltage loss.
Uses convergent device diagnostics such as Voc, FF, series resistance and light-intensity recombination slopes, with appropriate functional controls.
accepted_equivalents: Quasi-Fermi-level splitting or implied Voc
Electron-only and hole-only devices
Transient photocurrent or charge-extraction spectroscopy
Ideality-factor or Voc-versus-ln(light intensity) analysis
common_wrong_answers: Treating shorter PL lifetime as automatic proof of faster and cleaner extraction
Using energy-level alignment alone without demonstrating transport selectivity and device voltage preservation
Attributing a higher fill factor only to passivation while ignoring contact resistance and carrier selectivity

expected_answer: The interlayer needs a continuous electron-conducting pathway and a cascade energy alignment from the fullerene or perovskite to the cathode, while its valence levels suppress hole leakage. Increasing thickness or density may improve water blocking and Pb capacity but can increase series resistance, trap carriers or crack during coating; a conductive additive or hybrid architecture can decouple sorption/barrier functions from electronic transport. Metal-binding groups should provide stable contact chemistry without corroding or insulating the electrode, and Pb-chelating sites must retain capacity and fast kinetics in the acidic, halide-rich, water-exposed environment of a failed module rather than only in a clean model solution. Operational claims require large-area uniformity and contact-resistance mapping plus stabilized MPP ageing under light, heat and humidity with matched devices lacking the sorbent functionality. Containment claims require deliberately damaged or water-soaked devices, total Pb mass balance in the leachate and retained layers, spatial depth profiling of Pb migration, capacity/saturation and re-release tests, and evaluation after ageing; observing Pb near one interface without a leachate mass balance is not sufficient.
scoring_key_points: Balances electron-selective conductivity and energy alignment against the added resistance of a dense or thick barrier/sorbent layer.
Addresses moisture blocking, mechanically uniform coating and chemically compatible low-resistance contact to the metal electrode.
Requires Pb-binding capacity, kinetics, selectivity and non-release to be tested in realistic degraded-device chemistry and after ageing.
Separates operational-stability validation from breach/leaching validation using MPP stress, matched controls, depth profiling and quantitative Pb mass balance.
accepted_equivalents: Hybrid conductive-sorbent interlayer
Chelation, thiol coordination or heavy-metal adsorption sites
ToF-SIMS or another quantitative depth-profile method
Damaged-module leachate assay with inductively coupled plasma mass balance
common_wrong_answers: Maximizing sorbent thickness without considering electron transport or module series resistance
Claiming environmental safety from shelf-stability retention alone
Claiming complete Pb containment from an interfacial Pb signal without measuring leaked and retained Pb

expected_answer: A causal study must create matched controls rather than compare only two end-point materials. Film thickness, porosity, particle size, roughness, perovskite composition and crystallization should be held constant while crystallinity, exposed facet and vacancy density are varied independently where possible; complementary controls could passivate vacancies on the conventional particles or alter facet chemistry on otherwise single-crystalline particles. Bulk-transport dominance should be tested by Hall or conductivity measurements, mobility versus film thickness, temperature-dependent transport and device series-resistance scaling; a bulk mechanism predicts lower resistance and stronger benefits as the ETL current path or module area increases. Interface-recombination dominance should be tested by absolute PLQY/quasi-Fermi splitting, differential lifetime or transient absorption, interface loss velocity, diode ideality and saturation current, and interface-trap measurements; it predicts Voc and FF gains even when ETL resistance is matched. Optical absorption and integrated photocurrent should remain essentially unchanged. A mediation analysis across the control set should then ask whether FF follows mobility/series resistance after interface metrics are matched, or follows interfacial recombination metrics after conductivity is matched, with spatial potential and compositional maps used to detect hidden morphology-driven confounders.
scoring_key_points: Proposes matched or factorial controls that independently vary crystallinity/facet/defects while holding ETL geometry and perovskite processing constant.
Defines bulk-transport diagnostics and predictions using mobility, conductivity, thickness scaling and series resistance.
Defines interface-recombination diagnostics and predictions using PLQY/QFLS, carrier dynamics, ideality/J0 and interface-trap measures.
Requires unchanged optical generation plus cross-control mediation or correlation and spatial mapping to identify morphology-related confounding.
accepted_equivalents: Factorial design or orthogonal material controls
Implied open-circuit voltage or quasi-Fermi-level splitting
Interface recombination velocity
Kelvin-probe force microscopy or nanoscale potential mapping
common_wrong_answers: Assigning the mechanism from higher TiO2 mobility alone when all interface variables also changed
Using faster PL decay alone as proof of lower interface recombination
Attributing the fill-factor gain to improved absorption despite matched current generation

expected_answer: The ETL must first be shown to form a uniform, pinhole-free mesoporous network at module width with controlled particle dispersion, thickness, porosity and drying, while remaining compatible with scalable coating, perovskite crystallization and laser-scribe edges. The electrical model must separate intrinsic junction improvement from area-dependent losses: ETL and transparent-electrode sheet resistance, contact resistance, current-crowding, interconnect resistance, dead area and geometric fill factor should be measured and included in a distributed module model. Translation is credible only if spatial maps and statistics show uniform Voc, photocurrent and local shunt/series resistance, and if the cell-to-module loss budget preserves the expected FF advantage in matched control modules; stabilized output and independent certification are stronger endpoints than a single reverse scan. The stability decision must also move beyond dry-nitrogen small-cell operation by testing encapsulated and unencapsulated modules under combined light, heat, humidity and bias, inspecting scribe-line corrosion, adhesion and recovery. A go decision requires reproducible module-level FF and energy yield with acceptable process yield and no new failure mode relative to the conventional TiO2 control.
scoring_key_points: Requires scalable control of ETL dispersion, thickness, porosity, coating uniformity, perovskite compatibility and laser-scribe interfaces.
Builds a distributed module loss budget including sheet/contact/interconnect resistance, current crowding, dead area and geometric fill factor.
Uses spatial mapping, matched control modules, statistics and stabilized or certified output to verify preservation of the small-cell FF gain.
Adds realistic combined-stressor module stability and process-yield/failure-mode criteria rather than relying only on dry-N2 small-cell ageing.
accepted_equivalents: Cell-to-module efficiency-loss analysis
Distributed resistance or finite-element module model
Laser-scribe P1/P2/P3 compatibility assessment
Spatial electroluminescence, photoluminescence or lock-in thermography mapping
common_wrong_answers: Scaling the small-cell PCE directly by active area without an interconnection and resistance model
Comparing only champion modules rather than matched distributions and stabilized output
Treating dry-nitrogen small-cell retention as sufficient evidence of outdoor module durability

expected_answer: Temporal correlation alone is insufficient because trapped photocarriers can both change conductivity and exert lattice forces. The first test should resolve the onset and recovery of strain, carrier population, mobility and Voc/FF under stepwise illumination and dark relaxation over several intensities; a causal structural pathway requires a reproducible kinetic ordering and quantitative coupling, not only the same final time trend. Structural-topology controls should compare otherwise similar 2D families or spacer variants that differ in interlayer bonding and contractibility while matching absorption and photocarrier density; a non-contracting phase that still photodopes is a critical negative control. The variables should then be decoupled: impose comparable compression mechanically or chemically in the dark, suppress contraction by clamping or a rigid spacer while retaining photocarriers, or use electrostatic carrier injection to fill traps without illumination. Finally, measure out-of-plane band dispersion or band offsets, electron mobility and recombination/selectivity and test whether the observed barrier change quantitatively reproduces the Voc/FF gain in transport modelling. If performance follows strain when carrier density is controlled, the structural mechanism is supported; if it follows trapped charge despite suppressed strain, photodoping is dominant.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that simultaneous light-induced strain and conductivity do not by themselves establish causality and requires time-resolved onset/recovery across intensity.
Uses phase or spacer controls with different contractibility but matched absorbed photon density, including a non-contracting photodoping control.
Proposes a true decoupling perturbation: dark mechanical/chemical compression, structural clamping, or carrier injection without equivalent strain.
Requires quantitative changes in barrier/band alignment, mobility and device modelling to mediate the Voc/FF improvement while Jsc remains nearly constant.
accepted_equivalents: Causal mediation between strain, mobility and device voltage
Rigid-lattice or non-contracting structural control
Hydrostatic/uniaxial pressure or epitaxial clamping
Electrical gating or charge injection as a photodoping control
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that operando temporal correlation proves that contraction causes the performance increase
Using only a dark-heating control, which does not separate photocarrier effects from photostriction
Attributing unchanged Jsc to improved absorption rather than examining transport barriers and recombination

expected_answer: A valid workflow must characterize local order rather than relying on the average crystal structure. Candidate descriptors should include tilt sign, correlation-length anisotropy, domain morphology, the quasi-elastic spectral weight and relaxation time of the local distortions, A-site orientational order and hydrogen-bond topology, and the calculated distribution of local band-edge offsets. Temperature-dependent measurements should determine whether dynamic domains slow, lock into long-range ferroelastic twins or instead remain isotropic and transform without twin formation. Optical and transport validation should include temperature-dependent Urbach energy, PL linewidth and quantum yield, and diffusion or mobility. A candidate passes only if it preserves the target bandgap while showing small local band-offset variance, weak or short-lived quasi-elastic disorder, low correlation anisotropy, no strong precursor-to-twin continuity and robust transport across the operating-temperature range. Average symmetry can hide finite local domains, mean tilt angle cannot encode correlation topology, and one PL spectrum cannot separate static defects from reversible dynamic disorder.
scoring_key_points: Includes local tilt sign, correlation length or anisotropy, domain morphology and fluctuation lifetime rather than average symmetry alone.
Includes A-site orientation or hydrogen bonding and local electronic band-offset calculations as mechanistic screening descriptors.
Requires temperature-dependent structural and optoelectronic tests that reveal domain slowing, twinning pathways and reversible disorder.
Defines pass/fail logic linking low dynamic band-edge disorder and weak ferroelastic precursor behavior to preserved bandgap and transport.
accepted_equivalents: Pair-distribution-function, total-scattering or diffuse-scattering descriptors of local order
Spectral linewidth of quasi-elastic scattering as a proxy for correlation time
Local potential variance or band-edge fluctuation amplitude
Absence of a domain-to-twin inheritance pathway as a ferroelastic-stability criterion
common_wrong_answers: Screening only by Goldschmidt tolerance factor, average lattice constant or room-temperature XRD.
Selecting the smallest mean tilt angle without considering whether the remaining tilts form long coherent domains.
Using a high room-temperature PL intensity as the sole criterion without temperature or transport measurements.
Assuming that all cubic-to-lower-symmetry transitions have the same ferroelastic consequences.

expected_answer: Sn(II) oxidation to Sn(IV), together with tin-vacancy formation, should be tested first because it can generate excessive p-type carrier density, increase non-radiative recombination and dark current, depress quasi-Fermi-level splitting and accelerate time-dependent degradation even in a sealed device if oxidation occurred during precursor preparation or coating. It can be diagnosed by Sn(IV)/Sn(II) chemical analysis, Hall or conductivity measurements, carrier-density measurements and changes after precursor purification or reducing processing. Incomplete coverage or pinholes create direct contact pathways and low shunt resistance, principally lowering fill factor and often voltage; cross-sectional or plan-view microscopy, dark J-V, light-intensity-dependent J-V and thickness/coverage controls are decisive. Contact energetics should be examined by UPS/Kelvin-probe measurements and selective-contact controls: an unfavorable band offset limits voltage or extraction despite correct optical absorption and may be altered systematically by halide composition or contact choice. Agreement between EQE-integrated and measured current rules out a gross photocurrent-calibration error but does not distinguish these electrical loss channels.
scoring_key_points: Links Sn(II) oxidation or tin-vacancy self-doping to high carrier density, recombination, dark current, voltage loss and continuing instability.
Links incomplete coverage or pinholes to low shunt resistance and fill-factor or voltage loss, with microscopy and dark/light-intensity J-V as discriminating tests.
Links contact energy offsets to voltage or extraction loss and proposes UPS, Kelvin-probe or contact-substitution diagnostics.
Uses the consistent absorption/EQE/current evidence to exclude a gross optical-current mismatch while preserving the need for electrical failure analysis.
accepted_equivalents: Sn4+ impurity, Sn vacancies or degenerate p-type self-doping
Parallel-resistance loss, pinhole-mediated leakage or direct electrode contact
Quasi-Fermi-level splitting measurements as a voltage-loss diagnostic
Time-resolved photoluminescence or electroluminescence efficiency as recombination diagnostics
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all losses to the narrower bandgap without testing oxidation, shunts or contacts.
Claiming that agreement between EQE-integrated current and Jsc proves the device has no electrical losses.
Treating inert storage as proof that oxidation could not have occurred during precursor synthesis or film deposition.
Proposing only additional encapsulation without identifying the dominant loss mechanism.

expected_answer: The strategy should begin with high-purity Sn(II) salts, explicit removal or quantification of Sn(IV), oxygen- and moisture-limited synthesis and coating, and a chemically reducing or Sn(II)-buffered formulation that suppresses tin-vacancy formation without introducing deep traps. Deposition must produce continuous, sufficiently thick coverage with controlled crystallization, because a nominally high-mobility absorber cannot compensate for pinholes and low shunt resistance. Selective contacts should be chosen or modified to minimize interfacial recombination and unfavorable offsets while avoiding dopants or solvents that oxidize the tin perovskite. Qualification must compare equal-initial-performance devices and track Sn oxidation state, carrier density, dark current, shunt resistance, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, EQE-integrated current, J-V parameters and stabilized power under controlled oxygen, temperature and illumination stresses. A genuine improvement should retain current and fill factor while maintaining or increasing voltage, show lower Sn(IV) and carrier density, lower leakage and slower chemical change, rather than merely starting from a lower-current or thicker, optically underperforming device.
scoring_key_points: Prioritizes Sn(II) precursor purity, oxygen control and suppression of Sn-vacancy/self-doping chemistry.
Requires continuous morphology and high shunt resistance through controlled deposition and thickness rather than relying on intrinsic mobility.
Includes contact-energy and interfacial-recombination engineering that is chemically compatible with Sn(II).
Defines matched-initial-performance aging with chemical, electrical, optical and stabilized-power metrics that can distinguish true stabilization from performance sacrifice.
accepted_equivalents: Reducing additives, SnF2 or an Sn-rich chemical-potential strategy when justified as vacancy suppression
Glovebox or closed-line coating with quantified oxygen exposure
Maximum-power-point aging, shelf aging and thermal aging as complementary qualification stresses
Absolute PL or electroluminescence yield and QFLS as non-radiative-loss metrics
common_wrong_answers: Relying only on thicker encapsulation while ignoring oxidation introduced before encapsulation.
Accepting improved retention that results solely from a much lower initial current or efficiency.
Optimizing halide composition for voltage without checking morphology, oxidation state or current loss.
Reporting only normalized PCE retention without absolute Jsc, Voc, fill factor, leakage and chemical-state data.

expected_answer: Auger loss should emerge at high carrier density in both optical high-fluence and electrical measurements, producing a super-bimolecular or approximately cubic density dependence, accelerated early-time decay and an EQE roll-off that scales primarily with instantaneous carrier density. Injection imbalance or interfacial quenching can leave the neat-film PLQE high while degrading EL: signatures include divergence between PL and EL decays, transient-EL overshoot or delayed components, strong sensitivity to transport-layer thickness or injection barriers, and carrier accumulation at one interface. Joule heating and ion migration are slower and history dependent; they should show temperature rise, hysteresis, spectral or voltage drift, delayed recovery after bias removal, and strong dependence on pulse duty cycle and ambient temperature. Measurements should therefore combine fluence-dependent transient PL, current-dependent transient EL, charge-balance/contact controls, pulsed-versus-continuous operation, thermal imaging and bias-history tests. The bulk heterostructure should be optimized to keep rapid energy transfer and radiative bimolecular recombination dominant while avoiding transport bottlenecks and high-density accumulation.
scoring_key_points: Identifies Auger loss by high-density scaling in both optical and electrical excitation and by accelerated early-time decay.
Identifies injection imbalance/interfacial quenching by PL-EL divergence, transient-EL behavior and strong contact or transport-layer dependence.
Identifies heating/ion migration by slow, hysteretic, temperature- and duty-cycle-dependent spectral/voltage drift and recovery.
Proposes a combined fluence-, current-, pulse-, temperature- and contact-control matrix rather than relying on EQE roll-off alone.
accepted_equivalents: Exciton-exciton annihilation when the answer correctly frames it as a high-density non-radiative channel
Space-charge accumulation or unbalanced electron/hole injection
Bias-induced halide redistribution or ionic interfacial screening
Electrothermal degradation distinguished using pulsed operation and direct temperature measurement
common_wrong_answers: Calling every high-current EQE loss Auger recombination without fluence or contact controls.
Using high low-fluence PLQE to conclude that EL must remain trap-free at all current densities.
Interpreting a spectral shift as phase segregation without checking device temperature and bias history.
Listing mechanisms without predicting distinguishable temporal or scaling signatures.

expected_answer: The strong improvement after dry conditioning without a change in thickness or absorption points first to residual solvent or solvate trapped at the single-crystal/selective-contact interface. Such residue can create poorly contacted or ionically conductive regions, lower shunt resistance, raise low-frequency and dark-current noise, and make the response drift; drying should increase shunt resistance and SNR while leaving bulk absorption and, ideally, bulk mobility-lifetime properties nearly unchanged. This hypothesis can be tested by time-resolved dark I-V and impedance/noise spectra during conditioning, interfacial vibrational or chemical analysis, cross-sectional potential or current mapping, and a process control with deliberately varied drying. A bulk-trap mechanism should instead correlate with carrier lifetime, mobility-lifetime product, depth-dependent collection and persistent trapping signatures, and should not be removed solely by interfacial drying. An insufficient built-in field should produce systematic thickness-dependent collection loss and contact-polarity dependence; it should respond to contact work-function changes or a small external bias rather than mainly to solvent removal. The decisive diagnosis requires separating improvements in leakage/noise from changes in charge-collection efficiency.
scoring_key_points: Prioritizes residual interfacial solvate because dry conditioning improves leakage/SNR without changing absorption or thickness.
Predicts increased shunt resistance and reduced low-frequency/dark-current noise, supported by interfacial spectroscopy, impedance and spatial mapping.
Distinguishes bulk trapping through lifetime, mobility-lifetime, depth-dependent collection and persistent-trap signatures that drying alone should not remove.
Distinguishes insufficient built-in field through contact-polarity/work-function and thickness or small-bias dependence rather than conditioning dependence.
accepted_equivalents: Residual precursor complex, solvent-rich interlayer or interfacial ionic-conduction pathway
Thermally stimulated current, time-of-flight or transient photocurrent for bulk trapping
KPFM, electron-beam-induced current or scanning photocurrent for field/contact mapping
Noise spectral density and impedance phase as alternatives to simple dark-current measurements
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that high X-ray absorption guarantees high SNR and charge-collection efficiency.
Attributing the improvement to bulk defect healing without testing whether bulk lifetime or mobility changes.
Applying a large bias as the first diagnostic, thereby introducing gain, ionic drift and degradation.
Measuring only average photocurrent and ignoring shunt resistance, noise spectrum and spatial non-uniformity.

expected_answer: Harder X-rays require a larger absorption path, but increasing thickness lengthens carrier transit, amplifies trapping and spatial non-uniformity, and may exceed the distance over which the contact-built-in field collects charge efficiently at zero bias. A thicker device can therefore gain absorption while losing charge-collection efficiency, response speed and DQE. Shrinking the pitch below the lateral charge-cloud size causes charge sharing and pixel cross-talk, so nominal sampling density improves without a corresponding MTF gain. The redesign should combine high-quality thick or stacked absorber geometry with asymmetric low-noise contacts, field-shaping or segmented electrodes, guard structures or physical/electrostatic pixel isolation, and possibly depth-aware or charge-sharing reconstruction, while avoiding the high fields that trigger ionic migration and gain-related noise. Validation must report energy-dependent absorption/DE, charge-collection efficiency, NED and DQE versus dose and spatial frequency, MTF and charge-sharing kernels, response time, noise spectra, and long-term operation under zero or minimal bias. The optimum thickness and pitch must be derived from the coupled absorption-transport-resolution model rather than optimized independently.
scoring_key_points: Explains the thickness trade-off between hard-X-ray absorption and zero-bias transport, trapping, response time or collection-field reach.
Explains why pitch below the charge-cloud scale causes sharing/cross-talk and limits MTF despite finer lithographic sampling.
Proposes field shaping, segmentation/isolation, guard structures or reconstruction while preserving zero/minimal-bias stability and low noise.
Requires energy-, dose- and spatial-frequency-dependent DE/NED/DQE, MTF, noise, response-time and long-term-stability validation.
accepted_equivalents: Stacked thin single-crystal layers or tiled absorbers as an alternative to one very thick crystal
Small-pixel effect, coplanar-grid or depth-sensing concepts if adapted without high-field instability
Charge-sharing correction or event-centroid reconstruction
Higher-Z composition engineering if transport and chemical stability are also evaluated
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that calculated absorption alone determines detector efficiency at high photon energy.
Assuming that smaller pixels automatically yield higher spatial resolution regardless of charge-cloud size.
Recovering charge collection by applying a large electric field without accounting for ionic migration, gain noise and degradation.
Reporting sensitivity alone without normalized noise, DQE and spatial-frequency measurements.

expected_answer:
The A-site additive can improve electronic quality and damage structural quality through different defect channels. A strongly hydrogen-bonding or otherwise iodide-coordinating A-site cation can raise the formation energy of halide vacancies and reduce halide-vacancy-related traps. That explains the longer lifetime and lower trap-density signature. Because the cation is oversized, however, it expands and locally distorts the lattice. The crystal can lower this elastic energy by creating Pb vacancies or vacancy-associated complexes. Such a strain-relaxation channel produces a broader distribution of lattice spacings and orientations, so rocking-curve width and microstrain increase even though one class of recombination center has been suppressed. Pb-vacancy-related disorder and the associated ionic defect population can also destabilize the internal field and dark current.

The trace B-site species should be interpreted as a vacancy/strain compensator rather than a conventional electronic dopant. If it is isovalent and nearly radius matched to Pb, it can occupy or bind at Pb-vacancy environments and raise the energetic cost of forming additional Pb vacancies without generating deep gap states. The expected cascade is reduced microstrain and rocking-curve width, lower trap density, longer carrier lifetime or larger mobility-lifetime product, and less bias-induced dark-current drift, while the average bandgap and major diffraction peak positions remain nearly unchanged.

A decisive test requires defect-specific energetics and orthogonal bulk measurements. Calculations or defect-sensitive spectroscopy should show that the A-site additive raises halide-vacancy formation energy but lowers Pb-vacancy formation energy under a strain-relief configuration, whereas the B-site dopant raises the Pb-vacancy cost. High-resolution rocking curves, Williamson-Hall or reciprocal-space analysis, and spatial strain mapping should improve without a systematic lattice shift or secondary-phase peaks. Elemental mapping and composition analysis must verify dilute, distributed incorporation. Finally, Hall/Fermi-level measurements, conductivity versus temperature, and absorption/UPS controls should show no carrier-density shift expected from shallow doping. Radius-mismatched or electronically active B-site controls should fail to reproduce the combined strain, lifetime, and dark-current improvements.
scoring_key_points: Explain that the oversized A-site cation can suppress halide-vacancy traps while simultaneously generating elastic strain that is relaxed through Pb-vacancy formation.
Interpret the trace isovalent, radius-matched B-site dopant as a Pb-vacancy/strain compensator rather than as a source of free carriers.
Connect the mechanism to the joint signatures: narrower rocking curve and lower microstrain, improved lifetime/trap metrics, suppressed dark-current drift, and little average bandgap or phase change.
Require defect-energetic, diffraction/strain, composition, and carrier-density controls that rule out shallow doping and second-phase formation.
accepted_equivalents: Halide-vacancy passivation may be described as stronger anion coordination, increased vacancy formation energy, or reduced under-coordinated Pb/halide defect density.
Pb-vacancy formation may be described as a strain-compensation, elastic-relaxation, or defect-complex channel.
Reciprocal-space mapping, synchrotron microdiffraction, Raman strain mapping, or coherent X-ray imaging are acceptable alternatives to rocking-curve/microstrain analysis.
Hall, Seebeck, Kelvin-probe/UPS, conductivity activation, or photothermal-deflection measurements may be used to exclude ordinary electronic doping or a hidden phase.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that a longer PL lifetime proves the crystal has fewer defects of every type and therefore cannot have higher microstrain.
Treating an isovalent trace B-site species as beneficial only because it increases free-electron concentration.
Using unchanged conventional XRD peak positions alone to prove uniform dopant incorporation and absence of local strain.
Attributing dark-current stabilization solely to electrode contact improvement without testing bulk defect and strain signatures.

expected_answer:
The transfer must control the local defect state, not merely copy nominal feed fractions. A factorial or response-surface design should vary the A-site additive and trace B-site compensator independently around the laboratory optimum, while also varying growth rate, thermal gradient, supersaturation, cooling history, and boule position. These variables determine segregation, elastic strain, vacancy populations, and inclusion density. Feed composition must be linked to actual radial and axial composition by ICP, XRF, electron-probe or equivalent mapping; nominal concentration is not an acceptable process variable by itself.

Acceptance should be spatial and multiscale. Across the boule and finished array, high-resolution diffraction or microdiffraction should map rocking-curve width, mosaicity and microstrain. PL/TRPL, trap-density measurements, mobility-lifetime product, resistivity, and bias-dependent dark-current drift should be mapped at the same coordinates. X-ray attenuation, sensitivity, detection limit, linearity, temporal response and pixel crosstalk should be measured under calibrated dose. Imaging qualification should include MTF or an equivalent edge/line-pair metric, not only integrated current. A useful process window is one in which composition variance and structural/electrical tails, rather than only the mean, remain below limits.

Bulk and contact contributions require matched controls. The same crystal slices should receive alternative electrodes or surface treatments, and identical contacts should be applied to crystals spanning the composition/strain map. Contact-only test structures, surface-sensitive spectroscopy, and thickness-dependent dark-current or charge-collection measurements can reveal whether improvement is interfacial. If the dual-site composition is causal, strain, trap, mobility-lifetime, and ion-drift improvements should persist across electrode variants and through the bulk.

The stress matrix should independently and jointly vary temperature, electric field polarity and magnitude, X-ray dose rate/total dose, light or dark storage, humidity, and thermal cycling. Recovery after removing bias distinguishes reversible ionic polarization from permanent chemistry. Go/no-go criteria should require bounded pixel-level drift, retained sensitivity and MTF, no growth of composition/strain hot spots, and statistically stable yield after stress. Increasing dopant content is rejected if it improves average lifetime but creates segregation, secondary phases, resistive pixels, or wider performance distributions.
scoring_key_points: Optimize actual local A-site/B-site composition together with growth rate, supersaturation, thermal gradient, and cooling history rather than copying nominal feed ratios.
Use co-registered spatial maps of composition, microstrain/mosaicity, trap and mobility-lifetime metrics, dark-current drift, calibrated X-ray response, and imaging resolution across the array.
Separate bulk composition/strain effects from electrode or surface passivation through matched contact swaps, thickness dependence, and surface-sensitive controls.

Define multi-stressor temperature-bias-radiation-environment tests and statistical go/no-go criteria based on pixel distributions, retained sensitivity/MTF, drift, and absence of segregation or secondary phases.
accepted_equivalents: Design of experiments, Bayesian optimization, response-surface methods, or statistical process control are acceptable optimization frameworks.
XRF, EPMA, LA-ICP-MS, SIMS, or spatially resolved XPS/EDS may be used for radial and axial composition mapping.
Micro-XRD, reciprocal-space mapping, diffraction topography, Raman mapping, or birefringence imaging may be used to map strain and mosaicity.
Contact swaps, symmetric blocking contacts, surface-passivated versus unpassivated devices, or thickness scaling are acceptable ways to separate bulk and interface effects.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only the nominal dopant concentration while ignoring segregation and the thermal history of a larger boule.
Qualifying the array from mean sensitivity while ignoring pixel tails, spatial drift, crosstalk, or MTF.
Assigning every improvement to bulk strain engineering without matched electrode and surface controls.
Using a single high-temperature storage test as proof of radiation, bias, humidity, and operational stability.

expected_answer:
The short-time response is consistent with reversible ionic redistribution. Mobile ionic defects, often halide vacancies or associated species, drift under the internal electric field and illumination-modified defect landscape. Their accumulation at interfaces screens or reshapes the junction field, changes band bending and recombination, and therefore lowers measured voltage. When bias and light are removed, the concentration gradient can relax by back-diffusion, allowing the potential and voltage to recover. This process can produce hysteresis, low-frequency capacitance and transient current without requiring permanent chemical damage.

The long-time, incompletely reversible response indicates that redistributed ions have crossed from polarization into chemistry. Halide enrichment at one contact can react with a metal or transport layer, while metal ions can diffuse into the perovskite; interfacial redox, new defect formation, phase change or contact delamination then fixes part of the altered field and recombination landscape. Depth-profile accumulation is therefore meaningful only when compared with unstressed and polarity-reversed controls and when beam or sputter artifacts are excluded.

Changing a transport layer can eliminate scan hysteresis by reducing interfacial capacitance, accelerating electronic extraction, passivating recombination sites, or changing where ions accumulate. It may make the current-voltage measurement less sensitive to a still-mobile ionic population. Bulk migration through vacancies, grain boundaries or interfaces can continue and drive slow maximum-power-point degradation, especially if the new contact remains a chemical sink. Thus hysteresis is an imperfect reporter, not a direct measure of zero ion motion.

Decisive tests should vary bias polarity, stress duration, illumination and temperature, then measure recovery kinetics. A thermally activated, polarity-reversing potential/current response supports ionic drift. KPFM or operando potential mapping should be correlated with impedance/transient current and elemental depth or lateral maps before stress, after short stress, after dark recovery, and after long stress. Blocking-contact devices or compositionally identical films without reactive metals separate bulk mobility from electrode reactions. Isotopic or tracer experiments, if available, establish species identity. Irreversible chemistry is supported by new interfacial phases, metal/halide interdiffusion, non-recovering recombination, and failure that scales with total transported charge rather than only scan rate.
scoring_key_points: Assign the short-time, dark-recoverable voltage/potential change to field-driven ionic redistribution that modifies band bending and recombination.
Assign the long-time, non-recoverable response and halide/metal accumulation to interfacial redox, interdiffusion, new defects/phases, or contact damage.
Explain that a transport-layer change can suppress hysteresis by changing extraction, capacitance, recombination, or ion-accumulation sensitivity while bulk ion motion persists.

Use polarity, time, temperature, illumination, recovery, blocking-contact, operando potential, transient/impedance, and chemical-mapping controls to distinguish reversible migration from irreversible reaction.
accepted_equivalents: Ionic polarization, space-charge formation, field screening, or reversible interfacial ion accumulation are acceptable descriptions of the short-time mechanism.
Electrode corrosion, interfacial redox, metal diffusion, halide reaction, or chemically pinned ionic redistribution are acceptable irreversible mechanisms.
KPFM, electroabsorption, operando PL, EBIC, impedance, transient current, or capacitance may be used to monitor field redistribution.
ToF-SIMS, XPS depth profiling, XRF, EDS, neutron methods, or isotope tracing may be used to identify transported species and reaction products.
common_wrong_answers: Equating the disappearance of current-voltage hysteresis with complete elimination of ion migration.
Calling every reversible voltage change electronic trapping without testing polarity, temperature activation, or dark recovery.
Treating post-mortem depth profiles as sufficient without unstressed, reversed-polarity, or sputter-artifact controls.
Assuming that ion accumulation remains harmless and reversible regardless of stress duration or contact chemistry.

expected_answer:
A robust strategy must act on several terms of the ionic-transport problem. In the bulk, composition and processing should reduce the concentration of mobile defects through stoichiometry control, low-defect crystallization, and chemically appropriate passivation. Increasing the migration barrier can be pursued through lattice-stiffening or stronger local bonding, but excessive alloying can introduce strain, phase instability or electronic traps. Grain-boundary transport should be reduced by dense morphology and boundary-selective passivation or crosslinking; thick insulating boundary phases are unacceptable if they lower lateral electronic conductivity or create extraction bottlenecks.

Interfaces need chemically stable, electronically selective ion-blocking layers. These layers should prevent halides from reaching reactive metals and prevent metal diffusion into the absorber while maintaining tunnelling or transport-compatible thickness and band alignment. Passivators or dipolar layers must be screened for their own volatility, ionicity and field-driven motion. Electrode and transport-layer choices should remove chemical sinks rather than merely relocate the accumulation zone. Encapsulation controls water and oxygen, which can convert reversible redistribution into irreversible chemistry, but encapsulation alone does not stop field-driven motion inside the sealed device.

At module level, interconnect geometry, sheet resistance and local shunts should be optimized to avoid field hot spots. Maximum-power-point control, soft start, reverse-bias protection and thermal management can reduce the time spent under ionic driving forces. These operating measures complement, but do not replace, material mitigation.

Validation must separate mechanisms. Temperature- and bias-dependent transient current or impedance can estimate mobile-ion density and activation energy; blocking-contact structures test bulk transport. Operando potential/PL mapping and module electroluminescence locate field accumulation and interconnect hot spots. Short stress followed by dark or zero-bias recovery quantifies reversible polarization. Long light-bias-temperature stress with post-stress chemical depth profiling tests whether barriers prevent halide/metal reactions. The matrix should vary light, temperature, bias polarity, humidity and stress time independently before combining them. A pass requires lower mobile-ion signatures or higher activation energy, preserved electronic mobility and fill factor, reduced interfacial reaction products, stable maximum-power-point output, and no merely cosmetic reduction of hysteresis while chemical migration or long-term degradation persists.
scoring_key_points: Reduce vacancy concentration and fast grain-boundary transport through stoichiometry, crystallization, and selective passivation while preserving electronic mobility.
Use electronically compatible ion-blocking interfaces and chemically stable contacts that prevent halide/metal reactions rather than simply moving the accumulation zone.
Address module field hot spots and operating conditions through interconnect design, thermal management, MPP control and reverse-bias protection, with explicit trade-offs.

Validate mobile-ion density/activation barrier, reversible polarization, interfacial chemistry, and true MPP stability using independent temperature-bias-light-humidity tests and chemical/electrical mapping.
accepted_equivalents: Lattice stiffening, defect-complex formation, vacancy compensation, dimensional confinement, or stronger ionic bonding are acceptable bulk strategies if electronic penalties are considered.
Ultrathin oxides, 2D perovskites, self-assembled monolayers, polymers, graphene-like layers, or stable transport layers may serve as ion barriers if band alignment and resistance are validated.
Bias-poling transients, galvanostatic/potentiostatic methods, impedance, thermally stimulated current, or tracer diffusion may quantify mobile-ion behaviour.
EL/PL/KPFM/lock-in thermography maps and segmented module tests may be used to identify interconnect field or thermal hot spots.
common_wrong_answers: Proposing only thicker passivation or barrier layers without considering series resistance and charge extraction.
Using encapsulation as the sole ion-migration solution even though ions can move within a sealed device.
Reporting reduced hysteresis as sufficient proof of lower mobile-ion density or higher migration barrier.
Applying one combined damp-heat test without separating light, field, temperature and humidity contributions.

expected_answer:
Identical initial PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting shows that both treatments reduce non-radiative recombination under the measurement condition, but it does not establish the same binding geometry, residence time, selectivity, electronic alignment or operational stability. A small monodentate Lewis base can bind strongly to an exposed Pb site yet still desorb, exchange with mobile ions, diffuse into adjacent layers or reorient under field and heat. Because one bond defines the attachment, loss of that interaction removes the passivation function. Redistribution can expose defects, alter local electric fields and create ionic or dipolar hysteresis. Strong binding to Pb also does not guarantee passivation of halide-related defects or prevention of interfacial reactions.

The multidentate zwitterion can gain stability through multiple simultaneous interactions, electrostatic anchoring and a lower probability of complete detachment. Its internal charges may passivate complementary defect types and reduce ion transfer across the interface. The same size and ionic character can, however, form a thicker or less electronically transparent layer, increase tunnelling distance, change band bending, or impede carrier extraction, explaining the fill-factor penalty. Moderate per-bond strength can therefore yield higher operational residence and better ion blocking than a stronger single bond.

Mechanism-resolved evaluation should combine chemical and electronic probes. XPS, infrared/Raman, solid-state NMR or desorption measurements before and after heat/bias can test binding motifs and retention. Isotope-labelled or mass-spectrometric depth profiling can track molecular redistribution. PLQY/TRPL and absolute quasi-Fermi-level splitting quantify recombination, while UPS/Kelvin probe measures dipole and energy-level changes. Bias-dependent impedance, transient current and hysteresis tests probe ionic polarization. Ion-blocking should be assessed by tracer/depth profiles or metal/halide diffusion after stress. Charge-extraction time, conductivity, contact resistance and stabilized fill factor reveal a transport barrier. A causal ranking therefore requires retention of passivation and suppressed ion/reaction signatures under operation, not merely the largest initial PL improvement or computed adsorption energy.
scoring_key_points: Explain that equal initial PLQY/quasi-Fermi splitting measures recombination suppression but not binding multiplicity, residence time, selectivity, dipole stability, ion blocking, or transport compatibility.
Diagnose A as vulnerable to desorption, field/thermal redistribution and single-bond failure despite strong Pb binding, causing exposed defects and ionic/dipolar hysteresis.

Diagnose B as operationally stabilized by multidentate/zwitterionic anchoring and complementary ion blocking, with a possible extraction or resistance penalty from steric thickness and dipole effects.
Require orthogonal retention/chemistry, energy-alignment, ion-migration, diffusion, recombination and charge-transport measurements before ranking passivators.
accepted_equivalents: Chelation, cooperative binding, multiple anchoring groups, or avidity are acceptable descriptions of multidentate stability.
Desorption, ligand exchange, diffusion, reorientation, deprotonation, or electrochemical decomposition are acceptable failure modes for the monodentate molecule.
UPS, KPFM, surface photovoltage, electroabsorption, or capacitance-voltage may be used to probe interfacial dipoles and band bending.
ToF-SIMS, isotope tracing, XPS depth profiles, neutron reflectometry, or fluorescence labelling may be used to track molecular and ionic redistribution.
common_wrong_answers: Ranking passivators solely by the largest calculated adsorption energy or initial PLQY increase.
Assuming a zwitterion is automatically electronically benign because it improves stability.
Attributing all hysteresis to unpassivated traps without testing molecular or ionic redistribution under bias.
Using post-treatment PL alone to distinguish defect passivation from a dipole-induced change in carrier distribution.

expected_answer:
The selection problem is multi-objective. Molecular descriptors should include the identity and selectivity of binding groups for under-coordinated metal and halide defects, denticity and geometry, acid-base character, formal charge or zwitterionic balance, steric size, conformational freedom, dipole moment and orientation, redox and thermal stability, volatility, solubility and orthogonality to later solvents. Additional descriptors are packing density, tendency to form a 2D phase or insulating multilayer, permeability to ions, compatibility with the transport layer, and predicted residence or decomposition under field and illumination. No single descriptor, including adsorption energy, is sufficient.

Screening should proceed in stages. First, computation and solution/film spectroscopy identify plausible binding motifs and exclude unstable or electronically dangerous candidates. Second, controlled films are evaluated for chemical retention, PLQY, quasi-Fermi-level splitting, trap density, spatial uniformity, morphology and crystallization effects. UPS/Kelvin probe and charge-extraction measurements test band alignment and transport. Heat-, light- and bias-treated films are then analysed for desorption, redistribution, chemical decomposition and ion-blocking performance. Molecules that improve PL but create a thick resistive layer, unstable dipole or mobile ionic species are rejected before full devices.

Scale-up must control surface coverage rather than solution concentration alone. Slot-die or blade coating requires monitoring wet-film residence, drying rate, solvent orthogonality, rinse or wash steps, additive distribution and interaction with the next deposited layer. Large-area PL/EL, contact-angle, spectroscopy, thickness and sheet-resistance maps should set spatial control limits.

Device gates should use stabilized maximum-power-point output, not a champion scan, and compare multiple areas and batches. Stress should separate and combine heat, illumination, electric field, humidity and thermal cycling, with post-stress chemical and ion-distribution analysis. A candidate fails even with record initial efficiency if it shows rapid MPP loss, increased series resistance, spatial nonuniformity, passivator migration, interfacial reaction, or poor process latitude. The winning molecule is the one that maintains defect passivation, energy alignment, ion blocking and charge extraction across scalable processing and operational stress, with reproducible yield rather than the highest isolated efficiency.
