scoring_key_points: Define a multi-objective descriptor set covering defect selectivity, denticity, charge/dipole, sterics/packing, redox/thermal/field stability, volatility, solvent orthogonality, ion permeability and transport-layer compatibility.
Use sequential molecular/film screening for binding and retention, recombination, morphology, energy alignment, extraction, ion blocking, and stress-induced redistribution before full devices.
Control large-area surface coverage, drying, solvent compatibility and subsequent-layer interaction with spatial quality maps rather than copying a small-area solution concentration.

Gate candidates by reproducible stabilized MPP, resistance, uniformity, chemical retention, ion/reaction suppression and multi-stressor stability, rejecting champion-efficiency molecules that fail any critical objective.
accepted_equivalents: High-throughput computation, combinatorial coating, Bayesian optimization, or design-of-experiments approaches are acceptable screening frameworks.
Binding energy, pKa, donor number, electrostatic potential, dipole, molecular volume, decomposition potential and diffusion coefficient are acceptable descriptor examples.
PLQY/QFLS, SCLC, deep-level spectroscopy, impedance, transient extraction, UPS/KPFM, ToF-SIMS and microscopy are acceptable stage-specific tests.
ISOS-style or equivalent separated light/heat/bias/humidity protocols are acceptable stress gates if stabilized performance and post-stress chemistry are included.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the molecule with the strongest single-site adsorption energy and assuming all other properties follow.
Optimizing only film PLQY while ignoring charge-extraction resistance, dipole orientation and passivator mobility.
Transferring a spin-coated concentration directly to slot-die coating without controlling coverage and drying history.
Accepting a reverse-scan record efficiency without stabilized MPP, batch yield, large-area uniformity or post-stress chemical analysis.

expected_answer:
The four-terminal result establishes that the absorber pair can work when current matching and the monolithic interconnect are removed, but it does not identify which two-terminal loss dominates. The first step is an optical/current balance. Subcell-resolved EQE should be integrated with the actual illumination spectrum to predict the series current. Reflectance, transmittance and optical modelling should quantify parasitic absorption in transparent electrodes, transport layers and the recombination layer. Spectral perturbation or bias-light EQE can determine which subcell limits current. If the two-terminal short-circuit current follows the lower integrated subcell current and changes predictably with spectrum or temperature, current mismatch is causal.

The next step is to diagnose the recombination interconnect and series resistance. Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV separates recombination voltage loss from transport/series loss. Electroluminescence, luminescence-voltage analysis and dark JV can reveal non-radiative loss or leakage at the interconnect. Impedance, contact-resistance measurements and temperature-dependent JV test whether fill-factor loss arises from a resistive or barrier-like recombination layer. A voltage or fill-factor deficit that persists after optical current matching, and that responds to interconnect thickness or material while the subcells remain unchanged, supports an interconnect mechanism.

Subcell instability must be measured operando. Time-resolved, subcell-selective EQE, photoluminescence or electroluminescence should track the wide-bandgap band edge and quasi-Fermi splitting during light soaking. A reversible redshift or split emission with changing top-cell current indicates halide segregation; hysteretic recovery after dark distinguishes it from fixed optical design. The low-bandgap cell and interconnect should be monitored simultaneously so degradation is not misassigned.

Counterfactuals are essential: deliberately spectrally match the subcells without changing the interconnect; replace or vary the interconnect while keeping optical generation constant; and stabilize the wide-bandgap composition while retaining the same current design. The dominant loss is the one whose targeted intervention restores the predicted two-terminal current, voltage and fill factor. A single total JV curve cannot distinguish these coupled mechanisms.
scoring_key_points: Use subcell-resolved EQE integrated with the actual spectrum plus optical loss analysis to test current mismatch and parasitic absorption.
Use Suns-Voc/pseudo-JV, EL/luminescence, impedance and contact-resistance or interconnect-thickness controls to identify recombination-layer voltage and fill-factor losses.
Track subcell-selective spectra and quasi-Fermi splitting during light/temperature stress to identify reversible wide-bandgap phase segregation or other subcell instability.
Require counterfactual interventions that independently correct spectral matching, interconnect properties and top-cell stability before assigning the dominant loss.
accepted_equivalents: Bias-light EQE, luminescence coupling analysis, spectral response under filtered illumination, or calibrated spectral sweeps may be used for subcell current assignment.
Series-resistance mapping, transfer-length measurements, conductive AFM, impedance or temperature-dependent JV may diagnose the recombination interconnect.
Operando PL, EL, absorption, Raman or XRD may be used to monitor mixed-halide phase segregation in the top cell.
A three-terminal test structure or independently contacted recombination layer may serve as a counterfactual for interconnect versus subcell loss.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all two-terminal loss to current mismatch simply because the subcells are series connected.
Using the four-terminal efficiency difference as direct proof of a bad recombination layer without optical and stability diagnostics.
Interpreting a fill-factor loss only as series resistance while ignoring interfacial recombination or a transport barrier.
Measuring only the total tandem spectrum and failing to resolve which subcell changes during light soaking.

expected_answer:
The objective should be annual delivered energy and reliability, not peak efficiency at one spectrum and temperature. The starting point is a site-specific spectral and thermal model using measured subcell EQE, temperature coefficients, angular response and degradation rates. Bandgaps and top-cell optical thickness should be chosen to maximize integrated series current over the expected spectrum, not perfect current matching only at AM1.5G. Optical design can reduce parasitic absorption and improve angular robustness through transparent electrodes, transport layers, texture and light management, but added optics must not increase thermal load or processing damage.

A monolithic two-terminal stack offers lower optical/electrical complexity and potentially lower module cost, but it is vulnerable to current mismatch, interconnect loss, reverse-bias stress and degradation of either subcell. Its redesign therefore needs a low-loss recombination layer, stable wide-bandgap composition, conformal processing, bypass/reverse-bias protection, thermal management and MPP algorithms aware of tandem current limitation. Composition or interface engineering that suppresses halide segregation must be verified under operating carrier density and temperature.

A four-terminal stack sacrifices some optical area and adds contacts, wiring and power electronics, but it decouples currents and MPPs. It can yield more energy under variable spectra, partial shading or unequal degradation if the extra transparent-electrode absorption and conversion losses are smaller than the mismatch benefit. Three-terminal or power-electronically coupled submodules can provide intermediate decoupling. The architecture decision must include manufacturing yield, repairability and correlated versus independent degradation, not efficiency alone.

Required data include long-term outdoor subcell-resolved current/voltage, spectrum, temperature and irradiance; periodic EQE and luminescence to identify the degrading junction; reverse-bias and shading maps; and calibrated energy through the power electronics. Accelerated tests should combine spectral cycling, temperature cycling, high-intensity light soaking, reverse bias, humidity and interconnect stress, while retaining separate controls. A two-terminal design is preferred only if annual mismatch and coupled-degradation losses remain below the optical/electronic overhead of decoupling. Four-terminal or partially decoupled operation is preferred when variable spectrum, shading or asymmetric degradation produces a larger recoverable energy gain than the added contact and converter losses.
scoring_key_points: Optimize bandgaps and optical thickness for site-specific annual spectra, temperature and angular conditions rather than only AM1.5G current matching.
Address two-terminal recombination-layer loss, mixed-halide stability, conformal processing, reverse-bias protection, thermal management and tandem-aware MPP control.
Compare four-terminal or partially decoupled architectures by recovered mismatch/shading/degradation energy versus added transparent-contact, wiring and power-electronic losses.
Base the architecture decision on outdoor subcell-resolved energy and degradation data plus separated spectral-temperature-light-reverse-bias-environment stress tests.
accepted_equivalents: Three-terminal, voltage-matched, module-level DC optimizers, or submodule power-electronic coupling are acceptable partially decoupled options.
Site-specific spectral databases, measured spectral irradiance, ray-tracing, or validated energy-yield simulations may be used for annual optimization.
Bypass diodes, current-limiting protection, distributed power electronics, or active reverse-bias avoidance are acceptable shading protections.
Periodic EQE, EL/PL imaging, luminescence coupling, thermal imaging or reference-cell diagnostics may be used to localize subcell degradation outdoors.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing the architecture solely from the highest standard-test efficiency without annual spectral and temperature data.
Assuming four-terminal operation has no optical, contact, wiring or power-conversion penalty.
Fixing current mismatch only by thickening the top absorber while ignoring parasitic absorption, recombination and phase segregation.
Using one constant-temperature light-soak test to represent spectral variability, partial shading, reverse bias and outdoor degradation.

expected_answer: The treatment may only have increased the nucleation barrier or removed catalytic nucleation sites; the free-energy ordering of the black and yellow polymorphs could remain unchanged. Grain-boundary nucleation, an induction time, and sensitivity to light or moisture are hallmarks of an activated transformation whose rate can change without changing equilibrium. To separate thermodynamic from kinetic stabilization, measure both transformation kinetics and the long-time phase outcome across controlled temperature, humidity and illumination conditions. In situ diffraction or optical spectroscopy should provide conversion fractions and induction times, from which apparent activation barriers can be compared. A treatment that greatly slows conversion but converges to the same final phase fraction under sufficiently long or strongly driving conditions is primarily kinetic; a reproducible shift in the equilibrium phase boundary or long-time phase fraction, corroborated by free-energy or reversible transition measurements, supports thermodynamic stabilization.
scoring_key_points: States that unchanged equilibrium free-energy ordering can coexist with a larger nucleation or growth barrier.
Interprets grain-boundary nucleation and the induction period as evidence of an activated, catalysed transformation rather than proof of equilibrium stabilization.
Proposes controlled in situ phase tracking over temperature, humidity and/or illumination to obtain both rates and long-time phase fractions.

Uses the correct decision rule: changed rate or activation barrier with the same eventual equilibrium implies kinetic stabilization, whereas a shifted reversible phase boundary or equilibrium fraction implies thermodynamic stabilization.
accepted_equivalents: Classical-nucleation language such as increased interfacial energy, reduced heterogeneous nucleation density or a higher critical-nucleus barrier.
Operando GIWAXS/XRD, Raman, absorption or phase-resolved photoluminescence as the phase-tracking method.
Calorimetry, reversible temperature cycling or validated free-energy calculations as evidence for a changed thermodynamic phase boundary.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that slower degradation automatically proves the black phase has become the equilibrium phase.
Attributing the result only to encapsulation even though the intervention is strain relief and the exposure conditions are unchanged.
Suggesting only a single end-point diffraction scan, which cannot separate induction kinetics from equilibrium.

expected_answer: Use a structured set of single-lever and factorial controls rather than retaining the full recipe. First compare the unmixed parent, A-site-only, halide-only, 2D-interface-only and selected combinations while mapping composition, strain and phase across the module. Temperature-dependent, long-duration phase measurements without bias should test whether cation or halide mixing shifts bulk phase stability; bandgap and segregation maps are required because halide substitution can stabilize the lattice yet introduce optical non-uniformity or photo-segregation. Time-resolved conversion under controlled humidity, light and temperature should identify kinetic suppression by additives, strain relief or the 2D layer. Finally, bias-dependent operando phase/photoluminescence mapping, ion-distribution analysis and contact/interconnect controls should locate electrically driven ion migration or interfacial nucleation. Retain only levers that improve the relevant failure mode without unacceptable transport, bandgap or uniformity penalties, and verify the selected reduced recipe under combined module-level stress.
scoring_key_points: Requires single-lever or factorial controls that isolate A-site mixing, halide substitution and the 2D-rich interface instead of evaluating only the combined recipe.
Tests bulk thermodynamic stabilization using long-time or reversible phase-boundary measurements and spatially resolves composition, strain and bandgap.
Separately quantifies kinetic effects through time-resolved phase-conversion measurements under controlled environmental and illumination stresses.
Uses bias-dependent operando mapping and ion/interfacial diagnostics to identify electrically driven degradation, then selects levers by stability-versus-bandgap, transport and uniformity trade-offs.
accepted_equivalents: A fractional-factorial or response-surface design that still identifies main effects and critical interactions.
Kelvin-probe, ToF-SIMS, XPS depth profiling, scanning XRD/GIWAXS or hyperspectral photoluminescence for spatially resolved module diagnostics.
Replacing halide stabilization with cation or strain engineering if halide segregation dominates the scale-up failure.
common_wrong_answers: Keeping all three interventions and merely increasing encapsulation without locating the active failure mechanism.
Using efficiency retention alone as the decision metric, which conflates phase stability, contact loss and transport penalties.
Testing only unbiased films even though degradation is localized near biased interconnects.

expected_answer: The larger size and molecular shape can change cavity fit, octahedral tilt and phase-transition energetics, thereby altering the band structure and structural stability. The larger dipole and its rotational dynamics can modify local dielectric screening, energetic disorder or carrier-defect interactions, so the lifetime increase need not arise from the same mechanism that causes tilting. Greater hydrophilicity can independently increase water uptake or facilitate hydration/decomposition, explaining poorer humid-air stability even if electronic recombination improves. Causality should be tested with a matched series: cations of similar size but different dipole, similar dipole but different size/shape, and similar steric properties but different hydrophilicity or hydrogen-bonding chemistry. Structural probes, dielectric or molecular-dynamics-sensitive measurements, time-resolved spectroscopy, and quantitative water-sorption/degradation tests should then be correlated without assuming that one variable controls every response.
scoring_key_points: Assigns octahedral tilting primarily to steric fit, shape and lattice-coupling effects of the A-cation.
Treats dipole magnitude and rotational dynamics as a distinct route affecting dielectric screening, energetic disorder or carrier recombination.
Treats hydrophilicity or hydrogen bonding as an independent cause of moisture uptake and chemical instability.
Proposes matched molecular controls and orthogonal structural, dynamic/electronic and water-uptake measurements to deconvolute the descriptors.
accepted_equivalents: Using tolerance-factor or octahedral-factor language for the steric contribution, provided its limitations are acknowledged.
Quasi-elastic neutron scattering, solid-state NMR, dielectric spectroscopy or molecular-dynamics calculations for cation motion.
Dynamic-vapour sorption, quartz-crystal microbalance or controlled-humidity spectroscopy for moisture uptake.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that a larger molecular dipole directly and necessarily causes stronger octahedral tilting.
Interpreting longer photoluminescence lifetime as proof of improved operational stability.
Comparing only unrelated cations whose size, dipole and hydrophilicity all change together.

expected_answer: Begin from the steric constraint that a sufficiently bulky cation is unlikely to occupy the 3D A-site at high concentration and may instead form a low-dimensional phase or non-perovskite residue. Prepare concentration and deposition-order series, including bulk-mixed, post-treated and interface-restricted controls. Determine depth distribution and local phase identity using complementary diffraction/scattering, spectroscopy and chemical depth profiling; lattice-parameter changes alone are insufficient evidence of A-site incorporation. Relate the identified location to function through surface recombination, moisture uptake, band alignment and through-thickness conductivity or carrier-extraction measurements. If benefits arise from a thin quasi-2D/passivating region, adopt a controlled interfacial gradient or post-treatment with thickness below the transport-limiting regime; if genuine dilute 3D incorporation is verified, define a solubility window and monitor phase purity. Scale-up should control cation dose and drying kinetics and confirm spatial uniformity across the coated area.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes the steric likelihood of quasi-2D phase formation or interfacial residue rather than assuming unrestricted 3D A-site incorporation.
Uses concentration and deposition-order controls plus depth-resolved structural and chemical characterization to identify location and phase.
Links structural role to recombination, moisture resistance, band alignment and vertical transport/extraction measurements.
Selects a scalable interfacial gradient, post-treatment or verified dilute-incorporation window and includes uniformity/process-control checks.
accepted_equivalents: GIWAXS with angle variation, cross-sectional microscopy, ToF-SIMS, XPS depth profiling, solid-state NMR or vibrational spectroscopy as complementary location/phase probes.
Space-charge-limited current, time-of-flight, impedance, transient photocurrent or device-thickness dependence as transport tests.
A graded 2D/3D heterostructure or self-assembled surface layer when the bulky cation is excluded from the 3D bulk.
common_wrong_answers: Inferring A-site incorporation solely from a small XRD peak shift.
Maximizing bulky-cation concentration because voltage and moisture resistance improved at one loading.
Ignoring the possibility that a continuous low-dimensional layer can block out-of-plane carrier extraction.

expected_answer: Average symmetry can conceal local octahedral distortions and fluctuations. Departures from linear metal-halide-metal linkage reduce orbital overlap, alter band dispersion and can widen the bandgap or increase effective mass, explaining the blue shift and lower mobility. Static distortions should persist in local-structure measurements and remain comparatively insensitive to probe timescale or temperature, whereas dynamic tilts should show temperature- and frequency-dependent broadening, relaxation or anharmonic signatures. Reduced connectivity, such as 3D-to-layered or surface-fragmented networks, should produce distinct medium-range pair correlations, termination signatures and anisotropic transport. A suitable sequence combines total scattering/PDF or local X-ray absorption with temperature-dependent Raman/terahertz or time-resolved scattering, followed by dimensionality/termination-sensitive microscopy or scattering and directional transport. The conclusion should be based on convergent evidence rather than Bragg peaks alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains that identical average symmetry can hide different local octahedral distortions or dynamics.
Connects bond-angle deviation or connectivity loss to reduced orbital overlap, altered band dispersion, bandgap shift and mobility loss.
Distinguishes static from dynamic distortion using local probes plus temperature, frequency or timescale dependence.
Tests connectivity or termination separately with medium-range structural and anisotropic-transport evidence.
accepted_equivalents: Pair-distribution-function analysis, EXAFS, diffuse scattering or local electron diffraction for static/local structure.
Temperature-dependent Raman, terahertz spectroscopy, quasielastic scattering, NMR relaxation or ultrafast diffraction for dynamic tilting.
Comparing in-plane and out-of-plane transport or identifying layered/edge-sharing motifs as evidence of connectivity changes.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that the structures are identical because the Bragg diffraction patterns match.
Attributing both optical and transport changes only to defect density without testing the octahedral framework.
Using a single room-temperature spectrum that cannot distinguish frozen disorder from rapid motion.

expected_answer: One intervention should tune the bulk octahedral framework—for example, choose A-site or B-site chemistry and strain control that reduce excessive tilt fluctuations, local strain gradients or soft modes while preserving corner-sharing 3D connectivity. A second should control surfaces or grain boundaries, for example with a termination-matched ligand or ultrathin low-dimensional cap that suppresses under-coordinated octahedra and halide-vacancy-mediated rearrangement without forming a transport-blocking layer. The mechanism must be tested by correlating operando segregation kinetics with direct measurements of local octahedral coherence or dynamics under illumination, such as time-resolved diffraction/PDF plus Raman or terahertz signatures. Carrier lifetime and mobility must be measured independently: genuine framework stabilization should reduce structural/halide redistribution at comparable carrier density and should not require a large mobility loss. Spatially resolved composition and phase mapping should confirm that the effect is not only interfacial blocking.
scoring_key_points: Proposes a bulk intervention that controls octahedral tilt, strain, softness or coherence while retaining corner-sharing 3D connectivity.
Proposes a complementary surface/grain-boundary intervention that stabilizes under-coordinated octahedra without creating a thick transport barrier.
Uses operando structural/dynamic probes together with spatial halide-segregation measurements to test the octahedral-network mechanism.
Includes independent carrier-density and mobility/lifetime controls so apparent stability cannot be explained by suppressed excitation or transport alone.
accepted_equivalents: Compositional alloying, epitaxial strain, lattice-matched additives or cross-linking that stiffen relevant octahedral modes without disrupting 3D connectivity.
Operando GIWAXS, diffuse scattering, PDF, Raman, terahertz or ultrafast electron/X-ray diffraction under matched illumination.
Hyperspectral photoluminescence or nano-XRF mapping for spatial segregation.
common_wrong_answers: Converting the absorber into a thick 2D phase and ignoring the requirement for three-dimensional transport.
Calling a lower photoluminescence signal evidence of reduced segregation without controlling absorbed photon density or carrier density.
Using only a final device-efficiency measurement with no direct octahedral or composition-sensitive probe.

expected_answer: Total defect density does not specify defect identity, charge state, spatial location, energetic level or capture coefficient, and the measured lifetime may also be controlled by surfaces or interfaces. Defect formation must be assessed through formation energies or controlled defect-generation experiments to distinguish resistance to creating defects from tolerance of defects once present. Electronic harmfulness requires defect transition levels and wavefunction/band-edge analysis, while direct or inferred capture coefficients under controlled carrier density are needed because a shallow level can still be harmful if capture is fast and a deep level may be rare or weakly coupled. Temperature-, frequency- or field-dependent measurements can test dynamic lattice screening, polaronic response or defect reconfiguration. Bulk-versus-surface passivation controls and thickness or interface dependence are required to determine whether A's good lifetime is intrinsic or merely surface-passivated. A should be called defect-tolerant only for specified defect types and conditions when substantial defects produce limited non-radiative loss, not merely because the as-made film performs well.
scoring_key_points: Explains that total defect density omits defect identity, charge state, energy level, location and capture kinetics.
Separates defect resistance/formation thermodynamics from electronic defect tolerance using formation energies or controlled defect creation and transition-level analysis.
Requires carrier-capture measurements and dynamic lattice/screening tests under controlled conditions.
Uses surface/interface passivation controls and gives a conditional, defect-specific criterion for calling the material defect-tolerant.
accepted_equivalents: Deep-level spectroscopy, temperature-dependent photoluminescence, transient absorption, microwave conductivity or first-principles non-radiative capture calculations.
Polaron formation, dielectric screening or lattice reorientation as dynamic mechanisms that reduce carrier-defect interaction.
Thickness scaling, surface treatment controls or single-crystal-versus-film comparison to isolate surfaces and grain boundaries.
common_wrong_answers: Defining defect tolerance solely as having a low defect density.
Equating long photoluminescence lifetime with intrinsic bulk tolerance without surface controls.
Listing shallow defects, self-healing and passivation without measurements that distinguish their contributions.

expected_answer: Stage 1 should calculate or measure phase stability, dominant native-defect formation energies and chemical-potential dependence to identify whether harmful defects are difficult to create; this addresses defect resistance. Stage 2 should determine defect transition levels, orbital character and non-radiative capture coefficients for the dominant defects, then validate them with defect-specific spectroscopy under controlled carrier density; benign levels or weak capture despite appreciable defect concentration support defect tolerance. Stage 3 should introduce calibrated defects by irradiation, off-stoichiometry, electrochemical bias or thermal stress and track both defect population and optoelectronic recovery in time. Recovery without external passivant, with reversible defect annihilation or migration to benign configurations, supports self-healing; recovery only after chemical treatment indicates passivatability. Surfaces, grain boundaries and bulk must be separated, and the full matrix should be repeated across relevant temperature, illumination, atmosphere and defect types. The final classification must therefore be conditional and mechanism-specific, with explicit no-go criteria such as deep fast-capture defects, irreversible phase decomposition or recovery that merely masks damage at the surface.
scoring_key_points: Begins with phase stability and native-defect formation energetics across chemical potentials to assess defect resistance.
Combines transition levels, orbital character and capture coefficients with defect-specific experimental validation to assess tolerance after defects exist.
Uses calibrated damage plus time-resolved defect-population and property recovery to distinguish self-healing from external passivation.
Separates bulk/surface contributions, repeats across defect types and operating conditions, and gives conditional classifications with explicit go/no-go criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Electron/ion irradiation, photodoping, stoichiometry control, electrical stress or controlled impurity introduction as calibrated defect-generation methods.
Positron annihilation, EPR, deep-level spectroscopy, transient spectroscopy or operando structural probes for defect population and recovery.
Using bonding-antibonding band-edge analysis or lone-pair chemistry as a theory-guided screen, provided capture kinetics and experiments are still required.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring the material defect-tolerant because its pristine mobility is high.
Using only defect formation energies and ignoring whether formed defects introduce deep levels or fast capture.
Calling recovery after adding a passivation molecule self-healing, or extrapolating one benign defect to all defects and operating conditions.

expected_answer: The first step is to verify that the apparent current match is real. Subcell EQE in a series-connected tandem must be measured with appropriate selective optical bias and, where needed, electrical bias; the integrated currents should then be compared with transfer-matrix or other optical modeling over realistic spectra and angles. A genuine optical mismatch makes the lower-current subcell clamp the tandem current. Its signature is a predictable, monotonic change in tandem short-circuit current with spectrum, absorber thickness or optical spacer design, while the individual subcell quasi-Fermi-level splitting and contact selectivity can remain good. Optical mismatch alone does not normally generate a pronounced S-kink. A recombination-contact barrier instead causes carrier accumulation and a voltage drop between the subcells. Expected signatures include an S-shaped J-V curve that depends on irradiance, temperature and bias history; a large interfacial differential resistance or low-frequency capacitance; a gap between pseudo-fill factor from Suns-Voc and the measured fill factor; and redistribution of the subcell voltages under selective illumination. Excess non-radiative recombination in one subcell is identified by reduced PLQY or electroluminescence efficiency, lower quasi-Fermi-level splitting, a larger Voc deficit and recombination-related light-intensity or ideality-factor signatures. It will not be removed merely by changing the illumination spectrum to achieve current match. Combining bias-light EQE, optical modeling, subcell-selective luminescence/QFLS, Suns-Voc or pseudo-J-V, dark J-V, impedance and temperature-dependent J-V allows the three causes to be separated rather than inferred from the tandem J-V curve alone.
scoring_key_points: Verifies subcell current matching with correctly biased EQE and realistic optical modeling rather than accepting a single integrated-EQE result at face value.
Identifies optical mismatch by spectrum/thickness-dependent current limitation without requiring an S-kink or loss of subcell QFLS.
Identifies a recombination-contact barrier through charge accumulation, S-shaped J-V, measured-versus-pseudo-FF loss, interfacial impedance/capacitance and subcell-voltage redistribution.
Identifies subcell non-radiative recombination through PLQY/QFLS, electroluminescence, Voc-deficit and recombination-ideality signatures that persist after optical rematching.
accepted_equivalents: Transfer-matrix, finite-difference optical simulation or experimentally calibrated spectral-response modeling are equivalent if they quantify subcell generation correctly.
Transient photocurrent, charge-extraction, electroabsorption or operando potential mapping may substitute for impedance when they directly reveal interfacial charge accumulation.
Absolute photoluminescence, electroluminescence quantum efficiency or implied-Voc measurements may substitute for one another as subcell recombination diagnostics when interpreted consistently.
common_wrong_answers: Calling every low-current tandem a current-mismatch problem without explaining the S-kink or bias-light dependence.
Treating an integrated EQE current measured without subcell-selective bias as definitive evidence of current matching.
Using only steady-state PL quenching to claim either efficient extraction or low recombination.
Assuming that a recombination layer can affect only series resistance and cannot alter charge accumulation or subcell voltage sharing.

expected_answer: The preferred strategy is to recover useful optical generation while preserving a thin, transport-competent and morphologically stable organic junction. First, redesign the optical field: reduce parasitic absorption in transport and recombination layers, optimize antireflection and optical-spacer thicknesses, increase rear reflection or light trapping where compatible, and co-optimize the perovskite thickness or bandgap so that current matching is not imposed entirely on the organic cell. Second, improve the organic subcell at fixed or only modestly increased thickness by selecting higher-mobility, lower-disorder donor-acceptor systems with adequate exciton diffusion, controlled vertical composition and thermally stable nanoscale morphology. Third, transfer the complete stack to the scalable process rather than optimizing isolated coupons: enforce solvent orthogonality, conformal coating, low sheet resistance, low-resistance interconnection, low dead area and a thermal budget that does not remix the organic blend. Encapsulation and interfacial barriers must suppress oxygen, moisture and molecular diffusion without adding optical loss. The go/no-go criterion should be annualized tandem energy yield and stability, not peak simulated current. Required evidence includes subcell-resolved EQE under representative spectra and temperatures, area-dependent series resistance and fill factor, spatial current-uniformity maps, morphology and burn-in tracking, and MPP aging under spectrally variable illumination. A design is transferable only if current matching remains robust to spectrum, temperature, manufacturing variation and aging while the organic morphology and interconnect resistance remain stable.
scoring_key_points: Prioritizes optical-field and parasitic-loss engineering plus co-optimization of both subcells before simply thickening the organic absorber.
Preserves exciton collection and charge transport through a thin, high-mobility, low-disorder and morphologically stable organic active layer.
Addresses scalable-stack constraints including solvent orthogonality, coating uniformity, sheet/interconnect resistance, dead area, thermal budget and encapsulation.
Uses subcell-resolved current, area scaling, spatial uniformity, burn-in and spectrum-dependent MPP energy yield as go/no-go metrics rather than peak small-cell PCE.
accepted_equivalents: Optical spacers, nanophotonic light management, textured reflectors or index-matched interlayers are equivalent if they increase useful absorption without creating electrical or stability penalties.
Morphology-locking by crosslinking, high-glass-transition components or non-fullerene acceptor selection is acceptable when charge transport and photochemical stability are demonstrated.
Module energy yield modeling may replace an annual outdoor trial if it is calibrated with measured spectral, thermal and degradation responses.
common_wrong_answers: Recommending a thicker organic layer as the sole solution despite the stated transport and burn-in penalties.
Optimizing current matching only under AM1.5G while ignoring spectral and temperature sensitivity.
Ignoring resistance, coating nonuniformity and inactive interconnection area during scale-up.
Selecting the design with the highest initial small-area PCE without testing morphology or MPP stability.

expected_answer: The textured surface has a larger true area, a distribution of local curvature and chemically non-equivalent sites, so a recipe calibrated by nominal substrate area can under-cover valleys while over-accumulating molecules at peaks. The first intervention is therefore to engineer conformal chemisorption rather than increase concentration blindly. The anchoring group and spacer should bind robustly to the actual oxide surface, tolerate local curvature and form a dense but electronically coupled monolayer. Deposition time, solvent, concentration, water content and rinsing should be recalibrated to the real surface area; vapor-phase deposition, repeated dilute dosing or an ultrathin conformal oxide/primer can be preferable to one concentrated solution. A mixed-SAM or bilayer is acceptable if it fills pinholes without forming a thick tunneling barrier. Spatial coverage, orientation and potential must be mapped on the textured substrate using chemically and electrically resolved methods, and cross-sections should verify that subsequent perovskite coating does not expose peaks or leave voids. Integration must preserve the silicon passivation, optical texture, low-temperature budget and solvent orthogonality, and the SAM must withstand perovskite deposition, fullerene processing and later electrode steps. Qualification should include subcell-resolved QFLS/Voc, recombination and contact resistivity, spatial PL/EL or photocurrent uniformity, tandem EQE/current matching, yield statistics over area, and combined light-heat-bias MPP aging. The design passes only if coverage and energetics are uniform, measured FF approaches pseudo-FF, no multilayer-induced transport barrier appears, and performance and stability remain reproducible across the textured area.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that texture changes true area, curvature and site chemistry, producing simultaneous under-coverage and local over-deposition if a planar recipe is copied unchanged.

Proposes conformal molecular/deposition solutions such as robust anchoring, dilute or vapor dosing, calibrated rinsing, mixed SAMs or an ultrathin primer while explicitly avoiding an insulating multilayer.
Addresses full-stack compatibility with silicon passivation, optical texture, thermal budget, solvents and subsequent perovskite/fullerene/electrode processing.
Requires spatial coverage/energetics, contact selectivity/resistivity, subcell-resolved performance, area yield and combined-stress MPP stability for qualification.
accepted_equivalents: Atomic-layer-deposited ultrathin oxides, plasma-tailored surface hydroxylation or grafted polymer primers are acceptable if they remain optically and electrically benign.
Mixed anchoring chemistries or crosslinkable monolayers are acceptable alternatives to a single SAM when monolayer-scale thickness and charge transfer are preserved.
Spatially resolved electroluminescence, photoluminescence, LBIC or KPFM may be combined in different ways to demonstrate uniformity.
common_wrong_answers: Increasing SAM concentration in proportion to projected area without considering true area, adsorption saturation or multilayer formation.
Assuming that a good planar contact angle guarantees conformal molecular coverage on texture.
Ignoring damage to silicon passivation or optical current matching during contact redesign.
Qualifying the transfer from one champion tandem rather than area-dependent yield and stability statistics.

expected_answer: The three mechanisms must be varied independently rather than inferred from one multifunctional molecule. A useful molecular series keeps the anchor and steric size approximately constant while reversing or changing dipole moment; a second series keeps dipole and backbone similar while removing or weakening the defect-binding group; and a third control matches solvent, concentration and steric environment but is electronically and chemically inert. Pre-deposition and post-deposition application are critical processing controls: a modifier that works only when present during crystallization is more likely to act through nucleation or morphology, whereas a post-deposition effect localizes the action to the completed interface. A dipole-dominated mechanism should show a saturating vacuum-level/work-function shift, a corresponding change in band bending or contact selectivity, and a reduced QFLS-to-Voc loss with little change in bulk trap density or morphology; reversing the dipole should reverse the energetic trend. Passivation should be supported by specific chemical interaction, increased PLQY/QFLS and lifetime, reduced interfacial recombination current or ideality factor and fewer electrically active traps even for a molecule with little dipole. A morphology mechanism requires changed nucleation density, grain/texture distribution, residual strain or composition, and its performance effect should be reproduced by a morphology-matched processing control. Causal attribution is strongest when spatial or depth-resolved recombination and potential measurements locate the gain at the intended interface and when the orthogonal molecule series predicts the photovoltaic response.
scoring_key_points: Constructs orthogonal molecule series that separately vary dipole, defect-binding functionality and inert steric/process effects.
Uses pre-deposition versus post-deposition and morphology-matched controls to isolate crystallization-mediated effects.

Defines a dipole mechanism by reversible/saturating energetic shifts and reduced contact voltage loss without necessary trap or morphology changes, and a passivation mechanism by chemical bonding plus lower recombination/trap signatures.
Defines morphology causality through nucleation/texture/strain/composition changes and requires spatial or depth localization plus predictive control trends.
accepted_equivalents: Homologous molecular series, matched-pair analogues or isotopically labeled analogues are acceptable if they decouple the functional variables.
UPS/Kelvin probe, surface photovoltage or electroabsorption may establish dipole/band-bending changes; PLQY/QFLS, transient PL or electroluminescence may establish recombination changes.
GIWAXS, SEM/AFM, in situ optical scattering or nucleation imaging may be used to diagnose morphology and crystallization.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning the improvement to the largest observed work-function shift without testing passivation or morphology.
Using a solvent-only control as the only control for a multifunctional molecule.
Treating larger grains as automatically beneficial without measuring interface recombination or composition/strain.
Inferring passivation solely from PL quenching, which can also reflect extraction or new non-radiative pathways.

expected_answer: The recoverable voltage component points first to a field- and light-driven top-cell process. Mixed-halide segregation or ionic redistribution can create lower-bandgap domains, alter band bending and increase recombination under the filtered spectrum and operating bias of the tandem. It should produce time-dependent PL peak splitting or redshift, spatial luminescence heterogeneity, subcell-Voc or QFLS loss and substantial dark or reverse-bias recovery without requiring a change in silicon EQE. The persistent fill-factor and resistance loss instead implicates the recombination junction or adjacent contacts. Ion interdiffusion, contact oxidation/reduction, thermal decomposition, delamination or loss of tunneling/recombination functionality should increase contact resistivity or an interfacial impedance arc and should be visible by cross-sectional chemical or structural analysis; it will not recover when halides remix. Shunting is a separate failure mode. It should lower shunt resistance, increase dark leakage, create localized electroluminescence/photoluminescence dark spots or lock-in thermography hot spots and often scale with area or defect density rather than only with interfacial resistance. The test sequence should combine selective-bias-light EQE and subcell voltage/luminescence measurements, time-resolved PL spectroscopy and dark recovery, Suns-Voc or pseudo-J-V versus measured J-V, impedance/contact-resistance analysis, dark J-V and spatial thermography/EL, followed by cross-sectional ToF-SIMS, XPS/TEM or equivalent chemistry. Top-cell-only and recombination-junction control stacks under the same spectrum, heat and bias are needed to attribute the concurrent reversible and irreversible components.
scoring_key_points: Links the reversible voltage/PL change to top-cell halide segregation or ionic redistribution and gives spectral, spatial, subcell-QFLS/Voc and recovery signatures.
Links the persistent FF/interfacial-resistance loss to recombination-junction or contact chemistry/interdiffusion/delamination and requires cross-sectional or impedance evidence.
Separates shunting through dark leakage, reduced shunt resistance and localized thermal or luminescence defects rather than treating all FF loss as contact resistance.
Proposes subcell-selective optical/electrical tests plus matched top-cell and recombination-junction controls under combined tandem-relevant stress.
accepted_equivalents: Photoluminescence peak splitting, electroluminescence spectral evolution or hyperspectral imaging are equivalent evidence for phase segregation when recovery is shown.
Transmission-line contact resistance, conductive-AFM, impedance spectroscopy or differential-resistance analysis may establish recombination-junction degradation.
Lock-in thermography, LBIC, electroluminescence or dark-current imaging may identify shunts if spatial localization is demonstrated.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning all degradation to the perovskite absorber because the silicon EQE is unchanged.
Calling any reversible voltage loss halide segregation without observing spectral or spatial evidence.
Treating increased series resistance and shunting as interchangeable causes of fill-factor loss.
Using only full-device J-V curves without subcell-selective or component-control measurements.

expected_answer: Single-junction lifetime is necessary but not sufficient because the tandem contact becomes part of an optical cavity, a current-matched series circuit and a recombination-junction process sequence. The first criterion is optical: the inorganic layer and its deposition must not add parasitic absorption or reflection that drives one subcell current-limiting over realistic spectra and angles. The second is electrical: band alignment, contact resistivity, tunneling/recombination with the interconnect and selectivity must remain adequate on the tandem's textured surface; a stable but resistive contact that lowers measured fill factor relative to pseudo-fill factor is a failure. The third is process and materials compatibility: deposition must not damage the silicon passivation, sputter or chemically attack the perovskite, exceed the thermal budget, promote interdiffusion, or create stress/delamination from roughness and thermal-expansion mismatch. The fourth is mechanism-preserving reliability. Component stacks and full tandems should be aged at MPP under combined light, heat and relevant humidity while subcell-resolved EQE, Voc/QFLS, contact resistance, spatial leakage and cross-sectional chemistry are tracked. Optical modeling, textured-substrate coverage tests and recombination-junction controls are required before full devices. The layer is a go only if it improves tandem energy yield and lifetime across area and manufacturing variation without shifting the dominant failure to current mismatch, contact resistance, shunting, silicon-passivation loss or interfacial chemical reaction.
scoring_key_points: Evaluates parasitic optical loss and spectrum-dependent current matching, not only the contact's single-junction stability.
Evaluates band alignment, selectivity, contact/recombination-junction resistance and measured-versus-pseudo-FF on the actual textured tandem surface.
Evaluates process compatibility with silicon passivation, perovskite damage, thermal budget, roughness, interdiffusion and mechanical stress.
Requires component controls and full-tandem combined-stress MPP aging with subcell-resolved, spatial and chemical diagnostics, using energy yield and failure-mode transfer as the go/no criterion.
accepted_equivalents: Transparent conductive oxides, ultrathin metal oxides or inorganic-organic bilayers may be evaluated under the same framework.
Annual energy yield, stabilized power output or degradation-corrected delivered energy are equivalent system-level decision metrics.
Mechanical cycling and damp-heat may be added to combined light-heat-bias stress when module packaging or thermal-expansion mismatch is the suspected limiter.
common_wrong_answers: Transferring the layer solely because it survives a longer single-junction thermal test.
Ignoring parasitic absorption and current matching because the contact is nominally transparent.
Measuring only initial tandem PCE and omitting pseudo-J-V, contact resistance or subcell diagnostics.
Assuming an ion-blocking layer cannot itself cause interfacial accumulation, delamination or a transport barrier.

expected_answer: The electrical boundary condition changes both electronic carrier population and the driving force for ionic redistribution. At open circuit, the quasi-Fermi-level splitting and steady carrier density are highest. This can accelerate non-radiative interfacial recombination, photo-redox reactions, halide segregation and reactions between accumulated ionic defects and transport layers or electrodes. At maximum power, carrier density is lower than at open circuit but a sustained internal field and current still drive mobile ions toward selective contacts, so field screening, band-bending changes and contact reactions remain possible. At short circuit, photocarriers are extracted and the device voltage is small, often reducing carrier-mediated chemical potentials and some forms of interfacial ion accumulation, although short-circuit current can still cause heating or electrode reactions in other systems. Reversible dark recovery is consistent with ion back-diffusion, relaxation of field screening or remixing of segregated phases. The incomplete recovery indicates an irreversible component such as decomposition, contact reaction, permanent trap formation or electrode corrosion. A decisive protocol stresses matched devices at open circuit, MPP, short circuit and selected fixed biases while continuously recording stabilized power, Voc, current, PL/EL spectra and spatial uniformity. Bias preconditioning, polarity reversal, dark-recovery kinetics and temperature dependence reveal ionic timescales and activation. KPFM or surface-potential mapping and ToF-SIMS/depth profiling test redistribution, whereas XPS, diffraction, mass loss or cross-sectional microscopy test irreversible chemistry. Pseudo-J-V versus measured J-V, impedance and QFLS distinguish recombination, transport and electrostatic screening. Mechanistic attribution requires correlation of recovery with ion/potential relaxation and persistence of chemical changes after the reversible component has disappeared.
scoring_key_points: Explains why open circuit raises carrier density and chemical driving forces, while MPP and short circuit impose different field, extraction and ionic boundary conditions.
Links reversible recovery to ion back-diffusion, field-screening relaxation or phase remixing and incomplete recovery to irreversible decomposition/contact/trap chemistry.
Uses parallel OC/MPP/SC/fixed-bias stress, preconditioning, dark recovery, polarity and temperature dependence to resolve electronic and ionic timescales.
Combines potential/ion-distribution measurements with chemical/structural probes and pseudo-J-V/QFLS/impedance to separate reversible electrostatics from irreversible loss.
accepted_equivalents: Open-circuit high injection, high quasi-Fermi-level splitting or high photocarrier chemical potential are equivalent descriptions of the electronic stress.
Transient capacitance, thermally stimulated current or impedance relaxation may substitute for KPFM when ionic redistribution is independently verified.
Electroluminescence, absolute PL, hyperspectral imaging or operando X-ray methods may be combined differently to track reversible phase/electrostatic changes.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that open circuit is benign because no external current flows.
Explaining all recovery as self-healing without identifying the irreversible residual damage.
Equating short circuit with zero internal field everywhere in the multilayer device.
Using only T80 curves without changing electrical boundary conditions or measuring ion/chemical state.

expected_answer:
The scale-up problem is a reaction–transport problem: local spacer activity, solvent residence time, temperature, and quench time vary across the web and therefore change both conversion depth and phase distribution. A robust process should meter the bulky-cation flux independently of wet-film thickness, use an orthogonal solvent with limited ability to dissolve the 3D absorber, and impose a narrow reaction window through controlled substrate temperature, short residence time, and a rapid solvent-removal or neutralization/quench step. Multi-zone drying or vapor treatment can reduce edge-to-center evaporation gradients. Spacer chemistry and concentration should be selected to favor high-n, vertically connected phases rather than an insulating low-n cap, and the web speed, coating gap, humidity, and solution age must be included in the control space.

An inline endpoint can combine hyperspectral reflectance/photoluminescence with low-angle scattering or grazing-incidence diffraction at representative cross-web positions. The endpoint should track emergence of the intended excitonic/structural signature and stop the reaction before low-n features or excessive converted thickness develop. Offline validation should include depth profiling, azimuthal orientation, water-vapor exposure, and cross-web device maps.

Acceptance requires a narrow distribution of converted-layer thickness, n-value composition, and orientation across the web; preserved absorber thickness and bulk 3D diffraction; high out-of-plane conductance and photocurrent; and improved humidity stability. A salt overlayer is rejected if organic-cation signal is present without the corresponding layered-perovskite diffraction/optical signature, if it washes away without changing the underlying lattice, or if it provides hydrophobicity but no reproducible phase-conversion depth.
scoring_key_points: Frames scale-up as coupled spacer delivery, solvent residence, temperature, and quench control, with measures to suppress cross-web evaporation and reaction gradients.
Selects chemistry and drying conditions that produce a thin high-n, vertically transport-compatible converted region rather than a thick low-n cap.
Defines an inline endpoint based on phase-sensitive optical and/or diffraction signals sampled across the web.
Sets acceptance and falsification criteria that verify lattice conversion, uniform depth/orientation, retained photocurrent, and humidity stability rather than a removable salt coating.
accepted_equivalents: Spatially resolved Raman spectroscopy or ellipsometry may replace hyperspectral PL if calibrated to n-value and conversion depth.
A vapor-phase spacer treatment with controlled partial pressure and residence time is acceptable in place of solution slot-die treatment.
Laser or flash quenching is acceptable if it reproducibly terminates conversion without thermally damaging the stack.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling the spin-coating recipe only by increasing solution volume or web speed.
Using contact angle as the sole endpoint, which cannot prove dimensional conversion or transport compatibility.
Maximizing the amount of 2D phase without a limit on low-n fraction or converted-layer thickness.

expected_answer:
Open-circuit PLQY probes recombination under photogenerated, approximately balanced carrier populations and does not guarantee balanced electrical injection, low contact resistance, stable interfaces, or efficient escape of generated photons. First, internal radiative efficiency under electrical injection should be estimated from calibrated electroluminescence, emitted spectrum, current density, and—where possible—optical modeling or integrating-sphere measurements. Electron-only and hole-only devices, injection-dependent capacitance/impedance, contact-selective quasi-Fermi-level measurements, and changes in EL onset voltage can test carrier balance and contact barriers. Injection imbalance is supported when one carrier current is limiting, charge accumulates near a contact, EL onset is high, and contact modification improves EL without changing optical outcoupling.

Outcoupling should be tested with angle-resolved emission, integrating-sphere measurements, transfer-matrix or electromagnetic modeling, and controlled changes in transport-layer refractive index or surface texture. Poor outcoupling is indicated when internal radiative efficiency is high and stable but most power remains in waveguided, substrate, or plasmonic modes; an optical extraction layer then raises external EQE with little change in voltage, carrier lifetime, or defect signatures.

Current-induced defect generation is tested by time-resolved EL/PL during constant-current stress, pre/post absolute PLQY, spectral shifts, hysteresis, and recovery after removing bias. A falling internal radiative efficiency, increasing non-radiative recombination, or irreversible contact/perovskite chemical change at constant optical geometry indicates electrical-stress damage. The mechanisms can coexist, so the diagnosis should compare external EQE, inferred internal efficiency, injection balance, and their time dependence at the same carrier density.
scoring_key_points: Explains why high open-circuit PLQY under optical excitation does not guarantee balanced electrical injection, stable contacts, or high photon escape probability.
Diagnoses injection imbalance/contact barriers using carrier-selective devices, electrical spectroscopy, EL onset, or contact-sensitive quasi-Fermi-level measurements.
Diagnoses optical outcoupling using calibrated angle/integrating-sphere measurements and optical modeling or controlled index/texture changes.
Diagnoses current-induced non-radiative degradation through time-dependent internal efficiency, PLQY, spectra, hysteresis, and recovery at matched carrier density.
accepted_equivalents: Magneto-electroluminescence, electroabsorption, or spatial EL imaging may supplement injection-balance diagnostics.
Reciprocity-based internal luminescence analysis is acceptable if parasitic absorption and non-ideal injection are explicitly treated.
Near-field optical measurements may substitute for optical-mode modeling.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing low EL EQE entirely to low material PLQY despite the stated high open-circuit PLQY.
Using only the EL spectrum or brightness without separating internal radiative efficiency from outcoupling.
Assuming photovoltaic contact selectivity automatically implies balanced high-current LED injection.

expected_answer:
Scale-up must separate or tightly coordinate solution speciation, nucleation, solvent removal, and crystal orientation. The precursor should use a solvent/additive system whose complexation and volatility create a reproducible induction time and narrow nucleation window. Concentration, spacer-to-metal stoichiometry, water content, solution age, meniscus temperature, coating speed, wet-film thickness, gas-knife profile, substrate-temperature zones, and annealing history must be controlled. A staged drying sequence can first homogenize the wet film, then trigger rapid crystallization before components segregate; alternatively, antisolvent vapor or controlled vacuum can impose a spatially uniform supersaturation. Spacer chemistry and substrate interaction should be tuned to favor the target n while promoting vertical or edge-on connectivity required for out-of-plane transport.

Inline monitoring should sample both down-web and cross-web positions. Hyperspectral reflectance/PL can track excitonic resonances and their width; Raman or ellipsometry can monitor solvent/complex removal; and grazing-incidence scattering at selected points can track low-angle phase peaks and azimuthal orientation. Calibration against cross-sectional composition, depth-resolved optical spectra, and device maps is required because a surface-sensitive or averaged measurement may miss a buried minority phase.

The decision rule should require agreement among at least two orthogonal phase-sensitive signals, bounded spatial and depth variation in the target n-value, absence of secondary excitonic/structural signatures above a defined detection limit, acceptable orientation distribution, preserved out-of-plane mobility, and uniform device performance. A film is rejected even if average XRD appears single phase when hyperspectral maps, depth probes, or transport reveal localized or buried phases, broad n-distribution, or insulating orientation.
scoring_key_points: Controls solution speciation and stoichiometry together with coating speed, wet thickness, evaporation/gas flow, temperature zoning, and annealing to narrow the nucleation/crystallization window.
Uses staged or triggered drying to prevent vertical and down-web component segregation while tuning substrate/spacer interactions for transport-compatible orientation.
Defines spatially resolved inline optical/speciation monitoring plus diffraction/orientation sensing calibrated to depth-resolved offline measurements.
Applies a multi-signal rejection rule requiring uniform target n-value, no hidden secondary phases, acceptable orientation/out-of-plane transport, and uniform device performance.
accepted_equivalents: Slot-die, blade, gravure, or vapor-assisted deposition strategies are acceptable if they control the same reaction–drying time scales.
Inline X-ray scattering may be replaced by rapid electron diffraction or calibrated polarized optical anisotropy where practical.
A machine-learning process controller is acceptable if trained on physically interpretable phase, solvent, and orientation signals.
common_wrong_answers: Scaling only by matching final dry thickness while ignoring wet-film residence and crystallization kinetics.
Using one average XRD scan as the sole phase-purity criterion.
Maximizing phase purity without checking orientation and out-of-plane transport required by the device architecture.

expected_answer: The two hypotheses must be separated by combining electronic-extraction probes with ion-sensitive, history-dependent probes on matched devices. For an electronically blocking cap, quasi-Fermi-level splitting or contact-free PL lifetime can remain high because recombination is suppressed, while charge-extraction transients slow, interfacial impedance or contact resistance rises, and the J–V curve develops an S-shape or thickness-dependent series loss. Spatial KPFM, ToF-SIMS, or composition-sensitive mapping performed before and after biased heating should show little redistribution; the loss should correlate mainly with cap thickness, orientation, or band offset and should not strongly reverse after de-poling. For failed ion blocking, the dominant signatures are bias-history dependence, low-frequency ionic capacitance or transient current, reversible hysteresis, and stress-induced movement of halide, A-site ions, or spacer species in ToF-SIMS/KPFM/operando PL maps. The degradation should be stronger at open circuit or under the field condition that accumulates ions and should partially recover in the dark or under reverse poling. A decisive study therefore uses the same thermal history at open circuit, short circuit, and MPP; a thickness/orientation series for the cap; and a transport-matched non-low-dimensional passivation control.
scoring_key_points: Separates contact-free recombination quality from contact-limited extraction using QFLS/PL plus transient extraction, impedance, or S-shaped J–V diagnostics.
Identifies ionic failure through bias-history dependence, low-frequency ionic response, reversible hysteresis, or direct post-stress ion/spacer redistribution mapping.
States opposite correlations: blocking loss tracks cap thickness/orientation/band offset, whereas ionic loss tracks electric-field condition and can show de-poling recovery.
Includes matched stress and control design, such as OC/SC/MPP comparison, a cap-thickness series, and a transport-matched passivation control.
accepted_equivalents: Transient photocurrent or time-resolved microwave conductivity may replace other extraction probes if interpreted as contact-sensitive versus contact-free.
Operando electroabsorption, scanning Kelvin probe, isotope-labelled ToF-SIMS, or bias-dependent PL may be used as ion-redistribution evidence.
A non-2D ligand, ultrathin insulating interlayer, or orientation-controlled low-dimensional phase is acceptable as the transport control.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that a long PL lifetime alone proves the device interface is electrically good.
Attributing all hysteresis to ion migration without testing bias history or directly probing redistribution.
Recommending only another efficiency measurement without a matched thermal and electrical stress matrix.

expected_answer: The redesign should be spatially selective rather than increasing the low-dimensional fraction everywhere. At scribe edges, where water and electric field concentrate, a chemically robust low-dimensional or perovskitoid-rich barrier should be combined with edge sealing to interrupt moisture and ionic pathways. Within the active area, sparse grain-boundary decoration or a graded quasi-2D/3D region can raise migration barriers and passivate defects without creating a continuous insulating network. The illuminated surface should use an ultrathin, vertically oriented, energetically compatible cap, or a gradient that returns rapidly to 3D character, so that the 3D phase remains the continuous vertical transport backbone. Validation must include spatially resolved EL/PL and sheet-resistance maps before and after stress, cross-sectional or isotope-labelled ion profiling from scribes into the active area, and stabilized MPP measurements under damp heat plus reverse-bias cycling. Go requires suppressed edge-propagation length and ion redistribution, no new S-shaped J–V or meaningful Jsc/FF penalty, and retained spatial uniformity and stabilized power; a design that merely improves shelf life while sacrificing current or allowing biased edge propagation is a no-go.
scoring_key_points: Assigns a robust low-dimensional barrier specifically to scribe edges and a sparse or graded low-dimensional treatment to grain boundaries rather than the entire bulk.
Preserves a continuous 3D vertical transport pathway through ultrathin, oriented, or rapidly graded surface phases with compatible band alignment.
Uses spatial module diagnostics that track edge propagation, ion movement, luminescence uniformity, and stabilized electrical output under combined stress.
Defines go/no-go criteria that require both migration suppression and negligible Jsc/FF or transport penalty.
accepted_equivalents: A 1D or mixed-connectivity perovskitoid may replace a conventional 2D edge barrier if its chemical and transport compatibility is justified.
Selective inkjet, vapor, or self-limiting deposition at scribes and grain boundaries is acceptable as the placement method.
Electroluminescence, lock-in thermography, LBIC, hyperspectral PL, or isotope tracing may be combined to quantify propagation.
common_wrong_answers: Adding a thicker 2D layer uniformly across the module without addressing the current penalty.
Treating encapsulation alone as dimensionality engineering and ignoring grain-boundary or field-driven transport.
Using only small-area shelf-life data as the scale-up acceptance test.

expected_answer: Nanoscale segregation can produce a strong minority-phase PL signal without a detectable bulk XRD peak because carriers funnel into small low-bandgap domains. The decisive sequence is time-resolved hyperspectral PL mapping under controlled excitation density and electrical boundary condition, paired with an independent temperature measurement and a composition- or strain-sensitive nanoscale probe. Segregation should show delayed nucleation and growth of spatially localized red-emitting domains, stronger formation when carriers accumulate at open circuit, suppression when carriers are extracted at short circuit, and dark recovery. Nano-XRD, cathodoluminescence, photoinduced absorption, or ToF-SIMS after frozen-in illumination should reveal correlated local compositional contrast even if conventional XRD is unchanged. Trap filling is typically prompt and saturating, changes intensity or the high-energy tail without producing persistent composition-correlated low-energy domains, and need not show slow dark remixing. Carrier heating gives an excitation-dependent high-energy distribution on ultrafast timescales, not a slowly growing red phase. Uniform lattice heating gives a spatially uniform, promptly temperature-tracking bandgap redshift and should be reproduced by dark heating to the same measured temperature. Repeating the test at matched sample temperature, pulsed versus continuous excitation, and OC versus SC therefore distinguishes the mechanisms.
scoring_key_points: Explains why a nanoscale minority low-bandgap phase can dominate PL while remaining invisible to conventional XRD.
Requires time-resolved and spatially resolved PL under OC/SC and excitation-density control, with delayed localized red-domain growth and dark recovery as segregation signatures.
Includes an independent temperature control and distinguishes uniform thermal redshift and ultrafast carrier heating from slow segregation.
Adds a composition- or structure-sensitive local probe, or an equivalent frozen-in illumination experiment, to corroborate halide redistribution.
accepted_equivalents: Operando nano-XRD, scanning PL, cathodoluminescence, photothermal deflection, or transient absorption may replace the named local probes.
Reverse-bias extraction or selective-contact half-stacks may replace the OC/SC comparison if carrier accumulation is controlled.
A carrier-density threshold and Arrhenius analysis of remixing are acceptable additional segregation evidence.
common_wrong_answers: Rejecting segregation solely because conventional XRD shows no extra peak.
Calling any redshift phase segregation without controlling sample temperature and excitation density.
Using only steady-state PL at one bias condition.

expected_answer: The stable PL spectrum and QFLS make absorber phase segregation or bulk recombination less likely but do not clear the contacted top cell. The matrix should retain standalone top and bottom cells, top-cell half-stacks with each selective contact, a recombination-junction test diode, a four-terminal optical stack, and the complete two-terminal tandem fabricated in the same run. Subcell EQE before and after stress establishes current matching and bottom-cell optical or processing damage; luminescence-based pseudo-JV, Suns-Voc, or subcell electroluminescence separates voltage/recombination loss from series-resistance loss. Impedance, transfer-length/contact-resistivity measurements, bias-dependent PL quenching, and temperature-dependent dark J–V isolate selective-contact or recombination-junction resistance. Bottom-cell lifetime/EQE measured before and after the top-cell thermal and solvent sequence checks process damage. Go requires no light-induced bandgap drift at the carrier density relevant to the tandem, stable top-cell QFLS and contact selectivity, a low and stable recombination-junction resistance with negligible optical loss, matched subcell currents over the expected spectrum and temperature range, and no bottom-cell performance loss from top-cell processing. A stable standalone absorber is insufficient if the two-terminal stack develops contact resistance or current mismatch.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched witness structures that isolate top absorber, each selective contact, recombination junction, bottom cell, and complete 2T tandem.
Applies subcell-resolved EQE and luminescence/pseudo-JV diagnostics to separate current mismatch, recombination, and series-resistance losses.
Checks bottom-cell damage from the top-cell process and directly measures contact or interconnect resistance under temperature and bias.
Defines go/no-go criteria covering phase stability, contact selectivity, interconnect loss, current matching, and bottom-cell preservation.
accepted_equivalents: A mechanically stacked 4T reference, spectral response decomposition, or calibrated luminescent coupling analysis may be used for subcell isolation.
TLM, conductive AFM, impedance spectroscopy, or dedicated interconnect diodes are acceptable resistance diagnostics.
Maximum-power tracking under spectral and thermal cycling is an acceptable current-matching stress test.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing the tandem loss to halide segregation despite an unchanged spectrum and without subcell diagnostics.
Testing only the complete tandem and attempting to infer every failure mode from its total J–V curve.
Using initial current matching at 25 °C as the sole scale-up criterion.

expected_answer: A useful design is a 2×2 functionality matrix rather than a comparison with only an untreated film. The full zwitterion contains both a perovskite-binding/passivating end and an HTL-facing charged end. A passivation-only analogue should retain the perovskite-binding group and molecular size but have a neutral or dipole-cancelled HTL-facing group. A dipole-only analogue should reproduce the dipole magnitude and orientation tendency while lacking the defect-binding functionality, and a matched non-binding, non-dipolar molecule controls morphology and solvent effects. Localization and orientation must be verified by depth profiling or XPS on separated interfaces, while UPS/KPFM or electroabsorption reports work-function shift and band bending. Chemical passivation should lower trap density and non-radiative voltage loss, increasing QFLS/ELQY or the slow recombination lifetime even if the work function barely changes. A pure dipole effect should shift the contact potential and accelerate selective extraction or improve FF/Jsc, but need not produce the same trap-density or ELQY gain. Synergy is demonstrated when the full molecule produces both classes of signatures and outperforms the sum or envelope of the single-function controls, with the correct dipole direction and no insulating transport penalty.
scoring_key_points: Proposes a crossed control set containing full, passivation-only, dipole-only, and matched inert or non-dipolar molecules.
Separates chemical passivation metrics such as QFLS, ELQY, trap density, or recombination lifetime from dipole metrics such as UPS/KPFM work-function shift and band bending.
Verifies buried-interface localization and orientation rather than assuming the molecular dipole points in the desired direction.
Defines synergy as simultaneous non-radiative-loss reduction and selective-extraction improvement beyond single-function controls without added series resistance.
accepted_equivalents: End-group protonation, tethered orientation, constitutional isomers, or external-field alignment may implement the functionality matrix.
Surface-photovoltage, electroabsorption, or capacitance profiling may replace KPFM/UPS for electrostatic alignment.
Absolute PLQY, electroluminescence efficiency, or QFLS from calibrated PL are equivalent passivation metrics.
common_wrong_answers: Comparing only the full molecule with an untreated control and assigning both mechanisms from performance alone.
Using a work-function shift as proof of trap passivation.
Using a longer PL lifetime as proof of faster extraction without accounting for contact-free recombination.

expected_answer: The molecule cannot be transferred by concentration matching alone because the oxide or SAM presents different Lewis acidity, hydroxyl density, surface charge, and binding sites. First, determine adsorption geometry, protonation state, and dipole direction on the new contact using spectroscopy, computation, and KPFM/UPS; redesign the contact-facing anchor if necessary while retaining a perovskite-passivating group. The resulting dipole must improve hole-selective alignment and electron blocking without making an insulating multilayer or chemically reducing/oxidizing the Pb–Sn absorber. Second, verify interface localization, coverage, QFLS/ELQY, extraction time, contact resistivity, and dark leakage in half-stacks before full tandems. Third, stress complete cells at 85 °C under MPP and compare OC/SC controls while monitoring work function or surface potential, EL/PL, impedance, and depth profiles of the molecule and mobile ions. A no-go result includes dipole reversal or drift, desorption or diffusion into the absorber, proton-transfer or NiOx/SAM reaction, increasing contact resistance, Sn oxidation, charge accumulation, or a gain in initial Voc accompanied by FF loss or rapid MPP degradation.
scoring_key_points: Re-evaluates anchoring, protonation, and dipole direction on NiOx or the SAM instead of assuming the PEDOT:PSS orientation is preserved.
Requires half-stack proof of localization, energy alignment, passivation, selectivity, and low contact resistance before tandem integration.
Uses heat-and-bias stress with spatial/electrostatic, recombination, impedance, and molecular/ionic redistribution diagnostics.
Defines no-go modes including orientation drift, chemical incompatibility, molecule migration, transport barrier, Sn oxidation, or unstable MPP despite higher initial efficiency.
accepted_equivalents: DFT or molecular dynamics, vibrational sum-frequency spectroscopy, NEXAFS, or angle-resolved XPS may be used to establish orientation.
NiOx surface functionalization or a redesigned bifunctional anchor is acceptable if the dipole direction and passivation function are preserved.
Operational stress at a realistic tandem current density and temperature may replace the exact 85 °C protocol if justified.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the same molecule must orient identically on every hole contact.
