Residual sulfate/hydrazinium may be measured by XPS, ToF-SIMS, ion chromatography, NMR, or vibrational spectroscopy.
Drying-rate dependence may be framed with solvent-removal time, supersaturation rate, or a dimensionless reaction-to-drying ratio.
common_wrong_answers: Choosing the dose that gives the flattest Sn/Pb profile regardless of conversion completeness or transport.
Assuming stronger Sn-O bonding is always beneficial and cannot create an electronic or ionic penalty.
Transferring the same mass concentration to a different Sn fraction or coating speed without kinetic recalibration.

expected_answer: The two mechanisms act at different stages and should be separated by preserving one chemical motif while removing the other. A hydrazinium salt with a non-sulfate counterion tests hydrogen bonding and cation effects without strong Sn-O coordination. It may alter precursor association or iodide mobility, but if sulfate is essential for rate matching and Sn2+ stabilization, it should show weaker changes in time-resolved Sn-phase crystallization, Sn4+ formation, and vertical Sn/Pb uniformity. A sulfate salt with an inert cation tests the anion’s coordination and oxidation resistance. It may reduce Sn oxidation, but it will not necessarily reproduce the interlaced FA-hydrazinium-iodide hydrogen-bond network or the same crystallization kinetics. Post-crystallization application is the most direct temporal control. If it lowers Sn4+ and improves surface recombination but does not remove the pre-existing Sn-rich top region, it isolates chemical passivation from crystallization regulation. In contrast, the full additive present in the Sn precursor should delay Sn-rich nucleation or intermediate conversion until it approaches the Pb-rich crystallization timescale. Time-resolved XRD or GIWAXS during antisolvent and annealing, together with in situ optical scattering, should measure this rate matching. Cross-sectional TEM/EDS or ToF-SIMS must then show a flatter Sn/Pb profile before extensive annealing-driven redistribution could occur. Direct Sn2+ stabilization should be quantified independently by Sn 3d XPS, oxidation-sensitive spectroscopy, controlled oxygen exposure, and comparison of Sn-I, Sn-F, and Sn-O chemical environments. Front/back PL and TRPL are useful downstream consequences but cannot alone identify whether the cause is compositional homogeneity or oxidation suppression. The strongest assignment requires factorial evidence: kinetic synchronization correlating with profile uniformity, and sulfate-dependent resistance to Sn2+ oxidation correlating with lower p-type defect density and voltage loss. If either control reproduces only one branch, the full molecule’s superior device response follows from the coupled mechanisms rather than generic surface passivation.
scoring_key_points: Uses hydrazinium-without-sulfate and sulfate-without-hydrazinium controls to isolate cation/hydrogen-bond and sulfate/Sn-coordination functions.
Uses post-crystallization treatment to distinguish chemical passivation from crystallization-rate regulation.
Requires time-resolved structural kinetics plus depth-resolved Sn/Pb composition to prove selective rate matching.
Requires independent Sn2+/Sn4+ chemistry and recombination measurements to quantify oxidation stabilization and connect it to Voc/FF.
accepted_equivalents: Hydrazinium chloride or another noncoordinating-anion hydrazinium salt is an acceptable cation control.
An alkali sulfate, ammonium sulfate, or another sulfate donor is acceptable if ionic strength and pH are matched.
Depth-resolved EDS, ToF-SIMS, XPS sputter profiling, or cross-sectional nano-XRF are accepted composition probes.
common_wrong_answers: Using only steady-state PL to claim that crystallization kinetics were synchronized.
Assuming a uniform final Sn/Pb profile proves that redistribution did not occur during annealing.
Treating lower Sn4+ as sufficient evidence that the additive also controlled the initial crystallization sequence.

expected_answer: The monotonic optical and lattice shifts report increasing average FA incorporation, but they do not imply monotonic electronic quality. Acetonitrile in the antisolvent can partially remove oleylammonium from CsI-terminated surfaces, creating accessible A-site vacancies. FA+ has stronger binding at these sites than Cs+, so moderate FAI drives rapid surface-to-core substitution. This expands the lattice, red-shifts the bandgap, passivates vacancy-related surface charge, and can flatten the energetic landscape. The zeta potential moving toward neutrality is consistent with removal or compensation of negatively charged surface sites. At the optimum, the native ligand shell remains sufficiently intact, particles retain discrete identity, and improved orientation and reduced traps increase mobility and PCE. At excessive FAI, the same solvent/ionic chemistry crosses a boundary. Continued ligand displacement or desorption exposes Pb-rich surfaces, changes the zeta potential positive, promotes aggregation or random packing, and creates undercoordinated Pb or Pb0. Trap-assisted relaxation and interparticle energy transfer then increase the Stokes shift and shorten useful carrier lifetime, even though the ensemble PL and XRD continue to red-shift because average FA content is still rising. To distinguish exchange from particle growth, compare TEM size distributions, pair-distribution functions, and quantum-confinement trends; a lattice shift at constant size supports composition change. To verify A-site substitution, use quantitative Cs/Pb and N/Pb XPS, solid-state NMR, elemental mapping, and depth-resolved HRTEM. Ligand integrity requires FTIR/NMR of oleyl groups, thermogravimetric ligand quantification, and surface-sensitive XPS. Transient absorption and excitation-dependent PL can reveal energy transfer to defective or compositionally distinct subpopulations. GIWAXS, SCLC mobility, trap-density measurements, and Pb0 XPS connect shell damage to film transport. The optimum therefore occurs where enough vacancies are exchanged and passivated to tune the bandgap, but the ligand coverage remains above the threshold needed for chemical stability and controlled electronic coupling.
scoring_key_points: Explains ACN-enabled ligand removal/A-site vacancy formation followed by stronger FA binding and vacancy-assisted exchange.
Connects the intermediate optimum to preserved ligand coverage, reduced traps, improved orientation, and controlled interdot coupling.
Identifies excessive FAI as causing ligand desorption, Pb-rich/Pb0 defects, aggregation or random packing, and defect-mediated energy transfer.
Proposes composition-, size-, ligand-, and ultrafast-dynamics measurements that distinguish exchange from growth and shell damage.
accepted_equivalents: Vacancy-assisted substitution may be described as surface-initiated FA-for-Cs exchange driven by stronger A-site binding.
Particle growth controls may include TEM, SAXS, absorption line-shape analysis, or pair-distribution measurements.
Ligand-shell integrity may be assessed by FTIR, solution/solid NMR, XPS, TGA, or quantitative ligand desorption analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming monotonic PL redshift proves that every additional FA ion improves device quality.
Attributing the high-FA PCE loss only to a smaller bandgap without addressing ligand loss and Pb0 formation.
Using XRD peak shift alone to distinguish alloying from size, strain, or mixed-population effects.

expected_answer: The original molecule should be decomposed into independent design modules rather than transferred unchanged. The perovskite-facing head must retain selective coordination to undercoordinated Pb and possibly hydrogen bonding to A-site or halide species. Its acidity should be weak enough to remove damaged surface material only within a controlled window; excessive proton activity or residence time can dissolve the surface, change I/Pb stoichiometry, and create mobile ionic residues. The central backbone should set the dipole and electronic coupling without introducing a thick tunneling barrier. The ETL-facing group must be redesigned for the chemistry of the polymeric contact. If the ETL contains pyridine, carbonyl, imide, thiophene, or fluorinated segments, complementary hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole interaction, π-stacking, or covalent click chemistry can replace fullerene-specific association. The group should not disrupt polymer packing or react with the coating solvent. Adsorption calculations and solution spectroscopy can screen candidate pairs, but the final criterion is interfacial function in the complete stack. Qualification should use a structure-property ladder: a perovskite-only head, an ETL-only tail, the full bridge, and a nonbinding analogue, all with matched thickness and acidity. XPS/NMR/FTIR should verify perovskite coordination; interfacial Raman, contact-angle, and spectroscopy should verify interaction with the new ETL. UPS/KPFM and surface-photovoltage measurements should confirm preserved band bending, while PLQY/QFLS and EQEEL quantify recombination. EIS, transient extraction, and temperature-dependent J-V should ensure that the bridge does not form an electron barrier. Peel/fracture tests and cross-sectional imaging should quantify adhesion and coating integrity. Processing stability requires rinse and solvent-resistance tests before device fabrication. Long-term heat-light-bias and humidity aging should track bridge redistribution, acid-induced decomposition, ETL morphology, contact resistance, and interfacial recombination. The molecule should be rejected if initial passivation is retained but FF becomes thickness-sensitive, if the ETL solvent removes or redistributes the bridge, or if the interface gradually acidifies, accumulates ions, or delaminates.
scoring_key_points: Decomposes the bridge into perovskite-binding, dipole/electronic, and ETL-binding modules and redesigns the ETL-facing chemistry for the new polymer.
Controls acidity and residence time to preserve surface-localized polishing/passivation without bulk or stoichiometric damage.
Uses function-separating molecular controls plus chemical, energetic, recombination, transport, and adhesion measurements in the complete interface.
Requires solvent-resistance and combined-stress aging with rejection criteria for migration, acid damage, transport barriers, or delamination.
accepted_equivalents: ETL-facing interaction may use π-stacking, hydrogen bonding, Lewis acid-base pairing, dipole matching, or mild covalent coupling.
Band-bending evidence may use UPS/KPFM, surface photovoltage, Mott-Schottky, or depth-resolved photoemission.
Bridge retention may be tested by labeled ToF-SIMS, XPS after rinsing, ellipsometry, fluorescence labeling, or equivalent methods.
common_wrong_answers: Using the PCBM-optimized molecule unchanged because it already passivates perovskite.
Selecting the most acidic molecule to maximize surface smoothing without checking stoichiometry or long-term ion generation.
Demonstrating only bare-film PL improvement and omitting electron-transfer, adhesion, and solvent-resistance validation.

expected_answer: The unchanged Jsc indicates that optical generation and short-circuit collection are already near saturation in both devices. The polymer’s gain therefore lies mainly in voltage and fill-factor losses. Higher electroluminescence efficiency, lower trap density, and an ideality factor near one indicate reduced trap-assisted and interfacial nonradiative recombination, which raises the quasi-Fermi-level splitting and Voc. Carbonyl and sulfur lone pairs can passivate undercoordinated Pb, while smoother coverage reduces local contact defects and leakage. Tighter packing and a continuous dopant-free film can lower contact inhomogeneity and series-related FF loss even when the pristine-film SCLC mobility is only comparable to doped spiro. A deeper HOMO can improve energetic selectivity by suppressing minority-electron leakage and aligning the contact with the perovskite valence band, but if it becomes too deep relative to the valence-band maximum it can create an energetic barrier for hole transfer. The distinction requires more than UPS values. Temperature-dependent J-V and contact resistance should reveal thermally activated extraction if a barrier exists. Transient photocurrent, charge extraction, and thickness-dependent FF should remain fast and weakly thickness-dependent for a beneficial contact. PL quenching and short interfacial TRPL can support rapid transfer, but they must be combined with high PLQY/QFLS in nonextracting geometries or with device EQEEL to ensure that quenching is not parasitic recombination. Loss decomposition should compare radiative-limit Voc, QFLS, external Voc, pseudo-FF, and measured FF. If QFLS and EQEEL improve, the polymer reduces nonradiative loss. If pseudo-FF improves but measured FF does not, transport or contact resistance remains limiting. Conversely, a too-deep HOMO would produce lower temperature-dependent extraction, charge accumulation, S-shaped J-V, or increased capacitance despite good passivation. The optimal polymer therefore combines selective alignment, chemical passivation, conformal morphology, and adequate interfacial transfer; no single energy-level number establishes that balance.
scoring_key_points: Uses unchanged Jsc to assign the main gains to reduced nonradiative Voc loss and FF/contact losses rather than optical generation.
Connects lower traps, stronger EL, near-unity ideality, and smoother coverage to passivation and suppressed interfacial recombination.
Explains that a deeper HOMO can improve selectivity but can become a hole-extraction barrier if the offset is excessive.
Uses temperature-, thickness-, transient-, QFLS/EQEEL-, and pseudo-FF-based tests to distinguish beneficial alignment from barrier-limited extraction.
accepted_equivalents: Energy selectivity may be described as reduced minority-carrier leakage, improved band alignment, or lower contact recombination velocity.
Barrier evidence may include S-shaped J-V, activated contact resistance, charge accumulation, slow extraction, or thickness-sensitive FF.
Nonradiative loss may be quantified by PLQY/QFLS, EQEEL, ideality factor, Suns-Voc, or radiative-limit voltage analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the deepest HOMO always gives the highest Voc and FF.
Using similar pristine-film mobility to conclude that transport cannot affect device FF.
Interpreting PL quenching alone as beneficial extraction without checking QFLS, EL, or parasitic recombination.

expected_answer: The polymer can influence mixed-halide stability through several competing pathways. Pyridine-Pb coordination may passivate undercoordinated lead and reduce vacancy-mediated halide motion, which should suppress segregation. Improved wetting and more uniform crystallization can also reduce local defect and strain gradients that nucleate iodide-rich domains. However, stronger interfacial anchoring may constrain lattice relaxation, creating residual or illumination-induced stress at the buried interface. Pyridine dipoles and altered surface energy can change local band bending or halide chemical potential, and nonuniform functional-group distribution can produce spatially varying nucleation. Any of these effects could create the observed low-energy PL shoulder and voltage nonuniformity. Optimization should vary pyridine fraction and linkage geometry independently while keeping molecular weight, film thickness, and surface energy as controlled as possible. A surface-energy-matched noncoordinating polymer separates wetting from Pb-N chemistry, while a small-molecule pyridine treatment on a neutral polymer separates direct passivation from backbone conformation. Depth-dependent GIWAXS and residual-stress measurements should determine whether the functionalized HTM changes buried strain. XPS or NMR verifies coordination, and SCLC or ion-migration measurements quantify defect and ionic changes. The decisive test is operando spatial and spectral tracking. Front- and substrate-side PL under calibrated illumination should reveal whether the low-energy phase begins at the buried interface. Hyperspectral PL, electroluminescence, Kelvin-probe mapping, and local photocurrent can correlate segregation with voltage loss. Time-resolved XRD/GIWAXS or nano-XRF can verify actual halide redistribution rather than trap emission. Bias polarity and temperature perturbations should test whether the process follows field-driven ion migration or purely photochemical phase instability. A successful polymer reduces the onset rate and amplitude of low-energy domains, keeps QFLS spatially uniform, and preserves trap-density, crystallinity, extraction, and MPP gains. The mechanism is falsified if a coordination-blocked analogue performs identically, if the PL shoulder appears without compositional redistribution, or if the instability tracks strain rather than vacancy density. The optimum may require less pyridine or a more compliant linkage than in the iodide-rich cell.
scoring_key_points: Explains both stabilizing pathways—Pb-defect passivation and uniform crystallization—and destabilizing pathways—constraint-induced strain, dipoles, or nonuniform nucleation.
Uses pyridine-fraction/linkage, wetting-matched, and coordination-blocked controls to separate chemistry, conformation, and surface-energy effects.
Requires buried-interface-sensitive operando spectral, spatial, structural, stress, and composition measurements to verify true halide segregation.
Defines falsification and acceptance criteria based on segregation kinetics, spatial QFLS, ion motion, and preservation of extraction/crystallinity benefits.
accepted_equivalents: Halide redistribution may be measured by hyperspectral PL, nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS after bias, operando diffraction, or compositional electron microscopy.
Interfacial strain may be assessed by depth-dependent GIXRD, Raman shifts, nano-beam diffraction, or mechanical modeling validated by measurement.
A coordination-blocked control may use methylated pyridine nitrogen, a sterically inaccessible N site, or a nonbasic positional analogue.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming stronger Pb-N binding must always suppress mixed-halide segregation.
Treating a low-energy PL shoulder as proof of halide movement without structural or compositional confirmation.
Changing pyridine content without controlling molecular weight, surface energy, film thickness, or linkage conformation.

expected_answer:
The original treatment cannot be assumed to be composition-neutral. Cs incorporation may stabilize the perovskite lattice and reduce A-site volatility, but too much Cs can create local wide-gap or nonperovskite phases. Chloride can accelerate crystallization, passivate halide vacancies, and modify texture, yet it can also alter intermediate chemistry and diffuse differently in a Br-rich film. Er is the least transferable component: a trivalent rare-earth ion may influence strain or defect charge compensation, but substitution at Pb2+ sites is energetically and electrostatically nontrivial and could generate compensating vacancies or segregated Er-rich phases.

For a wide-bandgap I/Br absorber, the main new risk is light-induced halide segregation. Any local Cs/Cl/Er-rich region, residual PbI2 conversion front, or strain gradient can become a nucleation site for I-rich domains. The treatment may also shift the optical gap or create an interfacial barrier that is negligible in the original absorber but costly in a current-matched tandem.

Screening should begin with a factorial composition matrix: intact Cs3ErCl6 QDs, Cs/Cl controls without Er, Er-containing controls without the QD structure, and QDs with adjusted halide chemistry. Use in-situ GIWAXS/PL to measure the treatment window and crystallization pathway. Quantitative XRF/ToF-SIMS and atom-probe or STEM-EDS should determine where Cs, Cl, and Er reside. UPS, absorption, and temperature-dependent transport should test band offsets and barriers. Under operating illumination, hyperspectral PL and operando XRD should quantify segregation kinetics and reversibility, while tandem-relevant current matching and Voc must be measured.

Retain the original QD only if it improves grain growth without detectable Er-rich phases, bandgap drift, or accelerated segregation. Use a composition-modified analog if Cs/Cl are beneficial but Er or the original halide ratio is not. Select a non-rare-earth reactive treatment when the same PbI2-management function can be achieved with lower compositional and supply-chain risk.
scoring_key_points: Explains distinct possible roles and risks of Cs, Cl, and trivalent Er in a mixed-halide wide-bandgap perovskite.
Identifies light-induced halide segregation, bandgap/current-matching shifts, and new secondary phases as transfer-specific risks.
Proposes component-resolved controls plus in-situ crystallization, spatial composition, band-alignment, and illuminated segregation measurements.
Provides criteria for retaining the original QD, modifying its composition, or replacing it with a simpler non-rare-earth chemistry.
accepted_equivalents: A rare-earth-free alternative may be a reactive halide salt, molecular complex, or nanoparticle if it reproduces controlled PbI2 conversion without harmful residue.
Wide-bandgap may be treated as approximately 1.7-1.85 eV if the answer preserves the mixed-halide tandem context.
Operando segregation analysis may use hyperspectral PL, electroluminescence, nano-XRF, or diffraction with adequate temporal resolution.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming chloride and cesium are universally stabilizing and therefore cannot cause composition gradients.
Treating Er as an inert spectroscopic label without testing charge compensation or secondary phases.
Assessing transfer only from initial small-cell PCE and omitting light-soaking and tandem current-matching tests.

expected_answer:
The 90 mV increase in absorber QFLS shows that non-radiative recombination inside the illuminated perovskite stack has been reduced, but external Voc can remain lower because the contacts do not extract the full electrochemical splitting. The missing 35 mV is a contact-selectivity or quasi-Fermi-level transfer loss. It can arise from residual surface recombination at the perovskite/carbon boundary, an insufficient back-surface-field barrier for electrons, Fermi-level pinning, or local regions where the carbon work function is not modified. Since Jsc is unchanged, the dominant gain is unlikely to be optical generation. The fill-factor improvement additionally indicates reduced contact resistance or reduced interfacial recombination under forward bias.

The loss budget should compare calibrated QFLS with Suns-Voc or pseudo-J-V. If pseudo-Voc approaches the QFLS while measured Voc remains lower, the remaining loss is contact-related. Electroluminescence efficiency and reciprocity analysis can independently estimate non-radiative voltage loss in the complete device. Dark saturation current, ideality factor, and impedance under varied illumination should separate recombination from series resistance. Temperature-dependent J-V and contact-resistance measurements can detect an extraction barrier. Mott-Schottky or capacitance profiling can support the field change but should not be used alone because fitted built-in voltage is model dependent.

Spatial nonuniformity is especially important for printable carbon electrodes. Kelvin-probe mapping, cross-sectional potential mapping, and local photocurrent or luminescence imaging should determine whether only part of the rear interface has the desired work function. A genuine dual-field improvement should raise QFLS, reduce the QFLS-to-Voc gap, increase recombination resistance, and improve pseudo- and measured fill factor without altering generation. If QFLS rises but the gap persists spatially, the perovskite-side passivation works while carbon-side field engineering is incomplete. If pseudo-FF improves but measured FF does not, resistive carbon transport remains dominant.
scoring_key_points: Interprets the QFLS increase as reduced absorber/contact recombination but recognizes that measured Voc can be limited by contact selectivity and quasi-Fermi-level transfer.
Locates the missing voltage in residual rear-interface recombination, insufficient electron blocking, Fermi-level pinning, or spatially incomplete carbon work-function modification.
Uses calibrated QFLS, Suns-Voc/pseudo-J-V, electroluminescence reciprocity, dark/impedance, and temperature-dependent measurements to build a voltage-loss budget.
Includes spatial diagnostics and distinguishes contact nonuniformity from series resistance and absorber recombination.
accepted_equivalents: Pseudo-J-V may be obtained from Suns-Voc or transient methods if the answer uses it to remove series-resistance effects.
Luminescence-based voltage loss may be expressed through external luminescence efficiency, radiative-limit Voc, or reciprocity analysis.
Carbon nonuniformity may be mapped by KPFM, scanning photocurrent, lock-in thermography, EL/PL imaging, or equivalent local probes.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that the full QFLS increase must appear as the same Voc increase.
Attributing the missing voltage to optical absorption despite unchanged Jsc.
Using only Mott-Schottky voltage as proof of the built-in field and ignoring contact selectivity and spatial variation.

expected_answer:
Conductivity is the product of charge density and mobility, so a larger spectroscopic doping yield does not guarantee a more conductive HTL. At low-to-moderate F4TCNQ loading, charge transfer creates Spiro-OMeTAD radical cations, increases hole density, and moves the Fermi level toward the HOMO. At high loading, additional ionized dopants can broaden the density of states through Coulomb disorder, deepen trapping, and reduce hopping mobility. Neutral or partially reacted F4TCNQ can also aggregate, creating spatially resistive domains. If implantation is incomplete, a steep vertical gradient may give a strongly doped top surface but leave the perovskite-side region underdoped; conversely, excess dopant at the perovskite interface can introduce quenching or chemical instability.

The variables must be separated experimentally. Doping yield and carrier density should be tracked by calibrated optical absorption, EPR, XPS/UPS, and, where feasible, charge-modulation or capacitance methods. Mobility and energetic disorder should be obtained from temperature-dependent hole-only transport, time-of-flight or SCLC analysis, and the field/temperature dependence of conductivity. A rising activation energy or broader Gaussian disorder parameter at high dose supports Coulombic disorder. GIWAXS, AFM, and nanoscale infrared or Raman mapping should test aggregation and host morphology. Depth-resolved FTIR/UPS and ToF-SIMS should reveal whether chemical doping and dopant concentration remain uniform through the HTL. C-AFM can identify disconnected conductive pathways.

The photovoltaic optimum is not the dose with the deepest HOMO or highest radical-cation signal. It is the dose that minimizes vertical transport resistance and energetic disorder while maintaining sufficient hole density, favorable alignment, low interfacial recombination, and thermal morphological stability. Device evidence should include QFLS-to-Voc transfer, pseudo-FF versus measured FF, temperature-dependent series resistance, and accelerated aging. A dose should be rejected if conductivity is sustained only at room temperature, if vertical gradients remain, or if mobility and stability decline despite higher nominal doping yield.
scoring_key_points: Uses conductivity = charge density x mobility to explain why stronger spectroscopic doping can coexist with lower conductivity.
Identifies high-dose mobility losses from Coulombic energetic disorder, dopant aggregation, and/or vertical concentration gradients.
Proposes separate measurements of doping yield/carrier density, mobility/disorder, morphology, and depth uniformity.
Defines the HTL optimum from vertical extraction, voltage/fill-factor transfer, and stability rather than maximum HOMO shift or oxidized-host absorption.
accepted_equivalents: Energetic disorder may be expressed as density-of-states broadening, increased hopping activation energy, Coulomb trapping, or reduced mobility edge transport.
EPR may be replaced by another radical-cation or charge-transfer quantification method if it distinguishes reacted from neutral dopant.
Time-of-flight, SCLC, impedance, or field-effect methods are acceptable mobility probes if their geometry and limitations are acknowledged.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a deeper HOMO automatically means higher conductivity.
Explaining the conductivity decline only by lower film thickness without checking charge density and mobility.
Choosing the highest F4TCNQ dose because it gives the largest oxidation peak.

expected_answer:
PEDOT:PSS conductivity, work function, acidity, and wetting are coupled but can move in different directions. Conductivity can increase if the modifier screens Coulomb attraction between PEDOT and PSS, removes or reorganizes insulating PSS at the surface, or induces a more extended PEDOT conformation. Acid neutralization can reduce corrosiveness and hydrophilicity but may also dedope PEDOT and lower conductivity. A redox-active modifier may oxidize or reduce PEDOT, changing carrier density. Separately, an oriented molecular dipole can reduce the apparent hole-extraction barrier without changing bulk PEDOT:PSS conductivity. Therefore, the observed combination cannot be assigned to a single generic “better contact” mechanism.

The study should use matched model films: PEDOT:PSS with the full molecule, a redox-inactive structural analog, a non-coordinating antioxidant analog, and pH-matched or ionic-strength controls. Four-point-probe and temperature-dependent conductivity should separate carrier-density and mobility changes; Seebeck coefficient, optical absorption, Raman, and XPS/UPS can assess PEDOT oxidation state and conjugation. Angle-resolved XPS and depth profiling should determine whether PSS is depleted or redistributed at the surface. Surface pH, acid release, and contact-angle measurements should quantify neutralization and wetting independently.

To isolate a dipole, compare work-function shifts for submonolayer versus thick modifier coverage and use Kelvin-probe or photoelectron measurements before and after washing. Interfacial hole-transfer dynamics, absolute QFLS, contact resistance, and electron-blocking leakage must be measured in complete stacks. A conductivity gain is useful only if the contact remains hole selective; increased dark leakage or reduced electron-blocking would indicate indiscriminate conductivity or an unfavorable energetic change.

PEDOT:PSS phase rearrangement is supported by PSS redistribution and mobility increase with little oxidation-state change. Acid neutralization changes pH/PSS chemistry. Secondary doping changes PEDOT charge-state signatures. A dipole shifts vacuum level without proportionate bulk conductivity change. The accepted mechanism may combine these effects, but each requires independent evidence.
scoring_key_points: Explains why conductivity, hydrophilicity/acidity, and hole-extraction barrier can arise from different and potentially opposing changes in PEDOT:PSS.
Distinguishes phase/PSS rearrangement, acid neutralization, PEDOT redox doping, and an interfacial dipole with matched molecular and chemical controls.
Uses transport, Seebeck/spectroscopic, depth-profile, pH/wetting, and work-function measurements to assign mechanisms.
Requires complete-device evidence that increased conductivity does not reduce hole selectivity or increase electron leakage.
accepted_equivalents: PEDOT:PSS phase rearrangement may be described as PSS segregation/removal, PEDOT conformational change, or enhanced interchain ordering.
Secondary doping may include oxidation-state change, counterion exchange, or redox-mediated carrier-density change.
Hole selectivity may be evaluated by dark leakage, electron-only blocking structures, recombination current, QFLS-to-Voc transfer, or equivalent diagnostics.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming lower contact angle directly causes higher PEDOT:PSS conductivity.
Attributing all work-function change to bulk doping without testing a molecular dipole.
Accepting higher conductivity as beneficial without measuring electron-blocking selectivity and dark leakage.

expected_answer:
Reverse bias is a distinct regime, not simply accelerated MPP aging. The electric-field direction and magnitude can drive the treatment's own cation and anion away from their designed locations, destabilize a surface secondary phase, and inject carriers that trigger redox reactions. Local shunts or shaded subcells can heat rapidly, increasing ionic mobility and metal diffusion. A layer that is beneficial at forward operating bias may become an insulating barrier or a site of field concentration under reverse bias.

Qualification should begin with single-cell step-stress tests using controlled reverse voltage/current, pulse duration, temperature, and illumination. Track leakage current, breakdown onset, recovery, electroluminescence, infrared hot spots, and local potential. Repeat with Ag, Cu, carbon, and transparent-conductive electrodes to separate metal-specific corrosion from perovskite ionic failure. Fragment-specific ToF-SIMS or labeled-ion profiling before and after stress should determine whether the salt loses spatial organization. XRD/GIWAXS and cross-sectional microscopy should test whether the secondary phase dissolves, thickens, or cracks. Ion-transport measurements before and after reverse stress should reveal whether mobile-defect density or barrier changes irreversibly.

Module tests should introduce calibrated partial shading to individual series cells while monitoring every subcell voltage. Include repeated shading cycles, damp heat, and thermal cycling because damage accumulation may be synergistic. Bypass diodes or subcell-level current-limiting designs should be evaluated as system protection rather than relying solely on chemistry.

Redesign options depend on the failure. If the salt redistributes, increase anchoring or use a less mobile counterion. If the secondary phase becomes a barrier, reduce dose or create a discontinuous/passivating monolayer. If metal corrosion dominates, adopt a more inert electrode or diffusion barrier. Acceptance requires a reverse-breakdown margin above the worst shaded-subcell voltage, no persistent ion/metal redistribution, limited hot-spot temperature, recovery without latent shunts, and retention of forward-bias PCE and MPP stability after repeated cycles.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes reverse bias/partial shading as a different field, injection, and heating regime that can redistribute the treatment and destabilize the secondary phase.
Defines single-cell reverse-bias step stresses with electrical, thermal, spatial, structural, and depth-composition diagnostics across different electrodes.
Extends qualification to series-connected modules with controlled subcell shading, voltage monitoring, cycling, and system-level bypass protection.
Provides mechanism-specific redesign and explicit breakdown, hot-spot, redistribution, latent-shunt, and forward-performance acceptance criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Reverse-bias protection may use bypass diodes, smaller subcells, current limiting, or another justified module design.
Anchoring may be achieved by covalent attachment, multidentate binding, polymer immobilization, or a less mobile ion pair if transport remains selective.
A discontinuous phase may be described as islands, a sub-monolayer, or localized grain-boundary conversion if field uniformity is verified.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming MPP stability guarantees partial-shading stability.
Applying one reverse-bias pulse and declaring success from immediate J-V recovery without latent-damage analysis.
Increasing treatment thickness to block ions without checking high-field extraction and breakdown behavior.

expected_answer:
The original pretreatment solves a process-specific wetting problem: it changes the polymer surface presented first to SnI2 in a sequential deposition. In a one-step ink, SnI2, organic iodide, additives, and coordinating solvent contact the surface simultaneously and for a much longer time during blade coating. ANI can dissolve into the wet film, alter precursor stoichiometry, nucleation, and local doping, while the new solvent can swell or reorganize the polymer. The same nominal dose and thickness can therefore produce excessive interfacial salt, nonuniform drying, or a transport barrier.

The transfer should define functions rather than copy recipes. A polymer-thickness series should be crossed with ANI surface coverage, solvent composition, substrate temperature, blade speed, wet-film residence time, and gas/thermal drying. Polymer swelling and mass loss should be measured in the actual ink solvents by ellipsometry, QCM, spectroscopy, or neutron/optical methods. Dynamic contact angle and surface-energy measurements should be made at coating temperature and on the relevant time scale, not only with a static droplet. ToF-SIMS or labelled ANI should determine whether the pretreatment remains at the interface or redistributes through the absorber.

In situ optical spectroscopy and GIWAXS should map nucleation and phase evolution, while large-area thickness, grain, stress, and pinhole maps quantify coating uniformity. The electronic acceptance tests should include spatial PLQY/QFLS, hole-extraction kinetics, contact resistance, SCLC mobility, sheet resistance under solvent exposure, and low-light as well as one-sun device maps. Controls should include no ANI, ANI added to the bulk ink at matched total amount, an inert wetting agent, and a polymer surface modified physically to match wettability without ammonium chemistry.

A robust window gives complete coverage without polymer dissolution, reproducible nucleation across coating direction, interface-confined or deliberately distributed ANI, low QFLS variance, and no extraction barrier. It fails if improved wetting is accompanied by polymer swelling, bulk stoichiometric shift, edge-to-centre nucleation gradients, residual-salt accumulation, or reduced fill factor. Scale-up qualification should use process capability across multiple coating runs, not the best strip.
scoring_key_points: Explains why one-step blade coating changes solvent contact, residence time, precursor sequence, ANI redistribution, and polymer swelling relative to two-step deposition.
Defines a multivariable process window over polymer thickness, ANI coverage, solvent, temperature, blade speed, residence time, and drying.
Requires in situ swelling/wetting/nucleation measurements, ANI depth mapping, spatial film-quality and electronic-uniformity diagnostics, and mechanistic controls.
Defines pass/fail criteria for coverage, polymer integrity, nucleation uniformity, QFLS/extraction, residual salt, and run-to-run process capability.
accepted_equivalents: Polymer swelling may be measured by QCM-D, ellipsometry, AFM thickness, neutron reflectometry, spectroscopy, or solvent-uptake mass change.
Physical wettability controls may use plasma, self-assembled monolayers, surface grafting, or an inert surfactant if electronic effects are checked.
Large-area uniformity may be assessed by PL/EL imaging, LBIC, hyperspectral mapping, sheet resistance, or segmented-device statistics.
common_wrong_answers: Use the same ANI concentration because wetting is a material property independent of coating method.
Increase ANI until the static water contact angle is minimized.
Polymer thermal stability guarantees solvent resistance during blade coating.
One champion large-area device is sufficient to define the process window.

expected_answer: The earliest failure is likely ionic and interfacial rather than a bulk optical collapse. Residual hygroscopic LiTFSI absorbs water through the HTL; incomplete complexation leaves a mobile Li+ fraction and water-assisted ionic conductivity. Under temperature and MPP bias, Li+ and halide vacancies redistribute toward interfaces. The accumulated ionic charge partially screens the junction field and changes local band bending, so extraction resistance and recombination rise. This first appears as increased series resistance, reduced recombination resistance, hysteresis, and fill-factor loss while absorption and Jsc remain largely intact. Illumination accelerates halide motion and interfacial redox chemistry. Defect-rich regions generated by ion accumulation become nonradiative recombination centers, lowering quasi-Fermi-level splitting and eventually Voc. Water and local electric fields then facilitate structural conversion of the metastable black inorganic perovskite to a yellow nonperovskite phase, causing the later optical and Jsc loss. The additive delays this sequence by passivating Pb-related defects and reducing the free Li+ population, but it cannot eliminate failure if coordination sites saturate, dissociate, or are spatially inaccessible. Operando impedance and bias-dependent transient current should reveal the early rise in ionic capacitance and transport resistance. Time-resolved ToF-SIMS or isotope-labelled Li mapping should show Li accumulation before the phase change, while GIWAXS/XRD and absorption track black-to-yellow conversion. PL or electroluminescence imaging should localize recombination before macroscopic discoloration. XPS of the metal contact and cross-sectional microscopy can test a competing electrode-corrosion pathway; corrosion without preceding ionic redistribution would produce a different signature. Dark storage lacks photocarrier-driven ion motion and redox reactions, while 65 °C aging in nitrogen excludes moisture and operating field. Neither reproduces the coupled light-humidity-bias stress that governs real operation.
scoring_key_points: Builds an ordered sequence from water uptake and incomplete Li coordination to ion redistribution and junction-field screening.
Connects early ionic/interfacial degradation to FF and recombination losses before bulk phase or Jsc failure.
Links later defect/redox evolution to black-to-yellow phase conversion and identifies the additive as delaying rather than eliminating failure.
Specifies operando ion, electrical, optical/structural, and electrode diagnostics and explains the limits of dark/N2 tests.
accepted_equivalents: mobile ionic charge may be described as interfacial polarization or electric-field compensation
operando GIWAXS may replace sequential XRD
Kelvin probe mapping may be used to follow local band-bending changes
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the first FF loss must be caused by reduced optical absorption.
Treating storage retention as equivalent to MPP stability.
Attributing all degradation to moisture without considering bias- and light-driven ion migration.

expected_answer: Undercoverage leaves patches of reactive NiOx exposed. Dangling bonds, oxygen-related defects, and Ni3+-rich sites can chemically interact with MAI and act as recombination centers at the buried interface. During heat and bias, these regions accumulate ionic charge, accelerate interfacial decomposition, and provide pathways for iodide migration toward the Ag electrode. The expected trajectory is an early loss of Voc and increased ideality factor, followed by stronger hysteresis and local dark or weak-EL regions. Impedance should show declining recombination resistance and increasing interfacial capacitance. Post-mortem XPS or ToF-SIMS should reveal exposed-NiOx reaction products, iodide enrichment along the device depth, and possibly AgI near the electrode. Overcoverage fails differently. A dense or nonuniform organic layer suppresses perovskite nucleation, producing incomplete coverage, small disconnected crystallites, or pinholes. Initially, some areas may be well passivated, but current is forced through a smaller effective contact area. This generates current crowding, local Joule heating, and shunt-prone paths. The dominant early signature is reduced Jsc or FF, spatially concentrated EL hot spots, and a broader device-to-device distribution rather than a uniform Voc loss. Impedance may show increased transport resistance in intact regions together with low-frequency shunt behavior at pinholes. Time-resolved PL/EL imaging is therefore diagnostic: undercoverage should correlate with chemically reactive, progressively darkening interface regions, whereas overcoverage should reveal nucleation voids and current hot spots from the beginning. Capacitance-frequency measurements can track the growth of interfacial trap populations for undercoverage; overcoverage is more likely to show geometric nonuniformity and transport bottlenecks. Cross-sectional ToF-SIMS, XPS, and electron microscopy should finally separate chemical reaction/AgI formation from physical voiding or incomplete film coverage.
scoring_key_points: Describes undercoverage as exposed reactive NiOx sites leading to interfacial recombination, ion migration, and possible AgI formation.
Describes overcoverage as nucleation suppression, incomplete coverage, current crowding, shunts, and transport resistance.
Predicts distinct electrical and spatial signatures for the two trajectories rather than treating both as generic degradation.
Uses time-resolved imaging, impedance/capacitance, and chemical/depth mapping to discriminate the mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: NiOx oxygen-vacancy or hydroxyl defects may be discussed with Ni3+ sites
Ag corrosion products may include AgI-rich interphases rather than crystalline AgI
lock-in thermography may replace EL hot-spot imaging
common_wrong_answers: Assuming more monolayer coverage is always more stable.
Predicting identical Voc-dominated decay for undercoverage and overcoverage.
Using contact angle alone to diagnose the failure trajectory.

expected_answer: In the 3D FASnI3 device, oxygen converts a fraction of Sn2+ to Sn4+ and shifts the defect chemistry toward acceptor-like states, especially Sn vacancies. The background hole density rises, the Fermi level moves deeper toward the valence band, and monomolecular recombination with photogenerated electrons increases. The immediate consequences are lower quasi-Fermi-level splitting and Voc, shorter carrier lifetime and diffusion length, and stronger nonradiative loss. Oxidation can also accelerate nonuniform crystallization, grain-boundary degradation, and interfacial reactions, so the initially electronic failure becomes morphological and chemical. A modest bulky-cation or quasi-2D component can slow oxygen and moisture ingress, passivate surfaces and grain boundaries, reduce Sn-vacancy formation, and improve film coverage. It may therefore preserve Sn2+ chemistry and suppress early voltage loss. The benefit is not unlimited. Low-n phases have wider bandgaps, larger exciton binding energies, and insulating organic spacers. If they become too abundant, poorly oriented, or broadly distributed, they impede vertical charge transport and inefficiently funnel carriers. The device then shows growing series resistance and FF loss even while oxidation is slower. Chemical oxidation should be monitored by Sn2+/Sn4+ spectroscopy, oxygen uptake, and phase-sensitive XRD/GIWAXS. Background doping requires Hall or Seebeck measurements, Fermi-level tracking, and injection-dependent PL/TRPL; a large hole-density rise with shortened diffusion length identifies self-doping. Spacer-limited transport is distinguished by orientation-resolved GIWAXS, depth-resolved phase mapping, temperature-dependent conductivity, and local vertical c-AFM. If Sn4+ remains low but resistance rises with an increased low-n fraction or parallel spacer orientation, the limiting failure is transport rather than oxidation. Thus, low-dimensional engineering trades chemical stability against electronic connectivity. The optimum suppresses oxygen-driven defect chemistry without creating a percolating insulating barrier or a harmful mixed-n landscape.
scoring_key_points: Traces oxygen-induced Sn2+ oxidation to Sn vacancies, high p-type background density, recombination, and Voc/diffusion loss.
Explains how chemical/electronic failure can propagate into morphology and interface degradation.
Explains both protective and transport-limiting effects of quasi-2D or bulky-cation components.
Specifies distinct measurements for oxidation state, carrier density/recombination, and spacer/phase-limited transport.
accepted_equivalents: iodine-related acceptor defects may be included with Sn vacancies
hollow perovskite protection may be discussed analogously if transport tradeoffs are addressed
mobility-lifetime product may replace diffusion length
common_wrong_answers: Claiming that a larger quasi-2D fraction always improves both stability and conductivity.
Attributing voltage loss only to morphological pinholes while ignoring self-doping.
Using XRD alone to quantify background hole density.

expected_answer: Incomplete removal in cooler regions leaves intact additive or sulfur-containing fragments at grain boundaries and interfaces. Residual coordination can initially slow crystallization or immobilize ions, but after device completion it may create insulating barriers, local dipoles, or chemically unstable complexes. Under light and bias, these regions accumulate charge, increase extraction resistance, and promote local nonradiative recombination. The early signature is FF loss, increased series resistance, stronger hysteresis, and spatially nonuniform PL/EL before a major change in absorption. Residual species may later redistribute or react with transport layers, lowering the effective ion-migration barrier locally despite a favorable area-averaged value. Excessive local heating produces a different failure. Halide and organic-cation loss, thermal decomposition, or rapid gas evolution can leave Pb-rich regions, microvoids, and buried-interface gaps. The film may appear crystalline in average XRD but contain mechanically weak, defect-rich hot spots. These sites accelerate halide-vacancy transport and interfacial redox reactions under bias. Voc and quasi-Fermi-level splitting then decline, while FF deteriorates through both recombination and poor contact. Repeated thermal cycling can enlarge voids or delaminate the interface. The two paths can be separated by spatially resolved diagnostics. ToF-SIMS or nano-XPS should reveal sulfur-rich cooler zones versus halide-depleted/Pb-rich hotter zones. Cross-sectional microscopy and acoustic or thermographic mapping should locate voids. Bias-dependent impedance and transient ion-current measurements should show transport resistance dominated by residue in the first case, but stronger recombination and ionic drift associated with thermally damaged regions in the second. Operando GIWAXS and mass-spectrometric exhaust monitoring during processing can identify the originating process nonuniformity. Thus, a high average migration barrier and short MPP test do not exclude local residue- or overheating-driven failure, especially when IPL temperature varies across area and thickness.
scoring_key_points: Describes incomplete removal as residual insulating/dipolar/chemical species causing charge accumulation, FF loss, and later ionic instability.
Describes overheating as volatile loss, Pb-rich defects, voids, and mechanically weak interfaces causing recombination and ion migration.
Predicts different temporal changes in Voc, FF, hysteresis, PL/EL, and structural chemistry.
Proposes spatially resolved sulfur/halide/Pb mapping, microscopy, and electrical/ionic diagnostics that distinguish the defects.
accepted_equivalents: residual N/S organics may be described as carbonaceous decomposition products
photothermal mapping may replace acoustic inspection
local QFLS mapping may replace PL/EL imaging
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a single area-averaged ion-migration barrier represents every IPL-processed region.
Predicting identical degradation for underheated and overheated areas.
Treating improved XRD crystallinity as proof that no voids or volatile-loss damage exist.

expected_answer: At the untreated buried interface, undercoordinated Sn4+ or Pb2+, oxygen-vacancy-related states, and local moisture create redox-active sites. Under heat and illumination, iodide can be oxidized to neutral iodine species or I2. Removing iodide leaves vacancies that increase ionic conductivity and expose undercoordinated Pb. Charge imbalance and reductive side reactions can then produce Pb0. The new vacancies and metallic/defective regions raise nonradiative recombination, lower local quasi-Fermi-level splitting, and enhance electric-field-driven halide migration. This is a positive feedback loop: ion migration supplies more iodide to reactive interfaces, while defect generation accelerates further redox chemistry. A multisite chelator/antioxidant can interrupt the loop at several points. Coordination to SnO2 defects and Pb2+ lowers the initial density of catalytic and recombination-active sites. Binding or adsorbing iodide/iodine species reduces their mobility and escape, while antioxidant chemistry suppresses conversion to I2 and Pb0. Improved crystallization and lower tensile strain reduce fast grain-boundary migration pathways. Better energy alignment and extraction also reduce interfacial carrier accumulation that drives redox reactions. The modifier has finite chemical and spatial capacity. If antioxidant groups are consumed, oxidized irreversibly, or binding sites saturate, iodide release and vacancy formation resume. The expected endpoint is renewed ionic polarization, growing Pb0/I2 signatures, and a transition from initially stable FF/Voc to accelerating recombination and structural decay. Humidity aging is most sensitive to water-assisted ingress and chemical oxidation; mass loss or I2 capture, XPS Pb0, and color/phase changes are informative. Thermal aging tests binding stability, modifier diffusion, and vacancy generation without strong photocarrier effects. MPP light soaking adds field-driven migration and interfacial redox; impedance, hysteresis, operando PL, and depth-resolved halide profiles should deteriorate before gross phase loss. Concordant protection across all three stresses supports a multi-link mechanism rather than a simple moisture barrier.
scoring_key_points: Builds the positive-feedback chain from iodide oxidation/I2 to vacancies, Pb0, recombination, and enhanced ion migration.
Explains how chelation, antioxidant/iodide management, crystallization/strain, and extraction interrupt different links.
Identifies finite modifier capacity or chemical consumption as a remaining long-term failure boundary.
Distinguishes humidity, thermal, and MPP diagnostics and their expected temporal signatures.
accepted_equivalents: I3− or volatile iodine species may be included with I2
Pb-rich reduced species may replace crystalline Pb0
modifier oxidation-state tracking may be proposed as a consumption diagnostic
common_wrong_answers: Treating iodide migration and iodine redox as unrelated degradation processes.
Assuming a chelator has unlimited antioxidant capacity.
Using humidity storage alone to claim suppression of field-driven ion migration.

expected_answer: The PBDB-T stability data support conclusions about the intrinsic compatibility of the PVDF:DH-modified absorber and interlayer with a relatively nonhygroscopic, nondoped hole contact. Improved retention can reasonably be linked to more complete PbI2 conversion, a more compact film, lower residual PbI2, and possibly more favorable internal-field or passivation effects. The data do not establish that the champion Spiro-OMeTAD/LiTFSI stack will show the same absolute lifetime or failure kinetics. Reintroducing LiTFSI adds water uptake and mobile Li+. Under heat, humidity, illumination, and bias, Li can redistribute toward the perovskite or electrode, modify local fields, and react with ionic or polar PVDF:DH fragments. The vertically segregated ReO4−-rich bottom region and fluorinated/polymer-rich top region may trap, repel, or concentrate Li in ways not sampled by the PBDB-T device. These interactions can change contact resistance, polarization, and ion migration. Spiro oxidation and dopant inhomogeneity add another source of conductivity drift. Any residual PbI2 can photolyze to Pb0, creating recombination centers even if dark storage is good. A matched matrix should cross absorber condition (control versus PVDF:DH bulk/interlayer) with hole contact (PBDB-T, undoped Spiro, and LiTFSI-doped Spiro). Each stack should undergo identical encapsulation, humidity-dark storage, 65–85 °C thermal aging, one-sun MPP, and combined damp-heat/light-bias stress. ToF-SIMS should follow Li and additive fragments; XRD/XPS should track PbI2/Pb0; impedance and four-point or hole-only transport should track contact resistance; PL/QFLS should separate absorber recombination from contact loss. If PVDF:DH improves every contact family, the absorber-level benefit is transferable. If the advantage collapses only with LiTFSI, the limiting failure is contact-specific and the PBDB-T result cannot be used as evidence for champion-stack durability.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes absorber/additive stability conclusions transferable from PBDB-T from champion-stack lifetime claims that are not transferable.
Adds LiTFSI moisture, Li migration, Spiro oxidation/conductivity, and additive-fragment interaction pathways.
Includes residual PbI2/Pb0 and contact-resistance failure in the champion stack.
Proposes a matched absorber-by-contact stress matrix with Li/additive, chemical, recombination, and transport diagnostics.
accepted_equivalents: a dopant-free small-molecule HTL may replace PBDB-T as the Li-free reference
operando neutron profiling may replace ToF-SIMS for Li
Moisture uptake may be measured by QCM or spectroscopy
common_wrong_answers: Claiming the PBDB-T retention directly proves equal stability for LiTFSI-doped Spiro.
Ignoring the different hole-contact chemistry because the absorber is unchanged.
Attributing all long-term improvement only to ferroelectric polarization.

expected_answer:
The emitter should minimize Sn vacancies and Sn4+ before device optimization. A quasi-2D or heterodimensional structure can confine excitons and reduce free-carrier leakage, but the phase distribution must be narrow enough to avoid multiple emissive wells and spectral broadening. Antioxidant or reducing chemistry, Sn-rich stoichiometry, and a solvent system that does not oxidize Sn2+ should be combined with rapid encapsulation. Because deeper confinement can impede transport, the dimensionality and organic spacer fraction should be optimized against conductivity and operating voltage rather than maximized.

The device stack should use injection layers whose effective barriers compensate the intrinsic p-type character. Electron injection must be strengthened without allowing excessive electron accumulation, while hole injection may require a blocking or lower-mobility layer. Carrier-only devices, capacitance-voltage measurements, and transient electroluminescence should confirm that the recombination zone remains in the emitter at increasing current. A graded or bilayer architecture can separate transport from radiative confinement. Optical outcoupling or a weak microcavity should increase external efficiency without forcing a narrow angular spectrum or changing the intrinsic emission assignment.

High radiance makes Auger recombination and Joule heating inseparable unless temperature is measured operando. EQE and spectral position should be recorded versus current density, pulse width, duty cycle, and substrate temperature. If short pulses recover EQE while the carrier density remains similar, heating is implicated; if roll-off scales with instantaneous carrier density even at constant temperature, Auger or exciton-polaron quenching is more likely. High-thermal-conductivity substrates, thin transport layers, and heat-spreading electrodes are therefore part of the emitter design.

Viability requires stable NIR-II peak position and linewidth, balanced injection, low voltage, limited Sn4+ growth, suppressed EQE roll-off, and reproducible lifetime at a specified radiance. A device that reaches high peak EQE only at negligible brightness or under very low duty cycle has not solved the high-radiance problem.
scoring_key_points: Combines Sn redox/vacancy control with a confinement strategy while recognizing the transport and spectral-distribution tradeoff.
Uses contact and transport-layer design to compensate p-type self-doping and maintain a controlled recombination zone.
Separates Auger loss from Joule heating using current-density, pulse, duty-cycle, and operando-temperature measurements.
Defines viability at specified radiance using roll-off, spectrum, voltage, oxidation, and lifetime metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Quasi-2D, quantum-well, or heterodimensional confinement are acceptable if transport penalties are discussed.
Thermal imaging, micro-Raman thermometry, or calibrated voltage-temperature methods are acceptable operando temperature probes.
common_wrong_answers: Proposing stronger quantum confinement without addressing increased resistance and phase-distribution broadening.
Reporting only peak EQE and wavelength without radiance-dependent roll-off and lifetime.

expected_answer:
The additive library should vary the nitrile electronic strength, number of cyano groups, spacer length, and counter-cation while keeping molecular size and ionic content as controlled as possible. Cyano-containing neutral molecules, ammonium analogues without cyano groups, and noncoordinating isomers are needed to separate Sn coordination from hydrogen bonding and generic ionic effects. DFT adsorption energies and charge-density analysis can rank candidates, but the target is an intermediate binding regime rather than the most negative adsorption energy.

Useful coordination should reduce Sn2+ oxidation and raise the formation energy of Sn vacancies without immobilizing precursor complexes or creating deep molecular states. This requires Sn2+/Sn4+ spectroscopy, vacancy/trap measurements, Hall carrier density, and calculated/experimental density of states. In a bromide-rich or Sn-Ge lattice, the Lewis acidity, lattice softness, and native-defect hierarchy differ from FASnI3; therefore the same molecule may overcoordinate Sn, retard conversion, produce residual low-dimensional phases, or segregate at grain boundaries.

Crystallization should be monitored in situ. An additive that delays nucleation enough to improve coverage may be beneficial, but excessive binding can leave solvent-adduct phases, small grains, poor connectivity, or insulating molecular layers. GIWAXS, microscopy, compositional mapping, and concentration sweeps should determine the process window. UPS/KPFM and carrier-only devices should verify that the additive does not create an extraction barrier or unbalance transport. Bias- and temperature-dependent transient current, ToF-SIMS, or impedance can test whether the ionic additive increases halide or cation migration.

Transferability requires a full analogue matrix: cyano versus noncyano, ammonium versus neutral, weak versus strong nitrile, and concentration series in both the original and new absorber. A successful candidate must improve oxidation state, vacancy/trap density, dark-current noise, and stability while preserving phase purity, mobility, extraction, and spectral response. Binding that improves XPS but raises voltage dependence, slows extraction, or creates hysteresis is overcoordination, not successful passivation.
scoring_key_points: Uses a chemically controlled additive library that separates cyano coordination from ammonium, ionic-strength, and size effects.
Treats optimal coordination as intermediate and tests oxidation, vacancy energetics, trap states, and carrier density.
Examines composition-specific crystallization, phase purity, band alignment, transport, and ion-migration penalties.
Requires cross-composition analogue and concentration controls plus device noise/stability validation before claiming transfer.
accepted_equivalents: Mixed Sn-Ge native-oxide effects may be included as an additional passivation variable.
Operando scattering, spectroscopy, or equivalent in-situ crystallization tools are acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the molecule with the strongest calculated adsorption energy as automatically best.
Assuming a mechanism transfers from iodide to bromide or Sn-Ge without remeasuring defect chemistry and energy alignment.

expected_answer:
The metric pattern first suggests a transport/contact failure rather than immediate bulk recombination: preserved open-circuit voltage indicates that the maximum quasi-Fermi-level splitting is not yet strongly reduced, whereas lower fill factor, current, and higher sheet resistance point to a growing extraction barrier or loss of lateral/vertical conductance. MXene oxidation can remove metallic states, change surface terminations, and disrupt the percolating network. Halide arrival may accelerate this process or create Ti-halide/oxide interphases that alter band alignment. Bulk perovskite degradation remains a competing mechanism and must be measured independently.

Use matched SnO2, SnO2/MXene, and conductivity-matched inert-carbon controls under heat-only, light-only, open-circuit, short-circuit, and maximum-power bias. Track four-terminal ETL sheet resistance, contact resistivity, temperature-dependent current-voltage curves, Suns-Voc/pseudo-JV, and operando impedance. If pseudo-fill factor remains high while measured fill factor falls, the loss is contact/transport dominated. Near-ambient-pressure or rapid-transfer XPS/XAS and Raman should quantify Ti oxidation and termination changes; cross-sectional ToF-SIMS or isotope-labelled halide should establish whether halide reaches and reacts with the composite. GIWAXS, absorption, PL quantum yield, and spatial lifetime mapping determine whether the absorber itself decomposes.

MXene oxidation is causal if resistance and barrier height rise before bulk optical degradation, scale with oxygen/water activity or electrochemical potential, and are suppressed by a diffusion barrier or oxidation-resistant termination. Halide reaction is causal if bias polarity controls halide accumulation and the Ti chemical change, with recovery or prevention when halide flux is blocked. The composite is intrinsically less stable than SnO2 if its unique Ti3C2Tx chemistry or percolation network degrades under otherwise identical stress and drives irreversible contact resistance or interfacial recombination not observed in pristine SnO2.
scoring_key_points: Ranks transport/contact degradation ahead of bulk recombination using the preserved Voc, FF/Jsc loss, and rising sheet resistance.
Uses matched-contact controls and bias/atmosphere-separated stresses to distinguish oxidation, percolation loss, and halide reaction.
Requires operando electrical measurements plus chemical depth profiling and independent bulk-perovskite diagnostics.
Defines intrinsic instability as a unique, irreversible MXene-related chemical or percolation failure preceding absorber degradation.
accepted_equivalents: Suns-Voc, pseudo-JV, or electroluminescence-derived pseudo-efficiency are equivalent ways to separate recombination from resistive loss.
XANES/EELS may replace XPS for Ti oxidation-state tracking if spatial and handling artefacts are addressed.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning every fill-factor loss to increased trap density in the perovskite.
Using ex situ Ti XPS alone without controlling air exposure or bias history.
Assuming higher initial conductivity guarantees better operational stability.

expected_answer:
The original locations cannot be copied mechanically because the selective contacts and desired majority carriers are reversed. At the bottom of a p-i-n device, the interface must support hole extraction while blocking electrons. A conductive Cl-terminated carbide that was beneficial beside SnO2 may be unsuitable if it donates electrons, disrupts the phosphonic-acid monolayer, or creates an n-type surface field. It should be retained only if its surface chemistry improves crystallization without shorting or reversing the hole-selective dipole. More plausibly, its Pb-Cl anchoring motif should be transferred to an electrically insulating or p-compatible scaffold. At the top perovskite/C60 interface, a pi-conjugated material may be useful if it passivates Pb defects while coupling electronically to C60 and preserving electron extraction; however, its frontier levels, thickness, and possible hole leakage must be re-optimized.

A minimal matrix includes the untreated p-i-n control, bottom-only, top-only, dual treatment, and chemically matched but electronically insulating analogues. Include a direct copy of the original materials and redesigned p-compatible/e-compatible variants. Verify phosphonic-acid monolayer coverage, wetting, modifier localization, and survival through subsequent solvent coating. Absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting on bare films quantify passivation; contact-selective PL/TRPL, transient photocurrent, surface photovoltage, and temperature-dependent JV quantify extraction barriers. UPS/Kelvin probe and capacitance-voltage measurements should establish the sign of band bending, while dark leakage and electroluminescence test selectivity.

Successful transfer requires improved nonradiative voltage loss and faster extraction at the intended carrier contact without increased series resistance, leakage, or hysteresis. If PLQY rises but contact-selective lifetime lengthens, pseudo-FF exceeds measured FF, or the surface field has the wrong sign, the modifier is passivating defects while creating a transport barrier. The transferable principle is chemically distinct treatment of both interfaces, not literal reuse of each material at its original location.
scoring_key_points: Explains why reversing device polarity changes the required band bending and majority-carrier selectivity at both interfaces.
Evaluates chemical and solvent compatibility with the phosphonic-acid bottom contact and C60 top contact.
Proposes a factorial matrix with original modifiers, redesigned analogues, single-interface, and dual-interface controls.
Defines success through simultaneous voltage-loss reduction, correct field direction, efficient extraction, and no added resistance or leakage.
accepted_equivalents: A NiOx-based p-i-n bottom contact may substitute for a phosphonic-acid contact if the same selectivity and compatibility analysis is performed.
Electron-selective conjugated analogues may replace the original top material if their defect-binding motif is preserved.
common_wrong_answers: Placing the original bottom modifier at the new bottom interface solely because both are buried interfaces.
Using stronger PL as the only criterion for successful transfer.
Ignoring whether the modifier dissolves, displaces, or electronically shorts the self-assembled monolayer.

expected_answer:
The strongest defensible claim is limited to the exact tested stacks and durations. The P3HT accelerated-aging result can show that the buried-interface treatment is compatible with a P3HT-based device under the stated double-60 condition, but it cannot establish thermal-humidity stability of the champion Spiro-OMeTAD architecture. Changing the hole conductor changes ion sources, hygroscopicity, dopants, oxidation chemistry, transport, and contact degradation. Likewise, a 500-versus-1000 h inconsistency prevents a precise retention-time claim until raw timestamps and sample histories are reconciled. The result may still support qualitative improvement over its matched control, but the longer duration must not be repeated as fact.

Audit the raw data, device identifiers, measurement timestamps, environmental logs, sample counts, and definition of retained PCE. Report both the last unambiguous common time point and the distribution across replicates, including failures. Separate storage from operation; a device measured intermittently under double-60 storage is not equivalent to continuous MPP at 60 °C and 60% RH. Confirm whether devices were encapsulated, whether humidity reached the active area, and whether controls used identical electrodes and HTLs.

The minimum causal repeat is a 2 x 2 design: modifier versus no modifier crossed with Spiro-OMeTAD versus P3HT, using identical perovskite, ETL, electrode, encapsulation, and batch-randomized fabrication. Run continuous MPP under controlled 60 °C/60% RH and, separately, dry heat and humid dark storage to identify stress interactions. Track Voc, Jsc, FF, series resistance, luminescence/QFLS, ion profiles, and phase evolution. The modifier stabilizes the original architecture only if modified Spiro devices outperform matched unmodified Spiro devices reproducibly under the combined stress, without the benefit being attributable to P3HT substitution. Until then, the evidence supports interface-treatment potential, not qualification of the champion stack.
scoring_key_points: Restricts claims to the exact HTL, stress mode, and unambiguous duration actually tested.
Explains why substituting P3HT invalidates direct stability inference for the Spiro-OMeTAD champion architecture.
Requires raw-data audit, replicate distributions, and reconciliation of the 500/1000 h discrepancy.
Proposes a modifier-by-HTL factorial repeat under continuous combined stress plus separated stress controls.
accepted_equivalents: A three-factor design including encapsulation is acceptable if modifier and HTL effects remain independently estimable.
T80 or energy-yield analysis may replace a single retention checkpoint if raw trajectories are reported.
common_wrong_answers: Reporting 91% after 1000 h without reconciling the conflicting caption.
Assuming stability measured with P3HT automatically applies to Spiro-OMeTAD.
Calling intermittent storage measurements equivalent to continuous MPP operation.

expected_answer:
Several favorable features remain transferable: a compact conjugated core, high intrinsic mobility, pinhole-free coverage, thermal robustness, and dopant-free or low-dopant operation. The Pb-passivation argument does not transfer automatically. Sn2+ is more redox-active and tin perovskites are commonly strongly p-type because of Sn vacancies. Electronegative O/F regions may coordinate Sn, but excessive electron withdrawal can deepen the HTM ionization energy, creating a hole-extraction offset relative to the shallower tin-perovskite valence band. Strong surface binding could also perturb Sn-I bonding or accelerate interfacial oxidation if the molecule concentrates oxygen, oxidants, or polar dopants.

Retain the morphology-controlling and conjugated transport framework, but redesign frontier levels and redox compatibility. Use a fluorination series with matched molecular shape and film-forming behavior, plus analogues in which the Lewis-base site is spatially separated from the electron-withdrawing fluorine. Consider replacing Li-TFSI doping with a dopant-free architecture or a nonoxidizing dopant. Add antioxidant or SnF2-compatible anchoring groups only if they suppress Sn4+ formation without increasing vacancies.

Compare lead and tin absorbers using the same HTM series at matched thickness. Measure solid-state ionization energy, interfacial dipole, contact resistance, and hole transfer; quantify Sn4+/Sn2+, Sn-vacancy-related carrier density, trap spectra, and oxygen sensitivity. Absolute PLQY/QFLS is especially important because tin films can show fast extraction and severe nonradiative loss simultaneously. Operando XPS or optical oxidation markers under heat/light test chemical stability. Fluorination remains beneficial only if it improves coverage and mobility while preserving low extraction barrier, lowering Sn4+ and trap density, and reducing rather than increasing p-type degeneracy or interfacial oxidation. If the nonfluorinated or weakly fluorinated analogue gives higher QFLS and lower resistance despite slightly lower mobility, the original fluorination optimum is lead-specific.
scoring_key_points: Identifies tin-specific differences: Sn2+ oxidation, shallow valence band, Sn-vacancy self-doping, and stronger redox sensitivity.
Separates transferable morphology/transport features from non-transferable Pb-defect and energy-alignment assumptions.
Proposes matched fluorination and binding-site controls with dopant/redox compatibility redesigned.
Defines success using extraction barrier, QFLS, Sn4+/Sn2+, vacancy/carrier density, mobility, and operational chemical stability.
accepted_equivalents: Germanium-tin or mixed Sn-Pb absorbers are acceptable intermediate transfer systems if composition-dependent band alignment is addressed.
XPS, Mössbauer-like tin spectroscopy, or chemical titration may be used to quantify Sn oxidation state.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming Lewis-base passivation of Pb and Sn is chemically identical.
Choosing the deepest HTM HOMO without considering the shallower tin-perovskite valence band.
Using high hole mobility alone as the criterion for success in a heavily self-doped tin absorber.

expected_answer:
The n=1 and n=5 observations probe different balances of confinement, dissociation, transport, and recombination. A sharp, intense band from the insulating-spacer n=1 material is consistent with strong dielectric confinement: electron and hole remain bound as an exciton and recombine radiatively within the inorganic slab. High PL intensity in that limit does not imply efficient free-carrier generation or out-of-plane extraction. A conjugated spacer that electronically participates near a band edge, provides pi-stacked pathways, or raises the effective dielectric screening can reduce the exciton binding energy and permit interlayer charge transfer. The resulting exciton is less localized, so the n=1 excitonic peak can broaden and weaken even when the material is more useful for photovoltaic transport.

Weak PL becomes evidence of loss only if it is accompanied by a reduced absolute photoluminescence quantum yield, shorter free-carrier lifetime, stronger sub-gap absorption, or increased trap-assisted recombination. In n=5 films, the longer lifetime and lower trap density indicate that the donor-acceptor spacer is not simply opening a nonradiative channel. Instead, vertical orientation, lower strain, stronger dielectric screening, and frontier-orbital coupling can jointly increase the fraction of mobile carriers while reducing defect-mediated loss. The higher voltage and fill factor then follow from lower nonradiative recombination and easier out-of-plane extraction.

The minimum discriminating set is temperature-dependent PL to extract exciton binding energy; absolute PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting under matched generation; transient absorption or field-dependent PL to monitor exciton dissociation; time-resolved PL interpreted with carrier-density dependence; and vertical conductivity or mobility measured on morphology-matched films. Structural orientation and thickness must also be controlled. The decisive conclusion is that PL intensity alone cannot rank these materials: one must separate radiative exciton population from free-carrier yield and nonradiative lifetime.
