The simultaneous rise in contacted-stack extraction rate, conductive-AFM current, fill factor, and balanced electron/hole mobility is therefore the key optimum signature.

At high dose, the appearance of strong low-angle diffraction and an excitonic absorption feature, together with lower JSC and FF, indicates excessive low-dimensional phase fraction or thickness. A continuous organic-spacer-rich layer then adds series resistance and blocks out-of-plane transport even if the bare-film PL remains strong. The distinction requires incidence-angle-dependent GIWAXS and cross-sectional TEM to determine phase depth, orientation, and thickness; XPS or ToF-SIMS depth profiles to quantify Br and bulky-cation penetration; and wavelength-dependent absorption/PL to identify true bandgap alloying. Br alloying should shift the 3D absorption edge throughout the sampled depth without necessarily producing a large contact resistance. Bulk 2D conversion should persist at higher GIWAXS incidence and alter film-wide excitonic spectra. Incomplete coverage should produce nanoscale current and potential heterogeneity, exposed 3D regions, and leakage rather than uniform series resistance. A transport barrier should show increased contact resistance, slower extraction after the electron contact is added, and thickness-dependent FF loss. The optimal dose is the one that raises QFLS/VOC while preserving or improving contacted cross-plane transport, not the dose giving the strongest layered-phase signal.
scoring_key_points: Interprets the dose series as low-dose defect passivation, intermediate-dose passivation plus transport-compatible surface RP formation, and high-dose blocking or excessive low-dimensional conversion.
Uses surface-sensitive structural and depth-composition measurements to separate surface confinement, orientation, Br incorporation, and bulk conversion.
Connects contacted-stack kinetics, cross-plane current, contact resistance, mobility balance, JSC, and FF to transport rather than relying on bare-film PL alone.
Defines distinct signatures for incomplete coverage, alloying, bulk 2D conversion, and a continuous transport barrier and states a simultaneous passivation/transport optimum criterion.
accepted_equivalents: A thickness-dependent tunneling-barrier analysis can substitute for direct contact-resistance extraction
Hard-X-ray photoemission or angle-resolved XPS may replace ToF-SIMS for depth-sensitive composition
Absolute electroluminescence and Suns-VOC may substitute for PLQY/QFLS measurements
common_wrong_answers: Selecting the highest PLQY or strongest RP diffraction as automatically optimal
Attributing all optical blue shifts to vertical orientation rather than Br incorporation or phase conversion
Using conventional theta-2theta XRD alone to infer the depth and orientation of an ultrathin surface phase

expected_answer:
A single Arrhenius fit to T80 is not defensible because T80 is an emergent endpoint that can switch among at least four rate-limiting processes. Nucleation may be defect-activated and strongly light dependent; propagation may depend on iodine concentration and a chemical-front activation barrier; escape or capture depends on package permeability and getter capacity; rupture depends on cavity volume, adhesion, and mechanical strength. Changing temperature can alter all four and can even change which mechanism controls the endpoint, producing a misleading apparent activation energy.

The minimum program should factorially vary temperature, light intensity, electrical operating point, internal free volume, electrode or encapsulant permeability, and getter loading. Replicated devices are essential because nucleation is stochastic. Time-resolved optical or electroluminescence imaging should provide lesion birth times, coordinates, radii, and coalescence. Gas analysis or iodine-sensitive optical probes should track volatile release; pressure or membrane-deflection measurements should quantify buildup; spatial XRD/Raman should confirm PbI2 formation; and electrical data should be decomposed into active-area loss, contact resistance, and surviving-region efficiency.

A hierarchical competing-process model should contain a nucleation hazard λ(T, photon flux, defect density), a propagation velocity v(T, iodine activity, bias), an escape/getter balance for iodine inventory, and a rupture threshold based on pressure and adhesion. The model should predict distributions of T95/T90/T80 and rupture probability, not only a mean lifetime. Separate activation parameters should be estimated in regimes deliberately chosen to isolate each process: low iodine inventory for nucleation, seeded lesions for propagation, inert iodine dosing for escape/getter calibration, and mechanical coupons for rupture.

Field extrapolation is acceptable only if the same mechanism and spatial signatures persist across the acceleration window, parameters remain stable when a stress level is omitted from fitting, and predictions are validated at an intermediate condition. Package changes require re-estimation of escape and rupture terms even if absorber chemistry is unchanged. Reporting should state uncertainty bands and the probability of catastrophic local failure. A T80 that lengthens because a permeable contact vents iodine but releases it into adjacent cells is not equivalent to intrinsic stabilization.
scoring_key_points: Explains that T80 mixes nucleation, propagation, volatile management, and mechanical rupture and therefore need not obey one Arrhenius law.
Defines a replicated factorial stress matrix including temperature, light/bias, free volume, permeability, and getter capacity with spatial, chemical, gas, pressure, and electrical observables.
Uses a hierarchical or competing-process model with separate nucleation hazard, front velocity, iodine inventory/escape, and rupture threshold parameters.
Requires mechanism invariance, intermediate-condition validation, uncertainty reporting, and requalification when packaging changes.
accepted_equivalents: A stochastic cellular-automaton or survival-analysis formulation may replace the stated hierarchical model
Membrane deflection, acoustic emission, or embedded pressure sensors may be used for rupture precursors
T95 or lesion-free survival probability may be used instead of T80 if defined consistently
common_wrong_answers: Fitting one lifetime endpoint versus reciprocal temperature without checking mechanism changes
Using only average PCE traces and no spatial lesion statistics
Treating increased venting as intrinsic absorber stabilization without accounting for iodine transfer or package consequences

expected_answer:
The device must be analyzed as two chemically distinct interfaces plus a redox-sensitive Sn-Pb bulk. The control ladder should include untreated, top-only, bottom-only, and dual-treated devices, each fabricated with the same absorber batch. Partial stacks terminated after the perovskite, electron contact, and hole contact should be stressed in parallel. The stress matrix should separate dry-N2 light/bias, dark heat, controlled oxygen, controlled humidity, and combined MPP conditions. This distinguishes intrinsic ion/contact evolution from Sn(II) oxidation and water- or acid-assisted reactions.

Operando absolute PL or electroluminescence imaging should localize voltage loss; Suns-VOC/QFLS separates absorber recombination from contact loss. Impedance, transient extraction, and four-terminal test structures should identify the origin of FF loss. Depth-resolved XPS or hard-X-ray photoemission should track Sn4+/Sn2+, Pb0, and interfacial dipoles at the top and bottom. ToF-SIMS should monitor EDA, glycine, halide, metal, and mobile-cation redistribution, with isotope labels if necessary to distinguish the modifiers from native ions. Cross-sectional microscopy and nanoscale potential mapping should identify roughening, delamination, or local barriers. PEDOT:PSS acidity and water uptake should be measured independently on bottom-interface coupons.

Protective persistence is demonstrated only if the modifiers remain spatially localized, their dipole/selectivity effects survive, Sn4+ growth and halide redistribution are suppressed relative to the relevant single-treatment controls, and the top- and bottom-specific recombination/resistance gains remain under stress. If the top treatment disappears or reacts with the electron contact while top-interface VOC loss grows, a more strongly anchored or contact-compatible passivator is needed. If bottom FF loss correlates with PEDOT:PSS water uptake, acidity, or additive displacement, the buried interface should be redesigned using an acid-neutral barrier or a different hole contact rather than simply increasing additive loading. If bulk Sn oxidation dominates all stacks under oxygen, antioxidant and encapsulation strategies are required. The qualification endpoint must combine retained QFLS-VOC, contact resistance, modifier localization, and Sn oxidation state, not PCE retention alone.
scoring_key_points: Uses untreated, top-only, bottom-only, and dual-treated devices plus partial-stack controls to localize protection and failure.
Separates dry light/bias, dark heat, oxygen, humidity, and combined MPP stresses and tracks QFLS/VOC, impedance, extraction, and spatial luminescence.
Requires depth-resolved chemical evidence for modifier localization, Sn oxidation, halide/metal migration, dipole persistence, and interface morphology.
Links top-contact, acidic bottom-contact, and bulk-redox signatures to distinct redesigns and defines a multidimensional stability endpoint.
accepted_equivalents: Cross-sectional nano-IR, X-ray photoelectron microscopy, or atom-probe methods may supplement ToF-SIMS
NiOx or a SAM may be used as an acid-free comparison but does not by itself prove transferability
Isotopically labeled glycine or diammonium species can be used to track modifier retention
common_wrong_answers: Concluding both modifiers remain effective from a single dual-treated PCE trace
Attributing all VOC loss to bulk Sn oxidation without top-interface QFLS-VOC analysis
Increasing bottom-additive concentration without testing PEDOT:PSS acidity, displacement, or transport resistance

expected_answer:
Dark humidity survival demonstrates that removing hygroscopic dopants and using a hydrophobic polymer can suppress one degradation route; it does not test thermal, photochemical, mechanical, or electrode-driven failure. The initial combination of FF loss with preserved VOC and QFLS points first to transport or contact resistance rather than bulk recombination. The program should compare dark heat, illumination at open circuit, dark current injection, and illuminated MPP at matched device temperature. Oxygen-free and controlled-oxygen versions distinguish intrinsic thermal relaxation from polymer photo-oxidation.

Polymer-only and perovskite/polymer partial stacks should be thermally cycled across the polymer glass-transition or side-chain-ordering range. GIWAXS, ellipsometry, AFM, and nanoscale mechanical mapping should test loss of face-on order, densification, dewetting, or pinhole formation. Temperature-dependent vertical conductivity and contact resistance should be tracked before and after stress. If morphology or orientation changes while the perovskite QFLS remains stable, polymer relaxation is implicated. UPS/KPFM and selective-contact dark-current measurements should test whether interfacial energetics or electron blocking deteriorate.

Metal dependence should be isolated using Au, a diffusion-barrier/Au stack, and an inert alternative electrode. ToF-SIMS and cross-sectional microscopy should track Au and iodide migration. Polymer photo-oxidation requires operando or post-stress XPS, FTIR/Raman, absorption, and electron-spin measurements, with recovery tests in inert conditions. Residual solvent should be quantified by thermal desorption or GC-MS and varied independently by drying protocols. Ion redistribution should show bias-polarity dependence, low-frequency impedance changes, and partial dark recovery without permanent polymer chemistry.

The operational-stability claim fails if the pristine polymer survives humidity yet develops irreversible resistance, loss of selectivity, electrode intrusion, or chemical oxidation under heat-light bias. A viable redesign may raise polymer thermal stability, improve anchoring and coverage, add a thin metal/ion barrier, or change drying. Acceptance requires stable FF/contact resistance and spatially uniform current under MPP, not only retained dark-storage PCE or contact angle.
scoring_key_points: Separates dark heat, light, current/bias, temperature, and oxygen stresses while using QFLS/VOC to distinguish bulk recombination from contact transport loss.
Tests polymer orientation, morphology, thermal transition, vertical conductivity, contact resistance, and selectivity before and after stress.
Uses metal/barrier controls and depth-resolved chemistry to distinguish Au/iodide migration, polymer oxidation, residual solvent, and reversible ion redistribution.
Defines why dark humidity survival is insufficient and gives mechanism-specific redesign and MPP acceptance criteria.
accepted_equivalents: A Cu or carbon electrode may serve as a metal-migration comparison if its own chemistry is controlled
Dynamic mechanical analysis or differential scanning calorimetry can establish polymer transition temperatures
Thermally stimulated desorption can substitute for GC-MS residual-solvent analysis
common_wrong_answers: Assuming dopant-free automatically means stable under heat and illumination
Attributing FF loss to bulk perovskite degradation despite preserved QFLS and VOC
Using only post-stress top-view morphology and ignoring buried contact and metal migration

expected_answer:
Shelf and outdoor retention can be dominated by encapsulation and low average stress, whereas MPP imposes simultaneous photocarrier, field, temperature, and current gradients. The failure tree should therefore compare untreated and heterostructured absorbers in a layer-ablation ladder: bare film, film with only the hole-selective SAM, film with only the electron-contact stack, complete device with an inert electrode, and complete Ag device. Additional controls should replace the SAM, PCBM/BCP, or Ag one at a time while preserving the surface treatment.

Operando hyperspectral PL or electroluminescence should map the emergence of I-rich domains and distinguish bulk phase segregation from contact-localized voltage loss. GIWAXS or grazing-incidence X-ray scattering during light/bias should track the low-dimensional peaks and 3D phase; disappearance, broadening, or n-value evolution of the surface phase indicates reconstruction. Depth-resolved ToF-SIMS/XPS should monitor EDA/MA, I/Br, Ag, and mobile cations. QFLS and Suns-VOC separate absorber recombination from contact loss, while impedance and transient extraction locate growing resistance. KPFM or surface-potential mapping can test whether the intended n-type surface dipole persists.

Mechanism-specific outcomes are distinct. A red-shifted bulk PL domain with stable 2D peaks and no contact chemistry indicates mixed-halide segregation. Loss or redistribution of EDA/MA and low-q peaks, accompanied by slower electron extraction, indicates 2D-layer reconstruction or dissolution. Stable absorber QFLS but increasing QFLS-VOC gap implicates a selective contact. SAM loss should appear at the buried interface and often reduce built-in potential or hole selectivity. Ag/iodide reaction should be suppressed by an inert electrode or barrier and show Ag/halide interdiffusion.

Acceptance requires the surface phase, bulk spectrum, QFLS-VOC gap, extraction time, and metal/halide profiles to remain stable under the same MPP stress. A treatment that only improves shelf storage or delays one failure while another layer controls T80 is not an operationally complete heterostructure solution.
scoring_key_points: Uses a layer-ablation and layer-substitution ladder to isolate absorber, 2D surface, buried SAM, electron contact, and Ag contributions.
Combines operando spectral imaging, GIWAXS, depth chemistry, QFLS/Suns-VOC, impedance, and extraction measurements.
Defines distinct signatures for bulk segregation, 2D reconstruction, SAM failure, electron-contact loss, and Ag/halide reaction.
Requires simultaneous stability of phase, surface chemistry, QFLS-VOC, extraction, and metal/halide profiles under matched MPP stress.
accepted_equivalents: A transparent inert top electrode or carbon electrode can substitute for the Ag-ablation control
Nano-XRD or cathodoluminescence may supplement operando PL for spatial phase mapping
Bias-dependent recovery tests may identify reversible halide segregation
common_wrong_answers: Using shelf stability as proof that the surface heterostructure controls MPP lifetime
Attributing all red-shifted emission to bulk segregation without checking contact-localized luminescence or 2D reconstruction
Replacing several layers simultaneously, which prevents causal assignment

expected_answer: Normal-incidence AVT is a scalar average and does not constrain the spectral shape of transmission at other angles. Semi-transparent cells often contain ultrathin metals, dielectric-metal-dielectric electrodes, transport layers, and cavity-like optical thicknesses. Their interference conditions depend on optical path length and polarization. At oblique incidence, resonances shift, s- and p-polarized transmission diverge, and a spectrum that is neutral at 0° can develop narrow color peaks or notches. A similar angular effect can arise from photonic crystals or thickness-tuned antireflection layers even if the absorber itself has no compositional change. The evaluation should therefore measure angle-resolved spectral transmittance and reflectance for both polarizations over the relevant solar and viewing cone, not only 400-700 nm at normal incidence. From each spectrum, calculate photopic AVT, CIE x-y or u′v′ coordinates, correlated color temperature, color-rendering metrics, and a color-shift metric such as ΔE relative to normal incidence. The same optical data should be integrated with the AM1.5 spectrum to predict angle-dependent photocurrent and near-infrared solar-heat transmission or rejection. Transfer-matrix or rigorous electromagnetic modeling should be fitted to measured layer thicknesses and optical constants so that the layer responsible for the angular resonance can be identified. Design should reduce high-Q cavity behavior: use less dispersive transparent conductors, broaden resonances with carefully chosen dielectric thicknesses or graded-index layers, control ultrathin-metal continuity, and shift absorber absorption toward the near-infrared rather than creating visible transmission through narrow interference windows. The optimization target is a Pareto surface across PCE, angle-averaged AVT, ΔE, CRI, and solar heat gain. A façade-ready device must meet limits over a defined incidence range, for example 0-60°, because a single normal-incidence PCE@AVT point cannot certify visual neutrality in service.
scoring_key_points: Explains angular color change through multilayer interference, optical-path shift, and polarization dependence.
Requires angle- and polarization-resolved spectra with AVT, CIE/ΔE, CCT/CRI, and NIR/solar-heat metrics.
Uses optical modeling tied to measured thicknesses and optical constants to identify the responsible layer.
Proposes low-dispersion/broadened optical designs and a multi-objective acceptance range rather than a single normal-incidence point.
accepted_equivalents: Transfer-matrix, scattering-matrix, or full-wave optical modeling are acceptable.
Color difference may use CIE ΔE76, ΔE2000, or an equivalent perceptual metric.
Solar heat gain coefficient or NIR rejection may replace a simple NIR transmittance metric.
common_wrong_answers: Normal-incidence AVT guarantees angle-independent color.
The color change must be caused by absorber degradation or halide segregation.
Maximizing visible transmittance at one wavelength is sufficient for a neutral window.

expected_answer: Improved orientation and lower elastic strain reduce some defect and recombination pathways, but they do not guarantee immobile halides. Vertically connected grains can even provide continuous migration pathways if vacancy concentration, local electric field, or interfacial chemical potential remains high. The coordinator may passivate SnO2 oxygen vacancies and template growth while leaving halide-vacancy transport in the mixed-halide bulk only partly changed. Under forward bias and illumination, ionic drift and photo-carrier-induced free-energy changes can therefore create I-rich emissive regions without altering the average crystal orientation. Bulk photo-segregation should produce a reversible low-energy PL shoulder whose growth depends on illumination intensity, temperature, and halide composition, accompanied by spatially resolved composition contrast or a split/shifted absorption response. It may be weak or invisible in conventional XRD because the segregated domains are small or low volume fraction. Time-resolved PL mapping, nano-XRF/SIMS after bias, and recovery in the dark are decisive. Field-driven interfacial accumulation predicts polarity dependence and localization near one contact. Bias-reversal experiments, cross-sectional Kelvin-probe or electroabsorption mapping, depth-resolved SIMS, and capacitance/ionic transient measurements should show charge and halide accumulation at the buried interface. If the shoulder forms only under a specific bias direction and persists after light is removed until ions relax, interfacial drift dominates. Residual PbI2 photodecomposition instead should generate Pb0/I2 signatures, irreversible PL loss or new nonradiative regions, and chemical changes detectable by XPS, Raman, or mass spectrometry. It need not produce a clean reversible red shoulder. The diagnosis must therefore combine reversibility, spatial/depth localization, bias polarity, composition mapping, and Pb0/I2 chemistry. The coordinator remains beneficial if it lowers strain and defects, but mixed-halide stability requires separate control of vacancies, fields, and residual PbI2 chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Explains that improved orientation/strain does not eliminate halide vacancies, fields, or connected ion-migration pathways.
Identifies reversible, light/intensity/composition-dependent low-energy emission and nanoscale composition contrast as bulk segregation signatures.
Uses bias polarity and depth-localized potential/composition measurements to identify interfacial ion accumulation.
Uses irreversible Pb0/I2 chemical signatures to distinguish residual-PbI2 decomposition.
accepted_equivalents: Ion migration may be described through vacancy-mediated drift-diffusion or chemical-potential gradients.
Nano-XRF, SIMS, cathodoluminescence, or hyperspectral PL are acceptable segregation maps.
Pb0 may be detected by XPS; iodine species by Raman, optical absorption, or mass spectrometry.
common_wrong_answers: Vertical grain orientation guarantees complete suppression of ion migration.
Unchanged average XRD orientation rules out phase segregation.
A red PL shoulder always proves irreversible chemical decomposition.

expected_answer:
The early Voc loss should first be localized. If the recovered absorber retains its original quasi-Fermi-level splitting while the intact device has lower Voc and electroluminescence efficiency, the dominant new loss lies at a contact or buried interface rather than in the absorber bulk. Operando front- and rear-side PL, contact-selective half-stack PLQY, Suns-Voc, and electroluminescence should show whether the voltage loss appears only after a particular contact is present. Depth-resolved XPS or hard-X-ray photoemission, surface-potential mapping, and contact replacement can then test for new interface defects, chemical reactions, or an energy-alignment shift. A rapid, non-recovering increase in the QFLS-Voc mismatch would support interface recombination.

The later hysteresis and fill-factor loss require an ionic branch. Repeat aging under open circuit, short circuit, maximum power, and reversed bias while keeping temperature and illumination fixed. A polarity-dependent onset, slow relaxation after bias removal, reversible surface-potential gradients, low-frequency capacitance changes, and redistribution of mobile ionic species by ToF-SIMS or operando Kelvin-probe measurements support ion accumulation and field screening. Recovery in the dark should restore field distribution and hysteresis without repairing a chemically damaged contact.

Irreversible electrode or transport-layer degradation is indicated by rising series resistance, permanent leakage or contact resistance, metal/halide interdiffusion, cracks, or chemical-state changes that do not recover after electrical relaxation. Four-point resistance, impedance over a wide frequency range, cross-sectional microscopy, and isotope- or element-resolved depth profiling should be tied to spatially resolved photocurrent and thermal maps.

Causality is established by reproducing each stage with selective stress: light without bias for photochemical interface damage, bias in the dark for ionic redistribution, and heat in inert conditions for contact instability. A valid sequence is early interface-recombination growth, followed by reversible ionic screening, with any residual non-recovering FF or leakage loss assigned to contact or electrode damage.
scoring_key_points: Uses unchanged recovered-absorber QFLS plus increased device QFLS-Voc loss to localize the early Voc decay to an interface.
Identifies ionic screening through bias-polarity dependence, slow relaxation, field/capacitance changes, spatial ion redistribution, and dark recovery.
Assigns irreversible residual losses to contact/electrode damage using resistance, chemistry, diffusion, and structural evidence.
Decouples light, bias, and heat stresses to establish temporal causality and the order of failure mechanisms.
accepted_equivalents: Operando surface photovoltage or electroabsorption may replace Kelvin-probe mapping for field redistribution.
Hard-X-ray photoemission, cross-sectional photoelectron spectroscopy, or interface-sensitive spectroscopy may be used for buried-interface chemistry.
A reversible bias-pulse or temperature-jump protocol is acceptable for separating ionic relaxation from permanent chemical damage.
common_wrong_answers: Attributes all degradation to bulk phase decomposition despite unchanged absorber QFLS and XRD.
Calls every slow electrical transient ion migration without testing bias polarity, spatial redistribution, or recovery.
Uses a single post-aging J-V curve and cannot distinguish reversible field screening from permanent contact resistance.

expected_answer:
The first branch is degradation of the engineered surface state. Angle-resolved XPS, ToF-SIMS, and depth-resolved photoemission should determine whether Cl and the ammonium-derived species desorb, diffuse into adjacent layers, or react. If the treatment is lost, the near-surface core-level gradient and work-function shift should collapse while the bulk electronic structure remains unchanged. Bare-film PLQY may still be relatively high if chemical passivation partly survives, but QFLS should fall sharply after PCBM deposition and the original conduction-band offset should reappear. Reapplying the surface treatment to a delaminated or freshly contacted absorber, or replacing PCBM on the aged surface, should restore Voc if this branch dominates.

A second branch is degradation within PCBM/BCP or at the Ag electrode. Rising series/contact resistance, reduced extraction in transient photocurrent, fullerene chemical changes, BCP crystallization or cracking, and Ag/halide interdiffusion would produce a later fill-factor loss. Replacing only the top transport/electrode stack while preserving the aged perovskite surface is a decisive intervention. If performance recovers without restoring the original surface Cl signal, the main limitation was above the perovskite.

Bulk phase instability must be probed below the detection limit of conventional XRD. Spatial PL, grazing-incidence or nano-XRD, absorption, Raman, and cross-sectional microscopy should look for local delta-phase nuclei, voids, or moisture-induced decomposition near edges and grain boundaries. Loss that persists after contact replacement and is accompanied by lower absorber QFLS or new local optical signatures supports this branch.

Humidity-only, heat-only, and combined-stress tests, with encapsulated and unencapsulated controls, establish synergy and ingress pathways. A plausible sequence is partial surface-treatment loss causing early Voc decline, followed by transport-layer/electrode resistance and FF loss; bulk phase conversion is assigned only if absorber-specific structural and photophysical evidence appears.
scoring_key_points: Tests whether surface-treatment loss collapses the near-surface electronic gradient and recreates contact-induced QFLS or alignment loss.
Uses selective top-contact replacement and transport/chemical diagnostics to identify PCBM, BCP, or Ag degradation as a later FF mechanism.
Probes local bulk phase or decomposition below conventional XRD sensitivity with spatial structural and photophysical measurements.
Decouples humidity and heat, includes ingress controls, and uses recovery interventions to establish the failure sequence.
accepted_equivalents: A peel-and-recontact experiment or fabrication of a fresh electron contact on the aged absorber is equivalent to the stated replacement test.
Nano-XRD, GIWAXS mapping, cathodoluminescence, or hyperspectral PL may identify local phase instability.
Surface photovoltage or KPFM may replace depth-resolved photoemission for tracking loss of the engineered band bending.
common_wrong_answers: Concludes that unchanged bulk XRD proves the absorber is stable and ignores local or interfacial failure.
Attributes both Voc and fill-factor losses to one generic moisture mechanism without selective replacement tests.
Treats the disappearance of Cl signal as proof of bulk CsPbI3 phase transformation.

expected_answer:
The bottom-contact branch is PEDOT:PSS. Its acidity and water uptake can corrode ITO, alter work function, and introduce moisture at the buried perovskite interface. Compare otherwise identical cells using neutralized PEDOT:PSS, a dopant-free inorganic or self-assembled hole contact, and a moisture-barrier interlayer. Substrate-side PL/QFLS, adhesion, ITO chemistry, and cross-sectional water or ion profiles should show whether degradation initiates from the bottom. If replacing PEDOT:PSS removes the early Voc decay under humidity, this branch is causal.

The absorber branch involves MA or iodine volatility and moisture-assisted decomposition. Track mass loss or evolved species, local PbI2 formation, absorption/PL changes, and grain-boundary chemistry with operando spectroscopy and spatial diffraction. A fresh-contact reconstruction on the aged absorber distinguishes permanent absorber loss from contact failure. Dark humidity, dry illumination, and combined stress determine whether water and photocarriers act synergistically.

The top-contact branch is split between PCBM and Au. PCBM oxidation, aggregation, or delamination should reduce electron mobility, increase contact-induced QFLS loss, and be partly recoverable by removing and redepositing the fullerene layer. Hydrophobicity may delay moisture ingress but does not prove chemical stability. Au/halide interdiffusion or electrode corrosion should produce metal or iodide depth profiles, permanent series resistance or leakage, and little recovery after only PCBM replacement. A diffusion-blocking buffer and an alternative inert electrode are decisive controls.

Ingress should be localized with edge-sealed, face-sealed, and fully encapsulated samples or isotopically labelled water. Front- versus rear-side luminescence and spatial failure maps indicate the initiating side. The early storage benefit can be assigned to removal of corrosive dopants and hydrophobic top coverage only if those controls delay ingress; long-term limitation is assigned to the layer whose selective substitution or replacement prevents or reverses the corresponding loss.
scoring_key_points: Tests PEDOT:PSS acidity/hygroscopicity with neutralized or alternative hole contacts and substrate-side chemical/QFLS diagnostics.
Separates irreversible MAPbI3 volatile/decomposition loss from contact failure using evolved-species, spatial phase, and fresh-contact reconstruction tests.
Distinguishes PCBM oxidation/delamination from Au-halide diffusion through selective layer replacement and diffusion-barrier controls.
Localizes moisture ingress by side/edge sealing and decouples humidity, light, and combined stress to assign early protection and long-term limits.
accepted_equivalents: NiOx, CuSCN, or a self-assembled monolayer may serve as the PEDOT:PSS replacement control.
C60 or another fullerene derivative may serve as a PCBM replacement if electron energetics are matched.
Deuterated water, humidity-sensitive tracers, or neutron imaging may localize ingress.
common_wrong_answers: Assumes the hydrophobic PCBM layer guarantees long-term humidity stability.
Attributes all loss to MAPbI3 decomposition without selectively replacing contacts.
Compares encapsulated and unencapsulated cells only, so the initiating interface and material liability remain unknown.

expected_answer:
The key is to track the same domains before, during, and after aging. Low-dose operando EBIC or scanning photocurrent, hyperspectral PL/lifetime imaging, surface-potential mapping, and registered nano-XRD or electron-diffraction maps should be acquired at fixed coordinates. Loss of percolation connectivity can occur through small changes at necks between 3D-like sub-grains without changing average phase fraction or PLQY. It should produce fragmentation of current pathways, increased local series resistance, and preserved bright emission in electrically isolated domains.

Strain relaxation or n-phase reorganization should shift local diffraction spacings, orientation, Raman stress signatures, or phase-selective transient-absorption kinetics while whole-film XRD remains dominated by the unchanged majority. Thermal-only aging and mechanically constrained samples test this branch. A reversible thermal or pressure treatment that restores local topology would strengthen the assignment.

Ion redistribution should be bias-polarity and illumination dependent. Same-location ToF-SIMS after marked aging stages, nano-XRF, Kelvin-probe maps, and spectral shifts should reveal halide or cation accumulation near domain boundaries or contacts. Dark rest or reverse bias may partially restore current if redistribution rather than permanent structural damage dominates. Local non-radiative hot spots instead show reduced lifetime and PLQY co-localized with lost current, increased sub-gap emission or ideality factor, and little recovery without repassivation.

Contact delamination or interfacial voiding should follow mechanical interfaces, alter local contact resistance, and be visible by cross-sectional microscopy or acoustic methods; replacing or recontacting the top layer should restore collection without restoring the absorber map. Average XRD and PLQY are insensitive because they integrate over electrically disconnected but structurally intact material. The accepted failure model must link spatial change to the order of electrical loss and demonstrate mechanism-specific recovery or selective contact repair.
scoring_key_points: Uses registered same-location current, luminescence, potential, and nanoscale structural maps rather than area averages.
Distinguishes percolation loss from strain/n-phase reorganization through connectivity metrics and local diffraction or stress signatures.
Identifies ion redistribution and local non-radiative hot spots by different bias dependence, composition, lifetime, and reversibility patterns.
Tests contact delamination with interface imaging and selective recontacting and explains why intact but electrically isolated domains preserve average PLQY/XRD.
accepted_equivalents: Conductive AFM, light-beam-induced current, or photoconductive AFM may replace EBIC for registered local collection.
Bragg ptychography, nano-GIWAXS, or 4D-STEM may provide local strain and phase mapping.
Acoustic microscopy or X-ray tomography may identify interface voids and delamination.
common_wrong_answers: Uses unchanged average PLQY to conclude that recombination and charge collection are unchanged.
Attributes disappearing current domains to phase loss without same-location structural evidence.
Calls every reversible current change ion migration and ignores connectivity or contact mechanics.

expected_answer:
Total residual PbI2 is not an adequate control variable because its location, continuity, chemical state, and local excess determine whether it acts as a passivating interlayer or a degradation nucleus. A thin, laterally uniform buried residue can reduce undercoordinated-Pb defects and improve contact selectivity. In contrast, bulk islands, surface-rich PbI2, or compositionally isolated regions can react with water and organic salts, promote local phase decomposition, create insulating barriers, or evolve into shunting defects under heat and bias.

The process window should therefore be defined by spatial descriptors rather than one integrated diffraction peak. Depth-resolved GIWAXS/GIXRD, cross-sectional nano-XRF or TOF-SIMS, and selective chemical mapping should quantify the residual fraction at the buried interface, in the absorber bulk, and at the top surface. PL or electroluminescence imaging, lock-in thermography, local ideality-factor mapping, and dark-current maps should verify that high-PbI2 regions do not coincide with recombination or leakage. Conversion-front kinetics should be tracked across the web to ensure that local drying or coating variations do not create bulk residues.

Freshness is a controlled factor: aged and fresh PbI2 and organic-salt solutions should be processed in a factorial design, with viscosity, water content, precursor speciation, and conversion time recorded. Operational qualification must include maximum-power-point light soaking with heat and controlled humidity, thermal cycling, and post-stress depth mapping, not shelf storage alone.

A production lot should pass only if buried PbI2 remains within a validated narrow range, bulk/surface islands stay below a spatial defect threshold, module electroluminescence and leakage maps are uniform, and accelerated stress does not increase PbI2-rich failure sites or produce statistically significant Voc/FF loss. Matching bulk XRD intensity alone is a no-go criterion.
scoring_key_points: Explains why residual PbI2 location and morphology, not total amount alone, determine benefit or harm.
Specifies depth-resolved and spatially resolved structural, chemical, and electrical acceptance metrics.
Includes fresh-versus-aged precursor controls and relevant precursor-state measurements.
Defines an operational-stress-based production go/no-go rule rather than relying on shelf storage or bulk XRD.
accepted_equivalents: controlled buried PbI2 interlayer
interface-localized excess lead iodide
spatial defect threshold based on EL or leakage mapping
common_wrong_answers: Treating all residual PbI2 as universally beneficial or universally harmful.
Using only average XRD intensity or average device efficiency.
Calling ambient storage retention sufficient proof of module reliability.

expected_answer:
The initial benefit and later failure are consistent with a finite strain budget. Moderate compressive strain can lower the free energy of the black phase and alter its band structure favorably. Thermal cycling, however, changes lattice parameters and can cross perovskite phase-transition regimes. If the perovskite, PbS, substrate, and contacts have different thermal-expansion coefficients, each cycle changes the interfacial stress. Repeated shear and normal stress can nucleate misfit dislocations, delamination, or cracks. Once the coherent strain relaxes irreversibly, the phase-stabilization benefit weakens; newly formed defects and cracks also provide ion-migration and recombination pathways, producing hysteresis and performance loss.

The redesign should reduce the amplitude and concentration of cyclic stress rather than maximize initial coherence. A compositionally graded or elastically compliant buffer can distribute mismatch over a larger thickness. Smaller coherent domains or nanocrystal-in-matrix geometries can retain local compressive strain while allowing global relaxation. A van der Waals template is attractive when orientational control is needed without strong in-plane clamping, although it may offer less deterministic band alignment and weaker mechanical adhesion.

Selection requires temperature-dependent reciprocal-space mapping and Raman spectroscopy to measure reversible and irreversible strain; in-situ PL/absorption to track phase stability; cross-sectional TEM after cycling to quantify dislocations; and acoustic, curvature, or nanoindentation measurements to determine modulus and interfacial fracture energy. Operando current-voltage hysteresis and ion-migration diagnostics should be correlated with crack formation.

Choose the lattice-matched route only if coherence survives cycling without defect accumulation. Choose a compliant buffer if controlled strain can be retained with low interfacial stress. Choose a van der Waals template when thermal mismatch dominates and phase stability can be maintained by local confinement or chemistry rather than rigid coherent strain.
scoring_key_points: Links thermal-expansion mismatch and phase transitions to strain relaxation, dislocations, cracks, ion migration, and hysteresis.
Proposes compliant, graded, or locally coherent designs rather than simply increasing lattice match.
Specifies temperature-dependent structural, phase, mechanical, and operando electrical measurements.
Provides conditional decision rules for lattice-matched, compliant-buffer, and van der Waals strategies.
accepted_equivalents: finite strain budget
local coherent strain with global compliance
thermomechanical fatigue
quasi-epitaxial van der Waals release
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a room-temperature lattice match guarantees thermal-cycle stability.
Treating phase stabilization and mechanical reliability as independent.
Recommending van der Waals growth as universally superior without checking adhesion and band alignment.

expected_answer:
The screen confuses a favorable fundamental gap with a favorable photovoltaic transition. In many double perovskites the lowest-energy transition is indirect, parity forbidden, or both. The material can therefore possess a 1.40 eV electronic gap yet have a much larger optical onset and a low absorption coefficient near the band edge. A long PL lifetime is not sufficient evidence of good collection: it may reflect a weak radiative transition, carrier localization, or low mobility rather than low recombination in a transport-relevant state.

Down-selection should begin with quasiparticle band structure including spin-orbit coupling, transition-matrix elements, and phonon-assisted absorption, not gap energy alone. Experimental absorption coefficient, photothermal deflection spectroscopy, temperature-dependent PL, and magneto- or electroabsorption should test forbidden or indirect transitions and exciton binding. Time-resolved microwave conductivity, Hall or field-effect measurements, diffusion-length mapping, and orientation-dependent transport should test whether the octahedral network supports mobile carriers.

The ideal-crystal defect result must be replaced by chemical-potential-dependent defect formation energies, charge-transition levels, and defect complexes under realistic growth conditions. Multivalent cations require explicit oxidation-state and redox-stability analysis under oxygen, moisture, light, and contact deposition. Thin-film viability must be evaluated through phase purity, grain connectivity, surface composition, and reproducible low-temperature synthesis.

Finally, interface-specific band alignment, contact reactions, and selective extraction should be measured in complete devices with matched transport layers. A material should advance only if it combines a strong allowed near-gap transition, manageable exciton binding, adequate mobility and diffusion length, stable oxidation state, controllable film morphology, and compatible interfaces. Low formation energy and an ideal 1.40 eV gap are screening inputs, not a photovoltaic verdict.
scoring_key_points: Explains the distinction between fundamental and optically allowed band gaps, including indirect/parity-forbidden transitions.
Interprets long lifetime cautiously and requires transport/exciton measurements.
Expands defect screening to realistic chemical potentials, redox stability, and thin-film morphology.
Adds interface/device gates and states a multi-objective advancement rule.
accepted_equivalents: optical gap versus fundamental gap
parity-forbidden band-edge transition
phonon-assisted absorption
transport-limited long lifetime
common_wrong_answers: Assuming any 1.4 eV calculated gap is optimal for solar cells.
Equating long PL lifetime with long carrier diffusion length.
Ignoring oxidation state, phase purity, and contact compatibility because ideal-crystal defects are shallow.

expected_answer:
The integrated operating point is determined by the intersection of the photovoltaic current-voltage curve with the combined electrochemical polarization of the photocathode, photoanode, resistive connections, and mass-transport losses. A better catalyst measured at one externally imposed potential may not change that intersection if another element is limiting. The large-area PV may have low fill factor and substantial series resistance; the BiVO4 photoanode may require most of the available photovoltage; or CO2 transport and local pH may cap the cathodic rate. The new catalyst may also shift selectivity without lowering the overpotential at the actual tandem current.

The diagnostic sequence should first measure stabilized J-V curves of the illuminated PV alone and three-electrode polarization curves of each electrode under the same illumination, electrolyte, area, temperature, and gas flow used in the tandem. These curves should be combined with measured wiring, ITO, graphite-epoxy, and contact resistances to predict the zero-bias intersection. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and current-interrupt measurements can localize ohmic versus charge-transfer loss.

Next, vary CO2 flow, pressure, buffer capacity, stirring, and electrode orientation while monitoring local pH and dissolved CO2. If the tandem current responds to mass-transfer variables but not catalyst exchange, the cathode is transport limited. Product analysis must report CO and H2 faradaic efficiencies at the actual operating point; a higher CO partial current in a potentiostatic test does not guarantee a higher syngas rate in the leaf.

Finally, decouple components by externally biasing the tandem or substituting a high-performance reference photoanode. The catalyst is system-limiting only if it reduces cathodic overpotential in the relevant current range and shifts the integrated operating intersection without causing selectivity or stability penalties.
scoring_key_points: Explains the integrated operating point as the intersection of PV output and total electrochemical polarization.
Identifies alternative limits: PV series resistance/FF, photoanode overpotential, contacts, and CO2 mass transport/local pH.
Uses matched component curves, EIS/current interruption, and controlled decoupling experiments.
Requires product faradaic efficiency at the actual operating point, not only catalyst activity at a fixed potential.
accepted_equivalents: load-line intersection
photovoltage budget
system-level current matching
mass-transfer-limited CO2 reduction
common_wrong_answers: Assuming higher catalyst current at one potential must raise zero-bias tandem current.
Comparing catalyst data measured under different area, electrolyte, or gas-flow conditions.
Using total photocurrent without measuring product faradaic efficiencies.

expected_answer:
Fracture energy measures resistance to propagation of a particular crack under a specific test geometry and environment. It does not measure moisture stability, ion migration, electrode corrosion, interfacial adhesion, fatigue, or barrier integrity. A bimodal grain structure can deflect cracks and increase cohesive toughness, yet its fine-grain regions may contain more boundaries that accelerate water ingress or ionic transport. The rapid plasma process may also leave residual stress or weak interfaces that are not captured by a cohesive-fracture specimen. On a flexible module, failure may initiate in the transparent electrode, transport layers, encapsulant, or patterned interconnect rather than in the perovskite bulk.

Qualification should therefore separate cohesive, interfacial, and system failure. Measure perovskite cohesive fracture energy, peel or blister adhesion at each interface, residual stress, and cyclic crack growth before and after controlled humidity and temperature exposure. Perform repeated bending at several radii under dry dark, illuminated dry, damp heat, and combined MPP-bias conditions. In-situ electroluminescence, resistance mapping, acoustic emission, and optical microscopy should identify the first failing layer.

Microstructure causality requires matched films with unimodal large grains, unimodal small grains, and the RSPP bimodal distribution at similar composition and thickness. Depth-resolved moisture uptake, TOF-SIMS ion profiles, and grain-boundary-sensitive spectroscopy should test whether fine-grain regions become environmental pathways. Barrier and encapsulation controls determine whether failure is absorber-intrinsic or packaging-limited.

The bimodal structure is beneficial only if it reduces crack growth and preserves stabilized module power under combined stress without increasing moisture uptake, ion redistribution, or interfacial delamination. High initial fracture energy accompanied by faster damp-heat electrical decay is not a robustness claim.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes fracture energy from operational, interfacial, environmental, and fatigue durability.
Identifies how bimodal grains can toughen mechanically yet increase boundary-mediated moisture or ion transport.
Proposes combined bending, humidity, heat, light, and bias tests with layer-resolved failure localization.
Uses matched microstructure and encapsulation controls and defines a power-retention-based decision rule.
accepted_equivalents: cohesive toughness versus interfacial adhesion
environment-assisted fatigue
grain-boundary moisture pathway
combined-stress module qualification
common_wrong_answers: Equating a single fracture-energy number with long-term module stability.
Testing bending only in dry dark conditions.
Attributing every flexible-module failure to the perovskite bulk without checking electrodes, interfaces, and encapsulation.

expected_answer:
Lower nonradiative recombination does not guarantee a lower device temperature because total heat generation and heat removal are separate balances. The treatment may replace a grain-boundary region with a low-thermal-conductivity organic phase or create thermal boundary resistance, reducing lateral and vertical heat dissipation. It may also absorb light parasitically, change optical interference, or increase current and Joule heating because the device now delivers more power. If the treatment modifies contact resistance, local Peltier or resistive heating can dominate. Infrared emissivity changes can also produce an apparent temperature difference without a real thermal change.

Diagnosis begins with calibrated thermography using emissivity-matched coatings or independent Raman/photoluminescence thermometry. Layer-resolved optical modeling and absorptance measurements should quantify whether the passivator or modified stack absorbs additional photons. Thermal conductivity and interface thermal resistance should be measured by time-domain thermoreflectance or scanning thermal microscopy on matched films. Simultaneous current, voltage, and local temperature maps under open circuit, short circuit, and MPP can separate recombination-related heat from Joule and contact heating. Dark electrical bias at the same current tests resistive heating without optical input.

Contact and sheet resistance should be mapped by four-point or transmission-line methods, while lock-in thermography identifies localized hot spots. A passivator-only film on an inert substrate controls emissivity and optical absorption.

The long-term interpretation changes because a treatment can improve initial electronic quality yet accelerate ion migration, interfacial chemistry, phase segregation, or thermomechanical stress through a hotter operating state. Operational stability should therefore be compared at both equal irradiance and equal device temperature. If the passivated device degrades faster only when allowed to self-heat, thermal management—not electronic passivation failure—is the missing design variable.
scoring_key_points: Separates heat generation from heat dissipation and identifies conductivity, optical, Joule/contact, and emissivity alternatives.
Uses calibrated independent thermometry, layer-resolved absorption, and thermal-property measurements.
Employs operating-point and dark-bias controls to partition recombination and resistive heating.
Links elevated temperature to ion, chemical, and stress degradation and requires temperature-controlled stability comparisons.
accepted_equivalents: thermal boundary resistance
emissivity artifact
equal-current dark-bias control
equal-temperature operational aging
common_wrong_answers: Assuming higher PLQY must make the full device cooler.
Using uncalibrated infrared temperature as definitive.
Ignoring increased current, contact resistance, and passivator absorption.

expected_answer:
A Tauc fit from one thickness is not sufficient. Variable-angle ellipsometry should be performed on several thicknesses with an optical model that includes roughness, anisotropy, and any oxide overlayer. Photothermal deflection spectroscopy or Fourier-transform photocurrent spectroscopy should extend the dynamic range below the apparent edge and quantify the Urbach tail. Polarization-resolved absorption on differently oriented films can test whether texture causes an apparent direct-transition signature.

Temperature-dependent absorption and PL should then separate excitonic, band-to-band, and defect-related emission. A free-exciton peak should show a reproducible binding-energy relation to the continuum and characteristic temperature broadening, whereas defect emission usually has stronger excitation-density dependence, longer or distributed decay, and thermally activated quenching. Excitation-wavelength-dependent and front/back PL can determine whether the 1.9 eV signal originates from the bulk, an oxygen-rich surface, or a secondary oxide. Spatially correlated Raman/XRD, PL, and oxygen-sensitive XPS or nano-SIMS should test whether bright regions coincide with oxide or oxygen-substituted domains.

The optical assignment must be connected to carrier transport. Time-resolved microwave conductivity or optical-pump THz spectroscopy should measure the mobile-carrier yield and mobility immediately after excitation; TRPL and transient absorption should quantify trapping and recombination. Hall/Seebeck measurements, surface photovoltage, and thickness-dependent photoconductivity can test whether carriers cross the film rather than recombine in isolated bright regions.

A useful absorber should show a high absorption coefficient at the fundamental edge, limited sub-gap absorption, mobile free carriers, and a diffusion or collection length compatible with device thickness. A small Stokes shift is supportive only if the PL follows the same phase and volume as the absorption edge and if oxygen variation does not create the emission. Bright defect-selective PL with poor photoconductivity would invalidate the inference of good photovoltaic quality.
scoring_key_points: Uses multi-thickness, anisotropy-aware ellipsometry plus a high-dynamic-range sub-gap absorption method.
Uses temperature-, fluence-, wavelength-, and depth-dependent PL/absorption to separate excitonic, band-edge, and defect/oxide emission.
Spatially correlates oxygen/phase mapping with optical response.
Requires mobile-carrier, transport, and collection evidence before treating a small Stokes shift as photovoltaic quality.
accepted_equivalents: PDS may be replaced by highly sensitive EQE, FTPS, or another validated sub-gap absorption technique.
TRMC, THz conductivity, Hall, time-of-flight, or a comparable free-carrier transport combination is acceptable.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding that a 100 meV Stokes shift proves defect tolerance without testing oxygen-rich regions or carrier mobility.
Using a single linear Tauc plot as definitive evidence of a direct fundamental gap.

expected_answer:
The starting point should be a global model constrained by orthogonal observables. Pump-THz-probe measurements should be repeated with excitation wavelengths that produce shallow and nearly uniform generation profiles, on several film thicknesses, and from both substrate and film sides. The depth-resolved rate equation should use the measured absorption coefficient rather than an assumed exponential profile. If the low coefficient is mainly a depth-averaging artefact, the extracted value will change systematically with excitation depth and thickness and converge when generation becomes uniform.

Rapid trapping is tested by combining THz conductivity with broadband transient absorption and calibrated time-resolved PL. A loss of THz signal without an equivalent loss of total excited-state population, together with delayed emission or thermally released carriers, indicates trapping into low-mobility states. Temperature-dependent measurements can reveal trap activation, while sub-bandgap photoionization or thermally stimulated current can quantify the reservoir.

Spatial electron-hole separation should be sensitive to electric field, asymmetric contacts, and excitation side. Contact-free films and electron- or hole-selective half-stacks should be compared under applied field. Long-lived charge-induced absorption, a persistent surface photovoltage, or field-dependent recovery with suppressed PL would support separated carriers rather than intrinsically slow recombination. Microscopic potential mapping after pulsed excitation can add spatial evidence.

An intrinsic non-Langevin mechanism is supported if the same low electron-hole annihilation coefficient is obtained after correcting the generation profile, if mobile-carrier and total-population measurements decay consistently without a hidden reservoir, and if the coefficient is weakly dependent on field and contact asymmetry. Its temperature dependence should then be compared with dielectric screening, polaronic coupling, and phonon-mode changes. The Langevin benchmark must use the independently measured sum mobility and dielectric constant under the same temperature and carrier-density conditions.
scoring_key_points: Varies excitation depth, film thickness, and illumination direction and explicitly models the nonuniform carrier profile.
Combines THz conductivity with total-population and luminescence probes to reveal THz-invisible trapping.
Uses field and selective-contact controls to identify spatial electron-hole separation.
Defines intrinsic non-Langevin behavior only after profile, trapping, and separation artefacts are excluded with matched Langevin parameters.
accepted_equivalents: Transient absorption may be replaced by another calibrated total-excited-population probe.
Surface photovoltage, electroabsorption, or time-resolved microwave conductivity may support the charge-separation analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Declaring non-Langevin recombination solely because the fitted coefficient is smaller than a textbook Langevin value.
Using only one pump wavelength and one film thickness while assuming every photoexcited carrier remains THz-mobile.

expected_answer:
The decision should maximize expected decision value, not the local derivative of LCOE with respect to an input. A parameter can be highly sensitive but already well known, or weakly sensitive yet so uncertain that resolving it changes the architecture choice. The current technoeconomic model should therefore contain probability distributions for saleable yield, material utilization, module efficiency, contact cost, degradation, service life, replacement, and learning rate, including correlations.

For each proposed experiment, estimate how its result would update those distributions and what decisions could follow. The yield campaign is valuable when process scrap and utilization dominate manufacturing-cost uncertainty and when the platform can be abandoned or redesigned if yield falls below a defined break-even surface. The outdoor campaign is preferred when lifetime/degradation uncertainty dominates delivered energy and when no short accelerated test can credibly constrain field failure. Because two years may still be shorter than commercial life, the campaign must target failure modes and improve a validated lifetime model rather than merely report retention.

The contact-redesign experiment is preferred when an expensive evaporated layer is a large and relatively certain cost driver, the replacement has a plausible low-capital process, and the main uncertainty is whether it preserves voltage, fill factor, yield, and reliability. The efficiency program is preferred only when efficiency is close to a threshold that materially changes area-related cost and LCOE, and when the gain is likely to survive module scaling without adding costly materials or reducing yield and lifetime.

Expected value of sample information can be calculated by simulating posterior decisions after possible experimental outcomes and comparing expected minimum LCOE or expected regret with the current decision. Experiment cost, duration, and opportunity cost must be included. A go/no-go threshold should specify which posterior combination of yield, lifetime, contact cost, and module efficiency justifies continued scale-up. The best experiment is the one most likely to change a consequential decision and reduce the probability of selecting the wrong architecture, not necessarily the experiment on the parameter with the steepest one-at-a-time sensitivity curve.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes value of information from nominal LCOE sensitivity by considering uncertainty, decision consequences, and actionability.
Models how each experiment updates distributions for yield/utilization, lifetime/degradation, contact cost/process, or module efficiency.
States scenario-specific conditions and break-even thresholds under which each of the four experiments is preferred.
Includes experiment cost, duration, posterior decision simulation, expected regret or expected LCOE, and architecture go/no-go decisions.
accepted_equivalents: Value may be quantified through EVSI/EVPI, real-options analysis, Bayesian decision theory, expected regret, or another formal decision framework.
Outdoor reliability may be replaced by a field-relevant multi-stress campaign if its mapping to lifetime uncertainty is justified.
Efficiency value may be evaluated through area-related BOS, encapsulation, and manufacturing costs rather than efficiency alone.
common_wrong_answers: Always fund the efficiency program because higher efficiency always gives the lowest LCOE.
Always measure the input with the largest one-way sensitivity coefficient.
Choose the cheapest experiment without considering whether its result can change a commercial decision.
Treat experiment duration and opportunity cost as irrelevant to R&D prioritization.

expected_answer:
An initial work-function mismatch creates a local electrostatic discontinuity and nonuniform carrier/ion distribution across the weak homojunction. Under illumination, charge accumulation and mobile ionic defects can screen or amplify the local field. Repeated redistribution changes band bending and extraction, increasing interfacial recombination and local electrochemical potential. If the interface also has weak adhesion, ionic accumulation and lattice distortion can raise local stress, reduce cohesive strength, and promote nanoscale separation or roughening. The newly created free volume and defective coordination then facilitate iodine loss, PbI2 enrichment, and further ion motion. Electrical, mechanical, and chemical changes can therefore form a positive feedback loop that ultimately increases resistance or recombination and lowers FF.

Direction of causality requires time-resolved, spatially registered measurements. Operando or repeated KPFM/surface-photovoltage mapping should establish whether work-function drift appears before topographic change. Simultaneous AFM or acoustic/fracture-sensitive measurements should detect the onset of roughening or adhesion loss. Angle- or depth-resolved GIWAXS/XRD, Raman, or composition mapping should determine when and where PbI2 enrichment begins. The same coordinates should be followed so co-localization is meaningful.

Perturbation controls are essential. Electrical boundary conditions should be varied at fixed light dose: open circuit, maximum power, short circuit, and externally applied bias. If work-function drift is field-driven, its sign or magnitude should follow bias and may partially relax in the dark before roughness appears. Mechanical controls with enhanced adhesion but similar work-function mismatch test whether roughening is necessary for chemical change. Dipole-matched but weakly binding controls test the reverse. A PbI2-suppressing chemical passivator that does not correct the mismatch can reveal whether PbI2 is downstream or independently initiating.

Causality is strongest when the temporal order is reproducible and selectively interrupted: correcting the mismatch suppresses early ion/potential drift; strengthening adhesion blocks roughening but not the initial electrical signal; and preventing PbI2 formation affects only later chemistry. If PbI2 appears first in unbiased samples, the proposed electrical-first sequence must be rejected. End-point correlations alone cannot establish the chain.
scoring_key_points: Builds a feedback sequence from work-function mismatch to charge/ion accumulation, altered band bending, stress/adhesion loss, roughening, PbI2 enrichment, and FF loss.
Requires time-resolved spatial registration of electrical potential, morphology/mechanics, and depth-sensitive chemistry.
Uses operating-point/bias perturbations and matched controls that separately tune dipole, adhesion, and PbI2 chemistry.
Defines causal interruption and temporal-order criteria, including outcomes that would falsify an electrical-first mechanism.
accepted_equivalents: Electrical mapping may use KPFM, surface photovoltage, electroabsorption, luminescence-based potential mapping, or another operando method.
Mechanical evolution may be followed by AFM, acoustic microscopy, fracture testing, strain mapping, or cross-sectional imaging.
Chemical evolution may be probed by angle-resolved GIWAXS/XRD, Raman, XPS with artifact controls, or compositional microscopy.
common_wrong_answers: Work-function drift, roughness increase, and PbI2 enrichment are three names for the same process.
Because all markers correlate with degradation, their causal order does not matter.
A stable final work function proves the interface has high mechanical adhesion.
PbI2 enrichment must always be the initiating event in FAPbI3-rich devices.

expected_answer:
The original molecular roles cannot be copied directly because the buried contact, carrier polarity, lattice chemistry, and dominant defects have changed. The head group should still interact selectively with a desired Sn-Pb perovskite facet or precursor intermediate, but its binding must not preferentially complex Sn2+ so strongly that it changes Sn/Pb incorporation or promotes disproportionation. The buried-contact end should be compatible with the hole-selective SAM: it may require hydrogen bonding, ionic pairing, or a covalent/coordination motif that fills SAM defects without displacing the monolayer or reversing its dipole. A sulfur group that is beneficial for SnO2 may oxidize, bind Sn strongly, or create deep states in the new system, so alternative soft donors or redox-buffering groups should be screened.

Segregation must be engineered rather than assumed. In an inverted stack, the additive should enrich at the bottom hole-contact/perovskite interface while leaving enough molecular population during nucleation to control orientation. Solvent affinity, molecular charge, spacer length, precursor coordination, coating direction, drying rate, and antisolvent or gas-quench history will determine this partitioning. Too much buried accumulation can form an insulating barrier; too much bulk retention can alter doping, ion migration, or phase stability.

The control set should separate three functions: a facet-selective analogue without buried-contact affinity, a contact-passivating/redox-stabilizing analogue without orientation control, and the bifunctional candidate. Additional controls should vary donor redox chemistry and dipole. GIWAXS and in situ crystallization measurements establish orientation; labelled depth profiling and contact spectroscopy establish segregation; XPS or operando optical/electrical probes quantify Sn4+ formation; absolute PLQY/QFLS and contact-resolved transients determine recombination and hole extraction. Mobility, series resistance, and tunnelling-barrier thickness must be measured.

In the tandem, EQE and stabilized maximum-power operation must verify current matching and absence of light-induced halide or Sn/Pb compositional redistribution. The ligand transfers successfully only if it suppresses Sn oxidation and buried recombination, preserves a favorable hole-contact dipole, improves or maintains transport, and gives orientation benefits across a reproducible coating window. A higher small-cell Voc is insufficient if the treatment narrows process tolerance, raises resistance, or shifts the subcell current balance.
scoring_key_points: Redesigns facet-binding and buried-contact functionality for mixed Sn-Pb chemistry, a hole-selective SAM, and Sn2+ oxidation risk rather than copying the SnO2 ligand.
Explains how solvent coordination, charge, spacer, drying, and coating direction control partitioning between nucleation and the inverted buried interface.
Uses function-separated and redox/dipole controls with orientation, labelled localization, Sn4+ chemistry, QFLS, extraction, mobility, and barrier measurements.
Requires tandem EQE/current matching, stabilized operation, compositional stability, and a reproducible process window before claiming successful transfer.
accepted_equivalents: Alternative donor groups may include phosphonic, carboxylate, pyridyl, thiocyanate, chalcogen, antioxidant, or other justified motifs compatible with Sn-Pb chemistry.
Buried localization may be measured by isotopic ToF-SIMS, angle-resolved spectroscopy, cross-sectional chemical mapping, or validated tracer methods.
Sn oxidation may be monitored by XPS with artifact controls, optical signatures, Mössbauer/XAS where feasible, chemical titration, or operando electrical indicators.
common_wrong_answers: Use the identical sulfur-ammonium molecule because all lead/tin halide perovskites have the same interface chemistry.
Maximize ligand accumulation at the buried interface regardless of tunnelling resistance.
A stronger preferred orientation automatically improves tandem current matching and stability.
Only the champion inverted-cell efficiency is needed to validate transfer of the bifunctional mechanism.

expected_answer:
Three failure classes must be separated. First, the ligand-stripped nanocrystal surface can reconstruct, oxidize, or lose polymer coordination; this would reopen Pb/I-related traps and increase nonradiative voltage loss. Second, mismatch in thermal expansion and polymer glass transition can generate interfacial shear, nanocrystal-film cracking, or delamination, especially during bending combined with thermal cycling. Third, the polymer/MoO3/metal side can undergo diffusion, redox chemistry, or work-function drift, producing an extraction barrier even if the absorber remains chemically intact.

Begin with material stacks rather than full modules: nanocrystal/polymer, polymer/MoO3, and complete nanocrystal/polymer/MoO3/metal structures. Subject them to isothermal aging below and above the polymer glass-transition region, then to repeated temperature cycling under inert and controlled-oxygen conditions. Add a mechanically strained set at the expected neutral-plane curvature. At selected intervals measure XPS or infrared signatures of polymer-QD coordination, absolute PLQY/QFLS, trap density, UPS/Kelvin-probe energetics, and metal/oxide depth profiles. Use cross-sectional microscopy, acoustic or optical delamination mapping, and resistance mapping to detect cracking and loss of contact. Full devices should be tracked by dark J-V, impedance, EL-EQE, EQE, and stabilized power.

Chemical depassivation is indicated by recovered trap signatures and lower QFLS before major resistance or visible cracking changes. Thermomechanical failure produces spatially localized shunts or open regions correlated with cracks and bending direction. Contact-energy drift produces increased series resistance, altered built-in potential, or injection asymmetry while film PL and structure remain largely unchanged. A credible qualification requires that the same failure signature appears in material stacks and devices, and that encapsulation or neutral-plane redesign suppresses the predicted mode rather than merely delaying all degradation.
scoring_key_points: Identifies distinct chemical depassivation, thermomechanical damage, and polymer/MoO3/metal energetic or diffusion failure modes.
Uses isolated material stacks plus complete devices to localize the failing interface.
Combines temperature, atmosphere, and mechanical-strain variables with chemical, structural, energetic, and electrical diagnostics.
Defines diagnostic signatures that distinguish trap reopening, cracking/delamination, and contact-energy drift.
accepted_equivalents: ToF-SIMS may replace another depth-profile method for metal or oxygen diffusion.
Dynamic mechanical analysis or ellipsometric glass-transition measurements may define the relevant polymer softening regime.
common_wrong_answers: Concluding stability from room-temperature inert storage alone.
Treating every fill-factor decline as nanocrystal degradation.
Testing thermal cycling without mechanical strain even though the intended product is flexible.

expected_answer:
The optimum current mismatch for a series-connected tandem is not a universal constant because the limiting subcell changes with spectrum, incidence angle, temperature, and degradation state. A slight bottom-cell limitation can maximize standard-condition efficiency if it places both subcells near favorable fill-factor regions, but the same design may waste top-cell photocurrent under blue-rich spectra or become strongly top-limited under red-rich or high-temperature conditions. Changes in perovskite thickness, nanoparticle scattering, transparent-electrode loss, and additive-induced morphology must therefore be included optically and electrically.

Build a coupled optical-electrical model calibrated with measured subcell EQE, reflectance, parasitic absorption, temperature coefficients, and two-diode parameters. Use time-resolved spectral irradiance and temperature data for representative climates to simulate hourly subcell currents, operating voltage, fill factor, and energy yield. The model should include distributions, not only champion parameters, and should allow series resistance, shunt resistance, and top-cell band gap to evolve during aging. Experimentally validate selected mismatch points using tunable-spectrum solar simulation, variable temperature, and incidence-angle sweeps. Subcell-resolved electroluminescence or luminescence coupling measurements can verify which junction limits under each condition.

The design variables should include perovskite thickness/band gap, front-electrode transmission, Si wafer optics, grid shading, nanoparticle coverage, and additive dose. The optimization target should be annual delivered energy per aperture area, optionally corrected for degradation and yield loss, rather than one-sun reverse-scan PCE. A design is preferred only if its predicted energy-yield advantage survives manufacturing variation and measured spectral tests. If the standard-condition bottom-limited setting frequently switches to severe limitation in realistic conditions, a smaller mismatch or broader current balance is superior even with a slightly lower certified PCE.
scoring_key_points: Explains why the current-limiting subcell changes with spectrum, temperature, angle, optics, and degradation.
Uses a calibrated coupled optical-electrical tandem model with measured subcell EQE and device parameters.
Requires tunable-spectrum and temperature validation of multiple designed mismatch points.
Replaces champion STC PCE with annual delivered energy yield, including variability and degradation where possible.
accepted_equivalents: Energy yield per module mass or per installed area is acceptable if the application and denominator are stated.
Spectral Monte Carlo simulations may substitute for site-resolved hourly data if validated against representative measured spectra.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that the 0.5 mA cm−2 mismatch remains optimal in every climate.
Optimizing only integrated Jsc while ignoring subcell fill factor and series resistance.
Using a single champion cell rather than distributions and manufacturing tolerances.

expected_answer:
Use electron contacts that change photocatalytic activity independently of band alignment and extraction. The core matrix should include the original compact TiO2, UV-passivated or surface-coated TiO2 with similar energetics, and a non-photocatalytic wide-band-gap electron contact adjusted to comparable work function and conductivity. For each contact, test full-spectrum illumination, UV-cut illumination with the same visible absorbed dose, and narrow-band UV at matched photon dose. A perovskite-only film on inert substrate provides the direct-photochemistry baseline. Encapsulation and atmosphere must be controlled so oxygen and moisture are not unintentionally varied.

Track stabilized device parameters continuously, but pair them with operando PL, UV-visible absorption, XRD, and chemical analysis of Ti, Pb, halide, and oxygen species. Radical or photocatalytic activity can be probed with spin trapping or a calibrated reporter reaction on the contact. Ion migration should be monitored by bias-dependent PL or potential mapping, transient ionic current, and depth profiles before and after illumination. Interfacial recombination can be followed by QFLS, EL-EQE, and impedance.
