TiO2 photocatalysis is supported if degradation follows TiO2 surface activity and is suppressed by an ultrathin inert coating or non-photocatalytic replacement without changing the perovskite optical dose. Direct perovskite photochemistry is supported if inert-substrate films and all contact variants show similar phase or chemical damage under equal absorbed UV dose. An ion-migration pathway is favored when degradation strongly depends on electric field or operating point, produces reversible or spatial halide redistribution before permanent chemical change, and is reduced by an ion-blocking interface even when UV absorption is unchanged. The mechanisms can coexist, but the matrix should identify the rate-limiting one and avoid assigning all UV loss to bulk film defects.
scoring_key_points: Uses contact variants that separate TiO2 photocatalytic activity from energy alignment and extraction.
Separates full-spectrum, UV-cut, and narrow-band UV exposure at matched photon or absorbed dose.
Includes chemical/radical, structural, recombination, and ion-migration diagnostics.
Defines distinct signatures for contact photocatalysis, direct absorber photochemistry, and field-dependent interfacial ion migration.
accepted_equivalents: SnO2, passivated TiO2, or another non-photocatalytic ETL may serve as the replacement if band alignment and resistance are matched.
Electron-spin resonance or a validated photocatalytic reporter may be used to detect reactive species.
common_wrong_answers: Attributing UV degradation to TiO2 solely because TiO2 is present.
Comparing UV-cut and full-spectrum tests without matching visible dose and device temperature.
Using only final PCE retention without chemical or ionic diagnostics.

expected_answer:
The structural-catalyst hypothesis predicts that electrical conditions which accumulate iodine or favor the interstitial charge state at one interface will create spatially localized δ-phase nucleation after an induction period. The initial electrical penalty may be modest because the defect is shallow, but once local face-sharing Pb-I motifs form, phase conversion should become autocatalytic or persist after the field is removed. Ordinary halide migration, in contrast, can produce reversible potential or luminescence gradients without a new crystal phase. PbI2-forming decomposition should generate a distinct diffraction/chemical signature and may depend more strongly on volatile loss or electrode reactions.

Use lateral or vertical devices with ion-blocking electrodes and controlled iodine chemical potential. Apply positive and negative bias in the dark, at open circuit under illumination, and at maximum-power-like fields while matching temperature. Operando micro-XRD/GIWAXS or Raman mapping should follow α-, δ-, and PbI2-related signatures at the biased interfaces. Simultaneous PL spectral imaging, Kelvin-probe mapping, and transient ionic current can track reversible ion redistribution. After stress removal, monitor dark recovery and reapply the opposite field. Include an interstitial-suppressing non-iodide passivation control, an iodine-rich treatment, and humidity/oxygen-controlled environments.

Defect-driven nucleation is supported if δ-phase appears preferentially where the field predicts iodine accumulation, its onset rate scales with iodine-interstitial population, and the structural change persists or continues after ionic potential gradients relax. Reversible halide migration is indicated by field-reversible PL/potential changes without δ-phase growth. PbI2 decomposition is identified by PbI2 formation, loss of organic/halide species, or electrode reaction rather than selective α-to-δ conversion. Activation energies from temperature-dependent induction times can be compared with calculated transition barriers, but agreement alone is not proof. The decisive result is a spatial and kinetic sequence from interstitial accumulation to persistent δ-nucleus formation.
scoring_key_points: Predicts localized, delayed, and potentially persistent δ-phase nucleation where bias drives iodine/interstitial accumulation.
Combines operando phase mapping with ionic-current, potential, and PL measurements under dark and illuminated bias conditions.
Includes iodine-rich and interstitial-suppressing controls plus field reversal and recovery.
Distinguishes persistent α-to-δ conversion from reversible halide redistribution and PbI2-forming decomposition by separate signatures.
accepted_equivalents: Operando electron diffraction or synchrotron nano-XRD may replace GIWAXS if beam damage is controlled.
Bias-poling followed by rapid ex situ phase mapping is acceptable when operando structural access is unavailable and timing is sufficient.
common_wrong_answers: Calling any hysteresis or PL shift evidence of δ-phase nucleation.
Using only I2-vapor stress, which does not test electrical accumulation.
Failing to distinguish δ-FAPbI3 peaks from PbI2 or other degradation products.

expected_answer:
The earliest changes can occur within the quantum-dot solid before average crystallography detects a new phase. Heat and illumination weaken dynamic ligand binding and promote ligand desorption or redistribution. This changes dielectric confinement and interdot spacing, creating a broader distribution of electronic coupling and local bandgaps. Simultaneously, photocarriers and internal fields drive halide vacancies or mobile ions toward surfaces and contacts. Local compositional redistribution and trap charging produce spectral broadening, red-shifted low-energy domains, hysteresis, and dispersive extraction. These changes may initially be reversible when the device is cooled or rested.

Continued ligand loss lowers the kinetic barrier to dot-dot necking, Ostwald ripening, or partial fusion. Coarsening reduces quantum confinement and produces the persistent red shift and larger crystallites. It may also release strain that had stabilized the black perovskite phase, allowing nonperovskite domains to nucleate. Surface vacancies exposed by ligand loss increase nonradiative recombination and provide faster ion-migration pathways, so structural and ionic degradation reinforce one another. Contact reactions can then become secondary sinks for mobile halides.

A discriminating study should combine operando PL spectral mapping and absolute PLQY, temperature-dependent transient photocurrent, impedance or ionic-current measurements, and in situ GIWAXS/GISAXS. Reversible disorder would relax after dark rest while dot size, scattering form factor, ligand coverage, and XRD remain unchanged. Irreversible coarsening would produce persistent GISAXS/TEM size growth, reduced ligand signatures by solid-state NMR, FTIR, or XPS, and a permanent absorption/PL red shift. Composition-sensitive mapping can separate halide segregation from pure size growth. Dark shelf tests omit photocarrier-driven ion motion, junction fields, and thermally activated ligand exchange. They can therefore certify ink or phase storage while missing the coupled light-heat-bias failure that controls operating lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Links illumination and heat to ligand redistribution, heterogeneous interdot coupling, ion motion, and early spectral/extraction changes.
Explains how continued ligand loss enables coarsening, loss of confinement/strain stabilization, and later phase conversion.
Distinguishes reversible electronic or ionic disorder from irreversible sintering using operando optical, transport, scattering, and ligand measurements.
Explains why dark shelf stability excludes the coupled drivers present under photovoltaic operation.
accepted_equivalents: quantum-dot fusion may be described as necking, ripening, or sintering
operando absorption may complement PL spectral mapping
nuclear magnetic resonance or thermogravimetric desorption may be used to quantify ligand loss
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the first PL red shift must already be a bulk XRD-detectable phase transition.
Treating ligand removal as universally beneficial because it improves coupling.
Using dry dark storage as evidence of operational stability.

expected_answer:
Regions that dry last can remain in a solvent-rich intermediate after the surrounding film has already nucleated and contracted. Delayed conversion produces locally different grain-boundary density, strain, orientation, and residual coordination chemistry even when the final average XRD is phase-pure. Coordinating solvent or nonvolatile adduct residues increase local polarity and water uptake. Under damp heat, those regions hydrate first, weaken Pb-halide bonding, and accelerate defect formation and ion migration. Ionic charge accumulation changes local band bending and raises nonradiative recombination, creating the early low-PL bands. Continued moisture exposure promotes voiding, secondary phases, contact corrosion, and eventually localized shunts or series-resistance loss that spread through interconnected module cells.

Average XRD, thickness, and efficiency are insensitive to a small-area tail. The controlling variable is the spatial distribution of intermediate lifetime and residual chemistry, especially at coating edges, meniscus transitions, and drying nonuniformities. In-line monitoring should therefore combine spatially resolved optical or IR signatures of solvent coordination with fast diffraction or reflectometry and thermal/airflow maps. Endpoint criteria should bound the maximum local intermediate persistence and residual-solvent signal, not only the average. Offline validation should use PL-lifetime mapping, micro-XRD/GIWAXS, ToF-SIMS or infrared mapping, and local impedance before and after damp heat.

Process remedies include zoned substrate temperature, controlled solvent activity, gas-knife uniformity, web-speed adjustment, and an additive/solvent pair whose conversion window is broad but whose residue is volatile. A short conversion-completion step may be triggered by the slowest region rather than a fixed line time. Success requires narrowing the spatial distributions of residue, trap density, and damp-heat degradation onset while retaining electrical uniformity. Raising the mean PL without removing the low-conversion tail would not solve the weakest-link failure.
scoring_key_points: Links late drying to persistent intermediates, residual coordination, local structural/electronic heterogeneity, and enhanced water uptake.
Builds the damp-heat sequence through trap generation, ion migration, recombination, voiding/contact failure, and module loss.
Explains why spatial tails are invisible to average XRD, thickness, and efficiency.
Proposes spatial in-line endpoints and process controls aimed at the slowest-converting regions rather than the mean.
accepted_equivalents: low-conversion regions may be described as solvent-rich bands, adduct-retention zones, or drying-front defects
Raman or hyperspectral imaging may replace infrared mapping
local electroluminescence may complement PL mapping
common_wrong_answers: Attributing failure only to average grain size.
Assuming phase-pure average XRD excludes residual solvent or minority intermediates.
Optimizing average PL while ignoring the spatial distribution and module weakest links.

expected_answer:
Reversible loss of the passivating state would occur if Pb–O or peroxide-derived surface species desorb, are reduced by the perovskite or contact, or exchange with halides during heating. PLQY and surface-oxygen signatures would fall together while absorption, morphology, and deep composition remain largely unchanged. Cooling alone may not restore the state, but a second mild peroxide treatment should recover the original PLQY and quasi-Fermi splitting with little cumulative penalty.

Latent overoxidation is different. An initially bright surface may contain unstable oxidized lead, iodate-like species, or halide-depleted regions that evolve into deep traps or volatile products during heating. This pathway should show irreversible Pb/I stoichiometric change, new oxygen chemical states, increased subgap absorption or trap-assisted recombination, and incomplete recovery after retreatment. A dose-dependent threshold and greater damage for stronger initial oxidation would support this mechanism.

Redistribution involves migration, clustering, or burial of the oxidized species rather than their disappearance. The total oxygen inventory may remain constant while angle-resolved or depth-resolved XPS, isotope-labeled H2^18O2 profiling, or cross-sectional spectroscopy shows a changed location. Spatial PL maps may evolve from uniform brightening to patchy recombination, and KPFM may reveal broadened surface potential. If the oxidized layer migrates into or reacts with a transport layer, device resistance and selectivity can degrade before the isolated-film PL collapses.

The experiment should track absolute PLQY/QFLS, TRPL, surface and depth chemistry, volatile products, and trap density through heating and retreatment. Untreated films, oxygen-only exposure, low- and high-dose peroxide, and films protected from contacts are required. Unchanged bulk XRD only excludes large-volume phase conversion; it cannot distinguish reversible surface chemistry from nanoscale overoxidation or redistribution.
scoring_key_points: Defines distinct mechanisms for reversible passivation loss, irreversible latent overoxidation, and spatial redistribution of oxidized species.
Uses retreatment/recovery behavior and dose dependence to separate reversible from cumulative chemical damage.
Requires isotope-labeled, depth-resolved, and spatially resolved chemistry rather than bulk XRD alone.
Links each pathway to characteristic PLQY/QFLS, trap, potential-uniformity, and device-resistance signatures.
accepted_equivalents: Pb–O loss may be described as reduction, ligand exchange, desorption, or chemical consumption
operando ambient-pressure XPS may replace sequential ex situ XPS
thermal desorption mass spectrometry may identify volatile oxidation products
common_wrong_answers: Assuming any decrease in PLQY proves bulk perovskite decomposition.
Calling the treatment reversible without demonstrating recovery by retreatment.
Using constant total oxygen as evidence that the passivating structure is unchanged.

expected_answer:
Once the oxidized Spiro-MeOTAD interfacial trap is neutralized, other thermally activated processes can control lifetime. Li+ and TFSI− can redistribute through the HTL and toward interfaces, changing local doping and screening the junction field. tBP removal and continued heating can also reorganize Spiro-MeOTAD, alter free volume, or reduce conductivity. These mechanisms initially increase series resistance and produce fill-factor loss before major optical or current changes. The APTES layer itself may condense into an inhomogeneous siloxane network, desorb from incompletely anchored sites, or react further with the HTL, creating patchy tunneling barriers. At longer times, Au diffusion or interfacial chemical reactions can add shunts, contact resistance, or recombination, explaining the smaller later Voc loss.

The branches should be ranked using repeated non-destructive measurements on the same devices: J–V decomposition, impedance over temperature and frequency, dark conductivity, capacitance, TPV/TPC, and spatial EL or lock-in thermography. A rising series resistance with stable optical QFLS points to HTL/contact transport; rising ideality factor and falling EL efficiency indicate renewed recombination. Depth-resolved ToF-SIMS should track Li, TFSI, aminosilane fragments, and Au. GIWAXS/DSC or nanoscale mechanical mapping of the HTL can reveal morphology evolution, while angle-resolved XPS, FTIR, or solid-state NMR tests silane bonding and condensation. Cross-sectional microscopy should be performed only after electrical failure locations are mapped.

Counterfactuals include Li-free or alternative-dopant HTLs, a stable noncondensing amine anchor, a metal-diffusion barrier, and APTES devices without tBP degassing. If APTES devices show the same Li or electrode sequence but delayed onset, it delays failure. If the first failure shifts to silane-rich high-resistance patches that are absent in controls, it changes the dominant mode and may introduce a new lifetime ceiling.
scoring_key_points: Builds a failure tree beyond radical-cation recombination, including ion redistribution, HTL transport/morphology, silane evolution, and electrode reactions.
Connects early FF-dominated loss to series/contact resistance and later Voc loss to recombination or metal chemistry.
Requires time-resolved electrical/spatial diagnostics and depth-resolved chemical/structural post-mortem analysis.
Uses dopant, anchor, electrode-barrier, and degassing counterfactuals to distinguish delayed failure from a newly introduced mode.
accepted_equivalents: LiTFSI redistribution may be described as dopant segregation or mobile-ion accumulation
conductive AFM may complement lock-in thermography for local resistance
Ni or carbon electrodes may substitute for Au in electrode-reaction controls
common_wrong_answers: Assuming all residual thermal decay must come from the original radical-cation trap.
Interpreting FF loss as proof of bulk perovskite decomposition.
Claiming improved intrinsic lifetime without identifying whether the failure mode has shifted.

expected_answer:
Strong multipodal adsorption can prevent wholesale desorption yet still permit local rearrangement. Under prolonged photovoltage, heat, and ionic flux, incompletely anchored molecules or strained tripods can tilt, cluster, hydrolyze, or exchange with halide-containing species. The total phosphorus loading may remain constant while the monolayer becomes laterally heterogeneous. Bare or edge-on patches reduce hole selectivity and create local charge accumulation at the TCO/perovskite interface. Accumulated holes and ionic charge alter band bending, increase trap-assisted recombination, and drive halide or A-site migration toward the buried contact. Reactive TCO sites exposed in low-coverage patches can then catalyze decomposition or form interfacial products. Voc and FF can therefore decline before enough bulk material changes to affect XRD.

Brief heat pulses mainly test thermal desorption and gross molecular stability without sustained photocarriers, electric field, or ion flux. A 100 h average MPP trace may also miss a slow spatial percolation process. Average phosphorus loading cannot detect redistribution from uniform coverage into islands or distinguish intact molecules from fragments.

The pathway should be tested with operando or periodically quenched EL/PL imaging, surface-potential or photocurrent mapping, and impedance to identify the first low-selectivity patches. Isotope-labeled monolayers and depth-resolved chemistry can track anchor/core integrity, while ToF-SIMS or X-ray fluorescence follows halide accumulation at the TCO. Orientation-sensitive spectroscopy before and after stress should test reorientation. Correlative cross-sectional microscopy should target mapped failing regions. A more strongly cross-linked or orientation-locked analogue should suppress patch formation; a deliberately diluted monolayer should accelerate the same spatial signature. The hypothesis is falsified if molecular orientation and coverage distributions remain invariant and degradation instead begins at the top electrode or bulk absorber with no spatial correlation to the buried contact.
scoring_key_points: Builds a buried-interface sequence from local monolayer rearrangement/fragmentation to coverage patches, charge accumulation, recombination, ion migration, and TCO reaction.
Explains why total anchor loading and bulk XRD can remain constant during spatial interfacial failure.
Identifies the missing stressors in brief heat and short inert MPP tests.
Requires spatial operando electrical/optical maps, orientation/core-integrity measurements, ion profiles, and matched molecular-density counterfactuals.
accepted_equivalents: patch formation may be described as islanding, local desorption, tilt disorder, or anchor exchange
operando Kelvin probe or scanning photocurrent may replace surface-potential mapping
buried-interface hard X-ray photoemission may complement post-stress chemistry
common_wrong_answers: Assuming strong adsorption energy prevents all interfacial reorganization.
Treating unchanged average phosphorus loading as proof of uniform coverage.
Equating short heat resistance with long-term light-bias stability.

expected_answer:
The inert MPP result demonstrates resistance to heat, illumination, and bias in the absence of external oxidants and water. Humid air introduces sorption, redox chemistry, and faster ionic transport. Water can enter through defects in the top contact or edges, plasticize or reorganize the organic HTM, and accumulate at the buried interface according to local surface energy. A highly planar molecule that packs well initially may either resist penetration or crystallize and open grain boundaries during prolonged exposure. Oxygen can oxidize the HTM, shifting its conductivity and energy levels. These changes first raise contact or series resistance, producing FF loss while the absorber still absorbs normally.

Water-assisted halide migration and interfacial redox then increase trap density and nonradiative recombination, causing Voc loss. Mobile iodide can react with Cu or facilitate metal diffusion, while moisture and depleted halide regions promote PbI2 formation and later Jsc decline. The sequence may be spatially localized at HTM crystallites, pinholes, or electrode defects even if average neat-film thermal stability is high.

Controls should include encapsulated and unencapsulated devices, dry oxygen, humid nitrogen, and combined humid air at matched temperature, light, and bias. A nonplanar analogue, a morphology-stabilized planar derivative, and an independent Cu-diffusion barrier separate HTM packing from electrode chemistry. Operando impedance, EL/PL imaging, contact resistance, and optical QFLS should establish whether FF loss precedes recombination. GIWAXS/AFM should track HTM crystallization or dewetting; ToF-SIMS/XPS should map water-derived oxygen, halides, and Cu. If the planar HTM remains morphologically uniform and outperforms controls in each isolated stress, planarity is protective. If failure nucleates at growing planar-HTM domains and is suppressed by amorphization or side-chain redesign, excessive packing has become the liability.
scoring_key_points: Adds humidity/oxygen-driven sorption, HTM redox or crystallization, enhanced ion motion, and Cu reaction to the inert-atmosphere failure picture.
Explains the ordered FF, Voc, PbI2, and later current-loss sequence through contact transport then recombination/chemical degradation.
Uses dry-O2, humid-N2, combined-stress, encapsulation, morphology, and electrode-barrier controls to isolate causes.
Defines when planarity is protective versus a crystallization/dewetting liability through operando morphology, ion, electrode, and electrical evidence.
accepted_equivalents: HTM crystallization may be described as domain coarsening, dewetting, or loss of amorphous continuity
Ag may replace Cu as the reactive-metal example if the contact stack differs
water uptake may be tracked by isotope-labeled humidity or quartz-crystal microbalance measurements
common_wrong_answers: Assuming 1000 h in nitrogen proves equal durability in humid air.
Attributing early FF loss directly to bulk PbI2 formation.
Calling planarity universally stabilizing without checking long-term HTM morphology and electrode chemistry.

expected_answer: Early in exposure, the dominant change may be near-surface loss of volatile or water-soluble FAI and a local shift in the Cs/FA ratio. If the Pb-I framework remains largely connected and the compositional excursion has not crossed a nucleation threshold for stable nonperovskite phases, restoring FA and iodide chemical potentials can repopulate vacancies and recover the perovskite phase. This is a stoichiometric, potentially reversible regime. Longer exposure introduces qualitatively different damage: oxygen converts exposed iodide into iodate-containing products, removal of those products creates Pb-I framework vacancies or voids, and phase segregation produces structurally distinct Cs-rich and FA-rich nonperovskites. Once material is physically lost, crystallites have coarsened into stable secondary phases, or contacts have delaminated, supplying FAI cannot reconstruct the original microstructure or interface. A strategy to delay this tipping point should target both branches of the coupled loop. A hydrophobic, ionically impermeable but electronically benign surface layer reduces water access and FAI extraction. An oxygen/redox barrier or iodide-preserving interlayer limits iodide oxidation. A shallow FAI or iodide chemical-potential reservoir could buffer initial stoichiometric loss, but it must not create mobile-ion or contact-instability penalties. Grain-boundary and scribe sealing are needed because inward propagation is likely fastest along connected defects. The intervention should be tested using pulsed humid-oxygen exposures of increasing duration followed by standardized recovery treatment. Operando surface/bulk GIWAXS, XPS or XRF for N/I/O balance, profilometry or microscopy for void formation, PL/QFLS, and complete devices for contact resistance and hysteresis should locate the recovery threshold. Success is not a visual return to the black phase. The treated sample must retain elemental mass balance, suppress iodate accumulation, avoid growth of nonperovskite phases at the surface and in the bulk, preserve morphology and interface adhesion, and recover electronic quality without repeated FAI dosing. A genuine loop interruption shifts the critical exposure time and reduces the rate of inward damage under continuous humid-oxygen stress; simple re-blackening after each cycle is only repair of an early symptom.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes reversible near-surface FA/I stoichiometric depletion from irreversible iodate formation, framework loss, voiding, and segregated phases.
Explains why chemical-potential replenishment can work before a structural or nucleation threshold but not after material loss or interface damage.
Proposes simultaneous water-access, oxygen/redox, defect-path, and optional stoichiometric-buffer interventions.
Defines pulsed-stress/recovery testing with chemical mass balance, phase, morphology, and electronic criteria beyond visual re-blackening.
accepted_equivalents: A sacrificial FA/iodide reservoir may be implemented by a surface salt, polymer-bound ion source, or reversible vapor treatment if it does not destabilize contacts.
Electronic recovery may be assessed by PLQY, QFLS, TRPL, mobility, device Voc/FF, or equivalent metrics.
Framework loss may be described as Pb-I vacancy formation, dissolution, porosity, or irreversible surface recession.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming all phase change is reversible because the film becomes dark again.
Using only a moisture barrier while leaving oxygen-driven iodide oxidation unaddressed.
Equating restored PL intensity with restored elemental composition and interface integrity.
Testing a single endpoint without mapping the exposure-duration threshold.

expected_answer: The absence of a large average bandgap shift does not exclude structural decomposition. A mixed-cation perovskitoid can preserve the same mean Pb-I composition while locally redistributing the small and spacer cations. Because the two cations occupy different crystallographic environments, unequal mobility or desorption during thermal cycling can change local occupancy, strain, and the balance between corner-sharing and face-sharing units. Nanoscale domains with different connectivity may therefore form before a new bulk phase is obvious. Such domains can broaden or split diffraction peaks, create local band offsets and transport barriers, and reduce fill factor while the spatially averaged absorption edge remains nearly unchanged. The first task is to map a true composition-temperature-processing phase diagram rather than rely on the nominal precursor ratio. Isotopically or chemically distinguishable cations, solid-state NMR, depth-resolved mass spectrometry, nano-XRD/electron diffraction, and spatial PL or cathodoluminescence should test whether the cations segregate or leave the film. Variable-temperature GIWAXS can reveal reversible versus irreversible connectivity changes and strain evolution. Mechanical and thermal-expansion measurements should determine whether repeated mismatch between organic and inorganic sublattices drives defect formation. Matched single-cation and nearby-size spacer controls establish whether the failure is specific to the mixed-cation occupancy scheme. A robust strategy would use a spacer pair whose size and hydrogen-bonding preferences provide a broad free-energy basin for the desired connectivity, not merely the best room-temperature crystal. Stronger but nonreactive anchoring, reduced cation volatility, controlled solvent coordination, slower crystallization, and texture-promoting nucleation can reduce local occupancy fluctuations. A small compositional buffer may be acceptable only if it does not introduce low-dimensional insulating domains. Before transfer to a new spacer family, the material should retain one connectivity distribution, uniform cation ratio, low strain, and stable spatial PL through repeated thermal cycles; device FF and series resistance should remain stable at fixed QFLS. Passing room-temperature light soaking or matching the initial 2.0 eV gap is insufficient. The design rule is transferable only when the targeted cation-size window also survives kinetic processing and thermal redistribution.
scoring_key_points: Proposes cation redistribution and local corner-/face-sharing connectivity changes as a hidden failure mode despite an unchanged average gap.
Uses nanoscale chemical, structural, strain, and luminescence mapping in addition to average XRD or absorption.
Builds a composition-temperature-processing phase map with matched single-cation and neighboring-size controls.
Defines a transferable design window based on nonvolatile, nonreactive cations, robust connectivity, texture, and cycle-stable device transport.
accepted_equivalents: Local phase separation may be described as occupancy disorder, connectivity domains, polytype formation, or nanoscale low-dimensional inclusions.
Spatial probes may include nano-XRD, electron diffraction, scanning PL, cathodoluminescence, Raman mapping, or equivalent methods.
Thermal robustness criteria may use fixed FF/series resistance, mobility, or extraction length at unchanged QFLS.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming an unchanged average bandgap proves the phase is homogeneous.
Extending the room-temperature cation-size rule without measuring cation mobility or thermal phase behavior.
Using only bulk powder XRD to exclude nanoscale connectivity domains.
Adding excess spacer indiscriminately even if it forms insulating low-dimensional phases.

expected_answer: The existing correlation is underdetermined because the spacer substitution changes several variables at once. A causal test needs orthogonal perturbations. First, prepare matched spacers that separate steric geometry from polarizability: an allyl-like cation with similar size and hydrogen-bonding but no heavy iodine, an iodine-containing analogue with a different chain geometry, and a nonhalogenated spacer adjusted to reproduce the interlayer distance. Single-crystal structures and dielectric measurements must verify which variables are actually matched. If deep emission tracks equatorial Pb-I-Pb distortion across chemically different spacers at similar interlayer dielectric environment, distortion is the stronger mediator. If it tracks spacer polarizability or interlayer dielectric contrast at similar inorganic geometry, dielectric/interlayer effects dominate. Pressure provides a second orthogonal axis. Hydrostatic or stacking-axis uniaxial pressure can reduce interlayer spacing and modify octahedral angles without changing chemical identity. Operando XRD or Raman should quantify both changes while transient absorption and time-resolved PL follow band-edge capture and sink-state lifetime. A distortion-controlled state should shift in formation rate or energy with the Pb-I-Pb angle and soft-mode spectrum, potentially showing strong temperature dependence and reversible pressure tuning. A dielectric or interlayer charge-separated state should be especially sensitive to layer spacing, dielectric constant, and field orientation; it may show large Stark shifts, polarization anisotropy, or electron-hole separation signatures even when local octahedral angles are nearly fixed. Polarization-resolved absorption/PL, electroabsorption, time-resolved microwave or terahertz conductivity, and surface-potential or charge-sensitive probes can test whether the sink state carries spatially separated charge. First-principles excited-state calculations should independently vary the inorganic coordinates and the organic dielectric environment, rather than relaxing both simultaneously. The strongest evidence is a mediation analysis across samples and perturbations: the trap formation rate and emission energy collapse onto one structural descriptor after controlling the other variables. A simple correlation between average bond angle and lifetime is not enough, because spacer chemistry can alter defect formation energies, dielectric confinement, and lattice dynamics concurrently.
scoring_key_points: Recognizes that spacer substitution confounds distortion, interlayer distance, dielectric response, and chemical defect formation.
Uses chemically matched spacer analogues to vary inorganic distortion and organic polarizability/interlayer spacing independently.
Uses pressure/temperature with operando structure and ultrafast spectroscopy to establish reversible causal coupling.
Specifies distinct signatures for distortion/self-trapping versus dielectric or interlayer charge separation and calls for calculations with independently varied coordinates/environment.
accepted_equivalents: Heavy-atom effects, dielectric confinement, interlayer charge transfer, or polaronic self-trapping are acceptable competing mechanisms if distinguished experimentally.
Pressure may be hydrostatic, uniaxial, epitaxial strain, or mechanically applied bending with calibrated structural response.
Charge separation may be probed by Stark spectroscopy, transient conductivity, surface potential, or equivalent techniques.
common_wrong_answers: Assigning the sink state solely from a bond-angle correlation.
Comparing spacers that change size, polarity, and hydrogen bonding without verifying matched variables.
Using steady-state PL alone to distinguish self-trapping from charge separation.
Assuming a longer interlayer distance automatically means stronger dielectric confinement without measuring dielectric response.

expected_answer: The degradation can be represented as a positive feedback among hole population, ionic configuration, and recombination. Let the local hole density increase the rate constants for vacancy-mediated iodide motion and for nonradiative recombination through stronger electron-phonon coupling or greater wavefunction overlap. Ion redistribution then creates defect-rich or compositionally altered configurations with even larger capture coefficients. At constant optical output, the external circuit compensates for the falling internal radiative efficiency by injecting more current, further raising hole density and ionic driving force. Because both the ionic rate and recombination coefficient depend nonlinearly on the evolving state, the observable decay can become superlinear even when each elementary step is thermally activated. The earliest warning should precede permanent composition change. Useful observables include a carrier-density-dependent shortening of PL or EL lifetime, growth of low-frequency lattice or electroabsorption signatures, a reversible shift in capacitance or ionic impedance, increasing voltage needed to sustain fixed luminance, and spatial accumulation of potential near the hole contact. A later stage adds hysteresis, halide-composition gradients, new defect luminescence, and incomplete recovery after rest. Time-resolved measurements under short duty cycles can determine whether electronic lifetime changes occur before measurable ion motion and whether the ionic state retains memory. Breaking the loop requires limiting peak local hole density and reducing the sensitivity of the lattice/defects to holes. Pulsed or adaptive drive can include recovery intervals chosen from the measured ionic relaxation time rather than merely lowering average current. A contact with high hole conductivity, low interfacial trap density, and minimal injection barrier prevents local charge pile-up; a thin ion-blocking but electronically transparent interlayer can suppress vacancy exchange. Bulk strategies include stronger lattice bonding, vacancy passivation, reduced mobile-halide concentration, and microstructures without fast interfacial ion pathways. The qualification should compare equal delivered photon dose and equal luminance, not equal current alone. Success requires lower peak interfacial hole density, unchanged initial radiative efficiency, reduced ionic impedance drift and composition movement, and a linear or sublinear damage accumulation over repeated on/off cycles. A strategy that merely reduces current while also reducing output does not demonstrate feedback suppression.
scoring_key_points: Builds a positive feedback in which holes accelerate ion motion and recombination, ionic redistribution increases defect-assisted recombination, and constant-output operation demands more injection.
Identifies early electronic, phonon/potential, capacitance/impedance, and drive-voltage observables before irreversible composition change.
Proposes duty-cycle control based on ionic relaxation plus conductive/selective contacts, thin ion-blocking interfaces, and bulk vacancy/lattice stabilization.
Defines equal-output or equal-photon-dose validation with reduced peak hole density, ion drift, and superlinear damage.
accepted_equivalents: Carrier lifetime may be monitored by TRPL, transient EL, differential lifetime, or equivalent techniques.
Ionic memory may be measured by hysteresis, capacitance, impedance, Kelvin-probe potential, or composition mapping.
Adaptive operation may use pulsing, reverse-rest, active bias control, or temperature-aware duty cycling.
common_wrong_answers: Treating ion migration and recombination as independent additive losses.
Lowering average current without matching optical output or photon dose.
Using a thicker transport layer despite increased resistance and charge accumulation.
Measuring only final efficiency or luminance without early-state electronic and ionic observables.

expected_answer: Edges can have undercoordinated ions, higher vacancy density, weaker organic-spacer packing, and direct access to the environment, so they can dominate ionic flux even when the basal planes are high quality. Chemical passivation should reduce halide-vacancy concentration and stabilize undercoordinated Pb without introducing electronically deep states. Candidate ligands or cross-linkers must bind selectively at exposed edges and remain immobile under bias. Physical encapsulation can block environmental exchange and mechanically constrain the edge, but a thick dielectric may concentrate the electric field at the passivation boundary or obstruct contacts. Increasing layer number may lower edge-to-volume ratio and change migration barriers, yet it also changes band structure, out-of-plane screening, and the optical signature. Geometry can reduce corner field enhancement by using rounded junctions, guard electrodes, wider separation from metal edges, or a field orientation parallel to rather than across the chemical boundary. The strategies should be compared on otherwise identical single-crystal devices. Atomic-resolution or nanoscale chemical mapping must verify edge coverage and initial junction sharpness. Bias-dependent PL plus direct composition mapping should determine onset voltage, flux, and spatial pathway. Conductive AFM or four-probe measurements test whether electronic mobility and contact resistance are preserved. Finite-element field simulations should identify whether the intervention redistributes the field to a hidden hot spot. Thermal imaging and matched-power controls exclude heating. A genuine suppression shifts the ion-migration activation energy or lowers halide flux at the same local field and temperature, not merely the applied voltage. It should reduce edge vacancy or defect signatures, maintain a sharp composition profile after repeated subthreshold and operational bias cycles, and preserve current, mobility, and luminescence. Delayed catastrophe would instead show increasing local field, abrupt breakdown at the passivation termination, chemical decomposition, or a sudden alloy front after a longer incubation time. Endurance tests should include polarity reversal, retention after rest, and post-mortem oxidation-state analysis. The optimal design may combine selective chemical passivation with a thin conformal barrier and rounded, field-uniform junction geometry; simply making the crystal thicker or coating the edge is insufficient unless local-field-normalized ionic transport is reduced.
scoring_key_points: Identifies edge vacancies, undercoordination, packing, and environmental access as causes of the fast ionic pathway.
Compares chemical passivation, physical barriers, layer-number changes, and geometry/field redesign with electronic and optical tradeoffs.
Requires local-field-normalized composition flux, activation energy, field simulation, thermal controls, and electronic-transport measurements.
Distinguishes genuine suppression from delayed field concentration or catastrophic degradation through endurance, retention, and post-mortem criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Edge passivants may be Lewis bases/acids, covalent cross-linkers, bulky ammonium species, or inorganic caps if they do not create deep electronic traps.
Geometry control may use guard electrodes, rounded corners, parallel fields, or increased contact setback.
Ion suppression may be quantified by threshold field, activation energy, tracer flux, junction broadening, or equivalent metrics.
common_wrong_answers: Claiming success from a higher applied-voltage threshold without calculating the local field.
Using a thick insulating edge coating that destroys lateral current injection.
Increasing layer thickness without accounting for changed band structure and edge-to-volume ratio.
Ignoring abrupt breakdown or chemical decomposition after a longer incubation period.

expected_answer:
The analysis should begin by separating the electrically series-connected subcells. Stress and monitor three structures in parallel: the complete tandem, a top-cell-equivalent perovskite device on an inert or representative recombination contact, and the finished TOPCon bottom cell with an optical filter reproducing its tandem operating spectrum. Additional dark-heat and light-only controls separate thermal changes from photocarrier-driven changes. In the tandem, periodic subcell-resolved EQE, luminescence coupling, spectrally resolved electroluminescence, and light-bias JV can identify which subcell loses voltage or current matching.

Perovskite-side burn-in is supported by bias- or illumination-history dependence, partial recovery in the dark or under reversed bias, evolving hysteresis, low-frequency capacitance, halide redistribution in ToF-SIMS, and changes in perovskite or transport-layer photoluminescence/work function. Selective-contact degradation should additionally alter extraction kinetics, interfacial recombination, or contact resistance without a corresponding decline in the isolated silicon cell. By contrast, loss of TOPCon hydrogen passivation should produce a persistent increase in silicon contact recombination or saturation current, reduced minority-carrier lifetime, and little short-time electrical recovery. Oxide or dopant/contact evolution would be accompanied by changes in contact resistivity, sheet resistance, junction leakage, or temperature dependence, potentially with structural or chemical changes at the poly-Si/SiOx/c-Si interface.

The decisive protocol therefore includes periodic Suns-Voc or implied-voltage measurements on the isolated bottom cell, contact-resistivity test structures aged with the same thermal history, and hydrogen/chemical profiling on sacrificial samples. A TOPCon failure assignment is justified only when the isolated silicon structure degrades under the same temperature and photon dose, the tandem loss tracks silicon pseudo-Voc or contact resistance, and perovskite-state variables remain comparatively stable. Early reversible burn-in confined to the tandem top stack should not be attributed to the silicon process merely because the bottom cell was newly optimized.
scoring_key_points: Uses complete-tandem, perovskite-only, and spectrally matched silicon-bottom-cell stress splits plus dark/thermal controls.
Identifies reversible, bias-history-dependent signatures of perovskite ion migration and contact degradation.
Identifies persistent silicon signatures of hydrogen-passivation loss or oxide/contact evolution using lifetime, recombination, and resistance metrics.
Requires subcell-resolved correlation before assigning tandem decay to the TOPCon process.
accepted_equivalents: Light-biased EQE, subcell electroluminescence, luminescence coupling, or another validated subcell-resolved method is acceptable.
Hydrogen profiling may use SIMS, deuterium tracing, FTIR on matched films, or an equivalent approach.
Persistent TOPCon degradation may be expressed as increased J0, reduced implied voltage, increased contact resistivity, or a consistent combination.
common_wrong_answers: Blaming the silicon bottom cell from tandem JV decay alone.
Calling all early burn-in irreversible chemical degradation without testing dark or bias recovery.
Comparing stress tests performed at different temperatures or spectral loads without matching the operating condition.

expected_answer:
A grain-boundary polymer can change the failure mode rather than simply extend lifetime. At an optimum loading, a retained macromolecular bridge may increase intergranular cohesion, blunt cracks, and keep electronically connected perovskite material across a boundary. Under humidity, however, absorbed water or residual solvent can plasticize the polymer, alter its coordination to Pb, lower its glass-transition temperature, and create a faster pathway for ions. Conversely, a stiff or highly cross-linked bridge with a thermal-expansion mismatch may prevent stress relaxation and concentrate strain at the polymer/perovskite interface, causing debonding or transgranular fracture during bending or thermal cycling.

The qualification matrix should cross polymer loading or molecular weight with mechanical strain amplitude, humidity, and temperature cycling. Include polymer-free films, a non-coordinating polymer with matched modulus and hydrophobicity, a small-molecule Lewis-base control, and a polymeric Lewis-base that does not form conductive composite bridges. Measure crack-onset strain, cyclic resistance, fracture energy or adhesion, and spatial PL/EL degradation during in-situ bending. Cross-sectional microscopy and chemical mapping after cycling should locate cracks relative to polymer-rich boundaries.

To identify plasticization, measure water uptake, dynamic mechanical response or glass transition before and after humidity, ionic conductivity under strain and humidity, and bias-driven iodide redistribution. A mechanically beneficial bridge should delay crack initiation, preserve c-AFM or device current across boundaries, and retain low ionic mobility. A water-plasticized pathway should show humidity-dependent softening and ion transport before catastrophic cracking. A brittle constraint should increase local strain and crack density despite low water uptake. Module-level acceptance must include repeated MPP operation during combined mechanical and damp-heat stress, not separate shelf tests. The process is acceptable only if mechanical reliability improves without increased ionic drift, series resistance, or irreversible polymer/perovskite delamination.
scoring_key_points: Identifies beneficial bridging, humidity-induced plasticization/ionic transport, and stress-concentrating brittle constraint as distinct possible outcomes.
Uses matched mechanical and chemical controls to separate coordination chemistry from polymer modulus and hydrophobicity.
Combines in-situ mechanical/electrical imaging with postmortem crack and polymer localization.
Requires combined-strain, humidity, temperature, and MPP qualification with explicit rejection criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Fracture energy may be assessed by peel, double-cantilever, four-point bend, nanoindentation fracture, or another suitable method.
Water plasticization may be diagnosed by DMA, sorption, glass-transition change, swelling, or humidity-dependent modulus.
Electronic continuity may be tracked by c-AFM, sheet resistance, local photocurrent, electroluminescence, or device-level series resistance.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a cross-linked polymer is automatically mechanically tougher under all conditions.
Testing bending and humidity separately and claiming combined-stress durability.
Using only post-stress efficiency without locating cracks or measuring ion migration.

expected_answer:
Reversible voltage loss suggests a state variable that can relax, but several mechanisms can produce it. Host or guest ions may redistribute under the electric field, temporarily changing surface dipoles, band bending, and defect occupancy. The complex may partially deassociate at elevated temperature and reform in the dark. Irreversible chemical decomposition, desorption, or loss of anchoring would instead produce cumulative structural and chemical changes. Transport-layer degradation can mimic interfacial failure while leaving the host-guest chemistry intact.

Use a stress matrix combining open circuit, short circuit, maximum power, and reversed bias at several temperatures, with identical photon dose. Track recovery kinetics after dark rest and after bias reversal. A field-driven redistribution mechanism should depend strongly on bias polarity and accumulated charge, show partial or full reversible recovery, and produce corresponding changes in KPFM/work function, low-frequency capacitance, or depth-resolved guest distribution. Temperature dependence can yield an activation energy for redistribution or decomplexation.

Direct chemical evidence is required before claiming decomposition. Compare pre-stress, stressed, and recovered films by solid-state NMR, FTIR/XPS, and mass or desorption analysis. Stable molecular spectra with reversible spatial redistribution support ionic or conformational reorganization; new chemical species, irreversible loss of host/guest signal, or weakened anchoring support decomposition. PLQY/QFLS and surface LDOS should determine whether passivation is lost, while contact-resolved transient extraction, impedance, and selective-layer controls identify transport-layer degradation.

A useful component-swap control is to age the same interface with alternative hole contacts and to age the hole contact on a stable reference absorber. If voltage loss follows the contact rather than the supramolecular signatures, the HTL is responsible. The mechanism should only be assigned when electrical recovery, chemical state, spatial composition, and bias/temperature dependence are mutually consistent; dark recovery alone is not proof of benign molecular reorientation.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes reversible field-driven redistribution/decomplexation from irreversible chemical loss and separate transport-layer degradation.
Uses bias polarity, operating point, accumulated charge, temperature, and recovery kinetics as mechanistic perturbations.
Requires direct chemical and spatial evidence before assigning decomposition or molecular migration.
Uses contact controls and optoelectronic measurements to localize the loss to passivation, band alignment, or the transport layer.
accepted_equivalents: Chemical-state measurements may include NMR, FTIR, XPS, ToF-SIMS fragments, thermal desorption, or validated mass analysis.
Spatial redistribution may be measured by labelled guests, ToF-SIMS, KPFM-correlated mapping, or another depth/lateral technique.
Alternative selective contacts are acceptable if their band alignment is independently controlled.
common_wrong_answers: Calling any dark-recoverable loss harmless without checking repeated-cycle accumulation.
Inferring molecular decomposition solely from lower device voltage.
Ignoring the possibility that the transport layer, not the supramolecular interface, is degrading.

expected_answer:
Particle interfaces create preferred nucleation sites and can change local solvent evaporation, precursor concentration, and conversion kinetics. Even if the final film is conformal, valleys, particle contacts, or regions with high local particle density may retain PbI2 or another intermediate. A small amount of residual PbI2 can passivate defects initially, but under illumination and heat it can transform, facilitate iodine loss, react with contacts, or create electronically inactive regions. Conversely, PbI2 observed after aging may be a product of perovskite decomposition rather than an initial reservoir.

The study should register pre-aging and post-aging maps to the same geometric locations. Use cross-sectional nano-XRD/GIWAXS, Raman or cathodoluminescence, ToF-SIMS, and electron microscopy to quantify PbI2, halide stoichiometry, particle density, and voids at tips, sidewalls, valleys, and particle interfaces. Initial-state mapping is essential: if PbI2 is already localized before stress and predicts later loss, it is a process residue; if it appears only after local current/PL degradation, it is likely a decomposition product.

Electrical consequence must be measured locally. Correlate PbI2 with PLQY/QFLS, local photocurrent, electroluminescence, contact resistance, and subcell EQE. Protective PbI2 should correlate with lower initial recombination and stable local operation up to an optimum amount. Harmful residual PbI2 should correlate with poor extraction, field concentration, or later phase growth. A degradation product should track iodine depletion, new voids, and loss of perovskite signal.

Process changes should tune conversion rather than remove the nucleation particles indiscriminately: adjust local precursor excess, annealing ramp, antisolvent/gas-quench timing, particle coverage distribution, or introduce a mild post-conversion step that consumes excess PbI2 without dissolving the conformal film. Acceptance requires retained tip coverage, unchanged current matching, low spatial PbI2 variance, and improved MPP stability across texture locations.
scoring_key_points: Links preferred particle nucleation to spatially nonuniform precursor conversion and possible PbI2 reservoirs.
Distinguishes initial residual PbI2, beneficial passivation, harmful transport effects, and PbI2 formed by degradation.
Uses registered pre/post spatial phase, composition, and local electrical mapping across texture locations.
Proposes conversion-focused process modifications with conformality, current-matching, and stability acceptance criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Nano-XRD may be replaced by microbeam diffraction, Raman, cathodoluminescence, or another phase-sensitive spatial method.
Local electrical loss may be assessed by photocurrent, EL, lock-in thermography, KPFM, or subcell-resolved mapping.
Post-conversion treatment may be chemical, thermal, vapor, or photonic if it preserves film coverage and interfaces.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming all PbI2 is either always beneficial or always harmful.
Using only a final averaged XRD pattern without pre-aging spatial information.
Reducing particle coverage until PbI2 disappears without checking that pyramid tips remain covered.

expected_answer:
The surface treatment and the bulk additive act on partly different state variables. The diammonium iodide can passivate under-coordinated surface sites and reduce non-radiative recombination, explaining higher PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting. However, it also leaves an iodide-rich top region. That region can increase the concentration or chemical activity of mobile iodide species, so the device becomes electronically cleaner but ionically less stable. The bulk additive need not produce a proportionate further decrease in electronic trap density to suppress hysteresis. Its cation can reversibly coordinate or hydrogen-bond to iodide, while chloride can occupy or neutralize iodine-vacancy-related migration sites. The main change is therefore a lower mobile-ion population and/or a higher hopping barrier, not merely fewer recombination centers.

Under a voltage pulse, the optimized device should show a smaller slow current component, a shorter or lower-amplitude post-pulse relaxation, and less history dependence; the fast electronic transient may change much less. Temperature-dependent measurements should yield an Arrhenius slope consistent with a larger ionic activation barrier and a stronger suppression of hysteresis at a given temperature. Dark or illuminated preconditioning should produce less persistent J–V displacement and less recovery drift because illumination-generated fields no longer redistribute ions as readily. Depth profiling should show the surface diammonium species concentrated near the top interface, whereas the bulk-additive cation and chloride-related signal should extend through the absorber and toward both interfaces. A decisive model would jointly fit pulse-relaxation time constants, scan-rate dependence and temperature dependence with separate electronic and ionic branches. Attributing all improvements to trap passivation would fail because it cannot explain the large activation-energy change and the spatial complementarity of a surface treatment and a bulk ion-binding additive.
scoring_key_points: Separates surface electronic passivation from an iodide-excess-driven increase in mobile-ion activity.
Explains the bulk cation/chloride pair as raising the migration barrier and/or lowering the mobile-ion population through iodide binding and vacancy filling.
Predicts reduced slow bias-relaxation, weaker preconditioning memory and a larger Arrhenius activation energy without requiring a proportional electronic trap-density change.
Predicts surface-localized diammonium species but bulk-distributed additive ions and identifies a coupled electronic–ionic kinetic model as the proper test.
accepted_equivalents: ionic trapping or ion binding for hydrogen-bond-mediated immobilization
vacancy passivation for chloride occupation of iodine-vacancy migration sites
a reduced mobile-ion density instead of, or in addition to, a larger hopping barrier
common_wrong_answers: Saying that higher PLQY alone proves ion migration is suppressed.
Assuming chloride improves performance only by changing the bandgap.
Predicting identical fast electronic and slow ionic transients.
Treating the surface and bulk species as spatially uniform without depth-profile evidence.

expected_answer:
The measurements probe different populations and electrical boundary conditions, so their characteristic times cannot be ranked as one universal carrier lifetime. In a perovskite/HTL stack, photoluminescence decays through both recombination and transfer of holes into the HTL. A much shorter TRPL decay after strain relief can therefore indicate faster interfacial hole extraction, provided that independent device measurements show lower recombination rather than a new non-radiative sink. The accompanying shorter transient-photocurrent time supports this interpretation because short-circuit or extraction conditions allow carriers to leave the absorber; faster decay of the photocurrent transient means the stored photocarrier population is removed more rapidly.

Transient photovoltage is measured near open circuit, where net extraction is suppressed. Its decay is governed more directly by recombination of the excess carrier population. A longer TPV lifetime after treatment is therefore consistent with slower recombination and a higher attainable quasi-Fermi-level splitting. The ideality factor moving from a trap-assisted value toward one is an independent signature that Shockley–Read–Hall recombination has been reduced. Together, the data describe faster useful extraction under current-producing conditions and slower loss under voltage-producing conditions.

Strain relief can produce this combination by flattening an unfavorable vertical band-edge gradient, improving contact coupling and reducing strain-associated deep defects. A bare-film TRPL experiment may even lengthen because no extraction layer is present; that result would reflect reduced bulk recombination, whereas the contact-stack TRPL can shorten because transfer dominates. Correct interpretation therefore requires a kinetic scheme with at least bulk radiative/non-radiative recombination, interfacial transfer and extraction terms. The claim is credible only when shorter contact-stack TRPL coexists with faster TPC, longer TPV, higher recombination resistance, improved electroluminescence or voltage, and no evidence for added interfacial quenching defects.
scoring_key_points: Explains that contact-stack TRPL includes charge transfer and can shorten because extraction accelerates.
Interprets shorter TPC as faster carrier removal under extraction/short-circuit conditions.
Interprets longer TPV and near-unity ideality factor as reduced recombination under open-circuit conditions.
Uses a multi-rate kinetic model and independent recombination diagnostics, rejecting the universal rule that longer optical lifetime is always better.
accepted_equivalents: interfacial quenching for charge-transfer-induced TRPL shortening
open-circuit small-signal lifetime for TPV lifetime
SRH suppression for the ideality-factor improvement
common_wrong_answers: Calling the shorter TRPL lifetime proof of worse non-radiative recombination.
Calling every longer transient lifetime improved extraction.
Ignoring the different open-circuit and short-circuit boundary conditions.
Explaining the four trends only by increased absorption.

expected_answer:
A separately deposited interlayer can passivate the perovskite surface, but it fixes the molecule mainly at one plane and may leave a weakly coupled boundary to the polymer. The blend permits the bifunctional molecule to partition dynamically during coating and drying. The coordinating end lowers the free energy of locating at the perovskite surface, while the conjugated or aromatic end remains compatible with the polymer and can participate in local chain organization. The result is a graded molecular bridge rather than a discrete insulating sheet: sufficient molecules reach surface defects, while their polymer-facing groups maintain electronic and structural continuity into the hole-transport layer.

Below the optimum concentration, coverage is incomplete. Residual under-coordinated sites sustain trap-assisted recombination, and the polymer still contacts the heterogeneous perovskite poorly. Increasing concentration raises passivated-site fraction and can improve local polymer registry or wetting, so voltage and fill factor rise. Around the optimum, the vertical profile contains enough interface-enriched bridge molecules to saturate high-affinity sites without disrupting the host’s percolating transport network.

Above the optimum, excess molecules remain in the polymer bulk or form aggregates. They can dilute conductive polymer pathways, introduce energetic disorder, impede interchain hopping, alter drying kinetics, or create a dipole/space-charge layer that accumulates carriers. If the passivating end binds too strongly, excess coverage may also make a dense tunnelling barrier. Consequently, conductivity and fill factor can fall even though XPS still indicates strong surface binding and PL may remain quenched.

The model predicts a concentration-dependent vertical composition measurable by angle-resolved XPS, neutron reflectometry or depth profiling; a saturating surface-binding signal; a non-monotonic conductivity/contact resistance; and polymer-order changes localized near the interface rather than a wholesale bulk phase change. The blend outperforms the preformed interlayer when co-deposition produces simultaneous defect saturation and polymer-side connectivity. Rescue by a molecule with only the passivating end, or by an inert spacer, should fail to reproduce the complete optimum.
scoring_key_points: Explains blend superiority through interfacial partitioning and simultaneous perovskite-side binding and polymer-side continuity.
Predicts incomplete defect coverage and persistent recombination below the optimum.
Predicts excess-molecule aggregation, dilution, energetic disorder or tunnelling resistance above the optimum.
Proposes measurable vertical enrichment, saturating binding and non-monotonic conductivity/contact resistance rather than a wholesale bulk-polymer transformation.
accepted_equivalents: interfacial segregation for thermodynamic partitioning to the perovskite surface
graded interface for the blended molecular bridge
percolation dilution or hopping disruption for the high-concentration transport penalty
common_wrong_answers: Treating the bridge solely as a conventional p-type dopant.
Assuming more passivating molecule must always improve performance.
Explaining the blend advantage only by a change in bulk polymer crystallinity.
Ignoring the possibility that a dense molecular layer becomes electrically resistive.

expected_answer:
Hysteresis arises when the electronic carrier distribution and slower ionic or capacitive polarization evolve on comparable time scales. If the electron contact extracts much more slowly than the hole contact, electrons accumulate at the electron-selective interface. The local field and interfacial recombination then depend strongly on scan direction and dwell history. Raising electron mobility and improving conduction-band alignment can reduce this imbalance, empty the interface more rapidly and make the electronic response less sensitive to the slower ionic state.

The optimum is not infinite mobility. Once transport through the electron contact is no longer rate limiting, further mobility provides little benefit. If the work function or interfacial dipole is shifted too far, the contact can become nonselective, reduce the built-in potential or facilitate minority-carrier leakage. Very high carrier density can also increase interfacial Auger or bimolecular loss, while a highly conductive but poorly passivated surface may transmit carriers quickly into a recombination-active interface. Excess chemical modifier can introduce an insulating chelate-rich phase or alter perovskite nucleation adversely. Thus voltage, dark leakage or recombination can worsen even while the ETL’s lateral or SCLC mobility rises.

Flux balancing predicts that the hysteresis minimum occurs when extraction time constants at the two contacts become comparable. Impedance should show reduced interfacial charge-accumulation capacitance, a shorter transport time and a larger recombination resistance, while the bulk ionic feature may remain present. Scan-rate dependence should narrow because the electronic bottleneck is removed, but temperature-derived ionic activation energy need not change greatly. Pure trap passivation instead should primarily lower recombination current, increase PL lifetime or QFLS, and reduce trap-related capacitance even if the extraction asymmetry remains. A decisive experiment independently varies mobility and surface passivation: for example, use matched-wetting ETLs with different mobility, and matched-mobility ETLs with different defect chemistry. The flux-balance model is supported when hysteresis correlates with the ratio of electron and hole extraction times rather than with electron mobility or trap density alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains hysteresis reduction through removal of electron-side charge accumulation and matching of electron/hole extraction time scales.
Rejects unlimited mobility as the objective and identifies over-shifted energetics, nonselectivity, leakage or interfacial recombination as high-mobility failure modes.
Predicts reduced accumulation capacitance and a hysteresis minimum near matched extraction times, without requiring a large change in ionic activation energy.
Distinguishes flux balance from trap passivation using independent mobility/passivation controls and correlations with extraction-time ratios.
accepted_equivalents: carrier-flux matching for extraction-time balance
transport resistance and chemical capacitance for the relevant impedance terms
minority-carrier blocking loss for excessive contact-energy shift
common_wrong_answers: Stating that the highest possible ETL mobility always gives the best device.
Equating reduced hysteresis with elimination of all mobile ions.
Using only PL quenching as proof of flux balance.
Ignoring the hole contact and built-in potential.

expected_answer:
A phase census does not determine device operation unless the spatial ordering of those phases is also known. Low-n domains have wider gaps and larger band offsets, whereas high-n domains are lower-gap collection sites. In Film A, photocarriers generated near the top can funnel toward high-n material closer to the electron-selective contact. This may shorten the electron extraction path, but holes must still reach the top contact without being trapped in low-gap regions or blocked by low-n barriers. In Film B, high-n wells near the hole contact may aid hole collection but can force electrons to cross more wide-gap interfaces before reaching the bottom electron contact. Thus the same PL lifetime can coexist with different minority-carrier transit times, interfacial carrier accumulation, and recombination losses.

Front/back excitation is diagnostic because it changes where carriers are generated relative to the gradient. Bias-dependent EQE or photocurrent measured from both illumination directions should reveal whether collection becomes worse when carriers are created on the side from which the minority carrier must traverse the unfavorable phase sequence. Time-resolved extraction or transient absorption collected from both surfaces should show different transfer and depletion kinetics even if ensemble PL is similar. Spatially resolved quasi-Fermi-level splitting can further reveal whether low-gap domains accumulate both carrier types and create local non-radiative sinks.

Swapping to a p-i-n architecture reverses which gradient is favorable. If the performance ranking of Films A and B also reverses, the dominant effect is phase-position/contact selectivity rather than an intrinsic difference in phase quality. If the ranking does not reverse, one should suspect additional asymmetries such as buried-interface defects, optical-generation profiles, or unequal vertical connectivity. The decisive conclusion therefore requires phase-depth mapping combined with direction-dependent transport, not PL alone.
scoring_key_points: Explains that identical phase fractions and PL do not fix transport because vertical band-offset ordering controls carrier pathways and accumulation.
Connects the two gradients to asymmetric electron and hole extraction in an n-i-p stack, including possible barrier crossing and low-gap trapping.
Predicts illumination-direction-dependent EQE/photocurrent or transient signatures that locate the unfavorable transport direction.
Uses selective-contact polarity reversal as a causal test and states how a reversed performance ranking would support the gradient mechanism.
accepted_equivalents: A vertical energetic cascade or phase-depth-ordering explanation is acceptable.
Front/back excitation may be described as substrate-side versus air-side illumination.
Contact reversal may be implemented by comparing matched n-i-p and p-i-n stacks.
common_wrong_answers: The two films must perform identically because their PL lifetime and phase fractions are identical.
Only the total low-n fraction matters; its depth location is irrelevant.
The film with the strongest low-energy PL must always have the highest fill factor.

expected_answer:
Ordinary geometric confinement weakens as a quantum dot becomes larger: the carrier wavefunction occupies a larger volume, Coulomb interactions decrease, biexciton Auger-Meitner recombination slows, and biexciton emission becomes increasingly competitive. In a purely geometric picture, the biexciton lifetime should lengthen and g2(0) should rise with edge length, causing large dots to lose antibunching even if their exciton quantum yield remains high.

Dynamic localization changes the relevant volume. If room-temperature soft-lattice fluctuations restrict the electron-hole wavefunction to an approximately size-independent nanometre-scale region, the effective Auger interaction can remain strong as the physical crystal grows. FAPbBr3 should therefore show a much weaker increase of biexciton lifetime and g2(0) with physical size than CsPbBr3. Large hybrid dots may retain high exciton brightness because the desired single-exciton radiative channel is not strongly quenched, while the biexciton is selectively removed by the faster non-radiative Auger channel. The central signature is thus size-decoupling: optical cross-section and count rate can increase with dot volume, but antibunching remains governed by the smaller localization volume.

Temperature provides a causal test. Cooling should suppress the thermally activated dynamic disorder and delocalize the wavefunction relative to the room-temperature localized state. In large FAPbBr3 dots, biexciton lifetime should then lengthen and g2(0) worsen toward the geometric-confinement trend. Small dots may remain antibunched because hard-wall confinement is already sufficient. The inorganic CsPbBr3 control should show a smaller or qualitatively different temperature response because it lacks the same hybrid-lattice dynamics.

The comparison must be made at matched absorbed excitation probability, surface passivation, charge state, and exciton quantum yield. A plateau of room-temperature g2(0) and biexciton lifetime versus physical size, followed by loss of that plateau on cooling or lattice stiffening, would strongly support phonon-controlled effective volume.
scoring_key_points: Contrasts geometric confinement, which weakens with dot size, with a size-independent dynamically localized effective volume.
Predicts weak size dependence of FAPbBr3 biexciton lifetime and g2(0), but stronger degradation in size-matched CsPbBr3 controls.
Explains why exciton brightness can remain high while biexciton emission is selectively quenched.
Predicts loss of the localization advantage on cooling/lattice stiffening, especially for large hybrid dots, with matched excitation and surface controls.
accepted_equivalents: Auger-Meitner recombination may be called biexciton Auger quenching.
The localization volume may be described through inverse participation ratio or wavefunction extent.
Lattice stiffening may be produced by cooling, pressure, isotopic substitution, or cation substitution.
common_wrong_answers: Larger physical dots must always have poorer single-photon purity in every material.
A low g2(0) necessarily requires a low exciton quantum yield.
Cooling should strengthen a mechanism that is explicitly driven by thermal lattice motion.

expected_answer:
The charge-separation descriptor is local and primarily describes how an organic bilayer interaction distorts an adjacent inorganic sheet. A larger in-plane Pb-I-Pb angle can increase orbital overlap, narrow the bandgap, and improve in-plane mobility within a well. A planar solar cell, however, extracts carriers across many layers and phases. Its fill factor can remain limited by vertical orientation, organic-barrier thickness, phase distribution, interwell energetic offsets, grain boundaries, and contact resistance. Therefore a genuine local CSD effect can coexist with unchanged out-of-plane mobility.

The additional descriptor should quantify vertical electronic connectivity rather than duplicate local octahedral geometry. Suitable forms include an effective interwell tunnelling/activation barrier, the fraction and tortuosity of vertically connected inorganic slabs, or a depth-resolved phase-and-orientation connectivity index. It should incorporate spacer dielectric character and interlayer distance where those control wavefunction overlap. For n>1 films, a phase-distribution term is also needed because low-n/high-n segregation can dominate transport even when each local sheet is structurally favorable.

Validation should proceed in stages. First, confirm that the n=1 structural trend transfers locally to n=4 by GIWAXS/PDF and spectroscopy rather than assuming identical crystal structures. Second, map phase fractions and depth-dependent orientation. Third, measure in-plane and out-of-plane conductivity over temperature to separate intrinsic band transport from activated interwell crossing. Transient extraction, time-of-flight, and impedance should determine whether vertical transit or contacts set the fill factor. Matched devices with varied contact work functions can isolate contact resistance.

CSD is predictive when higher values reproducibly improve local band structure and the film already possesses comparable vertical connectivity, phase distribution, and contacts. It is insufficient when those extrinsic variables vary or when the spacer that improves in-plane overlap simultaneously raises the vertical barrier. A multivariate model using both CSD and a vertical-connectivity descriptor should predict mobility and device metrics better than either alone.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes local/in-plane structural effects of CSD from vertical transport through a multilayer n=4 film.
Identifies orientation, interwell barriers, phase distribution, grain boundaries, and contacts as reasons for unchanged out-of-plane mobility.
Proposes a vertical-connectivity or effective-barrier descriptor in addition to CSD.
Defines a staged structural, anisotropic-transport, transient, and contact-control workflow and a boundary for CSD validity.
accepted_equivalents: The second descriptor may be an interlayer transfer integral, activation energy, percolation index, or vertical slab-connectivity metric.
Depth-resolved GIWAXS, tomography, or cross-sectional microscopy may map vertical connectivity.
Out-of-plane mobility may be measured by SCLC, time-of-flight, or vertical FET/diode methods with appropriate controls.
common_wrong_answers: High in-plane mobility guarantees a high fill factor in a vertical solar cell.
An unchanged out-of-plane mobility disproves every local structural effect of the spacer.
CSD alone should predict all n-values, morphologies, and device architectures without additional variables.

expected_answer:
Confinement raises the free-energy cost of forming a segregated nucleus through finite domain size and the host-guest interface.
