It does not make the illuminated free energy independent of carrier population. At the same absorbed generation rate, a longer carrier lifetime produces a larger steady-state carrier density. Those carriers preferentially lower their energy in a small iodide-rich, narrower-gap fluctuation, thereby increasing the electronic driving force for demixing and reducing the critical nucleation barrier. Composite L can therefore segregate sooner even though it has fewer traps and an identical structural confinement geometry.

Trap passivation has competing effects. It removes defect-assisted ion-migration pathways and local nucleation sites, which should improve kinetic stability. But it also prolongs carrier residence and increases quasi-Fermi-level splitting, which can strengthen carrier-induced thermodynamic instability. Which effect dominates depends on generation rate, recombination order, composition, temperature, and the interface penalty. Comparing samples only at equal incident power mixes these effects because their absorbed flux, PLQY, and steady-state carrier densities differ.

The decisive experiment should quantify carrier density directly. Absolute PLQY and calibrated quasi-Fermi-level splitting, combined with transient lifetime and charge-density-dependent recombination, can convert absorbed generation into steady-state density. Illumination should then be adjusted so that L and S are compared at the same carrier density, and separately at the same generation rate. Operando hyperspectral PL should measure segregation onset and growth; transient absorption or time-resolved PL can verify carrier occupation of emerging low-gap states. Temperature and pulsed-duty-cycle variation can separate thermodynamic carrier-density effects from cumulative ion motion and heating.

If L is less stable at equal generation but equal to or more stable than S at matched carrier density, the earlier red-shift arose from its higher carrier population, not failure of confinement. If L remains less stable at matched density, passivation may have changed ion diffusivity, interface energy, or hidden morphology despite nominally matched structure. A valid model must use carrier density, not incident power, as the illuminated thermodynamic variable.
scoring_key_points: Explains that a longer lifetime raises steady-state carrier density at the same absorbed generation rate.
Connects higher carrier density to stabilization of low-gap iodide-rich fluctuations and a reduced nucleation barrier.
Recognizes the competing benefit of trap passivation through fewer defect-assisted migration/nucleation pathways.
Requires absolute carrier-density calibration and compares segregation at matched carrier density as well as matched generation rate.
accepted_equivalents: Carrier density may be inferred from calibrated PLQY/QFLS plus recombination kinetics or from charge-extraction methods.
Carrier-induced free energy may be described as quasi-Fermi-level, polaron, or photocarrier stabilization of iodide-rich domains.
Duty-cycle or pulsed-excitation controls may be used to separate population effects from heating and cumulative migration.
common_wrong_answers: Fewer traps must always produce slower phase separation at every excitation condition.
Equal incident or absorbed power guarantees equal steady-state carrier density.
The confinement mechanism predicts phase stability independent of carrier lifetime and quasi-Fermi-level splitting.

expected_answer:
A power-dependent PL peak is not a direct thermometer unless the carrier distribution and band edges are independently known. In a degenerate or partially degenerate semiconductor, band filling raises the emission energy because electrons and holes occupy states away from the band extrema. For parabolic bands, the shift scales roughly with carrier density to the two-thirds power divided by an effective-mass factor. A larger low-temperature shift can therefore arise from a smaller effective mass, reduced thermal broadening, a sharper occupation edge, different carrier density at the same incident fluence, or fewer thermally activated traps, even if the energy-loss rate is unchanged.

Carrier-density calibration is particularly important in FASnI3 because absorption, recombination coefficients, self-p-doping, and trap capture vary with temperature. The same pump fluence may create different instantaneous and time-integrated carrier densities. Disorder and band-tail occupation also change with temperature; carriers may fill tail states before band states at one temperature but not the other. Temperature-dependent bandgap shifts must be subtracted from the excitation-induced shift.

Slow cooling is a dynamical claim. It requires energy-resolved transient emission or absorption that follows the high-energy distribution at matched carrier density and pump excess energy. A carrier temperature should be extracted from the high-energy tail with a justified distribution function, and its decay should be compared across temperatures after correcting for band filling and bandgap renormalization. Sub-picosecond measurements are needed to capture initial cooling, while nanosecond data establish any long-lived component.

Thus the 150 meV shift at 24 K supports stronger density-dependent state filling or a different non-equilibrium distribution, but it does not by itself determine the cooling time. Slower low-temperature cooling would require a demonstrably slower decay of carrier temperature or excess energy, not merely a larger peak displacement. Conversely, a large static shift with identical transient cooling would be fully compatible with band-structure and occupation effects.
scoring_key_points: Explains that a PL blue shift can arise from band filling and is not by itself a carrier-cooling time.
Includes effective mass, Fermi broadening, disorder/tails, and temperature-dependent carrier-density calibration.
Requires subtraction/control of bandgap shifts and comparison at matched absorbed carrier density and pump excess energy.
Defines slow cooling through time-resolved carrier-temperature/excess-energy decay rather than steady-state peak displacement.
accepted_equivalents: Burstein-Moss-like filling may be used as an equivalent term.
Energy-resolved TRPL, transient absorption, or time-resolved photoemission are acceptable dynamic probes.
Carrier temperature may be obtained from a high-energy Boltzmann/Fermi-Dirac tail with appropriate caveats.
common_wrong_answers: The larger 24 K blue shift proves a twofold longer cooling time.
Incident fluence is automatically equivalent to the same carrier density at all temperatures.
Band filling cannot occur in a disordered, self-doped tin perovskite.

expected_answer:
The test matrix must vary stressors independently before combining them. Use matched cells and mini-modules under light at open circuit, short circuit, and maximum power; dark heat; damp heat; thermal cycling; and humidity-only exposure. Encapsulated and unencapsulated devices, edge-seal coupons, absorber-only films, and contact half-stacks should be aged in parallel. Open circuit imposes a different internal field and carrier density from maximum power, while damp heat adds water transport and interfacial chemistry, so survival in one state does not predict the other.

Absorber phase instability should be tracked by operando or periodic GIWAXS/XRD, absorption, and hyperspectral PL. Composition-dependent phase changes that occur in absorber-only films under the same heat/light stress support a bulk branch. Grain-boundary ion transport is better identified by bias-polarity dependence, low-frequency impedance, surface-potential mapping, and spatially resolved halide or cation redistribution. A rise in hysteresis that relaxes after dark rest suggests a mobile-ion component, but irreversible spectral or chemical changes indicate more than polarization.

Buried-interface and contact failure require half-stack PLQY/QFLS, electroluminescence imaging, contact resistance, work-function mapping, and depth-resolved chemical analysis. Local voltage loss or hot spots that precede bulk diffraction changes point to interfaces. Encapsulation leakage should be mapped using water-vapour transmission coupons, calcium or humidity sensors, edge-versus-centre degradation fronts, and isotope-labelled moisture. Delamination requires acoustic microscopy, adhesion tests, and cross-sectional imaging to determine whether it is a cause or late consequence.

The programme should define a temporal failure map: first detectable water ingress, ion redistribution, QFLS loss, resistance change, phase change, and mechanical separation. Only the earliest spatially co-located signature with an appropriate isolated-stress control should be assigned as initiating failure. Report lifetime with temperature, humidity, illumination, electrical load, encapsulation, area, and retention criterion; a 1,000-hour open-circuit result is one protocol, not a universal commercial lifetime.
scoring_key_points: Uses independent and combined light, bias, heat, humidity, and cycling stresses with absorber, half-stack, seal, cell, and module controls.
Distinguishes bulk phase change and grain-boundary ion transport using structural, spectral, bias-dependent, impedance, and spatial-composition evidence.
Localizes interface/contact and encapsulation failures through QFLS/EL, resistance, chemical depth profiling, ingress sensors, and degradation-front mapping.
Requires temporal and spatial precedence and reports protocol metadata rather than extrapolating open-circuit light soaking to universal lifetime.
accepted_equivalents: Operando Raman or synchrotron scattering may replace conventional XRD for phase tracking.
Thin-film moisture dosimeters or embedded impedance humidity sensors are acceptable alternatives to calcium tests.
Electroluminescence or photoluminescence imaging may be used to map local voltage loss if calibrated against electrical data.
common_wrong_answers: Calls the module stable because it survived 1,000 hours under any single condition.
Attributes all damp-heat loss to the perovskite absorber without seal or half-stack controls.
Treats delamination observed at the end of the test as proof that mechanical failure initiated the degradation.

expected_answer:
The cycling waveform should be decomposed into isothermal holds and temperature transitions. Age matched devices at -40 °C, 85 °C, and room temperature without cycling, and compare them with full-cycle samples having identical cumulative hot time. If performance changes only during transitions, thermal-expansion mismatch and fatigue are implicated; if the same loss occurs during the 85 °C hold, thermal molecular disorder or desorption is sufficient.

Reversible molecular disorder should be identified by temperature-dependent work function, surface-potential heterogeneity on witness contacts, and reversible changes in contact resistance or electroluminescence after returning to room temperature. Molecular desorption is irreversible and should produce a cumulative loss of electrochemically measured coverage, phosphorous- or molecular-fragment transfer to the opposite fracture surface, and mass or chemical loss that does not recover after equilibration. A covalently linked contact should show smaller changes than a noncovalent or monolayer control.

Mechanical initiation requires interrupted cycling before visible delamination. Use acoustic microscopy, X-ray tomography, cross-sectional SEM, and double-cantilever-beam or peel tests to locate subcritical voids and quantify adhesion-energy loss. Spatial electroluminescence/PL and lock-in thermography should test whether dark spots co-localize with nascent voids. If QFLS decreases locally only where cracks appear while absorber-only witness films remain unchanged, buried-interface recombination is secondary to mechanical separation.

Bulk absorber degradation must be checked independently by absorption, GIWAXS/XRD, PLQY/QFLS on delaminated or contact-free films, and composition mapping. A valid sequence could be reversible molecular packing disorder during early cycles, cumulative desorption and adhesion loss, crack/void formation, then permanent interfacial recombination and FF loss. Alternatively, chemical absorber degradation may precede fracture; only early interrupted states can decide. The sequence should be reported by cycle count and temperature phase, not inferred from the final fracture surface.
scoring_key_points: Separates isothermal heat/cold holds from thermal transitions and matches cumulative hot time to identify fatigue versus heat-only processes.
Distinguishes reversible molecular disorder from irreversible desorption through recovery, coverage, surface-potential, and chemical-transfer measurements.
Captures subcritical cracks/voids and spatially correlates them with EL/PL, contact resistance, adhesion, and recombination before macroscopic delamination.
Uses absorber-only structural and QFLS controls and interrupted-cycle temporal evidence to establish failure order.
accepted_equivalents: Infrared thermography, scanning acoustic microscopy, or X-ray laminography may be used for non-destructive void detection.
Coverage may be quantified by cyclic voltammetry, radiolabelling, quartz-crystal microbalance witnesses, or quantitative XPS.
Interfacial fracture testing may use DCB, peel, or four-point bend methods if fracture location is chemically verified.
common_wrong_answers: Calls all thermal-cycle loss mechanical because delamination is visible at the end.
Uses reversible room-temperature recovery to rule out cumulative desorption or subcritical damage.
Attributes EL dark spots directly to bulk perovskite decomposition without spatial fracture or QFLS controls.

expected_answer:
The tandem must first be electrically decomposed. Use bias-light-dependent EQE to obtain each subcell current, selective illumination to perturb current matching, and subcell electroluminescence or luminescence coupling to estimate individual voltages. If selective light restores tandem fill factor and power while each isolated subcell remains efficient, the primary problem is current mismatch. A recombination-junction failure should instead produce added series resistance or non-ohmic voltage loss affecting both subcells, detectable by impedance, temperature-dependent J-V, and dedicated junction-only structures.

Delayed residual-solvent damage should be tested with solvent-residue depth profiles, thermal desorption, and cross-sectional microscopy at early ageing times. Voids or interfacial swelling that develop where coordinating solvent was trapped should correlate with local current loss and may accelerate under heat even without illumination. Process controls with longer solvent-release time but matched fresh efficiency are needed to test this branch.

The low-bandgap Sn-Pb cell requires oxidation-sensitive diagnostics: Sn4+ mapping, oxygen-isotope tracing, QFLS, and rear-side hyperspectral PL. A loss in bottom-cell current or QFLS with localized Sn oxidation identifies that subcell. The wide-bandgap top cell requires surface-sensitive, spatially resolved hyperspectral PL, nano-XRD, and halide-composition mapping because small segregated domains may be invisible in averaged spectra. Bias and dark-rest reversibility can distinguish reversible segregation from permanent decomposition.

Optical changes must also be excluded by measuring reflectance, transmission into the bottom cell, and parasitic absorption of the interconnect. The initiating layer is the one whose local chemical or electrical signature appears before tandem-current loss and is reproduced in an isolated subcell or layer stack. Final-state microscopy alone is insufficient. A defensible diagnosis combines temporal precedence, subcell-selective electrical loss, spatial co-localization, and selective recovery or barrier controls.
scoring_key_points: Uses subcell-resolved EQE, selective illumination, subcell voltage/luminescence, and junction-only controls to separate mismatch and recombination-junction failure.
Tests delayed residual-solvent damage with residue analysis, thermal desorption, void mapping, and matched-process controls.
Localizes Sn-Pb oxidation and sparse WBG halide segregation with subcell-specific chemistry, QFLS, and spatially resolved spectroscopy.
Requires temporal precedence, optical-loss exclusion, spatial co-localization, and selective recovery before assigning the first failing layer.
accepted_equivalents: Three-terminal diagnostic tandems or mechanically stacked reference tandems may substitute for some subcell-selective measurements.
Photoluminescence excitation tomography or filtered EL imaging may replace near-field hyperspectral mapping if small domains are resolved.
Transfer-matrix modelling is acceptable for optical loss only when constrained by measured spectra.
common_wrong_answers: Uses unchanged total Voc to conclude that neither subcell nor the recombination junction degraded.
Rules out halide segregation solely because the spatially averaged PL spectrum does not split.
Calls any tandem-current reduction current mismatch without measuring independent subcell performance.

expected_answer:
Humidity, heat, and thermal transitions must be separated. Age matched films, perovskite/chelate half-stacks, perovskite/chelate/C60 stacks, and full devices under dry heat, constant damp heat, humidity cycling at fixed temperature, and dry thermal cycling. If low-QFLS spots appear only during temperature transitions, mechanical fracture is favoured; if they appear under constant humidity, dissolution or water-enabled chemistry may be sufficient.

Chelate retention and integrity should be measured before large oxidation. Use quantitative XPS or labelled-diamine mass balance, GIWAXS/low-q structural signatures, nanoscale chemical mapping, and cross-sectional microscopy. Desorption or dissolution produces molecular loss; cracking preserves average amount but creates spatial gaps. Acoustic microscopy, AFM nanomechanics, or tomography can detect subcritical voids and cracks. Co-localization of these gaps with low-QFLS spots would place mechanical barrier failure before oxidation.

Ingress and oxidation require controlled isotopes and spatial chemistry. Use labelled water or oxygen, NanoSIMS/ToF-SIMS, and Sn2+/Sn4+ mapping. If isotope uptake appears first through barrier gaps and is followed by local Sn4+ and conductivity changes, ingress is secondary to cracking. A renewed Sn-rich surface can be tested by local Sn:Pb mapping; selective removal of excess Sn should disappear where the barrier remains intact but re-emerge at failed sites.

A direct chelate-C60 reaction is tested by ageing C60/chelate model stacks without perovskite and by spectroscopy for new adducts, energy-level shifts, or fullerene reduction. If contact resistance rises before molecular loss, cracking, or Sn oxidation, this branch may initiate failure. Interrupted tests at early cycle counts, followed by dry-rest and humidity-removal recovery, distinguish reversible water doping from irreversible oxidation. The initiating mechanism is the earliest spatially resolved change reproduced in its isolated stack and prevented by a targeted modification such as crosslinking, hydrophobic encapsulation, or a mechanically compliant overlayer.
scoring_key_points: Separates constant heat, constant humidity, humidity cycling, and dry thermal cycling across films, half-stacks, C60 stacks, and full devices.
Distinguishes molecular loss from barrier cracking through quantitative retention, nanoscale chemistry, mechanics, and co-localized QFLS mapping.
Traces water/oxygen ingress, renewed Sn-rich exposure, and Sn oxidation with isotope-resolved spatial measurements and temporal order.
Tests direct chelate-C60 chemistry in model stacks and uses interrupted stresses plus targeted prevention to identify the initiating event.
accepted_equivalents: Radiolabelled chelate, deuterated diamine, or quartz-crystal witness samples may replace one quantitative-retention method.
X-ray tomography, scanning acoustic microscopy, or conductive-AFM gap mapping may be used for barrier-crack detection.
Operando near-ambient-pressure XPS may combine ingress and oxidation tracking if spatial resolution is adequate.
common_wrong_answers: Attributes the failure to Sn oxidation because Sn4+ is high at the end of the test.
Calls average chelate retention proof that the barrier did not crack locally.
Assumes rising C60 contact resistance is caused by oxidation without testing chelate-C60 model stacks.

expected_answer:
The accelerated waveform should reproduce module electrical boundary conditions rather than apply an arbitrary constant reverse voltage. Use programmable shading of one or multiple subcells while the module operates near its maximum-power voltage, with controlled ramp rate, dwell time, recovery time, irradiance, temperature, and bypass-diode state. Include constant-voltage cell tests only as mechanistic references. Vary pulse duty cycle at fixed cumulative reverse-bias charge to determine whether peak field, time at bias, or recovery controls damage.

Reversible ionic polarization should be identified by immediate threshold or leakage shifts, low-frequency capacitance, surface-potential gradients, and relaxation during dark or zero-bias rest without chemical change. The persistent branch requires spatially registered leakage, electroluminescence, PL, and thermal imaging after selected pulse counts. If hot spots precede persistent leakage, Joule heating or interconnect resistance may initiate failure; if leakage precedes heating, electrochemical shunting is more likely.

Interconnect and scribe damage should be tested with four-terminal segment resistance, optical coherence or X-ray imaging, and control modules without Cu near the scribe. Mechanical edge defects should remain localized to the patterning geometry and may respond to thermal cycling even without reverse bias. Cumulative iodine-Cu chemistry requires time-resolved CuI/iodine-state mapping and Cu depth profiling at the same hot spots. Incipient filaments should produce nonlinear local conductance, random-telegraph behaviour, and metallic Cu signatures before full shorting.

Mechanism-faithful acceleration requires that the ordering of signatures match realistic shading: reversible ionic response first, then persistent CuI/leakage or edge damage, then hot-spot amplification and possible filament formation. Compare reinforced and component-ablated modules, Cu-free controls, and modules with altered interconnect geometry. Pass/fail criteria should include leakage growth per shading charge, recovery fraction, maximum local temperature, subcell PCE retention, and absence of persistent chemical/metallic shunts, not merely survival without catastrophic breakdown.
scoring_key_points: Uses realistic module shading waveforms with controlled peak bias, duty cycle, recovery, irradiance, temperature, and bypass conditions.
Distinguishes reversible ionic leakage from persistent damage through relaxation, capacitance, potential mapping, and absence/presence of chemical change.
Localizes Joule heating, interconnect/scribe damage, iodine-Cu chemistry, and incipient filaments with registered electrical, thermal, structural, and chemical maps.
Requires the accelerated test to preserve signature order and defines quantitative leakage, recovery, temperature, and subcell-retention criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Dynamic electronic-load emulation may replace physical shading if the subcell voltage/current waveform is validated against real shading.
Lock-in thermography, infrared microscopy, or distributed temperature sensors may be used for local heating.
Random-telegraph noise or local nonlinear I-V may serve as an incipient-filament marker if confirmed by post-mortem Cu mapping.
common_wrong_answers: Uses a single high reverse voltage because it produces failure faster, without matching module waveforms.
Attributes overnight recovery to healing of all damage and ignores a persistent chemical component.
Calls every hot spot a filament without determining whether interconnect resistance or Joule heating appeared first.

expected_answer:
The target profile should preserve a nearly acceptor-free region near the hole-selective contact, increase acceptor concentration toward the electron-collecting surface, and end in a continuous electron-selective cap. Because the new acceptor is anisotropic, molecular orientation must also support out-of-plane electron transport. A concentration gradient without an orientation gradient may create nominal contact area but poor vertical mobility.

The deeper electron affinity can improve electron transfer, but an excessive offset may waste voltage through energetic relaxation or create deep interfacial charge-transfer states. Strong visible absorption can alter generation and invalidate comparisons based only on Jsc. The acceptor may also collect holes if it penetrates too deeply, aggregate into isolated low-mobility domains, or disrupt precursor crystallization. Lower diffusivity improves profile retention but may prevent the graded distribution from forming during the short coating window.

A factorial screen should vary acceptor concentration, deposition timing, solvent selectivity, drying rate, and post-anneal. Depth-resolved composition and orientation should be measured by SIMS, angle-dependent GIWAXS/NEXAFS, and cross-sectional spectroscopy. Optical transfer-matrix analysis and EQE should separate parasitic absorption from collection. Absolute PLQY/QFLS, transient absorption, charge-extraction yield, electron and hole mobility, and contact resistivity should establish whether transfer is selective and productive. Planar, intentionally uniform bulk-mixture, and sharp-interface controls are required.

Acceptance requires higher extracted-electron yield and fill factor at unchanged or improved QFLS, no increase in hole leakage, a stable depth/orientation profile, and no crystallization penalty. If the deeper acceptor raises quenching but lowers external voltage or if strong absorption reduces current reaching the perovskite, the design should be rejected despite faster interfacial transfer.
scoring_key_points: Defines a hole-contact-excluding, electron-side-enriched, continuous and vertically oriented acceptor profile.
Identifies energetic relaxation, parasitic absorption, hole leakage, aggregation, anisotropy, and crystallization damage.
Uses profile/orientation, optical, QFLS, selective-transfer, mobility, and contact measurements with sharp and bulk-mixture controls.
Requires productive extraction without voltage, selectivity, optical, or profile-stability penalties.
accepted_equivalents: graded non-fullerene acceptor heterojunction
orientation-controlled electron-acceptor gradient
productive transfer rather than maximum quenching
common_wrong_answers: A deeper LUMO always improves both Voc and electron extraction.
The strongest-absorbing acceptor is best because it increases total absorption.
Low molecular diffusivity guarantees that a useful gradient will form.

expected_answer:
A texture series should be produced at matched composition, additive coverage, thickness, and initial QFLS, ranging from weakly textured to strongly out-of-plane oriented films. Flexible substrates and barrier stacks with different moduli and thermal-expansion coefficients should be crossed with the texture series. This separates intrinsic anisotropic lattice response from externally imposed mismatch. Grain size and residual strain must be matched or included as covariates.

Operando GIWAXS during bending and thermal cycling can measure orientation-dependent lattice strain, peak broadening, and irreversible texture loss. Digital image correlation, Raman/PL strain mapping, acoustic or optical crack detection, and cross-sectional microscopy should locate stress at vertical grain boundaries and interfaces. Electrical mapping should track local electroluminescence, sheet/contact resistance, QFLS, and stabilized power during cycling. A film may retain average diffraction texture while developing sparse electrically fatal cracks, so spatial diagnostics are essential.

If strong texture is mechanically harmful, failure should scale with the orientation-dependent strain component, substrate mismatch, and cycle amplitude, and should be reduced by a compliant interlayer or a substrate with better expansion matching. Redesign options include slightly broader orientation distribution, graded texture through thickness, elastic interlayers, smaller coherent-domain height, or molecular spacers that preserve electronic order while allowing interfacial slip.

The preferred design maximizes vertical transport subject to a fatigue constraint. Strong texture is accepted only if it retains its QFLS and fill-factor advantage after bending and thermal cycling without higher crack density, delamination, or ion-migration signatures. It should be rejected or softened if its initial electronic benefit disappears under realistic mechanical stress, or if a moderately textured film reaches similar stabilized power with substantially better fatigue life.
scoring_key_points: Uses a matched texture series crossed with substrate modulus and thermal-expansion mismatch.
Measures operando anisotropic strain, texture retention, cracks, interfaces, and spatial electrical performance.
Proposes compliant, graded, or moderately broadened texture redesigns that preserve vertical transport.
Defines a constrained optimum based on stabilized electronic gain and mechanical fatigue rather than initial PCE alone.
accepted_equivalents: texture-mechanics trade-off
graded orientation profile
compliant interlayer for anisotropic strain accommodation
common_wrong_answers: The most strongly oriented film is always the most stable.
Unchanged average GIWAXS texture proves there are no fatigue cracks.
Flexible-device qualification can be inferred from rigid-glass MPPT stability.

expected_answer:
The stabilizer dose must be re-optimized because the wide-bandgap ink has different halide chemical potentials, intermediate phases, and tolerance-factor constraints. A matrix should vary Br fraction, stabilizer concentration, humidity, and ink age while keeping thickness and optical gap targeted. Controls should include the cation with a non-formate anion, an inorganic formate, and a redox-matched non-A-site-compatible reductant. This separates iodine-redox control from incorporation of the organic cation.

Solution analysis should quantify I−/Br− complexes, I2/I3−, possible Br-containing oxidized species, Pb-halide coordination, and organic-cation deprotonation. In-situ GIWAXS and absorption/PL during coating should identify whether the stabilizer changes polytype sequence or creates low-dimensional impurity phases. Final composition and vertical/lateral Br/I distribution require calibrated XPS/ToF-SIMS and spatial PL-energy mapping.

Initial benefits should be evaluated with absolute PLQY/QFLS, bulk lifetime, surface recombination velocity, trap spectroscopy, and device transport. A higher initial QFLS is not enough if the additive creates a mobile-ion reservoir. Operational tests must combine one-sun illumination, elevated temperature, and electrical bias while monitoring PL/EL peak splitting, spatial segregation, hysteresis, ion-related capacitance, and stabilized current matching in the intended tandem.

Acceptance requires suppression of air-induced stoichiometric loss at a dose below the impurity threshold, unchanged or improved extraction, and no increase in light-induced spectral segregation or mobile-ion density. The chemistry should be rejected if the optimum is too humidity-sensitive, if the cation accumulates in a secondary phase, if Br/I gradients grow during operation, or if the recovered initial voltage is lost under bias despite good dark storage.
scoring_key_points: Re-optimizes dose across Br fraction, humidity, and ink age with counterion and redox controls.
Measures mixed-halide precursor chemistry, crystallization pathway, impurity phases, and Br/I spatial distribution.
Separates initial QFLS/trap recovery from mobile-ion and phase-segregation behaviour under operation.
Defines rejection by impurity formation, segregation, ionic accumulation, humidity sensitivity, or transport loss.
accepted_equivalents: wide-bandgap counterion-pair re-optimization
mixed-halide redox and segregation compatibility
operando PL/EL segregation gate
common_wrong_answers: A stabilizer that works for iodide-rich films can be used at the same molar dose in a bromide-rich film.
Lower iodine oxidation guarantees lower halide segregation.
Dark-storage stability is sufficient for a mixed-halide tandem absorber.

expected_answer:
In the n-i-p geometry, an upward near-surface bandgap gradient and associated field can deplete electrons from the defective top interface while leaving holes available for collection by the hole transport layer. Placing the same electron-repelling field next to an electron-selective contact in a p-i-n cell creates the wrong selectivity. Electrons may accumulate below the gradient, face an extraction barrier, and generate an S-shaped current-voltage curve, reduced fill factor, or bias-dependent collection even if the isolated film has a long PL lifetime.

One redesign is to reverse the energetic sign at the top contact. A composition or dipole gradient can be chosen so that the conduction-band edge becomes more favorable toward the electron transport layer while the valence-band offset still blocks holes. This must be shallow enough to avoid introducing a recombination-active mixed-halide region or an insulating low-dimensional barrier. A second redesign is to retain the electron-repelling field but move it to the buried hole-selective interface, where its polarity again supports carrier selectivity. The top electron contact can then use an ultrathin, electronically transparent passivation layer with negligible transport barrier. A third acceptable route is a fixed molecular or oxide dipole that creates the required contact-specific band bending without mobile halides.

Success cannot be judged from film TRPL alone because field-induced spatial separation can lengthen PL while slowing extraction. Depth-resolved UPS or Kelvin-probe profiling should establish the sign and magnitude of the band bending. Selective-contact PLQY or quasi-Fermi-level splitting should quantify non-radiative voltage loss, while contact-resolved transient photocurrent, transient photovoltage, bias-dependent EQE, impedance, and dark current should test extraction and blocking. Surface recombination velocity should be measured with the actual electron contact. The redesigned interface is successful only if it lowers contact recombination, preserves or accelerates electron extraction, avoids an extraction barrier across operating bias, and remains energetically stable during maximum-power operation.
scoring_key_points: Explains that an electron-repelling top field has opposite consequences at a hole-selective versus electron-selective contact.
Proposes at least two valid redesigns, such as reversing the top gradient, relocating the field to the buried hole contact, or using a fixed contact-specific dipole.
Separates lifetime/passivation metrics from charge-selective extraction and barrier diagnostics in the complete p-i-n stack.
Includes operational tests of band-bending polarity, recombination, extraction, and field stability under realistic bias.
accepted_equivalents: contact-polarity inversion
relocation of the surface field to the collecting-hole interface
immobile molecular-dipole or heterojunction field engineering
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that any wider-bandgap cap is beneficial regardless of which carrier the adjacent contact collects.
Using only isolated-film PL lifetime to select the p-i-n treatment.
Reversing the field without checking valence-band hole blocking or mixed-halide stability.
Making the low-dimensional layer thicker to improve passivation while ignoring tunnelling and series resistance.

expected_answer:
The three electrical conditions impose different carrier populations and electric-field profiles, so identical photon dose does not imply identical ionic driving forces. At open circuit, photocarriers accumulate and the electronic current is zero. Large quasi-Fermi-level splitting, interfacial charge accumulation, and partial screening of the built-in field can change vacancy charge states and promote local chemical reactions. If iodide vacancies drift and generate interstitial-iodide hole traps near the hole-selective interface, open circuit can strongly expose that feedback because holes are not continuously removed.

At maximum power, carriers are extracted and the internal field is intermediate. The same vacancy-mediated mechanism may persist, but its rate and spatial location can change because electronic and ionic currents coexist. Short circuit usually gives lower steady-state carrier density and a stronger extraction field; this may reduce carrier-assisted trap chemistry while still driving charged vacancies toward one interface. Therefore, a simple ranking cannot be assumed: open circuit may maximize photochemical trap generation, whereas short circuit may maximize field-directed redistribution. The key is to separate mobile-ion displacement from irreversible trap creation.

Use matched devices aged at open circuit, stabilized maximum power, and short circuit under identical spectrum, temperature, atmosphere, and integrated photon dose. During aging, record transient current after voltage steps, impedance or capacitance signatures of mobile ions, electroluminescence or PL maps, and contact-resolved extraction. At defined intervals, measure thermal-admittance trap spectra and perform depth-resolved halide/cation profiling. Dark-rest recovery distinguishes reversible ionic polarization from permanent lattice damage. Polarity-reversal or pulsed-bias experiments provide an additional test of field direction.

A universal absorber-compensation mechanism is supported if AX excess lowers the initial mobile-ion population and suppresses the same trap-generation pathway under all three bias conditions, even though kinetics differ. A bias-specific interfacial mechanism is indicated if the benefit appears mainly when the hole contact is forward-polarized or carrier-rich, with little effect on bulk ion metrics under the other conditions. Initial PCE must remain matched so that slower aging is not attributed to lower operating current or temperature.
scoring_key_points: Explains why open circuit, maximum power, and short circuit produce different carrier densities and ionic field distributions despite matched photon dose.
Distinguishes reversible ion redistribution from irreversible vacancy/interstitial trap generation and contact damage.
Defines a bias-controlled ageing protocol with operando ion, trap, spatial, and extraction measurements plus dark recovery or polarity reversal.
States criteria separating universal bulk vacancy compensation from a hole-contact-specific or bias-specific stabilization effect.
accepted_equivalents: bias-dependent ionic polarization
universal absorber defect-cycle suppression
contact-specific hole-extraction stabilization
common_wrong_answers: Assuming open circuit is always the harshest condition without measuring field and carrier-density effects.
Comparing ageing times without matching photon dose and temperature.
Equating reversible current recovery with repaired lattice defects.
Concluding that AX excess is universal from one open-circuit stress condition.

expected_answer:
The design objective is to reduce non-radiative and contact-related voltage loss while preserving the iodine-rich bulk bandgap. The absorber should therefore remain predominantly Sn-I, with oxidation suppressed through high-purity Sn(II) precursors, controlled reducing chemistry, low-oxygen processing and compositional strategies that decrease Sn-vacancy or Sn(IV) formation without creating deep states. Any bromide should be confined to a very thin interfacial or graded region if it improves contact stability or band bending; it should not dominate the optically active thickness.

Voltage recovery should then be pursued through selective contacts. Choose an electron contact with a small extraction offset but a strong hole-blocking barrier, and a hole contact whose work function is aligned to the iodine-rich valence band without oxidizing Sn(II). Insert ultrathin passivation layers that reduce interface recombination while remaining tunnelling-permissive. Because a narrow-gap bottom cell requires high current, use sufficient absorber thickness and optical management to retain near-infrared absorption, but verify that added thickness does not create incomplete collection. A tandem-compatible recombination interconnect must be transparent in the bottom-cell spectral range and chemically orthogonal to the Sn perovskite.

The proof is not a higher Voc alone. Measure absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting of the absorber before and after each interface, electroluminescence-derived non-radiative voltage loss, intensity-dependent Voc, dark current and impedance. EQE must retain the long-wavelength onset and integrated current of the iodine-rich absorber. UPS/Kelvin probe and depth-resolved composition should confirm that any Br enrichment is interfacial rather than bulk. In the tandem, light-bias or subcell-resolved spectroscopy should show that the bottom-cell voltage increases while its current-limiting spectral contribution remains unchanged. A solution that gains voltage by simply widening the bandgap fails the design objective.
scoring_key_points: Preserves an iodine-rich low-bandgap bulk while targeting Sn oxidation, vacancy chemistry and non-radiative loss.
Uses selective, chemically compatible contacts and ultrathin passivation rather than bulk bandgap widening as the main voltage lever.
Retains near-infrared absorption and collection through thickness and optical management with a low-loss tandem interconnect.
Requires QFLS/EL voltage-loss and EQE evidence proving voltage gain without loss of the bottom-cell spectral function.
accepted_equivalents: interfacial bandgap grading
non-radiative voltage-loss reduction
iodine-rich tin-perovskite tandem bottom cell
common_wrong_answers: Adding enough bromide to raise Voc regardless of current loss
Reporting only the tandem PCE
Assuming a deeper contact work function automatically improves selectivity

expected_answer:
The field should be increased electrostatically rather than by sustained external bias. One route is to enlarge the contact work-function asymmetry using highly selective, chemically stable electron- and hole-transport layers while suppressing carrier injection from both electrodes. A second is a graded or compensated junction: a shallow compositional or controlled doping gradient can distribute the built-in potential through the crystal instead of concentrating it at one interface. A p-i-n-like geometry with a thick, low-defect intrinsic region is preferable to heavy bulk doping, which narrows depletion width, increases dark conductivity and may introduce mobile ionic defects. Guard rings or vertical pixel electrodes can shape field lines and reduce lateral drift without raising the average field throughout the absorber.

The trade-offs are coupled. A larger work-function difference is useless if one contact becomes chemically reactive or injects carriers under X-ray illumination. Strong interfacial band bending can increase recombination if traps remain, while excessive doping raises capacitance and Johnson or shot noise. A steep field near one interface may accelerate local ion accumulation even at zero terminal voltage. The selective layers must therefore be thin enough for collection, robust against residual solvent and impermeable to electrode-metal migration.

Verify the mechanism with depth-resolved electrostatic potential, capacitance-voltage profiling, Kelvin probe or electroabsorption, and transient-current measurements from both illumination directions. Microbeam scans should map charge-cloud width as a function of absorption depth and pixel position. Resolution improvement should coincide with shorter collection time and reduced lateral spread, not merely with thresholding or lower gain. Compare zero-bias dark noise, NED, DQE and long-term drift before and after field engineering. A contact-only control with identical optical absorption but no increased built-in potential is essential. The design succeeds only if higher spatial resolution is retained under prolonged zero-bias operation without a new injection or ionic-stability penalty.
scoring_key_points: Uses contact asymmetry, graded junctions or field-shaping geometry to increase internal drift without sustained external bias.
Explains depletion-width, injection-noise, capacitance, recombination and ionic-stability trade-offs.
Requires depth- and position-resolved field/collection measurements plus microbeam charge-cloud mapping.
Demands simultaneous retention of zero-bias NED/DQE and long-term stability, not resolution improvement alone.
accepted_equivalents: built-in-field engineering
graded p-i-n single-crystal detector
field-shaped pixel or guard-ring architecture
common_wrong_answers: Applying a larger external bias
Using heavier doping without considering depletion width and noise
Claiming better resolution from image post-processing alone

expected_answer:
The third junction is worthwhile only if its incremental voltage and spectral utilization exceed every loss introduced by the additional stack. Begin with realistic, not ideal, optical-electrical simulation using measured absorption coefficients, parasitic absorption, luminescence coupling, external radiative efficiency, series resistance and temperature coefficients. Optimize bandgaps for the intended spectrum and climate. In a monolithic series-connected device, all three currents must match over a useful operating range; an optimum under one standard spectrum may underperform annually if the middle junction frequently limits current. Four-terminal or partially decoupled designs relax this constraint but add transparent contacts, wiring and area penalties.

The marginal voltage from the new junction must be discounted by its non-radiative voltage loss and by voltage or fill-factor loss in two recombination interconnects. Additional transparent electrodes and transport layers can remove photons that would otherwise reach the lower cells. The process sequence may damage an underlying perovskite or require orthogonal solvents, and conformal coating becomes harder on textured or large-area substrates. The weakest subcell also determines long-term yield: wide-gap halide segregation, low-gap Sn oxidation or interconnect corrosion can erase the theoretical benefit.

The decision package should include annual spectral/temperature simulations with uncertainty, sensitivity analysis to current mismatch and degradation, and comparison with the best two-junction architecture using the same area and aperture definitions. Experimentally, demonstrate each subcell's QFLS and EQE in the integrated stack, optical-loss accounting, low-resistance interconnects, stabilized output and module-relevant uniformity. Accelerated light/heat/bias tests must show that the third junction does not introduce a new dominant failure mode.

A practical rule is to proceed only when the lower confidence bound of predicted annual energy-yield gain remains positive after measured optical, voltage, resistance, inactive-area and degradation penalties are included. A higher ideal detailed-balance ceiling or small-area initial PCE is not sufficient justification.
scoring_key_points: Frames the third-junction decision as marginal voltage/spectral gain minus measured optical, electrical and stability penalties.
Includes realistic bandgap/current matching over annual spectra and distinguishes monolithic from electrically decoupled architectures.
Accounts for extra interconnects, processing compatibility, inactive area, large-area uniformity and the weakest-subcell lifetime.
Requires uncertainty-bounded annual-yield simulation plus integrated subcell QFLS/EQE, stabilized output and stress-test evidence.
accepted_equivalents: marginal-value criterion for a third junction
annual-yield-aware multi-junction optimization
confidence-bounded architecture decision
common_wrong_answers: Adding a junction because the detailed-balance limit is higher
Optimizing only AM1.5G current matching
Ignoring added interconnect and processing losses

expected_answer:
The candidate should be used as a controlled minority component rather than as a full A-site replacement. A compositional series should identify the highest incorporation level that preserves a single 3D perovskite network, solution stability and the target bandgap. The host A-site mixture can retain FA/Cs for structural fit, while the cyclic amidinium fraction is tuned to strengthen hydrogen-bond coupling, reduce volatility and potentially stiffen the lattice. Solvent coordination, precursor temperature and crystallization rate must be adjusted to prevent selective precipitation. If the cation has limited bulk miscibility, a deliberately graded profile with a low bulk concentration and a thin enriched surface or grain-boundary region is preferable to uncontrolled low-dimensional inclusions.

Structural validation must go beyond average diffraction. Depth-resolved GIWAXS, solid-state NMR and nanoscale chemical mapping should establish whether the cation is incorporated, segregated at boundaries or converted into a distinct low-dimensional phase. Vertical mobility, contact resistance and thickness-dependent collection must verify that any surface-rich layer remains electronically permeable.

Mechanism discrimination requires three linked tests. First, temperature-dependent NMR, Raman or quasi-elastic scattering can determine whether A-cation and octahedral dynamics change. Second, bias- and light-dependent isotope tracing, time-of-flight SIMS or transient ionic-current measurements can quantify halide and A-site redistribution. Third, selective removal or thickness variation of the surface-rich phase can test whether stability is simply caused by a transport-blocking cap. Operando PL mapping and GIWAXS under illumination should correlate local segregation with composition and strain.

The design is accepted only if halide segregation is suppressed at an incorporation level that retains 3D connectivity, vertical extraction and spectral stability, and if the benefit persists when optical absorption and surface-barrier effects are normalized. A stable but resistive quasi-2D cap is not a successful transfer.
scoring_key_points: Chooses minority or graded incorporation to balance A-site benefits against solubility and low-dimensional phase formation.
Requires depth-resolved proof of incorporation, segregation and preserved three-dimensional connectivity.
Separates lattice-dynamic, ion-migration and surface-blocking mechanisms with orthogonal operando measurements.
Defines success as simultaneous suppression of segregation, preserved bandgap and efficient vertical extraction.
accepted_equivalents: partial A-site substitution
surface-enriched but electronically thin cation profile
hydrogen-bond-mediated lattice stiffening
operando halide-segregation mapping
common_wrong_answers: Assuming complete substitution is optimal because the new cation is more hydrophobic.
Treating any low-dimensional phase as beneficial without testing vertical transport.
Using improved steady-state PL alone to claim suppressed ion migration.

expected_answer:
The electronic structure of a halide perovskite is determined by overlap along connected metal-halide-metal pathways. Equal mean bond angle therefore does not imply equal electronic disorder. In film A, correlated tilts create a spatially coherent distortion field. The band-edge shift produced by one octahedron is similar to that of its neighbors, so carriers experience an anisotropic but comparatively smooth potential landscape. Transport can be faster along the direction with stronger orbital overlap, and the absorption edge can remain sharp despite broken cubic symmetry. In film B, randomly oriented tilts generate short-range fluctuations in orbital overlap and local band-edge energy. That disorder broadens the density-of-states tail, increases carrier scattering and lowers mobility without requiring a larger average tilt.

The structural evidence should quantify both amplitude and correlation length. Three-dimensional diffuse scattering, pair-distribution-function analysis over variable real-space ranges, and coherent or nanobeam X-ray diffraction can distinguish correlated tilt domains from uncorrelated local distortions. Temperature-dependent measurements should reveal whether the correlations are static, dynamic or near a soft-mode transition. Polarized Raman or terahertz spectroscopy and molecular-dynamics-informed simulations can connect specific octahedral modes to the observed anisotropy.

Conventional confounders must be matched or measured. GIWAXS pole figures and polarized microscopy should quantify crystallographic texture; cross-sectional microscopy and grain statistics should exclude grain-size differences. Defect density and capture coefficients should be compared using injection-dependent PL, thermal admittance or deep-level spectroscopy rather than inferred from lifetime alone. Direction-resolved conductivity or terahertz mobility should be measured relative to the tilt-correlation axis.

A decisive result is that mobility anisotropy and Urbach energy track the octahedral correlation length across temperature or processing series while mean angle, texture, grain size and defect metrics remain constant. If anisotropy instead follows macroscopic texture, the octahedral-correlation explanation is not established.
scoring_key_points: Explains why octahedral tilt correlation length controls spatial coherence of orbital overlap and band-edge disorder.
Connects correlated tilts to anisotropic transport and random tilts to Urbach broadening and scattering.
Uses diffuse scattering/PDF or equivalent methods to quantify correlation beyond average crystallography.
Includes explicit controls for texture, grain size and defect capture, with a falsifiable correlation-length signature.
accepted_equivalents: cooperative octahedral tilting
correlated structural disorder
spatially coherent band-edge modulation
diffuse-scattering correlation length
common_wrong_answers: Equating identical mean bond angle with identical electronic structure.
Attributing anisotropy only to preferred crystal orientation without measuring it.
Using PL lifetime as the sole measure of defect density.

expected_answer:
Water-vapour transmission rate is an external barrier metric and does not identify the chemical fate of the small amount of water that enters. The workflow should therefore use controlled doses of H2^17O, D2O or H2^18O, selected according to NMR sensitivity and feasibility, while keeping humidity activity identical. 2H NMR can distinguish relatively mobile water, hydrogen-bonded water and deuterium incorporated through exchange with organic cations; 1H/2H cross-polarization and relaxation can identify changes in cation motion. If available, ^17O NMR can directly probe molecular water, hydrate-like environments and oxide-containing degradation products. 13C/15N-labelled organic cations provide a complementary route to detect loss, fragmentation or altered local coordination, while 207Pb and halide-sensitive measurements track new inorganic phases.

Time-resolved spectra should be collected during uptake, dry purge and thermal recovery. Reversible hydration should produce water-related signals and dynamic changes that disappear on drying without a persistent new Pb or organic-cation environment. Proton/deuteron exchange will remain after free water is removed but can occur without framework decomposition. Organic-cation volatilization should reduce integrated labelled-cation intensity or create volatile products, whereas irreversible decomposition should generate persistent new 207Pb, halide or ^17O environments and should correlate with nonrecoverable voltage or fill-factor loss.

Depth information is essential. Use sacrificial mini-modules with layers sampled from edge, interconnect and centre regions, or spatially selective NMR/microcoils, and combine with isotope-depth profiling. The encapsulation designs must be tested under heat, illumination and electrical bias because reactive consumption can differ at equal ingress rate.

An acceptance rule should specify maximum isotope uptake at critical locations, maximum retained exchanged-water fraction after purge, absence of persistent decomposition resonances, and bounded electrical loss after repeated cycles. Scheme A may pass if hydration is fully reversible and does not accumulate; scheme B fails if small ingress produces irreversible chemistry, even when its nominal transmission rate is lower.
scoring_key_points: Uses isotope-labelled water and nucleus-specific NMR to distinguish free/bound water, exchange and decomposition.
Includes time-resolved uptake, purge and recovery to separate reversible hydration from persistent chemical change.
Adds spatial/depth sampling and combined operational stress rather than relying on bulk, static spectra.
Translates spectroscopy into quantitative module acceptance limits tied to accumulation and irreversible electrical loss.
accepted_equivalents: D2O tracer NMR
^17O-labelled water
labelled organic-cation mass balance
persistent post-purge resonance as irreversible chemistry
common_wrong_answers: Equating lower water-vapour transmission rate with better chemical stability.
Calling all retained deuterium decomposition without considering exchange.
Reporting only a final bulk spectrum without uptake/recovery kinetics or spatial sampling.

expected_answer:
Defect tolerance concerns the consequences of specific defects under defined carrier and environmental conditions, not a single lifetime value. At low injection, both materials can appear similar because traps are unoccupied, passivated at the surface, kinetically inaccessible or below the sensitivity limit. Material A may contain many shallow defects whose levels remain near a band edge and have small multiphonon capture coefficients. Material B can contain fewer defects yet suffer strongly once a deep centre changes charge state or becomes activated at elevated temperature. Large lattice relaxation increases electron-phonon coupling and can lower the capture barrier, producing injection- and temperature-dependent recombination.

The minimum experimental set should measure defect populations and recombination kinetics separately. Quantitative composition/defect assays, thermal admittance or deep-level transient spectroscopy, and controlled irradiation or off-stoichiometry series can vary defect density. Injection-dependent absolute PLQY and time-resolved PL over temperature should extract the transition from monomolecular to radiative and Auger regimes. Temperature-dependent capture kinetics, ideally combined with photoinduced current or capacitance measurements, can identify activation barriers and charge-state transitions. Surface-passivated and thickness-varied samples are needed to isolate bulk from surface capture.

Theory should calculate defect formation energies across chemical potentials and Fermi level, thermodynamic transition levels, structural relaxation coordinates and non-radiative multiphonon capture coefficients. Static density-of-states calculations alone are insufficient. The predicted deep centre in B should show a large configuration-coordinate displacement and a capture coefficient consistent with the measured temperature dependence.

Dynamic screening must be tested rather than assumed. Frequency- and temperature-dependent dielectric response, polaron signatures, or ultrafast spectroscopy can show whether carrier-lattice screening reduces Coulomb capture in A. The materials can be called differently tolerant only after normalizing for defect concentration and surfaces and demonstrating that the intrinsic capture harm per relevant defect remains lower for A across operating injection and temperature.
scoring_key_points: Explains why defect tolerance is condition-, defect- and capture-specific rather than equivalent to low-injection lifetime.
Separates defect concentration, energetic depth and multiphonon capture through injection- and temperature-dependent experiments.
Requires formation energies, charge transitions, relaxation coordinates and capture coefficients in theory.
Includes controls for surfaces and a direct test of dynamic dielectric or polaron screening.
accepted_equivalents: configuration-coordinate analysis
non-radiative multiphonon capture coefficient
shallow-but-abundant versus deep-but-rare defects
condition-specific defect tolerance
common_wrong_answers: Calling A more defect-tolerant solely because it has a longer lifetime under one condition.
Using defect formation energy or density of states alone to predict recombination.
Ignoring surface recombination and charge-state occupancy.

expected_answer:
A two-terminal tandem should be designed for lifetime-integrated current balance, not exact current matching at time zero. The organic blend should be selected not only for bandgap and initial EQE but also for low burn-in, stable morphology and photochemical robustness. A slightly current-rich organic subcell at commissioning can be rational if its predictable early loss brings the stack toward balance, provided the excess does not create severe voltage or fill-factor penalties. The perovskite composition and interfaces should minimize slow spectral drift, halide segregation and contact-induced loss so that its current trajectory is also predictable.

Optical design should provide controlled adjustability without requiring thicker organic films. A spectrally selective optical spacer, textured light management, reflective rear contact or ternary organic blend can redistribute absorption while preserving exciton collection. The recombination contact must remain optically transparent, low resistance and chemically isolating; degradation there can mimic subcell mismatch and must be diagnosed separately. If feasible, module layout can include subcell-thickness or optical-spacer variants across a small design window rather than one nominally perfect match.

Qualification requires subcell-resolved ageing under realistic spectra, temperature cycles and maximum-power-point tracking. Periodic EQE with bias light, electroluminescence, tandem J-V reconstruction and optical spectroscopy should extract each subcell’s current and voltage trajectory. Dark-rest and controlled annealing steps should distinguish reversible morphology or ionic changes from irreversible photochemistry. The measured trajectories should feed an annual energy-yield model using site-specific spectra and temperature, including mismatch clipping and series-connection losses.

The preferred stack is the one with the highest projected energy delivered before a defined failure criterion and acceptable uncertainty, not the highest initial PCE. A design with slightly lower initial current but slower, better-correlated subcell degradation can outperform an initially matched stack whose currents diverge rapidly.
scoring_key_points: Optimizes lifetime-integrated current balance and recognizes distinct organic burn-in and perovskite slow-decay trajectories.
Proposes absorber and optical interventions that manage mismatch without simply thickening the organic layer.
Requires a stable, transparent recombination contact and tests it separately from subcell degradation.
Uses subcell-resolved ageing and site-specific energy-yield modeling rather than initial PCE as the decision metric.
accepted_equivalents: lifetime current matching
ageing-aware tandem optimization
spectral optical spacer
energy-yield rather than champion-efficiency selection
common_wrong_answers: Matching the subcells only at the beginning of life.
Compensating burn-in solely by making the organic absorber thicker.
Attributing all nonlinear tandem loss to the current-limiting subcell without testing the recombination contact.

expected_answer:
Oxidative treatment can increase the average NiOx work function and improve precursor wetting, yet also create highly oxidized surface sites, hydroxyls or Ni-related defects that react with iodide and the organic perovskite components. Interfacial iodide oxidation or acid-base/redox chemistry can generate iodine species, undercoordinated Pb and PbI2-rich regions. These reactions add non-radiative recombination centres even while the nominal valence-band alignment appears more favorable. The molecular passivant can coordinate reactive Ni or Pb sites and suppress recombination without restoring the original work function, showing that chemical passivation and energetic alignment are separable.

Faster interfacial PL decay is ambiguous. It can represent efficient hole transfer, but it can also result from rapid trap-assisted recombination at a damaged interface. Absolute PLQY, quasi-Fermi-level splitting and time-resolved emission must be interpreted together. Beneficial extraction should reduce PL lifetime while preserving high PLQY under selective-contact conditions and produce collected current; a damaged interface lowers both PLQY and implied voltage.

The evidence set should include UPS/Kelvin-probe mapping for work function and spatial uniformity, XPS or operando photoelectron spectroscopy for Ni oxidation state, iodine species and Pb chemical states, and depth-resolved diffraction or spectroscopy for PbI2 formation. Compare untreated, oxidized, passivated-only and oxidized-plus-passivated contacts with matched perovskite morphology. Transient photocurrent/photovoltage, contact-selective PLQY, temperature-dependent ideality factor and impedance can distinguish extraction barriers from recombination. A chemically inert high-work-function reference contact is a critical control.

Causality is established if voltage and non-radiative loss track reactive interfacial species rather than average work function, and if suppressing those species restores quasi-Fermi-level splitting and stability while extraction remains efficient. Wetting improvements must be decoupled using processing adjustments that reproduce morphology without changing NiOx chemistry.
scoring_key_points: Identifies NiOx/perovskite redox or acid-base chemistry as a source of PbI2 and interfacial recombination despite favorable work function.
Explains why rapid PL quenching can mean either extraction or non-radiative trapping and invokes absolute PLQY/quasi-Fermi splitting.
Uses chemical-state, energetic and carrier-dynamics measurements with matched morphology controls.
Requires an inert high-work-function control and a causal correlation between reactive species, voltage loss and recovery.
accepted_equivalents: NiOx-induced iodide oxidation
reactive high-valence nickel surface sites
contact-selective photoluminescence yield
chemical passivation independent of work-function shift
common_wrong_answers: Assuming a higher work function automatically improves Voc.
Interpreting the shortest PL lifetime as the best extraction interface.
Attributing PbI2 solely to bulk crystallization without probing the buried contact.

expected_answer:
The work-function shift of a molecular layer is a collective interfacial property, not simply the gas-phase dipole of one molecule. Spacer length and rigidity control tilt angle, conformational disorder, intermolecular distance, anchoring geometry and the fraction of molecules that form an ordered monolayer. Dense packing can increase the areal dipole, but dipole-dipole depolarization can reduce the effective moment per molecule. Flexible spacers may adopt multiple orientations or form multilayers, whereas rigid spacers may improve order but create incomplete coverage if sterically mismatched. The same spacer also changes tunnelling distance and may expose or passivate different surface defects.

A causal series should hold the anchor and terminal functional group constant while varying spacer length and rigidity systematically. Surface density must be quantified independently by XPS, radiolabeling, quartz-crystal methods or calibrated desorption. Near-edge X-ray absorption, polarized infrared spectroscopy or angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy can measure orientation and order. UPS and Kelvin-probe force microscopy should map both average work-function shift and lateral heterogeneity. Contact-angle and microscopy data should test whether apparent energetic changes merely follow morphology or contamination.

Defect passivation must be separated using molecules with matched packing but an electronically inert terminal group, together with absolute PLQY, surface recombination velocity and chemical-state spectroscopy. Conversely, a dilute mixed-monolayer series can vary surface density while preserving orientation. Capacitance and temperature-dependent transport can reveal whether longer spacers create a tunnelling barrier despite favorable energetics.

A transferable rule requires the effective dipole per unit area, orientation distribution, depolarization behavior, coverage and electronic coupling to predict work function and voltage across substrates and processing conditions. Correlation with calculated isolated dipole alone is insufficient. The rule is credible only if it predicts a withheld molecule or a second contact material and if device voltage follows the measured interfacial quasi-Fermi-level loss rather than morphology changes.
scoring_key_points: Explains work-function shift as a collective function of surface density, orientation, packing and depolarization.
Uses orthogonal measurements of coverage, orientation, work-function heterogeneity and transport barrier.
Separates defect passivation and morphology from dipolar energetics with matched controls.
Requires predictive validation on a withheld molecule or second substrate for a transferable structure-property rule.
accepted_equivalents: Helmholtz areal-dipole relation
dipole depolarization
monolayer tilt-angle distribution
mixed-monolayer density series
common_wrong_answers: Ranking molecules solely by calculated gas-phase dipole moment.
Inferring monolayer coverage from contact angle alone.
Attributing higher Voc to work-function shift without measuring non-radiative interfacial loss.

expected_answer:
In a series-connected two-terminal tandem, partial shading reduces the photocurrent of the affected region while the rest of the string continues to drive current. The shaded tandem segment can therefore be forced away from its normal maximum-power point and, depending on string design and bypass protection, into reverse bias. Local power dissipation is concentrated at nonuniform current paths and edges, producing hot spots. In the perovskite top cell, the combined electric field, carrier imbalance and temperature can accelerate mobile-ion redistribution and mixed-halide segregation, consistent with a local red shift. Ion accumulation and heat at the recombination contact can alter its stoichiometry, create interfacial barriers or promote diffusion, leaving a persistent resistance increase even if the silicon bulk remains intact.

A pre-existing shunt would show localized leakage before shading and would typically intensify heating at the same site immediately. Establish baseline dark lock-in thermography, reverse-bias electroluminescence, local dark-current mapping and high-resolution potential mapping. Then apply controlled shading while recording local voltage, current and temperature with sufficient time resolution. Vary shaded fraction, string current and bypass-diode configuration to determine the electrical threshold for failure.

Mechanism separation requires subcell-selective and recovery measurements. Spatially resolved PL/EQE and composition mapping before, during and after stress can track reversible or persistent halide segregation. Dark or thermal recovery of the spectral shift with unchanged contact resistance would separate ionic/phase redistribution from contact chemistry. Cross-sectional ToF-SIMS, XPS or electron microscopy should test ion accumulation and interdiffusion at the recombination junction. Four-terminal or segmented test structures can independently measure top-cell, bottom-cell and interconnect response.

If leakage appears only after the event, follows contact damage and does not reproduce the original heating threshold, it is a consequence rather than the initial cause. If baseline shunt maps predict every hot spot, the shading mechanism is secondary.
scoring_key_points: Explains how partial shading in a series tandem can impose reverse bias and localized Joule heating.
Links field and heat to perovskite ionic/halide redistribution and persistent recombination-contact damage.
Uses pre-stress leakage maps and controlled shading thresholds to test a pre-existing shunt alternative.
Employs subcell-resolved recovery, composition and interface measurements to distinguish reversible segregation from irreversible junction change.
accepted_equivalents: reverse-bias hot-spot stress
string-current-driven shaded-cell failure
field-assisted halide segregation
recombination-junction interdiffusion
common_wrong_answers: Assuming the silicon subcell must be the damaged component because it carries the string current.
Calling every hot spot a pre-existing shunt without baseline mapping.
Using only post-mortem tandem J-V data without subcell or spatial resolution.

expected_answer:
The cavity changes the optical density of states and the angular-spectral escape channels rather than the intrinsic generation or recombination physics alone. In emission mode, constructive interference can direct photons into a narrow wavelength and angular range, so the measured forward electroluminescence may rise even if the total emitted photon flux changes little. The same reciprocal optical structure modifies absorptance for incident sunlight. If the cavity suppresses absorption outside a narrow resonance, reflects oblique rays, or increases field intensity in parasitic transport or electrode layers, the solar short-circuit current falls.

Photon recycling complicates interpretation. A reflective cavity can return internally emitted photons to the perovskite, increasing the probability of reabsorption and raising the internal photon residence time. This can support a larger quasi-Fermi-level splitting when non-radiative recombination is low, but it can also increase parasitic absorption or delay escape. Directional EL therefore does not automatically mean a higher external quantum efficiency integrated over all angles.

The required measurements are absolute, angle-resolved and mode-matched. Integrating-sphere EL should determine total external photon flux, while angle-resolved spectra reveal redistribution into the detector cone. Absolute PLQY and ELQY at matched carrier density distinguish changes in internal radiative efficiency from optical extraction. Spectroscopic ellipsometry plus transfer-matrix or electromagnetic modelling should partition absorption among perovskite, electrodes and transport layers. Angle-resolved EQE under illumination tests reciprocity with the emission pattern.

A genuine extraction improvement requires increased hemispherically integrated ELQY without a corresponding rise in parasitic absorption, together with acceptable broadband and angular solar EQE. A brighter on-axis signal with unchanged integrated flux is beam shaping, not an intrinsic emission-efficiency gain.
scoring_key_points: Explains the reciprocal effect of a cavity on emission channels and solar absorptance.
Distinguishes total photon extraction from angular redistribution and includes photon recycling/parasitic absorption.
Links reduced Jsc to spectral/angular rejection or absorption in non-active layers.
Specifies integrating-sphere, angle-resolved, matched-carrier-density and optical-loss measurements.
accepted_equivalents: Kirchhoff/optical reciprocity reasoning
Hemispherically integrated ELQY
Transfer-matrix or full-wave optical loss decomposition
common_wrong_answers: Assuming brighter forward EL proves higher internal radiative efficiency
Attributing Jsc loss to electronic contacts despite unchanged contacts
Ignoring angular dependence of both emission and absorption

expected_answer:
Conventional phase purity and local structural uniformity are not identical. A film can have one average composition and one dominant repeat distance while containing coherent intergrowths, missing or extra inorganic slabs, spacer-registry faults, or local transitions between RP-like and DJ-like stacking. Because these defects remain crystallographically coherent and may occupy a small volume fraction, their scattering can merge with the dominant Bragg series rather than form a resolvable second set of peaks. A narrow room-temperature absorption edge also does not exclude localized states or small domains that become optically distinct at low temperature.

The film should therefore be described cautiously as single-average-phase unless local and diffuse-structure evidence rules out intergrowth disorder. The characterization hierarchy should start with reciprocal-space mapping and incidence-dependent GIWAXS, looking for diffuse rods, asymmetric peak shapes and depth-dependent spacing. Total scattering with pair-distribution-function analysis can detect local Pb-X connectivity and spacer separation inconsistent with the average unit cell. Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy or electron diffraction should map slab-number changes directly, but beam damage controls are essential.

Solid-state NMR, vibrational spectroscopy or X-ray absorption can probe distinct organic-spacer environments and local octahedral coordination. Temperature-dependent PL, transient absorption and spatially resolved spectroscopy should determine whether broadened low-temperature emission arises from energy transfer into rare intergrowths or from generic defects. Correlation of the same regions by structural and optical microscopy is especially strong.

A true single-n population should show one local slab periodicity, minimal diffuse scattering, one spacer environment and no delayed spectral transfer to lower-energy domains. Persistent local spacing changes or energy-funnelling signatures indicate structural phase disorder even when conventional XRD appears phase-pure.
scoring_key_points: Distinguishes average crystallographic phase purity from local stacking/intergrowth disorder.
Explains why coherent faults may not generate separate conventional XRD peaks.
Proposes local and diffuse structural probes, not only ensemble diffraction.
Links structural findings to temperature-dependent and spatially resolved optical signatures with clear decision criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Single-average-phase with stacking disorder
Pair-distribution-function analysis
Correlative STEM/nano-PL or equivalent local structure-property mapping
common_wrong_answers: Declaring phase purity from one low-angle XRD series
Treating every broad emission feature as a second n-phase
Using only room-temperature absorption and PL

expected_answer:
