The choice should maximize annual stabilized energy yield and reliability, not the one-sun reference PCE. The optical model must use the target climate’s spectral distribution, angle, temperature and albedo to calculate subcell current matching over time. A 1.75 eV top cell may be optimal under the reference spectrum yet spend much of the year current-limited or overdriven under real spectra. The 1.68 eV cell may recover some current disadvantage under red-shifted or diffuse conditions.

Electrical quality must be separated from bandgap. The quasi-Fermi-level splitting, non-radiative voltage loss, contact losses and temperature coefficients of both compositions should be measured at operating carrier densities. A wider bandgap is not useful if its additional theoretical voltage is lost to traps or interfacial recombination. Subcell-resolved EQE, luminescence and pseudo-JV analyses should be incorporated into the tandem model.

Stability must enter as a time-dependent state variable. Light-induced halide redistribution can change the effective bandgap, voltage, current matching and recombination junction loading. Accelerated tests should combine relevant spectrum, temperature and MPP bias, with recovery periods to distinguish reversible segregation from irreversible defect formation. The model should propagate measured degradation and spectral shifts into annual energy yield rather than applying one arbitrary T80.

Module constraints are also decisive: thickness uniformity, compositional tolerance, large-area PL homogeneity, interconnection loss and thermal gradients. Composition H is selected only if its extra field energy yield remains after voltage deficit and segregation penalties and if process control is credible. Composition L is preferred if its lower nominal current is outweighed by higher voltage utilization, stable bandgap and predictable module performance. A bandgap-only or STC-only comparison is scientifically incomplete.
scoring_key_points: Uses climate-specific annual spectral and thermal energy-yield modelling instead of STC efficiency alone.
Includes QFLS, voltage deficit, contacts and subcell-resolved current matching rather than bandgap only.
Treats halide redistribution and degradation as time-dependent changes to bandgap and tandem balance.
Includes module-scale uniformity and process-tolerance criteria in the final decision.
accepted_equivalents: Bankability or energy-yield optimization
Time-dependent current-matching model
Subcell-resolved luminescence and EQE diagnostics
common_wrong_answers: Always choosing the 1.75 eV composition because it is closer to the ideal tandem bandgap
Comparing only initial champion PCE
Ignoring reversible and irreversible spectral evolution under bias

expected_answer:
The observations suggest that the initial chemical passivation remains partly effective—consistent with retained Voc—but the interfacial electrostatic and transport landscape is degrading. Thermal diffusion or proton-transfer reactions can disorder the oriented sulfanilic-acid population, reducing dipole uniformity and creating lateral variations in band alignment. Molecule or fragment migration into the Pb-Sn absorber can introduce ionic scattering, alter local stoichiometry or expose new defects. At the acidic PEDOT:PSS side, changes in protonation or sulfonate interactions may modify HTL conductivity and interfacial contact resistance. Increased Sn4+ near the hole contact indicates oxidation coupled to local chemical reactions or enhanced access of oxidizing species, which can create deep defects and resistive regions. The combined result is current crowding and FF loss before a large average QFLS penalty appears.

The redesign should immobilize the dipole while reducing chemical reactivity. Options include covalently tethering a zwitterionic dipole to the HTL or using a bifunctional molecule with a stronger, non-labile surface anchor and a spacer that prevents proton exchange with the perovskite. The acid-base strength should be tuned so that the molecule is ionized and oriented at fabrication conditions but does not catalyse Sn oxidation. A dense but sub-monolayer-scale network can suppress diffusion without becoming insulating. An ultrathin redox-stable buffer between PEDOT:PSS and the dipole may also isolate acidity while preserving tunnelling and band alignment.

Qualification should combine temperature-dependent ToF-SIMS, KPFM maps, UPS, Sn oxidation-state depth profiles, contact resistivity, impedance and local EL under MPP bias. Go criteria include stable dipole magnitude and spatial variance, no molecular penetration beyond the interface, unchanged Sn4+/Sn2+ ratio, and retained FF and QFLS. Initial PCE improvement alone is insufficient if the dipole is chemically or spatially metastable.
scoring_key_points: Builds a coupled mechanism involving dipole disorder, molecular migration, HTL chemistry and local Sn oxidation.
Explains why FF can decline before a large average Voc or QFLS loss.
Proposes immobilized, acid-base-tuned and redox-stable molecular/interface redesigns without creating an insulating barrier.
Defines thermal-MPP diagnostics and stability criteria for dipole uniformity, migration, oxidation and transport.
accepted_equivalents: Covalently tethered zwitterionic dipole
Redox-stable ultrathin buffer
Spatially resolved KPFM/EL and oxidation-state depth profiling
common_wrong_answers: Attributing all FF loss to bulk recombination
Increasing molecular thickness without checking tunnelling resistance
Evaluating only pre-stress work-function shift

expected_answer:
Acquire all maps in a common coordinate system before patterning the final electrode. Record absorber thickness/topography, reflectance and excitation-intensity maps first, because apparent PL variation can arise from optical interference or local absorption. Then measure calibrated PLQY or QFLS before and after C60, Kelvin-probe potential, C60 thickness or composition, and time-resolved PL. The informative variable is the local change caused by C60, not raw PL intensity. A negative post-C60 QFLS change accompanied by faster nonradiative decay indicates contact-induced recombination; rapid PL quenching with preserved QFLS can instead indicate extraction.

Convert the same area into a dense array of addressable microcells or use local electroluminescence, light-beam-induced current and luminescence-derived implied voltage. Register each pixel to the pre-device maps and quantify local Voc, series resistance, shunt behaviour and pseudo-FF. Use multivariate or hierarchical regression to test whether the C60-induced QFLS loss predicts electrical loss after controlling for thickness, roughness, grain structure and distance to edges. Hold out regions or wafers for validation so the relation is predictive rather than fitted post hoc.

Causality requires an intervention. Deliberately vary C60 deposition uniformity or introduce the tailored 2D layer on patterned regions of the same substrate. If the treatment selectively reduces the post-C60 QFLS variance and the same regions show narrower Voc/FF distributions, the link is strengthened. A passivating but blocking layer would raise PL uniformly yet increase local series resistance and reduce photocurrent. A genuinely homogenized contact should reduce both QFLS loss variance and transport-loss variance without sacrificing extraction. Champion efficiency alone is insufficient; the decisive result is a reproducible spatial covariance that disappears when the causal contact heterogeneity is removed.
scoring_key_points: Uses spatially registered optical, topographic, energetic and electrical maps on the same regions.
Controls optical-thickness and absorption artefacts and analyzes the C60-induced QFLS change rather than raw PL intensity.
Links local maps to microcell Voc, pseudo-FF, series resistance or photocurrent with multivariate predictive statistics.
Requires an intervention that reduces both contact-heterogeneity metrics and the corresponding electrical yield loss.
accepted_equivalents: Hyperspectral PL, Suns-PL or calibrated EL may be used for local QFLS
Conductive AFM or scanning photocurrent can replace a microcell array for local transport
Partial-correlation, mixed-effects or machine-learning regression is acceptable if held-out validation is used
common_wrong_answers: A brighter PL map automatically proves a better electron contact.
Correlating two unregistered maps from different devices is sufficient.
A lower PL standard deviation alone proves higher module yield.

expected_answer:
First match bandgap and absorptance. Prepare control and pseudohalide films with the same thickness, compositionally verified halide ratio and optical bandgap; derive the radiative-limit voltage from calibrated absorptance or EQE rather than assuming it is unchanged. Measure absolute PLQY and QFLS on inert, non-quenching substrates over a range of excitation densities. A bulk benefit should appear in neat films as a higher QFLS or lower nonradiative voltage loss at matched carrier density, and it should scale with absorber thickness or generation profile in a way consistent with reduced bulk recombination.

Then add interfaces sequentially: hole contact/perovskite, perovskite/electron contact, and the complete stack. The incremental QFLS loss after each contact identifies interface-specific penalties. Repeat with at least two chemically different hole contacts and two electron contacts. If the pseudohalide gain persists in neat films and remains similar across contact choices, it is primarily bulk. If the gain appears only after one contact, it is interfacial chemistry or energy alignment. Time-resolved PL, transient absorption and spatially resolved lifetime can test whether lifetime improves throughout the film rather than only near a surface.

Use Suns-Voc or pseudo-JV to separate recombination from transport, and compare electroluminescence-derived nonradiative loss in complete devices. Depth-resolved defect spectroscopy or surface passivation of both samples can provide an additional control: saturating surface recombination should not erase a true bulk difference. Structural orientation and microstrain must be measured because texture can alter optical outcoupling and contact formation. The decisive signature is a reproducible neat-film QFLS gain at matched radiative limit, followed by only small and comparable interface-loss increments, with device Voc tracking that gain. A higher raw PL intensity, longer lifetime on one contact, or a small bandgap shift alone cannot establish a bulk mechanism.
scoring_key_points: Matches bandgap, absorptance, thickness and carrier density and calculates the radiative-limit voltage.
Measures neat-film QFLS/PLQY before adding contacts and then quantifies incremental loss after each interface.
Uses alternative contact materials, surface-passivation controls and thickness/depth diagnostics to localize recombination.
Defines a bulk mechanism by persistence across contacts and translation from neat-film QFLS to device Voc/pseudo-JV.
accepted_equivalents: Photoluminescence quantum yield, electroluminescence efficiency or reciprocity-based voltage loss may be combined
Two-photon excitation or depth-resolved cathodoluminescence can probe bulk recombination
Intensity-dependent lifetime or transient photoconductivity may support the bulk assignment
common_wrong_answers: A higher device Voc automatically proves lower bulk defect density.
Comparing raw PL intensity without matching absorption and excitation density.
Using only one complete device stack, which cannot locate the recombination change.

expected_answer:
The unchanged average dark current does not exclude discrete trap-mediated events, and steady PL can miss low-density shallow traps. Measure dark-count spectra and temperature dependence before and after dose. Newly created shallow traps should introduce or strengthen Arrhenius components, change gate-width dependence and produce characteristic delayed-event correlations while shunt resistance remains high. Drive-level capacitance profiling, thermally stimulated current, admittance spectroscopy or deep-level transient methods can quantify the new trap energies and spatial distribution. Repeat surface passivation and compare one-step/two-step grain-engineered structures to determine whether damage is surface-, grain-boundary- or bulk-dominated.

Contact or shunt damage should appear in local leakage maps, reduced shunting resistance, altered capacitance, asymmetric response after device inversion or electrode replacement, and possibly hot spots even if the mean dark current is small. Use bare detector pulses from a calibrated laser to remove the scintillator from the chain. If laser photon-counting performance is stable but gamma spectra degrade, inspect scintillator light yield, decay time, optical transmission and coupling grease or interface. Conversely, if an injected electronic test pulse shows broadened baseline or threshold drift, the front-end electronics or radiation-induced offset is responsible.

Dose-rate, total-dose and annealing experiments distinguish transient trapped charge from permanent defect creation. Dark or thermal annealing that restores the original activation spectrum supports reversible occupancy; persistent DCR with new trap signatures requires material repair. Possible redesigns include radiation-hard surface ligands, larger grains, a barrier layer protecting the top surface, segmented replaceable pixels and periodic low-temperature or optical detrapping cycles, provided these do not increase after-events.

Acceptance requires restored DCR, pulse-detection probability and energy resolution under the same gate and electronics, plus stable shunt resistance. Any claimed recovery must be tested after renewed irradiation because a one-time anneal may only empty traps rather than prevent their recreation.
scoring_key_points: Uses temperature, gate-width and correlation spectroscopy to identify radiation-created shallow-trap events despite unchanged average current/PL.
Separates contact/shunt damage with local leakage, resistance, capacitance and electrode/control measurements.
Decouples detector, scintillator/optical coupling and electronics using calibrated laser and electronic test-pulse controls.
Defines dose/annealing tests and a redesign or recovery path verified by repeated irradiation and photon-counting metrics.
accepted_equivalents: Thermally stimulated luminescence/current or noise spectroscopy may identify shallow traps
A reference photodiode can monitor scintillator light-yield loss
Pixel replacement, sacrificial surface coatings or periodic optical reset are acceptable redesigns
common_wrong_answers: Unchanged PL and dark current prove that radiation did not damage the perovskite.
All gamma-spectrum degradation is assigned to the scintillator.
A single dark anneal proves permanent radiation hardness.

expected_answer:
Begin with matched phase-pure oriented and isotropic films of similar thickness, grain size, residual additive and initial defect density. Measure the orientation distribution and exposed surface facets. Fabricate both vertical devices, where the electric field is mainly normal to the film, and lateral devices, where it is in-plane. If ion migration is anisotropic, the bias-induced redistribution time and activation energy should depend on the field relative to the crystal orientation. Use transient ion-drift, low-frequency impedance, Kelvin-probe potential mapping and isotope-labelled halide depth/lateral profiling under reversed polarity.

For moisture, compare capped devices, uncapped films and deliberately facet-selective model surfaces under controlled humidity. Time-resolved GIWAXS, mass uptake, hyperspectral PL and chemical mapping should identify hydration, yellow-phase formation and additive loss. A texture benefit should persist after matching surface roughness and grain-boundary density; otherwise reduced ingress may simply reflect fewer boundaries. For interfacial reactions, use at least two hole contacts and two electron contacts. XPS/UPS and cross-sectional microscopy after light-bias-heat stress determine whether the (100) surface reacts differently or forms a more stable energetic contact.

Apply open-circuit, short-circuit and maximum-power stresses because ion distributions and interfacial redox differ with internal field. Rotate or invert the device stack where feasible so the same oriented absorber presents opposite growth surfaces to the contacts. A helpful texture would show lower mobile-ion response, slower phase or chemical evolution and smaller QFLS/Voc loss in the relevant field direction. A harmful texture could provide low-barrier channels normal to the electrodes, causing faster polarization despite excellent initial crystallinity.

Conclude only from matched, phase-pure controls. If orientation changes stability only with one contact, the mechanism is facet-specific interface chemistry; if it changes both lateral and vertical ion kinetics consistently, anisotropic bulk transport is more likely.
scoring_key_points: Uses matched phase-pure oriented and isotropic films and controls grain boundaries, roughness and residual additive.
Compares vertical and lateral field directions with ion-drift, potential and isotope-tracing measurements.
Separates bulk anisotropy, moisture ingress and facet-specific contact reactions through capping and contact swaps.
Defines beneficial or harmful texture by correlated ion/phase/chemical kinetics and QFLS/device degradation.
accepted_equivalents: Operando nano-XRD or scanning X-ray fluorescence may map ion redistribution
Deuterated water may trace humidity ingress
Single-crystal facet devices can supplement textured-film comparisons
common_wrong_answers: Strong texture is automatically more stable because XRD peaks are sharper.
A single vertical MPP test can distinguish bulk anisotropy from contact chemistry.
Comparing oriented additive films with mixed-phase controls isolates the effect of orientation.

expected_answer:
Do not operate the display at a globally fixed voltage. Calibrate each pixel or representative pixel group over temperature using current-voltage-luminance, EQE, spectrum and thermal maps. Build a model that separates the temperature dependence of injection from the temperature dependence of radiative efficiency and series resistance. Use closed-loop current or luminance control with a local temperature sensor, limiting both current density and electrical power. A feed-forward voltage table can provide the initial setting, but optical feedback or periodic calibration is needed because ageing changes injection barriers.

At low temperature, compensating only by raising voltage may destroy the sub-bandgap advantage or trigger tunnelling, leakage and current crowding. Prefer longer duty cycle or moderate pulse-width modulation within a safe peak-current envelope, and use balanced transport layers so both carriers rise together. At high temperature, reduce voltage/current to avoid runaway because thermally assisted injection can create positive feedback. Pixel-level series resistance, current spreading and thermal conduction must be uniform across the flexible substrate.

Qualification should compare fixed-voltage, fixed-current and closed-loop matched-luminance operation. At each temperature measure EQE, spectrum/FWHM, leakage, surface temperature, transient overshoot and spatial luminance uniformity. Colour stability confirms that compensation preserves band-edge emission rather than activating defect or exciplex channels. Lifetime tests must be run at matched luminance and matched ambient temperature with recorded electrical power; otherwise a cooler device may simply be dimmer. Thermal cycling and bending should check sensor drift, interface fatigue and pixel-to-pixel calibration changes.

The strategy succeeds only if closed-loop operation maintains luminance and colour while keeping junction temperature and cumulative charge below qualified limits, and if the low-voltage device still outlives a conventional control at matched luminance. If compensation requires voltage near or above the optical bandgap at low temperature, the architecture needs lower injection barriers or a less temperature-sensitive contact rather than more aggressive drive.
scoring_key_points: Rejects fixed-voltage operation and uses temperature-aware current/luminance feedback with power limits.
Addresses low-temperature under-injection and high-temperature positive feedback without losing sub-bandgap operation.
Requires matched-luminance measurements of EQE, spectrum, leakage, spatial heating and transient behaviour across temperature.
Qualifies lifetime under thermal cycling/bending and defines redesign if compensation requires excessive voltage or current.
accepted_equivalents: A calibrated feed-forward controller with periodic optical recalibration is acceptable
Pulse-density modulation or duty-cycle control may replace PWM
On-panel thermistors, resistance thermometry or infrared feedback can provide temperature sensing
common_wrong_answers: Use 1.7 V at every temperature because that is the reported turn-on voltage.
Increase voltage until luminance matches without monitoring leakage or junction temperature.
Compare lifetime at equal voltage rather than equal luminance and ambient temperature.

expected_answer:
The direction-dependent transient shift is initially more consistent with transport through a static vertical bandgap gradient. Top excitation creates carriers in the Br-richer, wider-bandgap surface region; those carriers can relax or diffuse toward the slightly I-richer, lower-bandgap interior, producing a progressive redshift. Substrate-side excitation begins closer to the lower-bandgap region, so little additional spectral shift is expected. This asymmetry should appear immediately in a fresh film and should be reproducible at low fluence without requiring prolonged illumination.

Phase segregation has different signatures. It generates new I-rich and Br-rich domains during illumination, so a distinct low-energy PL or bleach feature should grow with cumulative photon dose, often on a slower timescale than sub-nanosecond carrier transfer. Once domains span the optical probing depth, the low-energy feature should become less dependent on which side is excited. It should also show intensity, temperature, and defect-density dependence, and may partially recover in the dark. A static gradient should instead retain nearly the same depth profile before and after low-dose spectroscopy and should not create a new emissive phase during extended light soaking.

The decisive evidence set should combine front/back transient absorption with time-resolved and steady-state PL under controlled light-soaking and dark recovery. Depth-resolved composition or bandgap mapping is also required, using cross-sectional nano-XRF, depth-resolved cathodoluminescence, angle-dependent photoemission, or carefully artifact-corrected ToF-SIMS. A uniformly composed control with comparable texture separates directional funneling from crystallinity effects. The diagnosis favors benign funneling only if the initial composition gradient is stable, the redshift is pump-direction dependent and ultrafast, and no dose-dependent low-energy phase emerges.
scoring_key_points: Explains why top-side excitation of a static Br-rich-to-I-rich gradient produces a redshift while substrate-side excitation does not.
Contrasts ultrafast, direction-dependent funneling with dose-dependent, slower, and eventually direction-insensitive phase segregation.
Uses prolonged-illumination PL/TA plus dark-recovery behavior to test whether a new low-energy phase forms.
Requires an independent depth-resolved composition or bandgap measurement and an appropriate uniform-composition control.
accepted_equivalents: Static energetic grading may be described as downhill carrier transfer, energy cascading, or depth-dependent bandgap funneling.
Phase segregation may be described as photoinduced halide demixing or formation of I-rich emissive domains.
Cross-sectional nano-XRF, cathodoluminescence, angle-resolved spectroscopy, or artifact-controlled ToF-SIMS are acceptable depth probes.
common_wrong_answers: Treating every redshift as proof of halide segregation without considering excitation direction or timescale.
Claiming that a static gradient is proven by a single ToF-SIMS profile without optical-history or artifact controls.
Using improved XRD crystallinity alone to distinguish carrier funneling from phase segregation.

expected_answer:
The FAPbI3 result cannot be transferred by assuming that stronger Pb-ligand coordination blocks all halides equally. In a Br-I alloy, terpyridine may change the relative formation energies and migration barriers of iodide and bromide defects, alter the surface Br/I ratio, or stabilize a surface phase with different band offsets. A successful treatment must therefore suppress the formation of low-bandgap I-rich domains rather than merely trap one halide near the surface and drive segregation into the bulk.

The first stage is a composition-specific mechanism screen. DFT or calibrated defect calculations should compare I and Br vacancy/interstitial formation and migration in the untreated and reconstructed surfaces. Angle-dependent GIWAXS, XPS, and depth-resolved compositional mapping should establish whether a single 0D surface phase forms and whether Br/I stoichiometry changes during annealing. Operando PL and transient absorption under sustained illumination should track low-energy phase emergence, while isotope or bias-stress depth profiling tests halide redistribution.

The second stage evaluates electronic compatibility. Ligand dose and thickness must be swept while measuring QFLS, contact-dependent PL quenching, transient extraction, ideality factor, EQE, and series resistance. A high-gap or electrically isolated 0D layer is acceptable only if it lowers nonradiative recombination without blocking the carrier collected at that interface. In a tandem, spectral EQE and stabilized MPP must confirm that the top-cell current is not reduced enough to upset current matching.

Finally, vapor dose, temperature, and reconstructed-phase uniformity must be mapped across large substrates. Go criteria are suppressed light-induced low-energy emission, no adverse Br/I redistribution, preserved or increased QFLS and fill factor, maintained tandem current matching, and a uniform stable surface phase after thermal-light cycling. Any hidden shift of segregation into the film interior or spatially varying extraction resistance is a no-go.
scoring_key_points: Explains why I and Br defect energetics and redistribution must be tested separately rather than extrapolated from pure iodide FAPbI3.
Requires operando spectroscopy plus depth-resolved composition to distinguish suppression from relocation of halide segregation.
Defines a ligand-thickness electronic window using QFLS, extraction, resistance, and EQE/current-matching metrics.
Adds module-scale uniformity and thermal-light cycling with explicit go/no-go criteria.
accepted_equivalents: Photoinduced phase segregation, halide demixing, or low-energy I-rich domain formation are equivalent terms.
Nano-XRF, ToF-SIMS with controls, cross-sectional EDX, or isotope tracing are acceptable depth-composition methods.
A four-terminal tandem may use subcell power retention instead of strict two-terminal current matching.
common_wrong_answers: Assuming that a higher iodide-migration barrier automatically suppresses Br-I phase segregation.
Checking only initial PCE without measuring spectral current matching or low-energy emission under light soaking.
Ignoring treatment nonuniformity and composition shifts across a module-sized substrate.

expected_answer:
The study should include a concentration series below, at, and above the performance optimum, together with an iodide-only control that changes iodide chemical potential without adding the same redox couple and an oxidizing control that mimics redox activity without supplying equivalent iodide. Fresh devices must be matched for morphology and initial efficiency so that aging differences are not simply consequences of starting quality. The central question is whether the optimized process leaves a repaired lattice with little mobile iodine or a metastable reservoir of I2/I3−.

Stress conditions should separate mechanisms: maximum-power illumination at elevated temperature probes field- and carrier-assisted migration; open-circuit light soaking increases carrier density and photochemical driving force; dark heat tests thermal redistribution; reverse-bias or alternating-bias pulses accelerate ionic motion; and controlled humidity tests iodine-mediated contact reactions. Periodic dark rest can identify reversible ionic redistribution.

Operando measurements should include stabilized power, hysteresis, ideality factor, dark current, electroluminescence or PL spectral changes, impedance/low-frequency capacitance, and optical or Raman signatures of molecular iodine or polyiodides. A redox-active reservoir may produce reversible voltage shifts, growing hysteresis, low-frequency capacitance, iodine-related spectral features, or bias-dependent recovery before major efficiency loss. Post-mortem XPS and ToF-SIMS should map I2/I3−-related species, iodide accumulation, and metal or contact reaction products at both interfaces. Electrode corrosion and HTL oxidation must be checked directly.

Go criteria require that the optimized dose retain its lower electronic trap density and voltage advantage without increasing mobile-ion signatures, iodine accumulation, contact reaction, or concentration-dependent degradation relative to the iodide-only control. A dose that performs best initially but shows accelerated bias-dependent drift, interfacial iodine enrichment, or corrosion is rejected as transient redox doping rather than robust defect repair.
scoring_key_points: Uses below/optimal/above multiiodide doses plus iodide-only and redox-specific controls.
Separates MPP, open-circuit light, dark heat, bias, and humidity stresses to probe distinct migration and redox pathways.
Specifies operando electrical/optical signatures and post-mortem depth/chemical analysis of iodine and contact reactions.
Defines a go/no-go criterion requiring retained trap/voltage benefit without added mobile-ion, redox, or corrosion liabilities.
accepted_equivalents: Polyiodide, molecular iodine, or iodine-redox reservoir are equivalent descriptions.
Raman, UV-visible absorption, XPS, or electrochemical potential measurements may detect iodine redox species.
SIMS, XRF, or cross-sectional chemical mapping may be used for post-mortem depth analysis.
common_wrong_answers: Using shelf storage alone to claim long-term reliability.
Comparing only zero and optimum additive doses without an excess-dose or iodide-only control.
Accepting reversible dark recovery as proof that no irreversible contact damage is occurring.
